Commands are the primary means of initiating SAME instrument operations.  Commands to an instrument are 
typically formatted into an array of data and inserted into command packets and then transmitted from the ground 
operation station or from the crew display on the MSG MLC on-board the ISS.  When command packets reach the 
DACU the command data within is extracted and interpreted and the appropriate software functions are executed. 
The command requirements below deal mainly with the functions required by the instrument and not with how those 
functions are implemented or with how the command data is formatted.  See SAME-DOC-005,  Software Interface 
Control Document, for the latter information.

5.0 
SUBSYSTEM REQUIREMENTS 
5.1 
Sample Carousel 
5.1.1 Sample Selection 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall control a motor to rotate the sample carousel to a specified 
sample number. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-1-1-2] 
The DACU shall use four proximity sensors to confirm correct positioning 
of the correct sample carousel. 
5.1.2 Sample Positioning 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-2-1-1] 
The DACU shall mate the selected sample tube with the smoke generation 
duct and the sample contacts with heater wire coil contacts by controlling a 
linear actuator. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-2-1-2] 
The DACU shall confirm correct mating of a sample tube and sample 
contacts by monitoring the resistance between the two heater wire coil 
contacts. 
5.2 
Sample Heater (Heater Wire Coil) 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-1] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall control the 
sample surface temperature and duration of the heating. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-2] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall achieve 
steady state temperature of the heater within 5 seconds. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-3] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall set the 
temperature of the heater wire coil to any temperature between 50 and 500 
degrees Celcius. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-4] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall provide 
active temperature control of the heater. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-5] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall control the 
heater temperature and duration so as not to ignite the sample. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-6] 
The DACU shall measure and store the sample temperature at least once per 
second. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-7] 
The DACU shall measure and store the gas plume temperature at least once 
per second.  
5.3 
Camera and Lighting 
5.3.1 Lighting 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-3-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall control power to any combination of the camera lights. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-3-1-1-2] 
DELETED.

5.4 
Aging Chamber 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston upward velocity to 
achieve 1 to 10 cm/s average flow velocity in the smoke generation duct. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-2] 
The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston upward movement by 
controlling a solenoid on the vacuum line, by sensing and controlling a 
mass flow controller on the vacuum line, and by sensing a pressure 
transducer monitoring the drive side pressure of the piston. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-3] 
The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston downward velocity in 
order to provide smoke at the rate required for the particular diagnostics in 
use. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-4] 
The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston downward movement by 
controlling a solenoid on the GN2 line, by sensing and controlling a mass 
flow controller on the GN2 line, and by sensing a pressure transducer 
monitoring the sample side pressure of the piston. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-5]

a specified portion of the residence time.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 18
5.12 
Miscellaneous Diagnostic Measurements 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-12-1-1-1] The DACU shall record the air flow speed in the smoke generation duct 
with a range of at least 0 to 15 cm/s using calibration coefficients as 
necessary. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-12-1-1-2] The DACU shall record the MFC settings and the pressure transducer data 
at the rate of at least 0.1 Hz to be used in the calculation of the air flow 
speed. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-12-1-1-3] The DACU shall record the air flow speed in the smoke generation duct.

items.title: PSI-101_Reference Data_SAME_Software Requirement Document_004 Rev D.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 19
6.0 
OFF-NOMINAL AND CONTINGENCY REQUIREMENTS 
6.1 
Maintenance Mode Operation 
The software will contain provisions to allow experiment operations to continue in the event of the following: 
[SAME-SW-REQ-6-1-1-1-1] 
In the event of a loss of the ability to write to the data hard drive, the system 
shall continue to accept uplink commands and transmit status data to ensure 
safe operation. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-6-1-1-1-2] 
In the event of a loss of ethernet communication between the DACU and 
the MLC, operations shall continue.  Data recorded on the flight avionics 
may be manually commanded for retransmission once communication is 
regained. 
6.2 
Caution and Warning 
Three discrete bits in the health and status packet are used to indicate to MSG the presence of a payload condition 
warranting a warning, caution, or advisory classification and reaction.  See MSFC-RQMT-2888, MSG Investigation 
Interface Requirements Document, Section 3.11 for details of each level.  The specific payload conditions that result 
in warning and caution levels are determined by the Payload Safety Review Panel (PSRP) during Phased Safety 
Reviews.  Automatic safing will be performed if the warning or caution bit is set. The advisory bit can be used to 
reflect errors and off-nominal conditions seen only in the low rate telemetry data to the health and status data.  If, 
due to limited communication coverage or communication error, the health and status data is received while the low 
rate telemetry is not, then these off-nominal conditions will still be noted and time-tagged. 
6.2.1 Warning 
There are no conditions that constitute a “Class 2 -Warning” condition and a subsequent set of the Warning bit in the 
Health and Status packet payload ECW. 
6.2.2 Caution 
There are no conditions that constitute a “Class 3 - Caution” condition and a subsequent set of the Caution bit in the 
Health and Status packet payload ECW. 
6.2.3 Advisory 
There are no conditions that constitute a “Class 4 - Advisory” condition and a subsequent set of the Advisory bit in 
the Health and Status packet payload ECW. 
6.3 
Automatic Safing 
[SAME-SW-REQ-6-3-1-1-1] 
In the event of a GN2 regulated pressure reading of over 21 psig, the DACU 
shall automatically shut off the main GN2 valve. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-6-3-1-1-2] 
In the event of a vacuum pressure reading of over 19 psia, the DACU shall 
automatically shut off the main vacuum valve.

items.title: PSI-101_Reference Data_SAME_Software Requirement Document_004 Rev D.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 20
7.0 
CREW DISPLAY REQUIREMENTS 
7.1 
Graphic Standards 
The development and approval process for the project crew display follows the guidelines in SSP 58700-ANX5, 
U.S. Payload Operations Data File Management Plan, Annex 5: Payload Display Review, and in SSP 58700-
ANX6, U.S. Payload Operations Data File Management Plan, Annex 6: Payload Developers Review Guide. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-7-1-1-1-1] 
The crew display shall meet all applicable standards defined in SSP 50313, 
Display and Graphics Commonality Standard. 
7.2 
Interfaces 
7.2.1 Host Computer 
[SAME-SW-REQ-7-2-1-1-1] 
The crew display shall be able to run on the MSG Laptop Computer with 
features and operating system as described in MSFC-RQMT-2888, 
Microgravity Science Glovebox Investigation Interface Requirements 
Document, Section 3.3.5. 
7.2.2 MLC Server 
 
[SAME-SW-REQ-7-2-2-1-1]

items.title: PSI-101_Engineering Documents_SAME_Wire_Report.pdf
items.text:
SMOKE Experiment 
Ignitor WIre Characterization Study 
April 2002 
Purpose: 
The purpose of this report is to document the results of a study conducted in search of the 
ideal type of wire to be used for the hot wire ignitors for the Smoke Experiment. 
 
Objective: 
The objective of this study was to find a wire with a consistent, linear resistance versus 
temperature characteristic and with a “significant” slope. 
 
Scope: 
This study was conducted in the Phase A Laboratory (Bldg 77, Room 154A) on 
commercially available wire.  The ignitor manufacturing technique and the pyrolization 
of samples is beyond the scope of this study. 
 
Procedure: 
Each type of wire was mounted on a test fixture.  The test fixture was then placed into a 
ThermCraft laboratory oven.  The oven was programmed to ramp up to a set point, hold 
the set point for fifteen minutes, and then ramp to the next set point until the final 
temperature of approximately 800 oC was attained.  (See oven cycle graph in Appendix 
C.)  Resistance readings were taken near the end of  each “dwell” period.  Several of the 
wire types were subjected to additional tests to examine the effects of the previous 
thermal cycle(s). 
 
The test fixture held approximately thirty-four inches (0.86 meters) of wire. 
 
A stainless steel sheathed type-k thermocouple (Omega Part No. KQSS-116U-24) was 
placed inside the oven in close proximity to the wire under test.   
 
Leads of high temperature furnace wire (#18 AWG) were brought out of the oven to 
enable the test conductor to measure the resistance of the wire under test.   
The resistance of the leads and the terminations was characterized by subjection the 
fixture and leads to a thermal cycle with a copper bus bar shorting the terminals of the 
fixture. 
 
The fixture resistance was subtracted from the total resistance reading for each test point 
to determine the net resistance of the wire under test. 
 
The results were recorded in an Excel Workbook.  Several different data plots were 
prepared and studied.

items.title: PSI-101_Engineering Documents_SAME_Wire_Report.pdf
items.text:
SMOKE Experiment 
Ignitor WIre Characterization Study 
April 2002 
 
Summary and Conclusions: 
This study examined the characteristics of eight types of wire: anodized mild steel, pure 
iron, Alomega (similar to Alumel), -Stainless steel, pure platinum, platinum-rhodium, 
tungster-5%rhenium, and tungsten-26%rhenium.  Traditional heating wires, Nichrome 
and Kanthal were also included for comparison. 
 
Pure platinum has close-to-ideal characteristics.  However the cost of the material may be 
prohibitive. 
 
Alomega and stainless steel ran a close second. 
 
Mild steel, iron and tungsten-composites oxidized in the oven and their characteristics 
changed significantly from one thermal cycle to the next. 
 
Nichrome and Kanthal have too flat a slope to meet the objectives. 
 
Further testing will be conducted to determine the optimum wire type and wire diameter.  
Representative test samples will by pyrolized using various ignitor configurations.  The 
quality and quantity of the smoke will be visually evaluated. 
 
Test Results: 
The tests were conducted in the Phase A Lab from February 6, 2002 through March 20 
2002, by Len Miller and Nathan Funk of Zin Technologies, Inc. 
 
The individual results for each test were tabulated and plotted.  For those wires subjected 
to more than one thermal cycle, the comparative results were plotted.  Finally, an overall 
plot of the combined results was prepared.   
 
The entire Excel Workbook, with tabulated test results and plots thereof, is included in  
Appendix A of this report.  
 
Photographs of the laboratory apparatus are in Appendix B and a graph of the thermal 
cycle is in Appendix C.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 3 
2.2 
SAME Experiment Background 
Since the very beginning of the manned space flight program, NASA engineers and scientists have gone to great lengths to 
prevent fires from occurring on spacecraft. They have done this by adapting fire safety systems and procedures developed 
on Earth to the unique conditions and operating environment of spacecraft. However, microgravity combustion experiments 
have shown that fire can behave very differently in space and the best methods to prevent, detect, and extinguish fires on a 
spacecraft may be very different than those used on Earth. 
In 2000, NASA's Bioastronautics Initiative began with the objective of ensuring and enhancing the health, safety, and 
performance of humans in space. As part of this effort, the  Life Support and Habitation Branch at NASA Glenn Research 
Center is responsible for developing and implementing a research plan to significantly improve fire safety on spacecraft and 
in space habitats. This goal will be achieved by applying a significant amount of fundamental knowledge and the 
experimental capability of microgravity research to spacecraft fire safety questions. 
Spacecraft smoke detectors must detect smoke with a variety of particulate types. Hydrocarbon fuels typically produce soot, 
while overheated plastics produce droplets of recondensed polymer fragments. Paper and silicone rubber produce a smoke 
that is composed of liquid droplets of recondensed pyrolysis products. Differences in the nucleation and growth processes 
for these different types of smokes create particles that have different sizes and properties. 
The Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment that flew in the Glovebox on STS-75 demonstrated that the  smokes 
with solid particulates created in microgravity formed longer chains, and aggregated into larger particles than those created 
in normal Earth gravity. This is surmised to have occurred because of the increased residence time in the high concentration 
smoke regions and to have affected the responses of the two spacecraft smoke detectors (ISS and STS) utilized in that 
experiment. 
To develop smoke detectors that are sensitive to the type and size of smoke particles that will be encountered in 
microgravity and to allow them to distinguish between dust and smoke, better knowledge of the size distribution and 
morphology of the particulates is required. 
2.3 
SAME Experiment Objectives 
The major goal of this experiment is to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulates achieve in microgravity and to 
relate the droplet size and distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. This will 
be accomplished by extending the Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) concept to provide a particulate count and mass 
density determination to the diagnostic array used to analyze these liquid smokes. The experimental design and practical 
application of this data will be enhanced by the development of a numerical code that will predict the smoke droplet growth 
as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment. 
The SAME experiment has the following (listed) objectives: 
1. Make measurements of three moments of the particle size distribution for the μg smoke from several 
materials found in spacecraft considering the effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time 
(near the source) and smoke aging. The primary targets are materials that produce liquid smoke particulate 
but solid smoke producers will also be considered.  
2. Make measurements of the effect of µg and 1-g on the size distribution of liquid aerosol smokes (using an 
idealized smoke e.g. DBT) to provide data for numerical model comparison.   
3. Evaluate the performance in µg of the two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detector designs for the test 
conditions. 
4. Evaluate other smoke detection/sensing devices at NASA’s request for the test materials 
2.4 
SAME “Firsts” for NASA 
• 
Measurements of microgravity smoke: Diagnostics such as the P-Trak and the DustTrak will be used to measure 
particle count and particle mass concentration, respectively.  Both devices are manufactured by TSI.  With the aid of 
these instruments (and others), microgravity smoke will be characterized. 
• 
The use of rapid prototype materials for manned flight experiment hardware. 
• 
Use of an automatic, remotely adjustable, ‘particulate friendly’ dilution system.

items.title: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 4 
2.5 
The SAME Risk mitigation experiment – DAFT  
The objective for the risk mitigation experiment, DAFT (Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test), is to provide a 
microgravity technology demonstration of the P-Trak Ultrafine Particle Counter manufactured by TSI.  The P-Trak is a 
hand held air quality monitor which is capable of counting particles whose mean diameter is in the range of 1.0 to 0.05 
microns. 
After extensive market research performed by both the Engineering and Science teams, it has been determined that the P-
Trak is the only commercially available hardware that can perform this particle count while maintaining the weight, 
resource, and space limitations for an MSG experiment.   
P-Trak measures particle number concentrations in real-time  while storing that data in a memory maintained by an on-
board battery. These measurements are made in units of particles per cubic centimeter (pt/cm3) versus traditional aerosol 
measurements of milligrams per cubic meter (mg/m3) made by photometers.  P-Trak operates by using the particles in the 
aerosol as seeds to condense droplets of alcohol (a condensate nuclei counter).  These droplets have many times the average 
diameter of the original particles, and may, therefore, be easily counted with standard optical techniques.  The potential 
problem is that these droplets are directed through a nozzle to facilitate the counting, and some of these droplets (a 
predictable percentage) collide with the walls and form a film. In a gravity environment, this film is recycled by ‘falling’ 
down hill. 
In microgravity, the distinct possibility exists that these droplets will form a film that will bridge and block the nozzle, 
effectively plugging the flow of droplets and preventing the device from functioning, or obscuring the optics.  Furthermore, 
there is some concern that the droplets inside the optics chamber may get trapped in an internal circular motion and be 
counted more than once, producing an erroneously high count. 
The modification that was implemented in order to counteract these potential problems was: 60. 0.006” grooves were 
machined down the length of the inside of the condenser.  These grooves were designed to provide a mechanism in which 
the smoke particle/ alcohol mixture can wick its way back to reservoir end to simulate the effects of gravity, hence, 
inhibiting the possibility of the fluid to inhibit the functioning of the unit. 
The modifications to account for and eliminate this problem have been devised and implemented, however, it is not possible 
to test the effectiveness of these modifications in any of the available ground based facilities and/or the KC-135 due to the 
duration of the nominal operation time required (minutes per instance).  This testing, and the verification of the accuracy of 
the instrument functions on orbit, are the core of the DAFT experiment. 
Two P-Trak units are included in DAFT flight hardware, one being only flight hardened, and the other with the modified 
condenser and flight hardened. 
To successfully accomplish P-Trak functional demonstration, additional hardware (which will not be explained in detail 
here) has to be delivered to the ISS. This hardware includes a dust concentration monitor (DustTrak), data cables, fill 
assembly, sample bag assemblies, sample holders, virtual impactor, alcohol reservoir, battery packs, a HEPA filter 
assembly, and appropriate tubing. 
The P-Trak utilizes isopropyl alcohol as a condensate, and its use must therefore, be carefully monitored and requires a 
specific agreement for that use on the ISS which is contained within a Volatile Usage Agreement (VUA) created for the 
experiment.

4.1 
Hardware Subsystem Description 
The major planned components of SAME are as follows. They are organized by the assembly level, and the order in which 
they are currently planned to be installed into the MSG.: 
1. 
Fluids Control Box Assembly (67198MABA220) 
The Fluids Control Box (FCB) installs on the back wall of the MSG in the upper left section. It is a fan cooled 
enclosure made from aluminum that contains most of the fluids control devices and monitoring devices including 
solenoids, pressure regulator, pressure transducers and mass flow controller. It interfaces directly with the MSG 
fluids resources (VES and GN2) and the Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU), and distributes the fluids 
resources accordingly. Please refer to the SAME Fluids Schematic (67198PABA000) for more information on its, 
and the other fluids system functions. 
2. 
Sample Plate Assembly (Experiment Support Plate Assembly) 67198ABA100 
This assembly, when fully integrated, contains all of the major functional systems of SAME. It is a mounting plate 
which includes the mounting hardware for the Sample Carousel, the Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU), the 
Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) and the Aging Chamber Assembly (ACA). Permanently mounted to it 
are: 
• 
The Smoke Generation Tube 
• 
The Video Camera and Controller 
• 
The Sample Positioning system including: 
o 
the Sample Turning Module 
o 
the sample engagement  mechanism 
o 
the sample position indicator

items.title: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 6 
3. 
Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) (67198MDBA165) 
The DDA is attached to the Sample Plate Assembly and the Aging Chamber Assembly by the crew and contains: 
the ISS and STS smoke detectors and the sampling ports that supply the P-Trak Enclosure and the Commercial 
Diagnostics Enclosure (and port(s) added for any additional diagnostics required). The DDA has a very low 
internal volume, and the flow of the sample aerosol through it is controlled by regulating and balancing the 
requirements of the active diagnostics in the DDA with the exhaust rate of the Aging Chamber piston, as 
controlled by its mass flow controller. It also contains a port, protected by a HEPA filter, that is connected to the 
VES for exhaust and purging. 
4. 
Aging Chamber Assembly (67198MABA150) 
The Aging Chamber Assembly contains the cylindrical, metallic Aging Chamber, the pneumatically activated 
Inlet and Outlet Gate Valves and the Inlet and Outlet Elbows, which connect to the Smoke Generation Tube and 
the DDA, respectively. A Rulon piston, internal to the chamber, moves the sample into and out from the internal 
volume, and that flow is controlled by a mass flow controller which regulates the pressure or vacuum flow 
accordingly.  Sampling ports are provided in the elbows for use by the Thermal Precipitator, and the unit contains 
a Mixing Fan to insure that the contents are homogenous before disbursal to the DDA. 
5. 
Data Acquisition and Control Unit (DACU) (67198EABA660) 
The DACU is the central control unit for SAME. The baseline software is resident there, and, although many of 
the other packages contain their own relay and control cards, ultimately it is the DACU that interfaces with the 
Ethernet and the MLC to orchestrate the performance of the experiment. It also collects and stores data for 
subsequent downlink through the MSG systems, and controls the MSG Video Recorder to provide a taped record 
of the pyrolysis event. 
6. 
P-Trak Enclosure (67198MABA500) 
The P-Trak Enclosure is a flight hardened assembly containing a TSI P-Trak modified to take advantage of the 
VES system and to function in a microgravity environment. Although it interfaces with the DDA, the DACU, the 
Fluids Control Unit and the Power Distribution and Control Unit, it is basically a smart box that can operate 
independently and store its own data.  
7. 
Commercial Diagnostics Enclosure (CDE) (67198MABA600) 
The CDE houses two of the SAME diagnostics, the TSI DustTrak and a First Alert ionization smoke detector. 
Both units have been hardened for flight and have been modified to utilize the VES to drive the sample. The 
DustTrak has also been modified to utilize MSG air to provide its ‘sheath air’ in order to decrease the amount of 
aerosol required by the unit. Like P-Trak, the DustTrak portion of this device can operate independently and store 
its own data. The modified First Alert cannot.  
8. 
Dynamic Diluter (DD) (67198MABA180) 
The DD is a custom designed component that provides dilution of the aerosol from the DDA before its 
introduction into the P-Trak (and possibly the DustTrak). It works by utilizing a laminar flow element to measure 
the amount of sample being introduced and using that information (from a differential pressure transducer) to 
increase or decrease the diluent flow to achieve the desired concentration. The dilution setpoint may be altered by 
software and adjusts to the desired setting in approximately 5 seconds. 
9. 
Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU) (67198EABA680) 
The PDCU is the central disbursement point for the commands, power distribution and data collection for SAME. 
It contains the power converters, main relays and terminal data connections for the entire system and interfaces the 
DACU with the various systems and devices constituting the experiment.

SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 7 
10. Sample Carousel Assembly (67198MABB400) 
The Sample Carousel Assemblies (5) each contain six (6) Sample Tubes that interface the samples to the Smoke 
Generation Tube and allow the capture of the smoke in the Aging Chamber. Sample Carousels are sequentially 
installed onto the mounting locations on the Sample Plate Assembly, and the mechanisms contained by it identify 
the individual sample numbers, rotate the carousel to the correct position and engage the Sample Tube, which 
allows the sample to be in a position to be energized.  The samples themselves are composed of five (5) materials: 
Teflon, Kapton, Silicone, Cellulose and DiButyl Phthalate (which being a liquid, is contained within a small 
section of cotton lampwick) in small, cylindrical sections, that are wrapped with coils of wire (baseline: stainless 
steel) that both provides the heat energy to the sample when energized and measures its temperature (by its 
varying resistance). 
These samples are removed from the tubes for weighing, both before and after the experiment (before launch and 
after being downmassed) to quantify the actual mass loss during pyrolysis. 
11. Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU) (67198MABB300) 
The TPU is a device that captures actual samples of the aerosol particulate on Transmission Electron Microscope 
(TEM) grids for examination when returned from the ISS. The units (4) are number matched to the samples in the 
carousel, to take samples from both the Inlet and Outlet Elbows leading to and from the Aging Chamber. 
12. Alcohol Wick Storage Container (67198MABD700) 
The Alcohol Wick Storage Container is a custom manufactured aluminum vessel to contain the alcohol wick 
required by the P-Trak during the time (launch, non-ops) when it is not in direct use. Only one is nominally 
required, but two are included to provide one as a backup. 
13. Hoses 
SAME utilizes ISS GN2 and the VES system both as resources for the experiment process and as systems to 
power its devices. These resources are distributed to the components from the FCU via the hoses, which are 
nominally operated at +/- 15 psig. In order to conserve weight and volume, and provide ease of operation, acrylic 
hoses and quick disconnects will be used for the distribution of pressure and vacuum throughout the system (not 
typical Teflon with stainless steel overbraid). 
14. Harnessing 
All harnessing will conform to applicable standards and be designed to minimize the crew time needed to make 
the required experiment connections, without sacrificing reliability. 
15. SAME Service Kit 
This is a place holder. SAME has not yet defined any servicing requirements. 
4.2 
Video Recording Devices 
Video recordings of the smoke evolution process are very important for establishing proper operation of the test apparatus 
and for debugging the system operation.  Furthermore, the video provides a helpful demonstration of the variability in 
smoke evolution. Experience with CSD showed dramatic cases where clearly visible smoke streams were not always 
detectable by the smoke detectors while invisible smoke streams were readily detected. Normal video resolution is 
acceptable if the smoke is illuminated by forward scattered light from an appropriate light source. Video will be viewed on 
and recorded by the MSG video Monitor/Recorder. 
4.3 
On-Orbit Crew Operational Functions 
The crew will be asked to assemble the experiment from provided subsections, load software, reload Sample Carousels, 
Thermal Precipitator Modules, and alcohol for the particle counter, enter parameters, initiate the experiment, and 
disassemble the experiment.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 8 
5.0 
SAME SOFTWARE CONTROL 
5.1 
Software Controlled Operational Functions 
The DACU is the central point for SAME control.  It is ultimately responsible for all experiment operations and interfacing 
with the environment external to SAME.  It contains all of the logic necessary to autonomously operate the experiment as 
well as receive, validate, and process commands from the MSG.  The DACU periodically transmits the status of the Smoke 
system to the MSG, which then forwards it to the ground.   The software can autonomously control the progress of 
preprogrammed test, manage and store all science and system files on the local data storage medium, control the MSG 
video recorder capturing Smoke images, and copy the files to the MLC for downlink.  The software inside the DACU is 
also responsible for providing diagnostic information and manual control of all sensors and controls using the GSE port. 
Please refer to the SAME Baseline Software Requirements Document (SAME-DOC-004) for more detail. 
5.2 
Data Collection 
Data is collected and stored in the DACU until it is time to downlink the information.  The Thermal Precipitator Module, 
which collects samples of the smoke, will be bagged and returned for analysis.  Sample Carousels are retained so that the 
samples can be weighed after return to Earth. 
6.0 
SAME OPERATIONS 
6.1 
Operations Flow 
1. Experiment Setup- The experiment will be shipped in individual subassemblies that will be assembled inside of 
the MSG.  Parts will be inserted through the MSG side ports starting with the upper, back components.  After 
the MSG ports are covered and the rack is returned to nominal position, the Experiment Software is installed 
onto the MSG Laptop. 
2. Perform Experiment- The first steps in performing the experiment are to load the desired Sample Carousel, load 
or replenish the alcohol wick in the particle counter, and install a new Thermal Precipitator Module.  Next, the 
start-up check out routine is performed.  After the uplink parameters are sent, the experiment is initiated.  Then, 
the baseline uplink parameters are modified, as required, for the next test and the experiment is initiated again 
until all six samples in the Sample Carousel have been used.  The next number matched Sample Carousel and 
Thermal Precipitator Module will then be loaded and the experiment will continue as such until complete. 
3. Shutdown and Repack Experiment- When all the Sample Carousels have been used and all the experiments 
have been performed,  the final Sample Carousel and Thermal Precipitator Module will be capped and bagged.  
In reverse order of installation, the experiment hardware will be repackaged for downmassing. 
6.2 
Detailed Operations 
Please refer to the SAME Operations Concept Document (SAME-DOC-009) for a more detailed description of all 
Operations functions. 
6.3 
Timeline 
Since the experiment is designed for operations controlled from the ground, once the components have been installed in the 
MSG, timeline concerns have mainly to do with the acquisition of command windows and with weekly or semi weekly 
service sessions by the crew.  
SAME will follow the standard ISS procedures for scheduling activities aboard the station including OCR and iURC 
submittals and conferences with the ISS Cadre.

For questions and issues regarding the compliance of the experiment with the Science and other requirements, please refer 
to the SAME Engineering Requirements Document, SAME-DOC-002. 
7.0 
SAFETY CONCERNS & PREVENTATIVE MEASURES 
7.1 
Overall Strategy 
Safety analysis is being performed for the SAME (formerly Smoke) hardware in accordance with the safety policies and 
safety requirements for flight hardware (NSTS1700.7B and ISS Addendum). This assessment is being prepared using 
NSTS 13830C as a guideline for data submittal. Hazards not eliminated by design are addressed in either the latest revision 
of standardized hazard control report JSC Form 1230 for ISS and launch/landing phase of the mission or in a Unique 
Hazard Report, JSC 542B. For the most part, the SAME experiment uses generic hazard controls for electrical power 
hazards, sharp edges, EMI (testing), rotating equipment (smaller than 8 inch diameter rotors and less than 8000 RPM), Fire 
Detection and suppression, and touch temperature. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001).

items.title: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 
10 
7.2 
Pressurized Systems  
The pressure system includes the aging chamber, the system for moving the piston in the aging chamber (valves, regulator, 
lines, hoses, relief devices) and the Dynamic Diluter. All of the parts will be designed to meet the requirements of 
NSTS1700.7 ISS addendum, NASA-STD-5003, SSP 30558, and SSP 52005 for pressurized hardware. Pressurized lines 
and fittings will be designed to a factor of safety of 4.0 X System MDP of 200 psid (ISS N2 limiting pressure). Pressurized 
system components will be designed to a factor of safety of greater than or equal to 2.5 X System MDP of 200 psid. Down 
stream of the pressure reduction the MDP is 20 psig. These components are designed with the same factors of safety. See 
table of components and factors of safety and hazard report SMOKE-04. Materials will be selected and evaluated for stress 
corrosion and/or fluid compatibility in accordance with SSP 30233, Space Station Requirements for Materials and 
Processes. In the event of loss of power all solenoids will close including the mass flow controllers, therefore the system will 
not over pressurize. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001) specifically hazard report 
SMOKE-04. 
7.3 
Structures 
The SAME experiment is launched in stowage and contained in MSG for on orbit use. The structural aspect of SAME is 
primarily sealed containers and vented containers. Pressure systems are covered in section 1.2. SAME structural failure is 
addressed in Hazard Report SMOKE STD 01 in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001). 
7.4 
Materials 
The ZIN Tech Engineering Team will assure that reasonable measures have been taken with regard to material selection for 
the experiment‘s design, and selected materials are safe for the intended manned space flight application in their respective 
usage environment. A material flammability assessment will be performed per NSTS  22648. The flight unit will be offgas 
tested. The SAME Project Team will prepare the standard Materials Identification & Usage List (MIUL) and MUA’s. ZIN 
Engineering will review and approve material evaluation prepared by the SAME Project, and submit it to 
NASA/GRC/SMAD for concurrence. Upon material evaluation approval, NASA/GRC/SMTD will issue the Material 
Certification Letter in accordance with the guidelines established in the  applicable Material and Processes (M&P) 
Intercenter Agreement prior to flight hardware fabrication. Further information can be found in Hazard Report SMOKE 
STD 01 in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001). 
7.5 
Frangible Materials (Glass) 
All of the hardware which contains glass will undergo a vibration test in the stowed configuration at workmanship or 
protoflight levels and a post-test visual inspection to verify ability to survive launch loads. The duct with the video camera 
lens and LEDs installed will be stowed with clear plastic for crew inspection after launch. 
7.6 
Release of Experiment By-products into the Cabin Atmosphere 
The P-Trak needs a cartridge with an alcohol-saturated wick for its operation; therefore, a risk of contaminating the ISS 
environment has to be considered.  The amount of alcohol released will be carefully controlled and limited. The Project 
Team will submit a Volatile Usage Agreement request to JSC/OC (Material and Processes) for disposition and approval.  
All payloads are to submit their usage requests to a single approval authority at JSC because alcohol usage is a cumulative 
risk, and it will be necessary to process VUA through a single approval authority to track the total quantity of alcohol being 
used. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SMOKE-SDP-001). 
The pyrolysis products of Teflon currently have a JSC Tox level 3 for 5 minutes after creation. After this point the particles 
coalesce and drop to tox level 0. A hazard report has been generated to address this issue. The smoke is contained in the 
smoke tube and aging chamber for 5 minutes. All the smoke is expelled through HEPA filters, some of which dumps into 
the ISS vent the rest of it into the MSG. The MSG is the second containment of the smoke if the aging chamber where to 
leak. Finally the MSG is under a negative pressure which would prevent the smoke from leaking in the event of an MSG 
leak. Hazard Report SAME-08 has been written and submitted to the PSRP for review.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 
11 
7.7 
Non-Ionizing Laser Radiation 
The ISS Smoke Detector, the P-Trak and the DustTrak contain lasers as a part of their diagnostics systems.  These lasers are 
of Class 1 lasers, and the laser beams are fully contained. These items are not removed from their original housings and are 
used in the applications for which they are intended. There is no crew access to the lasers at any time.  The lasers meet 
ANSI Z136.1-2000 standards for Class 1. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001).  
7.8 
Ionizing Radiation 
The STS Smoke detector and the First Alert Smoke Alarm each contain 1 micro curie of Americium-241.  These items are 
not removed from their original housings and are used in the applications for which they are intended. More detail can be 
found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001). 
8.0 
PRODUCT ASSURANCE 
In order to assure the overall quality and performance of the systems created by the project team, Product Assurance will be 
provided by the ZIN Quality team and will include but not be limited to oversight of the manufacturing and assembly 
processes, investigations into materials and their compatibilities, compliance with the Safety requirements, assessment of 
the systems controls (i.e. Software) and inspection of the final products. The specific methods and strategies planned can be 
found in the following documents: SAME Product Assurance Plan (SAME-PLN-003) and Same Software Assurance Plan 
(SAME-PLN-006). Please refer to them for more detail. 
9.0 
PROJECT PLAN 
The SAME Project Plan (SAME-PLN-001) contains information regarding the Project organization and its levels, 
schedules, budget and a top level description of the project Science goals and the Engineering concepts. Please refer to that 
document for questions regarding those subjects

Conclusions
For the conditions tested, the materials emit most of their particulate in the submicron range.
A valid database now exists for design  of future smoke detectors
Particle dimensions vary strongly as a result of aging or flow residence time and temperature (for Kapton)

Dust rejection may be achievable by detecting at the sub-micron level.
Given the effects of aging and the slow mixing seen in spacecraft, it is probably unwise to focus entirely on small particle sizes for fire detection
Size selective smoke detection will improve reliability and false alarm rejection. Either by classifying the particles or by measuring multiple 
moments. 
Addition of gaseous species detection could  be helpful but requires further 
study.

SAME-DOC-003 Rev A 
 1 
1.0 
INTRODUCTION 
The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) instrument is an experiment payload planned for 
the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) located on the International Space Station (ISS).  Throughout 
this document the term “project” is used to refer to the SAME project in its role as payload developer.   
1.1 
Purpose 
The purpose of this Software Description Document is three-fold: 
(1) to describe the Software Management Plan (SMP) for the project  
(2) to identify what product specification and procedure documentation will be produced as part of the 
software effort for the project, and  
(3) to identify and describe the records that will be produced as part of the software effort. 
This document is intended to be used as a roadmap of the software development effort, describing some 
aspects of the road within the document itself and, as applicable, pointing to other software documents 
and records which will be completed as the project progresses. 
The basis for this document, including structure, are two Glenn Research Center (GRC) Manuals, GRC-
P2.6.4 and GRC-M2.6.4.  Refer to these documents for more detailed background information and 
terminology definitions. 
1.2 
Scope 
This Software Description Document establishes the project's management processes for the software to 
be developed by the project to satisfy its requirements.  It also contains requirements to be satisfied by the 
providers of all software purchased, contractually acquired, developed, or maintained for the support or 
execution of the project.  And except for software and hardware interfaces used to estimate capabilities 
and schedules for the availability of support resources, it does not apply to software applications that 
provide company-wide capabilities not specific to this project. 
The term "software" as used in this document includes code, documentation, associated data, and 
"firmware", which is software installed in a medium that cannot be dynamically changed. 
The project software is comprised of several software “packages”, each executing on a separate platform.  
Located within the MSG will be a microcontroller-based data acquisition and control unit (DACU) that is 
responsible for direct control of the experiment.  Connected to this controller is the MSG Laptop 
Computer (MLC) which will contain software to provide a crew interface into the DACU.  Ground 
support software will be developed to collect and analyze on-orbit data at the GRC Telescience Support 
Center (TSC).  Test software may be developed to assist in the development and testing of hardware 
subsystems.  This document is applicable to all of these packages.  Any specific exceptions will be 
identified in the appropriate section.

Development: Implement the design, i.e., code the software. Devise and perform unit-level testing. 
Perform any agreed upon inspections or walk-throughs. Finalize and release integration and software 
system-level test procedures.  Perform informal regression testing as features are added. 
System Testing: Perform software system-level testing, record errors, and fix problems. Document 
changes to the design, to the requirements, and to the code.  
Release: Perform any agreed upon customer demonstrations/tests. Record and store the version of the 
release. Finalize, review and sign-off on any user documents. Get customer agreement on delivery—a  
release authorization. For High and Critical Control Level, a version description document is required. It 
is highly recommended for Medium control software efforts as well.  This project will supply a version 
description document. 
Support: Provide agreed upon level of version support to customers. Record and address any problems. 
Review requests for added features. Determine the need for updates and follow this procedure for any 
additional development.  (Updates to the flight software are not possible for this project, but changes to 
ground support software and others are not unlikely).  Provide operation assistance to users of the 
software. 
2.2.2 Schedule 
The software development schedule is closely tied to the project schedule.  See SAME-PLN-001, Project 
Plan.  Following are software development tasks and milestones described in relation to the project 
milestones and phases. 
2.2.2.1 SCR/RDR Phase 
During this project phase the software requirements document and supporting software interface control 
document will be drafted.  The software management plan and the software assurance plan will be created 
and approved. 
2.2.2.2 PDR Phase 
During this project phase the software requirements document and software interface control document 
will be finalized and approved.  The software design document will be started with emphasis on the 
architectural design.  Development hardware and software will be acquired and assembled into the 
development system. The design document will be completed and signed off after a software design 
review in time for the PDR itself. Preliminary test plans will be written and reviewed.  Coding of software 
will begin with emphasis on supporting individual sub-systems of the functional model which is to be 
completed by PDR.  Functional model software will be baselined. 
2.2.2.3 CDR Phase 
During this project phase the flight, crew, and ground software will continue to be developed with testing 
of sub-systems as hardware is available.  The software acceptance test will be created, approved, and run 
on completed software with a complete system.  Flight and ground software is baselined and a Software 
Readiness Review is conducted.  Approval of the crew display by NASA’s Payload Display Review 
Team, including a usability test, will be acquired.  Integrated testing with MSG, as required, will be 
performed.  The operations manual will be written. Software will support the mission sequence test and 
respond to scientist requests for changes as necessary.  Final loading of software, release and validation 
will be performed in time for the Verification Readiness Review (VRR).

2.2.2.4 Post Pre-ship Review 
During this period ground software and tools supporting ground operations and data processing can be 
created or enhanced. The Operations Manual will also be enhanced. 
2.2.2.5 Mission Operations 
During mission operations the software team will support operations, trouble-shooting, and further create 
or enhance ground software as desired.   Downlinked data will be archived. 
2.2.2.6 Post Mission Operations 
After the mission is over, downlinked data will be safely stored.  Data storage media brought back from 
the ISS, if any, will be backed up and data will be retrieved, compared to downlinked data, and safely 
stored. 
2.2.3 Release Process 
A project software release is a complete package of every software module created that is necessary to 
operate the onboard payload system, payload crew display, payload ground control system, or any test 
support software (see SAME-PLN-008, Ground Support Equipment Plan).  A software release is under 
version control and configuration management in such a way that the project can say for certain that the 
software that is being used is the software that was tested.  If necessary, a past or present configuration 
can be reproduced using the records generated during a software release and the files stored in the 
software repository or configuration management system. 
Refer to SAME-PLN-002, Configuration Management Plan, for software release requirements. 
2.2.4 Simulations 
Where possible and as available, ISS program simulators provided to the project will be utilized.  As 
required for validation and assurance, the project may develop its own software and/or hardware 
simulators.  An MSG software simulator has already been developed by ZIN and will be used in place of 
MSG during development and testing. 
2.2.5 Development Environment 
Figure 2 shows a block diagram of the software development environment.  Aspects of this environment 
are described below.

Figure 2 – Software Development Environment 
2.2.5.1 Hardware 
Project software will be developed on an x86 computer running Windows XP or better using the tools 
listed below.  Compiled embedded control software and the operating system image for the DACU will 
be transferred to the DACU CPU’s data storage over a private ethernet network.  The DACU CPU is an 
x86 single board computer located on a PC/104 electronics board.  The DACU can be run by resetting or 
re-powering or, in debug mode, by initiating payload software from the development computer.  An 
RS422 interface between the development computer and DACU CPU simulates and tests the 
communication link between the payload and MSG. 
2.2.5.2 Operating Systems 
Embedded control software for the DACU will be developed to run under the QNX Real-Time Operating 
System (RTOS) by QNX Software Systems Ltd.  (The QNX RTOS is also known as Neutrino.)  It is a 
scalable, POSIX compliant, deterministic, and multi-threaded operating system.   
Custom project software for the MSG Laptop Computer will be developed to run under Windows NT 4.0, 
or as directed by MSG (an upgrade is possible in the near future). 
Custom project software for ground control at the TSC will be developed to run under Windows XP and 
will use the Telescience Research Kit (TreK) from MSFC to communicate with ISS command and data 
interfaces.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-003 Rev A 
 8 
2.2.5.3 Languages 
Wherever possible the project will use C++ as the programming language. 
2.2.5.4 Coding Standard 
The project will use 60081-STD-0066, BXF Software Coding Standard, to provide coding guidelines to 
promote style consistency, ease of reading, and maintainability by different programmers. 
2.2.5.5 Compilers 
Embedded control software for the DACU will be compiled using QNX Momentics Integrated 
Development Environment (IDE) version 6.x.x by QNX Software Systems Ltd. 
Custom project software for the MSG Laptop Computer and custom software for ground control will be 
developed using Microsoft Visual Studio .NET. 
2.2.5.6 Version Control / Software Repository 
All project software, including low control level software, will be placed under version control.  Version 
control allows the project to maintain a database of the source code, library modules, and COTS 
packages.  This database will provide change tracking information and simultaneous user access.  The 
version control database will be automatically archived using the existing ZIN network backup system. 
Version control will be achieved using Subversion by tigris.org. 
2.3 
Verification and Validation Plan 
Verification addresses whatever steps a project is going to use to assure that the requirements are 
completely and correctly incorporated in the software product.  Validation states how the project intends 
to get confirmation that what is being designed, built, and delivered meets those requirements. 
The project will perform verification by inspection.  SAME-DOC-006, Software Design Document, will 
provide traceability to each specific requirement in SAME-DOC-004, Software Requirements Document.  
Verification will be completed prior to source code implementation and will involve a design review as 
specified in SAME-PLN-006, Software Assurance Plan. 
The project will perform validation by testing.  SAME-TST-001, Software Acceptance Test, will be 
developed and executed to ensure that the software performs as expected.  In addition to nominal 
operations, this test will validate appropriate reaction, as defined by the software requirements, to off-
nominal and boundary conditions.  A mission sequence test will be developed and executed at the project 
level to ensure validation of the entire system, hardware and software.  The crew display will be 
additionally validated by a usability test at Johnson Space Center (JSC).  Integrated testing of the 
experiment with MSG will be performed as well, as required by MSFC-RQMT-2888, MSG Investigation 
Interface Requirements Document.  Prior to, and in-between releases of software, informal module testing 
will be performed to ensure functionality of each module. 
2.4 
Organizational and Technical Interface Descriptions 
This section describes all interfaces between the development organization and the users, customers, 
product assurance, and suppliers.  Interface descriptions define the boundaries of responsibility for each 
part of the software product and the way that technical information will be transmitted between all parties.

SAME-DOC-003 Rev A

2.4.1 Project Manager (GRC) 
The GRC Project Manager is responsible for the overall management of the project including milestone 
reviews, cost review, schedule, technical status, issues, and technical interchange to assure understanding 
of all requirements 
2.4.2 Principal Investigator and Science Team (GRC, NCMR, NIST)  
The Principal Investigator’s (PI) team is responsible for specifying the science requirements for the 
experiment.  These requirements will be captured in SAME-DOC-002, Engineering Requirements 
Document.  The science team will review and accept the verification and validation of the SAME 
software. 
2.4.3 Project Lead/Lead Engineer (ZIN) 
The Project Lead will provide a management function for the monitoring, control, and reporting of the 
project effort.  The Project Lead shall provide to NASA reporting and insight into the project status, and 
technical performance.  Acting also as the Project Lead Engineer, the Project Lead is responsible for 
coordinating issues between the various project disciplines. 
2.4.4 Lead Software Engineer (ZIN) 
The Lead Software Engineer is responsible for software requirements gathering, overall design, 
implementation and testing of the various software systems.  The Lead Software Engineer ensures that 
software is provided for system verifications, such as environmental testing. The Lead Software Engineer 
coordinates with the Ground Operations Engineers to achieve needed ground software support. The 
Software Lead is also responsible for maintaining the software schedules. 
2.4.5 Ground Operations Engineers (ZIN and TSC) 
The Ground Operations Engineers assist the Lead Software Engineer in obtaining the necessary command 
and data interfaces at the TSC.  The Ground Operations Engineers also provide ground software and 
procedures used for viewing data of the MSG host system onboard ISS. 
2.4.6 GRC Safety and Mission Assurance Directorate (SMAD) 
SMAD is responsible for NASA programmatic oversight related to Safety, Reliability, Quality Assurance 
and Security.  It provides advice and guidance in the planning and implementation of Security and 
supports flight projects to assure all safety requirements are met and mission success is consistent with 
the Center's goals. 
2.4.7 ZIN Quality Assurance 
ZIN Quality Assurance is responsible for implementation of the ZIN quality system during the life of the 
project.  It is responsible for ensuring that the quality assurance requirements identified in SAME-PLN-
006, Software Assurance Plan, and in SAME-PLN-003, Product Assurance Plan, are met.

SAME-DOC-003 Rev A 
 10
2.4.8 ZIN Configuration Management Officer 
The ZIN Configuration Management Officer is responsible for implementation and maintenance of 
Configuration Management on both project software and software documents.  These duties shall be 
performed in accordance with SAME-PLN-002, Configuration Management Plan. 
2.5 
Acquisition Activities Plan 
Not required for medium control level software. 
2.6 
Training Development Plan 
Not required for medium control level software. 
2.7 
Software Assurance Plan 
In order to ensure conformance of software to established requirements, development methodologies and 
standards a software assurance plan shall be developed.  Refer to SAME-PLN-006, Software Assurance 
Plan. 
2.8 
Risk Management Plan 
Risk management is addressed at the project level through SAME-PLN-001, Project Plan.  However, 
procedure P04003, Design Control Procedure for Software, of QM001, ZIN Technologies Quality 
Manual requires that the software risk level be assessed, and that will be done here. 
Following the guidelines of P04003 it is determined that the software risk for the project is Medium.  A 
medium level of risk is characterized as “In-use software failure risks significant property damage or 
significant negative impact upon the customer”.  The influencing point in this decision is the fact that 
samples are destroyed in testing and therefore science data losses during the test cannot be recovered by 
re-running the sample test.  There is not a risk of significant property damage, only of negative impact 
upon the customer. 
2.9 
Configuration Management Plan 
For released software the configuration management plan is contained within SAME-PLN-002, 
Configuration Management Plan, which also contains requirements for releasing software.  Prior to 
release, software will be stored and tracked using the version control method specified in Section 2.2.5.6.   
2.10 
Delivery and Operational Transition Plan 
Not required for medium control level software.

SAME-DOC-003 Rev A 
 11
3.0 
PRODUCT SPECIFICATION 
There are number of software-related product specification documents recommended by GRC-P2.6.4.  
The manner in which these are implemented by the project are listed below. 
3.1 
Concept Documentation 
Not required for medium control level software.  Refer to SAME-DOC-001, Concept Description 
Document, for the project-level concept. 
3.2 
Requirements Documentation 
The project will develop SAME-DOC-004, Software Requirements Document, which will contain all 
software requirements pertaining to systems, facility, safety, operations, telemetry, software interfaces, 
functionality and performance.  This document will also contain any limitations or constraints on the 
system and will specify the required responses to off-nominal and boundary conditions. 
3.3 
Design Documentation 
The project will develop SAME-DOC-006, Software Design Document, which will contain both the 
architectural software design and the detailed software design.  It is expected that these sections will be 
added at separate times. 
The architectural design will lay out the basic structure for the software defining the high level interfaces 
between software and hardware and any other systems as well as define the domains, objects, modules, 
functions and operations needed to meet the requirements.  Operational scenarios and use cases will be 
documented as part of the design to assure the design covers all the aspects of operation. Timing diagrams 
and flow charts will be used to convey the architecture and the real-time command and data flow.  
Network diagrams may be used to describe the physical and data interactions on the network in the final 
installation. 
The detailed software design will specify details that are worked within and between the modules, classes, 
and/or objects. For Object Oriented Design (OOD), the public versus private sectors will be determined. 
Parameter and variable types and values will be established. Global versus private flags, variables, and 
parameters will be determined. Methods, attributes, calculations, and algorithms will be captured. 
3.4 
Version Description 
The project will create Version Description Documents (VDD) to capture the as-built state of released 
software. A VDD will be necessary for each ground support software and flight software release and will 
be captured in SAME-DOC-010, Ground Software Version Description Document, and SAME-DOC-
011, Flight Software Version Description Document, respectively.  VDDs are not required for test support 
software.  The VDD will indicate compatability with other package versions.  For example, “This version 
of ground software will work with versions 1.0–2.5 of flight software.” Additional requirements for the 
VDD are listed in SAME-PLN-002, Configuration Management Plan.  It is suggested that the VDD 
contain the sections shown below.

PROCEDURES 
See the Validation and Software Assurance Plan in previous sections for the use of procedures by the

Testing Procedures 
The project will develop SAME-TST-001, Software Acceptance Test,  which will perform all internal

5.0 
RECORDS 
This section describes how the recommended software records listed in  Table 2 are implemented and 
handled in this project.  Most of these records are a result of following subsections of the software 
management plan, Section 2.0. 
5.1 
Project Approval/Work Authorization 
A record of approval/work authorization for the software effort of the project is part of the record for the 
entire project.  Refer to the project level document, SAME-PLN-001, Project Plan. 
5.2 
Design Review Records 
During software design reviews, with occurrence as dictated by SAME-PLN-006, Software Assurance 
Plan, minutes will be taken and a summary report will be generated that is signed off by all design review 
members.  At this point SAME-DOC-006, Software Design Document, will be modified to either 
reference a document containing the summary report or the report content itself will be appended to 
SAME-DOC-006.  In addition, for each review a memo describing the results of the review will be sent to 
the GRC Project Manager. 
Minutes from other software meetings will be stored and backed-up electronically. 
5.3 
Review or Board Records 
Record of project level reviews and board response, for example the Verification Readiness Review and 
the Pre-Ship Review, are kept at the project level according to SAME-PLN-001, Project Plan. 
5.4 
Problem Reports / Corrective Action Reports 
As specified in SAME-PLN-006, Software Assurance Plan, the project will record and track to closure 
any problems found in software using procedures P13001, Procedure for The Control of Nonconforming 
Product, and P14001, Corrective and Preventive Action Procedure, of QM001, ZIN Technologies Quality 
Manual.  The project shall use the non-conformance tracking and corrective action reporting as described 
in the Quality Manual once the software has passed software acceptance testing. 
5.5 
Verification and Validation Results 
Verification results consist of the record from the software design review.  See Section 5.2 for more 
information. 
Internal validation results for the project software releases will be in the form of a signed Software 
Acceptance Test Report.  Results of the validation accomplished by the mission sequence test will be 
generated at the project level according to SAME-PLN-003, Product Assurance Plan. 
External validation results, such as from the crew display usability test and any integrated MSG testing 
may exist as a memo or e-mail, in which case the text of the results will be stored electronically in a 
backed-up folder.

INTRODUCTION

items.title: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Operations Manual_007.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
2
2.0 
IN-FLIGHT FUNCTIONAL CHECKLIST 
This is a list of items that should be addressed after the hardware is installed in the MSG and before any 
samples are tested.  Not currently in any order. 
- 
Perform piston calibration and alter registry values as necessary.  See procedure later in this 
document.  Run a test with heater setpoint below R0 and no use of the thermal precipitors in order 
to confirm correct calibration. 
- 
Figure out good values for STSPumpFailureLowLimit and STSPumpFailureHighLimit registry 
values.  These depend somewhat on atmospheric pressure and should be adjusted for the ISS 
environment.  Correctly set, these values help detect failure of the STS pump. 
- 
Log some data with the P-Trak and DustTrak and confirm that their settings are correct.  For 
example: log interval, time constant, and date/time. 
- 
Record some video, downlink, and examine. 
- 
Experimentally determine the maximum setpoints that the mass flow controller will meet given 
ISS vacuum and GN2 sources.  Determine if any desired inlet velocities or diagnostic 
combinations are affected. 
- 
The registry value, DisableChecksumCheck, can be set to 1 to avoid the startup delay associated 
with calculating the checksum each time. 
- 
Revisit the decision about whether the heater controller offset correction will be done 
automatically as part of the test sequence or manually using the HeaterCorrectOffset utility prior 
to the test sequence.  Adjust the CorrectOffset registry value appropriately.

items.title: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Operations Manual_007.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
3
3.0 
STARTING THE SOFTWARE 
3.1 
Ground Computer 
On the ground computer you’ll need to first log on.  Then start TReK with SAME configuration files.  
Also start SAMEDisplay.  More TBD. 
3.2 
SAME Flight Software 
The software that controls the system starts automatically upon power on.  Within 30 seconds of turning 
on 120V power to the system there should be telemetry data received at the SAMEDisplay application.  
The GMT will be updating and startup messages will appear in the log window.  The Run Mode will 
change from Startup to Unitialized.

items.title: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Operations Manual_007.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
4
4.0 
TEST CHECKLIST 
This is a list of important things to do or confirm prior to, during, and after the running of a sample test.  
Placement of a highly visible printout of this list on console is recommended.  Steps depend on whether 
sample heater offset correction is being done automatically or manually.  Check the CorrectOffset registry 
value to find out (0=manual, >0=automatic). 
- 
Once per carousel open the gate valves and turn on the diagnostics for TBD minutes.  Downlink 
the data and verify correctness. The purpose is to collect baseline measurements of the MSG work 
volume required by the science team. 
4.1 
With Automatic Heater Offset Correction 
- 
Power on the system, wait for telemetry reception. 
- 
Send the Initialize command. 
- 
If the desired sample is not engaged, engage it using the Self Test command. 
- 
Turn on the 12VDC Heater Power. 
- 
Note the sample resistance and compare to ground measured resistance.  If they differ 
significantly, TBD.  Determine the setpoint. 
- 
Look at test parameters and change as necessary.  Use manual positioning option, but carousel and 
sample number must be correct. 
- 
Start the test. 
- 
When the test pauses check the following: 
o A “sample type is confirmed” message appears in the log. 
o The offset correction returned a value less than 50uV in the log. 
o The sample resistance is still good.  Within TBD % of before. 
o The desired diagnostics are powered and readings are nominal. 
o GN2 regulated pressure and vacuum pressure are good.  Range is TBD. 
- 
If the offset correction returned a value greater than 50uV, abort the test and restart.  If the offset is 
still greater than 50uV, change the CorrectOffset registry value to 0 (manual) and use the manual 
heater offset correction checklist instead. 
- 
Resume the test. 
- 
Watch the log for details about when the sample heater will start.  When it does, be ready to send 
an Abort command. 
- 
Watch the sample resistance and compare to the desired setpoint and MaxRt.  The software will 
too, and will abort heating if the resistance/temperature gets too high.  But watch anyway and send 
the Abort command in the highly unlikely event of too high resistance/temperature. 
- 
After sample aging, during exhaust, watch the output of the diagnostics for unexpected results. 
- 
After test is complete, power on any P-Trak or DustTrak that was used and retrieve the latest 
logged test ids.  Turn back off. 
- 
As desired, force a transfer of the current housekeeping and log files to the MLC.  Their transfer 
during power down has a slight chance of failing.  Doing it here ensures success. 
- 
Perform any other desired OS or system maintenance, such as directory listings or self tests. 
- 
Disengage the sample. 
- 
Send the Shutdown command with Shutdown option and power off system, or proceed to next 
test.

items.title: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Operations Manual_007.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
5
4.2 
With Manual Heater Offset Correction 
- 
Power on the system, wait for telemetry reception. 
- 
If the desired sample is engaged, DO NOT send the Initialize command. 
- 
If the desired sample is not engaged, send Initialize, engage sample using the Self Test command, 
and send Shutdown command with Restart option to bring system back to uninitialized state. 
- 
Send the OSCommand command with parameter ‘/root/HeaterCorrectOffset_g’.  If this command 
returns 0 in the log, then proceed, otherwise repeat until it does.  (Look at the value returned, not 
the details message which always says the same thing.)  See section 7.5 for details about the 
HeaterCorrectOffset utility. 
- 
Send the Initialize command.  
- 
Turn on the 12VDC Heater Power. 
- 
Note the sample resistance and compare to ground measured resistance.  If they differ 
significantly, TBD.  Determine the setpoint. 
- 
Look at test parameters and change as necessary.  Use manual positioning option, but carousel and 
sample number must be correct. 
- 
Start the test. 
- 
When the test pauses check the following: 
o A “sample type is confirmed” message appears in the log. 
o The sample resistance is still good.  Within TBD % of before. 
o The desired diagnostics are powered and readings are nominal. 
o GN2 regulated pressure and vacuum pressure are good.  Range is TBD. 
- 
Resume the test. 
- 
Watch the log for details about when the sample heater will start.  When it does, be ready to send 
an Abort command. 
- 
Watch the sample resistance and compare to the desired setpoint and MaxRt.  The software will 
too, and will abort heating if the resistance/temperature gets too high.  But watch anyway and send 
the Abort command in the highly unlikely event of too high resistance/temperature. 
- 
After sample aging, during exhaust, watch the output of the diagnostics for unexpected results. 
- 
After test is complete, power on any P-Trak or DustTrak that was used and retrieve the latest 
logged test ids.  Turn back off. 
- 
As desired, force a transfer of the current housekeeping and log files to the MLC.  Their transfer 
during power down has a slight chance of failing.  Doing it here ensures success. 
- 
Engage the next desired sample using the SelfTest command.  Engaging the next sample here 
shortens the time for starting the next test. 
- 
Perform any other desired OS or system maintenance, such as directory listings or self tests. 
- 
Send the Shutdown command with Shutdown option and power off system, or proceed to next 
test.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
6
5.0 
RUNNING A TEST 
5.1 
Initialization 
Select the Initialize button on the System tab, sending the Initialize command, and wait until the Run 
Mode changes from Unitialized to Ready. 
5.2 
Setting parameters 
From the Testing tab, select Change… to change to the set of test parameters you want to look at.  Create 
a new test by selecting the CreateNew button.  Select Set anywhere in the window to change the 
parameter for the selected test. 
The Test Setup group box is the way to choose which diagnostics to use.  Select the Pri. or Sec. radio 
button to see the difference in setup between primary and secondary aging.  
Heater Control Setpoint should be set after knowing the unheated resistance of a sample, a.k.a. R0.  
Nominal setpoints are a multiple, Rt/R0, of R0 depending on sample type: 
 
Sample Type 
Setpoint Multiplier, Rt/R0 
DBP 
TBD 
Kapton 
1.380 
Lampwick 
1.245 
Silicone 
1.327 
Teflon 
1.440 
 
To find the R0 of a sample, engage the sample to the inlet tube either by manual blocking or using the 
SelfTest command with EngageSample option (on System tab).  Then on the Smoke Generation tab turn 
on the 12 VDC Heater Enable (right click on the ‘LED’ and select ‘Set On’).  Sample Resistance will 
settle to a valid measurement within 4 seconds. 
5.3 
Registry File Concerns 
Assuming you’ve set the test parameters to a specific carousel number, sample number, heating setpoint 
and duration, you may think you are ready to go.  You may not be.  There are a bunch of sample-related 
limit checks that may cause an error or warning prior to heating.  There are also many timing constants 
that affect the system behavior.  These can be changed by selecting Set Registry… on the System tab.  
See SAME-DOC-005, Software Interface Control Document for key names and descriptions. A system 
timing simulator, currently located in SAMEFluidModel.xls, will be available on console to help see the 
effect of registry value changes.  Testing with the engineering unit is also recommended. 
Alternately, registry values can be changed by editing the registry.txt file on the DACU.  This file is 
located in the /config directory.  Also in that directory is registry.orig.txt which contains the original 
registry settings. 
Important:  Changes to registry values will not take effect until you restart the software.  Follow the 
steps for shutting down, below, but use the restart parameter option.

SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
7
5.4 
Running the Test 
From the Testing tab select Start… and enter the test number to run, if it hasn’t already been entered in 
the field, and select Send. 
After sample positioning and aging chamber setup has occurred the test will pause so you can examine 
the log for any warnings or errors.  Then send the Resume button.  The test should proceed to finish.  You 
can abort anytime by sending the Abort command.  An abort causes all valves to be turned off as well as 
all diagnostics. 
5.5 
Shutdown 
It is recommended that the system be gracefully shut down using the Shutdown button on the System tab, 
then cut power about 2 minutes later.  Current housekeeping and log files are transferred to the laptop 
during the first minute.  Use the second minute to ensure that the system did not restart, looking for the 
restart of low rate telemetry packets and updating GMT.  If the system restarts, select Shutdown again or 
send the OS command with parameter, ‘/bin/shutdown –b’.   
5.6 
Self-Tests 
The flight software has a few operations available through the SelfTest command.  These may be useful 
for other than self-test purposes, for instance to engage a sample to the inlet tube to check R0.  Parameters 
depend on the self test:

items.text:
SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
8
6.0 
PROCESSING FILES 
6.1 
Transferring files from DACU to the MLC 
All files will be automatically transferred from the DACU to C:\ftp on the MSG laptop.  Housekeeping 
files (.hkp) are transferred on the hour and upon shutdown (with either the shutdown or restart option).  
The Log file is also transferred upon shutdown.  P-Trak, DustTrak, and heater files are transferred soon 
after they are created.   P-Trak and DustTrak files are not automatically created since their data is 
embedded in the housekeeping data.  To explicitly retrieve logged data select the Transfer Data button on 
the DustTrak and P-Trak tabs.  This should be done no more frequently than once per minute because the 
filename is derived from the GMT, including the latest minute, but not the latest second.  
If you need the data immediately or a file doesn’t get downlinked for some reason you’ll have to do it 
manually using one of two methods described here: 
6.1.1 Using SAMEDisplay and FTP Cmd command. 
You’ll need to identify what file you need and the directory it is in.  Files are stored in a directory named 
according to GMT year and day.  For instance /data/2006_132/.  The .log file will be named 
2006_132_00.log in this example.  Housekeeping files will be 2006_132_15.hkp, 2006_132_16.hkp, etc. 
according to the GMT. 
With the flight software and SAMEDisplay running (does not need to be Initialized), select the FTP Cmd 
from the System tab.  Type:  LCD /data/2006_132, for example, to change local directory (on the DACU) 
and send the command.  Then select FTP Cmd again and type:  PUT 2006_132_16.hkp, for example, and 
send the command.  Watch your letter case – it matters. 
6.1.2 Using SAME processor command line to transfer files 
For this to work you’ll need a keyboard and monitor connected to the GSE port on the SAME DACU.  
Also, verify that the switch on the SAME DACU is switched to Override position.  This is obviously a 
ground use only method. 
From the command line on the GSE monitor (if the software is running you can get another console 
window by typing <CTRL><ALT>n, where n is 1 or 2), navigate using cd and ls to the directory with the 
file you want to transfer.  Type:  ftp 192.168.1.1<Enter>.  Type: anonymous<Enter> for name and just 
<Enter> for password.  Then at ftp> prompt type: bin<Enter>, then type: put 2006_132_16.hkp, for 
example.  File should end up in C:\SAME Data on laptop.  After done transferring file(s), type: 
bye<Enter> on the DACU. 
You can also use the two above methods to transfer files to the DACU using GET and get instead of puts. 
6.2 
Converting Housekeeping file to engineering units 
Use SAMEFileConverter.  More instructions TBD.

7.0 
MISCELLANEOUS PROCEDURES AND INFORMATION 
7.1 
Obtaining a directory listing 
An example: 
- 
OSCommand(‘ls –l /data/2006_237 > /data/dir.txt’). 
- 
FTPCommand(‘LCD /data’). 
- 
FTPCommand(‘PUT dir.txt’). 
- 
Have MSG cadre downlink the file dir.txt. 
7.2 
Replacing the registry file 
Normally you would change individual entries using the SetRegistry command.  This method could be 
used to set the registry to a known state, perhaps a file under source control, using an uplinked file.  And 
this is the only way I could get the copied-over registry.txt file to ‘take’.  If the system is shut down nicely 
through the shutdown command then it appears to revert to the old registry file. 
 
- FTPCommand(‘LCD /config’). 
 
- FTPCommand(‘GET registry.new.txt’) 
 
- OSCommand(‘cp /config/registry.txt /config/registry.old.txt’) 
 
- OSCommand(‘cp /config/registry.new.txt /config/registry.txt’) 
 
- Do a hard shutdown: power off 
 
- Power on and the new settings should take effect. 
7.3 
Piston Calibration 
Piston calibration, a.k.a. piston characterization, is a process of adjusting some registry values so that 
piston rates and time marks are correct for current conditions.   This process should be performed 
whenever there is a change of hardware, especially the aging chamber and piston itself; a change of 
environment, such as the move to the ISS; a change of fluid source strength; or a change of hardware 
condition, perhaps after many tests have been run. 
7.3.1 Inlet Velocity 
Actual inlet velocity is required to match desired inlet velocity to within +/- 0.5 cm/sec.  Actual velocity 
is not a directly measured value.  It is a function of piston bottom to top travel time, chamber volume, and 
inlet tube diameter.  The equation is:

Increasing the registry value, FillLeakRateLPM, will increase the actual velocity.  To determine piston 
travel time, perform the following steps: 
- 
Run a test with the desired inlet velocity and no heating (setpoint set below R0 and/or heater 
duration set to zero and/or no sample engaged.) 
-

-
