items.text:
SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
6
5.0 
RUNNING A TEST 
5.1 
Initialization 
Select the Initialize button on the System tab, sending the Initialize command, and wait until the Run 
Mode changes from Unitialized to Ready. 
5.2 
Setting parameters 
From the Testing tab, select Change… to change to the set of test parameters you want to look at.  Create 
a new test by selecting the CreateNew button.  Select Set anywhere in the window to change the 
parameter for the selected test. 
The Test Setup group box is the way to choose which diagnostics to use.  Select the Pri. or Sec. radio 
button to see the difference in setup between primary and secondary aging.  
Heater Control Setpoint should be set after knowing the unheated resistance of a sample, a.k.a. R0.  
Nominal setpoints are a multiple, Rt/R0, of R0 depending on sample type: 
 
Sample Type 
Setpoint Multiplier, Rt/R0 
DBP 
TBD 
Kapton 
1.380 
Lampwick 
1.245 
Silicone 
1.327 
Teflon 
1.440 
 
To find the R0 of a sample, engage the sample to the inlet tube either by manual blocking or using the 
SelfTest command with EngageSample option (on System tab).  Then on the Smoke Generation tab turn 
on the 12 VDC Heater Enable (right click on the ‘LED’ and select ‘Set On’).  Sample Resistance will 
settle to a valid measurement within 4 seconds. 
5.3 
Registry File Concerns 
Assuming you’ve set the test parameters to a specific carousel number, sample number, heating setpoint 
and duration, you may think you are ready to go.  You may not be.  There are a bunch of sample-related 
limit checks that may cause an error or warning prior to heating.  There are also many timing constants 
that affect the system behavior.  These can be changed by selecting Set Registry… on the System tab.  
See SAME-DOC-005, Software Interface Control Document for key names and descriptions. A system 
timing simulator, currently located in SAMEFluidModel.xls, will be available on console to help see the 
effect of registry value changes.  Testing with the engineering unit is also recommended. 
Alternately, registry values can be changed by editing the registry.txt file on the DACU.  This file is 
located in the /config directory.  Also in that directory is registry.orig.txt which contains the original 
registry settings. 
Important:  Changes to registry values will not take effect until you restart the software.  Follow the 
steps for shutting down, below, but use the restart parameter option.

items.title: PSI-102_Science Documents_SAME_Operations Manual_007.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
7
5.4 
Running the Test 
From the Testing tab select Start… and enter the test number to run, if it hasn’t already been entered in 
the field, and select Send. 
After sample positioning and aging chamber setup has occurred the test will pause so you can examine 
the log for any warnings or errors.  Then send the Resume button.  The test should proceed to finish.  You 
can abort anytime by sending the Abort command.  An abort causes all valves to be turned off as well as 
all diagnostics. 
5.5 
Shutdown 
It is recommended that the system be gracefully shut down using the Shutdown button on the System tab, 
then cut power about 2 minutes later.  Current housekeeping and log files are transferred to the laptop 
during the first minute.  Use the second minute to ensure that the system did not restart, looking for the 
restart of low rate telemetry packets and updating GMT.  If the system restarts, select Shutdown again or 
send the OS command with parameter, ‘/bin/shutdown –b’.   
5.6 
Self-Tests 
The flight software has a few operations available through the SelfTest command.  These may be useful 
for other than self-test purposes, for instance to engage a sample to the inlet tube to check R0.  Parameters 
depend on the self test: 
 
Self Test 
Parameter Definition 
Disengage Carousel 
no parameters 
Increment Carousel 
no parameters, rotates carousel one position 
Engage Carousel 
no parameters 
Dynamic Dilutor 
Parameter1: setpoint in sccm 
Parameter2: duration in seconds 
ISS Detector 
no parameters 
Fill Chamber 
Parameter1>0:  Fill rate is this parameter divided by 10 in LPM 
Parameter1=0: Fill rate is ChamberSelfTestFillRate registry value 
Parameter2 not used. 
Exhaust Chamber 
Parameter1>0:  Exhaust rate is this parameter divided by 10 in LPM 
Parameter1=0: Fill rate is ChamberSelfTestExhaustRate registry 
value 
Parameter2>0:  Percentage to exhaust. 
Parameter2=0:  Exhaust entire chamber. 
Sample Heater 
Parameter1>0:  Duration in seconds 
Parameter1=0:  Get previous run’s data and save to file.  Do not heat 
sample.  (Useful for aborted heating sequences.) 
Parameter2:  not used.  Setpoint ratio, Rt/R0, is 
SampleHeatingSelfTestRatio registry value. 
STS Detector 
no parameters 
Watchdog Timer 
no parameters.  System will reset in 2 minutes.

items.title: PSI-102_Science Documents_SAME_Operations Manual_007.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
8
6.0 
PROCESSING FILES 
6.1 
Transferring files from DACU to the MLC 
All files will be automatically transferred from the DACU to C:\ftp on the MSG laptop.  Housekeeping 
files (.hkp) are transferred on the hour and upon shutdown (with either the shutdown or restart option).  
The Log file is also transferred upon shutdown.  P-Trak, DustTrak, and heater files are transferred soon 
after they are created.   P-Trak and DustTrak files are not automatically created since their data is 
embedded in the housekeeping data.  To explicitly retrieve logged data select the Transfer Data button on 
the DustTrak and P-Trak tabs.  This should be done no more frequently than once per minute because the 
filename is derived from the GMT, including the latest minute, but not the latest second.  
If you need the data immediately or a file doesn’t get downlinked for some reason you’ll have to do it 
manually using one of two methods described here: 
6.1.1 Using SAMEDisplay and FTP Cmd command. 
You’ll need to identify what file you need and the directory it is in.  Files are stored in a directory named 
according to GMT year and day.  For instance /data/2006_132/.  The .log file will be named 
2006_132_00.log in this example.  Housekeeping files will be 2006_132_15.hkp, 2006_132_16.hkp, etc. 
according to the GMT. 
With the flight software and SAMEDisplay running (does not need to be Initialized), select the FTP Cmd 
from the System tab.  Type:  LCD /data/2006_132, for example, to change local directory (on the DACU) 
and send the command.  Then select FTP Cmd again and type:  PUT 2006_132_16.hkp, for example, and 
send the command.  Watch your letter case – it matters. 
6.1.2 Using SAME processor command line to transfer files 
For this to work you’ll need a keyboard and monitor connected to the GSE port on the SAME DACU.  
Also, verify that the switch on the SAME DACU is switched to Override position.  This is obviously a 
ground use only method. 
From the command line on the GSE monitor (if the software is running you can get another console 
window by typing <CTRL><ALT>n, where n is 1 or 2), navigate using cd and ls to the directory with the 
file you want to transfer.  Type:  ftp 192.168.1.1<Enter>.  Type: anonymous<Enter> for name and just 
<Enter> for password.  Then at ftp> prompt type: bin<Enter>, then type: put 2006_132_16.hkp, for 
example.  File should end up in C:\SAME Data on laptop.  After done transferring file(s), type: 
bye<Enter> on the DACU. 
You can also use the two above methods to transfer files to the DACU using GET and get instead of puts. 
6.2 
Converting Housekeeping file to engineering units 
Use SAMEFileConverter.  More instructions TBD.

SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
9
7.0 
MISCELLANEOUS PROCEDURES AND INFORMATION 
7.1 
Obtaining a directory listing 
An example: 
- 
OSCommand(‘ls –l /data/2006_237 > /data/dir.txt’). 
- 
FTPCommand(‘LCD /data’). 
- 
FTPCommand(‘PUT dir.txt’). 
- 
Have MSG cadre downlink the file dir.txt. 
7.2 
Replacing the registry file 
Normally you would change individual entries using the SetRegistry command.  This method could be 
used to set the registry to a known state, perhaps a file under source control, using an uplinked file.  And 
this is the only way I could get the copied-over registry.txt file to ‘take’.  If the system is shut down nicely 
through the shutdown command then it appears to revert to the old registry file. 
 
- FTPCommand(‘LCD /config’). 
 
- FTPCommand(‘GET registry.new.txt’) 
 
- OSCommand(‘cp /config/registry.txt /config/registry.old.txt’) 
 
- OSCommand(‘cp /config/registry.new.txt /config/registry.txt’) 
 
- Do a hard shutdown: power off 
 
- Power on and the new settings should take effect. 
7.3 
Piston Calibration 
Piston calibration, a.k.a. piston characterization, is a process of adjusting some registry values so that 
piston rates and time marks are correct for current conditions.   This process should be performed 
whenever there is a change of hardware, especially the aging chamber and piston itself; a change of 
environment, such as the move to the ISS; a change of fluid source strength; or a change of hardware 
condition, perhaps after many tests have been run. 
7.3.1 Inlet Velocity 
Actual inlet velocity is required to match desired inlet velocity to within +/- 0.5 cm/sec.  Actual velocity 
is not a directly measured value.  It is a function of piston bottom to top travel time, chamber volume, and 
inlet tube diameter.  The equation is:

Increasing the registry value, FillLeakRateLPM, will increase the actual velocity.  To determine piston 
travel time, perform the following steps: 
- 
Run a test with the desired inlet velocity and no heating (setpoint set below R0 and/or heater 
duration set to zero and/or no sample engaged.) 
- 
Abort the test during or after the aging period. 
- 
Obtain the drive side pressure data during chamber fill and graph it.

SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
10
- 
Pick the points where the piston begins moving, characterized by the start of increasing pressure, 
and where the piston stops moving, characterized by drastically decreasing pressure. 
- 
Subtract the start time from the stop time and calculate velocity.  Adjust FillLeakRateLPM and 
repeat as necessary. 
7.3.2 Sample Heating Start Time 
Ideally, the start of sample heating is calculated so that the end of sample heating occurs before the piston 
reaches the top of the chamber.  Actually, even before that, so that most of the smoke in the inlet tube at 
the end of heating enters the chamber as well.  And really, even before that, so that some clean air follows 
the ‘last’ of the smoke and more of the smoke enters the chamber.  The amount of the latter clean air is 
determined by the BackEndCleanAirOffset registry value. 
Because there is no direct physical measurement of where the piston is in the middle of its stroke, the 
software must estimate when the stroke begins and how long the stroke will take.  Then it can back off 
from there to determine sample heating stop and start times.  The registry values, FillWaita.b, where a.b is 
0.0 to 5.0 by 0.5, help compensate for timing inconsistencies which are a function of fill rate in LPM.   
(These values were more drastically a function of fill rate before the FillLeakRateLPM registry value was 
increased from 0.0.  See section 7.3.1.).  
Piston chamber fill movement begins by evacuating the the drive side of the piston at a rate of 3.0 LPM 
until the drive side pressure reaches 13.2 psia.  These values have been determined to be reliable, but can 
be changed if necessary by altering the registry values, FillStartRateLPM and FillStartPressurePSIA.  
Then the software waits for a period determined by the desired fill rate, a function of inlet velocity, and 
the FillWait registry values.  For a fill rate of 3.0 the software waits for the value of FillWait3.0.  For rates 
in between, the wait time is interpolated.  After waiting this time the software marks the start of piston 
movement, logging a message for the user.  Sample heating and other start and stop times are based on 
this mark.  To determine the best FillWait registry values,

Perform the following steps for each rate, R= 0.5 to 5.0 by 0.5, and then estimate FillWait0.0 
interpolating by hand on a graph of the other values versus rate.

Fill the chamber using the SelfTest command and the rate.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
11
7.3.3 Secondary Aging Volume 
When a secondary aging period and volume are specified, the piston must stop a percentage of the 
distance between the top and bottom of the chamber.  There is no direct physical measurement of the 
running distance, therefore it is estimated from the exhaust rate over time.  The registry value, 
ExhaustPercentageCorrectionFactor, is applied to the running percentage.  To adjust this value, 
- 
Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber to a specific percentage.  For best results use the 
exhaust rate and secondary volume that will be used during the actual test.  Or use 5 LPM and 
50%. 
- 
Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber the rest of the way.  Use the same rate and 100%. 
- 
Calculate the time taken for each portion using log messages or pressure data and figure the 
percentage of total time taken by the second exhaust.  Adjust the registry value and repeat until 
this percentage is within the desired accuracy of the secondary aging volume percentage. 
7.3.4 Exhaust Rate 
It was verified that the system exhausts at a rate sufficient to achieve overpressure of the diagnostic duct 
for all combinations of diagnostic use except when using the STS detector with both DustTraks.  If this 
situation changes, the exhaust rate can be increased using the ExhaustOverpressureRate registry value. 
7.4 
Changing flight software during flight 
Description:  Transfer new version of flight software from MLC to DACU.  Uses crew time, SAME 
Utility Cable, and HyperTerminal application on MLC to perform ftp transfer, backup old flight software, 
and replace it with the new.  Reboots are necessary because the software runs automatically on startup 
and cannot be replaced while running.  Therefore, after making a backup, the software is removed so that 
it cannot autostart.  Then the new version is copied to the autostart name.  Upon reboot, the system finds 
the autostart name again, the new version of software, and operation proceeds normally. 
*Note that only the steps marked with an asterisk need to be done by the crew.  The others can be 
accomplished using the ground display and the OSCommand and FTPCommand. 
- 
Uplink or transfer from media, SAME_g.new to MLC’s C:/ftp directory. 
- 
*Connect SAME Utility Cable between DACU and COM port x of MLC 
- 
*On MLC, start HyperTerminal (HT) and configure to Connect using: COMx with 19200 bps, 
8 data bits, No parity, 1 stop bit, Xon/Xoff flow control.  In Settings tab, Emulation is auto-
detect.  Or a configuration file can be uplinked and the crew will just double-click that. 
- 
Power on SAME.  Wait for 30 seconds. 
- 
At HT,  press <Enter> and verify that a prompt, “#”, appears. 
- 
At ‘#’ prompt, type ‘cd /root<ENTER>’.  If you like, type ‘ls<ENTER>’ to show listing of the 
/root directory. 
- 
Type ‘ftp 192.168.1.1<ENTER>’.  At prompt for Name enter ‘anonymous’.  At prompt for 
Password just press <ENTER>.  Verify message saying ‘230 Anonymous user logged in’ and 
‘ftp>’ prompt. 
- 
At ftp> prompt, type ‘bin<ENTER>’. 
- 
Type ‘get SAME_g.new<ENTER>’.  Verify progress indication and return of ftp> prompt with 
no errors. 
- 
Type ‘bye<ENTER>’.   ‘#’ prompt appears.

items.title: PSI-102_Science Documents_SAME_Operations Manual_007.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
12
- 
At ‘#’ prompt, type ‘chmod 777 *<ENTER>’. 
- 
Type ‘cp SAME_g SAME_g.old1<ENTER>’.  Wait for prompt, approx. 20 seconds. 
- 
Type ‘rm SAME_g<ENTER>’. 
- 
Type ‘shutdown<ENTER>’.  Wait 30 seconds for DACU to reboot.   
- 
*At HT, press <Enter> and verify that a prompt, “#”, appears. 
- 
*At ‘#’ prompt, type ‘cd /root<ENTER>’.  
- 
*Type ‘cp SAME_g.new SAME_g<ENTER>’.  Wait for prompt, approx. 20 seconds. 
- 
*Type ‘shutdown<ENTER>’. 
- 
*Exit HT. 
- 
Ground team will confirm new version is running (or check log messages on Crew Display for 
report of version number), and then shutdown SAME. 
- 
*Remove cable.   
7.5 
Description of HeaterCorrectOffset Utility 
Sample heater offset correction is a feature of the sample heater microcontroller that reduces 
measurement error by automatically removing offset voltages from the signal path.  After offset 
correction is performed, all subsequent resistance measurements will include the offset correction.  Until 
the system is powered off, that is.  At power up the offset correction is zero.  Offset correction should be 
run for each sample while the sample is engaged with the inlet tube and sample heater contacts. 
Occasionally the offset correction circuitry produces a correction that is obviously too high.  The result is 
that subsequent reports of resistance are lower than actual.  This can be detected at the time of the test 
pause by looking at the sample resistance and by looking for the log message indicating the value of the 
offset correction.  It should be approximately 200uV or less. 
If the offset correction at the time of the test pause is too high, then the test must be aborted and restarted 
to give the offset correction circuitry a second chance.  To avoid this time-consuming detour a utility 
separate from the flight software has been developed.  It is HeaterCorrectOffset_g in the /root directory of 
the DACU.  It can be run from the flight software by sending the OSCommand command with a 
parameter of ‘/root/HeaterCorrectOffset_g’. 
The HeaterCorrectOffset utility applies 12VDC to the sample heater, waits a few seconds, and then 
requests an offset correction from the heater microcontroller.  If the returned offset is in range then the 
utility exits, otherwise it requests the offset correction again for several times until it is in range.  Either 
way, 12VDC is removed from the sample heater before the utility exists.  As long as system power (not 
12VDC) remains applied, the offset correction initiated by the utility will be used by the flight software.  
If the utility fails to correct the offset to within the desired range then it returns a -1 (which is reported in 
the flight software log as 65280), otherwise it returns a zero to indicate success. 
There is one caveat to running the HeaterCorrectOffset utility.  The flight software must be either not 
running, which will not occur during flight, or must be in the uninitialized state.  Once the software is 
initialized the utility cannot gain serial access to the heater microcontroller.  Thus the sequence 
gymnastics in section 4.0. 
Additionally, if the HeaterCorrectOffset utility is used, then offset correction prior to the test pause should 
be disabled.  Otherwise an incorrect correction here will negate the use of the utility.  Setting the 
CorrectOffset registry value to zero will disable automatic offset correction during the test, allowing the 
value created by the HeaterCorrectOffset utility to be used.

7.6 
Transfer and Installation of Crew Interface application  
FTPCommand(‘LCD /crewinterface’) 
FTPCommand(‘PUT SAMECrewInterfaceX.YInstall.exe’), where X.Y is the version. 
The transfer takes about 1.5 minutes and the file should end up in c:\ftp on the MLC. 
An EDLFSerialPort Incorrect Checksum error may appear in the log.  It can be ignored. 
 
At this point the MSG cadre will use their commands to run the install file.  The format is: 
 
 
 
 
SAMECrewInterfaceX.YInstall.exe /SP- /VERYSILENT 
 
,where X.Y is the version number. 
 
No user interaction is required with these options.  The crew interface and support files will be installed in 
c:\01 on the laptop.  See SAME-DOC-008, Crew Interface Description; SAME-PRO-002, Software 
Installation Procedure; and SAME-DOC-011, Flight Software VDD, for more information. 
 
The crew interface and support files are uninstalled by the MSG using the following: 
 
 
 
 
c:\01\unins000.exe /SILENT 
 
7.7 
Use of tar utility 
The tar utility can be used to assemble or disassemble collections of files on the DACU, much like 
WinZip does on a PC.  It may be useful to tar a collection of files into one file prior to downlink.  The 
executable is located in the /root directory on the DACU and therefore should be able to execute from any 
local directory.  It is not necessary to specify the path to tar.  Use the OSCommand and parameters 
according to http://www.qnx.com/developers/docs/6.3.0/neutrino/utilities/t/tar.html.

items.title: PSI-102_Science Documents_SAME_Operations Manual_007.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-007 
 
 
14
8.0 
KNOWN ISSUES 
- 
Aborting a test occasionally causes the software to restart.  If this should happen you’ll need to 
reissue the Initialize command. 
- 
Try to avoid running a test sequence through the change of hour (i.e. 12:45-13:05).  Transfer of 
the housekeeping file at the top of the hour takes a good bit of processor time and the processor is 
close to 100% capacity, possibly affecting diagnostic measurement retrieval. 
- 
It is recommended that the system be gracefully shut down using the Shutdown button on the 
System tab, then cut power about 2 minutes later.  However, about 20% of the time the software 
will hang or restart before completely shutting down.  If it restarts, issue the Shutdown command 
again or issue the OS command with parameter, ‘/bin/shutdown –b’.   If it hangs (you may only 
know this if you have a monitor connected to the GSE port) a hard power off will have to suffice.  
The operating system will clean up any file ‘litter’ on the next power up. 
- 
Maximum inlet velocity with the FillLeakRateLPM registry value equal to 0.30 is 9.8 cm/sec.  
Above this the software does not correctly use the FillWait registry values to time chamber fill 
operations, including sample heating start time.  10.0 cm/sec can be achieved if FillLeakRateLPM 
is 0.25 LPM or less.  But timing is affected in other ways and ground testing or flight testing 
without sample heating is recommended. 
- 
Whenever the P-Trak is on, the DACU requests a measurement from it once per second.  
Occasionally the P-Trak does not respond with a measurement and the DACU substitutes a -999 
value instead to mark this occurance.  If the P-Trak is logging during this time, that missing data 
can be recovered by issuing the Transfer Data command to retrieve the logged data. It is 
recommended that this be done for each test, soon (within days) after the test is complete. 
- 
The P-Trak memory can hold approximately 60 20-minute tests.  When all memory is used the 
unit does not respond with any serial measurements while logging.  In other words, continuous -
999 readings is one indicator of full memory.  It is suggested that memory be cleared after 50 
tests to be safe. 
- 
Sample heater offset correction occasionally produces an incorrect correction factor.  The result is 
that reported sample resistance is lower than actual.  For more information see section 7.5. 
- 
Using ground support equipment there was insufficient fluid flow during chamber exhaust to 
maintain overpressure of the diagnostic duct, as required, when the STS detector and both 
DustTraks are in use.  When the STS detector is used it is recommended that at most one 
DustTrak is used. 
- 
If the heater gives an “Abort on MaxRt” error, the system must be power cycled before 
proceeding.  Otherwise, as will be apparent, the resistance measurement will be in error. 
- 
When specifying inlet velocities below 2 cm/sec, the FillWait registry values may not be 
accurate.  The registry value, BackEndCleanAirOffset, must be adjusted to ensure correct heater 
timing.  For 1 cm/sec, a value of 170 seconds is good.  But run a test with no heating to be sure. 
- 
During ground testing the connection between the DACU and the MSGSimulator occasionally 
drops out.  Packet count numbers of the MSGSimulator no longer increment and change from 
green to blue. To reestablish the connection deactivate it and activate it again.

INTRODUCTION 
1.1 
Purpose 
This document defines the specific requirements to be satisfied throughout the implementation of the software for 
the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) instrument.  The information contained within this document 
provides the technical requirements to be implemented and enables the development team to assess whether or not 
the completed software complies with the requirements of the system.  The data included in this document provides 
the criteria for acceptance of the integrated software configuration. 
1.2 
Scope 
The requirements specified herein apply only to SAME instrument software and custom MSG Laptop Computer 
(MLC) software.  All ground based telemetry data processing and command uplink software requirements will be 
identified in future documents as required.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 2 
2.0 
INSTRUMENT OVERVIEW 
The SAME instrument is designed to quantify the size and distribution of smoke particulate in low gravity so that 
this information is available for the future design of effective low gravity smoke detectors.  The instrument will also 
be used to evaluate the performance of two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detectors and one commercial smoke 
detector.  Measurements will be made for the smoke from several materials found in spacecraft considering the 
effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time and aging. The primary targets are materials that 
produce liquid smoke particulate but solid smoke producers will also be considered. 
 
 
Figure 1 
SAME Instrument Assembly Inside MSG WV 
The instrument is installed and operated in the MSG Work Volume (WV) which provides a minimal level of 
containment (see Figure 1).  A general description of the major subsystems follows below.  See SAME-DOC-001, 
Concept Description Document, for more detail. 
• 
Sample Carousel Turning Module, Sample Carousel and Heater Wire Coil 
These components are used to select and heat a sample in order to generate smoke. 
• 
Camera 
A camera and light(s) are mounted to see the sample and production of smoke. 
• 
Aging Chamber 
The aging chamber has a piston and two gate valves for holding the smoke for a time before releasing it 
downstream.  The piston is moved by pressure and vacuum provided by MSG and controlled by SAME. 
• 
Thermal Precipitator Module 
This assembly collects samples of smoke on TEM grids for post-flight inspection.  It has access to smoke 
before and after the aging chamber.

items.title: PSI-102_Reference Data_SAME_Software Req Document.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 3 
• 
Smoke Diagnostics  
After the aging chamber, the smoke is passed to several diagnostics:  the TSI P-Trak™ particle 
concentration counter, the TSI DustTrak™, a residential-grade ionization detector, the ISS photoelectric 
smoke detector and the STS ionization smoke detector. 
• 
Fluids Control Unit 
Pressure and vacuum supplied by MSG is controlled for smoke aging chamber piston movement and for all 
other fluid flow to and from the diagnostic equipment. 
• 
System Diagnostics  
Besides the diagnostic instruments measuring smoke characteristics, there are pressure transducers, 
temperature gauges, and voltage and current sensors to monitor system performance. 
• 
External Interfaces  
External interfaces provided by MSG include power, video recording, temperature control, post-
pyrolization venting, nitrogen and air supply/vacuum, an RS-422 interface for commanding and telemetry, 
ethernet for file transfer, and a laptop for crew access to the SAME experiment.  A SAMS unit measures 
local µg and vibrations and forwards that data to the ground requiring no SAME or MSG processing. 
• 
Avionics 
Contained in the Data Acquisition Control Unit (DACU) box, the SAME avionics conduct automated 
experiments, controlling the other sub-systems to produce and analyze the smoke.  Commands from the 
ground are processed.  Experiment data is saved to files on a local storage medium and forwarded to MSG 
for subsequent downlink.  Housekeeping data is downlinked every second and supplied to MSG.  Off-
nominal conditions are reported to MSG and the ground.  In addition, a means for the crew to access 
SAME data and control is provided.

items.title: PSI-102_Reference Data_SAME_Software Req Document.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 4 
3.0 
AVIONICS OVERVIEW 
SAME avionics are located in the DACU within the MSG Work Volume (WV).  Cables will stretch to the SAME 
diagnostic hardware for control and feedback, to J311 of the WV for command and data transfer, and to J404 of the 
WV for ethernet connection to the MSG laptop computer (MLC) for file transfer and crew display operation.  There 
is also a cable for the camera. 
3.1 
Data Interfaces 
To interface to the MSG, and subsequently to ground systems, the DACU CPU will communicate primarily to the 
MSG Rack Controller, also known as the SPLC (Standard Payload Computer) using an RS-422 interface (see Figure 
2).  SAME will use this interface to receive uplink commands and send health and status (H&S) data and low rate 
telemetry (LRT) data. 
 
 
Figure 2 
SAME to MSG Data Interfaces 
Payload commands are transmitted from the ground through the ISS Payload MDM and eventually to the SPLC via 
MIL-STD-1553.  The SPLC abstracts this interface from the payload developer, relieving the burden of knowing the 
details about the 1553 bus and command validation. 
A packet containing SAME health and status is automatically transmitted in the reverse direction on the 1553 bus 
and is received on the ground.  Also included in the payload health and status packet is the Experiment Control 
Word or ECW, a single dedicated memory word that represents the status of the payload.  The ECW is monitored by 
various ISS subsystems and provides a quick alert if an off-nominal condition is indicated in it.

items.title: PSI-102_Reference Data_SAME_Software Req Document.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 5 
File-based SAME science data such as experiment measurement data and instrument ancillary data will be 
transferred to the MLC using FTP utilizing a 10BaseT ethernet connection.  Once these files are stored on the MLC, 
the MSG Operations Team at the Payload Operations Integration Center (POIC) will periodically initiate their 
downlink and forward them to the SAME Operations Team.  Since SAME is not permitted to transmit data on the 
ISS LAN, the DACU will automatically switch the active network connection from the MLC to SAME and ISS 
using a custom designed ethernet switch when the FTP transfer is required.  In its normal state, the MLC will be 
connected to ISS LAN. 
The camera looking at the SAME sample is hooked up via an NTSC cable to a feedthrough inside the WV which is 
then patched on the outside to a video recorder channel in the video drawer. 
3.2 
DACU Overview 
The DACU is the central point for SAME control.  It is ultimately responsible for all experiment operations and 
interfacing with the environment external to SAME.  It contains all of the logic necessary to autonomously operate 
experiments.  A brief list of its major responsibilities is as follows:  
1. Receive, validate and process commands from the MSG. 
2. Periodically transmit SAME system status and select parameters to the MSG. 
3. Transmit completed and requested data files to the MLC via FTP. 
4. Manage and store all science and system files on the local data storage medium. 
5. Autonomously control the progress of preprogrammed tests. 
6. Provide diagnostic information and manual control of all sensors and controls using the GSE port. 
7. Control the MSG video recorder(s) capturing SAME images. 
8. React to sensor(s) out of tolerance by notifying MSG and ground systems, and performing software inhibits 
or other actions as appropriate. 
3.3 
Crew Display Overview 
During long periods of LOS or failure of telemetry, it is beneficial to provide limited visibility into SAME 
operation.  Payloads may utilize the MLC to present payload status to the crew and provide a mechanism to control 
the payload directly from it.  Two options for providing the SAME Crew Display are possible.  Option 1 is the 
preferred solution at this time because of a likely delay in an upgrade to provide a dedicated ethernet link between 
the MLC and an experiment. 
3.3.1 Option 1 - Custom Win32 or Java Based Application 
All data transmitted to the SPLC via H&S and LRT is also transmitted to the MLC via the MSG 1553 bus, and is 
therefore available on the MLC.  SAME may develop a custom Win32-based or Java-based application that displays 
a limited set of the SAME downlink data for the crew to see and provides commanding to the SAME instrument. 
3.3.2 Option 2 - Embedded Web Pages 
A dedicated ethernet interface between the MLC and SAME may be leveraged to provide a web-based interface into 
the DACU using the MLC native web browser.  The operating system running on the DACU is capable of running 
an embedded web-server such as Apache or NASA’s Tempest servers.

items.title: PSI-102_Reference Data_SAME_Software Req Document.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 6 
4.0 
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS 
4.1 
System Status 
4.1.1 Update Rate 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-1-1-1-1] 
The DACU software shall update its internal status once per second. 
4.1.2 LED Status Indicators 
The DACU will control two LEDs mounted on the outside of the DACU enclosure using discrete outputs.  These 
LEDs are described in Table 1. 
 
Table 1 
Status LEDs 
LED Name 
Description 
OK STATUS 
Indicates nominal operation of the entire 
SAME apparatus. 
TEST RUNNING 
Indicates that a test is currently running. 
 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-1-2-1-1] 
The DACU shall illuminate the OK STATUS LED while the CPU is 
properly running.  If the software detects an internal fault or error condition, 
the LED shall be extinguished. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-1-2-1-2] 
The DACU shall illuminate the TEST RUNNING LED while a test is 
running.  Upon completion, the LED shall be extinguished. 
4.2 
Data Communication 
There are three two-way paths of data communications connected to the DACU.  An RS422 interface is used for 
communications with the SPLC.  An ethernet interface is used for communications with MLC.  An RS232 interface 
is available while not on orbit for development, maintenance, and debugging activities. 
4.2.1 SPLC Communications 
4.2.1.1 
Serial Port Configuration 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-1-1] 
A single bi-directional RS422 channel between the DACU and the SPLC 
shall be used to communicate with the MSG systems.  
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-1-2] 
RS422 serial port settings shall be 19200 baud, no parity, 8 data bits, and 1 
stop bit.

items.title: PSI-102_Reference Data_SAME_Software Req Document.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 7 
4.2.1.2 
Data Format 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-2-1] 
All data that the DACU transmits to and accepts from the SPLC shall 
conform to the ESTEC Data Link Format as specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-
0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document, section 3.5.1.1. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-2-2] 
All data that the DACU transmits to and accepts from the SPLC shall 
conform to the byte and bit order as specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, 
MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document, section 1.4.3. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-2-3] 
All data that the DACU transmits to and accepts from the SPLC shall 
conform to the word alignment as specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, 
MSG RC ASW Interface Control Document, section 2.3. 
4.2.1.3 
Health and Status Packet 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-3-1] 
Once per second, the DACU shall transmit to the SPLC a health and status 
packet containing information such as voltages, currents, and pressures 
necessary to verify safe and proper operation.  Included in this information 
are the C&W flags which indicate nominal or off-nominal operation to the 
rack systems.   
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-3-2] 
The content of the health and status packet shall conform to the format 
specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control 
Document. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-3-3] 
The Cycle Counter field in the health and status packet shall be incremented 
once per second up to the value 0xffff, then roll over to 0. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-3-4] 
The C&W flags fields in the health and status packet shall be asserted only 
upon the conditions listed in Section 6.2. 
4.2.1.4 
Low Rate Telemetry Packet 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-4-1] 
Once per second, the DACU shall transmit to the SPLC a low rate telemetry 
packet representing the current state of the instrument.   
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-4-2] 
The content of the low rate telemetry packet shall conform to the format 
specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW Interface Control 
Document. 
4.2.1.5 
Video Command Packet 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-5-1] 
The DACU shall have the ability to control MSG video drawer functions by 
sending video command packets to the SPLC.  The controllable video 
drawer functions are determined by the requirements of the video drawer 
command group, Section 4.4.5. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-5-2] 
The content of video drawer packets issued by the DACU shall conform to 
the format specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW Interface 
Control Document. 
4.2.1.6 
Time of Day Packet 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-6-1] 
The DACU shall accept time of day packets from the SPLC when they 
adhere to the format specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC ASW 
Interface Control Document.

items.title: PSI-102_Reference Data_SAME_Software Req Document.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 8 
4.2.1.7 
Experiment Command Packet 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-1-7-1] 
The DACU shall accept experiment command packets from the SPLC when 
they adhere to the format specified in MSG-ORIGIN-IC-0001, MSG RC 
ASW Interface Control Document. 
4.2.2 MLC Communications 
Upon completion of a science run, all data files will be stored on DACU internal storage.  A copy of these data files 
will automatically be forwarded to the MLC via FTP on a point-to-point cross-wired ethernet cable.  The SAME 
Operations Team will submit a request to the MSG Team at MSFC to downlink the files on the MLC at the earliest 
possible time.  The downlinked files will then be electronically forwarded to GRC.  Because the connection is made 
directly to the MLC, no bandwidth restrictions are necessary to ensure ISS LAN resource availability. 
4.2.2.1 
FTP Usage 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-1-1] 
All data files stored on the DACU local storage shall be automatically 
forwarded to the MLC via FTP for backup and downlink. 
4.2.2.2 
Network Details  
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-2-1] 
A dedicated standard 802.3 (10BaseT) ethernet connection from the MLC 
to the DACU shall be used to perform the FTP transfer. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-2-2] 
Communications with the FTP server shall be done utilizing a server IP 
address of 192.168.1.1, port 21. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-2-3] 
The DACU will automatically switch the ethernet source from MLC→ISS 
to MLC→SAME when communication to the MLC is required.  When the 
transaction is completed, the original MLC→ISS connection will be 
restored. 
4.2.2.3 
SAME File Maintenance  
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-2-3-1] 
The DACU shall provide the ability to remove SAME files from the FTP 
server as needed to ensure proper storage space utilization. 
4.2.3 Remote Console Communications 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-3-1-1] 
The DACU shall provide a telnet console login session on an RS232 port.  
All administrative features and capabilities available via telnet shall be 
supported. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-2-3-1-2] 
The telnet console RS232 serial port settings shall be, 19200 baud, no 
parity, 8 data bits, and 1 stop bit.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 9 
4.3 
Data Storage Requirements 
The data storage requirements reflect two main needs.  First, that a record of all status, measurements and events is 
preserved beyond the flight of the instrument.  And second, that individual values of status, measurements or events 
can be easily located in stored data. 
4.3.1 Storage Media 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall store all files on a media that can preserve all generated 
files for extraction after payload down-mass.  
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-1-1-2] 
The storage media shall have a capacity of at least 520 megabytes. 
4.3.2 File Conventions 
4.3.2.1 
Directory Structure 
Because the execution of ISS instrument experiments are highly scheduled, the date and time that procedures and 
ground commanding is performed is usually reliably recorded by NASA cadre and experiment ground operation 
teams.  As such, finding the data files for a previously run experiment or for a particular logged event is facilitated 
by a data storage structure based on the date.  Therefore, 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-2-1-1] 
All files created shall be organized into a hierarchical directory structure 
based on the date that files were created. 
4.3.2.2 
File Names 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-2-2-1] 
All files created shall have unique file names. 
4.3.3 Stored Data 
4.3.3.1 
Housekeeping Data 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-1-1] 
Once per second data relating to the status of the instrument shall be stored 
to a file. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-1-2] 
Each second of housekeeping data stored to a file shall be time-tagged. 
4.3.3.2 
Messages 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-2-1] 
Messages generated by the instrument shall be stored to a file. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-2-2] 
Each message stored to a file shall be time-tagged. 
4.3.3.3 
Experiment Results 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-3-1] 
Experiment results shall be stored to a file 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-3-2] 
Experiment results stored to a file shall be time-tagged. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-3-3-3-3] 
DELETED.

4.4 
Command Requirements 
Commands are the primary means of initiating SAME instrument operations.  Commands to an instrument are 
typically formatted into an array of data and inserted into command packets and then transmitted from the ground 
operation station or from the crew display on the MSG MLC on-board the ISS.  When command packets reach the 
DACU the command data within is extracted and interpreted and the appropriate software functions are executed. 
The command requirements below deal mainly with the functions required by the instrument and not with how those 
functions are implemented or with how the command data is formatted.  See SAME-DOC-005,  Software Interface 
Control Document, for the latter information. 
4.4.1 General Command Requirements 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-1] 
DELETED 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-2] 
DELETED

DELETED 
 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-3] 
At the start of execution of a command the DACU shall generate and 
downlink a message that includes the name of the command and its 
parameters. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-4] 
At the successful completion of a command the DACU shall generate and 
downlink a message announcing the successful completion. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-5] 
The DACU shall perform out-of-bound checking on all command 
parameters and reject commands with out-of-bound parameters. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-6]

[SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-7]

parameters. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-1-1-8] 
The DACU shall indicate when a command is being executed with bound 
checking suspended. 
4.4.2 System Command Group 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-4-2-1-1] 
The DACU shall accept a set of commands to perform system level 
operations.  The system group commands shall perform the operations listed 
in Table 3.

4.5 
Experiment Sequencing Requirements 
4.5.1 Miscellaneous Sequencing Requirements 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-1] 
Residence time of smoke in the aging chamber shall be controllable from 0 
to 100 (or greater) minutes per aging period. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-2] 
The DACU shall command the diagnostic instruments to sample the smoke 
once the diagnostic duct is filled from the aging chamber. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-3] 
The DACU shall control the timing of diagnostic measurements such that a 
steady state signal is achieved on all instruments. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-4] 
The DACU shall allow the option of multiple smoke samples from the 
aging chamber with separate aging times. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-5] 
The DACU shall purge the diagnostic duct between multiple smoke 
samples from the aging chamber. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-6] 
The DACU shall control the system to allow the P-Trak to sample air from 
the MSG work volume. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-1-1-7] 
The DACU shall control the system to allow the DustTrak to sample air 
from the MSG work volume. 
4.5.2 Test Matrix Modifiable Parameters 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-2-1-1] 
DELETED. 
 
4.5.3 Test Definition 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-3-1-1] 
DELETED. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-3-1-2] 
There shall be predefined tests with parameters as determined by the 
Principal Investigator. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-3-1-3] 
Additional tests shall be possible to define with parameters determined by 
uplink commands. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-4-5-3-1-4]

items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 15
5.0 
SUBSYSTEM REQUIREMENTS 
5.1 
Sample Carousel 
5.1.1 Sample Selection 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall control a motor to rotate the sample carousel to a specified 
sample number. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-1-1-2] 
The DACU shall use four proximity sensors to confirm correct positioning 
of the correct sample carousel. 
5.1.2 Sample Positioning 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-2-1-1] 
The DACU shall mate the selected sample tube with the smoke generation 
duct and the sample contacts with heater wire coil contacts by controlling a 
linear actuator. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-1-2-1-2] 
The DACU shall confirm correct mating of a sample tube and sample 
contacts by monitoring the resistance between the two heater wire coil 
contacts. 
5.2 
Sample Heater (Heater Wire Coil) 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-1] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall control the 
sample surface temperature and duration of the heating. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-2] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall achieve 
steady state temperature of the heater within 5 seconds. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-3] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall set the 
temperature of the heater wire coil to any temperature between 50 and 500 
degrees Celcius. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-4] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall provide 
active temperature control of the heater. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-5] 
The DACU in combination with the heater microcontroller shall control the 
heater temperature and duration so as not to ignite the sample. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-6] 
The DACU shall measure and store the sample temperature at least once per 
second. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-2-1-1-7] 
The DACU shall measure and store the gas plume temperature at least once 
per second.  
5.3 
Camera and Lighting 
5.3.1 Lighting 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-3-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall control power to any combination of the camera lights. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-3-1-1-2] 
DELETED.

items.title: PSI-102_Reference Data_SAME_Software Req Document.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 16
5.3.2 Camera 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-3-2-1-1] 
The DACU shall control the gain and gamma settings of the camera. 
5.4 
Aging Chamber 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston upward velocity to 
achieve 1 to 10 cm/s average flow velocity in the smoke generation duct. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-2] 
The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston upward movement by 
controlling a solenoid on the vacuum line, by sensing and controlling a 
mass flow controller on the vacuum line, and by sensing a pressure 
transducer monitoring the drive side pressure of the piston. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-3] 
The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston downward velocity in 
order to provide smoke at the rate required for the particular diagnostics in 
use. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-4] 
The DACU shall control the aging chamber piston downward movement by 
controlling a solenoid on the GN2 line, by sensing and controlling a mass 
flow controller on the GN2 line, and by sensing a pressure transducer 
monitoring the sample side pressure of the piston. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-4-1-1-5] 
The DACU shall control a mixing fan in the aging chamber to be on during 
a specified portion of the residence time. 
5.5 
Thermal Precipitator Module 
5.5.1 Valve Control 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-5-1-1-1] 
Using digital outputs the DACU shall control the valves of the thermal 
precipitator module so that at most only one valve is open at a time. 
5.5.2 Heater Control 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-5-2-1-1] 
Using a digital output the DACU shall control power to one thermal 
precipitator module heater at a time. 
5.6 
DustTrak 
5.6.1 Control 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-6-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall control the DustTrak via an RS-232 serial port. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-6-1-1-2] 
The DACU shall turn the DustTrak on and off by controlling the on/off 
keypad using custom electronics. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-6-1-1-3] 
The DACU shall control the DustTrak keypad using custom electronics. 
5.6.2 Data Reception 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-6-2-1-1] 
The DACU shall receive data from the DustTrak via an RS-232 serial port. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-6-2-1-2] 
The DACU shall sample DustTrak data at a minimum rate of 0.2 Hz.

items.title: PSI-102_Reference Data_SAME_Software Req Document.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-004 Rev D 
 17
5.7 
P-Trak 
5.7.1 Control 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-7-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall control the P-Trak via an RS-232 serial port. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-7-1-1-2] 
The DACU shall turn the P-Trak on and off by controlling its momentary 
on/off switch via custom electronics. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-7-1-1-3] 
The DACU shall control the P-Trak keypad using custom electronics. 
5.7.2 Data Reception 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-7-2-1-1] 
The DACU shall receive data from the P-Trak via an RS-232 serial port. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-7-2-1-2] 
The DACU shall sample P-Trak data at a minimum rate of 0.2 Hz. 
5.8 
Ionization Detector (Residential Smoke Detector) 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-8-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall record measurements from the ionization detector at a 
minimum rate of 0.2 Hz. 
5.9 
ISS Detector 
The ISS detector is an Allied Signal/HoneywellTM engineering model. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-9-1-1-1] 
The DACU shall control the ISS detector. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-5-9-1-1-2] 
The DACU shall sample the output of the ISS detector at a sampling rate of 
1 Hz or greater. 
5.10 
STS Detector

SAME-DOC-004 Rev D

6.0 
OFF-NOMINAL AND CONTINGENCY REQUIREMENTS 
6.1 
Maintenance Mode Operation 
The software will contain provisions to allow experiment operations to continue in the event of the following: 
[SAME-SW-REQ-6-1-1-1-1] 
In the event of a loss of the ability to write to the data hard drive, the system 
shall continue to accept uplink commands and transmit status data to ensure 
safe operation. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-6-1-1-1-2] 
In the event of a loss of ethernet communication between the DACU and 
the MLC, operations shall continue.  Data recorded on the flight avionics 
may be manually commanded for retransmission once communication is 
regained. 
6.2 
Caution and Warning 
Three discrete bits in the health and status packet are used to indicate to MSG the presence of a payload condition 
warranting a warning, caution, or advisory classification and reaction.  See MSFC-RQMT-2888, MSG Investigation 
Interface Requirements Document, Section 3.11 for details of each level.  The specific payload conditions that result 
in warning and caution levels are determined by the Payload Safety Review Panel (PSRP) during Phased Safety 
Reviews.  Automatic safing will be performed if the warning or caution bit is set. The advisory bit can be used to 
reflect errors and off-nominal conditions seen only in the low rate telemetry data to the health and status data.  If, 
due to limited communication coverage or communication error, the health and status data is received while the low 
rate telemetry is not, then these off-nominal conditions will still be noted and time-tagged. 
6.2.1 Warning 
There are no conditions that constitute a “Class 2 -Warning” condition and a subsequent set of the Warning bit in the 
Health and Status packet payload ECW. 
6.2.2 Caution 
There are no conditions that constitute a “Class 3 - Caution” condition and a subsequent set of the Caution bit in the 
Health and Status packet payload ECW. 
6.2.3 Advisory 
There are no conditions that constitute a “Class 4 - Advisory” condition and a subsequent set of the Advisory bit in 
the Health and Status packet payload ECW. 
6.3 
Automatic Safing 
[SAME-SW-REQ-6-3-1-1-1] 
In the event of a GN2 regulated pressure reading of over 21 psig, the DACU 
shall automatically shut off the main GN2 valve. 
[SAME-SW-REQ-6-3-1-1-2] 
In the event of a vacuum pressure reading of over 19 psia, the DACU shall 
automatically shut off the main vacuum valve.

SAME-DOC-003 Rev A 
 1 
1.0 
INTRODUCTION 
The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) instrument is an experiment payload planned for 
the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) located on the International Space Station (ISS).  Throughout 
this document the term “project” is used to refer to the SAME project in its role as payload developer.   
1.1 
Purpose 
The purpose of this Software Description Document is three-fold: 
(1) to describe the Software Management Plan (SMP) for the project  
(2) to identify what product specification and procedure documentation will be produced as part of the 
software effort for the project, and  
(3) to identify and describe the records that will be produced as part of the software effort. 
This document is intended to be used as a roadmap of the software development effort, describing some 
aspects of the road within the document itself and, as applicable, pointing to other software documents 
and records which will be completed as the project progresses. 
The basis for this document, including structure, are two Glenn Research Center (GRC) Manuals, GRC-
P2.6.4 and GRC-M2.6.4.  Refer to these documents for more detailed background information and 
terminology definitions. 
1.2 
Scope 
This Software Description Document establishes the project's management processes for the software to 
be developed by the project to satisfy its requirements.  It also contains requirements to be satisfied by the 
providers of all software purchased, contractually acquired, developed, or maintained for the support or 
execution of the project.  And except for software and hardware interfaces used to estimate capabilities 
and schedules for the availability of support resources, it does not apply to software applications that 
provide company-wide capabilities not specific to this project. 
The term "software" as used in this document includes code, documentation, associated data, and 
"firmware", which is software installed in a medium that cannot be dynamically changed. 
The project software is comprised of several software “packages”, each executing on a separate platform.  
Located within the MSG will be a microcontroller-based data acquisition and control unit (DACU) that is 
responsible for direct control of the experiment.  Connected to this controller is the MSG Laptop 
Computer (MLC) which will contain software to provide a crew interface into the DACU.  Ground 
support software will be developed to collect and analyze on-orbit data at the GRC Telescience Support 
Center (TSC).  Test software may be developed to assist in the development and testing of hardware 
subsystems.  This document is applicable to all of these packages.  Any specific exceptions will be 
identified in the appropriate section.

Additional high-level characterization of the software effort is required by procedure P04003, Design 
Control Procedure for Software, of QM001, ZIN Technologies Quality Manual.  Following the guidelines 
of P04003 it is determined that the Software Risk is Medium (see Section 2.8 for details).  The Software

percent of hardware design and development cost, but less than hardware design and development cost.  
The Software Complexity is also Medium, meaning that the software design and development can be 
accomplished by the Lead Software Engineer on a full-time support basis, perhaps with occasional

SAME-DOC-003 Rev A

Development: Implement the design, i.e., code the software. Devise and perform unit-level testing. 
Perform any agreed upon inspections or walk-throughs. Finalize and release integration and software 
system-level test procedures.  Perform informal regression testing as features are added. 
System Testing: Perform software system-level testing, record errors, and fix problems. Document 
changes to the design, to the requirements, and to the code.  
Release: Perform any agreed upon customer demonstrations/tests. Record and store the version of the 
release. Finalize, review and sign-off on any user documents. Get customer agreement on delivery—a  
release authorization. For High and Critical Control Level, a version description document is required. It 
is highly recommended for Medium control software efforts as well.  This project will supply a version 
description document. 
Support: Provide agreed upon level of version support to customers. Record and address any problems. 
Review requests for added features. Determine the need for updates and follow this procedure for any 
additional development.  (Updates to the flight software are not possible for this project, but changes to 
ground support software and others are not unlikely).  Provide operation assistance to users of the 
software. 
2.2.2 Schedule 
The software development schedule is closely tied to the project schedule.  See SAME-PLN-001, Project 
Plan.  Following are software development tasks and milestones described in relation to the project 
milestones and phases. 
2.2.2.1 SCR/RDR Phase 
During this project phase the software requirements document and supporting software interface control 
document will be drafted.  The software management plan and the software assurance plan will be created 
and approved. 
2.2.2.2 PDR Phase 
During this project phase the software requirements document and software interface control document 
will be finalized and approved.  The software design document will be started with emphasis on the 
architectural design.  Development hardware and software will be acquired and assembled into the 
development system. The design document will be completed and signed off after a software design 
review in time for the PDR itself. Preliminary test plans will be written and reviewed.  Coding of software 
will begin with emphasis on supporting individual sub-systems of the functional model which is to be 
completed by PDR.  Functional model software will be baselined. 
2.2.2.3 CDR Phase 
During this project phase the flight, crew, and ground software will continue to be developed with testing 
of sub-systems as hardware is available.  The software acceptance test will be created, approved, and run 
on completed software with a complete system.  Flight and ground software is baselined and a Software 
Readiness Review is conducted.  Approval of the crew display by NASA’s Payload Display Review 
Team, including a usability test, will be acquired.  Integrated testing with MSG, as required, will be 
performed.  The operations manual will be written. Software will support the mission sequence test and 
respond to scientist requests for changes as necessary.  Final loading of software, release and validation 
will be performed in time for the Verification Readiness Review (VRR).

2.2.2.4 Post Pre-ship Review 
During this period ground software and tools supporting ground operations and data processing can be 
created or enhanced. The Operations Manual will also be enhanced. 
2.2.2.5 Mission Operations 
During mission operations the software team will support operations, trouble-shooting, and further create 
or enhance ground software as desired.   Downlinked data will be archived. 
2.2.2.6 Post Mission Operations 
After the mission is over, downlinked data will be safely stored.  Data storage media brought back from 
the ISS, if any, will be backed up and data will be retrieved, compared to downlinked data, and safely 
stored. 
2.2.3 Release Process 
A project software release is a complete package of every software module created that is necessary to 
operate the onboard payload system, payload crew display, payload ground control system, or any test 
support software (see SAME-PLN-008, Ground Support Equipment Plan).  A software release is under 
version control and configuration management in such a way that the project can say for certain that the 
software that is being used is the software that was tested.  If necessary, a past or present configuration 
can be reproduced using the records generated during a software release and the files stored in the 
software repository or configuration management system. 
Refer to SAME-PLN-002, Configuration Management Plan, for software release requirements. 
2.2.4 Simulations 
Where possible and as available, ISS program simulators provided to the project will be utilized.  As 
required for validation and assurance, the project may develop its own software and/or hardware 
simulators.  An MSG software simulator has already been developed by ZIN and will be used in place of 
MSG during development and testing. 
2.2.5 Development Environment 
Figure 2 shows a block diagram of the software development environment.  Aspects of this environment 
are described below.

Figure 2 – Software Development Environment 
2.2.5.1 Hardware 
Project software will be developed on an x86 computer running Windows XP or better using the tools 
listed below.  Compiled embedded control software and the operating system image for the DACU will 
be transferred to the DACU CPU’s data storage over a private ethernet network.  The DACU CPU is an 
x86 single board computer located on a PC/104 electronics board.  The DACU can be run by resetting or 
re-powering or, in debug mode, by initiating payload software from the development computer.  An 
RS422 interface between the development computer and DACU CPU simulates and tests the 
communication link between the payload and MSG. 
2.2.5.2 Operating Systems 
Embedded control software for the DACU will be developed to run under the QNX Real-Time Operating 
System (RTOS) by QNX Software Systems Ltd.  (The QNX RTOS is also known as Neutrino.)  It is a 
scalable, POSIX compliant, deterministic, and multi-threaded operating system.   
Custom project software for the MSG Laptop Computer will be developed to run under Windows NT 4.0, 
or as directed by MSG (an upgrade is possible in the near future). 
Custom project software for ground control at the TSC will be developed to run under Windows XP and 
will use the Telescience Research Kit (TreK) from MSFC to communicate with ISS command and data 
interfaces.

2.2.5.3 Languages 
Wherever possible the project will use C++ as the programming language. 
2.2.5.4 Coding Standard 
The project will use 60081-STD-0066, BXF Software Coding Standard, to provide coding guidelines to 
promote style consistency, ease of reading, and maintainability by different programmers. 
2.2.5.5 Compilers 
Embedded control software for the DACU will be compiled using QNX Momentics Integrated 
Development Environment (IDE) version 6.x.x by QNX Software Systems Ltd. 
Custom project software for the MSG Laptop Computer and custom software for ground control will be 
developed using Microsoft Visual Studio .NET. 
2.2.5.6 Version Control / Software Repository 
All project software, including low control level software, will be placed under version control.  Version 
control allows the project to maintain a database of the source code, library modules, and COTS 
packages.  This database will provide change tracking information and simultaneous user access.  The 
version control database will be automatically archived using the existing ZIN network backup system. 
Version control will be achieved using Subversion by tigris.org. 
2.3 
Verification and Validation Plan 
Verification addresses whatever steps a project is going to use to assure that the requirements are 
completely and correctly incorporated in the software product.  Validation states how the project intends 
to get confirmation that what is being designed, built, and delivered meets those requirements. 
The project will perform verification by inspection.  SAME-DOC-006, Software Design Document, will 
provide traceability to each specific requirement in SAME-DOC-004, Software Requirements Document.  
Verification will be completed prior to source code implementation and will involve a design review as

items.text:
iii 
 
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) 
 
 
Abstract 
 
Leaks, fires, and spills are some of the most significant hazards that must be accounted for in the 
design of the environmental control and life-support system on spacecraft. While prevention is 
certainly the first line of defense against a fire, early detection of a overheat event or an actual 
fire allows the crew to respond before the hazard gets out of control. The limited options 
available for response to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an 
earlier stage of its development than is typical for terrestrial applications.  This report describes 
the outcomes of the Smoke Aerosol Measurements Experiment (SAME), an experiment 
conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) on the International Space Station (ISS) 
to characterize the size distribution of smoke particulate produced in low-gravity from a variety 
of overheated spacecraft materials The absence of gravity can impact not only the formation of 
the smoke particulate but also the aging and coagulation processes that occur as the particulate 
are transported from their source to a detector. 
 
Based on the results of an earlier flight project carried out in the Glovebox of the Space Shuttle, 
(Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD)), the soot particles generated and observed in low gravity 
environment tend to be larger in size than those in earth conditions. However, the preliminary 
results of CSD project were not conclusive because of a minor variation of the temperature of hot 
wire which heated the test sample to generate smoke, and also because the CSD apparatus could 
not measure the liquid drops existing in the smoke produced by several of the samples. 
Furthermore, the CSD project was not designed to provide on-orbit measurement of the particle 
size distribution. The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment was designed to obtain this data 
that could then be used to design the next-generation smoke detectors for space exploration 
missions. Unfortunately, because of the relatively small volume of the MSG, it cannot 
accommodate the instruments normally used in a ground-based laboratory to measure the size 
distribution of smoke particulate. Therefore, a new procedure was developed, the moment 
method, from which the characteristics of the particle size distribution can be inferred using a 
minimum number of portable instrument. 
 
The SAME experiments were conducted during Expedition 15 on the ISS.  Four materials, 
typical of those found in spacecraft, were tested including cellulose (lamp wick), Kapton, 
silicone rubber, and Teflon. A fifth material, dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) retained in a cotton wick 
was used as a reference. In order to simulate the detection of a pre-fire overheated-material event, 
samples were heated to temperatures below the ignition point. The smoke generation conditions 
were controlled to provide repeatable sample surface temperatures and air flow conditions. The 
transport time from the smoke source to the detector was simulated by holding the smoke in an 
aging chamber for times ranging from 10 seconds to 1800 seconds.  Smoke particle samples 
were collected on Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grids for post-flight analysis. The 
smoke properties were measured using particulate aerosol diagnostics that measure different 
moments of the size distribution. These statistics were combined to determine the geometric 
mean particle sizes and geometric standard deviation, which is sufficient to describe the entire 
smoke distribution if a lognormal distribution is assumed. For comparison, smoke detectors from

items.title: PSI-102_Reports_SAME_Final Science Report.pdf
items.text:
iv 
 
the ISS and the space shuttle were also included in the SAME apparatus. The experimental 
results show that, for the materials tested, a substantial portion of the smoke particles are below 
500 nm in diameter. The smoke transport model demonstrated that mixing dominates the smoke 
transport and that consequently detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity. The 
knowledge gained from SAME can be used to establish design requirements for smoke detectors 
used in future spacecraft.

items.text:
1 
1. 
Introduction 
 
Appropriate design of fire detection systems requires knowledge of both the expected signature of the 
events to be detected and the background levels of the measured parameters.  Terrestrial fire detection 
systems have been developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires.1, 2 Unfortunately, there is no 
corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and consequently current spacecraft fire detectors were 
developed based upon experience on normal gravity fire behavior and properties. This approach was 
necessary given the absence of data concerning microgravity smoke particulate. However planned 
spacecraft and their planned missions outside of low earth-orbit will require increased reliability of fire 
detection systems in addition to robust false alarm resistance.  Extended lunar-surface missions will 
require systems that are not influenced by lunar dust and other nuisance dust sources. 
The absence of buoyant flow increases the residence time in microgravity fires causing substantial 
changes in flame structure. Given the large changes in fire behavior seen in reduced gravity, it is 
reasonable to expect that the signatures and detection requirements of these fires will change. There are 
a number of factors that can be expected to affect the particle size distribution of the smoke from 
spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravity increases the residence time in 
microgravity fires and increases the transit time from the reaction zone to the detector.3 The materials 
used in spacecraft are different from those typically used in terrestrial applications where smoke 
properties were previously evaluated. More importantly, the limited options available to respond to a 
spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an earlier stage of its development than is 
typical for terrestrial applications.  All of these effects can be expected to change the smoke particle size 
distribution.  The objective of this work was to make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft 
fires to enable improved design of future detectors. 
2. 
Smoke Background 
 
Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes.  In 
particular for non-flaming combustion, the aerosol includes recondensed original material or pyrolysis 
products that can be either liquid or solid.  For flaming combustion, the aerosol includes soot particulate, 
condensed water vapor, and ash particles.  Soot particles dominate the smoke particulate in established 
flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer fragments are produced by 
smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fire growth.  Given the constrained space on any 
spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established 
flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot.   
 
The background regarding fire detection in US spacecraft is summarized in this paper but is discussed in 
more detail in papers by Friedman and Urban4, 5 In the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo missions, the crew 
quarters were limited and mission durations were short, consequently it was considered reasonable that 
the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The Skylab module, however, included approximately 30 
UV-sensing fire detectors.4 These devices were limited to line-of-sight and were reported to have 
difficulties with false alarms. 
 
Details of the ISS and STS detector requirements are described by Steisslinger et al.6 A brief overview 
of the requirements is given below.

items.title: PSI-102_Reports_SAME_Final Science Report.pdf
items.text:
2 
 
Space Shuttle Detectors: 
At the time the Space Shuttle Orbiter (Space Transportation System (STS)) was developed, smoke 
detection for terrestrial applications was becoming commonplace.1 In particular, ionization detectors 
were readily available but photoelectric 
(scattering or obscuration detectors) were 
generally unavailable due to the difficulty of 
producing stable light sources.  There were 
no data available concerning the smoke or 
dust particle size distribution in low-gravity 
and the database for normal-gravity smoke 
characteristics was a fraction of what is 
available today. Consequently, the STS 
smoke detector (Fig. 1) employed a variant 
of the accepted ground-based approach 
(ionization detectors).  The Orbiter has nine 
particle-ionization 
smoke 
detectors 
in 
avionics cooling air return lines in the mid-
deck and flight deck and the SpaceLab had 
six additional particle-ionization smoke 
detectors in the avionics lines.7 While the 
design rationale is not completely known, 
Celesco™ (later Brunswick Defense™) 
based their design on data that suggested 
incipient fires could be discriminated by looking for particulate in the 0.4 μm to 0.7 μm range.8  The use 
of a pump provided the opportunity to use a particle separator that rejected particulate larger than 1μm.  
This air pump increased the power requirements and reduced the operational life of the detector. The 
STS detector as built was designed to alarm at a particle loading of 2 mg/m3 for 5 seconds (based on 1 
micron particles) or a 0.022 mg/m3/s rise in concentration for 20 seconds9. 
 
ISS Detectors: 
The International Space Station (ISS) smoke detector design took advantage of the availability of stable 
laser-diode light sources, mirroring a trend in terrestrial detectors toward light scattering devices.  This 
provided the opportunity to produce a detector that required substantially less power, (1.5 Watts versus 9 
Watts for the orbiter detector)6 and, with no moving parts, was quieter with a much longer operational 
life. The choice was supported by data indicating that early smoldering fires produce larger particulate 
than established flaming fires.1 The ISS detectors (Fig. 2) are laser-diode, forward-scattering, smoke or 
particulate detectors. The sensitivity extends down to 0.3 μm but is greatest for particles larger than 1 
μm. The current requirements for the ISS call for two detectors in the open area of the module, and 
detectors in racks that have cooling air-flow.10 
 
The design developed for the ISS by Allied Signal™ (Fig. 2) consists of a 2-pass laser diode to sense 
forward scattered light (30 degrees). There is also a light transmission sensor to monitor the beam 
intensity. The system is designed to alarm based on the magnitude of the scattered light signal 
referenced to the beam intensity. The system is less sensitive to particles smaller than the wavelength of 
the laser (near IR) than it is to larger particles. The minimum reported sensitivity is 0.3 μm.6 The ISS 
detector was designed to alarm at 1% obscuration per foot using an Underwriters Laboratory (UL) 
Figure 1. Brunswick Defense™ smoke detector used in the 
NASA orbiter fleet. The inlet is on the right and the gas is 
expelled out the small plate on the top.

items.text:
3 
 
smoke box and white light extinction.  This 
was implemented using a transfer standard 
detector and a 0.5 m polystyrene-bead 
aerosol system that was used to set the 
amplifiers on each unit. The transfer 
standard was calibrated in the smoke box 
and then used to set the levels with the 
aerosol system. 
 
As a result of these design decisions, the ISS 
and the Orbiter detectors have particle 
sensitivities that do not overlap.  In both 
cases the designs were based upon the best 
available data at the time.  However, due to 
the 
complete 
absence 
of 
low-g 
data 
concerning the nature of particulate and 
radiant emission from incipient and fully 
developed low-g fires, different conclusions 
were drawn concerning the optimal design 
for spacecraft fire detection.  
 
As described by Friedman4 there have been 
six overheat and failed component failures in 
the NASA Orbiter fleet in addition to several 
similar incidents that have occurred on the 
ISS. None of these events spread into a real fire but as mission durations increase, the likelihood of 
failures increases. The experience on Mir in 1997 has shown that failure of oxygen generation systems 
can have significant consequences. As a result, improved understanding of spacecraft fire detection is 
critically needed.11 
 
Previous work on smoke particles from low-gravity sources by Urban et al.5 indicated that the 
particulate produced by low-gravity flames (soot or unburned fuel particles) tends to have larger size 
particles than in normal gravity.  Results from the CSD (Comparative Soot Diagnostics) Experiment5 
which studied smoke properties in low-gravity from several spacecraft materials suggested that liquid 
smoke particles could achieve sizes larger than 1 µm while solid particulate remained in the sub-
micrometer range.  However, the CSD experiment did not produce sufficient data concerning the size of 
the liquid smoke particles to guide detector design. The combined impact of these limited results and 
physical expectations is that, based on the increased smoke residence time in low gravity, direct 
knowledge of low-g combustion particulate is needed for the confident design of smoke detectors for 
spacecraft rather than extrapolation from 1-g data 
 
Any effort to detect fires must be able to discriminate against the ambient background and nuisance 
signals.  In the case of smoke detection, the background dust aerosol conditions must be considered. The 
only spacecraft background aerosol particulate measurements to date were made on the Orbiter on STS-
32 in 199012 and on the ISS.5

mirrors (one visible at top right (B)) and is then reflected back to 
the sensors in the enclosure (C).  One sensor detects the forward 
scattered light and is referenced by another sensor that looks 
directly at the incident beam.
