for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established flaming fires; consequently, the 
primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot and ash.   
B. Prior Spacecraft Systems 
In the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo missions, the crew quarters were limited and mission durations were short, 
consequently it was considered reasonable that the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The Skylab module, 
however, included approximately 30 UV-sensing fire detectors.1 These devices were limited to line-of-sight and 
were reported to have difficulties with false alarms.   
C. Space Shuttle Detectors 
At the time the Space Shuttle Orbiter (Space Transportation System (STS)) was developed, smoke detection for 
terrestrial applications was becoming commonplace.2 In particular, ionization detectors were becoming readily 
available but photoelectric (scattering or obscuration detectors) were generally unavailable due to the difficulty of 
producing stable light sources.  There was no data available concerning the smoke or dust particle size distribution 
in low-gravity and the database of normal-
gravity smoke characteristics was a fraction of 
what is available today. Consequently, the 
STS smoke detector (Fig. 1) employed a 
variant of the accepted ground based approach 
(ionization detectors).  The Orbiter has nine 
particle-ionization smoke detectors in avionics 
cooling air return lines in the mid-deck and 
flight deck and SpaceLab had six additional 
particle-ionization smoke detectors in the 
avionics lines.3 While the design rationale is 
not completely known, Celesco™ (later 
Brunswick Defense™) based their design on 
data that suggested incipient fires could be 
discriminated by looking for particulate in the 
0.4 to 0.7 μm range.4  Use of a pump provided 
the opportunity to employ a particle separator 
allowing rejection of particulate larger than 
1μm.  This air pump increased the power 
requirements and reduced the operational life 
for the detectors. 
D. ISS Detectors 
The International Space Station (ISS) smoke detector design took advantage of the availability of stable laser-
diode light sources, mirroring a trend in terrestrial detectors toward light scattering devices.  This provided the 
opportunity to produce a detector that required substantially less power, (1.5 Watts versus 9 Watts for the Orbiter 
detector)5 and, with no moving parts, was quieter with a much longer operational life. The choice was supported by 
data indicating that early smoldering fires produce larger particulate than established flaming fires.2 The designated 
detectors (Fig. 2) for the ISS are laser-diode, forward-scattering, smoke or particulate detectors. Their sensitivity is 
greatest for particles larger than 1 μm with sensitivity extending down to 0.6 μm. The current requirements for the 
ISS call for two detectors in the open area of the US Lab module, and detectors in racks that have cooling air-flow.6  
The design developed for the ISS by Allied Signal™ (Fig. 2) consists of a 2-pass laser diode to sense forward 
scattered light (30 degrees). There is also a zero degree obscuration system that is used as a measure of the beam 
strength.  The system is designed to alarm based on the magnitude of the scattered light signal referenced to the 
beam intensity. The system is less sensitive to particles smaller than the wavelength of the laser (near IR) than it is 
to larger particles. The minimum reported sensitivity is 0.3 μm.5 On the other hand, for a fixed mass concentration 
of smoke aerosol; the STS ionization smoke detector is more sensitive to smaller particle sizes.

NASA Orbiter fleet. The inlet is on the right and the gas is 
expelled out the small plate on the top.

As a result of these design decisions, the 
ISS and the Orbiter detectors are sensitive to 
particles in different size ranges.  In both 
cases the designs were based upon the best 
available data however, due to the complete 
absence of low-g data concerning the nature 
of particulate and radiant emission from 
incipient and fully developed low-g fires, 
different 
conclusions 
were 
drawn 
concerning the optimal design for spacecraft 
fire detection.  
As described by Friedman7 there have 
been six overheat and failed component 
failures in the NASA Orbiter fleet. None of 
these events spread into a real fire but as 
mission durations increase, the likelihood of 
failures increases. The experience on Mir in 
1997 has shown that failure of oxygen 
generation systems can have significant 
consequences. 
As 
a 
result, 
improved 
understanding of spacecraft fire detection is 
critically needed.8  
E. Background in Low Gravity Smoke 
The salient result on smoke particle size 
determination in low-gravity reported by 
Urban et al.9 is that particulate produced by 
low-gravity flames (soot or unburned fuel 
particles) tends to have larger size particles 
than in normal gravity.  Results from the 
CSD (Comparative Soot Diagnostics) Experiment9 which studied smoke properties in low-gravity from several 
spacecraft materials suggested that liquid smoke particles could achieve sizes larger than 1 µm while solid 
particulate remained in the sub-micrometer range.  The combined impact of these limited results and theoretical 
predictions is that, as opposed to extrapolation from 1-g data, direct knowledge of low-g combustion particulate is 
needed for more confident design of smoke detectors for spacecraft. 
F. Spacecraft Atmosphere Dust Background 
Any effort to detect fires must be able to discriminate against the ambient background and nuisance signals.  In 
the case of smoke detection, the background dust aerosol conditions must be considered. The only spacecraft 
background aerosol particulate measurements to date were made on the Orbiter on STS 32 in 199010 and on the ISS.9 
The STS measurements included the results from two cascade impactors and a light scattering device.  The two 
impactors reported a bimodal particle size distribution with ~ 40% of the particles in each of the 2.5 to10 μm and 
>100 μm ranges.  The other two ranges < 2.5 μm and 10 to 100 μm were very lightly populated.  Each impactor 
sampled approximately 15 m3 of air over approximately 30 hours.  These results showed substantially higher 
concentrations than typical indoor measurements (over a factor of 5 for the two most populated size ranges). These 
data were supported by the light scattering instrument which made 17 measurements in 12 locations, all of these 
reported mass concentrations ranging from 50 to 70 μg/m3.  The ISS results of Urban et al.9 were a secondary result 
of an experiment to validate the operation of an aerosol particle counter in low-gravity.  The measurements were 
made in the US Lab on Increment 10 and the particle count levels were at the noise level for the instrument (less 
than 5 particles/cc). The low particle levels in the < 2.5 μm bin for the STS and the low overall numbers for the ISS 
suggest a zone of opportunity for spacecraft fire detection since typical normal gravity fires produce substantial 
particulate in this size range.2,11  However more complete particle size statistics are needed.

II. SAME Experiment 
Although the CSD experiment produced useful information concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke 
particulate, the data set was not particularly large as the size statistics were obtained from TEM data and critical 
details were not obtained for the liquid droplet aerosols.  To rectify this concern, another experiment (Smoke 
Aerosol Measurement Experiment: SAME) was developed.  The SAME experiment sought to avoid the problems 
experienced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence 
upon sample return to Earth.  This is a challenging endeavor because existing aerosol instrumentation is typically 
large, incompatible with spacecraft experiment constraints, and may require substantial sample return to Earth.  As 
will be described below, an alternative approach was employed that used three discrete instruments to measure 
separate moments of the size distribution.  When combined, these moments provide useful aggregate statistics of the 
size distribution.  The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials in much 
the same manner as the CSD experiment however the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were 
more rigorously controlled.   
A. Moment Method 
The approach used by the SAME experiment is termed the ‘moment method’ for convenience.12  As will be 
described below, the approach consists of measuring three moments of the size distribution (zeroth, first and third) 
and using the properties of the log-normal distribution to estimate the geometric mean diameter and the standard 
deviation. 
The average particle size and an estimate of the width of the size distribution will be estimated from various 
moments of the size distribution. The number distribution, fN(D), is defined as

By combining these three moments it is possible to compute three mean diameters of the size distribution and the 
geometric standard deviation.  Validation of this approach is discussed in Cleary, Weinert and Mulholland.3 These 
statistics provide a strong basis for design of spacecraft smoke detectors. 
 
B. Instruments  
These measurements were made using an assembly of three separate instruments. Two are industrial hygiene 
instruments manufactured by TSI and one is a modified residential smoke detector.   
The zeroth-moment instrument is a condensation nuclei counter P-Trak™  (TSI Inc.).  This device operates by 
passing the aerosol-laden particle stream through a region where it is saturated with isopropanol vapor and then into 
a cooler region where the vapor condenses onto the particles raising them all to a size where they are readily counted 
by a light scattering device.  This instrument is very robust and operates over a range of 0 to 105 particles/cm3 and 
20 nm to 1 μm diameter.  Some dilution is required since the smoke concentration ranges from about 0.5 × 106 to 5 
× 106. There was also a concern that the isopropanol condensate would not return to the wick in low-gravity.9 To 
mitigate this issue, the condensing section of the device was modified with very small grooves to improve 
conductance of the condensate back to the wick.  These changes were tested in a separate space experiment with 
good results indicating the modified device could be used successfully in low gravity.9 
The first-moment instrument is the ionization chamber from a residential smoke detector which uses an alpha-
particle emitter to generate ions in a region inside a DC electric field which causes the ions to drift producing 
current.  The presence of particulate reduces the current as a result of the attachment of the ions to the particulate.  
The mobility of the charged aerosol is too small for it to be collected on the ionization chamber electrode. The 
required particle concentrations are on the order of 105 particles / cm3 and no sample dilution was required.  
The third-moment instrument is a light scattering device DustTrak™ (TSI Inc.).  The device uses a 90 degree 
light scattering signal to quantify the aerosol mass density.  For terrestrial dust particulate this signal correlates well 
with the mass concentration, however additional compensation will be needed to account for the range of particle 
sizes that will be seen in the SAME experiment.  The device operating range is from 0.001 to 100 mg /m3.  These 
devices are equipped with an aerodynamic impactor at the inlet which captures particles larger than the selected size.  
The SAME experiment included 2 DustTraks™ one with a 1 μm impactor and one with a 10 μm impactor.  The 
difference in the signal from these two devices provided a measure of the fraction of the particulate that was larger 
than 1 μm.  In some cases dilution was required owing to the high smoke concentration levels. 
 
A schematic of the assembled hardware appears in Fig. 3.  Smoke was generated by overheating a small sample 
of material in the smoke generation duct for approximately 60 seconds.  During this interval, controlled flow was 
induced by a moving piston in the aging chamber which drew the smoke into the chamber.  The smoke was held in 
the chamber for a predetermined time, allowing the particles to coagulate.  The smoke was then pushed by the piston 
into the diagnostics duct where the moment instruments made their measurements. Also installed in the diagnostics 
duct were space shuttle and ISS smoke detectors.   As the smoke was monitored by the moment instruments, a

C. Experimental Results 
The system was installed in the 
Microgravity Science Glovebox, an ISS 
facility that provides many resources 
including: containment, power, data, video 
and uplink commanding.  The assembled 
hardware is shown in Fig 4.  Overall 30 
sample materials were tested.  These were 
comprised of six samples each of 5 
materials: Teflon™, Kapton™, silicone rubber, cellulose, and dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick. These 
samples were tested at different airflow rates, pyrolysis temperatures, and smoke aging durations.  The analog 
signals from the diagnostics were digitized at 1 
Hz.  At this time the used samples and TEM 
grids have just been received back from the ISS 
so mass-balances and TEM analysis have not 
been initiated.  The zeroth and first moment 
instruments have a limited dependence of 
particle diameter so they may be directly 
calibrated.  The third moment instrument (the 
DustTrak™) has a significant dependence on 
the particle diameter and the refractive index.  
An algorithm has been implemented to use the 
results of a Mie Scattering calculation with the 
measured results to iteratively converge on the 
value of the third moment that best fits the 
DustTrak™ signal and the other two moment 
measurements.  This work is currently 
underway so only results from the zeroth and 
first moment instruments will be presented 
here.  As discussed above, the ratio of the first to the zeroth moment is the count mean diameter (D0.5).  Values of 
D0.5 were calculated directly from the calibrated signals from the P-Trak and the Ion sensor and are shown in Table 1 
for the baseline runs of the 4 solid materials with the 
percentage increase over the sizes from a comparable test in 
normal gravity. 
III. Smoke Transport Model   
To assist in the interpretation of the SAME results and to 
provide a further understanding of the implementation of 
smoke detectors in spacecraft applications, a numerical model 
of the smoke transport and detection in the Destiny Laboratory 
(US Lab) of the ISS was developed.  The details of the model 
are discussed by Brooker et al.15 This study was conducted 
using FDS (Fire Dynamics Simulator) a fire modeling 
program developed by McGrattan et al.16,17  at NIST.  FDS 
(version 4.0.7 Linux) is a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) 
model that numerically solves a form of the Navier-Stokes 
equations for low speed, thermally driven flow with an 
emphasis on smoke and heat transport from fires.16 A detailed

conserved quantity representing the fraction of material at a given point that originated in the fuel stream) was 
utilized for this analysis. All solid surfaces were designated as inert with a thermal boundary condition of 293 K.

IV. Conclusion 
Smoke particulate produced in low-gravity was found 
to be typically 50% large in count mean diameter than 
similar conditions in normal gravity.  The resultant sizes 
were all below 300 nm suggesting that discriminating 
smoke from spacecraft dust possibly could be achieved by 
detecting in the sub-micrometer range.  Numerical 
modeling of smoke transport in the US Lab Module of the 
ISS predicted that actual detection times can be quite long 
and strongly dependent on location and the presence of 
obstructions.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 3 
2.2 
SAME Experiment Background 
Since the very beginning of the manned space flight program, NASA engineers and scientists have gone to great lengths to 
prevent fires from occurring on spacecraft. They have done this by adapting fire safety systems and procedures developed 
on Earth to the unique conditions and operating environment of spacecraft. However, microgravity combustion experiments 
have shown that fire can behave very differently in space and the best methods to prevent, detect, and extinguish fires on a 
spacecraft may be very different than those used on Earth. 
In 2000, NASA's Bioastronautics Initiative began with the objective of ensuring and enhancing the health, safety, and 
performance of humans in space. As part of this effort, the  Life Support and Habitation Branch at NASA Glenn Research 
Center is responsible for developing and implementing a research plan to significantly improve fire safety on spacecraft and 
in space habitats. This goal will be achieved by applying a significant amount of fundamental knowledge and the 
experimental capability of microgravity research to spacecraft fire safety questions. 
Spacecraft smoke detectors must detect smoke with a variety of particulate types. Hydrocarbon fuels typically produce soot, 
while overheated plastics produce droplets of recondensed polymer fragments. Paper and silicone rubber produce a smoke 
that is composed of liquid droplets of recondensed pyrolysis products. Differences in the nucleation and growth processes 
for these different types of smokes create particles that have different sizes and properties. 
The Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment that flew in the Glovebox on STS-75 demonstrated that the  smokes 
with solid particulates created in microgravity formed longer chains, and aggregated into larger particles than those created 
in normal Earth gravity. This is surmised to have occurred because of the increased residence time in the high concentration 
smoke regions and to have affected the responses of the two spacecraft smoke detectors (ISS and STS) utilized in that 
experiment. 
To develop smoke detectors that are sensitive to the type and size of smoke particles that will be encountered in 
microgravity and to allow them to distinguish between dust and smoke, better knowledge of the size distribution and 
morphology of the particulates is required. 
2.3 
SAME Experiment Objectives 
The major goal of this experiment is to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulates achieve in microgravity and to 
relate the droplet size and distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. This will 
be accomplished by extending the Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) concept to provide a particulate count and mass 
density determination to the diagnostic array used to analyze these liquid smokes. The experimental design and practical 
application of this data will be enhanced by the development of a numerical code that will predict the smoke droplet growth 
as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment. 
The SAME experiment has the following (listed) objectives: 
1. Make measurements of three moments of the particle size distribution for the μg smoke from several 
materials found in spacecraft considering the effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time 
(near the source) and smoke aging. The primary targets are materials that produce liquid smoke particulate 
but solid smoke producers will also be considered.  
2. Make measurements of the effect of µg and 1-g on the size distribution of liquid aerosol smokes (using an 
idealized smoke e.g. DBT) to provide data for numerical model comparison.   
3. Evaluate the performance in µg of the two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detector designs for the test 
conditions. 
4. Evaluate other smoke detection/sensing devices at NASA’s request for the test materials 
2.4 
SAME “Firsts” for NASA 
• 
Measurements of microgravity smoke: Diagnostics such as the P-Trak and the DustTrak will be used to measure 
particle count and particle mass concentration, respectively.  Both devices are manufactured by TSI.  With the aid of 
these instruments (and others), microgravity smoke will be characterized. 
• 
The use of rapid prototype materials for manned flight experiment hardware. 
• 
Use of an automatic, remotely adjustable, ‘particulate friendly’ dilution system.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 4 
2.5 
The SAME Risk mitigation experiment – DAFT  
The objective for the risk mitigation experiment, DAFT (Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test), is to provide a 
microgravity technology demonstration of the P-Trak Ultrafine Particle Counter manufactured by TSI.  The P-Trak is a 
hand held air quality monitor which is capable of counting particles whose mean diameter is in the range of 1.0 to 0.05 
microns. 
After extensive market research performed by both the Engineering and Science teams, it has been determined that the P-
Trak is the only commercially available hardware that can perform this particle count while maintaining the weight, 
resource, and space limitations for an MSG experiment.   
P-Trak measures particle number concentrations in real-time  while storing that data in a memory maintained by an on-
board battery. These measurements are made in units of particles per cubic centimeter (pt/cm3) versus traditional aerosol 
measurements of milligrams per cubic meter (mg/m3) made by photometers.  P-Trak operates by using the particles in the 
aerosol as seeds to condense droplets of alcohol (a condensate nuclei counter).  These droplets have many times the average 
diameter of the original particles, and may, therefore, be easily counted with standard optical techniques.  The potential 
problem is that these droplets are directed through a nozzle to facilitate the counting, and some of these droplets (a 
predictable percentage) collide with the walls and form a film. In a gravity environment, this film is recycled by ‘falling’ 
down hill. 
In microgravity, the distinct possibility exists that these droplets will form a film that will bridge and block the nozzle, 
effectively plugging the flow of droplets and preventing the device from functioning, or obscuring the optics.  Furthermore, 
there is some concern that the droplets inside the optics chamber may get trapped in an internal circular motion and be 
counted more than once, producing an erroneously high count. 
The modification that was implemented in order to counteract these potential problems was: 60. 0.006” grooves were 
machined down the length of the inside of the condenser.  These grooves were designed to provide a mechanism in which 
the smoke particle/ alcohol mixture can wick its way back to reservoir end to simulate the effects of gravity, hence, 
inhibiting the possibility of the fluid to inhibit the functioning of the unit. 
The modifications to account for and eliminate this problem have been devised and implemented, however, it is not possible 
to test the effectiveness of these modifications in any of the available ground based facilities and/or the KC-135 due to the 
duration of the nominal operation time required (minutes per instance).  This testing, and the verification of the accuracy of 
the instrument functions on orbit, are the core of the DAFT experiment. 
Two P-Trak units are included in DAFT flight hardware, one being only flight hardened, and the other with the modified 
condenser and flight hardened. 
To successfully accomplish P-Trak functional demonstration, additional hardware (which will not be explained in detail 
here) has to be delivered to the ISS. This hardware includes a dust concentration monitor (DustTrak), data cables, fill 
assembly, sample bag assemblies, sample holders, virtual impactor, alcohol reservoir, battery packs, a HEPA filter 
assembly, and appropriate tubing. 
The P-Trak utilizes isopropyl alcohol as a condensate, and its use must therefore, be carefully monitored and requires a 
specific agreement for that use on the ISS which is contained within a Volatile Usage Agreement (VUA) created for the 
experiment.

4.0 
SAME CREW INTERFACES 
4.1 
Hardware Subsystem Description 
The major planned components of SAME are as follows. They are organized by the assembly level, and the order in which 
they are currently planned to be installed into the MSG.: 
1. 
Fluids Control Box Assembly (67198MABA220) 
The Fluids Control Box (FCB) installs on the back wall of the MSG in the upper left section. It is a fan cooled 
enclosure made from aluminum that contains most of the fluids control devices and monitoring devices including 
solenoids, pressure regulator, pressure transducers and mass flow controller. It interfaces directly with the MSG 
fluids resources (VES and GN2) and the Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU), and distributes the fluids 
resources accordingly. Please refer to the SAME Fluids Schematic (67198PABA000) for more information on its, 
and the other fluids system functions. 
2. 
Sample Plate Assembly (Experiment Support Plate Assembly) 67198ABA100 
This assembly, when fully integrated, contains all of the major functional systems of SAME. It is a mounting plate 
which includes the mounting hardware for the Sample Carousel, the Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU), the 
Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) and the Aging Chamber Assembly (ACA). Permanently mounted to it 
are: 
• 
The Smoke Generation Tube 
• 
The Video Camera and Controller 
• 
The Sample Positioning system including: 
o 
the Sample Turning Module 
o 
the sample engagement  mechanism 
o 
the sample position indicator 
o 
the sample positioning lock mechanism 
o 
the Sample Carousel mounting system

items.title: PSI-102_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Doc.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 6 
3. 
Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) (67198MDBA165) 
The DDA is attached to the Sample Plate Assembly and the Aging Chamber Assembly by the crew and contains: 
the ISS and STS smoke detectors and the sampling ports that supply the P-Trak Enclosure and the Commercial 
Diagnostics Enclosure (and port(s) added for any additional diagnostics required). The DDA has a very low 
internal volume, and the flow of the sample aerosol through it is controlled by regulating and balancing the 
requirements of the active diagnostics in the DDA with the exhaust rate of the Aging Chamber piston, as 
controlled by its mass flow controller. It also contains a port, protected by a HEPA filter, that is connected to the 
VES for exhaust and purging. 
4. 
Aging Chamber Assembly (67198MABA150) 
The Aging Chamber Assembly contains the cylindrical, metallic Aging Chamber, the pneumatically activated 
Inlet and Outlet Gate Valves and the Inlet and Outlet Elbows, which connect to the Smoke Generation Tube and 
the DDA, respectively. A Rulon piston, internal to the chamber, moves the sample into and out from the internal 
volume, and that flow is controlled by a mass flow controller which regulates the pressure or vacuum flow 
accordingly.  Sampling ports are provided in the elbows for use by the Thermal Precipitator, and the unit contains 
a Mixing Fan to insure that the contents are homogenous before disbursal to the DDA. 
5. 
Data Acquisition and Control Unit (DACU) (67198EABA660) 
The DACU is the central control unit for SAME. The baseline software is resident there, and, although many of 
the other packages contain their own relay and control cards, ultimately it is the DACU that interfaces with the 
Ethernet and the MLC to orchestrate the performance of the experiment. It also collects and stores data for 
subsequent downlink through the MSG systems, and controls the MSG Video Recorder to provide a taped record 
of the pyrolysis event. 
6. 
P-Trak Enclosure (67198MABA500) 
The P-Trak Enclosure is a flight hardened assembly containing a TSI P-Trak modified to take advantage of the 
VES system and to function in a microgravity environment. Although it interfaces with the DDA, the DACU, the 
Fluids Control Unit and the Power Distribution and Control Unit, it is basically a smart box that can operate 
independently and store its own data.  
7. 
Commercial Diagnostics Enclosure (CDE) (67198MABA600) 
The CDE houses two of the SAME diagnostics, the TSI DustTrak and a First Alert ionization smoke detector. 
Both units have been hardened for flight and have been modified to utilize the VES to drive the sample. The 
DustTrak has also been modified to utilize MSG air to provide its ‘sheath air’ in order to decrease the amount of 
aerosol required by the unit. Like P-Trak, the DustTrak portion of this device can operate independently and store 
its own data. The modified First Alert cannot.  
8. 
Dynamic Diluter (DD) (67198MABA180) 
The DD is a custom designed component that provides dilution of the aerosol from the DDA before its 
introduction into the P-Trak (and possibly the DustTrak). It works by utilizing a laminar flow element to measure 
the amount of sample being introduced and using that information (from a differential pressure transducer) to 
increase or decrease the diluent flow to achieve the desired concentration. The dilution setpoint may be altered by 
software and adjusts to the desired setting in approximately 5 seconds. 
9. 
Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU) (67198EABA680) 
The PDCU is the central disbursement point for the commands, power distribution and data collection for SAME. 
It contains the power converters, main relays and terminal data connections for the entire system and interfaces the 
DACU with the various systems and devices constituting the experiment.

items.title: PSI-102_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Doc.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 7 
10. Sample Carousel Assembly (67198MABB400) 
The Sample Carousel Assemblies (5) each contain six (6) Sample Tubes that interface the samples to the Smoke 
Generation Tube and allow the capture of the smoke in the Aging Chamber. Sample Carousels are sequentially 
installed onto the mounting locations on the Sample Plate Assembly, and the mechanisms contained by it identify 
the individual sample numbers, rotate the carousel to the correct position and engage the Sample Tube, which 
allows the sample to be in a position to be energized.  The samples themselves are composed of five (5) materials: 
Teflon, Kapton, Silicone, Cellulose and DiButyl Phthalate (which being a liquid, is contained within a small 
section of cotton lampwick) in small, cylindrical sections, that are wrapped with coils of wire (baseline: stainless 
steel) that both provides the heat energy to the sample when energized and measures its temperature (by its 
varying resistance). 
These samples are removed from the tubes for weighing, both before and after the experiment (before launch and 
after being downmassed) to quantify the actual mass loss during pyrolysis. 
11. Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU) (67198MABB300) 
The TPU is a device that captures actual samples of the aerosol particulate on Transmission Electron Microscope 
(TEM) grids for examination when returned from the ISS. The units (4) are number matched to the samples in the 
carousel, to take samples from both the Inlet and Outlet Elbows leading to and from the Aging Chamber. 
12. Alcohol Wick Storage Container (67198MABD700) 
The Alcohol Wick Storage Container is a custom manufactured aluminum vessel to contain the alcohol wick 
required by the P-Trak during the time (launch, non-ops) when it is not in direct use. Only one is nominally 
required, but two are included to provide one as a backup. 
13. Hoses 
SAME utilizes ISS GN2 and the VES system both as resources for the experiment process and as systems to 
power its devices. These resources are distributed to the components from the FCU via the hoses, which are 
nominally operated at +/- 15 psig. In order to conserve weight and volume, and provide ease of operation, acrylic 
hoses and quick disconnects will be used for the distribution of pressure and vacuum throughout the system (not 
typical Teflon with stainless steel overbraid). 
14. Harnessing 
All harnessing will conform to applicable standards and be designed to minimize the crew time needed to make 
the required experiment connections, without sacrificing reliability. 
15. SAME Service Kit 
This is a place holder. SAME has not yet defined any servicing requirements. 
4.2 
Video Recording Devices 
Video recordings of the smoke evolution process are very important for establishing proper operation of the test apparatus 
and for debugging the system operation.  Furthermore, the video provides a helpful demonstration of the variability in 
smoke evolution. Experience with CSD showed dramatic cases where clearly visible smoke streams were not always 
detectable by the smoke detectors while invisible smoke streams were readily detected. Normal video resolution is 
acceptable if the smoke is illuminated by forward scattered light from an appropriate light source. Video will be viewed on 
and recorded by the MSG video Monitor/Recorder. 
4.3 
On-Orbit Crew Operational Functions 
The crew will be asked to assemble the experiment from provided subsections, load software, reload Sample Carousels, 
Thermal Precipitator Modules, and alcohol for the particle counter, enter parameters, initiate the experiment, and 
disassemble the experiment.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 8 
5.0 
SAME SOFTWARE CONTROL 
5.1 
Software Controlled Operational Functions 
The DACU is the central point for SAME control.  It is ultimately responsible for all experiment operations and interfacing 
with the environment external to SAME.  It contains all of the logic necessary to autonomously operate the experiment as 
well as receive, validate, and process commands from the MSG.  The DACU periodically transmits the status of the Smoke 
system to the MSG, which then forwards it to the ground.   The software can autonomously control the progress of 
preprogrammed test, manage and store all science and system files on the local data storage medium, control the MSG 
video recorder capturing Smoke images, and copy the files to the MLC for downlink.  The software inside the DACU is 
also responsible for providing diagnostic information and manual control of all sensors and controls using the GSE port. 
Please refer to the SAME Baseline Software Requirements Document (SAME-DOC-004) for more detail. 
5.2 
Data Collection 
Data is collected and stored in the DACU until it is time to downlink the information.  The Thermal Precipitator Module, 
which collects samples of the smoke, will be bagged and returned for analysis.  Sample Carousels are retained so that the 
samples can be weighed after return to Earth. 
6.0 
SAME OPERATIONS 
6.1 
Operations Flow 
1. Experiment Setup- The experiment will be shipped in individual subassemblies that will be assembled inside of 
the MSG.  Parts will be inserted through the MSG side ports starting with the upper, back components.  After 
the MSG ports are covered and the rack is returned to nominal position, the Experiment Software is installed 
onto the MSG Laptop. 
2. Perform Experiment- The first steps in performing the experiment are to load the desired Sample Carousel, load 
or replenish the alcohol wick in the particle counter, and install a new Thermal Precipitator Module.  Next, the 
start-up check out routine is performed.  After the uplink parameters are sent, the experiment is initiated.  Then, 
the baseline uplink parameters are modified, as required, for the next test and the experiment is initiated again 
until all six samples in the Sample Carousel have been used.  The next number matched Sample Carousel and 
Thermal Precipitator Module will then be loaded and the experiment will continue as such until complete. 
3. Shutdown and Repack Experiment- When all the Sample Carousels have been used and all the experiments 
have been performed,  the final Sample Carousel and Thermal Precipitator Module will be capped and bagged.  
In reverse order of installation, the experiment hardware will be repackaged for downmassing. 
6.2 
Detailed Operations 
Please refer to the SAME Operations Concept Document (SAME-DOC-009) for a more detailed description of all 
Operations functions. 
6.3 
Timeline 
Since the experiment is designed for operations controlled from the ground, once the components have been installed in the 
MSG, timeline concerns have mainly to do with the acquisition of command windows and with weekly or semi weekly 
service sessions by the crew.  
SAME will follow the standard ISS procedures for scheduling activities aboard the station including OCR and iURC 
submittals and conferences with the ISS Cadre.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 9 
6.4

The baseline experiment parameters will be resident in the software loaded into the DACU, however, it is anticipated that,

durations should be possible for some single samples, and the inclusion of this desirement will alter the published matrix.  
More test points are strongly desired as the test matrix below has no margin for repeats of test points and each parameter is 
not varied over more than two conditions.

7.0 
SAFETY CONCERNS & PREVENTATIVE MEASURES 
7.1 
Overall Strategy 
Safety analysis is being performed for the SAME (formerly Smoke) hardware in accordance with the safety policies and 
safety requirements for flight hardware (NSTS1700.7B and ISS Addendum). This assessment is being prepared using 
NSTS 13830C as a guideline for data submittal. Hazards not eliminated by design are addressed in either the latest revision 
of standardized hazard control report JSC Form 1230 for ISS and launch/landing phase of the mission or in a Unique 
Hazard Report, JSC 542B. For the most part, the SAME experiment uses generic hazard controls for electrical power 
hazards, sharp edges, EMI (testing), rotating equipment (smaller than 8 inch diameter rotors and less than 8000 RPM), Fire 
Detection and suppression, and touch temperature. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001).

items.title: PSI-102_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Doc.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 
10 
7.2 
Pressurized Systems  
The pressure system includes the aging chamber, the system for moving the piston in the aging chamber (valves, regulator, 
lines, hoses, relief devices) and the Dynamic Diluter. All of the parts will be designed to meet the requirements of 
NSTS1700.7 ISS addendum, NASA-STD-5003, SSP 30558, and SSP 52005 for pressurized hardware. Pressurized lines 
and fittings will be designed to a factor of safety of 4.0 X System MDP of 200 psid (ISS N2 limiting pressure). Pressurized 
system components will be designed to a factor of safety of greater than or equal to 2.5 X System MDP of 200 psid. Down 
stream of the pressure reduction the MDP is 20 psig. These components are designed with the same factors of safety. See 
table of components and factors of safety and hazard report SMOKE-04. Materials will be selected and evaluated for stress 
corrosion and/or fluid compatibility in accordance with SSP 30233, Space Station Requirements for Materials and 
Processes. In the event of loss of power all solenoids will close including the mass flow controllers, therefore the system will 
not over pressurize. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001) specifically hazard report 
SMOKE-04. 
7.3 
Structures 
The SAME experiment is launched in stowage and contained in MSG for on orbit use. The structural aspect of SAME is 
primarily sealed containers and vented containers. Pressure systems are covered in section 1.2. SAME structural failure is 
addressed in Hazard Report SMOKE STD 01 in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001). 
7.4 
Materials 
The ZIN Tech Engineering Team will assure that reasonable measures have been taken with regard to material selection for 
the experiment‘s design, and selected materials are safe for the intended manned space flight application in their respective 
usage environment. A material flammability assessment will be performed per NSTS  22648. The flight unit will be offgas 
tested. The SAME Project Team will prepare the standard Materials Identification & Usage List (MIUL) and MUA’s. ZIN 
Engineering will review and approve material evaluation prepared by the SAME Project, and submit it to 
NASA/GRC/SMAD for concurrence. Upon material evaluation approval, NASA/GRC/SMTD will issue the Material 
Certification Letter in accordance with the guidelines established in the  applicable Material and Processes (M&P) 
Intercenter Agreement prior to flight hardware fabrication. Further information can be found in Hazard Report SMOKE 
STD 01 in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001). 
7.5 
Frangible Materials (Glass) 
All of the hardware which contains glass will undergo a vibration test in the stowed configuration at workmanship or 
protoflight levels and a post-test visual inspection to verify ability to survive launch loads. The duct with the video camera 
lens and LEDs installed will be stowed with clear plastic for crew inspection after launch. 
7.6 
Release of Experiment By-products into the Cabin Atmosphere 
The P-Trak needs a cartridge with an alcohol-saturated wick for its operation; therefore, a risk of contaminating the ISS 
environment has to be considered.  The amount of alcohol released will be carefully controlled and limited. The Project 
Team will submit a Volatile Usage Agreement request to JSC/OC (Material and Processes) for disposition and approval.  
All payloads are to submit their usage requests to a single approval authority at JSC because alcohol usage is a cumulative 
risk, and it will be necessary to process VUA through a single approval authority to track the total quantity of alcohol being 
used. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SMOKE-SDP-001). 
The pyrolysis products of Teflon currently have a JSC Tox level 3 for 5 minutes after creation. After this point the particles 
coalesce and drop to tox level 0. A hazard report has been generated to address this issue. The smoke is contained in the 
smoke tube and aging chamber for 5 minutes. All the smoke is expelled through HEPA filters, some of which dumps into 
the ISS vent the rest of it into the MSG. The MSG is the second containment of the smoke if the aging chamber where to 
leak. Finally the MSG is under a negative pressure which would prevent the smoke from leaking in the event of an MSG 
leak. Hazard Report SAME-08 has been written and submitted to the PSRP for review.

items.title: PSI-102_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Doc.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A 
 
11 
7.7 
Non-Ionizing Laser Radiation 
The ISS Smoke Detector, the P-Trak and the DustTrak contain lasers as a part of their diagnostics systems.  These lasers are 
of Class 1 lasers, and the laser beams are fully contained. These items are not removed from their original housings and are 
used in the applications for which they are intended. There is no crew access to the lasers at any time.  The lasers meet 
ANSI Z136.1-2000 standards for Class 1. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001).  
7.8 
Ionizing Radiation 
The STS Smoke detector and the First Alert Smoke Alarm each contain 1 micro curie of Americium-241.  These items are 
not removed from their original housings and are used in the applications for which they are intended. More detail can be 
found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001). 
8.0 
PRODUCT ASSURANCE 
In order to assure the overall quality and performance of the systems created by the project team, Product Assurance will be 
provided by the ZIN Quality team and will include but not be limited to oversight of the manufacturing and assembly 
processes, investigations into materials and their compatibilities, compliance with the Safety requirements, assessment of 
the systems controls (i.e. Software) and inspection of the final products. The specific methods and strategies planned can be 
found in the following documents: SAME Product Assurance Plan (SAME-PLN-003) and Same Software Assurance Plan 
(SAME-PLN-006). Please refer to them for more detail. 
9.0 
PROJECT PLAN 
The SAME Project Plan (SAME-PLN-001) contains information regarding the Project organization and its levels, 
schedules, budget and a top level description of the project Science goals and the Engineering concepts. Please refer to that 
document for questions regarding those subjects

Conclusions
For the conditions tested, the materials emit most of their particulate in the submicron range.
A valid database now exists for design  of future smoke detectors
Particle dimensions vary strongly as a result of aging or flow residence time and temperature (for Kapton)
Particle morphology varies widely across the range of expected sample materials. Dependence on a single angle scattering device will be difficult.
MPASS – multi-moment approach shows promise for size segregating detector

items.title: PSI-102_Presentations_SAME-2_ParticleMorphology and Size Results.pptx
items.text:
30
Implications and Future Work
Dust rejection may be achievable by detecting at the sub-micron level.
Given the effects of aging and the slow mixing seen in spacecraft, it is probably unwise to focus entirely on small particle sizes for fire detection
Size selective smoke detection will improve reliability and false alarm rejection. Either by classifying the particles or by measuring multiple 
moments. 
Addition of gaseous species detection could  be helpful but requires further 
study.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-008 Rev A 
1 
 
 
1.0 INTRODUCTION 
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) is an experiment payload planned for the Microgravity Science 
Glovebox (MSG) located on the International Space Station (ISS).  The Crew Display (a.k.a. Human-Computer 
Interface or HCI) will operate on the MSG Laptop Computer MLC.  It provides the crew with information about the 
current status of the experiment and an ability to issue commands to control the system.  
The crew interface for SAME is intended to be used only in off-nominal conditions.  The nominal operation of the 
experiment will occur via ground commanding. 
1.1 
Purpose 
The purpose of this document is to describe the SAME Crew Display and to: 
 
1) Provide details about the implementation of the SAME Crew Display requirements found in SAME-DOC-
004, Section 7.0 
2) Satisfy the Preliminary and Candidate Display Deliveries as required for the Payload Display Review Team 
(PDRT) 
1.2 
Scope 
This document is limited to the operation of the SAME Crew Display.  Issues concerning general operation of the 
experiment via the software operating on the DACU or ground systems are not discussed here.

items.title: PSI-102_Reference Data_SAME_Crew Interface Description.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-008 Rev A 
2 
 
 
2.0 CREW INTERFACE 
2.1 
Purpose 
The purpose of the crew interface on SAME is to provide some basic information about the status of the experiment 
during off-nominal conditions, especially in case of loss of data telemetry and/or commanding from and to the 
ground.  This information is minimal in nature.  It represents the basic information that a crew member may be 
asked to report and commands they are asked to issue during off-nominal conditions. 
Section 3.0 provides flow diagrams showing the typical use of the crew interface.  In summary, those uses are: 
• 
Commanding and Telemetry Check.  Verification of SAME data transmittal and command reception. 
• 
Sample Positioning Check.  Used to debug unexpected sample positioning behavior that could use a crew 
member’s eye. 
• 
Gate Valve Check. Used to debug unexpected gate valve behavior. 
• 
P-Trak Configure.  Execute specified commands and verify specified results on the P-Trak to achieve 
reconfiguration and/or debugging. 
• 
Commercial Diagnostics Configure.  Execute specified commands and verify specified results on the 
Commercial Diagnostics unit to achieve reconfiguration and/or debugging. 
• 
Attended Operations.  Ability to power-up the SAME DACU, initialize the instrument, run a specified 
test, and shut down.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-008 Rev A 
4 
 
 
2.2.3 Payload Status Area 
This is an area reserved in the DGCS for payloads to present critical information that is shown at all times.  SAME 
will use this area to display information about the experiment and testing status.  
The Run Mode field displays the current running status of the SAME experiment.  Possible values are: 
STARTUP 
The DACU software is starting 
UNINITIALIZED The DACU software is waiting for the System Initialize command 
STANDBY 
The DACU software has been successfully initialized and is waiting for 
commands and is emitting housekeeping data. 
TEST RUNNING A test is currently in progress 
TEST PAUSED A test is paused 
SHUTDOWN 
The DACU software is in the process of shutting down. 
Table 2 - Run Mode Values 
 
The OK Status indicator replicates the physical LED labeled OK on the DACU housing. It represents the physical 
status of the experiment. When the indicator is lit the system is operational (e,g, powered, booted, ready to run); 
unlit indicates the system is not operational (e.g. not powered, in error). 
 
The Test Number field displays the current test number the DACU is running or prepared to run. 
 
The Elapsed Time field displays how long the current test has been running (HH:MM:SS). If no test is running the 
field will be blank 
 
The GPS field is required by SSP50313. It provides a time reference for payload operations.  
2.2.4 Status Bar 
 
 
 
 
The latest information message received from the DACU will be displayed here. In addition, it is added to the 
general message log (see 2.2.6). The message is specific to SAME and is composed of four comma-separated parts. 
The first part is the GPS time the message was generated on the DACU. Next is the level of the message which is 
either INFO or ERROR.   This is followed by the message text and optional detail text.  The last two fields make up 
the Description field in the general message log.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-008 Rev A 
5 
 
 
2.2.5 Workspace 
The workspace area is used for displaying information and controls for a given function. The contents will change 
based on the primary function selected. 
2.2.5.1 Welcome Screen 
The welcome screen is the first thing displayed when the crew display is started. There is no real content display, but 
it serves the purpose of positively identifying the SAME experiment. Once the operator selects a function from the 
primary button panel, the workspace will change to the new display. There is no way of displaying the welcome 
screen again without exiting and restarting the program. 
 
Figure 2 - Welcome Screen

items.title: PSI-102_Reference Data_SAME_Crew Interface Description.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-008 Rev A 
6 
 
 
2.2.5.2 Status Screen 
The summary status display is shown when the operator presses the Status button. It shows information about the 
state of SAME in addition to what is shown in the Payload Status Area (see 2.2.3). 
 
Figure 3 - Status Screen 
 
 
2.2.5.2.1 Sample Positioning Group 
The sample group consists of 3 fields. The Sample Number field is the number of the sample within the carousel 
being tested at that time. The Carousel Number field is the number of the carousel that is installed. A carousel 
holds six samples. The combination of the carousel and sample number uniquely identifies a particular test item. The 
Resistance field displays the measured resistance of the heater wire coil for the sample. This is used as a unique 
physical indicator of which sample is being tested. 
2.2.5.2.2 SAME Power Group 
MSG provides SAME with 120VDC. SAME converts this into 5 separate voltages using DC/DC converters. The 
SAME Power group consists of fields indicating the state of the 5 voltages. For all voltages, the possible state 
include ON and OFF.  In addtion the 12 VDC Heater, 12 VDC Misc, and 5 VDC can have a state of Enabled, which 
means that it was turned on, but has not yet been sensed as on. 
2.2.5.2.3 Ethernet Switch Group 
The MLC Ethernet connection is routed through a switch inside SAME. The switch connects the MLC to either the 
ISS LAN Backbone or to the SAME DACU. The purpose of this is to allow the DACU to transfer data files to the 
MLC via FTP. The switch is nominally controlled by the DACU; however the crew can manually activate the switch 
if necessary. When the DACU is unpowered, the switch connects the MLC to the ISS LAN. The Ethernet Switch 
group reports the state of the switch. There are three possible values:

items.title: PSI-102_Reference Data_SAME_Crew Interface Description.pdf
items.text:
SAME-DOC-008 Rev A 
7 
 
 
 
MLC to SAME 
The MLC network connection is connected to the SAME DACU 
(for the purpose of transferring files) 
MLC to LAN 
The MLC network connection is connected to the ISS LAN 
The above two states are achieved electronically by DACU commands 
Manual: MLC to SAME The manual switch has been used to force the MLC network 
connection to the SAME DACU. 
Table 3 - Ethernet Switch Position Values 
2.2.5.2.4 Gate Valves Group 
The Gate Valves group displays the status of two valves; the Inlet and Outlet valves. These can either be OPEN or 
CLOSED. 
2.2.5.2.5 Supply Group 
SAME uses the GN2 and vacuum resources supplied by MSG. SAME regulates the GN2 supply as needed. The 
Supply Group displays the status of these gas supplies and the vacuum state. The Main GN2 and Main Vacuum 
resources both have valves that are controlled by the DACU. The valve indicator fields show the state of these 
valves; OPEN or CLOSED. The pressure of the main GN2 supply, the vacuum, and the regulated GN2 are 
reported. 
2.2.5.3 Operations 
The Operations display allows for sending commands that affect the operation of the SAME experiment. There are 
two groups of these commands. 
 
Figure 4 - Operations Screen 
 
 
2.2.5.3.6 System Group 
These commands affect the entire SAME experiment.

items.text:
SAME-DOC-008 Rev A 
12 
 
 
2.2.6 Log 
The message log lists all the messages that have been received or generated by the interface. Messages originate 
from two sources: the DACU and the interface itself. The latest DACU message also appears on the Status Bar (see 
2.2.4).   By default messages are sorted by GPS with the latest messages at the top.  The window may be scrolled to 
see earlier messages.  Sorting order and column can be changed by selecting the column heading.  Sub-sorts are 
achieved by holding <CTRL> while selecting two or more headings.  An arrow in the heading indicates whether 
sorting is by decreasing (down arrow) or increasing (up arrow) order. 
 
Messages appear in the list with three pieces of information. First is the GPS timestamp of the message.  Second is a 
Level indicator. Messages are assigned one of the following levels: INFO, ERROR, or CONFIG. The final piece of 
information is the message description itself.  
 
Messages that originated from the DACU are always assigned an INFO or ERROR level. The DACU message is 
then summarized in a single text string with all the individual message fields identified. Messages originating from 
the interface can be CONFIG or ERROR level. 
 
 
Figure 7 - Log Window 
 
2.2.7 Help 
Selecting Help opens the Help window containing information similar to this document. 
 
 
Figure 8 - Help Window

1. Overview 
The Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) experiment was conducted on 
the International Space Station (ISS), in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), by 
astronaut Don Pettit during Expedition 30 in early 2012; see Figure 1.  SLICE 
investigated the structure and stability of laminar, gas-fueled, non-premixed flames in a 
coflow, where the gas-jet diffusion flame was positioned within a fan-driven flow duct. 
 
 
Figure 1.  Astronaut Don Pettit conducting SPLICE in the Microgravity Science 
Glovebox (MSG) on the International Space Station (ISS) on March 9, 2012 (i.e., GMT 
055), where that day’s testing including both SLICE and SPICE tests.  The MSG is 
covered so that the only experiment illumination is from the flame, (1) which Pettit is 
watching through a gap in the stray light cover, and (2) which can also be seen on the 
upper monitor on Pettit’s left.

items.title: SLICE final report 20161221.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2016) 
 
2016-DEC-21 
 
5 
 
 
The 12 bottles of gaseous fuel were completely consumed during 13 sessions 
(days) of testing.  There were approx. 120 ignitions, with roughly 4,000 high-
resolution photographs taken at roughly 700 flame conditions (where the 
photography was bracketed, i.e., with multiple photographs taken at a time under 
a range of settings). 
 
A fraction of the tests under SLICE were conducted for the Smoke Point In Coflow 
Experiment (SPICE) experiment, which had been previously conducted in 2009.  
Although they had unique objectives, SLICE and SPICE used the same experimental 
hardware (i.e., the SPICE hardware) and nearly identical procedures but they had 
different researchers and science objectives.  Together they came to be informally 
referred to (e.g., by Pettit) as SPLICE which could serve as an acronym for Smoke Point 
& Liftoff In Coflow Experiment.  Roughly a quarter of the 2012 SPLICE testing was for 
SPICE. 
 
SLICE is a precursor to the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, 
which is part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project 
which is in development for operation in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  
SLICE results are being used to maximize the scientific return of that upcoming space 
station experiment. 
 
 
 
2. Introduction 
 
a. Objectives 
The goal of the SLICE experiment was to improve our understanding of the physical 
and chemical processes controlling diffusion (i.e., non-premixed) flame structure and 
lifting phenomena (i.e., stabilization) and to provide for rigorous testing of numerical 
models including thermal radiation, soot formation, and detailed chemical kinetics. 
Good agreement between experimental and computational results had been 
demonstrated for lifted flames at moderate flame conditions, but that agreement 
broke down when the fuel was highly diluted or the soot production was high. SLICE 
was a precursor for the CLD Flame experiment, which is one of five experiments in 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project that are 
currently in development for conduct in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). A 
common goal of the two experiments is to improve computational techniques such 
that a broader range of flame conditions can be effectively modeled than is currently 
possible. 
 
The specific experimental objectives for SLICE were: 
For diffusion flames of methane, ethylene, and selected nitrogen dilutions of each 
fuel burning in a coflow of air: 
(1) Characterize the structure of the flame, especially its base (i.e., stabilizing 
region), from attached through lifted conditions as a function of the fuel, 
burner diameter, and flow conditions. 
(2) Identify the liftoff velocity limits as a function of the fuel and burner diameter.

A third objective, listed below, was abandoned a year in advance of spaceflight 
operations because it was determined from bench-top testing (for procedure 
development) that the planned fuel quantity was insufficient for this goal. 
(3) Characterize the hysteresis of flame lifting and reattachment (i.e., 
stabilization) with flow variations as a function of the fuel and burner 
diameter. 
 
b. Team Members 
Given that SLICE was a precursor to ACME’s CLD Flame experiment, the SLICE 
Principal Investigator (PI) and Co-Investigator (Co-I) were Yale University professors 
Marshall Long and Mitch Smooke, respectively.  Their students and research 
associates and the ACME Project Scientists (PSs), namely Dennis Stocker and 
Fumiaki Takahashi, made up the rest of the research team.  Bob Hawersaat was the 
Project Manager (PM) and Jay Owens was responsible for the flame imaging.  ZIN 
Technologies, Inc. had responsibility for the experiment development, crew training, 
and operations (ops) where the task lead was Tibor Lorik and the training and ops lead 
was Chuck Bunnell.  Carol Reynolds was the Payload Operations Lead for SLICE.  The 
initial analysis of the experimental data and the complementary normal-gravity (1g) 
testing was carried out by Bin Ma for his Ph.D. research.  On orbit, SLICE was carried 
out by astronaut Don Pettit, under the verbal direction of Stocker.  Contact information 
for these key personnel is provided in Table 1, where all but Smooke directly supported 
the on-orbit operations given that his role was in leading the computational modeling. 
 
For reference, the SPICE PI and Co-I were Dr. David L. Urban (NASA Glenn) and 
Prof. Peter B. Sunderland (U. Maryland), respectively, where Urban verbally directed 
crewmembers during the SPICE tests (i.e., Pettit in 2012).

c. Background  
SLICE was the fifth spaceflight experiment to investigate laminar gas-jet diffusion 
(i.e., non-premixed) flames.  And like the preceding experiments, the SLICE 
atmosphere consisted of ~21% oxygen (by volume) with a balance of nitrogen.   
Furthermore, the pressure was ~100 kPa in the 5 experiments, with the partial 
exception of the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP) experiment which also included 
testing at lower values.  Three of the predecessor experiments were conducted over 
a decade ago on the space shuttle, i.e., the Space Transportation System (STS), 
while the fourth was conducted on ISS, as listed in Table 2.  SLICE is especially 
related to two of those experiments, Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) and SPICE. 
 
Table 2: Pre-SLICE space experiments investigating laminar gas-jet diffusion 
flames, listed chronologically.

The four past experiments were focused on gravity’s effects on the flame structure, 
soot and stability limits, and vortex interactions.  The LSP and Turbulent Gas-jet 
Diffusion Flame (TGDF) experiments were both conducted in sealed combustion 
chambers, where the flame was in a quiescent atmosphere.  However, vortices were 
created in the TGDF experiment by varying the air entrainment through the 
mechanical variation of an iris diameter, where the iris was (1) orthogonal and 
coaxial to the burner and flame, and (2) positioned near the burner tube outlet.  
TGDF was an automated Getaway Special canister (GAS can) experiment that flew 
in the payload bay of the shuttle.  In contrast, LSP was carried out in Spacelab and 
Spacehab in 1997 and 2003, respectively.  LSP was operated by the crew and 
conducted within the Combustion Module facility, which is the space shuttle 
precursor to the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). 
 
In contrast to LSP and TGDF, ELF was conducted within a coflowing atmosphere, 
where the flame was enclosed within a small fan-driven flow duct with a 76.2-mm 
square cross-section.  ELF was crew-operated and conducted in a glovebox facility.  
These factors were also true for its successors SPICE and SLICE. 
 
NASA began conducting spaceflight combustion experiments in glovebox facilities in 
1992 with the United States Microgravity Laboratory 1 (USML-1) mission, i.e., STS-

items.title: SLICE final report 20161221.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2016) 
 
2016-DEC-21 
 
8 
 
50, in which the Middeck Glovebox (MGBX) facility was located in the Spacelab 
module rather than the shuttle middeck.  Microgravity flames tend to quench in the 
absence of buoyant convection, which normally transports air to flames, so the 
glovebox combustion experiments have typically incorporated fans to provide forced 
convection since that start.  An STS-50 example is the Wire Insulation Flammability 
(WIF) investigation, in which the wire and flame were centered within a fan-driven 
flow duct (i.e., with forced air flow parallel to the wire). 
 
In 1997, the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) investigation became the first glovebox 
experiment to be conducted in space with gaseous fuel.  Like all combustion 
glovebox experiments carried out on the shuttle, ELF was conducted in the MGBX 
facility, which was located in the middeck on its mission, the United States 
Microgravity Payload 4 (USMP-4) mission, i.e., STS-87.  The experimental hardware 
was designed to just fit within that facility, where this may be apparent in Figure 2.  
The 33x18x18 cm experiment module and other key hardware is shown in Figure 3. 
 
The ELF objectives to investigate the stability and structure of coflow laminar 
diffusion flames were very similar to the SLICE objectives.  ELF is very much a 
precursor to SLICE in terms of both hardware and science, even though experiments 
were separated by 15 years and their research teams were different.  However, 
Dennis Stocker was an exception in that he served as a Co-I and the PS for both 
experiments. 
 
 
Figure 2.  Steve Lindsey (left) assists Takao Doi (right) in conducting the Enclosed 
Laminar Flames (ELF) investigation on Nov. 29, 1997 during the USMP-4/STS-87 
space shuttle mission [STS087-E-5088]. 
 
SPICE was initiated as an extension of the LSP experiment to investigate the effect

items.title: SLICE final report 20161221.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2016) 
 
2016-DEC-21 
 
9 
 
of the air coflow on soot processes, i.e., in addition to LSP’s study with flames in a 
quiescent atmosphere.  The SPICE hardware was directly based on ELF’s hardware, 
where SPICE was originally planned as a shuttle experiment.  The ELF ground 
hardware that had been used for hardware development, crew training, and normal-
gravity (1g) comparison testing was modified so that it could serve the same purpose 
for SPICE.  Although SPICE was planned as a shuttle experiment, the project had a 
convoluted history, e.g., where it was stopped and restarted, such that it was 
ultimately conducted on ISS rather than the shuttle, even though the experiment 
module was designed for the MGBX rather than ISS’s Microgravity Science 
Glovebox (MSG). 
 
 
Figure 3. Bench-top photo of Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) spaceflight hardware 
and logo [NASA C-97-4013]. 
 
The SPICE hardware included significant improvements as compared to ELF.  While 
ELF had a fixed burner tube, SPICE had exchangeable tubes allowing variation of 
the burner diameter.  In ELF, the numerical data was physically displayed on the 
front of the module and was photographed along with the flame using a video 
camera.  Meanwhile in SPICE, the data was still recorded with the flame video, but it 
was overlaid electronically eliminating the need for the illuminated displays, as can 
be seen in Figure 4 (i.e., where there are no physical displays).  ELF used a second 
analog video camera to photograph the flame through the top window, while SPICE 
used a high-resolution digital SLR camera for the top-window photography.  SPICE 
had a retracting scale for photography that could be positioned at the flame axis, 
whereas ELF’s reference scale was on the top of the module, i.e., at a significant 
distance from the flame axis.  However, SPICE eliminated ELF’s retracting array of 
thermocouples and thin-filament fibers (for pyrometry) to include its retracting scale.  
SPICE also used larger fuel bottles because the MSG working volume was

significantly larger than that of the MGBX so greater amounts of fuel could be safely 
used.  Other differences are minor in comparison. 
 
 
Figure 4.  Bench-top photo of SPICE’s spaceflight experiment module, which is 
further discussed in the next section. 
 
When SPICE was conducted on orbit in 2009, e.g., as depicted in Figure 5, the 
SLICE researchers conducted limited trial testing in which it was verified that the 
SPICE hardware would enable accomplishment of the SLICE objectives.  Sample 
flame images of lifted flames are shown in Figure 6.  The testing was quickly 
followed by the preparation and submission of a SLICE proposal in June 2009 for a 
Rapid Turn Around Flight (RTA) Flight Opportunity.   Just weeks later, following an 
external review of the proposal, SLICE was selected by NASA Headquarters in July 
2009 for funding and development toward spaceflight.

Figure 5.  Astronaut Mike Barratt conducting the SPICE experiment in the MSG on 
May 16, 2009 [ISS019-E-017339]. 
 
 
Figure 6.  Photos of a lifted flame under different flow conditions from trial SLICE 
testing conducted during the 2009 SPICE operations (where the scale is not 
consistent).  The lifted nature of the flames can be discerned from the flame shape 
and the distance from the nozzle tip (which is not visible). While the flames on the left 
may look like attached flames, the outward fuel-lean flare of each flame’s base 
reveals its lifted nature. 
 
d. Hardware 
The SLICE experiment was conducted using the SPICE hardware, which remained 
on the ISS following its 2009 operations.  The hardware layout within the MSG is 
shown in Figure 7, where the major components are listed in Table 3 and identified in 
Figure 8.

Figure 8.  SLICE and SPICE hardware layout from a graphic used in crew training. 
 
The principal element of the hardware is the SPICE experiment module, which 
mounted to the floor of the MSG’s working volume, where a bench-top photograph is 
seen in Figure 4.  The bottom (i.e., ‘basement’) of the module includes a delivery 
system for the gaseous fuel, including a quick connect (for attaching a fuel bottle), 
particulate filter, pressure regulator, and mass flow controller (for 500 sccm on a N2 
basis), where these components can be seen with a bottle connected in Figure 9. 
 
The upper portion of the experiment module consists of the fan-driven flow duct in 
which the burner tube is located, and where there are top and front windows for 
flame photography.  The front window is hinged and opens to allow manual 
exchange of the burner tube and hot-wire igniter, where there are interlocks to 
prevent fuel flow and igniter actuation when it is open.  As seen from the front, the

items.title: SLICE final report 20161221.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2016) 
 
2016-DEC-21 
 
14 
 
ambient air from the MSG working volume flows from left to right, where it passes 
through the fan and is pushed through a flow straightener, into the duct, past an air 
velocity probe, through the duct screen, past the burner tube, through a heat sink, 
and out through the filtered soot trap.  This can be seen in part in Figure 10, e.g., 
where parts C1, H008, H010 are the fan, flow straightener, and heat sink, 
respectively.  Note that the velocity probe had a slow response time so the fan 
voltage was instead relied upon during the testing.  The flow duct has a 76.2-mm 
square cross-section with rounded corners, as seen in Figure 11. 
 
 
Figure 9. Illustration of the SPICE fuel delivery system showing the fuel bottle and 
the components in the bottom of the experiment module. 
 
Levers on the right end of the experiment module (when viewed from the front) are 
used to manually rotate the igniter to the burner tube and the photography scale (and 
focal target) to the duct center.  This end of the module also has a switch which can 
be used to disable (or enable) the fuel flow when the astronaut has their right hand in 
the MSG.  If the crewmember has removed their hand, the fuel flow can also be 
disabled (or enabled) using the control box.

SPICE’s power/video box assembly is mounted to the back wall of the MSG’s 
working volume.  It consists of a power box and video box with a common mounting 
plate.  The unit provides for power conversion and distribution, conversion of the 
video from a composite to S-video format, and the titler overlay of the numerical data 
onto the video.  The overlay includes the date and time, fuel flow, fan voltage, air 
speed, and radiometer output. 
 
The SPICE control box was located outside of the MSG through the use of a feed-
through connector.  It allowed the crew to enable or disable the fuel flow and igniter, 
and adjust the fuel flow rate, fan (i.e., coflow) speed, and radiometer gain.  The 
assembly, seen in Figure 14, also included a shutter release button for use with the 
digital SLR camera. 
 
 
Figure 14. SPICE control box assembly, including the shutter release button for the 
digital SLR camera. 
The 12 SPICE fuel bottles were refilled to support SLICE and the 2012 SPICE 
operations, where example photographs can be seen in Figure 15.  The bottles 
simply include a hand valve and quick connect for mating the bottle to the 
experiment module.  The bottles were filled with the fuels listed in Table 4, where the 
propane bottle was filled to lower pressure to avoid condensation of the fuel. 
 
Several hardware changes were made for SLICE, just as SPICE improved upon the 
earlier ELF investigation.  However, they were generally relatively minor in scope 
given that the SPICE hardware was mostly already on orbit and because SLICE was 
planned as an inexpensive experiment that would be quickly ready for spaceflight.  A 
simple example was the addition of two more burner tube sizes, with inner diameters 
of 2.1 and 3.2 mm.  The measured diameters of all of the burner tubes are listed in 
Table 5, to a resolution of 0.0064 mm, where it is a critical measurement because of 
its strong (inverse square) influence on velocity of the fuel jet (for a fixed fuel flow).  
Note that the burner tubes have constant inner diameters even though they have

The SLICE hardware included a Nikon D300s digital SLR camera as a replacement 
for the Nikon D100 that SPICE used during its 2009 operations.  While the previous 
camera was still on orbit, SLICE added a new camera which was characterized with 
a blackbody source to enable determination of the soot temperature via color-ratio 
pyrometry and the soot volume fraction from the temperature and absolute light 
calibration.  To balance the color planes in the flame photography and to avoid 
saturation, the camera had an optional blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which was
