items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2015) 
 
2015-DEC-24 
 
50 
 
6. Appendices 
a. 30-Day Operational Accomplishments Report 
b. Engineering Documents 
c. Drawings  
d. Procedure Outline 
e. Crew Briefing 
f. Video Overlay Recovery Plan 
g. Publications 
h. Presentations 
i. 
Webpages 
 
 
 
 
Appendix A. 30-Day Operational Accomplishments Report 
 
30-Day Operational Accomplishments Report 
International Space Station (ISS) 
Increments 29 and 30 
 
Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) 
Principal Investigator: Marshall B. Long, Yale University, New Haven, CT 
Project Scientist: Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH 
 
Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment (SPICE) 
Principal Investigator: David L. Urban, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH 
 
SLICE and SPICE use the same experimental hardware and nearly identical 
procedures but have different science objectives.  Together they came to be 
informally referred to as SPLICE which could serve as an acronym for Smoke 
Point & Liftoff In Coflow Experiment.  Roughly a quarter of the subject testing 
was for SPICE. 
 
 
I.  
Introduction 
The SLICE experiment investigates the structure of lifting and lifted flames, where flow   
conditions and the combustion chemistry cause the flame to detach from the burner and 
stabilize at a downstream position. It is a precursor to the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame 
(CLD Flame) experiment, where the SLICE results will be used to maximize the scientific 
return of that upcoming space station experiment.  The SPICE experiment is an outgrowth 
of the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP) experiment which flew on STS-83, STS-94, and 
STS-107.  SPICE investigates the smoke point phenomena in low gravity, a topic that was 
the subject of controversy before LSP established the clear existence of smoke points in 
low gravity.  SPICE extends these results to more conditions and fuel compounds.  
 
A. 
Hypothesis 
SLICE has a computational flame model, developed by Co-Investigator Mitchell D. 
Smooke et al. (of Yale University), which effectively served as the experiment’s 
hypotheses. And based on previous research, it was known that higher forced

items.title: SLICE final report 20151224.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2015) 
 
2015-DEC-24 
 
51 
 
velocities can be required to lift microgravity flames because of the absence of 
buoyant convection.  The hypothesis of the SPICE investigation was that smoke 
point behavior will be observed for co-flowing flames and that it will show 
dependence on nozzle diameter and coflow velocity.  
 
B. 
Objectives of Investigation 
The goal of the SLICE experiment was to improve our understanding of the physical 
and chemical processes controlling diffusion (i.e., non-premixed) flame structure and 
lifting phenomena (i.e., stabilization) and to provide for rigorous testing of numerical 
models including thermal radiation, soot formation, and detailed chemical kinetics. 
Good agreement between experimental and computational results has been 
demonstrated for lifted flames at moderate flame conditions, but that agreement 
breaks down when the fuel is highly diluted or the soot production is high. SLICE is a 
precursor for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, which is 
a part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project 
that is currently in development for conduct in the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR). A common goal of the SLICE and CLD Flame experiments is to improve 
computational techniques such that a broader range of flame conditions can be 
effectively modeled than is currently possible.  SLICE’s specific objectives were as 
follows: 
For diffusion flames of methane, ethylene, and selected nitrogen 
dilutions of each fuel burning in a coflow of air: 
(1) Characterize the structure of the flame, especially its base (i.e., 
stabilizing region), from attached through lifted conditions as a 
function of the fuel, burner diameter, and flow conditions. 
(2) Identify the liftoff velocity limits as a function of the fuel and burner 
diameter. 
 
The objective of the SPICE experiment was to find the laminar smoke-point 
properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the largest 
laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels under different 
nozzle diameter / co-flow velocity combinations.  Luminous flame shape 
measurements were also made to verify models of the flame shapes under coflow 
conditions.  
 
C. 
Previous Mission Experience 
The SPICE experiment was previously conducted in the Microgravity Science 
Glovebox (MSG) in early 2009 as part of Increments 18-20, where those operations 
included proof-of-concept testing for SLICE. 
 
 
D. 
Background/History of Project (Optional) 
While there are significant differences, SPICE and especially SLICE have similarities 
to the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) investigation which was conducted in the 
Middeck Glovebox (MGBX) on STS-87 in 1997.  In fact, the experiment assembly 
used by the subject experiments was designed for the MGBX (and not the MSG) and 
is directly based on ELF’s design.  Furthermore, the ground unit used for the SPLICE 
crew training, procedure and test matrix development, and other normal-gravity 
testing was originally used for those same purposes for ELF, although important 
upgrades were made. 
 
In terms of science, SPICE is directly related to the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP)

items.title: SLICE final report 20151224.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2015) 
 
2015-DEC-24 
 
52 
 
experiment which was conducted on STS-83 (1997), STS-94 (1997) and STS-107 
(2003) in facility that was a precursor to the CIR.  LSP studied laminar gas-jet 
diffusion flames in a quiescent atmosphere while SPICE is for similar flames in a 
coflow.  Meanwhile, SLICE and ELF were both studies of lifting and lifted coflow 
laminar diffusion flames, where ELF was focused on determination of the liftoff and 
blowout limits whereas SLICE was focused on the structure of lifting and lifted 
flames.  Furthermore, SLICE is a precursor to the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame 
(CLD Flame) experiment that is in development for conduct in the CIR as part of the 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
 
A. 
Discussion of Method/Protocol 
SLICE and SPICE are both crew-operated MSG experiments, where the 
crewmember was verbally directed by Stocker and Urban, respectively, during the 
testing based on the downlink of the experiment video.  Experiment variables 
included the burner tube diameter, the gaseous fuel (including any dilution), the fuel 
flow, and the air coflow.  The burner and fuel were fixed during each test, where the 
crewmember’s role after igniting the flame was to vary the flow conditions and take 
high-resolution still photos as directed.  Burn times were typically on the order of 1 
minute in duration, and after every two burns the MSG work volume was flushed with 
ISS cabin air as a safety measure.  At the end of each session, a calibration of the 
air coflow was conducted because it diminished over time as a result of soot 
accumulation in the exhaust plenum. 
 
An example of the experiment operations can be seen in the composite video of a 
single SLICE test at: 
http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/news/burming_questions.html 
The synchronized clip combines experiment video (of the flame), video of astronaut 
Don Pettit conducting the experiment, and the space/ground audio communication 
between Pettit and Dennis Stocker, the SLICE Project Scientist.  As can be seen in 
this example, the flow was adjusted throughout the experiment so that 
measurements could be made of the flame structure at a variety of flow conditions 
with the selected burner and fuel combination.  Typically, the fuel was held fixed 
(after a post-ignition adjustment), but in this example, the coflow was held fixed while 
the fuel flow was increased.  Generally, the flow was slowly increased as the flame 
approached the liftoff limit where it detaches from the burner and in some cases 
stabilizes above the burner but often blows out (i.e., extinguishes) as in this example.  
The liftoff and blowout limits are determined from analysis of the experiment video 
while the still photographs are used to determine the flame structure, including the 
soot temperature and volume fraction.  The computation of the latter also relied on a 
pyrometry calibration procedure, conducted during three sessions, in which Pettit 
photographed silicon carbide fibers heated by a flame. 
 
Most SPICE tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, 
and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the 
video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support crew in Cleveland. 
After the SPICE tests, the video record was analyzed to identify smoke point 
conditions. The associated coflow and fuel flow rates were obtained from digital data 
recorded in the video. The smoke point lengths were obtained from the video record 
and are the measured distance from the burner tip to the tip of the luminous flame on

items.title: SLICE final report 20151224.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2015) 
 
2015-DEC-24 
 
53 
 
the flame axis. 
 
III.  Results 
 
A. 
List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
The most significant anomaly was discovered when the hardware was set up in the 
MSG (on GMT 2012/020).  It was found that the experiment’s video data overlay had 
become stuck in a troubleshooting mode where it was scrolling hexadecimal 
characters rather than displaying the test conditions (e.g., fuel and air flows), etc.  
This critical data was not otherwise recorded or visible to the ground team directing 
the time-sensitive experiment operations.  Therefore, conducting the experiment in 
this condition would have been much more difficult, and would have resulted in a 
very large loss of science for the SLICE and SPICE experiments, as well as the 
subsequent Burning And Suppression of Solids (BASS) experiment which uses the 
same hardware.  Fortunately, a corrective procedure was developed by the SLICE 
team which was successfully implemented by Don Pettit (on GMT 2012/037).  Pettit 
reset the overlay to its normal mode by connecting test leads to the experiment’s 
video titler board and making a sequence of momentary electrical connections, 
mimicking the operation of a switch panel that was not part of the spaceflight 
hardware.  The anomaly occurred because a battery on the titler board had 
discharged since the hardware’s last use in 2009, where recharging of the battery 
alone did not return the overlay to the desired mode. 
 
A comparatively minor in-flight anomaly was the outcome of the fan calibration 
conducted at the end of the first session of testing (on GMT 2012/040).  Those 
results indicated much greater flows than those of any subsequent days or the end of 
the preceding session (on GMT 2012/037) which included both the video overlay 
reset and the soot removal procedure.  While the anomalous results appear to be an 
outlier, they were similar to those measured after the SPICE soot removal conducted 
in 2009, suggesting the possibility of a common cause.  Nonetheless, the reason for 
the anomalous higher flow readings is still not understood, although some simple 
tests were conducted as part of the in-flight operations to assess possible causes. 
 
B. 
Completeness/Quality of Data 
There were 13 sessions (i.e., days) of testing not counting the gathering and set-up 
of the hardware and the recovery of the video overlay, i.e., such that there a total of 
16 sessions.  In the 13 sessions, all 12 bottles of the gaseous fuel were completely 
consumed, where it was almost always one complete bottle emptied per session.  As 
such, the data collection was complete for SLICE and SPICE. 
 
The 13 sessions included 8 sessions for SLICE, 1 session for SPICE, and 4 sessions 
with tests for both experiments.  Collectively, over 100 tests were conducted (i.e., 
flames were ignited) and over 4,000 high-resolution digital photographs were taken.  
Those 14-megapixel photos included roughly 700 bracketed sets of flames photos, 
which were almost always at different test (e.g., flow) condition, where that is 
arguably the best indication of the quantity of data collected. 
 
The data quality was high with the exception that the flame images revealed a flow 
asymmetry, presumably in the coflow (and not the fuel flow) that caused the lifted 
flames to be always tilted, where that wasn’t observed in the SLICE proof-of-concept 
testing conducted as part of the SPICE operations in 2009.  Some tilt is acceptable if

items.title: SLICE final report 20151224.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2015) 
 
2015-DEC-24 
 
54 
 
the flame is near (e.g., within 1 cm of) the burner, but this was disappointing.  During 
the initial experiment set up, it was observed that a screen upstream of the burner tip 
had been pushed out of position.  While Pettit corrected this to the best of his ability, 
it is possible that dislocation of the screen may have been the cause of the flow and 
thus flame asymmetry.  Alternately, it might have been caused by air leakage around 
the experiment assembly’s front door which may have loosened since 2009. 
 
C. 
Status of Data Analysis 
The SLICE and SPICE testing resulted in a comprehensive data set with a variety of 
test conditions, including seven hydrocarbon fuels (accounting for various nitrogen 
dilutions), five fuel nozzle sizes, and a spectrum of flow conditions. A fully-
characterized color digital camera was used to image line-of-sight flame emissions to 
obtain flame properties such as the flame shape and size, lift-off height, as well as 
soot temperature and volume fraction. The data analysis carried out thus far includes 
quantitative determination of soot temperature and volume fraction for all sooty 
flames and lift-off height measurements for lifted flames. The data analysis is still 
ongoing, where a major remaining task is the conduct of comparison normal-gravity 
(1g) tests. While many 1g tests were conducted in advance of the ISS testing, the 
latter were conducted over a broader range of flow conditions.  Numerical simulation 
of the flames will also be performed and compared with experimental results. 
 
The SPICE data have been collected and transferred to the University of Maryland 
for detailed analysis by a graduate student employee.  This analysis will consist of 
careful review of the video record to identify images at the smoke point.  These 
images will then be used to determine the instantaneous flame size and the 
associated test conditions for that time will be extracted from the data. 
 
 
D. 
Preliminary Research Findings 
Due to the lack of buoyancy force, the microgravity (0g) flames are generally wider 
and less likely to lift off than their 1 g counterparts, and flames with higher dilution 
levels can be stabilized in microgravity. The soot residence time is also greatly 
enhanced in microgravity, which leads to lower soot temperatures and greater soot 
volume fractions.

Below is a nominally chronological list of selected engineering documents where it should be 
understood that there are other important documents that are not included.  However, it is 
important to note that SLICE did not have an Engineering Requirements Document (ERD) 
because of its streamlined development, where it was treated as a reflight of the SPICE 
experiment. 
 
The engineering documents which are particularly helpful for interpreting 
or understanding the SLICE results are marked with an outline like this. 
 
 
1. SPICE-RPT-002: Science Verification Report - May 2007 
The SPICE science requirements were included in SLICE, making this verification report 
important to the analysis of SLICE results.  It is notable that one science SPICE 
requirement was not met, where the report states: “There are 18 verification 
requirements. All requirements have been closed. One verification, Radiometer accuracy 
is not compliant.” [p. 5 of the pdf file] “The Radiometer is highly susceptible to EMI. 
Accurate readings can only be done by comparing the value prior to flame initiation and 
during flame activity.” [p. 17 of the pdf file] 
 
2. MSFC-ICD-3270 Revision C: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) Interface 
Control Document (ICD) for Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) - July 10, 
2008 
Although the SPICE ICD is an important engineering document, it should not be 
important for the interpretation of SLICE results. 
 
3. Memorandum SPICE-MEM-010: SPICE Flow Duct Velocity Measurements - June 6, 
2009 
This important memorandum describes coflow characterization of the flow duct 
performed in June 2008 prior to the hardware’s delivery to ISS. 
 
4. SLICE-PRO-001: Gas Supply Assembly Charging Procedure - February 2010 
This baseline document, which was later revised, identifies the fuels used in the SLICE 
experiment and explains the procedures for filling the fuel bottles. 
 
5. [SLICE-SDP-001]: ReFlight Safety Data Package - March 2010 
This baseline document was revised a few times before it was finalized.  It remains 
useful for understanding the experiment because of its overview of the hardware and its 
operation. 
 
6. SLICE-PRO-001 [A]: Gas Supply Assembly Charging Procedure – [May] 2010 
This is revision A of the fuel bottle filling procedure as can be seen on the signature 
page, but the document’s cover wasn’t updated and still shows the original February

17. SLICE-RPT-001: Nikon D300s Blackbody Characterization Report - October 2010 
This report describes the blackbody characterization of the digital still camera that was 
carried out to meet SLICE science requirement 4.7.3 (in the SRD) and includes the 
results.  The primary purpose of the characterization was to enable determination of the 
soot temperature via color ratio pyrometry using the camera’s color planes.  Additional 
absolute light calibration (discussed in the Data section of this document) allowed 
determination of the soot volume fraction.

Although this document dates from after the completion of SLICE, it shows how the

20. BASS-II Investigation On-orbit Anomaly - May 2, 2014 
This internal NASA presentation describes a 2014 anomaly in the Burning and 
Suppression of Solids II (BASS-II) experiment which was conducted on ISS in the same 
hardware as SLICE and SPICE.  The document is important because a leak was 
revealed when the hardware overheated.  While the leak almost certainly grew during 
this event, it may have existed (at a smaller size) during the SLICE testing and adversely 
affected the symmetry of the velocity field within the flow duct.

February 2013 
Page ii of vi 
 
PREFACE  
The Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) is a precursor to the Coflow 
Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, which is one of the four ACME (Advanced 
Combustion via Microgravity Experiments) investigations that are currently in development for 
conduct within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  The goal of the experiment is to 
investigate the structure of lifting and lifted flames, where the flame detaches from the nozzle 
and stabilizes at a downstream position.  The results will be used to minimize risk and maximize 
the scientific return of the CLD Flame Experiment.  The SLICE investigation was conducted in 
the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using the Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment 
(SPICE) hardware.

items.text:
Post Flight Report  
SLICE-RPT-002 Rev – 
February 2013 
Page 1 of 56 
 
 
1.0 
INTRODUCTION 
SLICE, the Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment, is a space station investigation of the 
structure of lifting and lifted flames, where flow conditions and chemistry cause them to detach 
and stabilize downstream of the burner. 
SLICE is a crew-operated combustion experiment that will be conducted within the Microgravity 
Science Glovebox (MSG) on the International Space Station (ISS). A flame of gaseous fuel, such 
as methane which is the primary component of natural gas, will be generated within a small fan-
driven flow duct. With guidance from the ground team, the astronaut will vary the fuel or air 
flow and take still photographs in parallel with video photography. The calibrated still 
photography will enable determination of the soot temperature and volume fraction. 
1.1 
Purpose  
The data will be used to improve modeling capability with the overall goal of increased fuel 
efficiency and reduced pollutant emission in practical combustion devices here on Earth. SLICE 
is a precursor to the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment which is in 
development for ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) as part of the Advanced Combustion 
via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. 
1.2 
Scope  
SLICE is a joint effort of Yale University, the National Center for Space Exploration Research 
(NCSER), NASA, and ZIN Technologies, Inc. The experiment is managed at the NASA Glenn 
Research Center (in Cleveland, OH), which is NASA’s lead for microgravity combustion 
research. If you are looking for more information about SLICE, please visit: 
http://issresearchproject.grc.nasa.gov/MSG/SLICE/

February 2013

3.0 
SLICE SCIENCE OVERVIEW 
3.1 
Background 
Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an important unresolved problem of combustion 
science that affects the durability and performance of power and propulsion systems, the hazards 
of unwanted fires, the pollutant emissions of combustors and the potential for developing 
computational combustion. 
Coflow laminar diffusion flames are especially valuable for studies of combustion because of the 
availability of accurate numerical modeling with that flame configuration. In particular, excellent 
agreement can be achieved when the flow conditions are such that the flame detaches and lifts 
above (i.e., moves downstream of) the nozzle. A coupled experimental and numerical 
investigation can enable validation and improvements to combustion modeling. Enhanced 
modeling capability is important because it can reduce time and cost in the design of practical 
combustion devices. Furthermore, flame attachment to (or detachment from) a burner or 
condensed-fuel surface is of essential importance in both combustion systems and fire safety. 
The flame attachment point controls the stability of the entire trailing diffusion flame. 
 
Figure 3-1— Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flames

Post Flight Report

February 2013

3.2 
Objectives 
For diffusion flames of methane, ethylene, and selected nitrogen dilutions of each fuel burning in 
a coflow of air: 
(1) Characterize the structure of the flame, especially its base (i.e., stabilizing region), from 
attached through lifted conditions as a function of the fuel, burner diameter, and flow conditions. 
(2) Identify the liftoff velocity limits as a function of the fuel and burner diameter. 
This will enable refinement of the flame diagnostic settings and test matrix for the CLD Flame 
experiment. It will also allow for a preliminary assessment of the numerical codes’ ability to 
predict the flame structure under the broader conditions that are only found in microgravity 
flames. The computation of attached flames will require modification of the numerical models to 
incorporate burner heat loss. 
3.3 
Science Requirements 
3.3.1 
Fuel Nozzles 
 All nozzles are replaceable on-orbit by the crew 
 Fuel nozzle installed orientation is in the axis of the flow duct 
 Fuel nozzles are circular with a constant internal cross section 
 Off-the-shelf tubes have inner diameter with a tolerance of better than the required ±0.1 
mm  
 The SPICE nozzles available include 0.4, 0.8, ,1.6, 2.1, and 3.2 mm  
 Burner tubes are made of 304 Stainless Steel

Oxygen Concentration 
Oxygen concentration information from Columbus and Node 3 will be monitored utilizing

3.3.4 
Pressure 
Cabin pressure information will be collected from both Columbus and Node 3 using, typically 
two, pressure transducers. 
3.3.5 
Acceleration 
SLICE testing will be scheduled around planned thruster firing or spacecraft dock or undock. 
The acceleration environment will be measured by SAMS during SLICE testing which will be 
installed in or near the MSG Work Volume. 
3.3.6 
Still Imaging 
 A Nikon D300s camera with a blue-green BG-7 filter that can installed or removed will 
be manifested for use with SLICE. 
 The Nikon D300s camera will be calibrated with a blackbody source 
o Calibration will be performed using the replacement LEXAN top window and with 
and without the BG-7 filter from 800 – 1200 ˚C in 100 ˚C increments.  See SLICE-
RPT-001. 
3.3.7 
Fiber 
There shall be a single ceramic SiC fiber with a diameter of less than 100 microns and shall be 
known to within ± 5 microns that can be located downstream and orthogonal to the fuel nozzle. 
 The fiber used will be an 80 micron diameter fiber

3.4 
Operational Requirments 
The standard test procedure was simplistic in nature.  The flame was ignited, then, the test 
operators relied on voice commands to adjust the fuel flows and air velocity until the flame 
extinguished.   
3.4.1 
Pyrometry Calibration 
The fiber is placed into position in the test chamber and a non-smoking flame is established so 
that the luminous portion of the flame is just below the fiber. Images are then taken with the still 
camera to provide a temperature measurement at the fiber position and an absolute intensity 
calibration.

3.5 
Success Critera 
3.5.1 
Minimum Success 
Still images are acquired for at least 15 different lifted flames with different combinations of fuel 
flow and air velocity with a single fuel, or at least 10 different lifted flames each of two fuels, or 
at least 5 different lifted flames each of 3 or more fuels.   
3.5.2 
High Success 
Still images are acquired of at least 30 different lifted flames total from at least 3 different fuels.  
The still images are acquired with a blackbody characterized camera for soot pyrometry or liftoff 
limits are determined for at least one fuel. 
3.5.3 
Complete Success 
Testing conducted with all 12 fuel bottles, with identification of stability limits and smoke points 
(within the range of the SPICE velocity limits).  Still images are taken of lifted flames with a 
blackbody characterized camera. 
The project would like to acknowledge the efforts of the SLICE Co-Investigator, Dennis Stocker, 
for generating the daily and weekly status updates.  The following sections includes a 
compilation of the status reports that were submitted to the Lead Increment Scientist (LIS) 
during the SLICE science operations conducted in the MSG on ISS.

4.0

4.1

Don, the SLICE team has developed a procedure to reset the video overlay from the hexadecimal 
trouble-shooting mode in which it is currently stuck to the normal display of data (e.g., flow conditions).  
We look forward to the conduct of that procedure and the start of testing next week. 
 
Daily Status Reports 
February 6, 2012 (GMT 037) 
Status Report Originator  
Dennis Stocker, SLICE PS/Co-I 
Science Status 
The procedure to reset the video overlay was successfully conducted 
thanks to Don’s “brain surgery” skills, and was followed by soot removal 
including fan calibration.  We are good to proceed with nominal science 
operations for SLICE and the subsequent MSG experiment, BASS, which 
uses the same SPICE hardware. 
Unexpected Events 
No significant surprises 
Science Look Ahead 
With today’s success, science ops with flames will begin during the next 
session using 100% methane as the fuel, where methane is the major 
constituent of natural gas and its chemical kinetics are well understood. 
Topics for Resolution 
None 
 
February 9, 2012 (GMT 040) 
Status Report Originator  
Dennis Stocker, SLICE PS/Co-I 
Science Status 
Science operations began today with 100% methane as the fuel.  There 
were 7 flames (i.e., test points) conducted as part of runs 1-2 before the 
fuel bottle was depleted (during the seventh test).  In this testing, data was 
acquired for approximately 35 flow conditions total, which is roughly what 
is expected for a single fuel bottle.  Eleven additional fuel bottles remain. 
Unexpected Events 
We observed significantly greater air flow in the fan calibration today than 
on GMT 037 (i.e., Monday).  Today’s results were very similar to results 
after soot removal during the 2009 SPICE ops which is reassuring, but the 
cause of the different results (i.e., GMT037 vs. 040) is currently not clear.  
Some possible causes include flow blockage on GMT 037, e.g., at or near 
the fan inlet, or “cleaning” resulting from the heat of today’s flames.  The 
SLICE fan calibration is nominally conducted at the end of all SLICE ops 
where we will be alert to future measurements and potential causes for the 
variation.

items.title: SLICE-RPT-002_Post Flight Report-.pdf
items.text:
Post Flight Report  
SLICE-RPT-002 Rev – 
February 2013 
Page 10 of 56 
 
 
Science Look Ahead 
Our next ops are with nitrogen-diluted fuel using 70% methane.  A 
major goal of the SLICE research is to extend our modeling 
capability to be able to accurately predict fuel-lean flames.  Before 
the normal flame testing, we’ll be doing a pyromety calibration 
where we’ll be photographing ceramic fiber(s) heated by the flame.  
That reference data combined with the soot pyrometry (via a color 
ratio technique) will allow us to determine the soot volume fraction 
from the still photos. 
Topics for Resolution 
A NCR was generated to identify the problem observed with the 
video overlay.  The NCR is SLICE-NCR-003.  The problem was 
that the video overlay data that is generated by the Video Titler Card 
located in the Video Unit of the Power/Video Unit Assembly 
displayed Hexadecimal data instead of the properly formatted data.  
The video Titler board contains a rechargeable battery that drained 
over the approximately 2 years that it was idle on ISS resulting in 
the Titler settings to reset to their factory default.  The Video Titller 
is capable of being configured to the users desired settings.  The 
crew procedure (MGUEMSGSLCEC001) was developed to allow 
the crew to enter the Titler menu, set the parameters properly, and 
save the settings.  Additonally the SLICE hardware was powered for 
approximately 4 hours to recharge the battery.  The crew procedure 
was successfully performed and even with powering down the 
hardware the settings are maintained.

4.2 
Weekly Overview – Week Ending 10 February 2012 
Status/Crew Member: 
Pettit 
Total Runs Planned: 
12 fuel bottles 
Runs Complete: 
1 bottle 
 
 
Don, thanks for your great job in recovering the video overlay data!  It would have been a big loss for 
both ops and science (for SPICE and BASS in addition to SLICE) to have proceeded without that data.  
Testing with the 100% methane went well, where our test matrix is only an estimate of what we might 
accomplish with each bottle.  In the 2 runs, we conducted 7 flames and got data for approx. 35 different 
conditions total - which was about what we had anticipated.  Based on my observations, I (Dennis) 
voiced up more flow conditions for some flames than I had originally intended where that limits the total 
number of flames accomplished.  We look forward to Monday's tests where we will press on to 70% 
methane, beginning with a pyrometry calibration which is needed for determination of the soot volume 
fraction from the still photos.  Meanwhile, we'll take advantage of this week's results to plan how to 
maximize our science return from future tests with the remaining 2 bottles of 100% methane. 
 
Daily Status Reports 
February 13, 2012 (GMT 044) 
Status Report Originator  
Dennis Stocker, SLICE PS/Co-I 
Science Status 
There was a late planning change where today’s testing was conducted 
with 40% methane instead of the 70% methane that had been planned.  
Review of the GMT 040 results made the SLICE PI concerned that 
microgravity-enhanced soot production would degrade the pyrometry 
calibration if the soot accumulated on the ceramic fibers.  Fuel dilution 
diminishes soot production, so the decision was made to begin with the 
most dilute fuel so as to avoid contamination of the silicon carbide (SiC) 
fibers.  Science operations began with the pyrometry calibration to get 
reference images of glowing ceramic fiber(s) – heated by a flame - that will 
allow determination of the soot volume fraction from the still photos of the 
flames.  Two calibration tests were conducted (i.e., test point 49 was 
repeated once) followed by four standard tests (i.e., flames) from run 8 
before the fuel bottle was depleted (during the final test).  Data was 
acquired for approximately 32 flow conditions total (from 6 flames total), 
which is similar to what was accomplished on GMT 040 and roughly what 
is expected for a single fuel bottle.  It must be understood that the number 
of tests (i.e., flames) conducted is very highly dependent on the flow 
conditions voiced up by SLICE.  More conditions than had been planned 
were voiced up today because the 0g flames didn’t lift when anticipated, 
and this diminished the number of tests conducted, i.e., flames ignited.  
Ten additional fuel bottles remain and the SLICE team is reassessing how 
to make the most out of that remaining fuel. 
Unexpected Events 
We are still seeing an inconsistency in the fan calibration, where today’s 
results suggest a significantly lower air flow than on GMT 040 but a little 
more than observed on GMT 037.  The calibration was conducted twice 
today with the glovebox both sealed (nominal) and open, but those two 
conditions gave nearly identical results.  The curves are all very similar in 
shape but offset from one another, where the cause of the variation is not 
yet understood.  It is not known whether the variation is because of 
inconsistencies in the actual flow, the measurement, or both.  The SLICE 
team is working to understand the data.

2 bottles as of GMT 047 
 
 
Don, thanks for your care with the ceramic fibers for the pyrometry calibration of the still photos, where 
that will enable our determination of the soot volume fraction in the flames.  In the testing on GMT 044, 
which was with 40% methane (diluted with nitrogen), a total of 6 tests were conducted, including two 
pyrometry calibrations and 4 standard tests, where the latter included 30 distinct flow conditions 
including several where the flame was lifting and partially detached from the  burner tube.  The 
microgravity flames have been found to be more stable, i.e., resistant to lifting, than anticipated so future 
testing will focus on smaller burner tubes, and thus higher jet velocities.  We’ve seen significant variation 
in the fan calibration curves, which is why we requested multiple fan calibrations on GMT 044 and 048.  
The two fan calibrations that you conducted on GMT 044 were nearly identical, but showed readings that 
were significantly lower than those on GMT 040 and slightly higher than those on GMT 037.  The 
existing curves, including pre-launch (in 2008) and during the 2009 SPICE ops, all exhibit a very similar 
shape but are often offset vertically.  Thus far, we don’t yet understand the cause of the variation, or 
even if the variation is in the flow itself or just the readings.  Next week’s testing includes 20% ethylene 
(diluted with nitrogen) and 100% propane, where the tests are focused on lifting (SLICE) and smoke 
points (SPICE), respectively. 
 
Daily Status Reports 
February 17, 2012 (GMT 048) 
Status Report Originator  
Dennis Stocker, SLICE PS/Co-I 
Science Status 
Today’s activity was conducted with 70% methane (diluted with nitrogen) 
and included two fan calibrations (conducted before and after the regular 
ops), a pyrometry calibration test (including 3 flow conditions) that will be 
used to determine the soot volume fraction from the digital stills, and 8 
standard tests (flames) including approximately 26 flow conditions.  
Through today’s selection of test points and voiced-up flow settings, 
results were acquired for a broader range of conditions than achieved in 
previous sessions.  More importantly, these tests included photography of 
lifted flames, which is the principal experimental objective for SLICE.   
While SLICE is clearly limited on fuel, good use was made of the bottle 
today. 
Unexpected Events 
None.  FYI, the two fan calibrations conducted today were very similar to 
each other, where the post-testing calibration was essentially identical with 
that on GMT 044.  They were also close to the calibration on GMT 037, 
making the calibration on GMT 040, with its significantly higher flows, an 
outlier.  Yet that day’s readings were very similar to those from a post-
cleaning calibration in the 2009 SPICE ops, suggesting the possibility in a 
systematic, but yet unknown, cause for the outliers. 
Science Look Ahead 
Monday’s testing is with 20% ethylene, where that fuel is of interest as a 
contrast to the methane because it is much more highly sooting.  Monday 
will not include a pyrometry calibration, as no more are planned for SLICE, 
but will focus on lifting and lifted flames. 
Topics for Resolution 
None

4.4 
Weekly Overview – Week Ending 24 February 2012 
 
Status/Crew Member: 
Pettit 
Total Runs Planned: 
12 fuel bottles 
Runs Complete: 
4 bottles as of GMT 054 
 
 
Don, thanks for your efforts and skill in capturing images of the lifted flames.  The microgravity flames 
have lifted at signficantly greater velocities than the normal-gravity flames, but upon lifting have been 
much less stable.  In the testing on GMT 048, which was with 20% ethylene (diluted with nitrogen), a 
total of 8 tests were conducted, including some repeats, with 32 distinct flow conditions including two 
where the flame was detached from the  burner tube.  As of GMT 054, a total of 27 standard tests (i.e., 
flames) were conducted including approximately 120 flow conditions.  The SLICE fan calibrations have 
shown minor day-to-day variation, where the calibration conducted on GMT 040 appears to be an 
outlier, and where the cause for the significantly higher flow readings on that day is unknown.  The 
results from GMT 040 are quite close to those obtained after the soot removal during the 2009 SPICE 
ops (on GMT 166), suggesting the possibility of a systematic cause.  The agreement of the typical 
SLICE results with those from the end of the 2009 SPICE ops seems to support this idea, but both could 
be coincidences.  Recent testing indicates that the higher flow readings from GMT 044 are not the result 
of either (1) the glovebox being open (i.e., where the gloveports are not sealed) or (2) the glovebox air 
circulation being on.  Much higher flow readings are observed when the front door of the SPICE 
experiment assembly is open, although that condition can lead to readings that significantly exceed 
those from GMT 040.  Next week’s testing includes more lifted flame tests with the 100% and 40% 
methane (diluted with nitrogen), but there will be a return to smoke point testing in future weeks.

Status Report Originator  
Dennis Stocker, SLICE PS/Co-I 
Science Status 
Today’s activities went very efficiently with Don accomplishing all of  Runs 
28 through 31 (19 tests).  We are intrigued by apparent differences in the 
smoke heights from the prior SPICE-1 testing (2 years ago) and will be 
evaluating the down linked still images to evaluate this. 
Unexpected Events 
None 
Science Look Ahead 
We will be returning to lifted flames (SLICE) on Monday GMT 058 using 
pure methane continuing on with lifted flames until Mid March when we 
would return to SPICE operations

This week's testing went very well, where we conducted a total of 25 lifting tests (i.e., ignitions), including 
approx. 140 flow conditions.  They were conducted on GMT 058 and 061 with 100% and 40% methane 
(diluted with nitrogen), respectively.  Importantly, the testing on GMT 061 included the right combination 
of factors - including Don's careful flow adjustments - to yield stable lifted flames, which can be simpler 
to numerically model and as such are the preferred flame configuration for this research.  Thanks too to 
Don for his great fisheye photos of the hardware setup within the glovebox.  The fan calibrations for both 
days gave similar results to previous sessions (with the exception of GMT 040), so flow degradation has 
not been an issue.  Next week's tests will include both lifting tests on Monday (GMT 065) and smoke 
point tests on Thursday (GMT 068) with 70% methane and 100% ethane, respectively.  Regarding the 
latter, ethane is the intermediate alkane between methane and propane and was not part of SPICE's 
2009 test matrix.

began with SPICE smoke point tests and conducted tests with 4 burner 
tubes very efficiently, including 4 ignitions and approx. 57 flow conditions 
(i.e., bracketed sets of photos).  Don was very quick at finding the test 
points so we were able to conserve fuel for SLICE.  Once these were 
complete we switched to SLICE operations, i.e., looking at flame lifting 
rather than smoke point determination.  Nine tests (i.e., flames) were 
conducted for SLICE, with 2 burner tubes and 34 flow conditions before 
the fuel bottle was depleted.  The fan calibration was within the observed 
day-to-day variation, although it was on the low side, suggesting the 
possibility of minor flow degradation from soot accumulation. 
Unexpected Events 
None 
Science Look Ahead 
Our next session will be on Monday (GMT 072) with the third and final 
bottle of 100% methane.  The tests will start with SLICE lifting tests and 
tentatively proceed to SPICE smoke point tests. 
Topics for Resolution 
None

items.text:
Post Flight Report  
SLICE-RPT-002 Rev – 
February 2013 
Page 19 of 56 
 
 
4.6 
Weekly Overview – Week Ending 09 March 2012 
Status/Crew Member: 
Pettit 
Total Runs Planned: 
12 fuel bottles 
Runs Complete: 
~7 fuel bottles 
 
 
As of GMT 068, we are roughly 60% through the SLICE and SPICE (i.e., SPLICE) testing.  Of the twelve 
fuel bottles, four are full, two are partially depleted, and six are empty.  The flame lifting testing on 
Monday with 70% methane included 10 tests (i.e., ignitions), not counting those which blew out at 
ignition, including approximately 50 flow conditions.  The fan calibrations continue to be similar from day 
to day (with the exception of GMT 040), so flow degradation has not yet been an issue although the 
sootiest fuel has been left to last.  The remaining testing will include a mix of lifting and smoke point 
tests, sometimes in the same session, e.g., on GMT 072.  Next week’s sessions include the third and 
final bottle of 100% methane and the second and final bottle of 20% ethylene, where both are currently 
full. 
 
Daily Status Reports 
March 12, 2012 (GMT 072) 
Status Report Originator  
Dennis Stocker, SLICE PS/Co-I 
Science Status 
Today, we again spliced together both SLICE and SPICE testing, where 
we burned the third and last bottle of 100% methane.  We began with six 
lifting tests (i.e., flames), where we took 40 bracketed sets of photos (i.e., 
at different flow conditions) and got measurements of lifting limits with the 
0.8-mm burner tube.  Then two smoke point tests were conducted with 
approx. 16 sets of photos before the fuel ran out.  It was interesting to see 
the smoking behavior with methane, as that had not been observed in the 
2009 SPICE ops when the hardware was limited to burners of 0.4-1.6 mm 
in inner diameter.  In this regard, soot behavior is too slow to fully develop 
in drop facilities and too sensitive to g-jitter in microgravity aircraft testing, 
so space-based testing is critical for this research.  The fan calibration 
indicated a small reduction in air flow, e.g., with a drop from 46-48 (typical 
range) to 44 cm/s when the fan is set at maximum flow. 
Unexpected Events 
None 
Science Look Ahead 
Our next session will be all SLICE lifting tests on Thursday (GMT 075) with 
the second and final bottle of 20% ethylene. 
Topics for Resolution 
None 
 
March 15, 2012 (GMT 075) 
Status Report Originator  
Dennis Stocker, SLICE PS/Co-I 
Science Status 
Today, the testing with 20% ethylene was for SLICE studies where we 
again successfully achieved the desired condition of stable lifted flames.  
Neglecting initial ignition attempts where the flame unexpectedly blew out 
at ignition, a total of 9 tests were conducted before the fuel was depleted, 
including approximately 78 flow conditions, i.e., bracketed sets of digital 
still photos.  The fan calibration gave similar results to that at the end of 
Monday’s session. 
Unexpected Events 
None 
Science Look Ahead 
Our next session will include both SLICE and SPICE (smoke point) tests, 
with 70% methane and 100% propane, respectively.  As a result, both 
Dennis Stocker and David Urban will be enabled.  The SLICE testing is 
with a pyrometry calibration, where the earlier results were not as self-

items.title: SLICE-RPT-002_Post Flight Report-.pdf
items.text:
Post Flight Report  
SLICE-RPT-002 Rev – 
February 2013 
Page 20 of 56 
 
 
consistent between the bracketed photos as desired. 
Topics for Resolution 
None 
 
March 19, 2012 (GMT 079) 
Status Report Originator  
Dennis Stocker, SLICE PS/Co-I 
Science Status 
Today, the testing was with two partial bottles with both SLICE and SPICE 
testing burning 70% methane and 100% propane, respectively.  
Collectively, there were 5 flames (including one pyrometry calibration) and 
28 bracketed sets of photos, i.e., flow conditions, totaling 300 high-
resolution photos (including the dark frame/current calibration).  It was 
particularly interesting to see the 70% methane flame at/near the smoke 
point, as that had not been expected with the diluted fuel.  The fan 
calibration showed a slight reduction in air flow. 
Unexpected Events 
None 
Science Look Ahead 
Our next and presumably final SPLICE session will be smoke point tests 
with 100% ethylene (the last of 12 bottles), where lifting tests aren’t 
planned unless SPICE is satisfied with their results and lets SLICE use the 
final remnant of fuel.  As a result, David Urban will be enabled, but Dennis 
Stocker will probably not be enabled. 
Topics for Resolution 
None 
 
March 23, 2011 (GMT 083) 
Status Report Originator  
Dennis Stocker (SLICE PS/Co-I) and David Urban (SPICE PI) 
Science Status 
Today’s testing was with the final fuel bottle, namely 100% ethylene, which 
was left to last because of its propensity for soot.  Both SPICE and SLICE 
tests were conducted with the fuel.  We were very fortunate to get a 
complete suite of smoke points for ethylene for all of the burner tubes.  
Don was able to smoothly operate the system through the last fuel bottle 
and we are excited to have finished the SPICE test matrix.  Lift off 
measurements were made for SLICE with the 0.4-mm burner, where we 
acquired liftoff limits (i.e., the velocities at which the flames lift) data for a 
total of 10 different fuel/burner combinations over the course of the SLICE 
experiment.   Additional SLICE tests were conducted with attached flames 
(on the largest burners) so that we would have flame data with high soot 
concentrations as a test for our modeling capability.  There were 5 SPICE 
and 6 SLICE flames ignited, including approximately 53 and 46 flow 
conditions (i.e., bracketed sets of photos), respectively.  Today’s testing 
yielding about 700 additional high-resolution photos, bringing the total 
SPLICE count to roughly 4,000.  Today’s fan calibration showed a 
dramatic reduction in the air flow, where that was presumably caused by 
the final SLICE tests.  The last two tests included conditions above the 
smoke point such that the flames emitted substantial soot. 
Unexpected Events 
None 
Science Look Ahead 
With today’s testing, SPLICE is now out of fuel and therefore complete, so 
Monday will be reconfiguration of the hardware for the Burning and 
Suppression of Solids (BASS) experiment, where that will presumably 
include the soot removal procedure. 
Topics for Resolution 
None

items.title: SLICE-RPT-002_Post Flight Report-.pdf
items.text:
Post Flight Report  
SLICE-RPT-002 Rev – 
February 2013 
Page 21 of 56 
 
 
4.7 
Weekly Overview – Week Ending 23 March 2012 
Status/Crew Member: 
Pettit 
Total Runs Planned: 
12 fuel bottles 
Runs Complete: 
11 fuel bottles as of GMT 082 
 
 
Don, it’s been a pleasure working with you on SPLICE.  We are thankful for your interest and dedication 
in making the research a success.  With the SLICE and SPICE testing on Monday, using respectively 
the remaining 70% methane and 100% propane, we got a wide range of data with bracketed sets of still 
photos at approx. 28 flow conditions (including the pyrometry calibration).  It was interesting to see the 
soot in the 70% methane flames, as that dilution wasn’t expected to approach or reach smoking 
conditions.  Yet with the near absence of buoyant convection in microgravity, the reduced velocities lead 
to longer residence times and enhanced soot production.  SPLICE testing will presumably come to a 
close on Friday (GMT 083) with smoke point tests using 100% ethylene.  However, as a reminder, 
SLICE is a precursor for an experiment in development for the CIR, so the results will be valuable for 
refining that study.  And perhaps we’ll be able to get approval for further SPLICE tests, but meanwhile 
we have a wealth of results to analyze.  Even neglecting the GMT 083 tests, we obtained over 3,000 
high-resolution still flame photos (of ~600 flow conditions), not including the scale, dark current, or 
pyrometry calibration photos.  FYI, the tilt of the lifted flames isn’t too much of an issue for modeling 
comparison when the flames are close to the burner, e.g., less than 1 cm per Co-Investigator Mitch 
Smooke.  And the broad range of conditions in the microgravity flames is helpful in revealing 
shortcomings in existing combustion codes for chemical kinetics, e.g., GRI-Mech.  We also look forward 
to hearing about the progress on our colleagues’ Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) experiment.  
Thanks and best wishes!

1. Overview 
The Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) experiment was conducted on 
the International Space Station (ISS), in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), by 
astronaut Don Pettit during Expedition 30 in early 2012; see Figure 1.  SLICE 
investigated the structure and stability of laminar, gas-fueled, non-premixed flames in a 
coflow, where the gas-jet diffusion flame was positioned within a fan-driven flow duct. 
 
 
Figure 1.  Astronaut Don Pettit conducting SPLICE in the Microgravity Science 
Glovebox (MSG) on the International Space Station (ISS) on March 9, 2012 (i.e., GMT 
055), where that day’s testing including both SLICE and SPICE tests.  The MSG is 
covered so that the only experiment illumination is from the flame, (1) which Pettit is 
watching through a gap in the stray light cover, and (2) which can also be seen on the 
upper monitor on Pettit’s left.

items.title: SLICE final report 20171226.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2017) 
 
2017-DEC-26 
 
5 
 
 
 
In the future, the photograph in Figure 1 and other SLICE photos will be shared at 
www.flickr.com/photos/space-flames. 
 
The 12 bottles of gaseous fuel were completely consumed during 13 sessions (days) of 
testing.  There were approx. 120 ignitions, with roughly 4,000 high-resolution 
photographs taken at roughly 700 flame conditions (where the photography was 
bracketed, i.e., with multiple photographs taken at a time under a range of settings). 
 
A fraction of the tests under SLICE were conducted for the Smoke Point In Coflow 
Experiment (SPICE) experiment, which had been previously conducted in 2009.  
Although they had unique objectives, SLICE and SPICE used the same experimental 
hardware (i.e., the SPICE hardware) and nearly identical procedures but they had 
different researchers and science objectives.  Together they came to be informally 
referred to (e.g., by Pettit) as SPLICE which could serve as an acronym for Smoke Point 
& Liftoff In Coflow Experiment.  Roughly a quarter of the 2012 SPLICE testing was for 
SPICE. 
 
SLICE is a precursor to the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, 
which is part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project 
which is in development for operation in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  
SLICE results are being used to maximize the scientific return of that upcoming space 
station experiment. 
 
 
 
2. Introduction 
 
a. Objectives 
The goal of the SLICE experiment was to improve our understanding of the physical 
and chemical processes controlling diffusion (i.e., non-premixed) flame structure and 
lifting phenomena (i.e., stabilization) and to provide for rigorous testing of numerical 
models including thermal radiation, soot formation, and detailed chemical kinetics. 
Good agreement between experimental and computational results had been 
demonstrated for lifted flames at moderate flame conditions, but that agreement 
broke down when the fuel was highly diluted or the soot production was high. SLICE 
was a precursor for the CLD Flame experiment, which is one of five experiments in 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project that are 
currently in development for conduct in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). A 
common goal of the two experiments is to improve computational techniques such 
that a broader range of flame conditions can be effectively modeled than is currently 
possible. 
 
The specific experimental objectives for SLICE were: 
For diffusion flames of methane, ethylene, and selected nitrogen dilutions of each 
fuel burning in a coflow of air: 
(1) Characterize the structure of the flame, especially its base (i.e., stabilizing 
region), from attached through lifted conditions as a function of the fuel, 
burner diameter, and flow conditions.

items.title: SLICE final report 20171226.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2017) 
 
2017-DEC-26 
 
6 
 
(2) Identify the liftoff velocity limits as a function of the fuel and burner diameter. 
A third objective, listed below, was abandoned a year in advance of spaceflight 
operations because it was determined from bench-top testing (for procedure 
development) that the planned fuel quantity was insufficient for this goal. 
(3) Characterize the hysteresis of flame lifting and reattachment (i.e., 
stabilization) with flow variations as a function of the fuel and burner 
diameter. 
 
b. Team Members 
Given that SLICE was a precursor to ACME’s CLD Flame experiment, the SLICE 
Principal Investigator (PI) and Co-Investigator (Co-I) were Yale University professors 
Marshall Long and Mitch Smooke, respectively.  Their students and research 
associates and the ACME Project Scientists (PSs), namely Dennis Stocker and 
Fumiaki Takahashi, made up the rest of the research team.  Bob Hawersaat was the 
Project Manager (PM) and Jay Owens was responsible for the flame imaging.  ZIN 
Technologies, Inc. had responsibility for the experiment development, crew training, 
and operations (ops) where the task lead was Tibor Lorik and the training and ops lead 
was Chuck Bunnell.  Carol Reynolds was the Payload Operations Lead for SLICE.  The 
initial analysis of the experimental data and the complementary normal-gravity (1g) 
testing was carried out by Bin Ma for his Ph.D. research.  On orbit, SLICE was carried 
out by astronaut Don Pettit, under the verbal direction of Stocker.  Contact information 
for these key personnel is provided in Table 1, where all but Smooke directly supported 
the on-orbit operations given that his role was in leading the computational modeling. 
 
For reference, the SPICE PI and Co-I were Dr. David L. Urban (NASA Glenn) and 
Prof. Peter B. Sunderland (U. Maryland), respectively, where Urban verbally directed 
crewmembers during the SPICE tests (i.e., Pettit in 2012).

SLICE Final Report (2017) 
 
2017-DEC-26 
 
7 
 
c. Background  
SLICE was the fifth spaceflight experiment to investigate laminar gas-jet diffusion 
(i.e., non-premixed) flames.  And like the preceding experiments, the SLICE 
atmosphere consisted of ~21% oxygen (by volume) with a balance of nitrogen.   
Furthermore, the pressure was ~100 kPa in the 5 experiments, with the partial 
exception of the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP) experiment which also included 
testing at lower values.  Three of the predecessor experiments were conducted over 
a decade ago on the space shuttle, i.e., the Space Transportation System (STS), 
while the fourth was conducted on ISS, as listed in Table 2.  SLICE is especially 
related to two of those experiments, Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) and SPICE. 
 
Table 2: Pre-SLICE space experiments investigating laminar gas-jet diffusion 
flames, listed chronologically. 
Experiment 
PI and Co-I(s) at the time of spaceflight operations 
Mission (year) 
Laminar Soot

(LSP) 
PI Gerard M. Faeth (University of Michigan) 
STS-83 (1997), 
STS-94 (1997), 
STS-107 (2003) 
Turbulent

(TGDF) 
PI M. Yousef Bahadori (Science Applications 
International Corporation) 
Co-I Uday G. Hegde (National Center for Microgravity 
Research) 
STS-87 (1997) 
Enclosed 
Laminar 
Flames (ELF) 
PI Lea-Der Chen (University of Iowa) 
Co-I Dennis P. Stocker (NASA Lewis Research Center) 
Co-I John E. Brooker (NASA Lewis Research Center) 
STS-87 (1997) 
Smoke Point 
In Coflow 
Experiment 
(SPICE) 
PI David L. Urban (NASA Glenn Research Center) 
Co-I Peter B. Sunderland (University of Maryland) 
ISS (2009) 
also conducted in 
2012 with SLICE 
 
 
The four past experiments were focused on gravity’s effects on the flame structure, 
soot and stability limits, and vortex interactions.  The LSP and Turbulent Gas-jet 
Diffusion Flame (TGDF) experiments were both conducted in sealed combustion 
chambers, where the flame was in a quiescent atmosphere.  However, vortices were 
created in the TGDF experiment by varying the air entrainment through the 
mechanical variation of an iris diameter, where the iris was (1) orthogonal and 
coaxial to the burner and flame, and (2) positioned near the burner tube outlet.  
TGDF was an automated Getaway Special canister (GAS can) experiment that flew 
in the payload bay of the shuttle.  In contrast, LSP was carried out in Spacelab and 
Spacehab in 1997 and 2003, respectively.  LSP was operated by the crew and 
conducted within the Combustion Module facility, which is the space shuttle 
precursor to the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). 
 
In contrast to LSP and TGDF, ELF was conducted within a coflowing atmosphere, 
where the flame was enclosed within a small fan-driven flow duct with a 76.2-mm 
square cross-section.  ELF was crew-operated and conducted in a glovebox facility.  
These factors were also true for its successors SPICE and SLICE. 
 
NASA began conducting spaceflight combustion experiments in glovebox facilities in 
1992 with the United States Microgravity Laboratory 1 (USML-1) mission, i.e., STS-

items.title: SLICE final report 20171226.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2017) 
 
2017-DEC-26 
 
8 
 
50, in which the Middeck Glovebox (MGBX) facility was located in the Spacelab 
module rather than the shuttle middeck.  Microgravity flames tend to quench in the 
absence of buoyant convection, which normally transports air to flames, so the 
glovebox combustion experiments have typically incorporated fans to provide forced 
convection since that start.  An STS-50 example is the Wire Insulation Flammability 
(WIF) investigation, in which the wire and flame were centered within a fan-driven 
flow duct (i.e., with forced air flow parallel to the wire). 
 
In 1997, the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) investigation became the first glovebox 
experiment to be conducted in space with gaseous fuel.  Like all combustion 
glovebox experiments carried out on the shuttle, ELF was conducted in the MGBX 
facility, which was located in the middeck on its mission, the United States 
Microgravity Payload 4 (USMP-4) mission, i.e., STS-87.  The experimental hardware 
was designed to just fit within that facility, where this may be apparent in Figure 2.  
The 33x18x18 cm experiment module and other key hardware is shown in Figure 3. 
 
The ELF objectives to investigate the stability and structure of coflow laminar 
diffusion flames were very similar to the SLICE objectives.  ELF is very much a 
precursor to SLICE in terms of both hardware and science, even though experiments 
were separated by 15 years and their research teams were different.  However, 
Dennis Stocker was an exception in that he served as a Co-I and the PS for both 
experiments. 
 
 
Figure 2.  Steve Lindsey (left) assists Takao Doi (right) in conducting the Enclosed 
Laminar Flames (ELF) investigation on Nov. 29, 1997 during the USMP-4/STS-87 
space shuttle mission [STS087-E-5088]. 
 
SPICE was initiated as an extension of the LSP experiment to investigate the effect

items.title: SLICE final report 20171226.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2017) 
 
2017-DEC-26 
 
9 
 
of the air coflow on soot processes, i.e., in addition to LSP’s study with flames in a 
quiescent atmosphere.  The SPICE hardware was directly based on ELF’s hardware, 
where SPICE was originally planned as a shuttle experiment.  The ELF ground 
hardware that had been used for hardware development, crew training, and normal-
gravity (1g) comparison testing was modified so that it could serve the same purpose 
for SPICE.  Although SPICE was planned as a shuttle experiment, the project had a 
convoluted history, e.g., where it was stopped and restarted, such that it was 
ultimately conducted on ISS rather than the shuttle, even though the experiment 
module was designed for the MGBX rather than ISS’s Microgravity Science 
Glovebox (MSG). 
 
 
Figure 3. Bench-top photo of Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) spaceflight hardware 
and logo [NASA C-97-4013]. 
 
The SPICE hardware included significant improvements as compared to ELF.  While 
ELF had a fixed burner tube, SPICE had exchangeable tubes allowing variation of 
the burner diameter.  In ELF, the numerical data was physically displayed on the 
front of the module and was photographed along with the flame using a video 
camera.  Meanwhile in SPICE, the data was still recorded with the flame video, but it 
was overlaid electronically eliminating the need for the illuminated displays, as can 
be seen in Figure 4 (i.e., where there are no physical displays).  ELF used a second 
analog video camera to photograph the flame through the top window, while SPICE 
used a high-resolution digital SLR camera for the top-window photography.  SPICE 
had a retracting scale for photography that could be positioned at the flame axis, 
whereas ELF’s reference scale was on the top of the module, i.e., at a significant 
distance from the flame axis.  However, SPICE eliminated ELF’s retracting array of 
thermocouples and thin-filament fibers (for pyrometry) to include its retracting scale.  
SPICE also used larger fuel bottles because the MSG working volume was

items.title: SLICE final report 20171226.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2017) 
 
2017-DEC-26 
 
10 
 
significantly larger than that of the MGBX so greater amounts of fuel could be safely 
used.  Other differences are minor in comparison. 
 
 
Figure 4.  Bench-top photo of SPICE’s spaceflight experiment module, which is 
further discussed in the next section. 
 
When SPICE was conducted on orbit in 2009, e.g., as depicted in Figure 5, the 
SLICE researchers conducted limited trial testing in which it was verified that the 
SPICE hardware would enable accomplishment of the SLICE objectives.  Sample 
flame images of lifted flames are shown in Figure 6.  The testing was quickly 
followed by the preparation and submission of a SLICE proposal in June 2009 for a 
Rapid Turn Around Flight (RTA) Flight Opportunity.   Just weeks later, following an 
external review of the proposal, SLICE was selected by NASA Headquarters in July 
2009 for funding and development toward spaceflight.

items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2017) 
 
2017-DEC-26 
 
11 
 
 
Figure 5.  Astronaut Mike Barratt conducting the SPICE experiment in the MSG on 
May 16, 2009 [ISS019-E-017339]. 
 
 
Figure 6.  Photos of a lifted flame under different flow conditions from trial SLICE 
testing conducted during the 2009 SPICE operations (where the scale is not 
consistent).  The lifted nature of the flames can be discerned from the flame shape 
and the distance from the nozzle tip (which is not visible). While the flames on the left 
may look like attached flames, the outward fuel-lean flare of each flame’s base 
reveals its lifted nature. 
 
d. Hardware 
The SLICE experiment was conducted using the SPICE hardware, which remained 
on the ISS following its 2009 operations.  The hardware layout within the MSG is 
shown in Figure 7, where the major components are listed in Table 3 and identified in 
Figure 8.

Figure 7.  Hardware set up for SLICE (and SPICE) in a fisheye photograph taken by 
astronaut Don Pettit through the MSG’s left gloveport on Feb. 20, 2012.

items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2017) 
 
2017-DEC-26 
 
13 
 
 
 
Figure 8.  SLICE and SPICE hardware layout from a graphic used in crew training. 
 
The principal element of the hardware is the SPICE experiment module, which 
mounted to the floor of the MSG’s working volume, where a bench-top photograph is 
seen in Figure 4.  The bottom (i.e., ‘basement’) of the module includes a delivery 
system for the gaseous fuel, including a quick connect (for attaching a fuel bottle), 
particulate filter, pressure regulator, and mass flow controller (for 500 sccm on a N2 
basis), where these components can be seen with a bottle connected in Figure 9. 
 
The upper portion of the experiment module consists of the fan-driven flow duct in 
which the burner tube is located, and where there are top and front windows for 
flame photography.  The front window is hinged and opens to allow manual 
exchange of the burner tube and hot-wire igniter, where there are interlocks to 
prevent fuel flow and igniter actuation when it is open.  As seen from the front, the

items.title: SLICE final report 20171226.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2017) 
 
2017-DEC-26 
 
14 
 
ambient air from the MSG working volume flows from left to right, where it passes 
through the fan and is pushed through a flow straightener, into the duct, past an air 
velocity probe, through the duct screen, past the burner tube, through a heat sink, 
and out through the filtered soot trap.  This can be seen in part in Figure 10, e.g., 
where parts C1, H008, H010 are the fan, flow straightener, and heat sink, 
respectively.  Note that the velocity probe had a slow response time so the fan 
voltage was instead relied upon during the testing.  The flow duct has a 76.2-mm 
square cross-section with rounded corners, as seen in Figure 11. 
 
 
Figure 9. Illustration of the SPICE fuel delivery system showing the fuel bottle and 
the components in the bottom of the experiment module. 
 
Levers on the right end of the experiment module (when viewed from the front) are 
used to manually rotate the igniter to the burner tube and the photography scale (and 
focal target) to the duct center.  This end of the module also has a switch which can 
be used to disable (or enable) the fuel flow when the astronaut has their right hand in 
the MSG.  If the crewmember has removed their hand, the fuel flow can also be 
disabled (or enabled) using the control box.

is to the left.  The schematic is an excerpt from drawing 60054mdfh001.

Figure 12. SPICE experiment module, as seen from the fan end (i.e., left end when 
seen from the front), where the air velocity probe and burner tube are visible 
because the fan housing was ‘removed’ to reveals the duct interior.  The schematic

SPICE’s power/video box assembly is mounted to the back wall of the MSG’s 
working volume.  It consists of a power box and video box with a common mounting 
plate.  The unit provides for power conversion and distribution, conversion of the 
video from a composite to S-video format, and the titler overlay of the numerical data 
onto the video.  The overlay includes the date and time, fuel flow, fan voltage, air 
speed, and radiometer output. 
 
The SPICE control box was located outside of the MSG through the use of a feed-
through connector.  It allowed the crew to enable or disable the fuel flow and igniter, 
and adjust the fuel flow rate, fan (i.e., coflow) speed, and radiometer gain.  The 
assembly, seen in Figure 14, also included a shutter release button for use with the 
digital SLR camera. 
 
 
Figure 14. SPICE control box assembly, including the shutter release button for the 
digital SLR camera. 
The 12 SPICE fuel bottles were refilled to support SLICE and the 2012 SPICE 
operations, where example photographs can be seen in Figure 15.  The bottles 
simply include a hand valve and quick connect for mating the bottle to the 
experiment module.  The bottles were filled with the fuels listed in Table 4, where the 
propane bottle was filled to lower pressure to avoid condensation of the fuel. 
 
Several hardware changes were made for SLICE, just as SPICE improved upon the 
earlier ELF investigation.  However, they were generally relatively minor in scope 
given that the SPICE hardware was mostly already on orbit and because SLICE was 
planned as an inexpensive experiment that would be quickly ready for spaceflight.  A 
simple example was the addition of two more burner tube sizes, with inner diameters 
of 2.1 and 3.2 mm.  The measured diameters of all of the burner tubes are listed in 
Table 5, to a resolution of 0.0064 mm, where it is a critical measurement because of 
its strong (inverse square) influence on velocity of the fuel jet (for a fixed fuel flow).  
Note that the burner tubes have constant inner diameters even though they have

The SLICE hardware included a Nikon D300s digital SLR camera as a replacement 
for the Nikon D100 that SPICE used during its 2009 operations.  While the previous 
camera was still on orbit, SLICE added a new camera which was characterized with 
a blackbody source to enable determination of the soot temperature via color-ratio 
pyrometry and the soot volume fraction from the temperature and absolute light 
calibration.  To balance the color planes in the flame photography and to avoid 
saturation, the camera had an optional blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which was

SLICE Final Report (2017) 
 
2017-DEC-26 
 
19 
 
generally but not always used during the SLICE operations.  To minimize 
uncertainties, SLICE used a new top window (i.e., to the experiment module) which 
was included with the BG7 filter in the blackbody characterization of the Nikon D300s 
camera. 
 
To enable the absolute light calibration necessary for determination of the soot 
volume fraction, SLICE flew an array of fine ceramic fibers that was mounted 
downstream of the burner within the experiment module’s flow duct.  It was mounted 
using an alternate top window with a fixture that was developed for holding solid fuel 
samples in the Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) experiment, which also 
used the BASS hardware.  The fiber array and window mounting are illustrated in 
Figure 16.  Two fiber arrays were flown, where the second was a spare because of 
the fragility of the fibers. 
 
 
Figure 16. (a) Fiber array, and (b) top-window fixture that was developed for holding 
solid fuel samples for BASS but instead held the fiber array for SLICE. 
 
e. Procedure 
The SLICE experiment was conducted manually by astronaut Don Pettit in early 
2012.  Using the simple hardware, Pettit ignited the flames, adjusted the fuel and air 
flow, and took still photographs of the flame per verbal directions from Dennis 
Stocker via space-to-ground communication.  The direct communication (without 
Payload Communication intermediaries) during those flame operations was 
established based on the SLICE crew training and the 2009 experience with Smoke 
Point In Coflow Experiment (SPICE).  Although their objectives and research teams 
differed, SLICE and SPICE were sister experiments, where SLICE was conducted 
with the SPICE hardware, although with some additional and upgraded components.  
Both experiments were conducted within the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) 
on the International Space Station (ISS). 
 
Before each round of testing, Pettit installed the specified burner tube and a supply 
bottle with the selected fuel. He then adjusted the fuel flow and air velocity as 
directed and ignited the flame. Several flame conditions were studied in each test; 
Petitt adjusted either the fuel flow or airflow to achieve different flame conditions.  
When directed, he photographed the flame with the high-resolution digital still 
camera.  The fuel flow was shut off upon completion of a test, e.g., which was 
typically when the flame quenched because of the flow conditions.  Throughout the 
operations, the ground team monitored the video downlink, which includes overlaid 
sensor data, to guide the crewmember in the testing.  The operations were directed 
from the Telescience Support Center (TSC) at NASA Glenn, to which Prof. Long and 
his graduate student Bin Ma were connected via teleconferencing.  Arrangements

items.title: SLICE final report 20171226.pdf
items.text:
SLICE Final Report (2017) 
 
2017-DEC-26 
 
20 
 
were made so that they had access to the video downlink at Yale.  Following the 
testing, the still images were downlinked to ground for analysis. 
 
While it hadn’t been expected or planned, a second camera view was provided in the 
downlink with an over-the-shoulder view of Pettit conducting the experiment.  At the 
time, there were only four video channels downlinked from ISS, where SLICE used 
two during the science (i.e., flame) portion of its operations.  This and the procedures 
in general can be seen in composite video at: 
http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/news/burming_questions.html 
To show the operations, the experiment (i.e., flame) video was combined with the 
over-the-shoulder video and the space-to-ground communication (i.e., audio) 
between Pettit and SLICE PS/Co-I Dennis Stocker.   
 
A detailed outline of the nine (9) SLICE procedures is provided in Appendix D, where 
the critical operations with the flames are entirely contained within procedure 2.005.  
The flow calibration in procedure 2.003 was also important to the experimental 
results, where the calibration was regularly conducted, e.g., during each session of 
testing, in order to correlate the fan voltage with the velocity in the duct.  The velocity 
was measured by an anemometer permanently mounted in the flow duct (upstream 
of the flame location) which had a time response that was too slow to be particularly 
useful during the flame testing.  The calibration was carried out repeatedly because 
air flow through the duct was seen to diminish over time because of soot 
accumulation in the exhaust plenum.  The other seven procedures are generally not 
important for interpreting the SLICE results because they deal with (1) the hardware 
set up, maintenance, and stowage plus (2) the handling of the camera media. 
 
It should be understood that the SLICE procedures apply to both the SLICE and 
SPICE experiments because additional SPICE tests were conducted in 2012, 
effectively as part of SLICE.  In 2012, the SPICE tests accounted for approximately 
one quarter of the combined total.  The only SPICE-specific procedure is part 4 of 
procedure 2.005, i.e., the Smoke Point Flame Test.  Part 2 of the same procedure, 
the Standard Flame Test, is for SLICE.  However, this flame portion of the testing 
was always conducted per verbal direction from the ground, so the SLICE and 
SPICE procedures were effectively identical.  As previously described, Dr. David L. 
Urban, the SPICE PI, directed Pettit during the SPICE tests instead of Stocker. 
  
The final procedure, 4.001, was developed after the on-orbit set up of the hardware 
on Jan. 20, 2012 when it was discovered that the video data overlay was incorrectly 
scrolling hexadecimal characters.  The video overlay was critical to the experiments 
because it was used to both display and record the numerical data, e.g., the fuel and 
air flow conditions.  The scrolling display mode occurred because an integrated 
battery had completely discharged since the hardware was last used in 2009.  
Although the battery was recharged, a sequence of temporary electrical connections 
had to be made - in the absence of switches - to return the overlay to the proper 
display mode.  The overlay was reset when the procedure was successfully carried 
out by Pettit on Feb. 6 GMT 037), after which testing began on Feb. 9 (GMT 040).  
The SPLICE testing continued twice per week until March 23 when the last of the 
fuel was consumed.  For reference, the SPICE hardware was next used for the 
Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) experiment, where it began just days 
after SLICE’s completion.

2017-DEC-26
