image is taken, the ruler is moved back to its home position. The ruler is mechanically linked to and 
controlled by a handle outside of the flow duct, at its front right corner. 
 
A hot wire igniter, a coiled Kanthal wire, was used to ignite the flame. During ignition, it is moved 
to the nozzle tip through a handle next to the ruler handle and electrically powered up with about 4 
amps of electric current that makes the wire bright red hot. Once the flame ignition is confirmed, the 
igniter is then moved away from the nozzle tip to its home position. The two handles are designed in 
such that only one of the two, the igniter and the ruler, can be moved to the nozzle at a certain time. 
This provides a safety feature of the system that prevents the ruler from being burned by the igniter. 
There is a small magnet mounted on the linkage to the igniter and a Hall-effect sensor mounted on 
the hinge of the front door. This sensor controls the igniter power circuits that when the front door is 
in open position or when the igniter is at its home position, the igniter power circuit is disabled. In 
other words, the igniter can be powered only if the front door is closed and the igniter is at the nozzle 
tip. The igniter is replaceable. When replacing the igniter, the astronaut must open the front door so 
that the igniter will not be powered during the replacement. 
 
There are 3 fuel nozzles made for the SPICE experiment. They all have the same length; 50 mm, 
with different inner diameters: 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm and 1.6 mm, respectively. Only one of the three 
nozzles is installed during a burn. Figure 4 is a photo of the igniters and nozzles in a storage box 
shipped to ISS. It can be seen that a nozzle has two parts: a thicker base with female threads in it and 
a piece of thin tubing extended from the base.  Thus the nozzle is threaded on a connector inside the 
flow duct, on the left hand side in Fig. 3. After installation, the nozzle is along the center line of flow 
duct. Its tip is about 54 mm from the screen at the left end of the flow duct. 
 
 
 
A thermopile radiometer, Oriel Model 71768, is placed in the far right corner downstream of the 
duct. It has a 90 degree view angle that can bracket the entire flame length. Since the radiometer 
signal is an integrated result of flame radiation, which is a complicated function of flame shape and 
temperature distribution in the flame, it can only provide a qualitative measurement of flame 
radiation. The flame radiation varies in a wide range depending on flame conditions so that the 
radiometer amplifier is equipped with a gain control switch to ensure the signal is detected with 
proper accuracy.

As shown in Fig 3, there are two rectangular boxes attached to the each end of the flow duct. The 
box on the left hand side has a 3” diameter electrical fan, Panasonic Model FBA08A12H1A, that 
blows air into the flow duct. A ceramic honeycomb flow strainer is installed downstream of the fan 
in the fan housing to break swirls.  An omni-directional anemometer, TSI model 8475-3-xx, is 
located inside the flow duct near the nozzle connecter to measure the air velocity. Several screens 
are located at the inlet of the fan, downstream of the anemometer and at the exhaust end of the 
chamber, respectively.  Note that the fan is installed upstream of the flame so that it will not be 
heated by the flame gases. The box at the right end of the flow duct contains a heat sink/hand guard 
and a fine screen that prevents excessive soot particles from entering the ISS MSG flow system.  
 
Attached to the flow duct is a fuel supply system illustrated in Fig. 5. As marked in the figure, 
items1 to 7 are the pre-assembled fuel bottle assembly each of which includes a DOT 150 ml 
stainless steel single end cylinder (SWAGELOK, 304L-055MS6-150), a ¼” diaphragm valve 
(SWAGELOK NUPRO # SS-DLS4), a quick connect, a Lanyard® clip, and connecting tubes. There 
was a long storage time from the delivery of fuel bottles from GRC to the actual execution of the 
experiments on ISS. Thus, a very low leak rate of fuel bottle assemblies is a critical requirement. 
There are total 12 fuel bottle assemblies which are stored in two separate containers.  The photo on 
the left of Figure 6 shows one of the fuel bottle containers that holds six fuel bottle assemblies and 
the photo on the right shows a single assembly. The six bottles in one container are filled with six 
different fuel gases to the maximum safety pressure for that fuel: ethylene (210 psia), methane (210 
psia), propane (110 psia), propylene (135 psia), 75% propylene (180 psia), 50% propylene (180 psia). 
The connection between the fuel bottle assembly and the rest of the flow system is through a couple 
of a ¼” Swagelok® quick-connect, items 7 and 8 in Fig. 5. Item 8 through 16 are the plumbing 
system included in the Experiment Assembly, underneath the flow duct in Fig. 3. Components in the 
plumbing include the male half of the quick-connect (item 8), a filter (item 10), a compact stainless 
steel pressure regulator (item 13, Process Valve, CPR1-1B01A3E178, 0-50 psig, P/N: 106153), a 
mass flow controller (item 15, MKS, Type 2179 MFC with a Positive Shutoff Valve, Model #: 
1179A52CS1BV-S, 0 - 500 SCCM, Standard Conditions: 0oC and 760 Torr), and stainless steel 
tubings. The mass flow controller sets the flow rate of the fuel gas based on the signal from the 
control box that astronaut holds during experiment.

Figure 12 is a photo of the two avionic box used in SPICE. The one labeled as “Power Box” 
converts ISS electric power supply (28 VDC) to various power sources needed by different parts of 
the SPICE apparatus. The “Video Titler Box” includes a titler that can display fuel flow rate, fan 
speed, air velocity, and radiometer gain on the same video screen as the flame, and circuits to 
process video output signal and still camera images to digital data for downlink and data storage. 
The module is also equipped with data logger and PCMCIA storage. 
 
B. Air velocity distribution in the flow duct 
An important feature of SPICE is that it has air co-flow surrounding the flames. SPICE is the first 
experiment that studies soot processes of laminar jet diffusion flame under long term microgravity 
condition with air coflow. Because the velocity distribution in or near the flame is complicated by 
the varying gas property and thermal expansion, the coflow air velocity can only be specified in far 
field and the inlet of the flow duct as boundary conditions of the flame under investigation. For this 
reason, the information of air velocity distribution before igniting of the flame is needed.  The air 
velocity was measured with an anemometer at different locations in the flow duct at different fan 
speed. The top window and the front window were replaced by two windows with holes on them to 
accommodate anemometer prob.  Figure 13 shows various hole locations through which air 
velocities were measured. Some expressions used in describing a spatial location are explained as 
follows. A “Station” refers to a plane perpendicular to the flow direction. The value of a “Station” 
indicates the distance between the nozzle tip and the plane. There are only two Stations in use: 13 
mm and 56 mm, defining two planes 13 mm and 56 mm downstream of the nozzle tip. “Height Off 
Floor” refers to the distance above the floor of the flow duct. The Floor of the flow duct is the lower 
wall of the flow duct, perpendicular to the front window. The three positions in Height Off Floor in 
use are 19 mm, 36 mm, and 57 mm define three planes in parallel with the flow duct floor. The 36 
mm one is in the middle of the flow duct so that it includes the nozzle. The third direction is 
expressed in terms of “Centerline”, “20 mm to the Inside” and “20 mm to the Outside,” which define 
three planes in parallel with the front window of the flow duct. There are totally 18 intersections of 
these three sets of planes. Air velocities were measured at these 18 locations at 6 different fan dial 
settings. Note that for the safety concern, even at 0 fan dial setting, there is a minimum DC voltage 
applied to the fan to maintain a low velocity air flow which prevents fuel gas from accumulating in 
the flow duct.

The measurement was carried out by inserting the probe into the two holes, 13 mm Station and 56 
mm Station, on the centerline of the top window. And three Height Off Floor locations were used in

The velocity difference increases with fan settings (average air velocity), whereas at the 56 mm 
Station, this center-dipping velocity profile evolves to a near linear profile with higher velocity at the 
bottom. This center-dipping is caused by the boundary layer around the nozzle.  Figure 15 shows the 
air velocity distribution in a horizontal plane at the center of the flow duct. The phenomenon of 
lower velocity along the center line can be seen in this plane too. Different from the velocity profile 
on the vertical plane, the center-dipping also shows at 56 mm Station.  
 
The flow field was further modeled with COMSOL, a commercial software. The air flow near the 
nozzle exit was shown in Fig. 16 for three different combinations of the nozzle velocity and co-flow 
velocity. The white lines in the plots are streamlines. The colors show the velocity map. Blue is for 
low velocity whereas red indicates high velocity. Although in each plot, velocity varies from blue to 
red, the absolute value of certain color is different between these velocity maps.  The nozzle ID in all 
the three cases is 1.6 mm and the average air velocity in the nozzle remains to be 50 cm/s whereas 
the coflow velocities are 0, 25 and 100 cm/s, respectively as stated below each plot. It can be seen 
that for the case of zero co-flow, the lateral air velocity profile becomes monotonically decay with 
its maximum value being at the center line. When the coflow velocity increases to 25 cm/s, a 
boundary layer around the nozzle becomes significant. Near the nozzle, in the radial direction the air 
velocity decreases with radius and then increases. As radius further increases to get near to the flow 
duct wall, the air velocity drops again. This type of velocity profile extends to quite large distance 
downstream of the nozzle. When coflow velocity increases to 100 cm/s, the coflow is significantly

small. In relative short distance downstream the nozzle, the velocity profile in radial direction

Thus the actual velocity distribution in the flow duct is quite complicated. It not only depends on the 
jet velocity and the coflow velocity, but also is affected by the heat released from the flame. The 
above discussion gives us a qualitative insight of the velocity field. Limited by the space in the MSG, 
SPICE experiment does not have velocity diagnostic capability to reveal the actual velocity in the 
presence of flame. 
 
SPICE FLIGHT TESTS 
The actual SPICE tests were conducted in SMG in twelve sessions from February 14, 2009 to June 
23, 2009. In each session, the SPICE science team and engineering team were in the TeleScience 
Center (TSC) in GRC to support the tests conducted on MSG. Real-time flame images were 
available as long as air-to-ground communication channel was available. In addition, the team was 
able to communicate with the astronaut who conducted the experiment to answer questions or to 
clarify any ambiguities. 
 
Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting the fuel 
flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and 
simultaneously by the ground support team in TSC. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two 
such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. The oxygen mole fraction of this 
cabin air is maintained within 19 – 24%. 
 
After the tests the video record was analyzed to identify smoke points. The smoke point lengths, LSP, 
(and the flow conditions) were obtained from the video record and are the measured distance from 
the burner to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis. The luminous flame tips were not 
sharply defined in most images, but rather transitioned from bright yellow to black over an axial 
distance of 2 – 5 mm. Luminous lengths were measured to the point where the centerline grayscale

intensity changed most rapidly between these yellow and black regions. This helped reduce the 
sensitivity of the measured lengths to camera exposures. 
 
Totally 526 flames were ignited and studied, which were much more than originally planned. The 
reason more flames can be studied was owing to the increasing familiarization for astronauts to the 
apparatus, so that the flame adjusting time and smoke point realization time became shorter and 
shorter. This leads to plenty unused fuel for new test points.  The entire test matrix and measured 
flame data are listed in Appendix A. 
  
The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of fuel 
or air. Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were generally more luminous than the others, 
attributed to increased soot volume fractions. Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, 
especially those with high air velocity, large burners, and long flames, and is attributed to coflow 
perturbations. This increased slightly the uncertainties in smoke points for these conditions. 
 
TEST RESULTS  
Smoke points were attempted for all fuels. The conditions for which smoke points were found are 
summarized in Table 1. In some cases (e.g., tests involving ethylene) the fuel supply was depleted 
before all desired conditions could be tested, as the supply was limited to two 150 cc bottles of each 
fuel at gage pressures of 760 – 1440 kPa. Smoke points were attempted with methane, but could not 
be obtained before the flames impinged on the copper plate at the end of the duct. 
 
 
 
Some smoke points (particularly for propane and ethylene) were identified by the onset of gradual 
dimming, reddening, and rounding of the luminous flame tip. Conversely, the brightest flames 
(particularly for propylene and propylene mixtures) normally did not display significant dimming 
and reddening near their tips, except when much longer than their smoke points. For these flames, 
smoke points were identified by the rapid transition to open-tipped flames. Open-tipped flames are 
common in microgravity when smoke points are far exceeded4 and are associated with flame 
extinguishment along the centerline and soot that escapes in an annular shell. For conditions 
sufficiently above the smoke points, quenched soot could be seen leaving the flames despite the dark 
background in the video.

15 
 
Figure 17 shows images for representative flames near their smoke points. Two sequences are 
shown, and in both, the smoke point occurs between the third and fourth images. In the top row, 
coflow velocity decreases from left to right at a constant fuel flow rate. This increases luminous 
flame length and leads to soot emission in the fourth image. The luminous length decreases in the 
fourth image owing to flame extinction and extensive reactant leakage. In the bottom row, fuel flow 
rate is increased at a constant coflow velocity, increasing luminous lengths. The luminous lengths of 
the flames in Fig. 17 are more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in coflow 
velocity. For a jet diffusion flame, the fuel flow rate is the limiting factor of the flame length because 
there is almost unlimited amount of oxidant (air in this case) available. This is why the flame length 
is more sensitive to the change of fuel flow rate. 
 
 
 
In Fig. 18 the measured smoke point lengths are plotted with respect to coflow velocity. For a given 
choice of fuel and burner diameter, an increase in coflow velocity generally increases the smoke 
point length. This behavior is attributed to decreased residence times and radiative losses as coflow 
velocity increases, and is an important issue for further consideration. The slope of the correlations 
in Fig. 18 generally decreases with increased sooting propensity. Figure 18 reveals that smoke points 
of nonbuoyant coflowing flames decrease with increasing burner diameter. This behavior also can be 
attributed to effects of residence time, as fuel velocity is proportional to d–2 when fuel mass flow rate 
is constant.

Also shown in Fig. 18 are smoke points of microgravity flames in still air.5 The limited smoke points 
at different diameters actually increase with burner diameter. When the present measurements are 
extrapolated to zero coflow velocity, the dependence on burner diameter diminishes. Normal gravity 
smoke points are also generally found to have only a weak dependence on burner diameter.5,6 
However, testing in normal gravity8 has shown that coflowing normal gravity smoke points for 
propylene  decrease with increasing burner diameter for the present range of diameters. The present 
smoke points generally were repeatable. An exception was the tests with the 0.41 mm burner (for 
which only propylene smoke points were possible). Testing on different days yielded different 
smoke points for this burner. 
 
The sooting propensity of the present fuels, identified from the smoke point lengths for fixed burner 
diameter and coflow velocity, generally increases from propane to ethylene, to 50% propylene, to 
75% propylene, and to propylene. This is consistent with normal gravity results in the same 
apparatus.7 The only exception was that, for the 0.76 mm burner, ethylene has a longer smoke point 
length than propane. The lower density of ethylene results in a decreased residence time, but this is 
unlikely to explain such a long smoke point relative to that of propane.

Eq. (2) for stoichiometric lengths and the past observations that flames at their smoke points 
typically have luminous lengths that are twice as long as their stoichiometric lengths. This choice of 
axes yields a reasonably good single correlation of the luminous lengths of all fuels. These results 
are similar to those of Lin and Faeth1 in that flames with low ua / uf are generally longer than those at 
otherwise matched conditions. This occurs in Fig. 19 for propylene, propane, and ethylene flames 
with the smallest burner, for which ua / uf < 0.08.

DISCUSSION 
 
Although it is convenient to classified all flames, laminar vs. turbulent and diffusion vs. premixed, 
into two categories based on their soot emission conditions, i.e., soot emitting flames and non-soot 
emitting flames, the conditions delineating the two or the conditions of onset of soot emission are 
difficult to define. Up to date, these conditions have been documented solely based on experimental 
observations.    Many efforts have been made to develop a universal method of defining the onset of 
soot emission, i.e., smoke point, conditions, in terms of primary parameters of the flame. But none of 
these efforts has been quite successful yet. The primary parameters of the flame mentioned here refer 
to parameters used to set the flame, not those generated by the flame. The primary parameters of jet 
diffusion flames include fuel type, fuel and oxidizer supply rates, ambient temperature and pressure, 
and configuration of the device where the flame takes place, such as nozzle diameter and dimensions 
of the combustion chamber. The flame temperature, gas velocity and species distributions as well as 
flame shapes and derived parameters such as heat generation and heat loss, are the parameters 
generated by the flame which is not considered as primary parameters.  If a method that relates 
smoke point to those primary parameters were found, we would be able to predict whether a flame 
emits soot or not based on the planned flame conditions.  In the course of pursuing such a universal 
method, a number of surmises of the mechanism of soot emission have been proposed to associate 
smoke point with certain flame generated parameters. Those surmises served as a middle step in 
hoping to help further development of the aforementioned method. The first surmise, and least 
controversial, is that smoke points occur when soot temperature drops below a critical temperature 
prior to soot burnout. This temperature is about 1300 K in normal gravity8,9 and 1000 K in 
microgravity.10,11 The second is that smoke point occurs when radiative loss fraction reaches 0.2 – 
0.4 for normal-gravity flames12-16 or 0.4 – 0.6 for microgravity flames.17 Since the radiative fraction 
of heat loss increases with fuel flow rate, smoke point will occur as the fuel flow rate is higher than

items.title: PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf
items.text:
18 
 
certain value. This is consistent with experimental observations. The third surmise is that the smoke 
point correlates to the ratio of luminous length divided by stoichiometric length. This ratio increases 
with flow rate. Once it reaches about 2, smoke point occurs.15,18,19 The last surmise suggests that 
smoke point correlates with the centerline flame residence time.  This is the most complex8-11,17,18,20-
24 surmise because flame residence time affects the soot processes in twofold. An increase in 
residence time can lead to soot emissions by increasing the time available for soot formation. 
Because this generally also increases the time available for soot oxidation, it has been proposed that 
smoke points are associated with conditions where the time available for soot formation exceeds that 
for soot oxidation to certain extent.21 This is difficult to prove because to evaluate the flame 
residence time requires the velocity distribution alone the centerline and the flame length, both of 
which are resulted flame parameters, not readily available from primary parameters of the 
experiment. In addition, the soot formation time and oxidation time are conceptually defined. 
Practically, these times are not measurable and they might be overlapped, i.e., for the same soot 
aggregate, adding and oxidizing carbon particles may happen simultaneously. Because of these 
difficulties and ambiguities, the fame residence time theory cannot be proved or disproved 
rigorously.  However, these obstacles do not prevent us from checking the residence time theory 
against the observed smoke point data with the help of some approximated velocity distribution and 
flame length information. More detailed discussion of this effort can be found in the publications 
resulted from the SPICE project listed in Appendices B through F. The results showed that although 
residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not yield quantitative 
correlations. 
 
 
CLOSING REMARKS 
Smoke points of 55 microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air were measured in earth 
orbit. The conditions emphasized small burners and the effects of coflow velocity. These flames 
allow extensive control over residence time, which is important in smoke point phenomena. The 
major conclusions are as follows: 
1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length. 
2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length. 
3. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased 
fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths. 
4. The sooting propensities of the present fuel mixtures in microgravity increase according to 
ethylene < propane < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene. This is the same as in 
normal gravity except for the exchanged positions of ethylene and propane. 
5. Consistent with past theory and experiments, luminous length at the smoke point is 
proportional to fuel mass flow rate. However there is a slight increase in luminous length as 
ua / uf decreases. 
6. Although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not 
yield quantitative correlations of smoke points. 
7. The present smoke point lengths scale with d –0.91 uair
0.41. Either a decrease in diameter or an 
increase in coflow velocity decreases residence time and radiative loss fraction, which in turn 
leads to a longer smoke point.

items.text:
Introduction 
•
Three investigations will be performed:   SPICE, SLICE, and BASS.   
•
These investigations will be performed inside the Microgravity Science 
Glovebox (MSG). 
•
SPICE is based on the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) hardware which 
flew on STS-87 in 1997. 
•
SPICE hardware is already on-orbit.  It has successfully completed all of its 
objectives with the collection of 200 data points in the first half of 2009. New 
fuel is being flown on ULF5 to support the SLICE and BASS experiments. 
•
SPICE hardware will also be used to perform SLICE and BASS. 
•
SPICE burns different fuels to investigate the point at which they begin to 
smoke.  
•
SLICE burns different fuels to investigate the structure of flames when lifted 
from the fuel nozzle.   
•
BASS burns different materials to investigate how they burn in microgravity.

The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find 
the laminar smoke-point properties of

SLICE Science Background 
•
The goal of the SLICE investigation is to investigate the structure of lifting 
and lifted flames; whereby the flame detaches from the nozzle and 
stabilizes at a downstream position.  
•
The results of the SLICE experiment will be used to minimize risk and 
maximize the scientific return of the CLD (Coflow Laminar Diffusion) 
Flame experiment, which is one of the four ACME (Advanced Combustion 
via Microgravity Experiments) investigations that are currently in 
development for conduct within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  
6 
The lifted nature of the flames can be discerned from the outward flare of the 
flame base in the example images below (which are not at the same scale) and 
the distance from the nozzle tip (which is not visible).

items.title: PSI-107_Presentations_IP-D Crew training 2011.pdf
items.text:
BASS Science Background 
•
The BASS investigation tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity burn as well 
if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being 
identical (ie. pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature).  
•
To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended 
microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft. If this 
hypothesis is true, it implies serious safety concerns over the utility and margin of 
safety provided NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 (upward flammability test used to evaluate 
materials intended for use in the habitable environments of US spacecraft).  Practical, 
realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames 
which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire 
burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).  
•
There are important differences in the suppression of fires in space compared to on 
Earth. On Earth it is understood that best results are generally obtained when the 
extinguisher “attacks” the base of the flame, which is both the stabilization point and 
the point of fresh air entrainment. For a fire burning in microgravity, the best point of 
application of suppressant may not be immediately apparent, especially for a partially 
obstructed flame or a wake-stabilized flame. Depending on the geometry of the flame 
and the characteristics of the extinguisher (distance from flame, dispersion angle) it is 
possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the 
flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen. 
7

items.text:
Earth Applications 
•
SPICE 
 
The smoke-point phenomena is a classical metric in the understanding of the heat 
release and spread rate of fires. It is commonly used in fire modeling on Earth and to 
understand the soot growth and emission by flames. The dominant characteristics of 
many flames of practical interest are nonbuoyant. SPICE seeks to extend our 
understanding by looking at the interaction of ambient flow with the smoke point, 
enabling us to better predict heat release from non-buoyant flames in practical 
combustors (e.g. jet engines and furnaces). 
•
SLICE 
 
The twin purposes for the SLICE research are increased efficiency and reduced 
pollutant emission in practical combustion devices. More explicitly, the experiment is 
being conducted to advance combustion modeling capability, which “allows system 
designers to improve efficiency and reduce harmful pollutants in ways never before 
possible” (as stated by an external reviewer of the SLICE experiment). In other 
words, the SLICE research is being conducted to advance energy technology and 
improve our global environment. 
•
BASS 
 
It is highly desirable to develop a new and/or improved Earth-based test method for 
material flammability. The data obtained in this experiment will begin to bridge the 
gap between the normal gravity method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual 
material flammability in microgravity 
9

SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
1 
1 INTRODUCTION  
 
The Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) Investigation will be operated onboard the 
International Space Station (ISS) in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG). A previous 
version of the SPICE design was called the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) experiment, which 
flew in the Middeck Glovebox on the Space Shuttle STS-87. The Enclosed Laminar Flames 
(ELF) experiment objective was to study fundamental phenomena related to the mechanisms 
controlling the stability and extinction of jet diffusion flames. The design modifications made as 
a result of a carrier change (Middeck GBX to ISS MSG) are considered significant enough that 
the SPICE Hardware is not considered Series Flight Hardware of the original ELF design. 
 
This Phase III Flight Safety Data Package (SDP) documents the hazards assessed for SPICE.  
This SDP documents compliance to NSTS/ISS 1700.7B and is prepared in accordance with 
NSTS/ISS 13830C. A brief overview of the experiment hardware and MSG interfaces is 
presented first, followed by a brief description of crew procedures.  Finally, a safety assessment 
of SPICE Hazards is presented.  Hazards that have not been eliminated by design have been 
addressed and documented in the Standard Hazard Form (JSC 1230 Form) or in a Unique 
Hazard Report (JSC 542B Form). Refer to Section 4 of this document for the SPICE Safety 
Assessment. Refer to Attachment B for the SPICE Standard Hazard Reporting Form, (JSC 
1230 Form). Refer to Attachment C for the SPICE Unique Hazard Reporting Forms, (JSC 542B) 
that support the SPICE safety assessment. 
 
1.1 APPLICABLE DOCUMENTS

NASA-STD-6001 - Flammability, Odor, Off-gassing, and Compatibility Requirements and Test 
Procedures for Materials in Environments that Support Combustion (same 
as NHB 8060.1)

items.text:
SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
4 
 
1.3 EXPERIMENT OVERVIEW 
 
The predecessor investigation to Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) was called 
Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) and was developed by NASA/GRC for flight on the Shuttle 
Spacelab during the Fourth United States Microgravity Payload (USMP-4 / STS-87) mission in 
November 1997. 
 
SPICE continues to study fundamental phenomena related to understanding the mechanisms 
controlling the stability and extinction of jet diffusion flames.  SPICE will stabilize an enclosed 
laminar flame, measure the overall flame shape to validate the theoretical and numerical 
predictions, measure the flame stabilization heights, and measure the temperature field to verify 
flame structure predictions. 
 
The differences in ELF and SPICE hardware are the following: 
 
 
The Gas Bottle Assembly size increased from 75 ml to 150 ml, and maximum pressure 
was reduced from 350 psi to 230 psi.  ELF bottles were open on both ends with a plug placed in 
one end and the valve in the other. For SPICE only one end of the bottle has an opening. 
 
 
The original fuel was 50/50 % methane. Propane, Ethylene, Propylene have been added 
as fuels. The increase in bottle size and decrease in pressure cause the worst case SPICE  
bottle to have three times the energy of an ELF bottle due to fuel.  Also the number of bottles 
increased from 6 to 12.  
 
 
 For the Experiment Assembly (EA) the Mass Flow Controller model was changed. 
 
 
There is a new Electronics power video box power box, a new video camera, a new still 
camera and there is an interface with MSG video drawer.  
 
1.4 PAYLOAD AND MISSION OVERVIEW 
 
The SPICE payload is currently scheduled to fly on the International Space Station (ISS) in the 
Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG).  The ascent flight on the NSTS is tentatively scheduled 
to be ULF2.  All SPICE hardware will be returned to earth at the same time on a future shuttle 
flight. 
 
 
1.4.1 SPICE Payload Hardware 
 
SPICE payload hardware is all new hardware that has been developed from the ELF 
experiment hardware design. 
  
SPICE consists of an Experiment Assembly (EA), 12 Gas Bottle Assemblies, a Nikon camera, a 
Video Camera, associated structural support for the cameras, Video Power Unit, and a number 
of stowage cases for the hardware and harnessing which includes a Control Box. SPICE is 
providing two bottle stowage cases, a component stowage case, and 2 tape bags. The rest of 
the hardware will be packed by JSC/MSFC. See figures 1 and 2 for hardware and figure 9b for a 
case diagram respectively.

items.text:
SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
5 
 
1.5 MICROGRAVITY SCIENCE GLOVEBOX (MSG) 
INTERFACES 
 
SPICE will interface with the MSG for structural support, containment and filtering, conditioned 
power and science data retrieval / storage / downlink. 
 
1.5.1 Structural Interfaces with MSG 
 
All SPICE hardware (see Figure 1) except the Control Box (see Figures 2 & 2A) will be mounted 
inside the MSG Working Volume. All components are stowed for launch.  The SPICE 
components mounted in the MSG are the Power-Video Unit, the Experiment Assembly, the 
Nikon Digital Still Camera & Mount and the Video Camera. All of the brackets are anodized 
aluminum. The SPICE Experiment Assembly (see section 2.1 for components) is mounted to 
the floor of the MSG. The SPICE Experiment Assembly has three aluminum angle brackets, 
each having one captive, M6 thumbscrew. One bracket attaches the 70mm grid on the MSG 
Airlock Lid and one to the 70mm grid on the MSG Cold Plate. The third bracket will be attached 
to the mid-section side of the Still Camera Mount.  
 
The Still Camera Mount base is attached to the 70mm grid on the MSG Cold Plate by an 
aluminum angle bracket that has two captive, M6 thumbscrews. The mid-section of the Still 
Camera Mount is then attached to the third bracket on the Experiment Assembly mentioned 
above.   
 
The Video Camera Mount Base is attached to the 70mm grid on the MSG Cold Plate by three 
captive, M6 thumbscrews. 
 
The SPICE Power-Video Unit comprised of a Power Conditioning Box Assembly and Video 
Titler Box Assembly that are mounted to an Adapter Plate which is mounted to the 70mm grid 
on the rear wall of MSG using two captive, M6 thumbscrews. 
 
A drawing of the SPICE engineering model inside the MSG is shown in Figure 2.

MSG is through the MSG W301 Video Extension. Requirements for SPICE Data & Video

The SPICE experiment uses the MSG J403 connector to interface the SPICE Control Box 
located external to the MSG Working Volume and the SPICE hardware inside the Working 
Volume (see figure 3a)  
1.5.5 MSG Thermal Interfaces 
Although the SPICE Experiment Assembly is mounted to the MSG Cold Plate. Cooling service 
provided by the Cold Plate is not required for SPICE operations. The heat dissipated by the 
burning process will raise the temperature of the air flowing through the Experiment Assembly 
only a few degrees. The heat will be then dissipated to the surroundings.   
1.5.6 MSG Working Volume and Air Filtration System 
The SPICE experiment combustion process is run with the MSG Working Volume configured in 
the normal mode (MSG Fans on lowest setting) with the side loading ports and glove ports 
installed. This mode provides one level of containment for combustion by-products (all by-
products are tox level 0).  At the end of the combustion process the MSG fans maybe changed 
to a higher speed and run for a 5-minute period in order to re-circulate the Working Volume air 
and clean-up combustion byproducts using the Working Volume Air Filtration System.  
1.5.7 Crew Interfaces 
The crew interfaces with SPICE consist of set up, nozzle change out, video tape change out, 
IBM micro drive change out, fuel bottle change out, ignition, smoke point setting, still camera 
shots, and tear down. Section 3.0 describes the operations in more detail.  
2 SPICE HARDWARE & SOFTWARE DESCRIPTION 
 
The SPICE experiment will use the Microgravity Science Glove Box (MSG) facility in the 
International Space Station.  The SPICE payload consists of the following hardware: 
 
• 
One (1) Experiment Assembly, which is comprised of: 
- Interchangeable nozzles (0.4, 0.8 & 1.6 mm) - radiometer 
- Fan for Co-flow 
 
 
 
    - anemometer 
- Exchangeable hot-wire Igniter 
 
    - quick-connect fuel inlet 
- heat sink/hand guard 
 
 
    - mass flow controller 
- Pressure regulator 
- 
Tattletale Model 8 data logger (anemometer, fan voltage, fuel flow rate, radiometer) 
• 
One (1) Power-Video Unit, which is comprised of: 
- 
Power Conditioning Box 
- 
Video Titler Box 
- 
Adapter Plate 
• 
One (1) Control Box, which is comprised of: 
- Igniter enable switch 
 
 
- fuel enable switch 
- Data enable switch  
 
 
- radiometer gain switch 
- Fuel flow pot  
 
 
 
- fan velocity pot 
 
• 
Twelve (12) Fuel Bottle Assemblies comprised of: 
- 150 cc DOT bottle with hand valve and quick connect for attachment to Experiment   
Assembly. 
- Gas Bottle fuels are propane, ethylene, methane, propylene (100%), and nitrogen 
diluted propylene (75%, and 50%). 
 
• 
Four (4) Cables: 
- Power Cable  
 
 
- Still Camera Cable

SPICE utilizes the MSG power supply; two color monitors, two video recorders, and the MSG’s 
Working Volume containment capability since the SPICE experiment combustion process is run 
with the MSG Working Volume configured in the normal mode. 
   
SPICE is powered off MSG Secondary Power (+28, +12, -12 and +5 VDC).  The total power 
consumption is 27 W nominal with a peak of 42 W for less than 10 seconds (typical) during 
ignition.   
 
The following sections provide the description of the various SPICE components. 
 
2.1 EXPERIMENT ASSEMBLY 
 
The Experiment Assembly (see Figure 4) is composed of an aluminum rectangular chamber 
34.6cm X 17.0cm X 26.2cm with a ¼ inch polycarbonate Lexan 9034 window cover and the 
associated stainless steel plumbing system that regulates the flow of gas.  A commercial three 
(3) inch diameter fan at the inlet to the chamber provides the air Co-flow. The fans are Panaflo 
FBA08A12HIA axial fans with a nominal speed of 2950 RPM with plastic housing and blades. 
The fan is placed in an aluminum housing and metal screens are located at the inlet and exit of 
the fan, and at the exhaust end of the chamber.  A ceramic (Cordierite) flow straightener is also 
located in the fan housing. It is contained in a housing with a 100 mesh screen over it.  A heat 
sink/hand guard is also placed at the exhaust end of the Experiment Assembly. The heat sink is 
a piece of copper with holes in it. It is contained in an aluminum box with corrugated bronze 
mesh over the opening.  The experiment Assembly is also equipped with a data logger and 
PCMCIA (data card type of digital storage) storage. The Experiment Assembly Cover opens to 
facilitate Nozzle and Igniter hardware installation and change-out operations. The thermal mass 
of the Experiment Assembly precludes the potential to exceed touch temperature limits.  
 
The Experiment Assembly also includes the Fuel Delivery System (See Figure 4A), which 
consists of stainless steel assemblies and component parts such as the Fuel Bottle Assembly 
(1-7), a male half Quick Disconnect (8), Filter (10), Pressure Regulator (13), Mass Flow 
Controller (15), and applicable stainless steel tubing and adapter fittings (9,11,12,14,16).   See 
table 1 attached to Hazard Report SPICE-U2 for the Maximum Design Pressures (MDP) and 
other information concerning these components. .

2.2 VIDEO TITLER BOX 
 
The Video Titler Box is mounted on an aluminum adapter plate along with the Power 
Conditioning Box (see Section 2.3). The complete assembly is called the Power-Video Unit (See 
Figure 5). 
 
This Video Titler Box receives camera video and superimposes SPICE text messages on it.  
Experiment data is presented on the video for tape recording and for display to crewmembers. 
 
The Video Titler Box is an aluminum enclosure approximately 8 in. x 5.5 in. x 3 in.  The Video 
Titler Box has six (6) connections:  Power from Power Conditioning Box, Control (RS-232), two 
(2) video inputs, one each from the SPICE Video camera and D100 Digital camera and two (2) 
video outputs which are connected to the MSG Video Drawer via a MSG Working Volume front 
feed-through connector.  
 
Internal to the Video Titler Box are three (3) conformal coated printed circuit boards and 
associated wiring.  The circuit receives the two (2) video signals from the SPICE Video camera 
and Digital Camera adds text and outputs the appropriate video format to the MSG Video 
Drawer. The MSG Video Drawer contains the video monitoring equipment that will recorder the 
SPICE video signals received onto SPICE provided digital video tapes.    
 
Video Titler Box power is provided from the SPICE Power Conditioning Box (see section 2.3).  
Control of the Video Titler Box is via (RS-232) link to the SPICE Experiment Assembly. 
 
 
 
2.3 POWER CONDITIONING BOX 
 
This box is located in the Power/Video Assembly and is attached to the adapter plate. It 
provides SPICE with power conditioning elements required for proper SPICE operation with the 
MSG.  These include wire gauge/routing sites and additional circuit protection Fuses and spares 
(see Figure 5). Two captive Thumb Screws secure the lid of the box. Backing off the screws and 
removing the lid accomplish access to the fuses. Fuses can be replaced within the Power 
Conditioning Box without having to remove the Box from MSG.  
  
Power conditioning elements are housed in an aluminum enclosure (with lid) very similar to the 
Video Titler Box.  The Power Conditioning Box includes a power input cable that is connected to 
the MSG Working Volume J303 Power Connector.  A terminal board inside the Power 
Conditioning Box provides power distribution for +/-12, +5, and +28 VDC power provided from 
MSG. The Power Conditioning Box also contains a 28VDC to 9VDC Converter and Filter that 
provides 9VDC power to the NIKON D100 Camera. The filter, capacitors, and a resistor are to 
limit the inrush current when the camera snaps a picture.   
 
Two (2) 5 Amp Cartridge Fuses with one wired to the +5 VDC power and the other wired to +28 
VDC power are also located inside the Power Conditioning Box.  The fuses provide additional 
circuit protection to the SPICE Experiment Hardware that is wired to the +5 and +28 VDC 
power. The SPICE Experiment Hardware that uses +/- 12VDC power does not require 
additional circuit protection.

The Video Camera Assembly is comprised of a Panasonic WV-CP 654 Video Camera with

The Still Camera Mount (Figure 8) is made up of anodized aluminum pieces bolted together.

2.9 CABLE ASSEMBLIES 
 
SPICE has the following cable assemblies, Power Cable Assembly, Video Cable assembly, Still 
Camera Cable Assembly, and Feed-through Cable Assembly. These are all stowed in the 
SPICE Component Stowage Case. The wires are Teflon wires rated for 200 C and are bundled 
together with expandable cable mesh. See SPICE Wire Derating Analysis  60054-ANA-017. 
 
The Power Cable Assembly consists of the cables which run from the Power/Video Unit to the 
Experiment Assembly, to the Video Camera, and to the Still Camera. This cable supplies power 
to these units.  
 
The Video Cable assembly is a video data cable which connects the Video Camera to the 
Power/Video Unit for signals.  
 
The Still Camera Cable Assembly. This cable connects the Power/Video unit to the Still Camera 
for signal. 
 
The Feed-through Cable Assembly has 4 ends and is used for signals except for one 12 volt 
wire to the experiment assembly. One end connects to the MSG feed through connector to 
provide communication to the SPICE Control Box. The control box itself has a cable and 
connector which is permanently attached to the Control Box. The control box consists of two 10 
turn pots, three toggle switches, a feed through, a multi-positional switch which switches 
resistors to set the radiometer gain. Another end of the cable connects to the Still Camera to 
snap pictures. Another end connects to the Experiment Assembly to start data collection, 
enable fuel flow, set the radiometer, set the fuel flow, set the fan flow, and enable the ignitor. 
The fourth end connects to the Power/Video Unit. 
 
2.10 SOFTWARE SUMMARY 
 
Data gathering software resides in the Experiment Assembly’s Data Logger. The Control Box 
Assembly is equipped with switches for controlling the fan speed and fuel flow rate, and 
activates the Ignitor and data acquisition.  Video images are taken with a Video Camera.  The 
video data is recorded on a MSG provided video recorder.  Digital pictures are also taken of the 
top view through the Experiment Assemblies Lexan window cover. The video images, together 
with the digital data output of the data logger, are sent to a video box, which writes the digital 
data (air flow velocity, fuel flow, fan voltage, and time) on the video signal.  The video signal 
from this box is then recorded by the MSG video recorder and down linked. 
The SPICE experiment will fail-safe in the event of total or partial power loss, i.e., the hardware 
will not be damaged or pose any hazard in the event of a power disruption.  In the event of a 
total power loss, the SPICE experiment cannot be operated and the normally closed MFC will 
shut, cutting off fuel flow. Experiment sequencing is controlled by the crew. Software is only 
used for data recording in the SPICE Experiment.  
3 SPICE FLIGHT OPERATION 
The SPICE experiment currently has a CEF submitted for launch on ULF-2.  This manifest is 
currently being reviewed.  The experiment will be performed inside the Microgravity Science 
Glove-box (MSG) on the International Space Station.  On-orbit operations will consist of SPICE 
Hardware Set-up and Stowage, SPICE Operations, Fuel Purges, along with Bottle, Burner 
Tube, and Ignitor Assembly exchanges.  Instructions for off-nominal activities are being

items.text:
SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
26 
developed. Flight Operational Procedures are listed in Table 3 of section 3.1 The SPICE 
hardware including the Component Stowage Case will be soft stowed in the MPLM for launch 
and landing.  The Gas Bottle Stowage Cases with 6 bottles in each case will be delivered at 
approximately L-48 hours and launched in the Middeck.  The hardware configuration for 
stowage during launch and landing is still under development. The safety aspects of launch and 
landing will be covered in the safety section.  
 
3.1 DETAILED OPERATIONS 
 
The SPICE SET UP procedure provides instructions to install SPICE hardware in the MSG WV, 
configure the SPICE Control Box Assembly outside the MSG Facility, perform an ignitor test, 
and perform a still camera test.  
 
The SPICE STOW procedure provides instructions to disassemble and stow the SPICE 
Experiment after SPICE Operations have been completed. 
 
SPICE OPERATIONS procedure provides instructions to conduct combustion experiment tests 
according to the Test Matrix of Table 4 in section 3.2. 
 
The SPICE GAS BOTTLE EXCHANGE procedure provides instructions to remove and replace 
Gas Bottle Assemblies from the Experiment Assembly as required by the Test Matrix of Table 4. 
This includes configuring the MSG video recorders and SPICE Still Camera Assembly, 
activating the experiment, performing a flame test, powering down, and logging test data. 
 
The SPICE FUEL PURGE procedure provides instructions to conduct a fuel purge of the SPICE 
Fuel Delivery System so that any unburned gas remaining from the previous combustion 
experiment test is purged out and replaced with the next combustion test gas. 
 
The SPICE BURNER TUBE EXCHANGE procedure provides instructions to change out the 
previous Burner Tube diameter size with a new Burner Tube diameter size as required to 
support the Test Matrix of Table 4. 
 
The SPICE IGNITOR EXCHANGE procedure provides instructions to remove the used ignitor 
and install a new ignitor in the SPICE Experiment Assembly.  
 
Table 3 lists the flight operation procedures for the SPICE experiment and figure 11 provides 
the experiment flow.

SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
29 
This section addresses the hazards investigated for SPICE.  If the hazard has not been 
eliminated by design with its rationale captured in this section, its controls are documented in 
either the JSC 1230 Form or in unique hazard reports developed for the SPICE experiment.  
The SPICE Flight Payload Standardized Hazard Control Report (STD-SPICE-01) is discussed 
in Section 4.2 and the JSC 1230 form is provided in Attachment D. Unique Hazards Reports 
(SPICE-U1, SPICE-U2, SPICE-U3, SPICE-U4, SPICE-U5, SPICE-U6, and SPICE U8) are 
provided in Attachment E.  
 
This section is comprised of three parts, as follows: 
 
 
Section 4.1 – Discussion of the safety assessment approach for SPICE. 
 
Section 4.2 – Discussion of each section of the JSC Form 1230. 
 
Section 4.3 – Discussion of other safety hazards.  
 
Section 4.4 – Discussion of hazard report verification classifications. 
Section 4.5 – Discussion of SPICE test failures, anomalies and accidents. 
 
4.1 SAFETY ASSESSMENT APPROACH FOR SPICE 
 
Since SPICE is similar in functional design and operation with its predecessor ELF, this SPICE 
Phase II Safety Data Package was developed using the hazard reports documented in MSFC 
Document JA-2378 which was the ELF Phase III SDP for the USMP-4/STS-87 Shuttle Middeck 
Glovebox (MGBX) mission.   
 
The SPICE experiment also uses new fuels and mixtures and a revised Test Matrix than that of 
its predecessor ELF and a new hazardous material and combustion By-Product list has been 
submitted to JSC Toxicology for hazard evaluation and assessment. The new fuel mixtures and 
combustion By-Products applicable to SPICE experiment are provided in the JSC HMST 
Attachment A. 
 
4.2 STANDARD HAZARDS (JSC FORM 1230) 
 
This section discusses each Standard Hazard applicable to SPICE as shown in the STD-
SPICE-01 Hazard report (JSC Form 1230) Attachment B.

4.2.1 Structural Failure 
 
SPICE hardware is designed to meet the expected launch, on-orbit and return loads specified in 
MSFC-RQMT-2888, Paragraph 3.1.1.1, and Table 1 which is consistent with SSP 57000 
requirements. The stowage loads in MSFC-RQMT-2888 are based on a worst case condition of 
the Middeck and MPLM stowage loads. SPICE hardware will be stowed in soft transfer bags 
and transported in the MPLM for transfer to the ISS.  All the SPICE hardware will be soft stowed 
for return.  ZIN Tech Engineering has performed an analysis of test levels specified in NASA-
STD-7001 (NASA Payload Vibration Test Criteria) and MSFC-RQMT-2888 to define vibration 
test levels to encompass the launch and landing load levels the hardware will be exposed to 
and has created a composite vibration loading profile to envelope the levels defined in both 
MSFC-RQMT-2888 and NASA-STD-7001. The SPICE flight hardware has undergone 
acceptance vibration testing at these levels.  A test report has been prepared to confirm that the 
test was successfully completed. 
 
The SPICE hardware is also designed to meet the expected on-orbit loads during operation in 
the MSG.  SPICE hardware will be fastened to the MSG working volume using captive, 
threaded fasteners. This will meet the on orbit load requirements as specified in SSP 57000 and 
MSFC-RQMT-2888. The hardware inside the MSG will not be exposed to on-orbit kick loads 
during operation. The control box is subjected to crew induced loads and is capable of 
withstanding the loads per SSP 57000 and MSFC-RQMT-2888.  
 
The Gas Bottle Assembly Stowage Case and the SPICE component cases have two latches 
which keep them from opening in stowage. The case itself is packed in foam and placed in the 
stowage volume which will prevent the case from opening during launch, therefore they are not 
safety critical.  
 
SPICE structural failure is addressed in Section 1 of STD-SPICE-01.  
 
4.2.2 Structural Failure of Sealed Containers  
 
Structural failure of sealed containers containing hazardous materials are addressed in Unique 
Hazard report SPICE-U2 for Rupture/Leakage of the SPICE pressurized fuel delivery system.  
Contamination Hazard for release of hazardous sample fluids is addressed in Unique Hazard 
Report SPICE-U1. The SPICE Fuel Delivery System is designed to meet the requirements of 
NASA-STD-5003 for Fracture Control of pressure vessels and pressurized components.    
 
4.2.3 Structural Failure of Vented Containers 
 
The Experiment Assembly is open on each end (fan end and screen end) and has a removable 
polycarbonate Lexan Window Cover; therefore it will not contain an internal atmosphere and is 
not hermetically sealed.  The design of the Experiment Assembly will be reviewed to verify that 
it can maintain structural integrity in the event of a rapid depressurization / re-pressurization per 
SSP 52005B, Para. 4.1.12. (See Table 5). The window on the top of the EA is polycarbonate 
and is held on by two screws.  The window cover is held on the bottom by a metal hinge and on 
the top by two gun bolt type sliding latches. 
 
The designs of the Nikon Digital Camera, Video Camera, Gas Bottle Assembly and Component 
Parts Cases  will also be reviewed to verify that they can maintain structural integrity in the

The SPICE hardware is designed to meet the intent of SSP 50005 / NASA-STD-3000.  The

as well as the total integrated assemblies.

4.2.5 Shatterable Material Release 
 
Use of frangible material is limited to the fuses, flow straightener, Still Camera lens and Video 
Camera lens.  The SPICE Experiment Assembly Window cover is made out of Polycarbonate 
Lexan 9034 and is not shatterable.   
 
The camera lenses will be launched with protective covers on since the glass of the Still and 
Video Camera lens are recessed in their respective housings. During SPICE set-up Crew 
procedure the cameras will be installed into the MSG Working Volume before the protective 
covers are removed from the camera lens. The crew will assess/inspect the lens for damage at 
the time of removal. Once the caps are removed and assessment is acceptable the MSG 
Working Volume enclosure will then provide containment when the protective covers have been 
removed from the cameras during experiment operations.  These items have also been 
vibration tested and inspected.  
 
The flow straightener is made of Cordierite which is a ceramic and is contained inside the fan 
housing on the Experiment Assembly (EA). Similar to acceptable controls for optical glass, the 
EA is also packaged in a clear plastic bag and inspected by the crew after launch. If it were to 
break, the pieces could be seen through the window of the EA. The EA is inside MSG when 
removed from the bag and when operating. If any particles are fine enough to get through the 
screens they will be ingested in the MSG HEPA filters. Since intake and outlets are screened 
and inside EA there are no identifiable failure modes on orbit to damage the ceramic. The 3 X 3 
X 1 inch piece of Cordierite is also bound along the 3 X 3 perimeter which will prevent damage 
and break up of this honey comb type material. Similar to control of optical glass such as lenses 
(form 1230 section 5) the item is vibration tested and inspected for damage afterwards. See 
figures 13a and 13b. 
 
The fuses in the Power Box are also glass. They are wrapped in Kapton tape, which is never 
removed, to contain any breakage that might occur. They are contained inside the Power 
Conditioning Box.  The crew does not have access to the interior of the Power Conditioning 
Box.

4.2.6 Flammable Materials 
 
"A" rated materials in accordance with MSFC-SPEC-527/JSC 09604F are selected for 
experiment hardware to control the hazard associated with the use of flammable materials.  Any 
non-"A" rated materials will be used in a non-flammable configuration in accordance with NSTS 
22648, Flammability Configuration Analysis for Spacecraft Applications, or justified for usage via 
a Materials Usage Agreement (MUA).  Materials usage is documented on a Materials 
Identification and Usage List (MIUL).  Materials usage will be analyzed by NASA/GRC/SMAD 
M&P and certified for flight via the GRC/JSC Materials and Processes Intercenter Agreement.  
Flammability of fuels is addressed in paragraph 4.3.6.1. 
 
Flammable Materials are addressed in Section 6 of STD-SPICE-01.

SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
35 
 
4.2.7 Materials Offgassing 
 
Representative SPICE hardware, flight-like cables and other miscellaneous items have been 
toxic off-gas tested in accordance with NASA-STD-6001, Test 7. See letter ED36B(03-060)  
attached to 1230 form. Offgas test results will be analyzed by NASA/GRC/SMAD  and certified 
for flight via the GRC/JSC Materials and Processes Inter-center Agreement. 
 
Materials Off-gassing is addressed in Section 7 of STD-SPICE-01. 
 
4.2.8 Non-Ionizing Radiation (EMI) 
 
4.2.8.1 
Non-Transmitters 
 
SPICE is designed for compliance with the radiated and conducted emissions requirements 
specified in MSFC-RQMT-2888 as defined in SSP 30237, Space Station Electromagnetic 
Emission and Susceptibility Requirements.  All electronic assemblies have been tested for 
conformance to this specification including the determination of the maximum ripple voltage 
emissions appearing on the SPICE input power leads.  The power conversion box contains a 
filter to meet the requirements of MSFC RQMT-2888. This filter reduces the step from milliamp 
draw to 3 amp draw by the still camera when taking a picture. See figure 14. SPICE will only be 
operated inside of the MSG working volume.  The test results have been submitted to 
NASA/MSFC MSG personnel for their review and approval. An ISS Electromagnetic Emissions 
Panel approved Technical Interface Agreement has been sought for RE02 exceedance.  
 
EMI Radiation is addressed in Section 8.1 of STD-SPICE-01. 
 
4.2.8.2 
Lasers 
 
There are no lasers in the SPICE experiment. 
 
4.2.9 Battery Failure 
 
The Batteries used in the SPICE experiment meet the criteria of small commercial batteries 
stated in Section 9.2 of the JSC Standardized Hazard Report JSC 1230. The following 
SPICE hardware contains small commercial batteries that are verified as permanently soldered 
into their respective electrical circuits and have completed successful verification of in circuit 
voltage measurements and verification of circuit isolation from external power sources. 
 
The NIKON D100 Digital Camera contains Button Cell 20mmX3.2mm, type Li-Mn-O2, 3 Volts 
DC 65mAh, Maxell Model No.: ML2032T6. The battery is fully contained within the Digital 
Camera and cannot be accessed unless complete Camera disassembly is performed. The 
purpose of the camera battery is to maintain date, time and camera operational settings. The 
cell is soldered to board.   
 
The Horita Video Titler Card Cell consists of two cells in series. The cells are 15.5 X6.3 mm 
Rechargeable Nickel Metal Hydride cells  1.2 VDC each, 60mAh, Model Number GP60BVH, 
Manufacturer GP Batteries International LTD.  The cells will not be charged and are prevented

May 2008 
36 
from doing so by a pull up resistor. The battery is soldered to the board, fully contained with in 
the Video Control Box and cannot be accessed unless the Video Control Box is disassembled. 
The purpose of the Video Titler Card Cell is to maintain Video Titler operational settings.   
 
The Dallas Tattle-Tale Card I-Button Data Device, Model Number DS1994, contains a 
12.5mmX2.5mm Li-CFx Battery, 3VDC, 50mAh, Model No. BR1225, Manufacturer RAYOVAC. 
The Lithium Battery is soldered to the boards and fully contained within the I Button Data Device 
and the I Button Data Device is contained inside the Experiment Assembly. The purpose of the I 
Button Data Device Lithium (Li-CFx) Battery is to maintain experiment data memory when 
external power is removed from the Experiment Assembly. The documents for the I-Button Data 
Device state that it does not use any power to charge the lithium battery.  It has a limited life of 
greater than10 years based on the low power required to sit idle. Specifically there is a 
statement on page 46 that the ROM logic can be operated by the parasite power even after the 
lithium cell is exhausted in 10 years or more.  This implies that the other sections of memory 
may not be operational if the lithium battery dies.  When data is being exchanged with the I-
Button Data Device, the data line is used to charge a capacitor internal to the I-Button Data 
Device and that capacitor is used to power the read write operations.  Parasite power is an 
internal I-Button Data Device capacitor that is charged by the data line (converted RS-232).   
 
 
Battery Failure is addressed in Section 9.2 of STD-SPICE-01. 
 
4.2.10 
 Touch Temperatures 
 
SPICE hardware and electronics have been designed and tested to meet touch temperature 
limits of 49°C specified in the Interpretation Letter MA2-95-048. Also during on-orbit operation, 
the SPICE hardware is enclosed inside the MSG working volume with no direct crew contact 
with the SPICE Experiment Assembly during ignition or combustion processes (experiment 
runs).  Also during post experiment runs the airflow provided by the MSG Air Handling Unit 
(AHU) during by-product clean up will also aid in the dissipation of any residual heated air within 
the MSG working volume. SPICE by design does not require external cooling during experiment 
operations.  
 
A thermal test has been conducted to verify that the touch temperature limits of MA2-95-048 are 
met. The fuel nozzles were tested and found that the worst case nozzle reached 89 degrees C 
but cooled to 33 degrees C in less than 60 seconds after flame off. This was without EA air flow 
which will be present at the end of a burn decreasing cooling time. A wait time will be imposed 
before EA chamber access after flame off.   
 
Touch Temperature is addressed in hazard report U6.     
 
4.2.11 Electrical Power Distribution 
 
The electrical power distribution system meets station interface circuit protection requirements 
of SSP 57000 (through the MSG Working Volume secondary power sources) and payload wire 
sizing and circuit protection requirements of Interpretation Letter TA-92-038.  The SPICE 
hardware will receive circuit protection from the MSG conditioned power sources (28VDC @ 7 
Amps), (+/-12VDC @ 2 Amps) and (5VDC @ 4 Amps).  SPICE will provide additional circuit 
protection in the Power Conditioning Box (5-Amp fast-acting cartridge fuses) on the +28 VDC 
and +5 VDC power lines.  The SPICE +/- 12VDC power line does not require additional circuit

items.text:
SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
37 
protection (fusing) since the wire sizing is appropriately de-rated for the provided MSG 
conditioned power source. 
 
Besides the circuit protection provided by the MSG circuit breakers and SPICE Fuses, the 
DC/DC converters also provide additional protection by current limiting their output in the event 
of an over-current condition.  See schematic of the SPICE Power Distribution System attached 
to hazard report STD-SPICE-01, Section 11. See SPICE Wire De-rating Analysis 60054-ANA-
017. 
 
SPICE does not meet the Power Distribution Single Point Grounding requirements of MSFC-
RQMT-2888.  The Hitachi Video Camera HV-C20U-S4 video camera, (PN )7009.80.AA 
(specially modified for the MSG Program), the Nikon D100 Digital SLR Camera and other 
similar commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) cameras (modified or unmodified) violate SSP30240, 
3.2.1.2, Secondary and Tertiary Electrical Power (single point grounding) by connecting the 
incoming 12 Vdc power return to camera structure (the second time the 12 Vdc is grounded to 
structure). SPICE has submitted a Tailoring Interpretation Agreement for these occurrences. 
See schematics attached to hazard report STD-SPICE-01, Section 11.  
 
SPICE meets the bonding and grounding requirements of SSP 30245 and SSP 30240.  Bonding 
and grounding of the SPICE hardware is accomplished via several different methods; via the 
chassis conductor pin provided via Pin L at the P303 Power Connector (i.e., conductor bond 
path), via the overall shield on the P303 Power Cable (i.e., using a grounded backshell), and via 
the metal-to-metal bond of SPICE structure to the MSG mounting plate. See schematic attached 
to hazard report STD-SPICE-01, Section 11. 
 
The SPICE experiment will fail-safe in the event of total or partial power loss, i.e., the hardware 
will not be damaged or pose any hazard in the event of a power disruption.  In the event of a 
total power loss, the SPICE Experiment cannot be operated. The MFC is normally closed, so 
power loss will stop fuel flow. See Hazard Report SPICE-U5 for loss of power case effect on 
fuel flammability control. 
 
Power into SPICE is filtered to prevent surges on the MSG power supply. See Figure 14 for the 
28 volt power filter schematic.  
 
A temporary or intermittent loss of power will cause the SPICE control software to "reboot" (the 
unit will act as if it was being turn "ON" for the first time). 
 
Electrical Power Distribution is addressed in Section 11 of STD-SPICE-01.

4.2.12 Ignition of Flammable Atmospheres in the Payload Bay 
Not applicable, as the SPICE hardware is not mounted/transported in the the Shuttle Payload

4.2.13 Rotating Equipment 
 
The SPICE Experiment Assembly has one internal Fan to (1) study convective flow during 
combustion and (2) to remove combustion byproducts from the Experiment Assembly in 
between tests.  The fan is DC-powered and is made of fiberglass-reinforced plastic (See 
Sections 6 and 7 of STD-SPICE-01 for materials requirements).  The fan diameter is 3 inches, 
with a speed of 2950 RPM.  It is a brushless DC motor provided with 12 V. Although the Fan 
shroud is plastic it is also fully enclosed in aluminum housing with stainless steel mesh (Type 
304ss, 71% of open area) covering the fan inlet and outlet openings.  Analysis shows that this 
fan has a low kinetic energy level (<<<19, 310 J) and is fully contained with the Experiment 
Assembly according to NASA-STD-5003 requirements. 
 
Rotating Equipment is addressed in Section 13 of STD-SPICE-01.

encountered during mating/demating of SPICE power connector P303 is 29 VDC maximum

during SPICE ignition is 2.8 Amps on the +5 VDC power line.  Crew procedures require that the 
MSG circuit breakers that provide power to the MSG J303 connector be turned off prior to any 
crew interface with the SPICE Experiment.

and/or keying.  In addition, they will all be labeled to help identify the connector interface in

feature a scoop-proof design that completely encloses the pin/socket contacts during mating 
and de-mating operations.  Additionally, the powered side of the cable connectors on SPICE are 
terminated in sockets to provide protection against inadvertent shorting that could be caused by 
external debris.   
 
Mating/Demating of Power Connectors is addressed in Section 14 of STD-SPICE-01. 
    
4.2.15 Contingency Return and Rapid Safing 
 
The SPICE experiment is not in operation mode while stowed in Shuttle for launch and landing.  
While on orbit the SPICE hardware will be either stowed in the ISS stowage, or in operation in 
the MSG.  In either case, the SPICE hardware will not interfere with the IVA envelope or impede 
emergency IVA egress to the remaining contiguous pressurized volumes. 
 
Design analysis will be performed for the SPICE hardware and planned flight operations for 
compliance to MA2-96-190.    
 
Contingency Return and Rapid Safing is addressed in Section 15 of STD-SPICE-01.      
 
4.2.16 Release of Mercury from Bulbs into Crew Habitable 
Environment 
 
There is no mercury in any of the SPICE components.  
 
4.3 OTHER SAFETY HAZARDS 
 
The previous sections close discussion on the SPICE Flight Payload Standardized Hazard 
Control Report (STD-SPICE-01).   Additional potential hazards and SPICE unique hazards are 
discussed below. 
 
4.3.1 Pressurized Systems 
 
SPICE pressurized components are the Gas Bottle Assemblies and the Experiment Assembly 
Fuel Delivery System. These components do not interface with the nitrogen or vacuum sources 
of the MSG.  
 
Even though all of the components are rated for pressures well above 230 psi, the system MDP 
is determined by the point at which the fuel can turn to liquid. This pressure also considered the 
maximum temperature that the bottle could experience. SPICE pressurized lines and fittings will 
be designed to a factor of safety of 4.0 X System MDP of 230psid. SPICE Pressurized system 
components will be designed to a factor of safety of greater than or equal to 2.5 X System MDP

items.text:
SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
40 
of 230 psid. The gas bottles are DOT bottles with a rated pressure of 500 psi which will be 
pressurized to a maximum of 230 psi. To prevent overpressurization this will be verified after 
filling that the bottles are the correct mixture and at the correct pressure.  The bottles have been 
proof tested to 1000 psi. The Experiment Assembly is not sealed and will not pressurize in the 
event of full open flow from the mass flow controller. The maximum flow rate of the fuel system 
is 20 liters per minute. The fan that is used to cause flow is capable of 1120 liters per minute 
with a pressure drop of parts of a psi. Therefore the flow rate through the chamber is orders of 
magnitude greater than the maximum fuel flow into the chamber. Therefore the chamber will 
have no significant increase in pressure. See hazard Report SPICE U5 for analysis of pressure 
due to burning of worst case fuel load in the EA.  In the event of power loss the Mass Flow 
Controller is normally closed, therefore fuel flow will stop.  
Materials will be selected and evaluated for stress corrosion and/or fluid compatibility in 
accordance with SSP 30233, Space Station Requirements for Materials and Processes. 
Hardware will be built in conformance with approved design drawings and specifications. The 
gas bottles will be filled to approved procedures to insure that the proper mixture of gas is 
placed in the correct bottle and each bottle is filled to the correct pressure. 
The Gas Bottle Assemblies and the pressurized portions of the Experiment Assembly Fuel 
Delivery System will be proof pressure tested to 1.5 X MDP and Helium Leak tested for an 
acceptable leak rate of 1x10E-4 scc/sec Helium in order to validate structural integrity and 
containment by design. 
 
During on orbit operations, procedures will be provided to instruct the crew on proper Gas Bottle 
Exchange, Experiment Set-up and Operation to prevent Gas Bottle and Experiment Assembly 
Fuel Delivery System leakage. 
  
Reference Unique Hazard Report SPICE-U2. Flammability issues of the fuels are covered 
in SPICE-U4 and SPICE U5. Projectile issues are covered in SPICE-U3. 
 
4.3.2 Collision 
 
Calculations show that for the bottle under full pressure, the propulsive force of the worst case, 
a break off of a tube, only create 0.6 lbs of force for 0.23 seconds. The force required to break 
off the tube is 10 lbs at the worst case moment arm with all factors of safety. If the bottle is 
being held such that 10 lbs of force is on the bottle, the 0.6 lb propulsive force can easily be 
withstood. Each Gas Bottle Assembly by design incorporates a single fault tolerant design. The 
Diaphragm Valve and Quick Disconnect are in series on the Gas Bottle Assembly. Should the 
Diaphragm Valve fail the Quick Disconnect will contain the gas. The failure of the Quick 
Disconnect is backed up by the containment of the Diaphragm Valve. Both the Diaphragm Valve 
and Quick Disconnect would need to fail simultaneously in order for the Gas Bottle Assembly to 
become a projectile. In addition there is a cap on the QC which although is not a radial vent cap 
it will restrict the flow and disperse it at an angle reducing the force. Even if both failures 
occurred the Gas Bottle Tubing at the QD end incorporates a 90 degree bend that would 
prevent the Gas Bottle assembly from gaining any significant speed (<1.5m/s), and force 
(<0.6lbf) or direction that would present a collision hazard.  
Reference Unique Hazard Report SPICE-U3. 
 
 
4.3.3 On-Orbit Maintenance

SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
41 
The SPICE experiment hardware does not contain limited life items. No on-orbit maintenance is 
planned. 
 
4.3.4 Fire Detection and Suppression 
 
SPICE does not have any computer control of any FD& S functions and cannot interface directly 
with the ISS caution and warning system.  SPICE flammability hazards are controlled by 
material selection, containment, and wire de-rating and circuit protection, (See Section 4.2.6 
and 4.2.11). SPICE unburned Fuel contamination hazard is controlled under unique Hazard 
Report SPICE-U1. Structural Integrity of the SPICE Experiment Fuel Delivery System is 
controlled under unique Hazard Report SPICE-U2.  
SPICE will receive Fire Detection capability from MSG through its Working Volume Rear Wall 
Temperature Sensor. The crew is required to be present during any burn per MSFC-RQMT-
2888.  Fire Suppression capability is provided by MSG through the use of a station Portable Fire 
Extinguisher (PFE) expelling CO2 into the MSG Working Volume. See Attachment D for the 
completed Fire Detection and Suppression Reporting Form 1428 for the SPICE Experiment. 
4.3.5 Crew Interaction 
 
SPICE is designed such that any required access to SPICE hardware during flight or ground 
operations can be accomplished with minimum risk of injury to personnel.  SPICE hardware 
components are designed to provide enough clearance for crew interface and usage and do not 
create a pinch or accessibility hazard.  
 
The SPICE experiment complies with the requirements for Electrostatic Discharge (ESD) 
compatibility as specified in MSFC-RQMT-2888 document.  An analysis will be prepared to 
demonstrate that that electrical equipment and any parts susceptible to damage by ESD will fail-
safe when exposed to an Electrostatic Discharge (ED) equal or less than 4,000 Volts to the 
case or any pin on the external contacts.  These (ED) voltages might be the result of charges 
accumulated and then discharged from ground personnel or crewmembers during equipment 
installation or removal.   Reference unique hazard SPICE-U8.  
 
Table 5 provides a listing of the SPICE Standard and Unique Hazards that are controlled by 
operating procedures.
