items.title: PSI-107_Engineering Documents_SPICE_Phase III Flight Safety Data Package.pdf
items.text:
SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
45 
 
 
 
 
4.3.6 Release of Experiment Materials 
4.3.6.1 Unburned Fuel Release  
JSC toxicologist assessment of the fuels used in SPICE have a toxicity rating of 0 and a 
flammability rating of 4, See Attachment A, SPICE Hazardous Material Summary Table (HMST). 
Also see table 6 for levels of fuel in the lab module.  
 
A concern was raised at the Phase 0/I review concerning effects on the ECLSS due to leaks of 
these fuels. The action item to determine any issues with these gases in the quantities from 
SPICE was given. The results of the analysis are that leakage of the total amounts of these 
fuels is not an issue for ECLSS.  Reference the March 25, 2004 email from Tim Smith which is 
attached to hazard report SPICE-U1. Leakage of fuel from SPICE is being controlled by design 
and verified by Helium leak testing of the Fuel Delivery System and the bottle assemblies. The 
gases that have been analyzed for ECLSS will be used to fill the bottle assemblies by using 
approved procedures, by labeling each bottle assembly for contents, and then by sampling each 
bottle to test for the correct contents. 
 
Reference Attachment E Unique Hazard Report SPICE-U1. 
 
Flammability in the US Lab. Lean Flammability Limit (LFL) Calculations conducted on the 
HMST listed SPICE Fuel Concentrations that could be released inside the United States Lab 
(USL) Volume show that all 12 SPICE Gas Bottles could leak their entire contents into the USL 
Volume and still be below the LFL for the applicable Fuel. The MSG will be in the Columbus 
module at the time SPICE is run. This module has a smaller volume than the US Lab. A new 
HMST has been requested and new calculations were performed based on the volume of 64 m3 
that is being used by toxicology. See table 6 for the calculations.  
 
Flammability in Stowage. The bottles are launched packed in foam in stowage cases which 
are in turn packed in foam. The bottles have all been vibration tested in the stowage 
configuration and leak tested. The fittings are all commercial fittings rated for over 3000 psi. 
Also each Gas Bottle Assembly incorporates a single fault tolerant design, which would require 
the Diaphragm Valve and Quick Disconnect to fail simultaneously in order for the Gas Bottle 
Assembly to leak unburned fuel through the normal flow path. This fault tolerance is 
accomplished by having the Diaphragm Valve and Quick Disconnect in series on the Gas Bottle 
Assembly. Should the Diaphragm Valve fail the Quick Disconnect will contain the gas. The 
failure of the Quick Disconnect is backed up by the containment of the Diaphragm Valve. There 
will be no ignition sources in the Gas Bottle Assembly stowage cases (no electronics or 
batteries). The bottles will be electrically connected to the aluminum case by two redundant 
strips of aluminum tape attached to the foam which will contact each bottle. A calculation will be 
performed providing the necessary volume in stowage which must be clear of ignition sources 
assuming two worst case bottles leak. This is based on being below the LFL. See table 6. The 
current calculation with a 75 % packing factor (there is only 25 % void space) is 156 liters or a 
54 cm cube. This size is easily accommodated considering the amount of foam used. Once the 
fuel leaks into the MPLM or ISS stowage volume it was agreed that it will dissipate rapidly.  
 
Stowage for landing utilizes the same controls, including valve handle restraints. The restraint (a 
tie-wrap) is capable of withstanding 50 lbs of force, which is sufficient to prevent turning of the 
valve during launch and to prevent inadvertent turning during handling.  See figure 10b for a

items.title: PSI-107_Engineering Documents_SPICE_Phase III Flight Safety Data Package.pdf
items.text:
SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
46 
picture of the valve with the restraint. This picture is for demonstration of the concept, the flight 
version will be installed with considerations for the crew (e.g. sharp edges) They will be cut by 
the crew once the bottle is inside the MSG. The bottles are expected to be used to the point 
where no gas is available to leak out, therefore for landing there should be less fuel, but the tie 
wrap will be installed by the crew when the bottle is removed from the MSG. In addition to the 
tie wrap the foam cut outs for the bottles includes cut outs for the handles which will prevent 
them from turning.  
 
Reference Attachment E Unique Hazard Report SPICE-U4  
 
 
Flammability in the MSG.  This concern is divided into three concerns, fuel build up in the EA 
igniting, fuel leak into the MSG igniting and gas leak impinging on a crew member’s hand.  
 
For the concern of the EA filling with fuel and igniting during times with out crew access to the 
inside of the EA, the MFC has been leak tested at MDP to demonstrate that it will not leak into 
chamber when off, preventing fuel in the chamber from building up or flowing in quantities that 
could ignite. Air flow from the EA fans keep the EA internal fuel percentage below the LFL. The 
EA fan is on automatically upon power up of SPICE. Also the air flow rate is verified by the crew 
from the laptop which has a measured value of air flow rate displayed. The only ignition source 
in the EA chamber is the ignitor and the ignitor is not turned on until after the EA fan is verified 
on. The crew will turn on the ignitor before fuel flow which will eliminate fuel build up. In the 
event that the fan fails, the crew fails to verify the fan speed and there was an ignition source 
the total energy content of the EA chamber is well below the 14,240 ft-lb limit for a pressure 
vessel at worst case fuel mixture. See table 6.  
 
A flame out condition has been proposed to cause fuel build up if the fuel is not turned off or fuel 
is not ignited. For this condition to occur the EA fan would also have to be off.  Large amounts 
of air in the line could cause flame out.  An air bubble caused by changing bottles has been 
hypothesized as causing a flame out. The QC from manufacturer is “drip-less” meaning it has 
minimal air entrainment (0.3 cc). This air bubble would be pushed out in the first 2 seconds of 
operation before ignition was confirmed (before steady state operation), therefore the situation 
of a flame out or failure to ignite in 2-3 seconds would not be a surprise situation for the crew, it 
would be part of the ignition sequence. Only approved crew procedures will be used to monitor 
burn to adjust flame. In addition it has been shown that the air bubble would mix in the fuel line 
filter to a percentage of fuel/air that would not be an issue. See attachments to hazard report 
SPICE-U5 for analysis.  
 
For the MSG concern, in general Lean Flammability Limit (LFL) Calculations conducted on the 
HMST listed SPICE Fuel Concentrations that could be released inside the MSG Working 
Volume show that 2 SPICE Gas Bottles could leak their entire contents into the MSG Working 
Volume and still be below the LFL for the applicable Fuel, see table 6. Note only one bottle at a 
time will be permitted in the MSG. This assumes total mixing which is realistic considering that 
there is a minimum of 180 liters/sec of air flowing in the MSG caused by the MSG fans. The 
MSG fans are capable of the fuel concentrations below the LFL, and in addition the EA fan will 
mix the air in the MSG WV. See attachments to hazard report SPICE-U5 for analysis. There are 
no ignition sources inside MSG to ignite any leak from the gas bottles. The switches used for 
the SPICE inhibits and ignition will not produce any sparks or electrical ignition sources. SPICE 
is designed to minimize the potential for leaks, and with the use of approved crew procedures to 
ensure the MSG fans are running and only one bottle is permitted in MSG at a time there should 
not be fuel ignition in MSG. See unique hazard SPICE-U8.

items.title: PSI-107_Engineering Documents_SPICE_Phase III Flight Safety Data Package.pdf
items.text:
SPICE PHASE III FLIGHT SAFETY DATA PACKAGE  
 
 
 
                 
SPICE-SDP-003 
 
May 2008 
47 
In the case of MSG being powered down or power failing there is a concern that a pool of fuel 
which leaks out of the Bottle Assembly or EA will ignite when the MSG is powered on. This is 
addressed in the attachment to hazard report SPICE-U5 which shows that in the worst case the 
fuel will dissipate due to molecular action in less than 28 minutes, but other factors reduce that 
time. A slow leak would mean less fuel to dissipate or allow a longer dilution time. A fast leak 
would increase mixing due to gas velocity. Since the crew is necessary for the total operation of 
SPICE, when the crew leaves the MSG it will be required that the crew turn off the hand valve 
reducing the leak potential. In the event of a power loss, when power is restored to the lab, 
racks must be individually turned back on, this includes the MSG. If a wait time of ½ hour were 
implemented it would insure adequate dilution of the fuel.  
 
In the case of impingement the leak controls mentioned before for the bottles are still valid. In 
addition, the pressurized area of the EA will be leak tested to insure that it does not leak. The 
Quick Connects (QC) softgood seal resides on the bottle side of the connection which will be 
used only once. The EA side which will mate 12 times (once for each bottle) is the metal side, 
thus reducing the risk of leakage due to seal wear. Electronics are contained inside the EA. The 
only exposed item is a switch which is a 5 volt switch. 5 volt systems are frequently used in 
flammable atmospheres (mines) due to their inability to ignite them. In addition this switch is 
sealed. The ignitor throw is a lever that the crew moves to insert the ignitor into the fuel path 
and turn on the ignitor. It is a lever on a rod which goes inside the EA to move the ignitor. There 
is a hall effect sensor (digital) which senses the proximity of the ignitor to the nozzle area  and 
electronically turns on the ignitor. Therefore there are no sparks associated with turning on the 
ignitor. There are also no sparks in the proximity of the crew’s hand to light a fuel impingement.  
See figure 16. 
 
Each Gas Bottle Assembly will be filled per approved procedure which will ensure all bottles are 
filled with the proper fuel mixtures to appropriate pressures and labeled to identify filled bottle 
contents. Structural Integrity of the Gas Bottle Assemblies including the Experiment Assembly 
Fuel Delivery System is verified by conducting proof pressure to 1.5 X system MDP of 230 psid. 
The Gas Bottle Assemblies will meet a leak rate of less than 1X10E-4 scc/sec Helium. The 
Experiment Assembly Fuel Delivery System will be verified by a decay pressure test 
 
Reference  Unique Hazard Report SPICE-U5.   
 
In the case of the crew having access to the inside of the EA and fuel leaking into it and igniting, 
the fuel is controlled by the MFC which is inhibited by the window switch (open circuit when the 
EA window is open), fuel enable on control box is off, and  the fuel switch is off.  All of these 
inhibit the MFC. In addition the Gas Bottle Assembly valve will be turned off. There are no 
ignition sources other than the ignitor itself. The inhibit switches are all 5 volt and the hall effect 
switch for the ignitor is solid state digital. The ignitor is inhibited by a window switch, the control 
box ignitor inhibit and the fact that the ignitor throw is not thrown.  Also when ever there is power 
to the experiment the EA fan will be on, which keeps the chamber below the LFL. See figure 17.  
Reference Unique Hazard Report SPICE-U8.

4.3.6.2 Combustion By-Product Release 
 
JSC toxicologist assessments of the combustion by-products of Carbon Monoxide and Carbon Dioxide 
produced by the SPICE experiment have been given a toxicity rating of 0. See Attachment A, SPICE 
Hazardous Material Summary Table HMST.  To ensure that the combustion by-products are compatible

50 
 
 
 
4.3.7 Acoustic Noise 
Acoustic noise generated by the small fan in the Experiment Assembly will not be a hazard. The SPICE 
Experiment will be in compliance to the Acoustic requirements of the MSFC-RQMT-2888.  
4.3.8 Stowage 
The Gas Bottle assemblies shown in Figure 10 will be pre-packed using two Gas Bottle Storage Cases, 
shown in figure 9. Each Gas Bottle Storage Case will contain 6 Gas Bottle Assemblies and a third 
storage Case will be used for SPICE Component storage. See sections 2.6 and 2.7. 
The SPICE Experiment Assembly along with the Gas Bottle and Component Cases will be soft stowed 
in the MPLM for launch and landing.  Stowage for launch is planned at L-48 hours.  The hardware 
configuration for stowage during launch and landing is still under development and is in work in 
conjunction with MSG.  
 
 
4.4 SPICE TEST FAILURES, ANOMALIES AND ACCIDENTS 
SPICE has had no safety related test failures, anomalies and accidents involving Qualification or Flight 
Hardware. The only test failure is related to EMI susceptibility of the camera. 
 
4.5  AGREEMENTS FROM PHASE 0/1 REVIEW AND 
SUBSEQUENT REVIEWS 
 
The following agreements/action items were taken at phase 0/1. After each action item is an answer or 
reference to the SDP text or hazard report which addresses the comment.

Power Conditioning Box, and other nominal equipment changeouts. A maintenance safety assessment 
has been completed and is included as an attachment to unique Hazard Report U-7. 
3.2 The PO agreed to note that the hardware transfer case latches are not safety-critical, since the case 
will be soft stowed and packed in foam.  This information is now included in section 4.2.1. 
3.3 The PO agreed to provide more information and pictures, along with a safety assessment, for the 
valve handle tie-wrap. Figure 10 b shows the valve handle tie-wrap constraint as well as figures 
attached to the Hazard Report SPICE U-3. An assessment of the restraint is covered in paragraph 
4.3.6.1.  
3.4 The PO agreed to confirm that there would still be airflow if the Control Box Assembly fan setting 
were set to zero. The airflow is wired to be on whenever the experiment is powered. Also the 
procedures require the crew to confirm the air flow by reading the measured air flow value off the 
laptop. See hazard report U-5. 
3.5 The PO agreed to attach a shatterable materials matrix to the 1230 hazard reporting form.   This has 
been attached to the 1230 form. 
 
3.6 The PSEs agreed to provide a shatterable materials matrix example to the PO. This was provided 
by Daniel Porter and was used to generate the matrix for SPICE. 
 
3.7 The PO agreed to determine if they could use a flow straightener made of non-frangible materials.  
This was investigated. Substitute materials did not have the same properties and replacement of 
this item would be difficult. It would also cause the acceptance vibration test to be voided. See 
controls provided in the 1230 form section 5.  
 
3.8 The PO agreed to send correspondence from Nikon to the PSEs and coordinate with the PSEs to set 
up a working group meeting to discuss COTS battery systems and schematics with EP5. This has been 
initiated (there have been a few interactions with Nikon)  Removal of the battery from the camera 
before flight will be done.  The SPICE Project has determined that the removal of the battery 
reduces the reliability of the Camera and is seeking to keep the battery in place for flight.  
 
3.9 The PO agreed to provide the EMI waiver and all bonding, grounding, power, and wire sizing 
schematics as attachments to the 1230 hazard reporting form at Phase II. These items have been added 
to the end of the 1230 form. 
 
3.10 MSFC/FD31/T. Smith agreed to provide to the PO input from ECLSS concerning the effects of 
unburned fuels and combustion byproducts on the air scrubbers of Shuttle and ISS. Tim Smith 
provided this information and its conclusion has been included in 4.3.6.1 of the SDP.  
 
3.11 The PSEs agreed to compare SPICE to its predecessor, ELF, and other similar payloads to see how 
similar hazards were handled previously and how it may apply to SPICE. This was provided by John 
Fonner.

MINUTES FOR SMOKE POINT IN CO-FLOW EXPERIMENT PHASE II FLIGHT SAFETY REVIEW ON 
JANUARY 27,  
 
NASA JSC 
Payload Safety Review Panel 
Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment 
Phase II Flight Safety Review 
 
Minutes of Meeting 
January 27, 2005 
  
1.0 INTRODUCTION 
1.1 General:  The Payload Safety Review Panel (PSRP), chaired by JSC/NA3/S. Wolf, met on January, 
2005, with representatives of GRC, the Payload Organization (PO), and MSFC at the Regents Park III 
Conference Facility for a Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) Phase II Flight Safety Review 
(FSR). JSC/NC44/J. Fonner and M. Highsmith, the supporting Payload Safety Engineers (PSEs), 
introduced the meeting and attendees (see Attachment 1).   
1.2 Background: The Phase 0/I FSR was held March 3, 2004.  
1.3 Scope: This meeting focused on the Phase II FSR. The PSRP assigned no previous Action Items 
(AIs) to this payload. The PO also summarized the Phase 0/I agreement disposition.   
1.4 Conclusion: One agreement and one action item resulted from this meeting (see Attachment 2). All 
nine Hazard Reports (HRs) were signed and approved for Phase II. This meeting completed the Phase II 
FSR.  
 
2.0 SIGNIFICANT SAFETY DISCUSSION  
2.1 SPICE Science and Hardware Overview: SPICE continues to study fundamental phenomena to 
understand the mechanisms controlling the stability and extinction of jet diffusion flames. SPICE will 
stabilize an enclosed laminar flame, measure the overall flame shape to validate the theoretical and 
numerical predictions, measure the flame stabilization heights, and measure the temperature field to 
verify flame structure predictions. The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar 
smokepoint properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the largest laminar jet 
diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity 
configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the flame 
shapes under co-flow conditions. The soot point is a simple measurement that has been found useful to 
study the influence of flow and fuel properties on the sooting propensity of flames. This information 
would help support current understanding of soot processes in laminar flames and by analogy in 
turbulent flames of practical interest. Unfortunately, while the laminar smoke-point properties of 
buoyant jet diffusion flames at normal gravity (ng) are well known, corresponding information for 
nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus, the measurements of the laminar smoke-point 
properties proposed here would also reduce the risk of future experiments involving hydrocarbon-fueled 
laminar jet diffusion flames in spacecraft.  
2.2 SPICE Hardware Overview: Hardware soft stowed in during launch and landing includes:

• Fuel Bottle Assembly: Commercial DOT bottle with Diaphragm Valve, SS tubing, QC fitting. 
• Controller Box: External to MSG, controls: radiometer, Data Recording, Fuel Enable, Ignitor 
Enable, Fuel Flow set point, Fan Flow set point and camera shutter.

The PO indicated that the radiometer measures the temperatures of the flames. 
2.3 Integration and Operations: The PO indicated that the fan will operate for chamber cooling on-
orbit. The crew can verify that the igniter is on prior to turning on the gas. The PO anticipates 10-14 
hours total operational time for the experiment with a set-up time of 45-60 minutes. Each experiment 
run lasts just a few minutes. The PO is hoping for use of the hardware and the Microgravity Science 
Glovebox (MSG) for several hours at a time. The PO clarified that the fuel nozzle changeout is manual. 
The crew procedure hazards are listed in a table.  
2.4 Safety Assessment:  
2.4.1 Form 1428, Fire Detection and Suppression Reporting Form: Approved as discussed in the 
meeting.  
2.4.2 Form 622 - Reflown and Series Payload Hardware Reflight Assessment Reporting Sheet: Not 
applicable to this payload.  
2.5 Hazard Report Discussion: The PO provides crew procedure inputs to the Payload Operations Data 
File (PODF) at MSFC.  
2.5.1 Form 1230, Flight Payload Standardized Hazard Control Report: Approved as modified in this 
meeting. The MSG integrated/series assessment will appear at Phase III. The PO indicated that the 
controller box is velcroed in place inside the MSG and that there are no crew entanglement concerns 
with the cables associated with the hardware package. Associated with Shatterable Material Release, the 
PO indicated that the flow straightener is made of Cordierite (a ceramic) and is contained inside the fan 
housing on the Experiment Assembly (EA) with a 100 mesh screen over it. The EA will be packaged in 
a clear plastic bag and will be inspected for particles before use. Any particles that escape the EA mesh 
should be captured by the MSG filter and the MSG HEPA filter. The PO clarified that the minor 
electromagnetic exceedences affect the cameras, but this is a performance issue, not a safety issue. The 
PSRP recommended that the PO match the voltage rating of the fan with the power supply to the fan 
(12V supply).  
2.5.2 SPICE-U1, Contamination of Orbiter/ISS Habitable Areas by SPICE Unburned Fuels or 
Combustion By-Products Results in Injury/Illness: Approved as modified in this meeting. The PO stated 
that the by-products consist of carbon dioxide and water, both scrubbed by the MSG filters. The 
Hazardous Materials Summary Table (HMST) is attached and under review. The PO analyzed the 
amounts, kinds, and release rates of the fuel bottle contents and determined that the contamination

hazards are reasonably benign in this payload. The PO also stated that each bottle is individually proof 
tested.  
2.5.3 SPICE-U2, Pressure System Rupture: Approved as modified in this meeting. The PO indicated that 
each gas bottle has been leak tested and filled to an appropriate pressure corresponding to the fuel 
mixtures. The PO keeps a pressure vessel log on each bottle. The QC caps will be installed during 
stowage and transit to MSG.  
2.5.4 SPICE-U3, Projectile Hazard Gas Bottle: Approved as modified in this meeting. The PO deleted 
hazard cause 2 and controls 1.2, 1.3, and 1.4 as a result of the discussion.  
2.5.5 SPICE-U4, Fire and Detonation in MPLM and ISS Stowage: Approved as modified in this meeting. 
Crew procedures have the crew marking spent bottles to prevent the crew from grabbing an empty gas 
bottle for installation. The PO described the aluminum strip inside the bottle case that is the bonding 
strap to preclude electrostatic discharge inside the bottle case: the aluminum strip is stuck to the interior 
of the top of the case in such a way that it touches the metal of the bottles when the case is closed. The 
PO indicated that any labels on the bottles will be positioned to assure the metal-to-metal contact 
between the bottles and the grounding strip. Discussion of the temporary aisle stowage of the bottle case 
led the PSRP to assign AI 1 to the PO to determine if the Station-supplied fuel stowage location 
complies with the SPICE flammability assessment restrictions. The PO will provide more details at 
Phase III.  
2.5.6 SPICE-U5, Fire in MSG: Approved as modified in this meeting. The PSRP recommended that the 
PO delete the 14,242 foot pounds reference in favor of the estimates in the table as the limits of released 
energy from the gas bottles. The pressure release exceeds the MSG interface control document limit, 
which makes this a catastrophic hazard rather than the usual critical designation.  
2.5.7 SPICE-U6, Touch Temperature Injury: Approved as modified in this meeting.  
2.5.8 SPICE-U7, Maintenance Assessment Hazard Controls: Approved as modified in this meeting.  
2.5.9 SPICE-U8, Flame Impingement During Crew Access: Approved as modified in this meeting. The 
PO clarified that the igniter cools down within less than 30 seconds. The PO has not seen the nozzles 
work loose due to gas flow –a matter of running torque versus seating torque—and indicated that gas 
flow pressure is not high enough to cause a problem. The PO has four inhibits on fuel flow and three 
inhibits on ignition. The PO agreed to provide a logic diagram depicting all of the inhibits that prevent 
fuel ignition at Phase III (Agreement 3.1).

Phase III.

items.title: PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport.pdf
items.text:
Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment 
“SPICE” 
Microgravity Science Glovebox 
Increment 19-20 (30 Day Report) 
Investigators: David Urban NASA GRC, Peter Sunderland: Univ. Maryland 
Project Scientist:  Zengguang Yuan, National Center for Space Exploration Research 
Project Manager: Robert Hawersaat NASA GRC 
 
I.  
Introduction 
 
A. 
Hypothesis 
The hypothesis of the SPICE investigation is that smoke point behavior 
will be observed for co-flowing flames and that it will show 
dependence on nozzle diameter and coflow velocity. 
 
B. 
Objectives of Investigation 
The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar smoke-point 
properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the 
largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels 
under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity configurations.  
Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify 
models of the flame shapes under co-flow conditions.  
 
C. 
Previous Mission Experience 
 
N/A 
 
D. 
Background/History of Project (Optional) 
 
The SPICE experiment was an outgrowth of the Laminar Soot Processes 
Experiment (LSP) which flew on STS 83, 94, and 107.  SPICE utilized the 
design heritage and modified the hardware from the Enclosed Laminar Flames 
Experiment (ELF) which flew in the Middeck Glovebox on STS 87. 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
 
A. 
Discussion of Method/Protocol 
 
Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, 
and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in 
the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support crew in 
Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the 
MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air.  After the tests the video 
record was analyzed to identify smoke point conditions. The associated 
coflow and fuel flow rates were obtained from digital data recorded in the 
video. The smoke point lengths, LSP, were obtained from the video record 
and are the measured distance from the burner tip to the tip of the luminous 
flame on the flame axis.

items.title: PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport.pdf
items.text:
III. Results 
 
A. 
List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
 
SPICE operated very successfully with the only significant anomaly being the 
accumulation of soot in the outlet screen which changed the flow behavior in 
the duct.  This was corrected by a crew member using the vacuum to clean the 
outlet screen on June 15. 
B. 
Completeness/Quality of Data 
During Increment 18 SPICE conducted 108 test points completing its nominal 
test matrix. During Increments 19/20 SPICE conducted 155 additional test 
points the provided improved resolution of the smoke points and allowed us to 
explore further limits in the parameter space. 
C. Status of Data Analysis:  The data from the down linked video have been analyzed 
for flame length and smoke point flow rate.  These have resulted in a meeting apper 
and a draft journal paper.  More work will be conducted with analysis of the digital 
luminance data from the Nikon.   
 
D. 
Preliminary Research Findings: 
 See attached paper below

items.text:
1 
2009 Fall Technical Meeting  
Organized by the Eastern States Section of the Combustion Institute  
and Hosted by the University of Maryland College Park 
October 18-21, 2009 
Laminar Smoke Points of  
Microgravity Coflow Diffusion Flames 
K.T. Dotsona, P.B. Sunderlanda, Z.–G. Yuanb, D.L. Urbanc 
aDepartment of Fire Protection Engineering, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA 
bNational Center for Space Exploration Research, Cleveland, OH, USA 
cNASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, USA 
 
Laminar smoke points were measured in nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in air coflow aboard the 
International Space Station as part of the Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPICE). Smoke points were found 
for ethylene, propane, propylene, and mixtures of 50 and 75% propylene by volume in nitrogen. Burner diameters 
were 0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm and coflow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. These flames afford good control over 
residence time via variations in dilution, burner diameter, and coflow velocity. Increasing coflow velocity decreases 
luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. 
Smaller burners have longer smoke points for coflowing flames. These trends can be explained qualitatively by 
considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate 
divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases.  
1. Introduction 
Soot formation is an important unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to 
be responsible for up to 50,000 premature deaths in the U.S. [1] and is believed to contribute to 
climate change and glacial melting [2]. Radiation from soot in flames allows reading by candle-
light but also contributes to heat loads in engines and the spread of unwanted fires. Smoking 
flames emit carbon monoxide, which is the major cause of death in fires [3].  
The smoke point is the condition (or length) where a flame begins to emit soot. Smoke points 
indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal gravity, laminar smoke 
points have been measured for many gaseous and condensed fuels [4–9]. Laminar smoke points 
have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions [10] and radiative loss factions [11] of 
turbulent diffusion flames. Yang et al. [12] found that gas turbine soot emissions correlate very 
well with a threshold sooting index (TSI) based on fuel molecular weight divided by the laminar 
smoke point. Smoke points have been shown to correlate with the smoke release from turbulent 
buoyant flames [13] and have been applied to developing general soot models for computational 
combustion simulations [14] and heat release measurements [15]. 
In a 1988 paper [16], Glassman predicted that smoke points would not occur in nonbuoyant gas-
jet flames. He based this on the assumption that residence time scales with the square root of fuel 
flow rate in normal gravity but is independent of flow rate in microgravity flames. Subsequent 
work [17] observed smoke points of nonbuoyant flames aboard a parabolic aircraft and used 
numerical predictions to show that residence time increases with flame length for nonbuoyant 
flames without co-flow. Urban et al. [18] reported smoke points of microgravity flames observed 
on a space shuttle. Microgravity smoke point measurements are difficult in parabolic aircraft

items.title: PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport.pdf
items.text:
2 
owing to g-jitter and in drop facilities owing to limited test times. 
Attributing smoke point behavior to total residence time helps with qualitative explanations of 
smoke point behavior but to date has not yielded successful quantitative correlations [8]. This 
may be because smoke points arise from a competition between the times available for soot 
formation and soot oxidation. Delichatsios and co-workers suggested that smoke point length is 
proportional to soot formation time [19–20]. Quantitative correlations may also be possible from 
an examination of radiative losses, which have been observed to be 20 – 30% for normal-gravity 
smoke point flames and to increase with adiabatic flame temperature [5]. 
Soot is transported in flames by convection and thermophoresis. By varying the burner diameter, 
coflow velocity, and fuel dilution, flame shape and residence times in the soot formation and 
soot oxidation regions can be changed. A decrease in coflow velocity will generally increase 
entrainment of flow towards the flame axis. 
Kent and Wagner [21] found that smoke burn out in the oxidative region of the flame ceases 
when the tip of a buoyant diffusion flame cools to approximately 1300 K. Urban et al. [22] found 
that the tip of a nonbuoyant (microgravity) flame reaches 1000 K at its smoke point. In buoyant 
flames this decrease in temperature is attributed primarily to heat conduction, while in 
nonbuoyant flames it is attributed largely to radiative quenching [23]. The radiative quenching 
effect causes a visible tip opening in nonbuoyant smoke points of flames of relatively long 
residence time [22]. 
A recent 2.5 s drop tower study by Jeon et al. [24] found that for small coflow velocities the soot 
volume fraction increases with coflow velocity. This was attributed to an increase in 
temperature. Lin and Faeth [7,25] studied the effects of coflow velocity on weakly-buoyant 
flames near the smoke point. They observed flames in normal gravity, but at low pressures to 
reduce the effects of gravity. They found that increasing the coflow velocity reduced soot 
volume fractions and increased the smoke point length. This was attributed to decreased flame 
residence time and modified soot pathlines. Refs. [7 and 24] both showed that luminous flame 
lengths decrease with increasing coflow velocity. Their burner diameters, 7 and 10 mm, 
respectively, were much larger than those considered here. 
Faeth and co-workers [25–27] applied the flame shape analyses of Spalding [28] and 
Mahalingam et al. [29] to nonbuoyant gas-jet flames to obtain

neglected. With this in mind, Eqs. (1–2) can be rearranged to

Thus motivated, the objectives of this study are: 
1. to 
measure 
nonbuoyant 
smoke 
points 
of 
propane, 
ethylene, 
propylene, 
and 
propylene/nitrogen mixtures, 
2. to identify the effects of coflow velocity and burner diameter on the smoke points, and 
3. to correlate the luminous flame lengths. 
2. Experimental 
The Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) module was brought to the International 
Space Station (ISS) in 2008. It was operated in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) by 
various crew members in 2009. Smoke points were attempted for all fuels for fuel jet diameters 
of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm. The conditions for which smoke points were found are summarized in 
Table 1. In some cases (e.g., tests involving ethylene) the fuel supply was depleted before 
desired smoke points could be found, as the supply was limited to two 75 cc bottles of each fuel 
at gage pressures of 760 – 1440 kPa, depending on the fuel. 
 The SPICE module contains a rectangular duct that has an approximately 76 mm square cross 
section with rounded corners. A DC fan supplies coflowing air from the glovebox contents. The 
air passes through a honeycomb and screen to reduce swirl and then enters the duct. The air and 
combustion products leave the duct through a perforated copper plate followed by a copper 
screen. The screen is 50 mm upstream of the burner discharge and the plate is 120 mm 
downstream. Fan voltage is varied to control the coflow velocity, which is measured with a hot-
wire anemometer between the inlet honeycomb and screen. This anemometer was calibrated in 
normal gravity using a hot-wire anemometer 36 mm downstream of the duct entrance. Fuel flow 
rate was adjusted manually and controlled with a mass flow meter. The flames were ignited with 
a hot-wire ignitor. Video was recorded with an analog color video camera and downlinked in real 
time. Still images were recorded with a 12 bit Nikon™ D100 single-lens reflex color digital still 
camera (with 3008 × 2000 pixels) with a 60 mm lens. 
Most of the tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting 
the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and 
simultaneously by the ground support crew in Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after 
each two such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air.  
After the tests the video record was analyzed to identify smoke point conditions. The associated 
coflow and fuel flow rates were obtained from digital data recorded in the video. The smoke 
point lengths, LSP, were obtained from the video record and are the measured distance from the 
burner tip to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis. The luminous flame tips were not 
sharply defined in most images, but rather involved a transition from bright yellow to black 
across an axial distance of 2 – 5 mm. Flame height was thus measured to the point where the 
centerline grayscale intensity changed most rapidly between these yellow and black regions. This 
helped reduce the sensitivity of measured flame height to camera exposure settings. 
Smoke points were obtained for five fuels, as summarized in Table 1. Smoke points were

items.title: PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_30-DayPostFlightReport.pdf
items.text:
4 
attempted with methane, but could not be obtained before the flames impinged on the plate at the 
end of the duct. Also shown in Table 1 are the ranges of various parameters for which 
microgravity smoke points were observed. 
3. Results and Discussion 
Some smoke points, propane and ethylene in particular, were identified by the onset of gradual 
(rather than sharp) dimming and reddening of the luminous flame tip in the downstream 
direction. Rounding of the tip also was associated with the smoke point. For conditions 
sufficiently above the smoke point, quenched soot could be seen leaving the flame. The brightest 
flames did not always display significant reddening or darkening near their tips, except well 
above the smoke point. This occurred for the pure propylene and propylene mixtures, and the 
smoke point was identified by the rapid transition to an open-tipped, soot emitting flame.  
The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of 
fuel or air. Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were generally more luminous than 
those of methane, ethylene, and propane, attributed to their higher propensity to form soot. The 
smoke point transition was more abrupt in the propylene-based fuels than for propane or 
ethylene. Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, especially those with high coflow, 
long length, and low fuel velocity, and is attributed to non-uniform coflow. This effect was small 
and did not prevent clear measurement of flame length. 
Figure 1 shows images for representative flames near their smoke points. Two sequences are 
shown, and in both the smoke point occurs between the third and fourth flames. In the top 
sequence, coflow velocity decreases from left to right at constant fuel flow rate. This increases 
luminous flame length and reduces the smoke point leading to soot emission. The luminous 
length decreases in the fourth image owing to incomplete combustion. In the bottom sequence 
fuel flow rate is increased at constant coflow velocity, increasing flame length as expected. As 
seen in Fig. 1, luminous length is more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in 
coflow velocity.

items.text:
SPICE-MEM-010 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Page 1 of 2 
 
Memorandum SPICE-MEM-010 
 
 
 
 
 
TO: 
 
Tibor Lorik, SPICE Project Lead, ZIN Technologies, Inc. 
 
FROM: 
Kevin Magee, Project Engineer, ZIN Technologies, Inc. 
 
SUBJECT: 
SPICE Flow Duct Velocity Measurements 
 
DATE:  
July 6, 2009 
______________________________________________________________ 
 
This Memo addresses the SPICE flow duct velocity measurements, which were performed by Kevin 
Magee on the flight hardware from June 16-24, 2008.  A hot wire anemometer probe was used to 
measure the air velocity at various points within the flow duct.  This probe was passed into the duct 
through a special multi-piece top window with probe ports at the desired locations.  Unused ports were 
taped shut on the inside and outside to prevent leakage and minimize flow disturbances.  The window 
itself was assembled and sealed with Kapton tape around its perimeter. 
 
The probe used was a TSI, Inc., Model 1261A miniature boundary layer probe (S/N# 012077) with a 
T1.5 (coated tungsten platinum) wire and a 56 ohm control resistor to give a 260oC operating 
temperature.  Its calibration was performed in a free jet facility on April 28, 2006. 
 
Measurements were taken at two axial stations of 13 and 56 mm as measured by the permanent scale 
bonded to the floor of the duct.  These locations are where the tip of the probe was located, not where 
the ports were located since the probe curves forward into the air flow.  At each axial station, 
measurements were taken at three width locations: the duct centerline, 20 mm off the centerline 
towards the back wall (called the “inside” position), and 20 mm off the centerline towards the front 
window (called the “outside” position).  At each width position, measurements were taken at three 
heights: 19, 36, and 57 mm off the floor of the duct.  It should be noted that the 36 mm height 
corresponds to the height of the nozzle, which was installed for the tests.  However, no flow out of the 
nozzle was done during the tests.  All locations are shown in Figure 1. 
 
At each measured position, the anemometer probe’s velocity readings were recorded for FAN dial 
settings of 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10.  The FAN and AIR readings were also noted.  Plots were then created 
to compare the probe velocity, AIR reading, and FAN reading for the different FAN dial settings.  
Velocity profile plots were also generated at the various axial stations in both width and height.  These 
plots and the raw data can be found in the spreadsheets at the following location. 
 
(Z:) Zindata1\zinapp\Shares\MRDOC\60107_086_SPP\SPICE\Duct Flow Data

items.title: PSI-107_Presentations_IP-C Crew training 2010.pdf
items.text:
INTRODUCTION 
•
Three investigations will be performed:   SPICE, SLICE, and BASS.   
•
These investigations will be performed inside the Microgravity Science 
Glovebox (MSG). 
•
SPICE is based on the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) hardware which 
flew on STS-87 in 1997. 
•
SPICE hardware is already on-orbit.  It has successfully completed all of its 
objectives with the collection of 200 data points in the first half of 2009. 
Spare gas onboard will now be used to collect additional data.  New fuel is 
being flown on ULF5 to support the SLICE and BASS experiments. 
•
SPICE hardware will also be used to perform SLICE and BASS. 
•
SPICE burns different fuels to investigate the point at which they begin to 
smoke.  
•
SLICE burns different fuels to investigate the structure of flames when lifted 
from the fuel nozzle.   
•
BASS burns different materials to investigate how they burn in microgravity.

items.title: PSI-107_Presentations_IP-C Crew training 2010.pdf
items.text:
The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find 
the laminar smoke-point properties of 
nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the 
properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion 
flames that do not emit soot) for two fuel types 
under different nozzle diameter / co-flow velocity 
configurations.  
 
SPICE will stabilize an enclosed laminar flame, 
measure the overall flame shape to validate the 
theoretical and numerical predictions, measure 
the flame stabilization heights, and measure the 
temperature field to verify flame structure 
predictions. 
SPICE Science Overview 
4

Target Setting: The target setting is just above the setting that 
produces a distinct edge (only a small portion of the tip will emit 
smoke). The smoke will probably emerge from the center of the tip 
but may emerge at the tip edges (horns) for the larger nozzle. The 
pictures show the onset of smoke points for various fuels on the 
KC-135. The size of the flame when it emits smoke is a fuel 
property. The expected size sequence will be Propylene, Ethylene, 
Propane and Methane (probably no smoke point). The diluted 
propylene smoke points will be longer than pure propylene. 
 
SPICE Smoke Point Determination Cue Card  
Background:  The smoke point is the flame length, 
above which, soot particles are no longer consumed in 
the flame and instead emerge through the flame tip 
and glow as they cool. The glowing soot causes a 
change from a sharp edge to a gradual transition 
between the bright flame and black background. 
 
Advisory note: For the test points with the 0.4 mm 
nozzle, the possibility exists that the flame could blow 
off. When this happens, the blue flame-base no longer 
touches the nozzle. When the base of the flame starts 
to separate from the nozzle, reduce the flow rate until 
it is well attached as the smoke height is not 
achievable.

SLICE Science Background 
•
The goal of the SLICE investigation is to investigate the structure of lifting 
and lifted flames; whereby the flame detaches from the nozzle and 
stabilizes at a downstream position.  
•
The results of the SLICE experiment will be used to minimize risk and 
maximize the scientific return of the CLD (Coflow Laminar Diffusion) 
Flame experiment, which is one of the four ACME (Advanced Combustion 
via Microgravity Experiments) investigations that are currently in 
development for conduct within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  
6 
The lifted nature of the flames can be discerned from the outward flare of the 
flame base in the example images below (which are not at the same scale) and 
the distance from the nozzle tip (which is not visible).  
Are CLD or ACME the approved names?  I could not find them.  (these 
payloads are in-development and haven’t touched  the ops world yet)

items.title: PSI-107_Presentations_IP-C Crew training 2010.pdf
items.text:
BASS Science Background 
•
The BASS investigation tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity burn as well 
if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being 
identical (ie. pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature).  
•
To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended 
microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft. If this 
hypothesis is true, it implies serious safety concerns over the utility and margin of 
safety provided NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 (upward flammability test used to evaluate 
materials intended for use in the habitable environments of US spacecraft).  Practical, 
realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames 
which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire 
burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).  
•
There are important differences in the suppression of fires in space compared to on 
Earth. On Earth it is understood that best results are generally obtained when the 
extinguisher “attacks” the base of the flame, which is both the stabilization point and 
the point of fresh air entrainment. For a fire burning in microgravity, the best point of 
application of suppressant may not be immediately apparent, especially for a partially 
obstructed flame or a wake-stabilized flame. Depending on the geometry of the flame 
and the characteristics of the extinguisher (distance from flame, dispersion angle) it is 
possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the 
flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen. 
7

items.title: PSI-107_Presentations_IP-C Crew training 2010.pdf
items.text:
Earth Applications 
•
SPICE 
 
The smoke-point phenomena is a classical metric in the understanding of the heat 
release and spread rate of fires. It is commonly used in fire modeling on Earth and to 
understand the soot growth and emission by flames. The dominant characteristics of 
many flames of practical interest are nonbuoyant. SPICE seeks to extend our 
understanding by looking at the interaction of ambient flow with the smoke point, 
enabling us to better predict heat release from non-buoyant flames in practical 
combustors (e.g. jet engines and furnaces). 
•
SLICE 
 
The twin purposes for the SLICE research are increased efficiency and reduced 
pollutant emission in practical combustion devices. More explicitly, the experiment is 
being conducted to advance combustion modeling capability, which “allows system 
designers to improve efficiency and reduce harmful pollutants in ways never before 
possible” (as stated by an external reviewer of the SLICE experiment). In other 
words, the SLICE research is being conducted to advance energy technology and 
improve our global environment. 
•
BASS 
 
It is highly desirable to develop a new and/or improved Earth-based test method for 
material flammability. The data obtained in this experiment will begin to bridge the 
gap between the normal gravity method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual 
material flammability in microgravity 
9

items.text:
vi 
ABSTRACT
The primary scientific explorations of this thesis work are to better understand (a) 
microgravity  fire-suppression of untested extinguisher, (b) combustion kinetic model 
refinement of renewable fuel butanol (C4H9OH) isomers, and (c) directly induced cool 
flame dynamics of higher n-alkane fuels from an isolated small droplet combustion 
perspective employing computational fluid dynamics with comprehensive chemical 
kinetics. The chronological development of the research direction shifts from a relatively 
small fuel like methanol (CH3OH) to heavier straight paraffinic fuel n-decane (n-C10H22). 
The first installment of the thesis is directed towards answering the feasibility of then-
newly considered fire suppressant xenon (Xe) for microgravity space application by the 
National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Methanol was used as model 
fuel to assess the combustion behavior under xenon-rich environment. The 
comprehensive analysis revealed that xenon promotes longer burning time and higher 
flame temperature compared to existing other diluents/extinguishers and can support hot 
flame with much lesser oxygen content than its counterparts. The exceptionally low 
thermal diffusivity of xenon is identified to be responsible for the significantly higher 
peak gas temperature and prolonged burn time. This detailed analysis clearly debilitates 
the potential of xenon as a next-generation fire-suppressant for microgravity applications 
and helped NASA in safeguard financial investment for International Space Station (ISS) 
experiments using xenon.

items.title: PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
items.text:
vii 
The second installment of the thesis outlines the efforts directed towards 
improving the gas phase kinetic model of butanol isomers based on droplet combustion 
experiments and computations. This is a unique contribution where the traditional gas-
phase experiment/theory-driven kinetic model is further refined in light of critical 
recommendations from the droplet combustion analysis. The comprehensive kinetic 
model of Sarathy et al. (Combust. Flame, 2012) is one of the two widely used model for 
butanol isomers which has been extensively validated against homogeneous gas phase 
experiments. The numerical simulation of the butanol droplet combustion experiments at 
atmospheric conditions predicted the faster burning rate and larger flame diameter using 
the above model. An exhaustive perturbation analysis is carried on chemical, 
thermodynamic and transport parameters influences (while simultaneously isolating their 
cross-influences) to pinpoint the root cause of faster burning tendency of the model. The 
synthesized results from this huge variable-matric perturbation revealed that the isomer-
specific species transport parameters were culpable, and recommendations were made to 
update those Lennard-Jones potential parameters. Once updated, the computational 
predictions significantly improves for the Sarathy et al. model based on the feedback 
from droplet combustion.  
The final segment of the thesis discusses the direct initiation of cool flame 
combustion for submillimeter-sized higher n-alkane droplets (n-heptane and n-decane) 
for possible terrestrial experiments without the necessity of radiative extinction as 
frequently encountered onboard the ISS experiments. It has been found that the 
dimensionality of the droplet (Do = 0.5 mm) statistically reduces the possibility of 
achieving direct cool flame burn for the droplet by simply varying the ignition energy

items.title: PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
items.text:
viii 
initiation. Therefore, it was conceptualized that a combination of a reduced ignition 
source and induction chemistry modulation may hold the possibility of direct initiation of 
cool flame for n-C7H16 and n-C10H22 even in ground-based drop tower experiments. To 
facilitate this idea, we numerically investigate the droplet combustion under selective 
ozone (O3) augmented ambient where O3 serves as an induction chemistry modulator 
through its liberation of atomic O via molecular decomposition. The available atomic O 
then reacts with the surrounding fuel producing OH radical, and eventually water and 
heat. This latter heat input acts as a secondary thermal feedback to the droplet surface 
maintaining steady surface burning rate which then stabilizes the cool flame very near the 
droplet surface. It was found that the fuel physical properties, especially flash point, play 
a decisive role in determining the nature of the initial cool flame dynamics and the ozone 
requirements. Higher flash point fuel (here, n-C10H22) is likely to undergo initial dumped 
cool flame oscillation than its lower value counterpart (n-C7H16) and will require higher 
O3 loading under identical ambient. In the near-limit condition, such directly introduced 
cool flame fails to attain a steady burn and enters into a continuously evolving oscillatory 
cool flame. Analyses further indicate that the dynamic interaction of degenerate chain 
branching and chain termination/propagation reaction classes of QOOH (Q=CnH2n) 
species associated with the low-temperature kinetic regimes, and continuous fuel leakage 
across the flame location contribute to the ever-increasing trends of the oscillation 
magnitude.

items.text:
ix 
PREFACE
This thesis reports the combustion behavior of sphero-symmetric small droplets 
for two different classes of fuels (oxygenated alcohols and n-alkanes) under diversified 
ambient conditions with the individual unique objective for each study. The research 
outcomes from this dissertation work were timely published in the leading combustion 
field-specific journals. The author prepared the thesis chapters 3-7 (in consultation with 
the thesis adviser) from those published articles with necessary amendments following 
the guidelines from the graduate school of the University of South Carolina, SC, USA. 
As a consequence, chapter relevant thorough background information from literature is 
provided at the beginning of each chapter. However, an abridged critical review of the 
droplet combustion literature is also included in the 1st chapter to complement the 
rationale of this Ph.D. work. It should be noted that the necessary approval from the 
publishing agencies and collaborators were sought in advance for this dissertation. The 
list of correlated chapters and the associated published article can be found on page 11.

1.1 PROBLEM STATEMENT 
The efficient conversion of fossil fuels to useful energy has been an active area of 
research ever since the development of steam engine by Sir James Watt and the post-
industrial revolution [1]. Since then, fossil fuels have incredibly the preferred choice of 
energy production in the form of ‘shaft output’ from the prime movers (i.e., engines, gas 
turbines, propellers, boilers and so on). Consequently, it is anticipated that the fossil fuels 
(gaseous and condensed phase) will also remain the automatic choice of ground, marine 
and aviation transportation systems for forth-coming future [2]. Such a prolific use of fossil 
fuels is primarily due to their extraordinary energy density irrespective of any defined 
metric (unit mass or volume basis) as illustrated in Figs. 1.1 and 1.2. Therefore, despite the 
resurgence of renewable energy sources in recent times (solar, wind, tidal, biomass etc.), 
combustion technology will remain the principal source of energy conversion for centuries. 
 
 
Figure 1.1 Comparison of energy content per unit volume for different fossil fuels and battery types 
(normalized against the conventional gasoline). Courtesy- United States energy information 
administration (https://www.eia.gov).

items.title: PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
items.text:
3 
 
 
Figure 1.2 Comparison of volumetric energy density for different energy sources. The plot is 
recreated after the reported data in reference [3]. Data for wind is for 5 m/s.  
 
 
However, the boon of combustion technology is not a singular entity and is often 
rationally criticized for contributing to the harmful emissions, posing detrimental effects 
on the environment as well as human health. Therefore, modern combustion technology 
simultaneously aims for higher conversion efficiency and lower perilous emission to tackle 
the ever stringent regulatory constraints [4, 5]. In relation to the fuel combustion, its 
ignition, flame development, and pollutant formation are inevitably interconnected. 
Therefore, the fundamental insights regarding the flame dynamics and species evolutions 
(including the harmful ones) are typically studied in standardized combustion and/or 
oxidation settings at desired thermodynamic states (P, T). Historically, such fundamental 
endeavors are carried out extensively using shock tubes [6], flow reactors [7], jet-stirred 
reactors [8], rapid compression machines [9], burner stabilized premixed flames [10] and 
opposed diffusion flame burners [11].  Although these test facilities are far from practical 
ideality for combustion devices, they offer unique opportunities to individually study 
ignition, flame characteristics and species evolution (i.e., reaction kinetics). In addition,

items.title: PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
items.text:
4 
due to their simplified flow field, the detail kinetic analysis is possible for these zero- or 
one-dimensional problems. While these experimental platforms and associated kinetic 
analyses serve as the foundational stage for the combustion research, they have two major 
concerns- (a) the studies have to be conducted in gas phase reactant mixtures, and (b) they 
are either steady state [7, 8, 10, 11] with transport effect, or transient in nature [6, 9] 
ignoring altogether the transport effect. Therefore, there exists a natural gap in studying the 
fuel combustion considering both the unsteady flame dynamics and the transport effect. 
The investigation of isolated single fuel droplet combustion in absence of (under 
significantly reduced) gravity offers a unique opportunity to probe liquid fuel combustion 
under unsteady transport dependent environment [12]. With such an advantageous 
canonical configuration, the physical problem becomes classical Stefan flow problem [13] 
where enthalpy and species transports are one-dimensional in radial coordinate. 
Computationally, such a facile reacting fluid domain can be modeled with detailed kinetics 
[14, 15], even to validate associated submodels, e.g., radiation model [16, 17], transport 
model (multicomponent vs. mixture average) [18] and water dissolution model [15, 19-
21].  
Interestingly, although one-dimensional droplet combustion may appear simple in 
configuration, it has relevance to the complex spray environment by incorporating moving 
boundary effects, unsteady heat conduction and mass diffusion in the droplet and 
surrounding gas, variable properties (dependent on temperature and composition), phase 
equilibrium at the interface, radiation dynamics, and a detailed kinetic mechanism for the 
combustion process. Traditionally, isolated droplet combustion studies (with or without the 
gravity) are conducted to understand the fuel ignition, burning rate characteristics, flame

items.title: PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
items.text:
5 
dynamics and spreading [22-24]. Therefore, there is a need to explore the outer regime of 
conventionality to apply droplet combustion approach, namely- (a) fire extinguishment, (b) 
kinetic model validation and improvement, and (c) new combustion technology study. This 
thesis work is dedicated to exploring these less-ventured pathways where computational 
droplet combustion can enhance the understanding of liquid fuel combustion. 
 
1.2 LITERATURE REVIEW 
 
Study of single isolated or array of isolated droplets has existed nearly seven 
decades since the pioneering work of G.A.E. Godsave [25, 26].  These initial investigations 
were primarily empirical in nature, therefore covering a wide range of fuels, e.g., benzene, 
tertiary butyl benzene, decalin, n-heptane etc. Along the line, Kumagai and coworkers were 
the forerunners in studying the combustion behavior of isolated droplet under reduced 
gravity environment [27, 28]. These investigators are the first to conduct research on 
spherical diffusion flames in absence of gravity and formulated a theoretical framework to 
study it numerically. In an independent study, Goldsmith and Penner [29] improved the 
simplified model of Godsave and also performed extensive experimental investigations 
[30] to delineate the role of increased ambient oxidizer, pressure and temperature on 
burning rate. To further excel in understanding the droplet combustion in terms of high-
pressure, Spalding [31] proposed a transient theoretical model to determine the frame 
locations and burning rate at elevated pressure conditions. By deploying statistical 
formulations, Willams [32] then tried to predict the droplet growth, new droplet formation, 
collision and aerodynamic forces on droplets under spray condition. He further explored 
the validity of typical droplet burning steady-state assumptions and showed that these

items.title: PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
items.text:
6 
simplifying assumptions can lead up to 20% error in predictions [33]. In contemporary 
time, researchers also engaged continuous photography and video recording techniques 
[34] to understand the dynamics of droplet combustion. As the importance of droplet 
combustion became more prominent from spray perspective, researchers like Hottel et al. 
[35] experimentally pursued the combustion behavior of different heavy fuels. 
The pivotal works of the fifties (i.e., till 1960) played an instrumental role to 
motivate the researchers to study droplet combustion with multifaceted research objectives. 
Combustion of the droplet and its subsequent burning behavior has been studied for rocket 
combustor application [36], high-pressure systems [37-39], denotation configuration [40], 
super-critical condition [41], evaporation model development [42] and for the ignition and 
extinction of droplets [43, 44]. Kassoy and Williams are the first to propose a theoretical 
formulation accounting for variable property effect on droplet combustion along with finite 
rate chemistry [45], and showed that numerical predictions improved significantly over 
constant fluid property approach.  
A critical evaluation of the presented studies suggests that while these improved 
our understanding of droplet combustion, they are based either convective experiments 
(forced or/and natural) or simplified computations, both of which required further research 
to address complicated spray environment. Consequently, there had been a necessity to 
address more practically relevant droplet combustion studies. In their innovative 
experiments, Faeth and Lazar [46] conducted tests for droplet combustion of alcohol and 
paraffinic fuels in the downstream of the flat flame burner to emulate droplet burning under 
gaseous product distribution environment. These authors also extended their research 
efforts towards bipropellant droplet combustion near critical point condition [47]. In an

items.title: PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
items.text:
7 
independent study, Kumagai et al. [48] conducted a ‘paradigm-shift’ study of isolated 
droplet combustion under free-fall condition retaining the spherical flame configuration to 
decoupling the role of external convective perturbation. Concurrently, Aldred and 
coworkers [49] experimentally explored the transient dynamics of relatively smaller 
droplet combustion with a conclusion of the inadequacy of the-then existing theoretical 
models. In the form of theoretical treatment, Law [50] proposed an asymptotic analysis of 
ignition and extinction of liquid fuel droplet which was then further improved to account 
the internal mixing considering the unsteady effect of multicomponent droplet [51]. Based 
on this contributing works, Law and Sirignano [52, 53] developed fully transient droplet 
combustion model. Crespo and Linan [54] also deployed asymptotic analysis to explore 
the effect of unsteady effects of droplet combustion and evaporation. In pursuit of 
developing more realistic theoretical models, Law et al. [55] improved their previous 
formulations incorporating the convective effect to unsteady multicomponent model. By 
the late 1970s, an emulsion of water-fuel mixture received attention across the combustion 
communities due to its relevance to practical application, and it was venture as a binary 
mixture under droplet configuration [56-58]. At this point, the research direction steered 
towards a better understanding of the role of reaction chemistry on droplet combustion 
through finite rate kinetics [59, 60]. Expressing the hot flame chemistry with single 
irreversible reaction step, Sirignano [61, 62] refined the previously developed single 
droplet theory under convective environment. Comprehensive details of the literature 
discussed so far can also be found in the review article of Law [63] and Faeth [64]. 
With the advancement of computational tools and diagnostics capabilities, freely 
falling [65] and micro- and/or reduced-gravity [66-68] droplet combustion gained

items.title: PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
items.text:
8 
popularity due to its geometrical constraint with well-defined boundary conditions. The 
works lead by F.L. Dryer at the Princeton University were the first to deploy computational 
fluid dynamics (CFD) in analyzing sphero-symmetric droplet combustion invoking 
detailed kinetics [69, 70]. These authors have successfully demonstrated the necessity of 
detailed kinetics in reproducing the experimental targets against reduced- or micro-gravity 
tests [71]. At this point in time, a careful synthesis of four decades of droplet combustion 
research (1950s-1990s) illustrates that the research thrust was first initiated by the 
empirical terrestrial experimentation (with or without gravity) which simultaneously led to 
the theoretical development of isolated droplet combustion phenomena. Subsequently, the 
role of chemistry was included in numerical consideration through single-step finite rate 
chemistry, and finally the development of CFD analysis with detailed kinetics. 
Beginning in the early nineties (the 1990s), the research direction with isolated 
droplet combustion shifts from global observational and/or fundamental targets to 
individualistic physical phenomena base understanding. To accommodate such objectives, 
methanol (CH3OH) was a generic choice of fuel due to its simplified chemistry and non-
sooting tendency [16, 19-21, 72-81]. To a lesser extent, ethanol was also studied for 
reduced gravity ambient [15]. These relatively recent studies primarily enriched our 
knowledge for specific physical cases, e.g.- water dissolution, diffusion and internal mixing 
limit, radiation influence on burning etc. Subsequently, researchers across the globe 
contributed to pushing the frontier limit of isolated sphero-symmetric droplet combustion 
for complex fuels and their mixtures [14, 18, 82-91] considering the necessity of 
practicality and to explaining the emergence of new combustion concepts (e.g., multiphase 
cool flames [92, 93]). To highlight the phenomenal scientific contributions originating

items.title: PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
items.text:
9 
from the isolated droplet combustion study over the last three decades is beyond the scope 
of this literature review, and is well documented in the review articles of Aggarwal [23] 
and Sirignano [24], and in respective chapters hereafter. However, a careful reexamination 
of all these major studies shows that the isolated droplet combustion can be further 
deployed to harness deeper insight for (a) fire suppressant effectiveness, (b) 
improving/refining detailed chemistry to complex fuels, and (c) oscillatory behavior of low 
temperature driven cool flames.  This existing knowledge gap  was the main intrinsic 
motivation to pursue this dissertation work in the field of isolated droplet combustion 
employing high fidelity CFD code with detailed kinetics. 
 
1.3 SCOPE AND ORGANIZATION OF THE THESIS WORK 
 
Since the seminal works of Godsave [25, 26], attention for isolated droplet has been 
given exclusively for large diameter droplets (order of several millimeters, 
analytical/experimental/computational) including the experiments conducted onboard the 
international space station [89]. To facilitate a gravityless environment for large diameter 
droplets, testings were primarily conducted in either space shuttle experiments or in the 
ISS as a terrestrial test site would demand very high drop tower free-fall height. To the 
contrary, smaller droplets (Do < 1.0 mm) require much less drop hight, thus opening the 
opportunity to do the testing in ground-based facility avoiding the expansive space-based 
testing [94]. This thesis work focuses on the numerical analysis of small diameter droplet 
combustion for a variety of practical fuels to extend the potentiality of droplet combustion 
in understanding the fire dynamics, reaction kinetics, and cool flame combustion.

10 
 
Chapter 1 briefly introduces the general problem statement of this thesis work, 
followed by its scopes and organization. This chapter also registers the significant archival 
publications arising from this Ph.D. research. 
 
Chapter 2 outlines the details of the numerical framework of the one-dimensional 
droplet combustion code that has been used in this thesis. This chapter first introduces the 
general conservation equations followed by the descriptions of the sub-models 
incorporated here, namely- radiation, diffusion, fiber heat feedback and water dissolution 
models. 
 
Chapters 3-7 contain the core sections of this thesis research. As already hinted, the 
broader goal of this investigation is to extend the droplet combustion capability to the field 
of fire extinction, reaction kinetics and new combustion concept (here, the cool flame of 
the smaller droplet). In chapter 3, the potential of an untested fire extinguisher gas- xenon 
(Xe), for microgravity application is explored through the computation of droplet 
combustion. Methanol has been used as model fuel for this study and a prior validation of 
the computation was made against NASA ISS FLEX-563 test data containing 63% (v/v) 
of xenon. Necessary recommendations were made to the NASA for xenon’s limiting 
viability as a next-generation fire suppressant. 
 
Chapter 4 and 5 discuss the combustion analysis of n-butanol and its isomers 
primarily focusing on the kinetic aspects as viewed from smaller droplet burning 
perspective. These studies are also complemented by the experimental counterpart 
performed by the collaborators at the Cornell University (led by Professor C.T. Avedisian) 
in a drop tower facility supporting small droplet combustion (Do < 0.6 mm).

items.title: PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
items.text:
11 
 
Chapter 6 shifts the research direction towards the numerical exploration of a 
concurrent new research topic- ‘cool flame’ from multiphase droplet perspective. Cool 
flame phenomena in droplet configuration have been investigated previously for large 
diameters only with a preceding extinction of the precursor hot flame. Here, we advance 
the mechanistic concept of directly instituted cool flame for sub-millimeter sized n-alkane 
(n-C7H16, n-C10H22) droplets without the necessity of radiative extinction of the hot flame. 
Subsequently, in chapter 7, the cool flame has been studied in a near-limiting condition 
where a quasi-steady cool flame transitions to an ever-increasing oscillatory flame. The 
inception, growth, and dynamics of such an oscillatory flame are discussed at length in this 
chapter. Finally, chapter 8 serves as the closure of this thesis highlighting major 
contributions and recommendations for future research direction.

2.1 MATHEMATICAL FORMULATION 
The transient, sphero-symmetric droplet combustion model simulating liquid phase 
droplet oxidizing in an infinite medium is thoroughly described in the following section in 
consultation with the previously published articles [1-3]. All the physical submodels those 
are considered in the isolated droplet combustion code is schematically illustrated in Fig. 
2.1.  Coupled mass, energy and species transport equations are simultaneously solved  in 
both the phases liquid and gas phases. The governing equations and associated submodels 
are described in the forthcoming sections.

model.

2.8 WATER DISSOLUTION EFFECT 
There are distinct classes of fuels (e.g., methanol and ethanol) for which selective 
combustion generated products from the flame front (e.g., water, H2O) can dissolve back 
in to the liquid droplet  [19]. The solubility of water in fuel, active -OH group and fuel 
chain length and structure all together dictate the water dissolution effect. Therefore, for 
such fuels, the role of liquid phase mass-transport must be considered as this directly 
contributes to the water absorption phenomena and its subsequent effect on the quasi-
steady state (QSS) and flame-extinction burning phase. The liquid mass Peclet number, as 
defined below, is used to characterize the effects of liquid-phase transport.

A lower value of liquid mass Peclet number preferentially transfers the condensed 
water interior to the droplet resulting in higher water accumulation (referred as ‘Well-
mixed Limit’). To the contrary, for higher value of Pel,m, only a thin layer of absorbed water 
is formed at the droplet boundary without significant water accumulation (known as 
‘Diffusion Limit’). The droplet burning rate (Kb) is computed as part of the solution, thus 
the value of the Pel,m is dictated primarily by the value of effective liquid diffusivity (Dl). 
In the model, only the value of Dl is empirically calculated [2, 19]. It should be emphasized 
that all other model variables are remained as detail as possible. 
 
2.9 NUMERICAL METHODS 
The complete set of coupled partial differential and algebraic equations are 
discretized first in space and then integrated in an automated fashion as a set of coupled

items.title: PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf
items.text:
34 
ordinary differential-algebraic equations in time. Spatial discretization is performed 
according to a node-centered finite volume scheme with a second-order accuracy. The gas-
liquid interface demarcates the volume boundaries for which the inner zone represents the 
condensed phase liquid fuel and the outer zone represents the gas phase ambient and the 
far field. The discretized mass flux is represented on cell interfaces and not cell centers, in 
the manner traditionally referred to as a staggered grid to avoid oscillatory solutions. 
Numerical integration of the final set of discretized equations is performed using a fifth 
order backward difference formula and a variable time step utilizing a fully implicit 
multipoint interpolation. This method is appropriate for the large range of time scales and 
overcomes stability constraints imposed by a chemically reacting system and automatic 
time-step variation.
