5.4.4 COMPARISON OF DROPLET COMBUSTION EXPERIMENTS AND 
PREDICTIONS 
To provide clear comparisons with the experimental results, Figure 4 (a)-(d) 
compares the predicted droplet diameters with measured values (cf. Figure 2 (b)) using 
the LLNL (dash red lines) and MIT (solid black lines) kinetic models. The experimental 
data shown in these plots include the error bars showing the standard deviations 
computed from three individual experiments (cf. Figure 2 (a)). For n-butanol (Figure 4 
(a)), the D2 predictions using both models yielded similar burning curves with the 
absolute (D/Do)2 values slightly smaller than the experimental values. Though the 
absolute droplet diameter values from DNM are below the error bars, the slope (burning 
rates) near the end are very similar to experimental results. This would suggest that the 
slight discrepancy may stem from the earlier stage of the combustion process (i.e. t/Do2 < 
0.8 s/mm2). 
Figure 5.4 (b) and (c) suggest that the MIT model better predicts the iso- and sec-
butanol data compared to the LLNL model, which reflects the extensive validation of the 
MIT model with gas phase sec- and iso-butanol combustion properties. It is clear that the 
droplet diameters predicted using the LLNL model are significantly smaller than the 
measurements for iso-, sec- and tert-butanol while predictions from the MIT model are 
relatively better matched with the data (Figure 5.4 (b)-(d)). Furthermore, burning rates 
(slope of the data) predicted from the MIT kinetic model are in reasonable agreement 
with the experimental results for iso- and sec-butanol.

regression for (a) n-butanol, (b) iso-butanol, (c) sec-butanol, and (d) tert-butanol. Initial droplet 
diameter: n-butanol (0.56 mm), iso-butanol (0.55 mm), sec-butanol (0.53 mm), and tert-butanol 
(0.52 mm). Ambient condition for simulation: P = 1 atm, T = 298 K. 
 
The numerical predictions for tert-butanol from both models (Figure 5.4 (d)) do 
not agree well with the data, though the MIT model is much closer to the measurements. 
Even considering validations of these kinetic models against premixed experimental 
combustion targets, both the LLNL and MIT models were found to not be in especially 
good agreement [16, 17]. This suggests that there are possible limitations in the kinetic

items.text:
112 
schemes due to limited insight into the mechanistic pathways associated with combustion 
of tert-butanol. Notably, from here onwards, the primary objective of this study will be to 
extensively investigate sec-, iso - and tert-butanol droplet combustion. Therefore 
subsequent discourse is mainly directed towards these isomers essentially precluding the 
already studied n -butanol [47]. 
The numerical predictions of instantaneous burning rate and peak gas temperature 
profiles for sec-, iso- and tert-butanol deploying both the chemical kinetic models are 
presented in Figure 5.5. In addition, the droplet burning rate calculated from the 
experimental dataset, delineated by solid symbol, is juxtaposed in respective subplots 
(Figure 5.5 (a)–(c)). As shown in the figure, predictions from Sarathy et al. (i.e., LLNL 
model) has a consistently higher burning rate for all the isomers compared to Merchant et 
al. (i.e., MIT model) predictions. Interestingly, opposite to the experimental observation, 
there is no ‘quasi-steady state’ burning period for the LLNL model. Instead, irrespective 
of the isomers, the model exhibits continuously increasing burning rate trend. All three 
isomers behave in a near-identical fashion with a sudden dip in the burning rate at the end 
indicating flame-out due to fuel depletion. In contrast, predictions from MIT model 
qualitatively regenerate the experimental profile and quantitatively reproduce the 
experimental observation, especially for sec- and iso-butanol though discrepancy is 
discernible for tert-butanol indicating faster burning rate. This also suggests that there is 
room for model refinement for the tert-butanol. A closer look at the tert-butanol burning 
rate also reveals that Merchant et al. predicts a flame extinction at the very last stage of 
the burn period.

items.text:
 Dynamics of near-limit cool flame burning of isolated submillimeter (Do = 
0.5 mm) n-C7H16 droplet is numerically studied.
Reduced ambient O2 mole fraction (10%) is considered to facilitate near-
limit condition.
Under selective O3 seeding (5%), the droplet briefly attempts to initiate 
stable cool flame before entering continuous oscillatory cool flame burn.
Local depletion of O2 (<13.5%) near the droplet initiates the pulsing 
behavior with initial small fluctuation in flame temperature.
The oscillation is found to increase in magnitude with time, and at each 
successive cycle.
Dynamic interaction of degenerate chain branching and chain propagation 
/ termination reaction classes of QOOH (within NTC region) is responsible 
for the observed oscillation.
Continuous fuel leakage through the flame location assists the oscillation 
to grow in radial direction with time.

items.text:
Supplementary Slide # Governing Equations
The complete set of coupled partial differential and algebraic equations are 
discretized first in space and then integrated in an automated fashion as a set 
of coupled ordinary differential-algebraic equations in time.
Spatial discretization is performed according to a node-centered finite 
volume scheme with a second order accuracy.
The innermost liquid node is centered at the origin, providing the required 
no-flux condition.
The discretized mass flux is represented on cell interfaces and not cell 
centers, in the manner traditionally referred to as a staggered grid to avoid 
oscillatory solutions.
Numerical integration of the final set of discretized equations is performed 
using a backward difference formula with a variable order of up to fifth order 
and a variable time step utilizing a fully implicit multipoint interpolation.

items.title: PSI-117_Presentations_PSI_Users_Group_Cool_Flames_in_Space_03302026.pdf
items.text:
The numerical effort to study counterflow flame configuration has been predominantly centered 
upon OPPDIF module of CHEMKIN chemical kinetic package
This module implements a similarity transformation approach that reduces the flow field to a 
one-dimensional/ plug flow problem with the following assumptions:
Radial component of velocity is linear in radius 
Dependent variables become functions of the axial direction only
What are the physical conditions that can be 
represented by this assumption?
High Reynolds number flow configuration: High strain rate (a) 
Thin flame sheet: Hot flame (high activation energy)
Limitations of the conventional numerical approach
Low Re: Low strain rate (a ~100 s-1) 
Finite Flame Thickness: low activation energy)
Cool flames

items.text:
17
Summary
• The experimental results and detailed predictions support that 
there exists two possible modes of quasi-steady cool flame 
droplet burning behaviour: “Warm” in the NTC regime and “Cold” 
in the low temperature regime.
• The helium concentration is critical for the observed 
characteristics – promoting the second stage burn or completely 
supressing it. 
• A dynamic coupling between heat generation and heat loss in 
the system.   
• The low temperature kinetics is distinctive and different in the 
second and third stage.
• Experimental observation with n-dodecane at higher pressure 
and helium exchange validates the “a priori” numerical 
predictions of a three stage behaviour inferred from n-heptane 
simulations.

• Two-stage hot-cool flame burning mode transitions are demonstrated to exist for the three 
fuels, and the maximum flame temperature at which transition to the second stage occurred 
was universally found to be ~ 1200K. 
• Hot flame characteristics of all three fuels indicate that predicted extinction phenomena are all 
very similar.
• Cool flame extinction properties are significantly affected by the n-alkane molecular weight, 
and the chain length of the n-alkane has significant effect on the cool flame reactivity - larger n-
alkane exhibited more robust cool flame (i.e., higher temperature) and hence smaller extinction 
diameters.
• Universally, de,CF for each fuel varies linearly with initial droplet diameter, but unlike de,HF these 
relationships do not collapse to a single function.
• n-Dodecane droplet combustion reveal a strong dependence of observations on ambient 
pressure. Single, two-stage hot-cool flame combustion transitions to a multi-cycle combustion 
behavior at ambient pressures above one atmosphere, and eventually into a hot - “Warm” flame 
transition.

items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
3 
 
1. Introduction 
The purpose of this report is to provide a description of the experimental hardware and operations of 
used in the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project that is sufficient for 
informed interpretation of the experimental results.  In contrast, it is not the intent of this document to 
review the project management, engineering development, design process, etc. although such aspects 
may be briefly addressed. 
 
The ACME suite of experiments are being carried out on the International Space Station (ISS) in the 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  ACME features investigations with gaseous fuels, such as methane and 
ethylene.  In addition to the fuel state, the current ACME experiments use laminar, non-premixed (i.e., 
diffusion) flames for their studies.  To simplify analysis, these flames are furthermore either axisymmetric 
or spherically symmetric, depending upon the experiment. 
 
Currently, ACME includes six independent experiments of which the first five were selected for testing in 
spaceflight by NASA while the sixth was selected by the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space 
(CASIS) and the National Science Foundation (NSF). 
 
The CIR facility was launched in 2008 and with the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) was 
used for a series of liquid-fueled experiments from 2009 to 2017.  The facility was reconfigured and set 
up for ACME testing by the ISS crew in September and October 2017, where over 25 astronauts from 
Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and the United States have thus far supported the project’s 
research.  As of this writing, over one thousand ACME flames have been ignited on the ISS, where that 
began in Nov. 2017.    It is expected that the planned ACME testing will be completed in 2021, when the 
CIR operations should subsequently shift to the Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) project. 
 
The discussion of the CIR hardware herein is limited, but the research facility is described in various 
documents, such as those listed below.  These are listed in reverse chronological order, where the oldest 
predate the facility’s completion and have become outdated in some regards.  References 1, 2 and 4 also 
discuss ACME, but were all prepared prior to the completion of ACME’s spaceflight hardware. 
1. Suleyman A. Gokoglu, Daniel L. Dietrich, Dennis P. Stocker, Paul V. Ferkul, Sandy L. Olson, Michael 
C. Hicks, Amelia Rai (editor), Neesha Hosein (editor), and Cory Duke (designer), “Combustion 
Science: A Researcher’s Guide to International Space Station,” NASA Publication NP-2015-10-034-
JSC (2015). 
2. J.M. Hickman, D.L. Dietrich, M.C. Hicks, V. Nayagam, V., and D. Stocker, “FLEX: A Decisive Step 
Forward in NASA's Combustion Research Program,” 1st Annual International Space Station 
Research and Development Conference, Denver, Colorado 26-28 June (2012). 
3. “Unlocking Mysteries in Microgravity: NASA Glenn Provides the Keys with the Fluids and 
Combustion Facility,” NASA fact sheet FS-2011-06-035-GRC, PS-00538-0611 (2011). 
4. T.F. O'Malley, W.A. Sheredy, and D.P. Stocker, “Combustion Research on the International Space 
Station,” 59th International Astronautical Congress, Vol. 2, pp. 756-766 (2008). 
5. Terence F. O’Malley, Karen J. Weiland, Craig A. Myhre, Frank G. Gati, Myron E. Hill, and John H. 
Snead, “The Fluids and Combustion Facility and First Payloads: The Multi-User Droplet 
Combustion Apparatus and the Light Microscopy Module: Enabling Research on the ISS,” 57th 
International Astronautical Congress,  IAC-06-A2.1.07, 2-6 Oct. 2006, Valencia, Spain (2006). 
6. T. O’Malley and C. Myrhe, “The Fluids and Combustion Facility Combustion Integrated Rack and 
the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus: Microgravity Combustion Science Using Modular

ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
4 
 
Multi-User Hardware,” 53rd International Astronautical Congress, The World Space Congress 
2002, IAC-02-J.5.05, 10-19 Oct. 2002, Houston, Texas (2002). 
7. Terence F. O'Malley and Karen J. Weiland, “The FCF Combustion Integrated Rack: Microgravity 
Combustion Science Onboard the International Space Station,” NASA Technical Memorandum 
TM--2002-210981, AIAA-2001-4927, September 2002. 
8. Robert L. Zurawski and Nora G. Bozzolo, “ISS Fluids and Combustion Facility: Combustion 
Integrated Rack: Payload Accommodations - Principal Investigator’s Guide,” NASA report, 
September 2000. 
 
The CIR facility was preceded by the Combustion Module (CM) which flew on the space shuttle Columbia.  
In 1997, the combustion research facility was within Spacelab on the STS-83 and STS-94 (Microgravity 
Science Laboratory) missions.  It was subsequently reconfigured and flew in 2003 within SPACEHAB, again in 
the shuttle’s payload bay, in the STS-107 mission.  The Combustion Module investigations included Laminar 
Soot Processes (LSP), Structure Of Flame Balls At Low Lewis-number (SOFBALL), and the Water-Mist Fire 
Suppression Experiment (Mist).  Although all three experiments burned gaseous fuel, each had its own 
chamber insert, whereas ACME features a single modular chamber insert to accomplish multiple 
investigations.  A significant difference between the CIR and its shuttle precursor is that the ISS tests are 
remotely commanded from the ground without crew involvement, which wasn’t the case with the 
Combustion Module research.  But in all cases the crew are required to configure the necessary hardware. 
 
While extensive, this report is far from exhaustive but there are other reports which provide additional 
detail useful for interpreting ACME’s experimental results.  Some key examples include the following:   
Camera characterization 
 
CFI Intensified Camera Package Characterization Report  
DRAFT REPORT 
 
Data Camera Characterization Report 
ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A 
Optical instrument characterization 
 
BRE Radiometer Characterization Report 
ACME-RPT-012 
 
Cool Flames Radiometer Characterization Report 
CIR-RPT-4600 
 
PMT Characterization Report 
ACME-RPT-013 
 
Radiometer Characterization Report 
ACME-RPT-011 
Requirement verification 
 
ERD Verification Report 
ACME-VER-002 Rev. B 
 
Inspection Verification Report 
ACME-VER-001 Rev. A 
Software and non-imaging data 
 
Software Interface Design Document 
ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D 
 
Abbreviations are addressed at the end of this report, but ERD stands for Engineering Requirements 
Document and many of the engineering requirements were directly derived from ACME’s science 
requirements.  Meanwhile, key hardware dimensions, for example of the burners, and other details are 
confirmed in the Inspection Verification Report.  Also note that the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) and Cool 
Flames radiometer reports are specific to certain ACME experiments, whereas the other reports are 
general to all of ACME. 
 
ACME Project Scientist Dennis Stocker (216-433-2166, dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov) may be contacted 
with questions about the ACME project.

items.title: PSI-159_Engineering Documents_ACME Engineering Implementation Rpt..pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
5 
 
2. Engineering Overview 
 
A. General Description 
This section provides a general description of the ACME engineering from the ‘3.0 Experimental’ 
section of the following 2014 conference paper: 
Dennis P. Stocker, Fumiaki Takahashi, J. Mark Hickman, and Andrew C. Suttles, “Gaseous 
Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station,” Spring 
Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Tulsa, OK, 16–
18 March 2014. 
 
IMPORTANT: The 2104 paper from which this section was extracted proceeded completion of the 
spaceflight hardware which was mostly launched in 2017.  As a result, it does not accurately 
describe the final engineering in some regards.   Therefore updates, clarifications, additional 
details, shortcomings, references, etc. have been included in boxed notes like this following the 
original description.  As a minor note, the sizes of figures were adjusted in this report, but none 
were cropped. 
 
As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to 
accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners.  Besides the chamber insert, 
other ACME-unique hardware includes a high-definition color camera and an avionics package, 
which is for data acquisition and control. 
 
 
Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber 
insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS.

items.title: PSI-159_Engineering Documents_ACME Engineering Implementation Rpt..pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
6 
 
 
ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of 
burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter.  As 
depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 
to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 
and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two 
flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm).  Most burners 
will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux 
transducers.  The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring 
of the pressure differential across the outlet surface.  The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable 
tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for 
precise positioning. 
 
 
Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, 
porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. 
 
Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated 
gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm.  
However, only the larger gas-jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests.  The burners are 
addressed in detail in section 3.C. 
 
Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, 
presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and 
supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local 
flame quenching. 
 
Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing.  Most tests have been conducted 
using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion 
experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR.  However, some tests were conducted with 
a coil igniter tip, where that included the second round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator 
(BRE) and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiments, with the 
exception of the latter’s first day testing.  The CFI-G investigation will also use the coil igniter tip.  
For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. 
 
The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the 
delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner.  The 
maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on 
a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines.  The crew can exchange the mass 
flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy.  The gas delivery 
system enables on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow,

items.title: PSI-159_Engineering Documents_ACME Engineering Implementation Rpt..pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
7 
 
inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames, 
although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments.  Gases can also be 
delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as 
the blending of different fuel gases.  CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME 
will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) 
that can be released into the combustion chamber. 
 
Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent.  Furthermore, the fuel 
diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit.  Ultimately, oxidizer flows 
of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a 
maximum of 5 slpm.  ACME has not used gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as indicated above; the 
bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control.  
 
ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and 
two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in 
use on orbit.  All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber.  Collectively, the 
imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot 
volume fraction; and operational support.  However, it is unlikely that all functions would be 
exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. 
 
Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of 
the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning 
mirror).  Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development.  The analog 
camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations.  Light-
emitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both 
support the operations and provide reference images.  The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 
30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent 
control of the zoom, iris, and focus.  The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly 
with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging.  Color imaging can 
also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to 
avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green.  The natural flame 
color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and 
measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24].  Alternately, CH* 
imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm 
bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM).  A 450-nm 
bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract 
interfering broadband soot emission.  However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such 
subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame 
conditions. 
 
The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, 
is not archived in space.  The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center.  Its 
gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction.   
 
The sensitivity of the color digital camera, often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data 
Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times 
and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second.  The clear “filter” is

items.title: PSI-159_Engineering Documents_ACME Engineering Implementation Rpt..pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
8 
 
of fused silica.  Unfortunately, the thickness of the blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter and the added 
antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it does not balance the 
intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature 
determination.  Meanwhile, rather than the 450-nm bandpass filter described above, the high 
definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging formaldehyde emissions.   
For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A).   
 
Imaging of the dim hydrogen flames in the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames 
(s-Flame) experiment was particularly challenging with these, if not all, cameras.   
 
Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral 
(HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which allows for imaging at 
multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired band.  This 
camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frames per second 
(fps).  Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss 
through the LCTF.  Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where 
ACME is equipped with a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers.  The fibers are 
orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired 
position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video.  During set 
up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal to either ACME’s color digital 
camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF.  An alternate fiber array including a platinum wire 
will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination with preflight calibration will 
enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24]. 
 
In contrast to the preceding paragraph, ACME did not use a HiBMs camera for pyrometry, but 
instead relied on use of ACME’s color DataCam for such temperature measurements.  For an 
example of how this can be done, see the techniques described in the following papers:   
P.B. Kuhn, B. Ma, B.C. Connelly, M.D. Smooke, and M.B. Long, “Soot and Thin-filament Pyrometry 
Using a Color Digital Camera,” Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 33 (2011) 743-750.  
B. Ma, M. B. Long, “Absolute light calibration using S-type thermocouples,” Proceedings of the 
Combustion Institute, 34 (2) (2013) 3531-3539. 
 
Thus far, TFP tests have been conducted with 14-micron fibers spaced apart by 5 mm for a total 
span of 20 mm (in the case of 5 intact ceramic fibers), neglecting optional translation of the array.  
Tests have been conducted using arrays with and without the platinum wire in the furthest 
downstream position.  Tests have also been conducted with some of the fibers broken and 
subsequently removed, leaving only three fibers in the final testing for the BRE and Coflow Laminar 
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiments and at least the initial testing for the Cool Flames 
Investigation with Gases (CFI-G). 
 
CIR has a second HiBMs camera, without a filter, that will be used in combination with CIR’s 
illumination package for alternate measurements of the soot volume fraction.  This will be 
accomplished via an extinction technique previously employed in microgravity [3,6,26], where the 
camera and the collimated light source (with its two fiber-coupled laser diodes) are positioned at 
opposite windows.  The images are recorded at 1024x1024 and 30 fps.  Thus far, the primary 
purpose of this combined system has been the measurement of the droplet diameter for 
determination of the droplet burning rate.

items.title: PSI-159_Engineering Documents_ACME Engineering Implementation Rpt..pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
9 
 
 
A HiBMs camera without the Liquid Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF) has been used throughout much, 
but not all, of ACME’s operations.  In the first round of the CLD Flame experiment, it was used 
without a filter for flame imaging, but this proved to be largely unsuccessful because the camera 
is very insensitive to blue.  Afterward, it was equipped with a red filter corresponding to the CIR 
illumination package for the rest of the ACME testing.  Unfortunately, that filter is sufficiently 
broad that significant incandescence can pass through the filter limiting its utility for 
determinations of soot volume fraction via light extinction, e.g., through the technique described 
in the following papers: 
D.L. Urban, Z.G. Yuan, P.B. Sunderland, K.C., Lin, Z. Dai, and G.M. Faeth, “Smoke-Point Properties 
of Nonbuoyant Round Laminar Jet Diffusion Flames,” Proceedings of the Twenty-Eighth 
Symposium (International) on Combustion 28 (2000) 1965-1972.  
F.J. Diez, C. Aalburg, P.B. Sunderland, D.L. Urban, Z.-G. Yuan, G.M. Faeth, “Soot properties of 
laminar jet diffusion flames in microgravity,” Combustion and Flame, 156 (2009) 1514-1524.  
P.S. Greenberg and J.C. Ku, “Soot Volume Fraction Imaging,” Applied Optics, 36 (22) (1997) 5514-
5522. 
Nonetheless, soot volume fraction can also be determined from the color DataCam images. 
 
During ACME operations, the HiBMs camera is typically archived at 15 fps because of data limits 
for transfer and downlink operations.  And because operations are constrained by the data limits, 
image data from this camera are sometimes deleted without downlinking to enable additional 
testing.  And in some testing, HiBMs images aren’t even acquired given their lesser value. 
 
Unfortunately, the HiBMs backlight illumination is significantly obstructed by the bracket for the 
electrode mesh further limiting its utility for the E-FIELD Flames experiment.   This was a design 
trade-off necessitated primarily by ACME’s large number of cameras and other optical 
instruments. 
 
CIR’s Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) package is a monochrome camera with an intensifier 
(for 280-700 nm) and a 310-nm bandpass filter (with a 10-nm FWHM) for OH* imaging.  Again as 
a result of the signal loss through the filter, binning is employed such that the OH* images are 
recorded at 512x512 and 30 fps. 
 
During ACME operations, the LLL-UV camera has only been used for the Structure and Response 
of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment. 
 
While not discussed in the preceding section, another intensified camera was used throughout 
ACME testing, although its image data was sometimes deleted or not even acquired to allow the 
performance of additional tests.   This was the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) camera which was 
generally configured with its CH* filter, where an exception is some s-Flame testing with 
particularly dim flames.  Due to design trade-offs, its Field of View (FOV) was partially obstructed 
by the arms of the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array when it was moved inwards to the 
flame.  More information about this camera can be found in its characterization report, CIR-RPT-
4600. 
 
The ACME chamber insert will also be equipped with non-imaging optical diagnostics including 
both thermopile radiometers and Photomultiplier Tubes (PMTs).  There is a crew-exchangeable

items.title: PSI-159_Engineering Documents_ACME Engineering Implementation Rpt..pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
10 
 
linear array of radiometers of which there are two versions supporting the initial set of 
experiments.  The array has a fixed position which is parallel to the chamber axis and centered 
(along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows and thus most of the other 
instrumentation.  One array is equipped with a single wide-view radiometer with two narrow-
view radiometers that are downstream and two more that are upstream, where all views are 
orthogonal to the chamber axis, as depicted in Figure 4.  The narrow-view radiometers are 
intended to support studies of gas-jet flames, where ACME can accommodate shorter burners, 
making the “lower” detectors useful.  The other array, also seen in Fig. 4, provides for three wide-
view measurements of the flame, where one view is masked to nominally block radiant emission 
from the burner.  It was specifically designed for the BRE experiment but will be a resource 
available to other ACME experiments.  Given that the radiometer array can be exchanged by the 
crew, alternate arrays could be developed.   
 
 
Figure 4: Crew-exchangeable radiometer arrays on the ACME chamber insert: (top) standard 
(ACME) array of 5 radiometers, and (bottom) array with three radiometers, designed for the BRE 
experiment, where the lowest detector is masked to avoid view of the burner.

items.title: PSI-159_Engineering Documents_ACME Engineering Implementation Rpt..pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
11 
 
A third radiometer array was developed for the CFI-G experiment, where it is important to 
understand that only a single radiometer array can be used at a time. 
 
The narrow-view radiometers in the standard array are only fully sensitive in small spots, but they 
are each sensitive in a much greater Field of View (FOV) than represented in the preceding figure.   
They do not have lenses; their FOV is a result of an aperture where most of their FOV is within the 
penumbra which is only visible to a portion of the sensor.  Figures representing the measured FOVs 
of the as-built standard and BRE radiometer arrays are found in section 3.F of this document.   
 
Unfortunately, the radiometers in the BRE array typically saturated in the first round of BRE 
testing, so the standard array was used in its second round.  However, those radiometers similarly 
saturated in many of round 2 tests.  In this regard, each of ACME’s BRE and standard radiometers 
have a fixed gain.  Meanwhile, each sensor in the radiometer array developed for the CFI-G 
investigation has two fixed gains, i.e., a high gain and low gain.   
 
For more information about the standard radiometer array used for most ACME testing, see the 
Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-011).  Meanwhile, you can learn about the other 
radiometer arrays from the BRE Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-012) and the 
Cool Flames Radiometer Characterization Report (CIR-RPT-4600).    
 
An additional wide-view radiometer, that is fixed and not crew exchangeable, is positioned 
downstream of the burner and flame at 30o from the chamber axis.  This detector is primarily 
intended to support the spherical flame experiments and will have a quicker response than the 
more sensitive detectors that will used in the linear arrays.   Like the radiometers on the two linear 
arrays, it will have a spectral range of nominally 0.2-11 micron and its field of view will be 
established by an appropriately selected aperture. 
 
The FOV of the off-set radiometer is also shown in section 3.F.  Learn more about this sensor from 
the Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-011).   
 
To detect the quenching of dim flames, the chamber insert will be equipped with a set of three 
PMTs.  Each PMT will have a wide-angle view, a sight line that is orthogonal to the chamber axis, 
and will be centered (along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows so that it is 
aligned with most of the other instrumentation.  The PMTs’ spectral range will be 230-700 nm, 
i.e., visible and near ultraviolet, but one will have a 310-nm bandpass filter and another will have 
a 430-nm bandpass filter (where both are with a 10-nm FWHM).  The pair of detectors will enable 
measurement of OH* and CH* emission, respectively.  The third PMT will be equipped with a 
neutral density filter to prevent saturation.  Like many other components, the PMT array can be 
removed from the chamber insert by the crew. 
 
Unlike the radiometers, each PMT had a readily adjustable gain.  However, the PMT signals 
sometimes saturated when the gains were set too high.  See the PMT Characterization Report 
(ACME-RPT-013) to learn more about the three Photomultiplier Tube (PMTs).   
 
The chamber insert is also equipped with six far-field thermocouples to measure the spread of 
the thermal field in the spherical flame experiments.  They are of limited utility for other 
experiments because they are positioned upstream of the burner tip.  Therefore, they will

items.title: PSI-159_Engineering Documents_ACME Engineering Implementation Rpt..pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
12 
 
generally not be installed by the crew to reduce the chance of accidental damage.  There will be 
two versions of a four-thermocouple rake to allow a choice of near and far measurements.  Other 
arrays could be designed to support future experiments, but they cannot extend downstream of 
the burner tip without interfering with other (e.g., optical) measurements. 
 
The two lone thermocouples, which are both at nominally 200 mm from the center of the spherical 
burner, have been installed throughout ACME testing.  The tip of one was seen to be slightly bent 
early in testing, as discussed and depicted in section 3.G of this report.   
 
Only the short (or far) version of the radiometer rake has been used thus far, where factors include 
the need for crew time to switch between rakes and the heat loss that could result from 
thermocouples in the long (close) rake.  The short (far) rake’s thermocouple tips should nominally 
be at 45, 60, 100, and 100 mm from the spherical burner center.  For thermocouples at the same 
distance from the burner center, the angle between the rays from the burner center to the two 
thermocouples should be 90 degrees.  The bead size of the thermocouples was not measured, but 
it is undoubtedly at least twice the size of the 0.2 mm diameter wire. 
  
The two thermocouples closest to the burner outlets on each four-thermocouple rake are type B, 
while the others are type K. 
 
Experiment-unique hardware is also mounted on the chamber insert.  For example, to 
accommodate the E-FIELD Flames experiment, the insert is equipped with a high-voltage supply 
and a crew-removable electrode mesh which can be set between +10 and -10 kV.   The circular mesh 
is orthogonal to the chamber axis and is positioned (during set up) at either ~35 or ~50 mm 
downstream of the insulated burner.  The ion current between the burner and electrode mesh will 
be determined via measurement of the voltage drop across a known resistor and application of 
Ohm’s Law. 
 
Additional images of the chamber insert can be seen in subsequent sections of this report.  The 
hardware specific to E-FIELD Flames is discussed further in section 2.B. 
 
Additional supporting measurements will be made, where the chamber pressure is a simple 
example.  The ACME experiments will use the CIR’s gas chromatograph for pre- and post-test 
analysis of the chamber atmosphere, e.g., for oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, 
and fuel gases.  Acceleration measurements will be provided by the Space Acceleration 
Measurement System (SAMS) [27], which is the primary instrument for such measurements on 
ISS and previously served that role for the space shuttle. 
 
The CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) was not used for the CLD Flame or 
E-FIELD Flames investigations and thus far was only sometimes used during BRE, Flame Design, 
and s-Flame testing.  Its use requires significant time and as such effectively reduces the number 
of tests that can be conducted.  However, estimates of the chamber contents were computed 
assuming that the fuel in a normal flame test (for example) was either fully or not at all oxidized, 
e.g., for unsustained ignition in the latter case. 
 
The CIR facility was equipped with a 3-axis SAMS sensor head and the acceleration measurements, 
along with relevant documentation, are accessible via the home page for the Principal Investigator

items.title: PSI-159_Engineering Documents_ACME Engineering Implementation Rpt..pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
13 
 
Microgravity Services (PIMS), https://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/pims/home/.  To be clear, the 
acceleration measurements are not archived with the ACME experiment data in the Physical 
Sciences Informatics (PSI) website, www.nasa.gov/PSI.  
 
All ACME experiments will be constant volume (i.e., rather than constant pressure) studies, where 
the chamber’s free volume will be about 90 liters.  Burner flows will generally be constrained to 
limit the pressure rise, and tests will typically be 0.5-2 minutes in duration. 
 
The chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed hardware. 
 
The ACME experiments will be configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  Instead, the 
experiments will be commanded from the ground, specifically from the Telescience Support 
Center (TSC) at the NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio.  They can be conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it will also be possible to 
effectively operate the experiments in a “manual” mode, where changes can be made in response 
to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream.  For 
example, a flow rate could be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit.  Step and ramp 
changes can be made in the flow rate(s) or electric field potential.  The TFP fiber array can be 
translated uniformly through a soot-free flame to get a continuum measurement of the 
temperature field.  In summary, ACME’s experiment control will allow for broad flexibility.   
 
The TSC is now also referred to as the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC).  Thus far, the 
ACME tests have always been conducted in a nominally automated mode. 
 
B. Overview for E-FIELD Flames 
While focused on the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) 
experiment, this section provides a good general description relevant to all ACME experiments.  
This text is from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ section of the following conference paper: 
Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on 
Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of 
the Central States Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. 
See the paper itself for the references, etc. as they not included in this report.  As a minor note, the 
sizes of some figures were adjusted in this report, but none were cropped.  The figures have not 
been renumbered herein but are effectively 5-8 for this report (rather than 1-4). 
 
In contrast to the preceding section, this paper was written after the beginning of E-FIELD Flames 
(and CLD Flame) operations on the ISS.  However, additional details are again included within this 
section in boxed notes like this. 
 
The E-FIELD Flames experiment is being conducted in 2018 within the ISS’ Combustion Integrated 
Rack (CIR) [15], which was launched in 2008 and used from 2009 to 2017 for a series of droplet 
combustion experiments [16].  The CIR facility is similar in size to a vending machine as can be 
seen in Figure 1.  It includes a 100-liter combustion chamber capable of operation at pressures of 
up to 300 kPa.  The chamber features a ring of 8 sapphire windows and is equipped with a set of 
reconfigurable imaging systems.  The CIR was designed with gas delivery, venting, thermal control, 
electrical power, data handling, image processing and storage, and vibration isolation to enable 
combustion research with gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels.

items.title: PSI-159_Engineering Documents_ACME Engineering Implementation Rpt..pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
14 
 
 
Figure 1: European Space Agency (ESA) astronaut Paolo Nespoli installing the chamber insert for 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) in the Combustion Integrated 
Rack (CIR).  This photograph [ISS053e098207] was taken on the International Space Station (ISS) 
on 12 Oct. 2017. 
 
E-FIELD Flames is one of the six unique experiments featuring non-premixed laminar flames of 
gaseous fuels which currently make up the ACME project [17].  A modular set of hardware, 
including the critical chamber insert depicted in Figures 2 and 3, was developed to carry out the 
ACME investigations in the CIR facility.  The 0.4-m diameter ACME chamber insert provides 
common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and a 
retracting resistively-heated igniter.  The igniter has a crew-exchangeable tip and arm (to 
accommodate the various burners) and stepper-motor drive for radial positioning.  The chamber 
insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the far left of Figures 2-3 behind an orange 
hose and black cables) for delivering fuel, oxidizer (or an inert), and nitrogen to the burner or 
chamber.  The crew can exchange the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate accuracy for 
the desired flow ranges.  ACME’s gas delivery system enables on-orbit dilution of the gaseous fuel 
or oxidizer with nitrogen (available from the space station), but not both simultaneously.  
However, bottles of premixed fuel and oxidizer are also used, where the CIR’s standard bottle 
sizes are 1.00, 2.25, and 3.80 liters.  Fuels are stored in 1-liter bottles, while the 21/79 
oxygen/nitrogen mixture (on a volume basis) used by E-FIELD Flames comes in 3.80-liter bottles.  
The ACME experiments are constant volume studies, where the chamber’s free volume, with the 
insert installed, is about 90 liters.  Burner flows are generally constrained to limit the pressure rise 
and vitiation of the atmosphere, where typical ACME tests are only 0.5-2 minutes in duration.

ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
15 
 
 
Figure 2: NASA astronaut Joe Acaba reviewing procedures to align the hot-wire igniter on the 
ACME chamber insert to his left, in a photograph [ISS054e014660] taken by NASA astronaut 
Mark Vande Hei on 5 Jan. 2018. 
 
 
Figure 3: Solid model representation of the ACME chamber insert.

items.title: PSI-159_Engineering Documents_ACME Engineering Implementation Rpt..pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
16 
 
The E-FIELD Flames experiment is being conducted with two different burners: a simple gas-jet 
burner and a coflow burner, which can be seen in Figure 4(a).  The results discussed in this paper 
are only from the first of the experiment’s tests conducted with the coflow burner.  The stainless 
steel fuel tube in the burner has inner and outer diameter of 2.2 and 2.4 mm, respectively.  The 
coflow burner’s steel outer tube has an inner diameter of 25 mm, where the annulus outlet is a 
6.4-mm thick Hastelloy X honeycomb with 0.05-mm foil thickness and 0.81-mm cell size.  The 
coflow burner’s inner tube protrudes 3.1 mm beyond the surface of the honeycomb outlet.  While 
the inner tube is being used exclusively for fuel flow in E-FIELD Flames, valves in the ACME 
chamber insert allow the fuel, oxidizer, and nitrogen to be directed to either tube, making this 
burner capable of inverse flame testing. 
 
 
Figure 4: (a) Detail of the ACME chamber insert featuring the coflow burner (in the image 
center) used by the E-FIELD Flames experiment.  This is from a photograph [ISS053e096074] 
taken by ESA astronaut Paolo Nespoli on 12 Oct. 2017 after he installed the burner on the 
chamber insert. (b) Detail of the ACME chamber insert where the copper electrode mesh, used 
by the E-FIELD Flames experiment, can be seen above the coflow burner.  This is from a 
photograph [ISS055e001252] taken by NASA astronaut Scott Tingle on 8 March 2018 following 
his installation of the electrode mesh. 
 
In this study, a high-voltage electric field is generated between the burner and a copper electrode 
mesh located above (i.e., downstream of) the burner outlet, as can be seen in Figure 4(b).  The 
circular mesh is energized at up to 10,000 volts with either polarity, where the burner serves as 
the electrical return and the flow of flame-produced ions completes the circuit.  The ion current 
between the burner and electrode mesh is measured from the voltage drop across a known resistor 
and application of Ohm’s Law.  With and without the copper ring, the electrode mesh is 8.9 and 
8.4 cm in diameter, respectively.  The square copper weave has 7.1 wires/cm, a wire diameter of 
0.43 mm, and a 48% open area.  The mesh permits gas to pass through while also acting as an 
electrical element.  The electrode mesh is mounted 37 mm above the coflow burner tip and is 
centered on and orthogonal to the chamber axis.  The ACME chamber insert can also

items.title: PSI-159_Engineering Documents_ACME Engineering Implementation Rpt..pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
17 
 
accommodate an alternate electrode position of 52 mm above the coflow burner tip, but the 
closer position is being used to produce the highest field strengths. 
 
The slow response time of the high-voltage power supplies (recommended in the ACME 
Integrated Science Requirements Document, i.e., ISRD) did not meet the requirements necessary 
to achieve the requested time response performance, and as such inhibited determination of the 
flame’s response time to rapid changes in the electric field strength. 
 
The negative and positive high-voltage power supplies were to have been coupled, as described 
for example in Appendix C of the ISRD.  However, switching between the two high-voltage power 
supplies led to excessive Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) in ground testing so the power 
supplies were completely decoupled, where only one was installed at a time.  As such, testing was 
limited to a single polarity at a time in contrast to the experimental plans documented in the 
experiment’s Science Requirements Document (SRD) and the ACME ISRD. 
 
ACME’s non-imaging measurements are recorded at 125 Hz.  The measured test conditions 
include the chamber pressure and temperature, the three gas flow rates, and the electrical 
potential of the electrode mesh.  Acceleration measurements are provided by the Space 
Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) [18], which is the primary instrument for such 
measurements on ISS and previously served that role for the space shuttle. 
 
The flame behavior is observed optically with a variety of instruments.  For most ACME 
experiments, including E-FIELD Flames, the radiant emission is measured with 6 thermopile 
detectors with a spectral range of nominally 0.2-11 microns.  Five radiometers are in a crew-
exchangeable linear array that is mounted parallel to the chamber axis.  The other detector is 
downstream and off axis from the burner.  Chemiluminescent emission is measured with a set of 
three Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules.  Their spectral range is 230-700 nm, i.e. in the visible 
and near ultraviolet, but two are equipped with narrow bandpass filters for measurement of OH* 
and CH* emissions, respectively.  The third PMT is equipped with a neutral density filter to prevent 
saturation, although the gain values for all three PMTs are independently and readily adjustable.  
Like many of the components, the array of PMT modules can be removed from the chamber insert 
by the crew.  In addition to their scientific value, PMT measurements are used operationally to 
detect ignition and automatically deactivate and retract the igniter.  The radiometer or PMT 
measurements can similarly be used to detect extinction and automatically end the gas flow and 
test. 
 
Imaging measurements of the flames complement the optical sensors described above.  Color 
imaging is provided by an analog color camera within the chamber and a high-definition (1360 x 
1024), 12-bit color camera mounted outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench.  The latter is 
equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus.  It has a 
filter barrel with a fused silica window (for color imaging), a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, 
and bandpass filters for imaging CH* and HCHO (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence.  The digital 
color camera was characterized prior to launch for color-ratio pyrometry and measurement of the 
soot volume fraction, via the techniques of [19, 20].  The camera makes soot pyrometry possible 
as well as Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP), where the chamber insert is equipped with a translating 
array of silicon-carbide (SiC) fibers.  A 14-micron fiber array can be seen at the top of Figure 4(b).  
However, the fibers interfere with the electric field preventing the use of Thin Filament Pyrometry 
in the E-FIELD Flames experiment.

items.title: PSI-159_Engineering Documents_ACME Engineering Implementation Rpt..pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
18 
 
 
Two intensified monochrome cameras mounted outside the combustion chamber are available 
for ACME use, although only one is being used by E-FIELD Flames.  It is a high-definition 
(1390x1040), 12-bit camera equipped with a filter barrel similar to that used by the digital color 
camera discussed in the preceding paragraph, although it doesn’t have a blue-green filter.  The 
CH* filter has been used in the intensified photography of the E-FIELD Flames tests.  While unused 
by E-FIELD Flames, the CIR is also equipped with a high-definition (1024x1024) camera with an 
intensifier extending into the ultraviolet which can be equipped with a bandpass filter and 
corresponding optics for OH* imaging. 
 
Finally, a high-definition (1024x1024), 12-bit monochrome camera is mounted outside the 
chamber opposite a collimated light source with two fiber-coupled laser diodes emitting red light 
of 650-655 nm.  This camera has a bandpass filter corresponding to the illumination source, 
allowing for determination of soot volume fraction through an extinction technique previously 
employed in microgravity research [21-23].  Unfortunately, because of trade-offs demanded by 
limited chamber volume and large number of instruments and components, the collimated light 
is obstructed substantially by the electrode mesh mount, limiting the utility of this camera for the 
E-FIELD Flames experiment.

3. Engineering Details (selected) 
This section provides additional details about some of the key engineering elements, including the 
chamber insert (pp., 20-22), gases and gas delivery (pp. 22-25), burners (pp. 25-50), igniter tips (pp. 50-
51), optical layout (pp. 51-56), radiometers (pp. 57-58), and thermocouples (pp. 59-60).  Most of the 
engineering subsystems are depicted in Figure 9, which is color-coded for ACME and the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) facility in which the ACME research is being conducted.  Thus far, ACME has not used 
the HiBMs-2 camera as shown in the chart, but the project instead has taken advantage of the Cool Flames 
Investigation (CFI) intensified camera, a CIR asset developed for the CFI experiment.   While not shown in 
the figure, ACME has also sometimes used the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) 
for the BRE, Flame Design, and s-Flame experiments.  This is limited to pre- or post-test measurements of 
the chamber atmosphere for oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and fuel gases.

items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
22 
 
 
Figure 12.  Solid model representation of the chamber insert’s interior as seen looking away from 
the burner toward the opposite end plate.  Note that the electrode mesh was only installed for 
the E-FIELD Flames experiment, where it obstructed use of the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) 
fiber array.  Furthermore, its mounting bracket interfered with illumination for possible soot 
volume fraction measurements via light extinction. 
 
B. Gas Delivery 
The tests are conducted using nitrogen available from the ISS and fuel, oxidizer, and inert gas 
bottles launched from Earth specifically for use with the CIR facility.  This approach includes both 
the burner flow and the chamber atmosphere, where combustion tests were not conducted with

compressed nitrogen is available as a space station resource.  Again, this discussion neglects gases

As discussed in the Hardware Overview, there are four types of burners, where two types were 
fabricated in different sizes and multiple spaceflight copies were made and used of the spherical 
burner.  Meanwhile there is only a single spaceflight copy of the coflow burner.

Additional details can be learned from the burner drawings listed in section 6.F.  
 
1. Gas-Jet Burners 
The fabricated gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 
1.3 and 2.1 mm, where two spaceflight copies of each were fabricated because of 
concerns that they might be damaged.  However, only a single copy of the larger diameter 
burner has thus far been used during the spaceflight tests, where that use was limited to 
the second round of the E-FIELD Flames testing.  This gas-jet burner was used to allow 
comparison with tests carried out with the coflow burner in E-FIELD Flames’ first round.  
The same commercial stainless-steel tubing used for the coflow burner’s inner tube was 
also used for the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner.  However, it is important to note that the 
nominal inner diameter (ID) in both cases was 2.16 mm, i.e., approximately 2.2 mm rather 
than 2.1 mm.  While potentially confusing, this met the tolerance requirement for the 2.1-
mm gas-jet burner.  Meanwhile, the nominal outer diameter (OD) was 2.41 mm, again for 
the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner and the inner tube of the coflow burner.  It is also important 
to understand that the gas-jet burner is slightly taller than the coflow burner, where the

burner). 
 
The gas-jet burner features an extremely fine, sheathed, type-K thermocouple mounted 
on the tube exterior with its tip 5 mm upstream of the burner outlet.  In contrast, the 
coflow burner was not equipped with the thermocouple because of concerns that it might 
result in flow and thus flame non-uniformity.

2. Coflow Burner 
The coflow burner is effectively a 2.1-mm gas-jet burner within a large tube, where gas 
could also flow from the annulus between the two tubes.  The stainless-steel fuel tube in 
the burner has inner and outer diameter of 2.16 and 2.41 mm, respectively.  The coflow 
burner’s steel outer tube has an inner diameter of 25 mm, where the annulus outlet is a 
6.4-mm thick Hastelloy X honeycomb with 0.05-mm foil thickness and 0.81-mm cell size.  
The coflow burner’s inner tube protrudes 3.1 mm beyond the surface of the honeycomb 
outlet. 
 
 
Figure 15.  The coflow burner aboard the space station, where the inner tube extends 
downstream of the annular outlet featuring a fine honeycomb. The white cable with the 
black connector on the right is for grounding, while the yellow connector on the left was 
used to secure the cable for the burner thermocouple, even though the coflow burner 
isn’t equipped with a thermocouple.  [Cropped detail from ISS064e028847] 
 
The coflow burner has thus far only been used for the CLD Flame and E-FIELD Flames 
experiments, where in both cases the inner tube was used exclusively for fuel flow.  
However, ACME’s gas delivery manifold allows the fuel, oxidizer, and nitrogen to be 
directed to either tube, making the burner capable of inverse flame testing, as can be 
seen in section 3.B. 
 
CLD Flame tests were always conducted with an oxidizer coflow, but some E-FIELD Flames 
tests with the coflow burner were conducted with no coflow.  That enabled a three-way 
comparison with the tests conducted with a coflow and those with the gas-jet burner 
(which of course were without a coflow).  
 
As previously mentioned, the coflow burner is slightly shorter than the gas-jet burner, 
where the electrode mesh used for the E-FIELD Flames experiment was nominally 35 and 
37 mm downstream of the gas-jet and coflow burners, respectively (based on the outlet 
of the inner tube in the case of the coflow burner).  Given the two situations, the electrode 
mesh can appropriately be described as positioned nominally 36 mm downstream of the

two burners. 
 
Unlike the other burners, the coflow burner was not equipped with a thermocouple 
because of concerns that it could adversely result in flow and thus flame asymmetry. 
 
The final tests from E-FIELD Flames’ first round on 17 May 2018 featured sooty 100% 
ethylene (C2H4) flames and a positively-charged electrode mesh which ‘pushed’ the 
flames toward the burner leading to significant soot deposition on the coflow burner.  
Figure 16 reveals that soot accumulated on the burner’s inner tube to the extent that its 
shape was effectively altered and would impede the surrounding coflow.  Meanwhile, the 
honeycomb coflow outlet was blackened in the central region near the inner tube, as seen 
in Figure 16, where that soot could have obstructed and reduced the coflow in the most 
important region.  
 
 
Figure 16.  The coflow burner outlet imaged with the backlit HiBMs camera on 25 May 
2018.   The inner tube, from which the fuel exits in normal flame testing, has been coated 
with soot. 
 
 
Figure 17.  The coflow burner outlet (as seen in the display of a handheld digital camera) 
from a high-definition video downlink from the ISS on 19 June 2018 prior to the burner 
cleaning.  The central portion of the burner’s outlet, including the honeycomb is 
blackened by soot. 
 
A procedure to clean the coflow burner was developed on the ground and implemented

images can be seen in Figure 18, Arnold used a toothbrush, piece of insulated wire, 
flashlight, vacuum sweeper, and mask (for personal protection).   After the cleaning, the 
CLD Flame Principal Investigator Marshall Long subsequently declared that “we are 
satisfied that the burner will be able to provide flow conditions similar to those that have 
been measured in our lab before the burner was placed in orbit.” 
 
 
 
Figure 18.  Images from the coflow burner cleaning carried out by astronaut Ricky Arnold 
on 19 June 2018.  In the left image [ISS056e021501], a piece of insulated wire is used to 
ensure that the inner tube’s interior is unobstructed by soot.  In the right image 
[iss056e021495], a flashlight is used to verify that the honeycomb is not blocked by soot.  
 
The spaceflight burner’s flow profile was characterized by the CLD Flame team at Yale 
University prior to its launch, where measurements were made along the four different 
lines shown in Figure 19 where the velocities of the inner and annular flows were

measurements were made for each of those velocity pairs at 0.5, 5, and 10 mm 
downstream of the burner’s inner tube, where those results are respectively presented 
in Figures 20-24, 25-29, and 30-34.  The black dashed lines in the subsequent plots of 
velocity profiles represent the inner and outer tubes of the burner. 
 
Select measurements were also made for 11 mismatched velocity pairs at 0.5 mm 
downstream of the inner tube, where those are presented in Figures 35-45 (of which the 
first five are with no inner flow).  Additional measurements may be found in the Dec. 2016 
document titled ACME CLD burner hot wire anemometry measurements.

titled ACME CLD burner hot wire anemometry measurements. 
 
3. Spherical Burners 
The spherical burners have thus far been used for the CFI-G, Flame Design, and s-Flame 
experiments.  In contrast to initial plans, spaceflight burners were only fabricated with a 
6.35-mm porous sphere.  It was initially expected that flames which were more spherical 
might be generated with larger diameter porous spheres, but 2.2-s drop testing indicated 
that 6.35-mm diameter spheres were as good or better than the larger sizes in creating 
spherical flames. 
 
Multiple copies of the spherical burner were launched to the ISS because of concerns that 
they might be damaged and/or might prove to yield flames which aren’t sufficiently 
spherically symmetric. 
 
The porous spheres were fabricated from sintering 316 stainless steel with 10-micron 
media grade, for which the porosity is approximately 41% and the density is 4.6 g/cm3.   
More specifically, each sphere was formed by sintering together sintered disks, where the 
supply tube should extend to the sphere’s center.  Neglecting the interior of the supply 
tube, there is presumably no cavity within the porous sphere. 
 
Each sphere was furthermore sinter-bonded to its stainless-steel supply tube.  As a side 
effect, the tubing lost its temper and became very pliable because of the high 
temperature required for the bonding.  Therefore, a close-fitting support tube, with an 
outer diameter of 1.8 mm, was added to the design.  It doesn’t quite extend to the porous 
sphere as can be seen in Figure 46.  The gap between the support tube and the burner is 
often obvious in flame imaging because the supply tube is more reflective than the 
support tube. 
 
Each burner was equipped with an extremely fine, sheathed, type-K thermocouple which 
was embedded as much as ~1 mm into the porous sphere.  The thermocouple hole was 
0.76 to 1.0 mm deep (and 0.25-0.30 mm in diameter) where the thermocouple was meant 
to be inserted fully, i.e., until reaching the hole’s bottom, but that may not be its exact 
position.  The junction is of course not at the extreme end of the sheathed thermocouple, 
but it is very fine and presumably close.  If the porous sphere is imagined as a globe with 
the supply tube as the south pole, the thermocouple is inserted in the lower hemisphere, 
between the equator and pole as seen in Figure 46.

Figure 46.  A spherical burner, prior to launch, showing the positioning of the slightly 
embedded thermocouple.  The gap between the support tube and porous sintered sphere 
can also be seen.  The white cable with the black connector on the left is for grounding, 
while the yellow connector is for the type-K thermocouple. 
 
The spherical burners were first used for the Flame Design experiment, where the first 
flame tests were conducted on 25 April 2019.  However, after several days of testing it 
was concluded by the investigators that the flames were insufficiently symmetric at high 
burner flow rates to meet the science objectives.  At the high flow rates, the flame ceased 
to be spherically symmetric and its center didn’t coincide with the burner’s center.  The 
results indicate that the sintered attachment of the sphere to the supply tube was more 
porous than the sintered sphere itself, where the flame was shifted toward the supply 
tube. Therefore, the spherical burner was replaced on 14 June 2019 where the shift was 
from serial number 1002 to 1003.  The subsequent burner (s/n 1003) showed similar 
behavior, but to a significantly reduced degree. As a result, some of the early Flame Design 
testing was repeated after the burner swap.  This burner (s/n 1003) has thus far been 
used for all subsequent spherical flame testing including the tests for the s-Flame and CFI-
G experiments.

4. BRE Burners 
In terms of both size and instrumentation, the two BRE burners are significantly different 
than the other existing ACME burners.  The outlet diameters of the two burners are 25 
and 50 mm, where the latter burner is shown in Figure 47.  The overall burner diameters 
are even larger, for example because each burner is encompassed with 6 mm of ceramic 
insulation. 
 
 
Figure 47.  The 50-mm BRE burner prior to launch.  The white cable with the black 
connector on the right is for grounding, while the yellow connector on the left was used 
to secure the cable for the burner thermocouple, where the measurements from the BRE 
burner’s thermocouples and heat flux transducers were transmitted through the black 
cables.  The two heat flux transducers can be seen in the perforated outlet plate as black 
‘circles.’  The two light dots in the same ‘row’ as the two transducers are the tips of 
embedded thermocouples.

S1101MFA1245.  The dimensions for the ceramic insulation are in inches. 
 
While the 25-mm BRE burner, depicted in Figure 48, has an outlet diameter corresponding 
to the coflow burner, it is nonetheless larger and more complex.   
 
The perforated copper outlet plate of each BRE burner is 5.3 mm thick and has two 
sheathed type-K thermocouples (0.25 mm in diameter) embedded so their tips are at the 
blackened outer surface.  This design allows the outlet plate to be used for calorimetric 
measurements of the burner heating by the flame.  In this regard, note that the BRE 
burners - including their instrumentation - are not water-cooled, where that was not

For flow control, each BRE burner has a ceramic honeycomb, 25 mm thick, upstream of 
the outlet plate.  Each ceramic element is sandwiched between two layers of perforated 
brass which are 0.4 mm thick and have staggered holes which are 0.4 mm in diameter 
yielding a 22% open area.  The perforated brass is visible in Figure 49. 
 
 
Figure 49.  The 50-mm BRE burner with a coil-type igniter tip inserted above it during set-
up by astronaut Chris Cassidy on 27 Aug. 2020. The center and offset heat flux 
transducers, which include thermocouples, are within openings in the perforated outlet 
plate and pointed out by green arrows.  The tips of two additional thermocouples are 
visible as faint dots between holes in the black outlet below the transducers, as pointed 
out by the red arrows.  [Cropped detail from ISS063e078811] 
 
As seen in Figure 49, the BRE burners are each equipped with two Medtherm heat flux 
transducers, of the Schmidt-Boelter type, which each include a type-T thermocouple.  The 
Medtherm calibrations for the four transducers are included in Figures 50-53.  The sensors 
pass through the holes in the outlet plate, where one is in burner’s center and the other 
is offset, where their radial positions are indicated in Table 4.  The 25- and 50-mm burners 
respectively have sensors with outer diameters of 1/16 and 1/8 inch, where the model 
and serial numbers are also provided in the table.

and 2 type-B thermocouples.  Furthermore, the BRE wiring wasn’t optimized to minimize 
mixed connections.  The thermocouples and wiring are described in Table 5, where

mismatched connections.

The flow from the two spaceflight BRE burners was characterized at the University of 
Maryland prior to the burners’ launch.  Flow profiles were measured 10 mm downstream 
from the burner outlet along four lines across the burner surface, namely N-S, NE-SW, E-
W, and SE-NW, where the offset heat flux transducer is to the north (N) as shown in the 
subsequent figure.  The flow profiles were made for the 25- and 50-mm burners with 3 
and 12 slpm of nitrogen, respectively.  At these flow rates, it can be seen in Figures 55 
and 56, respectively, that flow from both burners was nominally axisymmetric.  While it 
was nominally flat across the center of the 25-mm burner, the characterized flow was 
significantly depressed in the center of the 50-mm burner.  However, the 50-mm burner 
was only used on 2 of the 17 days in which BRE flames were ignited.  Furthermore, the 
50-mm burner flow (i.e., of both fuel and nitrogen, if any) in the spaceflight testing was 
always less than 0.5 slpm total (on a nitrogen basis), in great contrast to the 12 slpm used 
in the characterization.  As such, it is likely that the flow profile was more uniform than 
that seen in Figure 56.

D. Igniter Tips 
Two types of crew-exchangeable igniter tips have been used during ACME testing.  Most tests 
were conducted with a tip featuring a simple loop of Kanthal A-1 wire (0.25 mm in diameter) 
which was resistively heated with specification of the voltage and duration.  A pre-heat voltage 
and duration, e.g., prior to burner flow, can also be specified.  The second type features a small 
coil of Kanthal A-1 wire (0.32 mm in diameter), where it was used in the final six s-Flame test days 
(in June-July 2020) and throughout the second round of BRE testing (in Sept. 2020 to Jan. 2021).  
The coil igniter tip is also being used in the CFI-G investigation. 
 
 
Figure 57.  A standard ACME igniter tip prior to launch.  The igniter tip’s white ceramic insulator 
is 4.75 mm in diameter and the pin-to-pin spacing (as measured from their centers) is 2 mm.

the Fields of View (FOVs) are not clearly presented in those reports, so they are shown graphically 
in this section for the standard, offset, and BRE radiometers, but not the CFI-G radiometer array. 
 
Note that the ACME burners vary in length, where the subsequent figures show a spherical 
burner, for which the porous sphere should be nominally centered at the intersection of the CIR 
window axes, the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) FOVs, and standard radiometer array’s central 
radiometer.  The other ACME burners were shorter in length so that the burner-stabilized flames 
would be approximately centered relative to most of the optical instrumentation.  More 
specifically, the outlets of the existing BRE, coflow, and gas-jet spaceflight burners are respectively 
about 10, 12, and 10 mm ‘below’ (i.e., upstream) of plane defined by the axes of CIR chamber 
windows.

thermopile detectors are of the same make and model, but the FOV is restricted by an additional 
aperture (not a lens) in front of each of the four outer radiometers.

G. Thermocouples 
The thermocouple rakes, of which there are two versions with different probe lengths (referred 
to as far and near or alternatively short and long), were developed for ACME’s spherical flame 
experiments.  The four thermocouple tips on each rake are nominally at the distances below from 
the center of the burner’s porous sphere 
 
Far/short 
45, 60, 100, 100 mm 
 
Near/long 
13, 25, 50, 100 mm 
In the far/short case, the two thermocouples at 100 mm distance are in orthogonal directions 
from the spherical burner. 
 
 
Figure 69.  Thermocouple rake dimensions. 
 
The size of the exposed thermocouple beads was not measured, but it should be at least twice 
the 0.2-mm wire diameter. 
 
The two innermost thermocouples (i.e., closest to the spherical burner) on each rake are type-B, 
while the outer thermocouples are type-K.  In contrast, only the two thermocouples at 13 and 25 
mm were intended to be type B, where this discrepancy is documented in deviation ACME-DEV-
026. 
 
There are also two separate thermocouples which are each at nominally 200 mm distance from 
the center of the spherical burner where these have thus far been always installed.  However, 
they are located far upstream of the burner outlets and as such will be of limited value for 
experiments with the other burner types. 
 
Thermocouple 2 (at 200 mm, on the relay side) was reported to be bent by about 10 degrees on 
3 April 2018, about 10-15 degrees on 22 May 2018, and about 30 degrees on 19 June 2018.  The 
next three reports indicated the same bend, and the procedures were changed to cover the tip

B. Deviations and Waivers 
Engineering design requirements have their source in the spacecraft, CIR facility, safety, and of 
course the experiments’ science.  But all of them could not be readily addressed.  A list of deviation 
and waiver documents is subsequently provided, including the reason for each request. 
 
ACME-DEV-002 
Engineering model will not be exposed to high oxygen concentrations during the course 
of testing and validation, so this requirement is not necessary for this build 
ACME-DEV-004 
In order to avoid scrapping and remaking the S1101MFD2206 Zoom Lens Housing, a 
deviation is required to replace item C13, QTY 6, on S1101MFA2200, from NAS1101E00-
3 Screw, Machine-Flat Fillister Head .060-80 UNJF-3A x .188 Length to NAS1101E01-3 
Machine-Flat Fillister Head .073-64 UNJF-3A x .188 Length on S/N 1001 and 1002.  Also, 
Revision C of S1101MFD2206, per ACME-ECO-182, will not be incorporated on S/N 1001 
and 1002. 
ACME-DEV-005 
This deviation will enable us to use these parts for the GIU, without having to scrap and 
rework the Thermocouple rakes. 
ACME-DEV-006 
This deviation enables the two brackets currently fabricated to be used for EM and flight 
with minimal rework. 
ACME-DEV-007 
The NCR and Deviation allow for the use of the covers without having to refabricate parts, 
at a significant impact to schedule. 
ACME-DEV-008 
To protect the expensive and delicate flow straightener from undue damage and stress 
from machining. 
ACME-DEV-009 
Two assembly fasteners will not engage the locking features of their locking inserts. 
ACME-DEV-011 
Two of the inserts on this assembly, as identified in ACME-NCR-055 and in the attached 
PDFs, are missing their locking features. This deviation allows for the use of item C19
