parameter 'GevTimestampTickFrequency'. 
 
4. High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package 
The HiBMs camera was used in combination with an opposed backlight, i.e., the CIR’s 
collimated illumination package.  The resultant imaging was used in preceding droplet 
combustion experiments for measuring droplet diameter, but it may also be useful for 
determining the soot volume fraction via light extinction.  However, the camera’s red filter, 
corresponding to the red illumination, appears to be broad enough to permit significant soot 
incandescence to pass through the filter.  As a result, this imaging is unlikely to be useful for 
soot volume fraction measurements for all conditions.  After post-processing on the ground, 
the images were made available in the TIFF format and as such are readily opened.  The 
grayscale images were typically archived at 15 fps. 
 
It is important to understand that this camera’s images are of limited value for BRE because 
of the general lack of soot with exception of ignition.  But even considering that, the soot 
volume fraction can be computed using images from the ACME DataCam as discussed in that 
camera’s section.  
 
In initial ACME testing with the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, this 
monochrome camera was used without a filter, but that was abandoned because the camera 
is nearly insensitive to blue.  The red filter was installed on 5 March 2018 and used throughout 
all subsequent ACME testing. 
 
 
C. Test Parameters and Other Files 
Files discussed in this section include the following: 
CIR chamber calculator file 
Test parameter file 
Notes 
Test timing 
Logs 
 
1. CIR chamber calculator file 
In great contrast to other file types, there is just a single file for each of BRE’s two rounds of 
testing:  
 
Final ACME Chamber Calculator - 2019-01-31 to 2019-04-09.xlsx 
 
Final ACME Chamber Calculator - 2020-07-22 to 2021-02-03.xlsx 
which provide estimates of the composition of the combustion chamber before and after each 
BRE test, and more generally for every Fuel/Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) action 
involving gas flow into or out of the chamber.  As a result, this includes filling and venting 
operations, plus recirculation of the chamber contents through the adsorber cartridge filled 
with 13x molecular sieves. 
 
More specifically, the chamber calculator provides the chamber pressure before and after 
each operation involving flow into or out of the chamber.  While the standard ACME data 
output files (discussed in section 4.A.1) provide the chamber pressure throughout each test,

items.title: PSI-20_Science Documents_BRE_data_interpretation_20220804.pdf
items.text:
ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 
 
20 September 2021 
 
20 
 
 
that measurement is from a pressure transducer that hasn’t been calibrated in years.  
Meanwhile, the calibrations of the corresponding CIR pressure transducers are checked every 
six months and those calibrations are updated if needed.  Therefore, the chamber calculator 
is the more reliable source of the chamber pressure. 
 
The pressure in the CIR chamber is measured by four different CIR pressure transducers, of 
which one (PT29) is a different model used for safety.  The output of the other three 
transducers were used to obtain an average chamber pressure.   However, the output of one 
of those (PT28) was clearly an outlier from the other two (PT16 and PT17) as well that of PT29.  
Therefore, the average pressure recorded in the chamber calculator file was later based on 
just PT16 and PT17.  
 
For BRE, the chamber calculator also provides concentration estimates of the following gases 
within the chamber before and after each test and FOMA operation: 
Oxygen & nitrogen: 
O2, N2 
Fuels:  
 
CH4, C2H4 
Combustion products: CO2, H2O 
The latter are based on telemetry from the three Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) on the ACME 
chamber insert for the flow of fuel, oxygen (or inert), and nitrogen. 
 
In a test, the chamber calculator assumes either complete combustion or no combustion, 
where in the former case the reactant flowing from the burner is transformed into carbon 
dioxide and water vapor (or water vapor alone if the fuel was hydrogen).  Failed or 
unsustained ignitions were typically set to assume no ignition.  Short-lived flames were often 
treated as having complete combustion, even if a significant fraction of the reactant didn’t 
burn.  However, adjustments can be made to account for partial combustion by appropriate 
selection of the ‘Burn Fraction’ in column AL. 
 
With recirculation of the chamber contents, the calculator assumes that the carbon dioxide 
and water vapor are completely adsorbed, i.e., removed from the chamber.  Meanwhile, it 
assumes that any unburnt fuels are not adsorbed. 
 
Researchers can of course make their estimates of the chamber contents where the chamber 
calculator should nonetheless be referenced for its record of fills, venting, and recirculation.  
Note that the chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed 
hardware.  Unfortunately, it is not yet possible to compare chamber calculator estimates with 
measurements that were sometimes made with the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph 
Instrumentation Package (GCIP).  Concentrations from the latter are not yet available as 
explained in section 4.A.3 of this document. 
 
2. Test parameter file 
Each BRE test was controlled by a software script and corresponding parameter file, named 
for example ‘as run21028C1.txt,’ specifying settings for imaging, ignition, gas flow, and more.  
The parameter file and script are discussed extensively in the ACME/BRE Experimental 
Procedure document, which should be referred to for information on this file type.  But note 
that the ACME.log files should be the best way to verify the as-run test parameters, where 
the separate parameter files are unfortunately not completely reliable.  They have not always

items.text:
ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 
 
20 September 2021 
 
21 
 
 
been saved and when the file saving was automated, they have still sometimes had missing 
entries. 
 
3. Notes 
Notes of various types are available for test days, where not all types were collected or 
necessarily prepared for each test day.  It is important to understand that the notes, whether 
handwritten or typed, may include mistakes.  It is better to rely on automated logs, metadata 
files, and parameter files or of course the measurements themselves when possible. 
 
The daily test point logs, with names such as ‘19039 daily test point log.pdf,’ chronologically 
list the tests and the image data acquired which was to be downlinked.  Typically, image data 
was not downlinked without successful, i.e., sustained, ignition.  As an example, image data 
wasn’t downlinked if the test aborted prior to ignition.  However, the reverse is not always 
true.  Image data was sometimes downlinked when ignition was unsuccessful and as a result 
the test point log is only a clue as to what transpired.  Furthermore, note that image data 
from certain selected cameras, e.g., the HiBMs camera, was sometimes not downlinked due 
to the limit of how much data could be reasonably downlinked in a subsequent two-shift day. 
 
Notes with names such as ‘19039 flow traces.pdf’ include preliminary plots of the flow rates 
(as seen on a console during testing) and other flame diagnostics, typically along with 
additional information about the tests.  
 
The test parameter notes, with names such as ‘19039 test parameter notes.pdf,’ show the 
parameter values which were planned in advance of the test day and the changes made 
during the test day. 
 
The test sheets, with names such as ‘19039 test sheets.pdf,’ are summary notes about the 
conduct of each tests conducted that day. 
 
4. Test timing 
Timing files with names such as 19039C1_TP.txt can be a convenient way to determine the 
phases of the test in which the images were acquired.  An example BRE file is presented here.  
Regarding the closing table, it should be understood that IPSU1 and IPSU2 were respectively 
used to archive the HiBMs and LLL-UV images, but the LLL-UV camera wasn’t used for BRE.  
Meanwhile, IPSU5 (also known as IPSU-G) was used to archive the ACME DataCam and CFI 
intensified camera images.  Normally far more CFI intensified than DataCam images were 
acquired because of the longer exposure times used for the latter camera.

5. Logs 
There are four primary types of automated logs of which two, with names like the following, 
may be helpful. 
 
2021-01-28_12-28_ACME.log 
2021-01-28_12-18_IPSUG.log 
As a reminder, the IPSU-G is the processing and storage unit for the images from the ACME 
DataCam and CFI intensified camera. 
 
Meanwhile, the two logs of commands, with names like the following, are unlikely to be useful 
for interpreting the BRE results. 
 
2021-01-28_12-30_ACMECommands.log 
2021-01-28_12-23_IPSUGCommands.log 
Each of the four log files are created for each day of testing, rather than for each test, although 
there are sometimes multiple log files (of the same type) covering separate portions of a test 
day.  They are text files (despite the log suffix) and as such can be readily opened. 
 
The ACME.log files should be the best way to verify the test parameters, where the separate 
as-run parameter files are unfortunately not completely reliable.  A portion of the log 
corresponding to a single test, 21028C1, is presented here, where this can best be interpreted 
after becoming familiar with the contents of the ACME/BRE Experimental Procedure 
document.  But the test parameters and timing of the test are obvious in the excerpt.

Appendix A 
Nomenclature 
This document’s key abbreviations are listed here. 
ACME 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (project including s- Flame) 
AOI 
Area of Interest (e.g., for image acquisition of just a portion of the camera FOV) 
ASCII 
American Standard Code for Information Interchange 
BRE 
Burning Rate Emulator (an ACME experiment) 
CCD 
Charge-Coupled Device (such as a camera sensor) 
CIR 
Combustion Integrated Rack (ISS facility in which ACME experiments are conducted) 
CFI 
Cool Flames Investigation (a droplet combustion experiment preceding ACME in the CIR) 
CFI-G 
Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (an ACME experiment selected by CASIS and NSF) 
CLD Flame 
Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (another ACME experiment) 
CSV 
comma-separated values 
DataCam 
Data Camera (for ACME experiments, characterized for pyrometry, etc.) 
E-FIELD Flames Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames 
Fiji 
Fiji Is Just ImageJ (a version of ImageJ preloaded with many plug-in features) 
Flame Design 
another ACME experiment 
FOMA 
Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (CIR’s gas management subsystem) 
FOV 
Field of View 
fps 
frames per second 
GCIP 
Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package 
GIPOC 
Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center 
GMT 
Greenwich Mean Time 
HiBMs 
High Bit-depth Multi-spectral camera (of the CIR facility) 
HOBJ 
Halcon object (binary uncompressed format; used for the DataCam)  
ImageJ 
Image Processing and Analysis in Java (open-source image processing software)  
IPSU 
Image Processing and Storage Unit (CIR subsystem) 
IPSU-G 
IPSU for Gigabit ethernet cameras 
ISS 
International Space Station 
LLL-UV 
Low Light Level Ultraviolet camera (of the CIR facility) 
MFC 
Mass Flow Controller 
NTSC 
National Television System Committee 
OMA2 
Optical Multi-channel Analyzer 2 (open-source software for image processing and display) 
ops 
operations 
PaRIS 
Passive Rack Isolation System 
PIMS 
Principal Investigator Microgravity Services 
PMT 
Photomultiplier Tube (where ACME is equipped with three PMT modules) 
PT 
pressure transducer 
psia 
pounds per square inch 
s-Flame 
Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flame (another ACME experiment)  
SAMS 
Space Acceleration Measurement System 
slpm 
standard liters per minute (a measure of the mass or molar flow rate of a gas) 
TFP 
Thin-Filament Pyrometry (a technique for making gas-phase temperature measurements) 
TIFF or TIF 
Tagged Image File Format (used by the CFI, HiBMs, and LLL-UV cameras) 
TM 
thermistor 
TS 
Transport Stream (a video format)

ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME- REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014 
Page ii of vii 
 
PREFACE  
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) is a next generation mini-
facility designed to support Principal Investigators (PI) interested in studying various aspects of 
advanced gaseous combustion in a microgravity environment.  ACME will be integrated into the 
Fluids and Combustion Facility’s (FCF) Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) onboard the 
International Space Station in the US Lab Module. 
The ACME mission is to perform microgravity experiments to study fire suppression/flame 
extinguishment investigations using the Combustion Integrated Rack.  The ACME will allow 
investigation using pure fuels and mixtures of fuels at various chamber atmosphere pressures, 
compositions, and oxygen concentrations.  The microgravity environment allows for 
measurement and observation of flame formation and extinguishment processes that cannot be 
made in sustained gravity.  The modular design of the ACME allows for flexibility in 
configuring for specific experiments and easy maintainability of the hardware.  This hardware 
will provide the apparatus for dispensing, deploying and igniting fuel.  When new experiments 
are proposed the additional experiment specific hardware will be provided.  This requirements 
document reflects such a case, including only the new requirements of the ACME investigation.

ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 1 of 117 
 
 
1.0 
INTRODUCTION   
1.1 
Purpose 
This document will define the engineering requirements necessary to successfully complete 
science and safety requirements.  This document will be used by the ACME design engineers to 
develop the systems necessary for ACME.  Interface and carrier requirements levied on ACME 
will be documented in the ACME ICD, FCF-ICD-CIR-ACME.  ACME will use the existing 
Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) hardware and software platform design 
already developed as a baseline for meeting the requirements found in this document where 
applicable.  Due to the reuse of the MDCA platform design, ACME operational safety concerns 
will be addressed in existing MDCA documents where applicable.  Requirements in this 
document levied on the ACME carrier, the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), will be 
communicated to the ACME-CIR Interface / Sustaining Engineering Team 
1.2 
Scope 
This Engineering Requirements Document assesses the system requirements and lessons learned 
of the existing Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) and Flame Extinguishment 
Experiment requirements needed to successfully build the hardware and develop avionics 
software and how these requirements are implemented.  The Engineering Requirements 
Document (ERD) will provide information regarding the ACME experiment and ensure that 
requirements are quantifiable, verifiable and specific.  The ACME ERD consists of six sets of 
requirements:  Science Requirements, Operational Requirements, FCF/CIR Integration 
Requirements, Derived Requirements, Software Requirements and Safety Requirements.

ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 4 of 117 
 
 
3.0 
REQUIREMENTS MANAGEMENT 
3.1 
Preparation for Requirements 
The preparation for developing proper project requirements is an important first step.  Preparing 
in this sense means establishing procedures for identifying, approving, allocating and managing 
changes to requirements.  This document along with the ZIN Requirements Management 
Procedure (P04005) is meant to facilitate this process.  Other project documentation supports this 
effort and their completion is also required.  A project shall use the following documents and 
procedures during the requirements development process: 
 ZIN Requirements Management Procedure P04005 
 SpaceDOC II Systems Engineering Management Plan (SEMP) or a Project SEMP as 
necessary  T04001 
 ZIN Requirements Database T04003 
 Project Concept of Operations (ConOps)  T04002 
 Project Engineering Requirements Document (ERD)  
3.1.1 Stakeholder Analysis 
An understanding of a customer’s needs and goals for a project is paramount to the requirements 
development process.  Ultimately, it is the customer who will be using the hardware built to the 
specifications laid out by the requirements a project develops.  A customer’s satisfaction with the 
performance of the developed hardware and the benefits the hardware’s operation provides to 
stakeholders is the ultimate measurement of a projects success.  Therefore, a project shall 
perform a stakeholder analysis in the early phases (Pre-phase A or Phase A) of the project life 
cycle. 
3.1.1.1 
Identify Stakeholders 
Project requirements are elicited from Project Stakeholders. A stakeholder is any entity with a 
legitimate interest in the project.  They are any person or organization that is actively involved in 
a project, or whose interests may be positively or negatively affected by execution or completion 
of the project. Some stakes an entity may have in your project are: Interest, rights, ownership, 
knowledge, impact or influence, contribution, etc. Examples of stakeholders can include: 
 ZIN Technologies (further broken into Project Manager, QA Manager, Resource 
Manager, etc.) 
 Principal Investigators and Project Scientists 
 Customer 
 NASA (further broken into GRC, JSC, ISS, etc.) 
 Product users 
 Product integrator 
Stakeholders shall be identified and documented in a Project SEMP using the Project SEMP 
template T04001.

items.text:
ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 5 of 117 
 
 
3.1.1.2 
Identify Level 0 Stakeholder Requirements 
To initiate the requirements elicitation process a project should discuss and develop a short list of 
the main goals and products of the project. Ideally there would be less than 10 and around 4 or 5 
main Level 0 requirements. This step should immediately follow the identification of the Project 
Stakeholders. 
3.2 
Obtaining Requirements 
Once the preparations for developing requirements have been made early in the life cycle of a 
project, the engineering team can begin to develop a set of requirements that will guide the 
design and development of the systems necessary to fulfill the Project Stakeholder’s needs.  
These “build-to” or engineering requirements begin to take shape typically in Phase A of a 
project life cycle and continue to be developed throughout the design phase of the project. 
3.2.1 Identifying All Stakeholder Requirements 
After the initial, Level 0, stakeholder requirements have formed a foundation for discussion, a 
project can initiate the collection of all stakeholder requirements. Inputs for identifying more 
detailed stakeholder requirements will include: Source documents, stakeholder needs and project 
constraints such as cost, schedule and hardware/software solution restrictions. Stakeholder 
requirements can also be found in interface documents, concept documents developed by the 
project, ZIN organizational and industry standards, test results and design maturation 
discussions, stakeholder meetings, etc. At this point in the project trade studies are ongoing and 
specific hardware and software solutions are beginning to be formulated. 
Requirements shall be properly documented with traceability and captured in a Requirements 
Development Matrix Database using the ZIN template T04003. Traceability shall include (as 
appropriate): 
 The source document identity 
 The paragraph title 
 The sentence number  
The requirements will then further be documented using this template as the project’s 
Engineering Requirements Document, which is generated from the database. 
Figure 1 shows the various sources of project requirements in a block flow diagram.  This 
section should also make apparent what requirements are housed and maintained by the project 
engineering team and which are external requirements that are not included in this document but 
must also be considered during the design process.  Note the color coded differentiation between 
internal project documents and external documents.

3.3 
Analyzing Requirements 
Once all stakeholder requirements have been collected and organized it is essential that these 
requirements be analyzed.  Ensuring that the requirement statements meet the necessary standard 
of quality for communication and implementation is part of this process.  Projects shall review 
their requirement statements for quality and validity.

items.text:
ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 7 of 117 
 
 
3.3.1 Requirement Quality 
Requirement statements shall be clear and concise and decomposed to such a level that there is 
only one requirement in each requirement statement. Requirements shall use the word “shall” to 
clearly identify the demand upon the project team. Some tips to identify poor requirement 
statements are: 
 Use of superlatives such as best, most 
 Subjective language such as “user friendly”, “easy to use” 
 Vague pronouns 
 Ambiguous adverbs and adjectives such as “almost always”, “significant”, “real-time”, 
“various”, “few”, “many”, “appropriately” 
 Open-ended, non-verifiable terms such as “provide support”, “as a minimum”, “but not 
limited to” 
 Comparative phrases like “better than” or “higher quality” 
 Loopholes such as “if possible”, “as appropriate” 
 Other indefinites such as “etc.”, “to be determined (TBD)” 
At the time a requirement is identified, a verification method shall also be identified and 
documented in the Requirements Database. Verification methods include test, inspection, 
demonstration and analysis. This will encourage the writers of the requirement to evaluate 
whether they have written a verifiable requirement and provide an instant check of the 
requirement’s value. This step shall be done early in the project, typically in Phase B of the 
project life cycle. 
3.3.2 Requirement Validation 
As mentioned above, understanding stakeholders’ needs and goals is an important step in 
forming requirements.  Ensuring that your requirements are written in a way that fulfills these 
expectations is the next step.  Along with understanding the manner in which the requirement 
will be verified it is also important to analyze whether or not the requirements and the solutions 
they offer align themselves with stakeholders initial operational and programmatic goals. 
Requirement validation requires forethought as to whether or not the hardware that the 
engineering requirements will produce can perform in a manner that fulfills the stakeholders 
goals.  Simplified, validation becomes the question: Are you building the right hardware?  For 
example, have your requirements properly captured the precision and accuracy needs of a 
particular measurement device?  All project requirements shall be validated against stakeholder’s 
requirements.  This includes any transition or derived requirements.   
3.4 
Approving Requirements 
The approval of the ERD serves as an official method of communication between the 
engineering team and the NASA Project Manager.  Communication between the engineering 
team and NASA stakeholders will have invariably been occurring throughout the requirements 
formulation process.  However, the ERD approval is where these requirements are formally 
agreed upon and baselined.

items.text:
ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 8 of 117 
 
 
3.5 
Maintaining Requirements 
Maintenance of requirements is one of the most essential steps to a project’s requirements 
development effort.  Even after the ERD has been baselined there could be many instances when 
it would need to be updated. A new stakeholder could be identified, maturation of the product 
design could bring about new derived requirements from within the engineering team, and of 
course frequent review of the requirements could result in finding flaws in the requirement 
statements that can be fixed.  
Following the logic of this process it is easy to see how many of the project’s fundamental 
documents are affected by the requirements. Therefore, when a requirement is modified or 
added, each document discussed in this process is also subject to change. 
This step shall happen regularly in the Project Life-Cycle to constantly ensure the integrity of the 
end product. Requirements documents, the Requirements Development Matrix and associated 
project documents shall be updated prior to major project gateway reviews at a minimum.

5.0 
ACME HARDWARE PRODUCT DESCRIPTION 
The ACME investigation will be using the MDCA hardware and software concepts and design 
when appropriate. The ACME hardware consists of three hardware system domains, the 
Chamber Insert Assembly (CIA) System, the Avionics Package (AVP) System and the ACME 
Imaging Packages (IMAG) System.   
The CIA provides the mechanism for the combustion event.  The ACME CIA Flow subsystem, 
which interfaces with the CIR Fuel/Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA), provides gas 
mixing and flow control.  The AVP is the center of control and power distribution for ACME.  
And, the IMAG provides imaging of the combustion event including that provided by the carrier 
(CIR). 
The ACME PBS numbering convention for the systems in Figure 2 corresponds to the ACME 
Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) numbering for traceability across the ACME Project 
Lifecycle.  The number convention utilizes a SSC (System/Subsystem Classification) followed

items.text:
ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 11 of 117 
 
 
 
5.1 
ACME Chamber Insert Assembly (CIA) System 
The ACME CIA System provides all the necessary hardware and interfaces to perform science 
on one platform.  The available interfaces are the CIR Water Thermal Cooling System (WTCS), 
and the CIR Fuel/Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA).  Most experimental functions occur 
within the CIA structure and many associated subsystems are found on the CIA.  The CIA 
consists of the Experiment Mounting Structure (EMS) which is the functional hardware and 
upon which the various subsystems are structurally based.  Other subsystems found on and 
around the CIA include the Gas Flow System (FLOW), Exchangeable Gas Burner System 
(Burner), Ignition System (IGN), Engineering Analog Camera System (OpsCam), Diagnostics 
System (DIAG), Measurement System (MEAS), E-Field System (E-FIELD). 
 
 
FIGURE 3. 
ACME Chamber Insert Assembly (CIA) Design 
5.2 
Experiment Mounting Structure (EMS) System 
The EMS provides the main structure for the CIA and acts as the primary mechanical interface 
with the CIR combustion chamber.  It consists of two endplates, support structure, and extraction 
handles.

items.title: PSI-20_Engineering Documents_ACME_Engineering Requirements Doc Rev K.pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 12 of 117 
 
 
 
5.3 
Cooling Plate System 
ACME will use two cold plates mounted to the Experiment Mounting Structure interfacing with 
the CIR Water Thermal Control System (WTCS).  One cooling plate can be attached to each end 
plate.  The hardware to accommodate this is identical to that used on MDCA System.  The 
cooling plates are plumbed together using rigid tubing, and attached to the IRR WTCS interfaces 
with flexible hoses and quick disconnects. 
5.4 
Gas Flow System (FLOW) 
There is a reconfigurable flow system on the CIA that is auxiliary to the CIR FOMA.  Gases are 
received from FOMA via quick disconnects on the Interface Resource Ring (IRR).  The gases 
are directed through interchangeable Mass Flow Controllers, which are replaced as experiments 
require.    Gases are then directed through a series of switching and isolation valves to the burner 
or directly vented into the chamber for chamber fills. 
5.5 
Gas Burner System (Burner) 
The burner system consists of three different types of exchangeable burners made from varying 
inner and outer diameter stainless steel tubing supported by an electrically insulating ceramic 
base.  There are 4 types of burners:  Spherical (3), Gas Jet (7), Co-flow (1) and Burning Rate 
Emulator (2).  Each burner tip is smooth and without burs or sharp edges to aid in the gas 
deployment.  The burners are mounted with a coupling that allows exchangeability of the burners 
and maintains the precise alignment of the system.  Spherical and Gas-Jet burners also include 
burner temperature thermocouples. 
5.6 
Ignition System (IGN) 
The Ignition System will reuse the design of the MDCA System igniter, with a different 
deployment scheme. 
The ignition system consists of a hot wire igniter subassembly mounted to a deployment arm.  A 
Haydon-Kerk linear actuator motor and driver board controls the position of the deployment arm.  
The igniter tip is mounted to an insulating ceramic structure attached to the end of the arm.  The 
entire top assembly is removed from the arm and replaced on an experiment basis to maintain the 
precise geometry necessary for igniter functionality and to reposition the igniter tip based on the 
burner tip’s position. 
5.7 
Analog Camera System (OpsCam) 
The Analog Camera System will be provided, internal to the combustion chamber, primarily as a 
near real-time visual aid to engineering for hardware operation monitoring and troubleshooting.  
In addition, this view will provide a near real-time “look” into the chamber for science 
throughout the flame combustion event. 
5.8 
Illumination System (OpsCam) 
The Illumination System consists of an array of high intensity, white light LEDs that receive 
power from the relay board hardware and are controlled by the Data Acquisition Unit.  The

items.title: PSI-20_Engineering Documents_ACME_Engineering Requirements Doc Rev K.pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 13 of 117 
 
 
illumination system intensity will be variable to avoid saturation of diagnostics.  This 
illumination system is provided to support the Analog Camera System. 
5.9 
Diagnostic System (DIAG) 
Two of the diagnostic systems the Radiometers, the Photomultiplier Tube Modules (PMTs), and 
the Thin Fiber Pyrometry (TFP) Array are located on the Insert.  This hardware supports 
Diagnostic Analysis of the Flames. 
5.10 Radiometer System 
The Radiometers will provide relative measure of flame radiation and emissions, over the 
wavelength range of 0.2 m – 11 m, throughout the combustion event.  The Radiometer System 
will be mounted on the CIA providing a direct view of the combustion event.  Data from the 
Radiometers will be handled by the Data Acquisition Unit mounted inside the Chamber.  Power 
via the Relay Board to the Radiometer System is provided by ACME AVP System (section 
3.4.2). 
5.11 Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) System 
The Photomultiplier Tube Package will provide high-sensitivity relative measurements of flame 
radiation and chemiluminescent emissions of electromagnetic energy over a wide range of 
frequencies and intensity levels throughout the combustion event as well as flame detection and 
extinction determination.  The PMT System consists of three Hamamatsu PMT modules, 
mounted on the CIA providing a direct view of the combustion event.  Additional filters will be 
required for the 2 PMT modules used for narrowband emissions.  Data from the PMT modules 
will be handled by the Data Acquisition Unit mounted inside the Chamber.  Power via the Relay 
Board to the PMT System is provided by ACME AVP System (section 3.4.2). 
5.12 Thin Fiber Pyrometry (TFP) Array System 
A Thin Fiber Pyrometry (TFP) Array arm mounted to a translating motor to move the array into 
and out of the flame.  The translating motor will be an Ultramotion brand linear stepper motor 
and encoder, similar to that used by MDCA System for its igniter.  The Array will be stowed out 
of the combustion area during E-Field testing, or when the Array is not required, but will not be 
removed from the chamber.  The array can be aligned with either the HiBMs-2 or ACME data 
color camera. 
5.13 Measurement System (MEAS) 
The ACME measurement system encompasses the measurement subsystems involved in 
detection and measurement of the experiments with the exception of diagnostic systems 
mentioned above in section 3.4.1.6 and CIR provided diagnostics.  The following sensors are a 
part of the Measurement System:  Far Field Thermocouple Array, Pressure Transducers for 
differential pressure measurement, and heat flux sensors for the BRE burners. 
5.14 E-Field System (E-FIELD) 
The E-Field system consists of two High Voltage (HV) sources (one negative and one positive 
polarity), a passive network, an insulated mesh electrode and an insulated burner electrically 
connected to the returns of the HV supplies.

5.15 ACME Avionics Package System (AVP) 
The Avionics Package System (AVP) provides power conditioning and power distribution, 
system control, data acquisition and CIR and ground interface for the ACME insert.  The AVP 
will house the main electronics for the ACME hardware and will be mounted on the CIR Optics 
Bench. 
 
FIGURE 4. 
ACME Avionic Package (AVP) Design 
5.16 Avionics Package (AVP) 
The Avionics Package will house the main electronics and data storage for the ACME hardware 
and will be mounted at the CIR PIL (PI location), using the standard Optics Bench interfaces.   
5.16.1 Main Computer System (MCS) – Control and Data Management 
A main computer processor is responsible for controlling CIA hardware, imaging hardware to 
execute test points as well as acquiring, storing, and downlinking experiment data.  Experiment 
control and sequencing will be uplinked from the ACME Ground System (AGS) software, at the 
TSC, to the ACME Main Processor (AMP) System software that is resident on the main 
processor in a PC/104 stack configuration.  The main processor communicates with the CIR

items.title: PSI-20_Engineering Documents_ACME_Engineering Requirements Doc Rev K.pdf
items.text:
ACME Engineering Requirements Document  
ACME-REQ-001 rev. K 
April, 2014  
Page 15 of 117 
 
 
Input/Output Processor (IOP).  The interface to the CIR IOP is necessary for transferring 
commands, downlinked data and images, through the International Space Station (ISS) 
communications system. 
5.16.2 Color Camera Data Store (CDS) System 
The ACME Color Camera data is stored on a hard drive in the AVP.  The hard drive is 
removable and replaceable on orbit. 
5.16.3 Power Distribution System (PDS)  
The AVP Power & Distribution System provides power to the equipment in within the AVP and 
the CIA via four 28VDC, 8 amp circuits from the CIR’s Electrical Power Control Unit (EPCU).  
In the AVP, the power is converted to the necessary voltages, regulated and filtered.  Power 
distribution and control within the Chamber is handled by a data acquisition unit and a pair of 
custom designed relay boards.  These devices handle all of the communications with the AVP as 
well as the activation of various components of the CIA. 
5.17 ACME Imaging Package System (IMAG) 
The ACME Imaging (IMAG) System provides all optical imaging and non-optical imaging 
information for acquisition and storage concerning each of the ACME experiments. 
5.18 Data Color Camera Imaging System (DataCam) 
The ACME Data Color Camera Package (see Figure 4) will provide a view of the combustion 
event.  The current Color Camera Package concept consists of an Allied Vision (formerly 
Prosilica) GC1380CH (30fps) camera.  The camera is external to the chamber mounted at a 
UML Location on the Optics Bench.  Power to the Data Color Camera Package is supplied via 
the UML location. 
5.19 CIR Imaging Subsystems 
ACME will utilize the CIR LLL-UV, HiBMS-1, and HiBMS-2 Packages.

6.1 
Internal Interfaces 
The internal interfaces between ACME and CIR are listed below and the requirements for these 
interfaces will be defined in ACME Interface Control Document for the Fluids and Combustion 
Facility, FCF-ICD-CIR-ACME. 
 Structural/Mechanical and Stowage

 Thermal Control 
 Exhaust Vent 
 FOMA Gas Delivery 
 Environmental 
 
6.2 
External Interfaces 
6.2.1 Launch Configuration Interfaces 
ACME provided hardware is non-operational in whatever launch vehicle is chosen to get it on-
orbit.  ACME hardware will be stowed in standard containers provided by ACME and will only 
have physical and structural interfaces with the containers. 
6.2.2 On-orbit External Interfaces 
ACME has no direct external interfaces on-orbit.  All interfaces with the FCF, US LAB, ISS and 
the ground are provided indirectly through CIR.

7.0 
ACME ENGINEERING REQUIREMENTS 
Engineering requirements are ACME’s build-to requirement response to science requirements 
levied by NASA.  This section is drawn from the information filled into the ZIN Requirements 
Development Matrix (T04003) using the Requirements Management Procedure (P04005.)  
ACME’s requirements are organized according to the project’s PBS.  This helps to keep the 
reader and reviewer thinking in terms of the whole system. 
The SSC_ID column is for useful organization and sorting of the system requirements in the 
Requirements Tracking Matrix (RTM) into categories by system, subsystem, or other traits for 
measurements and metrics that may be of interest.  The SSC (System/Subsystem Classification) 
is a three digit number which relates to the Product Breakdown Structure (PBS) which in turn is 
a subset of the Work Breakdown Structure (WBS).  The first digit of the SSC relates the 
requirement to the system assignment.  The second digit of the SSC relates the requirement to 
the subsystem assignment.  The third digit of the SSC is used to relate the requirement to the 
product classification or type:  flight hardware product (0), flight software product (1), or ground 
software product (2), in which they affect.  The SSC is followed by an underscore as a delineator 
and then a unique four digit identification number.  The underscore, versus the dash, is used to 
keep the SSC and ID married as one object in the database.  Requirements with like qualities of 
interest may be grouped together by ID number for ease of sorting.

chamber axis within ± 2mm.

CIR chamber axis within ± 3 degrees.

downstream of the chamber window axes.

ACME shall provide the electrode mesh 
positioned within ± 1mm 40mm downstream of 
the chamber window axes.

ACME shall provide the electrode mesh as an 
ORU and removable from the ACME Chamber 
Insert Assembly (CIA) during spaceflight.

2.5.1 
2.5.4

capable of an output of ± 10 kV DC at no load 
with an equivalent DC output impedance of 50 
Mega-ohms.

1.7.1 
Electric Field – DC Range Accuracy 
ACME shall provide an electric field generator 
such that the voltage monitoring signal of the 
output is within an accuracy of ± 0.12% with a 
temperature coefficient of± 200 ppm per degree 
Celsius.

between the BRE and spherical burner supply

ACME shall provide the pressure differential for

the reading.

chamber axis where the Field of View (FOV) 
plane includes the CIR chamber axis.

items.text:
Laminar Flames 
 
1
2022 Spring Technical Meeting  
of The Central States Section of the Combustion Institute 
May 15–17, 2021 
Detroit, Michigan 
 
Laminar Non-Premixed Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the 
International Space Station 
 
Dennis P. Stocker1,* 
 
1NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, Ohio 44135, USA 
*Corresponding Author Email: dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov 
 
Abstract: From late 2017 to early 2022, six independent studies with flames of gaseous fuels were 
conducted on the International Space Station (ISS) in the U.S. combustion research facility.  An 
exploration of flames at the extremes of high sooting and high dilution was conducted with a coaxial 
coflow burner, where the fuel and oxidizer velocities were typically matched.  An investigation of 
electric-field effects also used the same coflow burner as well as a simple gas-jet burner, with a 
circular electrode mesh, downstream of the burner, at voltages of either polarity up to 10 kV.  A 
study focused on material flammability in a quiescent atmosphere emulated the burning of 
condensed-phased fuels using cylindrical burners with a flat perforated outlet instrumented to 
measure the heat flux to the burner, i.e., emulated fuel.  Three studies of soot processes, flame 
dynamics, and low-temperature combustion used porous spherical burners, yielding a nominally 
one-dimensional flame structure.  The objectives and selected findings of each investigation will be 
briefly discussed after a short review of the advantages of studying combustion in microgravity, 
earlier ISS research, and the experimental hardware and its operation. 
Keywords: flames, microgravity, non-premixed, laminar 
 
1. Introduction 
Microgravity, i.e., apparent near weightlessness, is a unique environment for conducting 
combustion research.  Many flames are dramatically influenced by the near elimination of buoyant 
convection, where the resulting effects are often advantageous [1-2].  For example, it is possible 
to create spherically symmetric flames enabling one-dimensional analysis.  More generally, the 
effective elimination of flicker yields quasi-steady flames.  Furthermore, the length scales are 
increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of their structure.  Microgravity flames tend 
to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere than normal-gravity flames and exhibit a 
much broader range of characteristics.  For example, the long residence times in microgravity 
flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free due to 
radiative heat loss.  Even neglecting soot, microgravity flames can be appropriate for studies of 
limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  It is also possible to study 
momentum-dominated flames at low velocities.  And of course, microgravity is the appropriate 
environment for studies related to spacecraft fire safety. 
Although microgravity combustion research has long been conducted in drop facilities and 
research aircraft flying parabolic maneuvers, spacecraft like the International Space Station (ISS) 
offer significant advantages.  Drop durations, which are ~5 s or less in NASA drop facilities, are 
too short for soot to achieve quasi-steady conditions.  They are also too short to first establish a 
flame and then vary conditions such as the flow rate, for example, to investigate stability or 
extinction limits.  Meanwhile, low-momentum flames can be dramatically disturbed by the g-jitter

items.title: PSI-20_Presentations_ACME CSSCI paper 20220402.pdf
items.text:
Laminar Flames 
 
2
present in aircraft testing, which is nominally ±0.02 g for a ~20 s duration.  The jitter can be 
avoided by floating an experiment within the aircraft, but that reduces the test duration to mere 
seconds.  As a result, space-based testing is often necessary to get microgravity conditions of 
sufficient duration and quality for combustion research. 
The recent research was preceded by two earlier studies with laminar non-premixed flames of 
gaseous fuels conducted in the ISS’ Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using a crew-operated 
coflow apparatus consisting of a gas-jet burner centered within a fan-driven flow duct.  On-orbit 
tests for the Soot Processes In Coflow Experiment (SPICE) of David L. Urban and Peter B. 
Sunderland were conducted in 2009 and 2012 [3].  ISS testing for the Structure & Liftoff In 
Combustion Experiment (SLICE) of Marshall B. Long, Mitchell D. Smooke, Fumiaki Takahashi, 
and Dennis P. Stocker was carried out in 2012 [4-7].  This pair of studies were in turn preceded by 
three investigations with non-premixed flames of gaseous fuels conducted during space shuttle 
missions in 1997 and 2003 [8-16].  The flames were similarly laminar, although one study featured 
mechanically induced vortices. 
Tests for six independent experiments with flames of gaseous fuels were conducted on the ISS 
from Nov. 2017 to Feb. 2022 as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments 
(ACME) project [2].  On-orbit preparations began in Sept. 2017, neglecting SLICE which was a 
planned precursor to ACME’s Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) investigation.  
Table 1 provides an overview of each study, where the first investigator listed is the Principal 
Investigator.  Additional information, including preliminary findings, about each of the six 
experiments will be presented after a description of the experimental hardware and operations. 
The ACME experiments are primarily focused on energy and environmental concerns, but 
there is a secondary emphasis with the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment on spacecraft 
fire prevention.  The primary objective is to gain fundamental understanding that can enable 
improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion processes on Earth, for 
example through the development and verification of models for chemical kinetics and transport 
processes in computational simulations.  In addition to enhanced performance, improved modeling 
capability can lead to reductions in the time and cost for combustor design.  Some specific goals 
are to improve our understanding of combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum 
performance and low emissions can be achieved, cool flame chemistry, flame stability and 
extinction limits, materials flammability, oxygen-enriched combustion which could enable 
practical carbon sequestration, soot control and reduction, and the use of electric fields for 
combustion control. 
 
2. Methods / Experimental 
The ACME research was conducted using a single modular set of hardware with the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) [2].  That facility is shown on the left in Figure 1 with NASA astronaut 
Kate Rubins reconfiguring hardware for a different investigation on 3 Feb. 2021.  The CIR 
provides a nominally 100-liter combustion chamber, gas delivery, venting, water cooling, imaging, 
and other general functions needed to carry out an array of combustion research.  The facility was 
launched in 2008 and then used from 2009 to 2017 for a set of investigations featuring the 
combustion of liquid droplets.  That research notably led to the discovery of non-premixed cool 
flames [17-22] which inspired ACME’s Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G). 
ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a 
variety of burners (but only one at a time) on the chamber axis.  Tests were conducted with gas-

items.text:
Laminar Flames 
 
4
jet, coflow, and spherical burners, plus a fourth type developed for the Burning Rate Emulator 
(BRE) investigation.  The resistively heated igniter has a crew-exchangeable tip and arm (to 
accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive allowed for precise positioning and 
retraction from the flame. 
The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers, visible on the left of Fig. 2, for the 
delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium), and nitrogen to either the burner or the chamber.  
The crew exchanged the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges to improve flow 
control and accuracy.  The gas delivery system enabled on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer 
(but not both simultaneously), coflow, and inverse flames, where the oxidizer issued from the 
burner into the chamber filled with a gaseous fuel.  Gases were also delivered premixed to the 
space station where that was necessary in some circumstances, such as the blending of different 
gaseous fuels.  ACME tests were most often conducted with methane and ethylene where other 
fuels included hydrogen, ethane, propane, n-butane, and hydrogen/methane mixtures.  Nitrogen 
dilution was common, but tests for the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-
Flame) study were also conducted with helium as the inert in both the fuel and oxidizer. 
The chamber insert provided an assortment of non-imaging instrumentation such as a crew-
exchangeable array of thermopile detectors to measure thermal radiation.  There is also a set of 
PhotoMultiplier Tubes (PMTs) which provided measurements of chemiluminescent emissions 
from the excited-state species CH* and OH* as well as a broadband measurement.  A crew-
exchangeable thermocouple rake, intended for studies of spherical flames, can be installed.  While 
not shown in Fig. 2, the chamber insert is also equipped with a translating, crew-exchangeable 
array of 14-micron silicon carbide fibers for making measurements of flame temperature via Thin 
Filament Pyrometry (TFP) [e.g., 23-25,31-34]. 
 
 
Figure 2: ACME chamber insert used within the CIR facility 
 
Five different cameras and two illumination systems were used in the recent research, although 
usually only a fraction of them were used because of operational constraints.  There is an analog

items.title: PSI-20_Presentations_ACME CSSCI paper 20220402.pdf
items.text:
Laminar Flames 
 
5
camera mounted on the chamber insert from which color video was always downlinked in near 
real time during testing.  The other four cameras were mounted around the periphery of the 
combustion chamber.  A high-definition color camera, carefully characterized prior to launch, was 
always used.  Both provide flame imaging, but the high-definition camera can furthermore be used 
to optically determine the CH* concentration, flame or soot temperature (via pyrometry), and soot 
volume fraction [e.g., 23-25].  The latter can also be determined using a gray-scale camera with 
an opposed collimated light source via a light extinction technique [36-37].  Two intensified 
cameras were used, one filtered for OH* emissions, while the other allows for imaging of CH* or 
alternately CH2O* emissions associated with cool flame chemistry. 
All ACME experiments are constant volume (rather than constant pressure) studies, where the 
chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed hardware.  The tests 
were typically only a few minutes in duration, limiting the pressure rise, vitiation of the chamber 
atmosphere, and acquisition of data which was an operational constraint. 
The ACME experiments were configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  Instead, the 
tests were commanded from the ground, specifically from the NASA Glenn Research Center in 
Cleveland, Ohio.  They were conducted in a mostly automated mode with pre-programmed scripts.  
But the role of the crew was critical and over 30 crew members from Canada, Germany, Italy, 
Japan, Russia, and the United States supported the four and half years of ACME operations.  And 
about 50 people, including the investigators, were engaged in the ground operations. 
Weekly operations typically included a two-shift day for testing, a two-shift day to downlink 
the resulting image data, and a day in which an ISS crew member prepared the hardware for the 
next test day.  Replacement of gas bottles was the most common crew activity, where less frequent 
replacements included mass flow controllers and igniter tips.  But the transition to a different 
experiment sometimes required many changes. 
 
3. Results and Discussion 
Past research, including that conducted in microgravity, had revealed shortfalls in the ability to 
accurately model flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and 
dilute flames that are near extinction.  The objective of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD 
Flame) investigation is to extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by 
developing and experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels.  The 
dependence of normal coflow flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution was carefully 
examined for flames at both very dilute and highly sooting conditions.  Measurements including 
flame temperature, CH* concentration, soot temperature, and soot volume fraction were made of 
the structure of diluted methane and ethylene flames in an air coflow, where the fuel and air 
velocities are typically matched.  Lifted flames are a focus of the research to avoid flame 
dependence on heat loss to the burner, where examples from ISS testing can be seen in Fig. 3a.  
The results are applicable to practical combustion issues such as turbulent combustion, ignition, 
and flame stability. 
For sooty attached flames, preliminary results have revealed that the soot volume fraction can 
be several times greater in microgravity flames than in comparison normal-gravity flames.  These 
microgravity flames are also taller and wider.  Meanwhile, dilution limits for both methane and 
ethylene flames were extended in microgravity, where the microgravity flames are more stable, 
allowing for lifted flames at lower fuel concentrations. 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the chemi-ions produced 
by the combustion.  The direct ion transport and the induced ion wind can modify the flame shape,

items.text:
Laminar Flames 
 
6
alter the soot or flammability limits, direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutant emission.  The 
purpose of the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) study is to 
improve understanding of chemi-ionization in flames and the interplay between ion generation and 
ion-driven flows, and to explore how electric fields can be used to control non-premixed flames.  
The ISS tests were conducted burning pure and diluted methane and ethylene with both gas-jet and 
coflow flame configurations.  An electric field of either polarity was generated by creating a high 
voltage differential (up to 10 kV) between the burner and a flat circular mesh above (i.e., 
downstream of) the burner.  Measurements were made of the ion current through the flame and 
the flame’s response to electric forcing as a function of the field strength, fuel, and fuel dilution. 
 
  
 
Figure 3: Gas-jet flames shown at different scales: (a) composite overlay of three dilute methane 
coflow flames as a function of the matched fuel/coflow velocity, (b) example of the effect of the 
electric field strength on the flame size where the downstream mesh was negatively charged 
 
In contrast to normal-gravity tests, the microgravity flames exhibit a distinct peak ion current 
that corresponds to the most compact flame, where an example of the effect of the field strength 
on the flame size can be seen in Fig. 3b.  Soot generation could be suppressed and more broadly 
there are clear correlations between the flame luminosity, combustion intensity, and ion current in 
the ISS data.  It was found that highly diluted flames can be stabilized with very weak electric 
fields.  But at high field strengths, the flames exhibited corona and arc discharges. 
Unlike the other ACME experiments, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) research is focused 
on spacecraft fire prevention.  More specifically, its objective is to improve our fundamental 
understanding of materials flammability in still atmospheres as a function of material properties.  
The research examines extinction behavior, the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and 
the relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.  A 
flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where 
measurements were made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the vaporization 
of condensed-phase fuels is dependent.  In the ISS tests, pure or nitrogen-diluted ethylene and 
methane were used to simulate the burning of materials such as plastics by matching properties 
including the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface temperature, and smoke point.  
Testing included atmospheres with elevated oxygen concentrations and reduced pressures being 
considered for future crew vehicles.  An example dome-shaped flame can be seen in Fig. 4a. 
It was found that low-momentum microgravity flames can burn for minutes in the absence of 
an air flow or flame spread.  Although the flames can burn for minutes in elevated oxygen

items.text:
Laminar Flames 
 
7
concentrations, like those being considered for future spacecraft, they were found to self-
extinguish in concentrations below ~25% (by volume).  While smaller flames can burn for minutes 
at elevated oxygen concentrations, larger flames were generally seen to self-extinguish within 1.5 
minutes.  Although ethylene flames at elevated oxygen concentrations can burn for minutes, 
methane flames were seen to self-extinguish within a minute. 
 
 
 
 
Figure 4: Low-momentum flames shown at different scales: (a) pure ethylene BRE flame 
where the burner is illuminated from the left in red, (b) inverse flame encompassing the porous 
spherical burner, with an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowing from the burner into an 
ethylene/nitrogen atmosphere, (c) false-colored image of a diluted hydrogen flame, revealing the 
burner and glowing ceramic fibers for Thin-Filament Pyrometry  
 
The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve fundamental understanding of 
soot inception and control and thereby enable the optimization of oxygen-enriched combustion 
and the ‘design’ of non-premixed flames that are both robust and soot free.  A secondary goal is 
to obtain detailed quasi-steady measurements and evaluate the possible existence of steady flames.  
The tests were conducted with various concentrations of ethylene and oxygen to determine the role 
of the flame structure on the soot inception.  The effect of the flow direction on soot formation 
was assessed by studying both normal flames and inverse flames, in which the oxidizer flowed 
from the burner into an atmosphere of gaseous fuel.  The burner, including its supply tube, can be 
seen within an inverse flame in Fig. 4b. 
As expected in the normal-flame ISS testing, the flame size increases with reactant flow rate 
and decreases with ambient oxygen concentration.  Very small flames have low radiative loss and 
asymptotically approach steady-state behavior, where one flame lasted over 14 minutes until it 
was terminated due to operational constraints.  In contrast, large flames increase in size over time 
until the flame extinguishes because of radiative heat loss.  Before extinction, these flames 
experience an unstable oscillatory mode, in which they partially quench and reform.  The 
oscillations grow in magnitude until the flame fully extinguishes. 
The goal of the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) investigation 
is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics of non-premixed spherical flames, 
potentially through modification of kinetic and/or transport sub-models.  The spherical flames 
were ignited and allowed to transition naturally toward extinction, where a specific objective is to 
identify the extinction limits for both radiative and convective extinction (i.e., at high and low 
system Damköhler numbers, respectively).  Tests were conducted with either nitrogen or helium 
as the diluent in both the fuel and chamber atmosphere.  The fuel gases included hydrogen, 
methane, hydrogen/methane mixtures, and ethylene where an example hydrogen flame can be seen 
in Fig. 4c.

items.text:
Laminar Flames 
 
8
Both radiative and kinetic (i.e., convective) extinction of the spherical flames appear to have 
been observed.  Radiative extinction seems to occur at high flow rates and kinetic extinction at 
low flow rates.  The latter may seem counterintuitive but at low flow rates the flames are close to 
the burner where the velocities are highest.  With helium, rather than nitrogen, dilution of both the 
fuel and oxygen, the extinction limits are shifted and kinetic extinction is generally difficult to 
discern.   
The purpose of Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G), selected for spaceflight by the 
Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) and the National Science Foundation 
(NSF), is to observe non-premixed quasi-steady spherical cool flames on porous burners.  Non-
premixed cool flames had been discovered in droplet combustion research conducted in the CIR 
in 2012 but droplet combustion involves unsteady burning rates.  Although ignition and flame 
propagation in engines depend on cool flames, computational tools used to design the engines 
neglect cool flame chemistry.  Advances in low-temperature kinetic mechanisms could enable 
cleaner burning, more efficient internal combustion engines.  Tests were carried out with normal- 
and inverse-flame tests of ethane, propane, and n-butane. 
Cool flames were discovered in normal-flame CFI-G testing with n-butane as can be seen in 
Fig. 5 which features a sequence of images from an intensified camera filtered for formaldehyde 
emissions.  As expected, the cool flames are significantly smaller than the corresponding hot 
flames. 
 
 
Figure 5: Appearance of a cool flame, in intensified imaging, after the hot flame quenches in 
a normal-flame test with diluted n-butane 
 
4. Conclusions 
When ACME’s ISS testing ended in Feb. 2022, over 1,500 flames were ignited for its six 
experiments.  Early results have been presented and published and more papers will follow [e.g., 
23-33].  ACME’s open-source data is gradually being made available through NASA’s Physical 
Sciences Informatics website.  Data from the E-FIELD Flames and s-Flame investigations, the 
first studies for which ISS testing was completed, are currently available online.  CIR operations 
have shifted to the Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) project which is focused on 
flammability, flame spread, and spacecraft fire safety [2].

ACME Critical Design Review– 21 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
PDR RFA-001 Disposition  
RFA # 01 
Originator: Anita Tenteris 
Originator Concurrence:  23 September 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
One of the criteria for PDR is a preliminary limited 
life items list. Just because other experiments may 
not have such a list does not mean ACME should not 
have such a list. ACME presents a unique situation 
where experiments will occur in the same chamber 
as the Cube is located as well as tubing, wiring, 
cooling lines, etc. The project should to start 
identifying their materials lists from the Computer-
Aided Design (CAD) drawings so that compatibility 
issues/soft goods shelf life/limited life items can be 
identified early in the design cycle. Maybe testing 
would also be needed as well for materials with 
unknown compatibility? 
 
Identify the material 
compatibility and shelf life limits 
for the soft goods used in 
ACME and CIR 
 
It has been determined by the 
project that a materials analysis 
would not be done for PDR due to 
funding and resource limitations.  
The plan is to have this analysis 
and MIUL completed at CDR. 
  
Although the analysis was not 
complete at PDR, the ACME 
project is aware of potential issues 
with the Data Cube and other 
electronics and their compatibility 
with the gaseous fuels.  These 
issues are currently being tracked 
in the Risk Management 
Implementation Tool database.

ACME Critical Design Review– 22 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
PDR RFA-002 Disposition  
RFA # 02 
Originator: Anita Tenteris 
Originator Concurrence:  23 September 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
In many of the presentations, the presenters 
indicated CIR heritage for a choice of hardware. It 
seemed as though CIR was treated as a ‘black box’ 
that ACME hooks into. ACME fuels need to be 
compatible with CIR and also cause no issues to 
CIR. 
The following items need to be investigated further to 
assess compatibility: 
• ACME Venting compatibility with CIR hardware 
• Are the gases/liquids compatible with CIR 
hardware, particularly with the soft goods in the 
solenoid valves? The board was told the solenoid 
valves contained FKM o-ring. For the ACME 
gases, NBr is the recommended rubber for most of 
the gases, if not all. 
• What are the limited life items for CIR? Do any of 
the items need be replaced prior to ACME use? 
An assessment of the venting 
compatibility has been addressed 
and was deemed acceptable. 
 
As the project matures, CIR will 
assess compatibility of materials in 
their system with ACME gasses, 
products of combustion and any 
other applicable interactions. 
 
ACME anticipates this will be 
completed by CDR.

ACME Critical Design Review– 23 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
PDR RFA-003 Disposition  
RFA # 03 
Originator: Al Linne 
Originator Concurrence:  7 November 2013 
Statement of 
Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
There are no warnings to 
eliminate damage to the 
test hardware 
To minimize the likelihood of 
hardware damage, the flight & 
ground software designs 
should incorporate software 
requirements to identify invalid 
commands and command 
parameters that are outside of 
allowable limits and to alert 
operations personnel that 
invalid commands were 
entered. 
 
A complete software command list for the ACME hardware has 
been derived from operational requirements for the ACME 
system.  Operational limits have been defined for each 
command and incorporated into the software requirement set.  
The software requirements are documented in the Software 
section of the ACME Engineering Requirements Document 
(ERD) ACME-REQ-001.   
This list of signals is also documented in the ACME Data 
Dictionary Document (ACME-DOC-008).   
These documents will be available for NASA review and 
comment during the CDR.   
The approved operational limitations will be built into the 
ACME ground command station software at the TSC.  Every 
command sent by an operator will be checked against these 
established limits.  Commands that violate safe ranges will be 
rejected (on the ground) and the operator will receive an error 
message.  This ground software will be verified, as part of the 
overall ACME test and verification  campaign, to ensure no 
command can ever reach the ACME hardware that is outside 
of these safely established limits.

ACME Critical Design Review– 24 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
PDR RFA-004 Disposition  
RFA # 04 
Originator: Al Linne 
Originator Concurrence:  7 November 2013 
Statement of 
Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
A detonation analysis has 
not been completed. 
Perform a detonation analysis on the 
expected ACME gas mixtures. This 
should be done prior to the ACME Phase 
0/1 Flight Safety Review, since it may 
inform some of the hazard analysis. Also, 
the results of this analysis could drive the 
consumables usage and could limit the 
amount of science performed. 
An ACME detonation analysis has been performed 
for the Inverse Flame Experiment, which is the the 
worst case hazard.  It was chosen because of the 
possible oxygen interaction with ACME CIA 
hardware (i.e. materials compatibility).  The 
analysis validated that the present configuration 
could safely meet requirements.  The analysis has 
not impacted the design. 
 
A full detonation analysis of all experiments will be 
completed prior to the Phase 2 Flight Safety 
Review.

Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
A number of different oxygen 
percentages were discussed & 
identified in the PDR presentation 
and documentation. What oxygen 
percentage was used in the 
design and does this cover the 
ranges requested by the PI. 
Determine the worst case oxygen 
percentage (and pressure) that could 
potentially be in the CIR chamber with 
ACME installed, based on credible failures 
to CIR & ACME equipment and use this 
oxygen percentage as the design point for 
ACME. This will drive integrated 
safety/hazard analyses as well as ACME 
material compatibility. 
Also, based on the resulting worst case 
oxygen percentage determine if an 
oxygen compatibility assessment needs to 
performed for the ACME Chamber Insert 
Assembly. 
Oxygen compatibility with the ACME CIA has 
been assessed and is documented in the 
Draft Materials Identification/ Usage List 
(MIUL), which is a review item for the CDR.  
An Integrated Hazard Analysis has been 
completed and the worst-case oxygen 
percentages and pressures have been 
identified and addressed in the Hazard 
Report (see ACME Hazard Report 5, 
documented in ACME-SDP-001).

RFA # 06 
Originator: Alan Linne, Nechelle Grant, Terry O’Malley 
Originator Concurrence:  25 October 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
CIR hazards mitigations are being 
used by ACME. It was not clear 
that the ACME team had reviewed 
the CIR hazards and confirmed 
the mitigation steps are applicable 
to ACME.  There were no 
integrated hazards included in the 
ACME Phase 0/1 Flight Safety 
Data Package safety hazard 
analysis (ACME-SDP-001. 
The ACME and CIR teams should provide 
an integrated CIR/ACME Safety story. 
There are likely integrated safety hazards 
that exist in the integrated system and 
these should be identified and 
documented. Perform an integrated 
hazard analysis and prepare integrated 
hazard reports. The integrated CIR/ACME 
hazard analysis should be part of the 
Phase 0/1 Flight Safety Review. 
Also, a pressure switch, a solenoid valve, 
and a pressure regulator in the ACME 
system were included in the design on the 
N2 input to the chamber. Perform a 
integrated hazard analysis of this system 
(CIR & ACME hardware) to ensure system 
meets the intent of CIR hazard analyses. 
The Integrated Hazard Analysis has been 
completed with the participation of the CIR 
Team.  An Integrated Safety Data Package 
has been prepared and was included as input 
to the ACME Phase 0/1 Flight Safety Review.

ACME Critical Design Review– 27 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
PDR RFA-007 Disposition  
RFA # 07 
Originator: Terry O’Malley 
Originator Concurrence:  25 October 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
The ACME project plan did not provide 
sufficient detail of the end-to-end project 
planning. There was no evidence of a 
bottoms up cost estimate or a bottoms 
up schedule. Both of these are vital in 
ensuring the project has been thought 
through and that sufficient resources are 
available to successfully complete the 
project. The only budget shown was the 
program budget, and it may not be 
adequate complete the current scope of 
the ACME project. 
The ACME Systems Engineering 
Management Plan also did not provide 
sufficient detail of the end-to-end project 
technical management. It provided 
details through PDR/CDR, but not the 
project lifecycle. 
Update the Project Plan. Complete a 
bottoms up cost estimate and a 
bottoms up end-to-end schedule. 
Consider performing a parametric cost 
estimate. To be of value, these should 
be performed within 6 months of the 
PDR. 
 
Update the SEMP to include technical 
details through launch. Include things 
as spare required, environmental 
testing required, Ground/Flight Support 
Equipment etc. 
An updated Project Plan has been 
baselined, which includes a bottoms-up 
cost estimate and schedule.  An 
independent cost estimate by the GRC 
Cost & Economic Analysis Office has 
been performed and is in-line with the 
project plan.    
 
Updates to the SEMP will be made 
regularly as more information becomes 
available to the project team.  The SEMP 
is a living document that will be revisited 
as necessary.

ACME Critical Design Review– 28

PDR RFA-008 Disposition  
RFA # 08 
Originator: Terry O’Malley 
Originator Concurrence:  25 October 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
The ACME Engineering requirements 
document is incomplete. While it appears 
that the Science requirements have been 
thoroughly addressed, carrier 
requirements (both CIR & ISS) and 
safety and mission assurance have not 
been addressed in the ACME ERD. It is 
important to thoroughly identify all 
requirements which are imposed on the 
system and subsequently must be 
verified. A related concern is the number 
of requirements that must be verified. 
There are a large number of 
requirements on the system and the 
verification program could be extensive. 
Complete the ERD. This should be 
done within 6 months of the PDR to 
ensure the CDR design meets all 
requirements that are levied on the 
system. Environmental testing 
requirements should be included as 
part of this, waivers for fragile 
equipment should be identified early. 
When developing the verification 
program look for ways to combine & 
streamline the verification process. 
The document FCF-ICD-CIR-ACME 
addresses carrier requirements (both CIR 
and ISS).  ACME-REQ-001 points there. 
 
Safety and Mission Assurance 
requirements will be detailed in the ACME 
Hazards and Integrated CIR-ACME 
hazard reports.  Following the Phase 0/1 
Flight Safety Review, where these Hazard 
Reports are approved, the requirements 
will be incorporated into ACME-REQ-001. 
 
The verification process will group 
requirements by discipline identified to 
facilitate verification and validation.

The project has done a good job of 
writing operational requirements, but they 
have not yet been vetted with the PIs. 
This concern stems from RDR when the 
PIs were assuming operational 
requirements that the GRC science and 
engineering teams were not aware of. 
This concern follows on from the ACME 
RDR-004 RFA which has not been 
closed out as of the PDR. 
It is imperative that: 1) the currently 
documented operational requirements 
are vetted with each of the PIs; 2) the 
engineering team talks with each of the 
PIs. This will ensure that both parties 
fullly understand what is meant by 
each of the requirements, and also 
give the engineering team a chance to 
uncover additional operational 
requirements. 
 
Close out the RFA ACME RDR-004. 
The Project Scientist, Dennis Stocker, has 
vetted the operations requirements 
documented in ACME-SRD-001 with the 
respective Pis.  Dennis has also 
discussed the Ops requirements with the 
ACME engineering team to be sure they 
are well understood. 
 
The ERD revision including the updates 
with the operations requirements has 
been completed and released. 
 
This information should be sufficient to 
close RFA ACME-RDR-004.

Spherical Burner
 
Spherical Burner 
The upper part of the spherical burner will be supplied by Princeton 
University under the following conditions: 
 
1) Princeton University: Fabricate a 1/4”, 3/8”, and 1/2” spherical burner head with supply tube per ACME 
ISRD 1.2.1, 1.2.2, 1.2.5, and 1.2.6.  
2) Princeton University: Perform preliminary tests on the above spherical burner heads following ACME 
ISRD 1.2.3 as a guide and conferring with NASA ACME Project Scientist.  
3) Princeton University: Deliver accepted spherical burner heads to NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC).  
4) NASA GRC performs additional acceptance tests as necessary (microgravity).  
5) NASA GRC deliver acceptable spherical burner heads to ZIN Technologies Inc. as government furnished 
equipment (GFE.) via C727.  
6) Zin Technologies Inc.: Accept and serialize spherical burner heads from NASA GRC.  
7) Zin Technologies Inc.: Perform additional fabrication on S1101MFA1218, S1101MFA1223, and 
S1101MFA1228 per ACME ISRD 1.2.4, 1.2.6, and 1.2.7. This fabrication will produce the following top level 
assemblies: S1101MFA1216: 1/4” spherical burner assembly, S1101MFA1220: 3/8” spherical burner 
assembly, S1101MFA1225: 1/2” spherical burner assembly  
8) Zin Technologies Inc.: Deliver S1101MFA1216, S1101MFA1220, and S1101MFA1225 to NASA GRC via 
a DD1149.  
9) NASA GRC: Test and verify S1101MFA1216, S1101MFA1220, and S1101MFA1225 per ACME ISRD 
1.2.3.  
10) NASA GRC: Deliver verified spherical burner assemblies along with verification certification documents 
to Zin Technologies Inc. as GFE via C727.

ACME Critical Design Review– 151 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
Depress / Repress 
• Unless part of a pressurized system, all volumes are designed to 
adequately vent due to station / vehicle depressurization 
• Vented Containers will be verified by the stored energy method (SDP 
STD-ACME-1 17.a) where the volume has a stored energy < 3,063 ft-
lbs.  Volumes with a stored energy > 3,063 ft-lbs will have a depress 
rate calculated. 
 
• Depress rates are calculated* for each volume to show that the 
volume’s depress rate is greater than maximum station / vehicle 
depress rate so no pressure load is generated 
• Maximum depress rate is defined in section 3.1.1.2.1.5 part B of SSP-
50835 Rev C as 13.3kPa/s (1.93psi/sec) 
 
 
 
*AIAA Journal, October 1986, Vol. 24, No. 10, pg 1709-1711, “Formulas for Venting or Charging 
Gas from a Single Volume”, H.T. Yang

Goal 
 Use the space environment as a laboratory for strategic 
research & technology experiments in physics, chemistry 
and biology to support Agency goals & the Nation’s vision 
new for space exploration. 
 
Objectives 
• Develop the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the 
Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) to support physical and 
biological research on board the ISS. 
• Develop the Ground Infrastructure, Integration, 
Operations, Logistics & Maintenance plans required for 
FCF sustaining engineering and operations. 
• CIR provides the only large environmental chamber (100 
liters) on ISS in which the space environment, Lunar, Mars 
or other desired environment may be simulated (i.e., 
pressure, temperature, gaseous atmospheres, 
particulates, etc.) for long duration, on-orbit investigations 
and technology validations. 
• CIR provides easily reconfigurable diagnostics, 
customizable software, passive rack-level vibration 
isolation, and other subsystems that will support a wide 
range of investigations
