diffusive flames in microgravity. Small diameter jet flames of 0.4 – 2.7 mm yielded spherical 
flames of durations from 150 – 300 s (Ross, 2001). Also Sunderland et al. (1999) recorded 
flames for port diameters up to 3.3 mm, and Reynolds (Re) from about 10 – 1700 in 
microgravity. Their low Re flames were spherical, and the higher Re flames elongated. An 
empirical relationship indicated the flame length to port diameter was linearly proportional to the 
Re, with the constant of proportionality depending on fuel type. The constant was about 30% 
higher for the non-buoyant flames, perhaps due to the lower entrainment of air. 
It would appear that a spherical flame shape forms a stable steady flame for droplets, jets at 
low Re, and the candle with the cylindrical wick. Three-dimensional planar surfaces burning in 
microgravity are likely to remain stable when achieving a similar flame shape. Brahmi et al. 
(2005) used a gaseous burner to simulate burning in microgravity under flow conditions. They 
burned ethane over a 60 × 60 mm sintered bronze plate in oxygen-nitrogen atmospheres flowing 
over the plate at velocities of about 10 – 150 mm/s. They found, for 120 experiments under 
microgravity conditions, a mapping of fuel velocity with oxidizer velocity indicated three 
regions of flame shapes during burning. These regions are shown in Figure 1. The flames 
indicated an elliptical shape in Region I, parabolic in Region II and linear in Region III. The 
elliptical flames for points the (a) and (b) location of the mapping are shown in Figure 2. It is 
noteworthy that steady elliptical flames were produced for this planar geometry at nearly 
quiescent conditions (U∞ ~ 5 mm/s) in microgravity. Their establishment in quiescent flow needs 
to be demonstrated. 
Perhaps this evidence suggests a spherical-like flame can support steady diffusive burning 
in microgravity quiescent conditions for other configurations. 
 
1.4 
Overview of the use of burners to emulate burning of materials  
Orloff and deRis (1971), deRis et al. (1975) and Kim et al. (1971) pioneered the use of sintered 
metal burners for studying the burning of planar condensed-phase steady burning. As with the 
Brahmi et al. (2005) burner, the flow of the fuel is distributed uniformly over the burner. This

For a given ambient condition, the B number is principally a function of the heat of 
gasification, L. The burning rate per unit area is also principally a function of the B number in 
purely diffusive or convective burning. Of course flame radiation and surface reradiation disturb 
this simple dependence. Yet the relatively simple dependence could be emulated by the deRis 
burner, and shown to follow laminar-burning theory. So despite the imperfection of a uniform 
burner velocity, the results yielded theoretically supported results for burning and flame shape.  
In the deRis burner, the heat of gasification was determined by Eq. (1) with no external 
radiation and negligible reradiation. The latter was accomplished by cooling water through the 
burner’s sintered metal matrix. An energy balance on the cooling water, after considerable time 
to achieve thermal equilibrium of the burner, allowed an average flame heat flux to be 
determined. Nitrogen addition to the gaseous fuel also allowed for variations in the supplied fuel 
mixture mass flux.  
Because we were to follow this burner approach, we sought to establish some further 
support for its accuracy and to help allow us to develop a skilled approach. 
 
1.5 
Review of supporting work for BRE 
We shall review our work to date, and show how it has evolved from our original objective to the 
current application of quiescent microgravity burning. It will display our approach, exploration 
of burning in microgravity, and the development of the burner concept and prototype.

1.5.1  Study of flat surface burning in microgravity 
Initially this study was to consider burning in various gravity space applications, such as the 
Moon and Mars environments. An early consideration was to explore such conditions in aircraft 
gravity simulations. Thus, a test of the burner approach was to consider the burning on a flat 
plate at various inclinations, with burning on top and the bottom. This work allowed us to 
explore this burning configuration by tests with real fuels, with a burner, and through theoretical 
analyses. In short, the results help to establish the credibility and accuracy of the emulation with 
a burner, and the limitations of theory to predict the results. A brief summary of this work 
follows, and Bustamante et al. (2012) presented a recent paper covering it. 
For the inclined plate burning experiments, laminar burning was primarily examined. 
This was done using two liquid fuels, methanol and ethanol, each saturated into a porous ceramic 
wick plate as shown in Figure 3. The plate was oriented at angles of 0º (vertical), and +/_ 30, 60 
and 90º, with negative angles indicating burning on the bottom. Steady burning could be 
achieved for each of these conditions; however, for top burning in particular, at flow distances 
exceeding about 5 cm, the onset of unsteady instabilities occurred. This was not considered fully

The methane flow rate was matched to the average burning rate measured in the corresponding 
methanol wick test of the same configuration. Images for flame standoff distances were taken 
within 5 – 15 s of ignition to minimize the temperature rise of the surface. The surface

A better comparison of the flame standoff position between the methanol and the methane 
burner is shown in Figure 5 in which two instantaneous traces were made of each. Their 
similarity, even in the transition instabilities, is a measure of the accuracy of the burner in 
simulating the methanol flames. Notably there are some differences, in particular at +30 and 0º 
where the onset of the transition occurred early in the methanol flame. The onset of transition 
appears to have had an upstream thickening effect on the standoff position. The reason for the 
difference at -90º is unclear. 
Nevertheless, the ability of the burner to emulate the distributive aspects of the burning by 
these flame standoff comparisons is encouraging. It is noteworthy that theoretical analyses to 
achieve similar results are limited by the effects of transition instabilities, variable properties, 
and flame radiation. Even a DNS simulation (Raghavan et al., 2010) of this inclined plate 
burning was confined to considering only a 1 cm long plate. Hence, a practical way to emulate 
burning is using a burner, as it automatically accounts for the effects of instabilities, radiation, 
and property variations.

1.5.2 Preliminary results in microgravity 
In addition to the normal gravity wick burning experiment, several microgravity experiments 
were made. These were performed in the NASA Glenn 5-second drop tower, and in aircraft 
simulations of microgravity. These involved a wick 10 x 40 mm in size. In two drop-tower 
experiments at NASA Glenn, a blue ellipsoidal flame was established; then appeared 
unstable and extinguished during the 5 s drop. A photograph is shown in Figure 7. It was 
speculated that the instability may have been related to the wick placement as too close to the 
chamber wall.  
Also, ethanol flames on the same size wick were used in aircraft simulations of 
microgravity. We recognize that this simulation for microgravity will be less satisfactory than the

1.5.3 Burner design and validation in normal gravity 
A BRE burner prototype has been designed and constructed. Its size has been selected based on 
our flight and drop tower tests, and the burner size used by Brahmi et al. The prototype BRE 
burner was selected to have an operating face of 50 mm in diameter. Due to the anticipated heat 
flux variation over the surface while burning in microgravity or normal gravity, two sensors are 
used. An appropriate averaging of the two heat fluxes should provide the needed average heat 
flux for computing the heat of gasification. The burner is designed with water-cooling to 
maintain reasonable operating temperatures, but thermocouples will directly record the surface 
temperature of the burner allowing the reradiation heat flux to be computed. Brass and glass 
beads provide a porous matrix for metered fuel flow, and porous brass screen serves as its face 
and internal layers. Figure 10 shows photographs of the prototype BRE. It shows the face with a 
heat flux sensor near the center and near the edge. It also shows the fuel and water supply lines 
below. We will perfect the operation of the prototype and establish its accuracy compared to real 
burning of materials. This will provide credibility for the BRE to work for a normal gravity 
environment. In particular, the control of the surface temperature needs to be refined to be able to 
range over a proper range of real fuel temperatures, roughly 50 – 500 ºC. For now we will accept 
the temperatures we get with the prototype 
 
We recently tested the BRE prototype to see if it could emulate a 50 mm pool of 
methanol steadily burning. The mass loss rate of methanol was measured and the flame was 
photographed. To match the methanol with the BRE we would need to use a fuel gas with the 
same flow rate. Also to match the flame height and the consequently the heat flux, the fuel must 
have the same heat of combustion. In addition a consideration of the soot tendency was made 
that led to methane as the gaseous fuel. However, nitrogen must be added to the fuel stream so 
that the resulting fuel mixture has a heat of combustion matching that of methanol, 19.1 kJ/g 
(Tewarson). The gas burner BRE used a fuel mixture of 52% (volume) methane with 48% 
nitrogen to achieve the needed heat of combustion. The flow rate of the mixture was 33 cc/s flow 
rate to match the measure steady burning rate of the methanol of 11g/m2-s.  
If the BRE concept is correct, the two flames should be nearly identical in appearance,

parameters: ∆hc, L and qrr without any additional external heat flux. Of course, the smoke point 
would be a fourth parameter for consideration. The mapping can be done by operating the BRE 
with different gaseous fuels, including dilution with nitrogen. Valuable information on the 
conditions for ignition and extinction can be obtained as well, and their accuracy is superior to 
unsteady mass loss measurements of real solid and liquid fuels. It would be interesting to test the

the BRE flammability range would not allow for steady burning without the assistance of 
additional heat flux. It is possible to use Eq. (2) to determine the needed external heat flux to

19
atmospheric concentrations and pressure. In short, the BRE is an efficient way to assess burning 
under a variety of environmental conditions. Its exploration in microgravity can give valuable 
insight into material flammability in space flight. 
 
2. 
FLIGHT EXPERIMENT  
2.1 
Knowledge Lacking and Knowledge to be Gained by Flight Tests  
The proposed tests aboard the ISS will establish the range of steady burning conditions for 
condensed fuels in microgravity. We will identify the associated material properties and the real 
materials that are represented. Once established based on fuel properties, NASA Test 2 could be 
used as a basis for establishing comparable properties for real materials. This could elevate the 
role of NASA Test 2 over Test 1. This would close the loop of using a ground-based test to 
assess the true flammability of materials in microgravity.  
The BRE mapping of material flammability in microgravity would provide a scientific 
rationale for assessing the fire hazard. We intend to explore the range of heats of combustion 
form about 5 – 50 kJ/g, and heats of gasification from about 0.5 – 5 kJ/g. These properties 
embrace common materials including paper, plastics and liquids. In addition, the BRE concept 
could be exploited in follow-on tests concerned with flowing ambients and extinguishing agents. 
 
2.2 
Experimental Objectives  
The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity 
ambient in terms of material properties. The specific flight objectives are as follows. 
1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures 
on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various 
pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures Emphasize conditions that can be 
related to diverse condensed fuels. 
2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). 
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for ignition limits. 
4. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits. 
 
2.3 
Summary of Approach 
To accomplish the above objectives, three types of flight experiments are proposed: burning, 
ignition limit, and extinction limit. Additionally, preliminary flight tests will be performed to 
verify the experiment operations and for comparison with ground-based tests. 
For each burn test, conditions will be established for the chamber contents, namely choice 
of diluent, oxygen concentration, and pressure. Fuel flow will commence followed by ignition. 
The flames will be observed without varying the fuel or its flow rate. Because burner surface 
temperature and heat flux will vary during the burn, this will allow a broad range of conditions to 
be observed during a single test. 
For each ignition limit test, conditions will be established for the chamber contents. Fuel 
flow will commence followed by attempted ignition.  
For each extinction limit test, flames will be established followed by a gradual reduction in 
fuel flow rate until extinction. 
In addition to the flight experiments, ground based testing in normal gravity and in 
microgravity will continue. These tests will involve gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels. Detailed 
analysis and FLUENT computations will be performed. This will give us insight to the 
mechanisms that allow burning to be sustained.

2.4 
Science Data End Products 
The science data end products (SDEP) are the tables, figures, and analyses that will be reported 
in the archival literature (not the raw data from the experiment). To facilitate comparison of the 
planned SDEP with the objectives, they are summarized in Table 3. The science requirements 
and the experiment success criteria (see below) are developed from this list of SDEP. 
 
2.5 
Justification for Extended-Duration Microgravity 
As discussed above, NASA Test 1 and Test 2 are currently incapable of directly analyzing 
material fire hazards in spacecraft. While microgravity tests of condensed fuels have been 
performed and are planned, these are not expected to reveal sufficient information about the 
diverse condensed fuels that exist aboard the ISS. The BRE experiment seeks to remedy these 
deficiencies. 
The proposed tests cannot be performed in parabolic aircraft owing to considerable g-
jitter disturbances. While limited testing is possible in drop towers, the characteristic times for 
the gas phase (approximately 20 s) and the burner surface temperature (approximately 40 s) 
preclude consideration of quasi-steady conditions. The long duration testing in the ISS will 
facilitate the efficient operation of the BRE to exploit a relatively quick record of results over a 
range of flow rates. This will insure a complete flammability map in microgravity. 
 
3. 
EXPERIMENT REQUIREMENTS  
3.1 
Requirements Discussion 
Most of the BRE experiment requirements fall within the requirements established by the other 
ACME experiments, as detailed in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document 
(ISRD) (Stocker, 2010). Sections of the ISRD are referenced below, and the detailed require-
ments are either accepted, modified, or not applicable as indicated. In addition, background is 
provided for these requirements and they are justified vis-à-vis the experiment objectives.

BRE Burners 
The design of the BRE burners is critical to meeting the BRE objectives. The burners (e.g., 
Fig. 10) shall involve round porous frits through which gaseous fuel is fed. These frits shall have 
diameters of 25 and 50 mm. Each burner shall contain two heat flux meters flush with the frit 
surface and facing outward. The PI team has extensive experience with the design and use of 
these burners. They can either advise NASA on the design of the flight burners or provide these. 
The burners shall be positioned such that the burner axis is coincident with the CIR chamber axis 
within ±2 mm (i.e., along its length) and orthogonal to the CIR chamber window axes. The plane 
of the CIR chamber window centers shall be 10±2 mm downstream of (i.e., above) the burner 
outlet. 
ISRD Section 1.1: Accepted 
ISRD Sections 1.2-1.7: Not Applicable 
 
Burner Gas Delivery 
ISRD Section 1.8: Accepted 
ISRD Section 1.9: Accepted, with specific flow rates for BRE given as: 
Fuel 0 to 0.1 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) 
Oxidizer not applicable 
Inert 0 to 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) 
These requirements were established by observations of flames in normal gravity, in the 
NASA Glenn 5 s drop facility, and on the parabolic aircraft. 
 
Ignition 
ISRD Section 1.10: Accepted with the following specifics for BRE:  
Ignition disturbances should be minimized to allow undisturbed burning as quickly as is feasible. 
It is suggested that ignition should occur at a distance of 3 mm from the frit surface. BRE is 
unique among ACME experiments in its interest in ignition limits. For these tests it is essential 
that the igniter conditions be highly repeatable. 
 
Ambient Environment 
ISRD Section 1.11: Accepted 
Prior to each test, the chamber shall contain the specified gas composition, consisting of O2 and 
inert (N2 and CO2, desired) within ±0.01 mole fraction of each concentration. A cylindrical free 
area that is (1) at least 200 mm and as large as possible in diameter, (2) extends at least 100 mm 
and as far as possible downstream from the burner outlet, and (3) extends at least 50 mm and as 
far as possible upstream of the burner outlet shall be kept clear of solid objects. A second 
cylindrical free area (with the same axis as the first) that is (1) at least 150 mm and as large as 
possible in diameter and (2) extends at least 200 mm and as far as possible downstream from the 
burner outlet shall be kept clear of solid objects. The temporary insertion of the igniter and the 
presence of any probes (including TFP fibers) are allowed exceptions. Suggested methods to 
decrease bottled gas consumption rates include, as available, partial venting and filling, and 
scrubbing for CO2 and H2O. 
 
Data Recording 
ISRD Section 1.12: Accepted with addition of data recording of BRE heat flux sensors. Two heat

22
flux sensors are required, one at the center of the burner and the other midway between the 
center and the periphery. 
 
Monitoring Measurements 
The BRE monitoring measurements shall include: chamber pressure; chamber O2 concentration; 
gas flow rates; burner pressure differential; and acceleration. These shall be initiated before test 
operations begin and continue sufficiently past flame extinction to allow a baseline 
measurement. 
ISRD Sections 2.1-2.3: Accepted 
ISRD Sections 2.4 and 2.5: Not Applicable 
ISRD Section 2.6: Accepted 
 
Science Diagnostics Requirements 
The BRE science diagnostics measurements shall include: color imaging for operations; color 
imaging for data analysis (with a field of view of at least 90 mm in diameter); ultraviolet imaging 
(with a field of view of at least 75 mm in diameter); temperature (frit temperature at 2 locations 
with a range of 30 – 500 °C; hot soot-containing regions in a 85 mm diameter region; hot soot-
free regions in a 85 mm diameter region; and far-field); soot volume fraction (with a field of 
view of at least 45 mm in diameter); radiant emission; chemiluminescent emission; and post-test 
gas composition. 
Color imaging will be used to determine flame size, shape, color, and existence. In 
addition, it will provide confirmation of other diagnostics used for detecting extinction limits. 
Visibly luminous soot will be observed with color cameras. Because flames can be asymmetric, a 
second view would minimize ambiguity. The field of view will need to be sufficiently large to 
observe the entire flame while at the same time be sufficiently small to allow for resolution of 
the fine scale needed to identify the onset of soot inception. For this reason, zooming capability 
is desired.  
Accurate measurement of gas temperatures and the burner surface is essential. Flame 
temperature and temperature distribution are affected by fuel composition, flow rate, radiative 
losses, and heat loss to the burner. Temperature measurements are required to understand these 
effects. The proposed flames in quiescent ambient environments are prone to disturbance by 
intrusive probes (e.g., thermocouples). In addition, near the extinction limits, heat or radical loss 
to an intrusive probe can extinguish the flame. Nevertheless, thermocouple probes are accurate 
and are requested here for the purpose of validating the other temperature diagnostics. These 
probes may be removed for tests after this validation is complete. 
Flame extinction will be inferred by photomultiplier tubes and imaging. To ensure that 
extinction has occurred, flow rate will be changed to a condition for which a stable flame had 
previously been observed. If the flame does not reappear, it can be assumed that the flame had 
extinguished. UV emission will also be used to indicate the presence of a flame. While it is 
generally believed that the existence of a hydrocarbon flame can be detected by observation of 
blue emission, this may not be the case with microgravity flames because these flames are 
extremely weak and we are attempting to produce the lowest temperature diffusion flames that 
have been produced. 
ISRD Sections 3.1-3.3: Accepted 
ISRD Section 3.4: Accepted, with specific locations to coincide with the two heat flux 
measurements. Range of temperature measurements is from 30 – 500 °C. It is anticipated that the

3.5 
Post Flight Data Analysis Plan 
The proposed test matrix is intended to shed light on the burning of condensed fuels in 
microgravity. We plan to examine conditions that map out flammable conditions and burning 
rates of diverse condensed fuels. This will result in extensive image data.  
Much of the post-flight data analysis will occur during mission operations as the science 
team evaluates each set of test runs in preparation for subsequent runs. Analysis of these tests 
will include: tracking of flame size and shape; analysis of discrete signals (e.g., thermocouples, 
radiometers, photomultipliers, and pressure transducers) for evidence of the quasi-steadiness of 
the flames; analysis of the temperature profiles (thin filament, soot temperature, and far-field 
thermocouples) to evaluate quasi-steadiness; and de-convolution of soot volume fraction 
measurements. 
The flammability maps will be prepared on 3-axis plots where the axes are burner heat of 
combustion, heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux (See Figure 13). Flame temperatures near 
extinction will be determined either by de-convolution of the soot temperature data or by thin 
fiber pyrometry.

items.title: PSI-20_Engineering Documents_BRE_procedure_20210520.pdf
items.text:
ACME/BRE Experimental Procedure 
 
20 May 2022 
2 
 
1. Introduction 
The narrative description of the experimental procedure is an excerpt from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ 
section of the following conference paper. 
Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on Flames in 
Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States 
Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. 
 
While the paper was written for the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) 
experiment, much of the discussion applies to ACME in general, including the BRE investigation.  The figure 
referenced in this excerpt is not included herein.  Clarifications and additional information, not in the 
conference paper, are included in boxed notes like this. 
 
The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  Thus far, ACME’s activity has 
included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities.  Most often the astronauts 
and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips.  In the latter case, the igniter 
tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the crew already has changes to 
make changes in the interior of the insert.  While these activities may seem mundane, the crew play a 
critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment.  As an extreme example, there were crew 
activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME 
experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  In contrast, only two 
crew days were required to reconfigure the hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the 
initial use of the same coflow burner.  Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks 
in advance, for which detailed procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. 
 
BRE has its own unique burners and it was the first ACME experiment conducted with large flames, as 
compared to those in the CLD Flame and E-FIELD Flames investigations.  That required changes to some 
optical elements for BRE as well as subsequent ACME experiments.  BRE was also the first experiment to 
use the CIR facility’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP).  As a result, the initial BRE set-
up included 9 days of crew activity, mostly by Canadian astronaut David Saint-Jacques, although that 
includes 4 days in which hardware was either gathered or stowed. 
 
All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center 
(GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio.  Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the testing.  The CIR 
hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer (DMO) consoles, and the 
ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console.  Two shifts of personnel are 
scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they typically last 14 hours with the many 
pre- and post-testing activities.  Given that the tests are remotely commanded, the operations are carried 
out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., from 7 AM to 9 PM.  A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are 
normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less.  Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per 
two weeks.  On intervening weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both 
gas bottles.  Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2-shift day for the RO 
and DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and 
that data is not missing.  Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew activity.  As 
a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week.  A team of four carry 
out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily operational plans typically 
exceed 50 pages on days including testing.

items.title: PSI-20_Engineering Documents_BRE_procedure_20210520.pdf
items.text:
ACME/BRE Experimental Procedure 
 
20 May 2022 
3 
 
The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in near real 
time but doesn’t allow for commanding.  In the case of E-FIELD Flames, arrangements were made so that 
the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the research team to participate 
in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters.  That team does not 
see the telemetry during the testing, but is in communication via phone and e-mail with their NASA 
research partners at the GRC ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC).  While there are many preparatory 
steps, the tests are ultimately conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files.  In 
advance of the test day, the UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep 
script and specifies other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings.  
It is also possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in 
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry.  For example, the electric field potential can be 
adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. 
 
Provisions have been made to enable the investigators from all ACME experiments to remotely view the 
analog video while they communicated verbally with NASA science personnel in the operations center.  
Thus far, all ACME flame tests, including those for BRE, have been conducted in an automated manner 
using software scripts and extensive parameter files. 
 
Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, the low 
rate results from several unavoidable factors.  After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz non-imaging data is 
downlinked for immediate review by the science team.  A small sample of images are often downlinked 
to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for those images are typically 
selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples.  The review helps to verify parameters 
or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the voltage range after determining where the 
ion current saturates for the given flame conditions.  After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber 
atmosphere after which the chamber is vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed.  
Midway through a day’s E-FIELD Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter 
cartridge filled with molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion 
products, e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products.  The tests are only 
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay 
Satellite (TDRS) System.  Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic communication outages with 
a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite to another) or can last as long as 30 
minutes. 
 
About eight flames were ignited per test day in BRE’s first round, neglecting the day in which no tests were 
conducted because the igniter had unknowingly failed at the end of the preceding test day.  The nominal 
durations were typically planned for 2 or 3 minutes but some tests were 5 minutes long.  Meanwhile the 
second round of BRE had roughly 15 tests conducted per day, but the durations were nominally 2 minutes 
at most. 
 
Unlike E-FIELD Flames, the BRE experiment also made use of the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph 
Instrumentational Package (GCIP) to measure species concentrations of the atmosphere in the combustion 
chamber.  There is no sampling probe and measurements are only made before, between, or after tests 
when the chamber atmosphere was ‘stirred’ through use of a fan.  The GC measurements were made on 
roughly 60% of the test days with flames in the first round, specifically on 19039, 19063, 19066, 19070, 
19087, and 19094.  In the second round, such data was acquired on less than half of the test days, 
specifically on 20247, 20261, 20279, and 20352.

items.title: PSI-20_Engineering Documents_BRE_procedure_20210520.pdf
items.text:
ACME/BRE Experimental Procedure 
 
20 May 2022 
4 
 
Like E-FIELD Flames, BRE made periodic use of the adsorber cartridge, for example between atmospheres 
and after GC measurements, if any, were made. 
 
A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a daily basis.  
The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame spread and material 
flammability.  That follow-on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, where each ACME experiment 
is allotted four months for testing.  Although it requires additional crew time, these allotments are split 
into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from testing for careful review of the early results 
so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of their second round.  This paper reports on early results 
from the first round of E-FIELD Flames. 
 
While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the available gas 
bottles that were and are launched to support the tests.  For E-FIELD Flames and most of ACME’s 
experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established in 2010.  At that time, 
NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of focused experiments with limited 
objectives rather than comprehensive experiments.  As such, the general target was 50 tests per 
experiment.  For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used 
to fill the chamber.  This resource constraint is exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair 
of redundant safety timers to limit the fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers 
can be set for the oxidizer flow in the case of inverse flame testing).  The timers can only be reset by 
venting the combustion chamber.  Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively 
corresponds to the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant).  For 
E-FIELD Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 
10 tests typically completed per day. 
 
The 999-second limit on the valve safety timers has thus far been common for all ACME testing.  However, 
the timers can be reset to 999 by nearly completely venting the chamber.  Sufficient time and gas resources 
are needed to vent and refill the chamber and still conduct tests afterward, but this was done on most BRE 
test days.  The only exceptions were 19039, 19063, and 19091 where in the last case no flames were ignited 
because the igniter had unknowingly failed at the end of the prior test day. 
 
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, such as 
the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours.  When necessary for the research, NASA 
does have continuous 24-hour/day operations for some non-CIR experiments.  But as discussed, the ACME 
tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is almost always limited to the planned 
durations. 
 
Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on-orbit hardware can store a limited amount of data.  
More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two-shift transfer and 
downlink day.  Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where image data from select 
cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge.  Nonetheless, the limit sometimes 
forces decisions to abandon recorded images. 
 
This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME 
experiments are conducted.  …

2. Test Sequence and Parameters 
All BRE tests conducted on the ISS were carried out using automated software which had its roots in 
ACME’s Integrated Science Requirements Documents (ISRD, RDR version, Rev. B) and Science Operations 
Requirements Documents (SORD, Rev. A).  The BRE Science Requirements Document (SRD) is of course 
pertinent but only that which was incorporated in the ISRD and SORD was used by the engineering team 
in developing the control software. 
 
The major phases of the test sequence are graphically displayed in Figure 1, which incorporates the 
optional pre-flow first implemented on BRE’s third test day.  The lines appearing in the figure represent 
the nitrogen flow rate, the fuel flow rate, the igniter position and power.  The lines that are more lightly 
shaded represent some optional changes to flow rates, for example the pre-flow.  However, the flow 
variations in the darkly shaded lines are also optional.  The phases are described in detail at the bottom 
of the schematic, where the nomenclature generally corresponds to the script parameter names.

items.text:
ACME/BRE Experimental Procedure 
 
20 May 2022 
11 
 
3. BRE Script 
For a deeper understanding of the experimental procedure, the final version of the JavaScript used to 
control the BRE tests is presented here.  Neglecting the first two days of testing, it was largely unchanged 
throughout the two rounds of BRE operations.  The minor changes included: 
~2020-03-17 
flow ramp hold was fixed so that the hold values were achieved exactly  
~2020-12-18 
ignition detection was disabled prior to igniter arm retraction so that the 
retraction wasn’t interrupted  
The first change was implemented between the first and second rounds of testing, while the second was 
made during the second round. 
 
The significant early change in the script was related to the comparatively large internal volume of the 
BRE burners which led to concern about understanding the composition of the gas initially flowing from 
the burner.  Therefore, on the second BRE test day (20 Feb. 2019, i.e., 19051), a no-flame ‘test’ was run 
before each flame test in which the burner was flushed with nitrogen.  A shortcoming of this measure was 
that the time between the nitrogen flushing and the start of the fuel flow was not precisely controlled.  
Therefore, the script was revised to allow specification of a ‘pre-flow’ with a specified wait time between 
the pre-flow and the start of the gas flow for the flame.  The revised version, which added four new 
parameters, was implemented on BRE’s third test day (25 Feb. 2019, 19056) and eliminated the need for 
the no-flame ‘test’ to flush the burner with nitrogen. 
 
With the addition of the scripted pre-low and wait time, the basic non-imaging data was captured during 
both the pre-flow and in the flame test, but not during the intervening wait period.  Therefore, one should 
pay close attention to the time stamp when reviewing BRE data prior to the start of the fuel flow because 
the listed time abruptly jumps. 
 
Note that the early portion of the script includes an example set of parameter values which are 
overwritten by values specified for each test. 
 
 
/** 
 * BRETest.js 
 * Script which executes a BRE test point. 
 *  
 * Assumptions: 
 *    - Cameras are configured except that data camera exposure and analog camera shutter 
 *      are set in this script, and the intensified camera gate and gain are set here. 
 *    - ACME Camera lens and filter is configured. Intensified Camera filter is configured. 
 *    - IPSUs being used, as specified in SystemDefineSetup command, are ready 
 *    - Mass flow controllers are enabled and zeroed 
 *    - PMTs are enabled 
 *    - ExtinctionDetectionConfigure and one of the ExinctionDetectionSet Action commands 
 *       has been issued and ExtinctinctionDetectionSetState(Disabled) 
 *    - Ignition detection parameters are set as desired using the IgnitionDetectionConfigure command. 
 */ 
 
//Hook up to the runScript signal to show where to start execution 
AcmeAvionicsController.runScript.connect(run);

4. Test Matrices 
For all ACME experiments, including BRE, the test planning was refined in multiple steps as described in 
this section.  Despite refinement, the experiments were always expected to address the science objectives 
approved in the ACME ISRD. 
 
A. Test Matrices: Years in Advance 
The test matrices found in section 5 of the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document 
(ISRD, RDR version, Rev. B) were the basis for planning the equipment and resources, such as gas 
bottles, needed to carry out each of the NASA-selected ACME experiments.  For BRE, the test 
matrices are found in section 5.5.  The investigators were each directed to define matrices with 
required testing which included at most one burner configuration and no more than nominally 50 
flames ignited.  Regarding these constraints specified by Project Scientist Dennis Stocker, the 
intent was to conduct focused rather than comprehensive research given the considerable 
resources required for testing on the International Space Station.    Meanwhile, there were no 
limits put on desired or highly desired tests because of NASA’s plan to only carry out tests 
designated as required.  
 
NASA Glenn’s ISS Control Board later decided to limit ACME testing to nominally 4 months of ISS 
testing per experiment which with preparatory operations, minor delays, repeat testing due to 
science loss, etc. were expected to typically occur in a total of 5 months.  This decision was made 
with the expectation that the required testing, e.g., as specified in the ISRD, could at least mostly 
be accomplished in that time period assuming the availability of crew and other needed 
resources. 
 
As part of his planning, Stocker instigated an alternating sequence of experiment testing, wherein 
investigators would get a break in their testing in order to analyze early results in depth and with 
that knowledge achieve higher science outcomes in their second round of testing.  As a result, 
each experiment was expected to get 2 months of testing per round, which meant nominally 8 
test days per round of testing.  Within that time constraint and available resources, experiments 
were ultimately permitted to plan for and conduct more tests than had been specified as required 
in the ISRD, despite the initial planning which ignored desired and highly desired testing. 
 
B. Test Matrices: Months in Advance 
At least a few months in advance of testing, ACME investigators were directed to submit a refined 
test matrix for the upcoming round corresponding to available hardware, gas bottles, and the 
agreed number of test days.  The refinement could be based on what is learned from 
experimental, analytical, or computational efforts which followed the 2013 ISRD.  Generally, this 
planning was done in detail comparable to that found in the ISRD, with the important exception 
that it had to furthermore establish the required hardware, including the specific mass flow

operations, including crew activity, could be adequately planned.  In this regard, it had to establish 
general operational plans for the chamber atmosphere on each day of testing including filling, 
scrubbing (via circulation through the adsorber cartridge), venting (whether partial or complete), 
and measurements, if any, with the Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). 
 
C. Test Matrices: Days in Advance 
Soon after BRE’s start, the investigators were required to submit their test parameters for all 
planned tests by noon Eastern at least three business days in advance of each scheduled test day.  
Those submissions included all of the test parameters within the script and additional ones 
outside of the script.  Most of the latter dealt with the camera settings which don’t change during 
a test, for example the filters used with the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) and the Cool Flames 
Investigation (CFI) intensified camera.  Outside of the script, the investigators were again required 
to specify the chamber atmosphere(s) and when GCIP measurements, if any, are planned.  It was 
expected that those correspond to the plan submitted months earlier, but some allowances were 
made for changes.  The script parameters, e.g., specifications of flow rates, didn’t need to 
correspond to those previously specified, but they normally had to correspond to the hardware 
and gas bottles planned months earlier and generally the chamber atmospheres as well by 
extension.

parameter values that differed in at least a few ways from those planned days earlier.

Relationship to NASA Flammability 
Tests 1 and 2 
• The Upward Flame Propagation (Test 1) is the dominant 
test for material flammability by NASA. 
 
– It tests the flame propagation of a vertical sample 30 × 6.4 – 
7.5 cm wide, under a small electric source heat flux of 75 
kW/m2.  
– The atmospheric conditions are controlled.  
– Burn length and time are recorded.  
– It is considered a pass-fail type test. 
 
• The NASA Test 2:  Cone Calorimeter with external heat 
fluxes of 25 – 75 kW/m2 to supplement information gained 
from Test 1.

Background of Combustion in 
Microgravity 
•
Experiments in Skylab (Ross, 2001; Kimzey, 1974) indicated sustained 
burning of thin paper and plastics. 
•
More recent experiments indicate flame spread on thin paper and plastic 
thin cylinders in microgravity (Ross, 2001).  
•
Opposed flow spread in a quiescent atmosphere has been shown to 
depend on material, thickness, and oxygen concentration (Ross, 2001). 
•
The burning of candle flames on the MIR (Ross, 2001) last for periods 
ranging from about 100 s to more than 45 minutes. A spherical flame 
formed around the wick.  
•
Droplet experiments by Kumagai and others (Ross, 2001). 
•
Small diameter jet flames of 0.4 – 2.7 mm yielded spherical flames of 
durations from 150 – 300 s (Ross, 2001).  
•
Sunderland et al. (1999) recorded flames for port diameters up to 3.3 mm, 
and Re from about 10 – 1700 in microgravity.  
•
Brahmi et al. (2005) used a gaseous burner to simulate burning in g. They 
burned ethane over a 60  60 mm sintered bronze plate in O2-N2 flowing 
at velocities of 10 – 150 mm/s. 
•
Bustamante (2012) aircraft and drop data on flat liquid-fueled wicks.

• The proposed tests aboard the ISS will establish the

items.text:
40 
Justification for Extended-
Duration Microgravity 
•
The proposed tests cannot be performed in parabolic aircraft 
owing to considerable g-jitter disturbances.  
 
•
Testing in NASA 5.2-s drop facility indicated possible approach to 
steady burning. 
 
•
The longer duration testing in the ISS will facilitate the efficient 
operation of the BRE to exploit a relatively quick record of results 
over a range of flow rates. This will insure a complete 
flammability map in microgravity.

Response to panelist recommendation 
• Recommend proposed ignition tests have a lower 
priority. Ignition eliminated 
 
• Prioritize the experimental diagnostics, to minimize 
complications in running the experiment and 
downloading data. Done 
 
• Focus on small burner designs for multiple reasons. In 
addition, a burner design with narrow external walls is 
strongly encouraged. Test matrix emphasizes 25 mm 
and we have reduced the edge effect.

items.text:
• Some repeated tests are recommended to establish 
uncertainty bounds and increase scientific credibility. 
Expect wide range of data points in flight.  
 
• The temperature range for the burner is not defined in the 
current science requirement documents. Take what we get. 
In document, the burner surface, temperatures at 2 
locations with a range of 30 – 500 °C.  
 
• The priority on O2 and pressure conditions ought to be on 
whatever the preferred conditions are for future space 
flight. Drop experiments should also help prioritize the test 
sequence. Included current NASA human flight atmosphere 
in test matrix

items.text:
• Experiments should be performed at nearly the same oxygen 
level. If tests at constant O2 are not possible, a method to 
convert experimental results obtained at one 
O2 concentration to another O2 level needs to be developed. 
Hope to have a theory for that.  
 
• As discussed above, a careful design of the burner, with a thin, 
low conducting, outside wall should allow the flame to sit 
closer to the burner and add stability to the flame tests. 
Reduce the edge 
 
• Fundamentally, there is no guarantee of achieving quasi-
steady flames. The PIs should consider how to collect and 
interpret data sets for which flames are sustained, but 
unsteady. Hope to have a theory to guide us

items.text:
BRE Operational Sequence 
 Action 
Approx. 
Time 
1. Ensure that the appropriate burner is installed. Preflow the 
burner fluent gas at the composition of the upcoming test point 
to flush the plumbing system. 
2. Establish chamber conditions. These consist of a set point 
pressure and species compositions, as specified in the test 
matrix. Conditions are obtained in four ways: from cabin air 
(desired); from the preceding test; from scrubbing and 
replenishing; or from a complete evacuation and recharge. 
3. Allow chamber contents to reach equilibrium. A hold time of 
5 minutes is required for quiescent, isothermal, and well-mixed 
conditions. 
4. Take reference images (if applicable). Establish framing rates for 
video cameras. Begin color imaging. Begin monitoring 
measurements and wait 15 s. 
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
68

items.title: PSI-20_Science Documents_BRE_science_concept_RDR_201306.pdf
items.text:
BRE Operational Sequence 
 Action 
Approx. 
Time 
5. Commence fluent flow at a value to be uplinked. The initial 
value should correspond to about 1 g/m2-s of hydrocarbon fuel.  
Energize igniter to ignite the flame and then retract the igniter. 
If ignition does not occur within 5 seconds, shut off the flow.  A 
new value of flow rate will be specified by uplink.  If the flame 
ignites, proceed to Step 6. Otherwise proceed to Step 7. 
6. Set the flow rate to the test flow rate.  Anytime during this step, 
if the flame extinguishes, or either heat flux sensor exceeds a 
critical temperature, stop the fuel flow.  Continue until the 
surface burner temperatures become quasi-steady.  Then 
reduce the flow rate in 10% increments of the test flow rate, 
hold for 15 s, and continue such reductions until extinction. 
7. Stop fluent flow.  Record reference images (if applicable). After 
60 s terminate color imaging and monitoring measurements. 
Select data for downlink and downlink data.

Science Success Criteria 
Minimum Success 
• Obtain color video, burner surface temperature, 
and burner heat flux for two C2H4 flames that 
burn for at least 20 s and then extinguish. 
 
High Success 
All of the above (BRE flight test matrix) plus: 
• Obtain a flammability map for C2H4. 
 
 
74

items.title: PSI-20_Science Documents_BRE_science_concept_RDR_201306.pdf
items.text:
Complete Success (i.e., completion of required test matrix) 
All of the above (BRE flight test matrix) plus: 
• Obtain a flammability map for CH4. 
• Measure peak temperatures (using filament and/or soot 
pyrometry) as a function of time for at least 5 flames. 
• Measure temperature distributions (using filament and/or 
soot pyrometry) at or near quasi-steady conditions for at 
least 5 flames.  
• Measure temperature distributions (using filament 
pyrometry) near the extinction limit for at least 5 flames. 
• Measure soot volume fraction profiles at (or near) quasi-
steady conditions and near the extinction limit for at least 5 
flames. 
75 
Science Success Criteria

items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
3 
 
1. Overview 
The Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is one of six independent experiments that 
make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are 
conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). 
 
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) and Co-Investigator are respectively Profs. Marshall B. Long 
and Mitchell D. Smooke, who are both in the Department of Mechanical Engineering & Materials Science 
at Yale University.  The ISS research benefitted greatly from the work of Dr. Jesse Tinajero, who was a Yale 
postdoctoral researcher during the spaceflight operations, and Dr. Davide Giassi, who as a Yale doctoral 
student did important preparatory work.  
 
Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME 
including CLD Flame and the rest of the ACME investigations.  In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki 
Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist.  For 
ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam 
who are also with CWRU. 
 
The ISS operations for CLD Flame were conducted in three separate rounds of testing, where the rounds 
were respectively conducted during Increments 53-54, 55-56, and 64. The third round was limited in scope 
and was carried out with a replacement 20-slpm mass flow controller for the oxidizer coflow to make up 
for the poor coflow performance in the first two rounds. 
 
Note that there was a direct precursor to the CLD Flame investigation, namely the Structure & Liftoff In 
Combustion Experiment (SLICE), which was conducted in the ISS’ Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) 
during Expedition 30 in early 2012.  Prof. Long was the Principal Investigator, while Smooke, Takahashi, 
and Stocker were Co-Investigators.  For more information about SLICE, readers are encouraged to consult 
its final report.  
 
 
2. Science Overview 
A. Background 
This background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document 
(SRD) of April 2010. 
 
The proposed work will build upon our ground-based microgravity studies in which advanced 
adaptive (parallel) computational algorithms and multidimensional imaging techniques were 
performed to characterize buoyant and nonbuoyant diffusion flames.  The computational work 
has facilitated the development of detailed soot models while the experimental work performed 
has built expertise in bringing two-dimensional, laboratory-quality diagnostics to a microgravity 
environment.  The experimental results of our previous microgravity combustion studies have 
provided the most rigorous testing of our combustion models to date.  Experiments were 
performed on the KC-135 of a nitrogen-diluted methane coflow laminar diffusion flame to 
measure flame chemiluminescence, temperature, major species, and soot distributions.  The 
results compared well with computations in the moderately dilute cases, but discrepancies were 
revealed in the case of the more dilute flames, particularly with the observed lift-off heights and

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
4 
 
extinction limits.  Additionally, the weak flames and the sooting flames were observed to be 
sensitive to the presence of g-jitter, making clear analysis difficult.  It is at these extremes of the 
fuel dilution spectrum that the most interesting effects can be observed.  Further, by extending 
the studies over a broad range of conditions, discrepancies between measurement and 
computation have been discovered that previous laboratory studies of this flame failed to reveal. 
 
We propose to concentrate this study on flame phenomena at the extremes of the fuel dilution 
spectrum – namely dilute flames near extinction and highly-sooting pure-fuel flames.  Previous 
work has shown that both weak flames and highly sooting flames require long periods of “clean” 
microgravity to reach a steady state.  The conditions aboard the International Space Station (ISS) 
will be ideal in this regard.  The intended flight experiments will provide insights into flame 
stability, extinction, and soot processes that are unavailable in ground-based microgravity 
facilities. 
 
Our project goals include the generation of improved computational models with improved soot 
submodels that are effective for both dilute flames and sooting flames that vary from low to high 
soot loading levels.  The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will be 
important for achieving both goals.  Experimentally, we plan to study methane and ethylene 
diffusion flames over a wide range of test conditions.  For the more dilute flames, measurements 
will be made of flame chemiluminesence of OH* and CH* to observe variations in lift-off height 
and flame shape as extinction limits are approached.  The sooting tendencies of the more fuel-
rich flames will be investigated using soot luminosity and laser extinction measurements to 
determine soot temperatures and soot volume fractions.  Flame temperatures in nonsooting 
regions will be measured using thin-filament pyrometry.  Based on observations, modifications 
can be made to the kinetics and soot model to match better the experimental results.  If the 
overall agreement of the measurements and computations is good, the results of the 
computations can be “mined” to provide insight on species (and hence chemical processes) that 
cannot be measured directly using the diagnostics available for the proposed experiment. 
 
B. Rationale for Microgravity 
This is the ‘Justification for Extended Duration Microgravity’ section (2.6) of the experiment’s SRD 
from April 2010.  References are not included in this document but can be found in the SRD. 
 
The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical 
kinetics in diffusion flames is central to nearly all aspects of combustion research: in the modeling 
of turbulent reacting flows, in understanding the processes by which soot formation and radiative 
transfer take place, and in the prediction of pollutant formation.  In addition, an understanding of 
those factors that affect flame extinction is critical in the suppression of fires, in improving engine 
efficiency, and in reducing emissions.  While normal gravity combustion studies can provide 
important information on combustion processes, the effects of gravitational forces can often 
complicate the interpretation of both computational and experimental results.  For example, 
most practical combustors are turbulent, and consequently momentum-dominated, while most 
laboratory-scale research burners have significant buoyancy contributions.  Therefore, studies of 
microgravity flames are of direct relevance to research in turbulent combustion since buoyancy 
effects are eliminated.  In addition to being inherently simpler, nonbuoyant flames have the 
advantage that hot gases are not accelerated by gravitational forces, which results in longer 
residence times and larger length scales.  These longer residence times have been shown to result

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
5 
 
in higher soot loading in microgravity flames compared to their normal gravity counterparts.  The 
larger spatial scales allow improved experimental resolution, which in turn gives a clearer, more 
spatially distinct view of the progress from soot inception and growth to eventual burnout.  Thus, 
microgravity data on sooting flames will provide a wide range of well-resolved conditions that will 
be critical for the development of submodels for soot formation that are capable of predicting 
both high and low soot loading levels. 
 
As we have seen from our previous microgravity work (see Fig. 2), very weak flames can be 
stabilized in a microgravity that extinguish under normal gravity conditions.  These flames are free 
of buoyant coupling of the flowfield or buoyancy-induced asymmetries, which can complicate 
comparisons between models and experiments under normal gravity conditions.  For these 
flames, small changes in the chemical kinetics were seen to have a significant effect on the 
agreement between measured and computed flame structure and lift-off height.  Once again, the 
microgravity environment allows us to investigate a wider range of flow and dilution conditions 
than would be accessible in a normal gravity environment; these data will be invaluable for our 
overall goal of developing improved kinetic mechanisms applicable to a wide range of combustion 
conditions. 
 
Section 1 discusses our previous experimental work in microgravity, which was carried out aboard 
the KC-135. The KC-135 was chosen over other ground-based microgravity facilities (such as a 
drop towers) due to the relatively long periods of microgravity available, which allowed adequate 
time for flame stabilization and integration of weak signals necessary for good signal/noise. 
However, the work also showed that both very dilute flames near extinction and sooty flames are 
sensitive to the g-jitter aboard the KC-135. 
 
Highly dilute fuel mixtures, which can only be stabilized under microgravity conditions, cannot be 
lit until microgravity conditions are reached. After ignition is established, the ignition source must 
be removed, and the flame allowed to stabilize.  Further, data acquisition of flame 
chemiluminescence requires total integration times of ~10 seconds to obtain sufficient 
signal/noise for good results when a tomographic inversion is used to reconstruct a two-
dimensional cross section.  Because flame luminosity is integrated along a line-of-sight, a low 
numerical aperture must be used, which results in a small optical throughput.  The combination 
of the time requirements for flame ignition, stabilization, and signal integration makes this 
experiment a poor candidate for drop tower facilities.  The most dilute of these mixtures 
previously studied exhibited unstable behavior aboard the KC-135 similar to that observed for 
sooting flames, with the lift-off height changing by several mm over the course of a parabola.   The 
longer periods of comparatively jitter-free μg available on the ISS will be critical for quantitative 
characterization of these weak flames.  A better understanding of the limits of extinction in these 
relatively cool flames will be important for improving kinetics mechanisms and understanding 
pathways to extinction.  Additionally, longer uninterrupted periods of microgravity will provide 
the opportunity to study a wider range of flow conditions without having to reset the 
experimental apparatus. 
 
For sooting flames, a number of experiments have shown that the overall flame structure is 
markedly different in space than in the shorter-duration periods of microgravity available in 
ground-based facilities [9].  Candle flames that were sooty in normal gravity, during aircraft 
testing, and in the high-quality microgravity of drop facilities, were observed to be blue in testing

items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
6 
 
on orbit in the Space Shuttle and Mir space station [36, 37].  If the experimental results obtained 
are to be used to validate the soot models, the long-term, low-jitter environment of space will be 
required. 
 
C. Science Objectives 
The proposed objectives text presented here is the ‘Experimental Objectives’ section (2.3) of the 
experiment’s SRD from April 2010. 
 
In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational 
models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, we have the following objectives: 
A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a 
function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off 
heights, temperatures and extinction limits. 
B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a 
function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas 
temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, 
and soot volume fractions. 
A more complete listing of the specific flame conditions that we will investigate is given in Sections 
2.4 and 3.3. 
 
D. Science Success Criteria 
This text is from the CLD Flame portion of the ‘Success Criteria’ section of the ACME Integrated 
Science Requirements Document (ISRD, ACME-SRD-001.B) from Sept. 2013, which is revision B of 
the version prepared for the Requirements Definition Review (RDR). 
 
Success of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame experiment will be judged on meeting the stated 
experimental objectives by acquiring results that lead to the stated data end products.  Three 
different levels of success – minimum, high, and complete success – are defined. An additional 
level of success is defined as satisfying our overall project goals, which is not required for complete 
experimental success. 
 
6.1.1. Minimum Success 
Minimum success is defined to mean acquisition of sufficient scientific data from the 
experiment to perform a direct comparison with the numerical computations and publish 
at least one journal article.  This minimal level of success may be achieved by obtaining 
basic information about the flame characteristics from the color images or UV images, 
possibly for a subset of the flame conditions outlined above.  Meaningful subsets of the 
data might include data from a single fuel (methane or ethylene, but not both) or from 
either weak or sooting flames, but not both.  Data would remain valuable for comparisons 
with computational models, albeit not as complete as would be desirable.  For example, 
minimum success might come from obtaining data as follows: 
1. Color images of nonsooting flames only (SDEP A1). 
2. UV images of OH* luminosity from nonsooting flames (towards SDEP A2). 
This would provide data that would allow us to determine several of our science data end 
products including the following: 
- 
Observation of lift-off heights as a function of dilution level (SDEP A4). 
- 
Observation of extinction limits as a function of dilution level (SDEP A6).

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
7 
 
- 
Observation of flame shape and size (SDEP A5). 
- 
2D images of OH* concentrations (SDEP A2). 
- 
Peak concentrations of OH* as a function of fuel dilution (SDEP A3). 
Similar “minimum success” subsets of data could be defined for sooting flames only, or 
datasets from one fuel only. In any of these cases, a paper could still be published on the 
limited results and their comparison to the computations. 
6.1.2. High Success 
High success is defined  to mean acquisition of sufficient scientific data from the 
experiment to perform a direct comparison with the numerical computations and publish 
several journal articles.  In addition to the information obtained for a minimum level of 
success, a high level of success may be achieved by obtaining more detailed information 
about the flame characteristics from UV images for species concentrations and from soot 
diagnostics for soot volume fraction (for example): 
1. 2D images of soot laser extinction and associated reference images 
2. 2D images of multi-color soot luminosity (from pyrometry data). 
This would provide data that would allow us to determine several of our science 
data end products including the following: 
- 
2D images of soot volume fraction (SDEP B11). 
- 
2D images of soot temperatures (SDEP B9). 
6.1.3.  Complete Success 
Complete success is defined to mean acquisition of all data related to the experimental 
objectives.  In addition to the information obtained for a high level of success, a complete 
level of success may be achieved by obtaining complete information about the flame 
characteristics using the available diagnostic techniques, including full information on 
temperatures, extinction and sooting tendencies across the full range of flow conditions: 
1. Multi-color images of TFP data, including reference images. 
2. Images of soot extinction representing the peak soot volume fraction, including 
reference images. 
3. Soot luminosity images representing the peak soot temperature, including 
reference images. 
This would provide data that would allow us to determine several of our science data end 
products including the following: 
- 
Radial temperature profiles from TFP (SDEP A7 and B8). 
- 
Combined temperature fields from soot pyrometry and TFP (SDEP A7 and B8 with 
B9). 
- 
Peak soot volume fraction as a function of fuel dilution over the full range of flow 
velocities (SDEP B12). 
- 
Peak temperature as a function of fuel dilution over the full range of flow 
velocities (SDEP A8 and B10). 
 
 
3. Hardware Overview

Implementation’ which should be consulted for additional details.  References to other sections 
within the boxed text of this section refer to the ACME Engineering Implementation document.
