items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
8 
 
 
This section provides a general description a general description of the ACME engineering from 
the ‘3.0 Experimental’ section of the following 2014 conference paper: 
Dennis P. Stocker, Fumiaki Takahashi, J. Mark Hickman, and Andrew C. Suttles, “Gaseous 
Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station,” Spring 
Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Tulsa, OK, 16–
18 March 2014. 
 
IMPORTANT: The 2104 paper from which this section was extracted proceeded completion of the 
spaceflight hardware which was mostly launched in 2017.  As a result, it does not accurately 
describe the final engineering in some regards.   Therefore updates, clarifications, additional 
details, shortcomings, references, etc. have been included in boxed notes like this following the 
original description.  As a minor note, the sizes of figures were adjusted in this report, but none 
were cropped. 
 
As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to 
accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners.  Besides the chamber insert, 
other ACME-unique hardware includes a high-definition color camera and an avionics package, 
which is for data acquisition and control. 
 
 
Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber 
insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS. 
 
ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of 
burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter.  As 
depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 
to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
9 
 
and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two 
flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm).  Most burners 
will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux 
transducers.  The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring 
of the pressure differential across the outlet surface.  The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable 
tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for 
precise positioning. 
 
 
Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, 
porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. 
 
Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated 
gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm.  
However, only the larger gas-jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests.  The burners are 
addressed in detail in section 3.C. 
 
Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, 
presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and 
supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local 
flame quenching. 
 
Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing.  Most tests have been conducted 
using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion 
experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR.  However, some tests were conducted with 
a coil igniter tip, where that included the second round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator 
(BRE) and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiments, with the 
exception of the latter’s first day testing.  The CFI-G investigation will also use the coil igniter tip.  
For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. 
 
The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the 
delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner.  The 
maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on 
a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines.  The crew can exchange the mass 
flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy.  The gas delivery 
system enables on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow, 
inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames, 
although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments.  Gases can also be 
delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as 
the blending of different fuel gases.  CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
10 
 
will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) 
that can be released into the combustion chamber. 
 
Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent.  Furthermore, the fuel 
diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit.  Ultimately, oxidizer flows 
of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a 
maximum of 5 slpm.  ACME has not used gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as indicated above; the 
bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control.  
 
ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and 
two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in 
use on orbit.  All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber.  Collectively, the 
imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot 
volume fraction; and operational support.  However, it is unlikely that all functions would be 
exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. 
 
Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of 
the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning 
mirror).  Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development.  The analog 
camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations.  Light-
emitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both 
support the operations and provide reference images.  The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 
30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent 
control of the zoom, iris, and focus.  The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly 
with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging.  Color imaging can 
also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to 
avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green.  The natural flame 
color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and 
measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24].  Alternately, CH* 
imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm 
bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM).  A 450-nm 
bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract 
interfering broadband soot emission.  However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such 
subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame 
conditions. 
 
The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, 
is not archived in space.  The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center.  Its 
gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction.   
 
The sensitivity of the color digital camera, often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data 
Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times 
and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second.  The clear “filter” is 
of fused silica.  Unfortunately, the thickness of the blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter and the added 
antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it does not balance the 
intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature 
determination.  Meanwhile, rather than the 450-nm bandpass filter described above, the high

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
11 
 
definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging formaldehyde emissions.   
For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A).   
 
Imaging of the dim hydrogen flames in the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames 
(s-Flame) experiment was particularly challenging with these, if not all, cameras.   
 
Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral 
(HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which allows for imaging at 
multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired band.  This 
camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frames per second 
(fps).  Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss 
through the LCTF.  Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where 
ACME is equipped with a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers.  The fibers are 
orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired 
position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video.  During set 
up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal to either ACME’s color digital 
camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF.  An alternate fiber array including a platinum wire 
will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination with preflight calibration will 
enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24]. 
 
In contrast to the preceding paragraph, ACME did not use a HiBMs camera for pyrometry, but 
instead relied on use of ACME’s color DataCam for such temperature measurements.  For an 
example of how this can be done, see the techniques described in the following papers:   
P.B. Kuhn, B. Ma, B.C. Connelly, M.D. Smooke, and M.B. Long, “Soot and Thin-filament Pyrometry 
Using a Color Digital Camera,” Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 33 (2011) 743-750.  
B. Ma, M. B. Long, “Absolute light calibration using S-type thermocouples,” Proceedings of the 
Combustion Institute, 34 (2) (2013) 3531-3539. 
 
Thus far, TFP tests have been conducted with 14-micron fibers spaced apart by 5 mm for a total 
span of 20 mm (in the case of 5 intact ceramic fibers), neglecting optional translation of the array.  
Tests have been conducted using arrays with and without the platinum wire in the furthest 
downstream position.  Tests have also been conducted with some of the fibers broken and 
subsequently removed, leaving only three fibers in the final testing for the BRE and Coflow Laminar 
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiments and at least the initial testing for the Cool Flames 
Investigation with Gases (CFI-G). 
 
CIR has a second HiBMs camera, without a filter, that will be used in combination with CIR’s 
illumination package for alternate measurements of the soot volume fraction.  This will be 
accomplished via an extinction technique previously employed in microgravity [3,6,26], where the 
camera and the collimated light source (with its two fiber-coupled laser diodes) are positioned at 
opposite windows.  The images are recorded at 1024x1024 and 30 fps.  Thus far, the primary 
purpose of this combined system has been the measurement of the droplet diameter for 
determination of the droplet burning rate. 
 
A HiBMs camera without the Liquid Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF) has been used throughout much, 
but not all, of ACME’s operations.  In the first round of the CLD Flame experiment, it was used 
without a filter for flame imaging, but this proved to be largely unsuccessful because the camera

12 
 
is very insensitive to blue.  Afterward, it was equipped with a red filter corresponding to the CIR 
illumination package for the rest of the ACME testing.  Unfortunately, that filter is sufficiently 
broad that significant incandescence can pass through the filter limiting its utility for 
determinations of soot volume fraction via light extinction, e.g., through the technique described 
in the following papers: 
D.L. Urban, Z.G. Yuan, P.B. Sunderland, K.C., Lin, Z. Dai, and G.M. Faeth, “Smoke-Point Properties 
of Nonbuoyant Round Laminar Jet Diffusion Flames,” Proceedings of the Twenty-Eighth 
Symposium (International) on Combustion 28 (2000) 1965-1972.  
F.J. Diez, C. Aalburg, P.B. Sunderland, D.L. Urban, Z.-G. Yuan, G.M. Faeth, “Soot properties of 
laminar jet diffusion flames in microgravity,” Combustion and Flame, 156 (2009) 1514-1524.  
P.S. Greenberg and J.C. Ku, “Soot Volume Fraction Imaging,” Applied Optics, 36 (22) (1997) 5514-
5522. 
Nonetheless, soot volume fraction can also be determined from the color DataCam images. 
 
During ACME operations, the HiBMs camera is typically archived at 15 fps because of data limits 
for transfer and downlink operations.  And because operations are constrained by the data limits, 
image data from this camera are sometimes deleted without downlinking to enable additional 
testing.  And in some testing, HiBMs images aren’t even acquired given their lesser value. 
 
Unfortunately, the HiBMs backlight illumination is significantly obstructed by the bracket for the 
electrode mesh further limiting its utility for the E-FIELD Flames experiment.   This was a design 
trade-off necessitated primarily by ACME’s large number of cameras and other optical 
instruments. 
 
CIR’s Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) package is a monochrome camera with an intensifier 
(for 280-700 nm) and a 310-nm bandpass filter (with a 10-nm FWHM) for OH* imaging.  Again as 
a result of the signal loss through the filter, binning is employed such that the OH* images are 
recorded at 512x512 and 30 fps. 
 
During ACME operations, the LLL-UV camera has only been used for the Structure and Response 
of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment. 
 
While not discussed in the preceding section, another intensified camera was used throughout 
ACME testing, although its image data was sometimes deleted or not even acquired to allow the 
performance of additional tests.   This was the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) camera which was 
generally configured with its CH* filter, where an exception is some s-Flame testing with 
particularly dim flames.  Due to design trade-offs, its Field of View (FOV) was partially obstructed 
by the arms of the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array when it was moved inwards to the 
flame.  More information about this camera can be found in its characterization report, CIR-RPT-
4600. 
 
The ACME chamber insert will also be equipped with non-imaging optical diagnostics including 
both thermopile radiometers and Photomultiplier Tubes (PMTs).  There is a crew-exchangeable 
linear array of radiometers of which there are two versions supporting the initial set of 
experiments.  The array has a fixed position which is parallel to the chamber axis and centered 
(along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows and thus most of the other 
instrumentation.  One array is equipped with a single wide-view radiometer with two narrow-

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
13 
 
view radiometers that are downstream and two more that are upstream, where all views are 
orthogonal to the chamber axis, as depicted in Figure 4.  The narrow-view radiometers are 
intended to support studies of gas-jet flames, where ACME can accommodate shorter burners, 
making the “lower” detectors useful.  The other array, also seen in Fig. 4, provides for three wide-
view measurements of the flame, where one view is masked to nominally block radiant emission 
from the burner.  It was specifically designed for the BRE experiment but will be a resource 
available to other ACME experiments.  Given that the radiometer array can be exchanged by the 
crew, alternate arrays could be developed.   
 
 
Figure 4: Crew-exchangeable radiometer arrays on the ACME chamber insert: (top) standard 
(ACME) array of 5 radiometers, and (bottom) array with three radiometers, designed for the BRE 
experiment, where the lowest detector is masked to avoid view of the burner. 
 
A third radiometer array was developed for the CFI-G experiment, where it is important to 
understand that only a single radiometer array can be used at a time.

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
14 
 
 
The narrow-view radiometers in the standard array are only fully sensitive in small spots, but they 
are each sensitive in a much greater Field of View (FOV) than represented in the preceding figure.   
They do not have lenses; their FOV is a result of an aperture where most of their FOV is within the 
penumbra which is only visible to a portion of the sensor.  Figures representing the measured FOVs 
of the as-built standard and BRE radiometer arrays are found in section 3.F of this document.   
 
Unfortunately, the radiometers in the BRE array typically saturated in the first round of BRE 
testing, so the standard array was used in its second round.  However, those radiometers similarly 
saturated in many of round 2 tests.  In this regard, each of ACME’s BRE and standard radiometers 
have a fixed gain.  Meanwhile, each sensor in the radiometer array developed for the CFI-G 
investigation has two fixed gains, i.e., a high gain and low gain.   
 
For more information about the standard radiometer array used for most ACME testing, see the 
Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-011).  Meanwhile, you can learn about the other 
radiometer arrays from the BRE Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-012) and the 
Cool Flames Radiometer Characterization Report (CIR-RPT-4600).    
 
An additional wide-view radiometer, that is fixed and not crew exchangeable, is positioned 
downstream of the burner and flame at 30o from the chamber axis.  This detector is primarily 
intended to support the spherical flame experiments and will have a quicker response than the 
more sensitive detectors that will used in the linear arrays.   Like the radiometers on the two linear 
arrays, it will have a spectral range of nominally 0.2-11 micron and its field of view will be 
established by an appropriately selected aperture. 
 
The FOV of the off-set radiometer is also shown in section 3.F.  Learn more about this sensor from 
the Radiometer Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-011).   
 
To detect the quenching of dim flames, the chamber insert will be equipped with a set of three 
PMTs.  Each PMT will have a wide-angle view, a sight line that is orthogonal to the chamber axis, 
and will be centered (along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows so that it is 
aligned with most of the other instrumentation.  The PMTs’ spectral range will be 230-700 nm, 
i.e., visible and near ultraviolet, but one will have a 310-nm bandpass filter and another will have 
a 430-nm bandpass filter (where both are with a 10-nm FWHM).  The pair of detectors will enable 
measurement of OH* and CH* emission, respectively.  The third PMT will be equipped with a 
neutral density filter to prevent saturation.  Like many other components, the PMT array can be 
removed from the chamber insert by the crew. 
 
Unlike the radiometers, each PMT had a readily adjustable gain.  However, the PMT signals 
sometimes saturated when the gains were set too high.  See the PMT Characterization Report 
(ACME-RPT-013) to learn more about the three Photomultiplier Tube (PMTs).   
 
The chamber insert is also equipped with six far-field thermocouples to measure the spread of 
the thermal field in the spherical flame experiments.  They are of limited utility for other 
experiments because they are positioned upstream of the burner tip.  Therefore, they will 
generally not be installed by the crew to reduce the chance of accidental damage.  There will be 
two versions of a four-thermocouple rake to allow a choice of near and far measurements.  Other

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
15 
 
arrays could be designed to support future experiments, but they cannot extend downstream of 
the burner tip without interfering with other (e.g., optical) measurements. 
 
The two lone thermocouples, which are both at nominally 200 mm from the center of the spherical 
burner, have been installed throughout ACME testing.  The tip of one was seen to be slightly bent 
early in testing, as discussed and depicted in section 3.G of this report.   
 
Only the short (or far) version of the radiometer rake has been used thus far, where factors include 
the need for crew time to switch between rakes and the heat loss that could result from 
thermocouples in the long (close) rake.  The short (far) rake’s thermocouple tips should nominally 
be at 45, 60, 100, and 100 mm from the spherical burner center.  For thermocouples at the same 
distance from the burner center, the angle between the rays from the burner center to the two 
thermocouples should be 90 degrees.  The bead size of the thermocouples was not measured, but 
it is undoubtedly at least twice the size of the 0.2 mm diameter wire. 
  
The two thermocouples closest to the burner outlets on each four-thermocouple rake are type B, 
while the others are type K. 
 
Experiment-unique hardware is also mounted on the chamber insert.  For example, to 
accommodate the E-FIELD Flames experiment, the insert is equipped with a high-voltage supply 
and a crew-removable electrode mesh which can be set between +10 and -10 kV.   The circular mesh 
is orthogonal to the chamber axis and is positioned (during set up) at either ~35 or ~50 mm 
downstream of the insulated burner.  The ion current between the burner and electrode mesh will 
be determined via measurement of the voltage drop across a known resistor and application of 
Ohm’s Law. 
 
Additional images of the chamber insert can be seen in subsequent sections of this report.  The 
hardware specific to E-FIELD Flames is discussed further in section 2.B. 
 
Additional supporting measurements will be made, where the chamber pressure is a simple 
example.  The ACME experiments will use the CIR’s gas chromatograph for pre- and post-test 
analysis of the chamber atmosphere, e.g., for oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, 
and fuel gases.  Acceleration measurements will be provided by the Space Acceleration 
Measurement System (SAMS) [27], which is the primary instrument for such measurements on 
ISS and previously served that role for the space shuttle. 
 
The CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) was not used for the CLD Flame or 
E-FIELD Flames investigations and thus far was only sometimes used during BRE, Flame Design, 
and s-Flame testing.  Its use requires significant time and as such effectively reduces the number 
of tests that can be conducted.  However, estimates of the chamber contents were computed 
assuming that the fuel in a normal flame test (for example) was either fully or not at all oxidized, 
e.g., for unsustained ignition in the latter case. 
 
The CIR facility was equipped with a 3-axis SAMS sensor head and the acceleration measurements, 
along with relevant documentation, are accessible via the home page for the Principal Investigator 
Microgravity Services (PIMS), https://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/pims/home/.  To be clear, the

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
16 
 
acceleration measurements are not archived with the ACME experiment data in the Physical 
Sciences Informatics (PSI) website, www.nasa.gov/PSI.  
 
All ACME experiments will be constant volume (i.e., rather than constant pressure) studies, where 
the chamber’s free volume will be about 90 liters.  Burner flows will generally be constrained to 
limit the pressure rise, and tests will typically be 0.5-2 minutes in duration. 
 
The chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed hardware. 
 
The ACME experiments will be configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  Instead, the 
experiments will be commanded from the ground, specifically from the Telescience Support 
Center (TSC) at the NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio.  They can be conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it will also be possible to 
effectively operate the experiments in a “manual” mode, where changes can be made in response 
to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream.  For 
example, a flow rate could be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit.  Step and ramp 
changes can be made in the flow rate(s) or electric field potential.  The TFP fiber array can be 
translated uniformly through a soot-free flame to get a continuum measurement of the 
temperature field.  In summary, ACME’s experiment control will allow for broad flexibility.   
 
The TSC is now also referred to as the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC).  Thus far, the 
ACME tests have always been conducted in a nominally automated mode. 
 
B. Hardware Shortcomings 
The primary hardware challenge for CLD Flame was the unsatisfactory performance of the Mass 
Flow Controllers (MFCs).  In particular, the MFC initially used for the oxidizer coflow behaved as if 
it momentary stuck in a few places, where the flow rate wouldn’t linearly ramp with time when 
commanded.  It tended to stick in some places and then abruptly overshoot where that was 
sometimes seen to extinguish the flame.   This prevented determination of extinction limits and 
led to the decision to prepare and launch a replacement MFC and add a short third round of CLD 
Flame testing.  The replacement was installed on 3 Feb. 2021 (21034).  The replacement’s control 
of the flow rate was much better as was verified during MFC testing on the subsequent day.  
However, it must be recognized that the majority of the investigation’s tests were carried out with 
the ill-behaving oxidizer MFC. 
 
Besides the issue with the oxidizer MFC, the fuel and especially nitrogen flows were sometimes 
found to oscillate.  Adjustments were subsequently made to (1) the cracking settings that control 
when the MFC valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) settings.  While the 
MFC tuning has been beneficial in some cases, it has not eliminated all gas flow problems.  It was 
seen that nitrogen oscillations tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow was implemented 
so that the oscillations would typically end before the flame measurements.  That approach was 
partially successful and was introduced between CLD Flame’s first and second rounds.  Later, a 
procedure of re-zeroing the MFCs prior to each test was also implemented between CLD Flame’s 
second and third rounds. 
 
Successful ignition was sometime an issue, especially early in the CLD Flame testing, where it was 
the first ACME experiment for which tests were conducted.  As a result, CLD Flame encountered

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
17 
 
issues which were resolved or better managed for later ACME experiments.  For example, ignition 
repeatedly failed in early testing and it determined in Dec. 2017 that the igniter arm was not 
properly aligned to the coflow burner, where the inner diameter of the fuel outlet was only 2.2 
mm.  The alignment was corrected by astronaut Joe Acaba with the help of Mark Vande Hei on 5 
Jan. 2018 (18005).  It helped enable the ignition of 57 flames that month in contrast to the 15 and 
11 flames ignited in November and December 2017, respectively. 
 
The hot-wire igniter tips degrade with repeated use and sometimes fail preventing subsequent 
testing until a crew member can replace it.  In early ACME – and thus CLD Flame - testing, the 
igniter sometimes failed during the last test of the day where the failure wasn’t discovered until 
the subsequent test day.  Such discoveries were made, for example, on both 29 Nov. 2017 (17333) 
and 15 Feb. 2018 (18046) when no flames could be ignited.  In later ACME operations, the igniter 
function was verified at the end of each test day to avoid such wasted test days.   Care was taken 
to limit igniter heating and retract it from the flame after ignition.  Furthermore, the igniter tip 
was proactively replaced on a periodic basis, when the crew made other changes on the ACME 
chamber insert. 
 
Even neglecting improper alignment and igniter tip failure, the flames did not always ignite.  
During ACME operations, it was common for the first test of the day to not ignite, presumably 
because the fuel line and burner hadn’t been sufficiently primed.  Ignition was also sometime 
been unsuccessful due to automated igniter deactivation and retraction caused by the igniter 
glow.  That was largely avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* 
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module.   The OH* chemiluminescence, in 
the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, 
which emits primarily in the infrared and visible spectrum.  However, the combination of igniter 
settings and PMT gains can lead to false ignition detection. 
 
As discussed in the preceding section (3.A), the ACME DataCam was unfortunately not as sensitive 
as had been hoped to the dim microgravity flames.  As a result, it was often used with long 
exposure times limiting the framing rate.  Furthermore, the blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter 
intended for use in the pyrometry didn’t meet objectives and was generally unused.  The filter’s 
thickness and the added antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it 
did not balance the intensity of the three color planes as intended. 
 
CLD Flame attempted use of the High-Bit Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera in its first round 
without a filter for flame imaging, but it proved to be highly unsuccessful because the camera is 
very insensitive to blue.  Afterward, it was equipped with a red filter corresponding to the CIR 
illumination package for the rest of the ACME testing.  However, the filter is sufficiently broad 
that significant incandescence can pass through the filter limiting its utility for determinations of 
soot volume fraction via light extinction.  Therefore, CLD Flame tests were often conducted 
without HiBMs imaging, or where the HiBMs data was deleted without downlinking, to allow for 
more testing without reaching data constraints. 
 
There were also issues with the Image Processing and Storage Units which effected CLD Flame 
operations.  The primary hard drive for the IPSU-G, for use with the Gigabit Ethernet (GigE) 
cameras, failed to boot in April 2018 during E-FIELD Flames operations.  The removed drive was 
reinstalled in the secondary position during CLD Flame operations on 14 Aug. 2018 (18226) by 
astronaut Ricky Arnold.  Unfortunately, it surprisingly caused the IPSU-G to again become

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
18 
 
unstable.  Therefore, the drive was removed on 22 Aug. 2018 (18234) by astronaut Alex Gerst, 
returning it to use, albeit without the intended storage capacity. 
 
The IPSU-1, used with HiBMs camera and the collimated illumination package, was only 
intermittently operable in Sept. 2018, at the end of CLD Flame’s second round.  It was not 
functioning on 6 Sept. 2018 (18249) or 10 Sept. 2018 (18253) but did work on 14 Sept. 2018 
(18257).  However, as previously discussed those capabilities were not seen as important for CLD 
Flame, so the testing continued unabated.  It was later determined to be an issue with a cable 
connection, which was corrected by astronaut Alex Gerst on 22 Oct. 2018 (18295) during E-FIELD 
Flames’ second round of testing.  In CLD Flame’s third round of testing, the HiBMs camera, 
illumination package, and IPSU-1 were not even used which is an indication of their limited value 
to the investigation. 
 
CLD Flame tests sometimes automatically aborted due to the controlling software script, where 
that was typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter.  As a result, there was little 
lost other than the time in the failed test attempt.  These aborts normally occurred because of 
communication issues with IPSU-1.  These aborts were infrequent, but there have been ACME 
test days when tests have aborted repeatedly.  
 
Soot deposition on the coflow burner was a temporary problem at the beginning of CLD Flame’s 
second round.  At the end of the E-FIELD Flame’s first round, testing with a positively charged 
electrode mesh pushed the flame down toward the burner.  A significant amount of soot 
deposited on the burner, both on the inner tube from which the fuel issued as well as the 
honeycomb in the burner annulus from which the oxidizer flowed.  The extent of the soot wasn’t 
appreciated until CLD Flame testing with flames resumed on May 25 (18145).  Additional 
evaluation tests were performed on May 31 (18151) when it was seen that the gas flow from the 
burner was affected by the soot buildup.  Therefore, a cleaning procedure was developed, 
approved, and carried out by astronaut Ricky Arnold on 19 June 2018 (18170).  Regular flame 
testing in the second round finally commenced on 5 July 2018 (18186), after a cable mating 
correction on 25 June 2018 (18176).  That was six weeks after the soot accumulation was 
identified as an issue, but useful scientific results were obtained on the 26 June 2018 (18177) 
evaluation day, so the burner cleaning effectively led to a 1-month delay. 
 
During Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) testing on 23 Dec. 2020, it was discovered that the lowest of 
the 14-micron silicon carbide fibers on the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array had broken.  
Recovery plans were developed and enacted on 18 Jan. 2021 to remove the broken fiber 
fragments from the harp-like array.  Unfortunately, the next fiber was broken during the delicate 
operations where the fibers are only spaced 5 mm apart.  Although ACME had alternate arrays, it 
also had months of remaining testing.  Therefore, the decision was made to continue with only 3 
fibers (instead of 5) for the final BRE testing and third round of CLD Flame tests.  This was a minor 
loss to CLD Flame given the small size of the experiment’s flames. 
 
In addition to sections 3.A-B, shortcomings are discussed in Appendices B and C of this report and 
in the ACME Engineering Implementation document.  The latter document includes images from 
the burner cleaning (in section 3.C.2), discussion of deviations and waivers (in section 4.B), etc.

items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
19 
 
4. Preliminary Results  
A. Changed Test Plans 
The most significant change in CLD Flame plans resulted from the poor performance of the Mass 
Flow Controller (MFC) used for the oxidizer coflow.  Its inability to provide a smooth ramped 
increase to the flow rate, and thus coflow velocity, prevented determination of extinction limits 
for a range of flame conditions.  As a temporary way to partially mitigate the science loss, tests 
were sometimes conducted where the coflow velocity was reduced rather than increased.  But 
given the science loss, the decision was made to prepare and launch a replacement MFC.  Those 
tests were ultimately conducted in early 2021, whereas the earlier tests were carried out in late 
2017 and 2018. 
 
Unwanted oscillations in the fuel and nitrogen flow were sometimes encountered and those led 
to operational changes which were partially successful.  The nitrogen oscillations were often 
observed to damp with time and the software script controlling the CLD Flame tests was modified 
between the first and second round of testing to accommodate a pre-flow of nitrogen with the 
goal of allowing any oscillations to diminish prior to the ignition of the flame.  Furthermore, a 
practice of re-zeroing the MFCs shortly before the start of each test was adopted.  Besides these 
measures, on-orbit adjustments were made to the MFCs’ cracking and Proportional-Integral-
Derivative (PID) settings. 
 
The use of long exposure times for the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) was adopted because of 
the dim nature of the microgravity flames.  The planned use of the blue green BG7 Schott glass 
filter with the DataCam for pyrometry was largely abandoned because the combination of the 
filter thickness and the added antireflective (AR) coating caused to great a reduction in the red 
color plane.  As a result of wear and breakage, different arrays of ceramic fibers for Thin Filament 
Pyrometry (TFP) were used during the three rounds of testing.   In the first round, the fifth fiber 
position (farthest downstream) had a platinum wire instead of a 14-micron Silicon Carbide (SiC) 
ceramic fiber like those in the four other positions.  In the second round, an array with five SiC 
fibers was used, while in the third round the array had only three fibers because two had broken. 
 
Testing began with the red filter removed from the High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera 
so that it could be used to image the flame rather than light extinction, e.g., for soot visualization 
and potential measurement, using the CIR illumination package.  However, it was discovered that 
the HiBMs camera was insensitive to blue light, where that’s the natural color of the hydrocarbon 
flames tested (neglecting any soot).  Therefore, after the first of CLD Flame testing, the red filter 
corresponding to the illumination package was installed to enable imaging with light extinction.  
However, CLD Flame employed a method featuring absolute light calibration to determine the 
soot volume fraction from the DataCam imaging.  As a result, HiBMs images were of limited value 
and were only sometimes saved or even recorded.  The camera wasn’t used at all during the third 
round of testing.  
 
Changes were periodically made to the software script controlling the tests.  An updated script 
was in use on 22 Dec. 2017 (17356) which added parameters for specifying the gain for each of 
the three Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules.  Conversely, that revision eliminated a parameter 
for accelerating the oxidizer coflow.  The script was revised again before the start of the second 
round of tests, where that update added a parameter allowing for a nitrogen pre-flow prior to the 
flame ignition, as previously discussed.  More importantly, the DataCam bracketing parameters

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
20 
 
were revised to allow for a multiplicative rather than additive change between exposures.  These 
changes are further discussed in the ACME/CLD Flame Experimental Procedure document, which 
also includes the final version of the script (used in the second and third rounds of testing) with 
an explanation of its parameters. 
 
B. Overview of Experiment Test Operations 
While not yet prepared, additional details will be made available in the ACME/CLD Flame 
Experimental Procedure document. 
 
The narrative description of the experimental procedure is an excerpt from the ‘Methods / 
Experimental’ section of the following conference paper. 
Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on 
Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of 
the Central States Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. 
 
While the paper was written for the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD 
Flames) experiment, much of the discussion applies to ACME in general, including the CLD Flame 
investigation.  The figure referenced in this excerpt is not included herein.  Clarifications and 
additional information, not in the conference paper, are included in boxed notes like this. 
 
The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  Thus far, ACME’s activity 
has included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities.  Most often the 
astronauts and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips.  In the 
latter case, the igniter tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the 
crew already has changes to make changes in the interior of the insert.  While these activities may 
seem mundane, the crew play a critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment.  As 
an extreme example, there were crew activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure 
the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion 
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  In contrast, only two crew days were required to reconfigure the 
hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the initial use of the same coflow burner.  
Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks in advance, for which detailed 
procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. 
 
As a correction, including two maintenance activities, there were 11 crew days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 
to prepare for the initial CLD Flame testing on the space station. 
 
All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations 
Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio.  Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the 
testing.  The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer 
(DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console.  
Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they 
typically last 14 hours with the many pre- and post-testing activities.  Given that the tests are 
remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., 
from 7 AM to 9 PM.  A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours 
of less.  Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks.  On intervening 
weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both gas bottles.  
Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2-shift day for the RO and

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
21 
 
DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors 
and that data is not missing.  Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew 
activity.  As a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week.  A 
team of four carry out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily 
operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing. 
 
The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in 
near real time but doesn’t allow for commanding.  In the case of E-FIELD Flames, arrangements 
were made so that the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the 
research team to participate in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s 
planned parameters.  That team does not see the telemetry during the testing, but is in 
communication via phone and e-mail with their NASA research partners at the GRC ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  While there are many preparatory steps, the tests are ultimately 
conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files.  In advance of the test day, the 
UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep script and specifies 
other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings.  It is also 
possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in 
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry.  For example, the electric field potential can 
be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. 
 
Provisions have been made to enable the investigators from all ACME experiments to remotely 
view the analog video while they communicated verbally with NASA science personnel in the 
operations center.  All ACME flame tests, including those for CLD Flame, were conducted in a 
nominally automated manner using software scripts and extensive parameter files. 
 
Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, 
the low rate results from several unavoidable factors.  After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz non-
imaging data is downlinked for immediate review by the science team.  A small sample of images 
are often downlinked to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for 
those images are typically selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples.  The 
review helps to verify parameters or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the 
voltage range after determining where the ion current saturates for the given flame conditions.  
After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber atmosphere after which the chamber is 
vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed.  Midway through a day’s E-FIELD 
Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter cartridge filled with 
molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion products, 
e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products.  The tests are only 
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and 
Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) System.  Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic 
communication outages with a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite 
to another) or can last as long as 30 minutes. 
 
Typically, on the order of 15 tests were conducted per CLD Flame test day. 
 
With CLD Flame’s significant oxidizer coflow, the chamber was normally filled with nitrogen and 
circulation through the adsorber cartridge was not important.  However, some test days featured

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
22 
 
testing where the chamber was filled with 21% oxygen (on a volume basis) and a balance of 
nitrogen.  
 
A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a 
daily basis.  The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame 
spread and material flammability.  That follow-on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, 
where each ACME experiment is allotted four months for testing.  Although it requires additional 
crew time, these allotments are split into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from 
testing for careful review of the early results so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of 
their second round.  This paper reports on early results from the first round of E-FIELD Flames. 
 
While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the 
available gas bottles that were and are launched to support the tests.  For E-FIELD Flames and 
most of ACME’s experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established 
in 2010.  At that time, NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of 
focused experiments with limited objectives rather than comprehensive experiments.  As such, 
the general target was 50 tests per experiment.  For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas 
constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber.  This resource constraint is 
exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the 
fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow 
in the case of inverse flame testing).  The timers can only be reset by venting the combustion 
chamber.  Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively corresponds to 
the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant).  For E-FIELD 
Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 
10 tests typically completed per day. 
 
The maximum limit of 999 seconds for the valve safety timers was used for all ACME testing. 
 
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, 
such as the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours.  When necessary for the 
research, NASA does have continuous 24-hour/day operations for some non-CIR experiments.  
But as discussed, the ACME tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is 
almost always limited to the planned durations. 
 
Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on-orbit hardware can store a limited amount 
of data.  More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two-
shift transfer and downlink day.  Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where 
image data from select cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge.  
Nonetheless, the limit sometimes forces decisions to abandon recorded images. 
 
This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME 
experiments are conducted.  … ]

C. Summary of Preliminary Results  
Temperature measurements in dilute, lifted flames 
The processing procedure for obtaining flame temperature measurements is summarized in 
Fig. 5.  An image of a heated SiC fiber taken during a space station fiber test is shown in Fig. 5(a).  
This is a single image taken from a series of images capturing a fiber sweeping through the center 
of the flame.  From the consecutive fiber images, a 2-D composite image is constructed and is 
shown in Fig. 5(b).  From this composite image, the temperature of the fiber is determined by 
performing color ratio pyrometry, Fig. 5(c).  From these fiber temperatures, a light calibration is 
performed to determine the absolute light calibration constant.  Figure 6 shows the calibration 
results for this fiber test and shows an excellent fit to the pixel data with reasonably low 
deviations.

Figure 6. Green camera signal vs fiber temperature results plotted along with the light calibration.  
From the light calibration, reference parameters of signal and temperature could be obtained and 
used to perform intensity ratio pyrometry to get an improved signal-to-noise intensity ratio fiber 
temperature measurement, Fig. 5(d).  The flame temperature measurement is obtained by 
applying a radiation correction to the fiber temperature results, Fig. 5 (e).  The radiation correction 
uses an energy balance between radiation and convection at the surface of the fiber, while 
assuming conduction is negligible. 
 
Figure 7 shows telemetry data from a microgravity test to determine the dilution limits of a 
nitrogen-diluted methane flame. The flame is ignited at 40% CH4 by volume and slowly diluted 
with excess nitrogen at constant velocity. As identified by the telemetry data, the opening of the 
valve connected to the nitrogen mass flow controller (MFC) is delayed, which causes an 
unintentional drop in total fuel mixture velocity. However, the valve eventually does open, and 
the conditions of fuel mixture gas flow fully recovers. Sometime after the recovery, the flame 
extinction event occurs. Assessment of the recovery determined that the initial drop in fuel

flames diluted with nitrogen, the extinction event occurred within a range of 24-27% CH4. The 
extinction event for ethylene flames diluted with nitrogen were found to occur in the range of 10-
12% C2H4. 
 
Figure 7. Telemetry data of a microgravity dilution limit test for a nitrogen-diluted methane flame 
at 40% CH4 by volume slowly diluted with nitrogen until extinction.  The region enclosed in the 
large circle indicates an initial flow issue where the nitrogen MFC valve struggles to open at the 
start of the dilution ramping stage.  However, the MFC eventually recovers, and the dilution limit 
is determined. 
 
Stable flames in microgravity were achievable at a dilution of 30% CH4.  As a comparison, stable 
flames in normal gravity are unachievable at this dilution.  This demonstrates the extension of the 
dilution limits when buoyancy is not present.  Microgravity flames were stabilized at 30% and 
flame and fiber images were obtained.  Results from these tests are shown in Fig. 8.  The color 
flame images in these figures show the deconvoluted signal after applying an Abel inversion.  This 
reveals the internal structure of the flame.  The lift-off behavior of these very weak flames is also 
observed as a function of increasing gas velocity.  The flame temperatures were measured and 
will be important for the analysis when studying the stabilization mechanism that creates the lift-
off behavior.

Comparison of Sooty Flames at 0 g and 1 g 
To investigate the effect of gravity on sooty flames, the experiments from the space station were 
recreated in a ground-based laboratory using copies of the microgravity flight hardware.  The 
testing, data processing procedures and analysis were recreated to have direct comparisons 
between the flames with and without the inclusion of buoyancy forces acting on the flames. In 
the discussion below, the velocities given are the average burner exit velocities measured during 
cold flowing conditions. 
 
Figure 11 shows a series of soot temperature profiles from microgravity and normal gravity 
ethylene flames diluted with varying levels of nitrogen and matching fuel mixture and coflow 
velocities fixed at 40 cm/s.  At high levels of dilution (60% N2 by volume) both the microgravity 
and the normal gravity have similar temperature profiles.  As the level of nitrogen dilution 
decreases, the height of the microgravity flames increases more rapidly, and the peak 
temperature shifts towards the sides. This is observed in Fig. 11(c) where the peak flame 
temperature shifts to the side and a cooler inner region forms.  This trend continues into the pure 
fuel condition shown in Fig. 11(d).  This trend of peak temperature shifting to the outer region of 
the flame has been observed in normal gravity conditions, however, it is not observed in the 
normal gravity flames produced from this ACME coflow burner.  The overall peak temperature 
decreases faster in the microgravity flames as dilution levels decrease.

D. Surprises and New Discoveries  
There are many aspects to diffusion flame combustion that are still not well understood at a 
fundamental level, and microgravity combustion has proven to be an effective environment from 
which to gain a deeper understanding.  The CLD Flame research has shown that microgravity 
flames can be 4-8 times sootier than their normal gravity counterparts and that the distribution 
of peak soot shifts from the centerline of the flame at normal gravity to the wings in microgravity.  
Such changes in the soot field are consistent with results from a variety of experiments on coflow 
flames in both ground- and space-based venues as well as different mass flow rates, burner 
diameters and fuels.  The increased soot loading and flame residence times lead to lower flame 
temperature in microgravity due to increased radiative losses.  
One of the project goals of CLD Flame was obtain quantitative measurements of sooting coflow 
diffusion flames in both normal and microgravity conditions on a burner with well characterized 
boundary conditions, and to use those measurements to improve computational models.  
Previous work had shown that existing computational models were unable to predict accurately 
the behavior of these systems.  With the new data provided, efforts are underway to generate 
new simulations matching the ACME test conditions under 1 g and 0 g conditions.  
A key element in the CLD Flame dataset is the availability of carefully measured boundary 
conditions, which are critical for comparison with computational models.  These were measured 
on both the ground-based copy as well as the flight copy of the coflow burners.  Figure 15 shows 
an example of one such velocity profile measured under cold-flow conditions at 0.5 mm above 
the fuel tube.  This was used as an input boundary condition for calculations of pure ethylene 
flames on 1 g and 0 g, and comparisons were made to the experimental data.  
 
Figure 15. Measured velocity profile for one flow condition used as the input boundary condition 
for computational modeling. 
The flames were computed on a domain 3.9 cm wide by 10 cm long.  The grids employed were 
highly nonuniform, with clustering of points near the inlet and the base of the flame, and, to some 
extent, near the steep gradients in the soot volume fraction.  The grid for the 1 g flame contained 
120 radial points and 138 axial points, while the grid for the 0 g flame contained 133 radial points 
and 149 axial points.  Experimentation has shown that these grids are adequate to achieve a stable

closeness of the measured and computed soot temperature fields (Fig. 16) is apparent.  The 
computed soot temperature is taken to be the portion of the temperature field where the soot

Despite the relatively good agreement in soot temperatures, the discrepancies between the 
experimental and computational results at the two gravity levels, shown in Fig. 17, remain 
significant.  Prior modeling efforts attributed the increased soot levels under microgravity to the 
increased flame residence times and to different trajectories of soot-forming streamlines through 
the flame.  However, a closer look at calculated flame residence times in 1 g and 0 g (Fig. 18) 
shows that for the relatively small flames considered here, the residence times (10 ms to peak 
soot) differ by a very small amount, with the times in the 0 g flame only about 5-10 percent longer 
than in the 1 g flame.  Thus, the residence-time argument, by itself, is not sufficient to explain the 
large differences in soot loading between the two gravity levels, and further refinement of the 
computational models is required. 
 
 
Figure 18. Computed soot volume fractions at 1g (left) and 0g (right), with residence time 
curves indicated in white at 5 ms intervals. 
 
E. Accomplishment of Approved Objectives 
CLD Flame had two main objectives as follows: 
 
A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames methane and ethylene, as a function 
of velocity and fuel dilution. 
 
B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of methane and ethylene diffusion flames with long 
residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution. 
 
Through the three rounds of testing of CLD Flame, both objectives were achieved, as seen in the 
examples above.  The first round of testing effectively began in January 2018 and concentrated 
on measurements in dilute methane flames, as well as characterization and calibration of the 
imaging systems.  The second round of experiments began in May 2018, and provided results on 
sooting methane and ethylene flames, as well as some data on weak, lifted ethylene flames.  
Because of issues related to the stability of the mass flow controllers, the quality of data on the 
extinction limits of the dilute methane and ethylene flames was not optimal.  Therefore, a third

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
35 
 
round of experiments began in February of 2021.  Improvements in the mass flow controllers 
allowed us to establish extinction limits for both fuels under a variety of flow conditions. 
 
The only deviation from the specifics of the science data end products as originally specified, 
related to chemiluminescence measurements.  The original SRD specified measurements of OH*, 
with CH* desired.  Because the quality of the images from the DataCam (which could detect CH*) 
were superior to those from the LLL-UV camera (for OH*), we concentrated on measuring and 
quantifying CH* rather than OH*.  Previous work has shown that these two radicals are spatially 
coincident in coflow diffusion flames.  Furthermore, the CH* spatial distribution is indicative of 
the flame front position, and its concentration is related to the total and local flame heat release 
rate. 
 
F. Additional Objectives Achieved 
Computational and Experimental Study of the Effects of Pressure and Fuel Dilution 
Since the CLD Flame experiments were carried out in an enclosed pressure vessel, there was an 
increase in pressure during each test due to the addition of fresh gas into the chamber (primarily 
from the coflow).  To understand better the effects of this increasing pressure, a combined 
computational and experimental investigation was conducted to characterize the influences of 
pressure, as well as fuel stream dilution on the structure, shape, and sooting behavior of coflow 
methane–air laminar diffusion flames under normal gravity conditions.  A series of 72 methane–
air coflow laminar diffusion flames with four levels of nitrogen dilution in the fuel stream (50, 55, 
60, and 65% methane) and 18 levels of pressure (1.0 to 2.7 atm in 0.1 atm increments) were 
assessed.  In general, very good agreement between the computations and the experiments was 
achieved for the temperature, the flame shape, and the soot volume fraction, and the numerical 
model successfully captured the effects of varying pressure and fuel stream dilution. The major 
conclusions of this research were as follows:  
 
• The maximum temperature increases with increasing methane concentration or 
pressure.   
• The lift-off height decreases significantly with increasing pressure, the modified flame 
length is roughly independent of pressure, and the flame radius decreases with pressure 
approximately as P−1/2.   
• The pressure and fuel stream dilution significantly affect the spatial distribution and the 
peak value of the soot volume fraction.  
 
Results of this study were published in Combustion Theory and Modelling. 
 
Software Development and Documentation 
As part of our NASA diagnostics development work, techniques were implemented for 
quantitative measurements of soot temperature, soot volume fraction, thin-filament fiber 
temperature, and concentration of CH* in axisymmetric flames.  These techniques require 
software for image acquisition and processing as well as careful characterization of the detection 
systems used.  The bulk of this is done using image processing software developed in our labs over 
a period of more than thirty years.  The “OMA” software has undergone continuous revision and 
extension and a version of the software for the Mac operating system has been available as open 
source since 2005 (http://oma-x.org).  All the ACME experiments used the same detectors, and 
many can use the same processing methods that we have developed to handle the raw data.  The

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
36 
 
detector calibrations and latest version of the processing software are available to all ACME 
investigators (and others as well through our open-source web site).  A User’s Guide that outlines 
the basic processing steps for soot temperature and volume fraction determination was prepared 
and posted on the NASA website.  The user’s guide includes examples of raw data and the steps 
required to obtain quantitative measurements as well as macro scripts consisting of basic OMA 
commands, which streamline the data processing.  While the most advanced user interface and 
display capabilities are for the Mac operating system, versions for the Linux and Windows 
operating systems are available that implement all the image processing algorithms and basic 
display capabilities. 
 
Due to the relatively low pixel density of the ACME detector, interpolating algorithms (a.k.a. 
demosaicing algorithms) have been tested as a way to maintain the original spatial resolution 
when converting raw images into color ones.  The "bilinear interpolation" and the "Malvar 
algorithm" have been implemented and added to OMA and their effectiveness tested against soot 
temperature measurements in a reference nitrogen-diluted ethylene flame.  The quantitative 
information returned by the demosaiced images was seen to be more accurate than the one 
computed without any interpolation, albeit with an increase in the overall image noise.  
 
G. Impacts, Benefits, and Products 
The main product from CLD Flame is a comprehensive dataset of microgravity and normal gravity 
coflow methane and ethylene diffusion flames.  These include weak, lifted flames near extinction, 
under a variety of fuel dilution levels and flow conditions.  The highly diluted, lifted flames tend 
to be non-sooting and differences in liftoff height and flame stability between 1 g and 0 g are 
significant (e.g., see Fig. 10 above).  This data will provide a stringent test for computational 
models seeking to predict flame extinction.  At the other end of the fuel dilution spectrum, the 
dataset includes robust, sooting flames, with different flow conditions and dilution levels, which 
provide different flame heights and levels of soot loading.  Once again, the contrast between 1 g 
and 0 g flames is remarkable and the lack of agreement between experimental and computational 
results points to deficiencies in current models of soot formation. 
 
The raw image data from CLD Flame has been processed to provide quantitative data on 
temperature in both the non-sooting and sooting flames using thin-filament and soot pyrometry, 
respectively.  An absolute light calibration of the camera and optical train allows further 
quantification of CH chemiluminescence in weak flames, as well as soot volume fraction in the 
case of sooting flames.  The flow conditions are matched in the 1 g and 0 g datasets, and in both 
cases, detailed near-field velocity measurements have been made.  These boundary conditions 
are critical as input to computational models wishing to compare experimental and predicted 
results. 
 
In addition to the raw data from 1 g and 0 g flames, processed data in the form of computer-
readable data files as well as final figures have been uploaded to the NASA website.  Examples of 
the more than 14 GBytes of data organized on the NASA website include the following: 
 
• 
Microgravity Testpoint Summaries 
• 
Normal Gravity Testpoint Summaries 
• 
Flight Burner Velocity Profiles 
• 
Ground Copy Burner Velocity Profiles

Appendix B. 30-Day Operational Accomplishments Report for ISS 
Increments 53-56 
15 Nov. 2018 
30-day Operational Accomplishments Report  
… for International Space Station (ISS) Increments 53-56 
This CLD Flame report covers operations in four increments, not just the 55 and 56 pair. 
 
ACME 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments 
CLD Flame 
Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame 
CLD Flame is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, which 
uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels in the 
ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). 
 
Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project 
Scientist, who is the primary contact for CLD Flame and ACME information. 
 
 
 
Principal Investigator (PI): 
Prof. Marshall B. Long, Yale University, New Haven, CT 
Co-Investigator (Co-I): 
Prof. Mitchell D. Smooke, Yale University, New Haven, CT 
PI team member: 
 
Dr. Jesse A. Tinajero, Jr., Yale University, New Haven, CT 
Lead collaborator: 
Prof. Sergey Minaev, Far Eastern Federal University, Vladivostok, 
Russia 
Project Scientist (PS):  
Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH 
PS team member: 
Dr. Uday G. Hegde, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, 
OH 
 
 
 
I.  Introduction 
The Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is conducted in the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via 
Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  In this experiment, the flame - burning a gaseous fuel 
- is surrounded by air flowing in the same direction as the fuel.  More specifically, the gaseous 
fuel flows from an inner tube which is centered within a much larger outer tube, where a 21/79 
mixture of oxygen and nitrogen (on a volume basis) flows from the annulus.  The testing is 
generally conducted where the fuel and velocities are matched.  Measurements are made of 
flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and stability.  Conducting the 
tests in microgravity allows for great simplifications in the analysis, enabling new understanding

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
42 
 
and the development of more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for use on 
Earth. 
 
The overall goal is to improve our understanding of the physical and chemical processes 
controlling diffusion (i.e., non-premixed) flame structure and lifting phenomena (i.e., 
stabilization) and to provide for rigorous testing of numerical models, including thermal 
radiation, soot formation, and detailed chemical kinetics.  Such understanding allows for detailed 
computational predictions, e.g., of pollutant formation, and enables the improvement of 
combustion efficiency and reduction of pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion. 
 
Research conducted in microgravity has revealed that our current predictive ability is significantly 
lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute 
flames that are near extinction. The general goal of the CLD Flame experiment is to extend the 
range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally 
verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels.  The dependence of normal coflow 
flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution is carefully examined for flames at both very dilute 
and highly sooting conditions.  Measurements are made of the structure of methane and 
ethylene flames in an air coflow, where the fuels are often diluted with nitrogen. Lifted flames 
are used as the basis for the research to avoid flame dependence on heat loss to the burner. The 
results of this experiment are directly applicable to practical combustion issues such as turbulent 
combustion, ignition, flame stability, and more. 
 
In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational 
models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, CLD Flame has the following objectives: 
A. Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as 
a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off 
heights, temperatures and extinction limits. 
B. Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a 
function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas 
temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, 
and soot volume fractions. 
 
The experiment characterizes the structure of the flame, especially its base (i.e., stabilizing 
region), from attached through lifted conditions as a function of the fuel (including nitrogen 
dilution) and flow conditions. The velocity limits where the flame detaches from the burner and 
later extinguishes are similarly identified as a function of the fuel.  An understanding of lifting 
and lifted behavior is valuable, because of the importance of flame stability to the safe operation 
of practical combustion systems. 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., 
gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  Length 
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.  
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
43 
 
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger 
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in 
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot 
free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and 
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  With these advantages, microgravity 
testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the 
gravitational environment of the combustion application. 
 
A precursor to the CLD Flame experiment was carried out during Expedition 30 in early 2012, 
namely the Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE).  The SLICE tests were conducted 
in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using the hardware from the Smoke Point In Coflow 
Experiment (SPICE).  The SPICE hardware was based on the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) 
investigation which was conducted in the Middeck Glovebox (MGBX) on STS-87 in 1997.  The ELF, 
SPICE, and SLICE investigated coflow flames by placement of a gas-jet burner within a small fan-
driven flow duct open to the glovebox facility.  Meanwhile, the CLD Flame experiment is carried 
out with a coflow burner within a sealed 100-liter chamber, with a coflow of compressed gas. 
 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
  
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
CLD Flame and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS 
crew.  The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  The 
most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) 
and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it may alternately 
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry 
stream.  For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or 
soot limit.  This was not done during Increments 53-56, where the console commanding 
during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed (in the analog 
ops video) that the flame had extinguished. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
44 
 
 
III.  Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
A total of 292 flames were ignited in two rounds of on-orbit testing, with 130 and 162 
respectively in the first and second rounds of the CLD Flame experiment.  Neglecting 
hardware set-up and engineering preparation, the first round took place from Nov. 2017 
to Feb. 2018, i.e., in Increments 53 and 54.  ACME testing subsequently shifted to the 
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment, and 
afterward returned for a  second round of CLD Flame tests, which took place from May to 
September 2018, i.e., during Increments 55 and 56.  The ‘interruption’ in the CLD Flame 
testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the 
initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize 
its scientific outcome. 
 
CLD Flame does not have subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are 
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  Both 
are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) 
is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the 
absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because 
of its carbon double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel and fuel 
mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel and 
nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched with 
methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a 
volume basis).  Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 
50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  But the ACME 
hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing 
for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.  In all cases, 
the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  
 
There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for CLD Flame, where all of the ISS results 
are electronically transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all currently 
planned ACME experiments. 
 
A summary log of the flames ignited for the CLD Flame experiment during Increments 53-
56, including a limited overview of the test conditions, is found on the next page in Table 
1.
