items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
46 
 
Pre-flight and post-flight activities are generally not addressed in this report. 
 
B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
1. Mission anomalies  
The primary hard drive for the CIR’s IPSU-G Image Processing and Storage Unit - for 
Gigabit Ethernet (GigE) cameras – failed to boot on April 27, 2018 (18117).  For ACME 
experiments, the IPSU-G is used for two key cameras, the ACME color digital ‘data’ 
camera (i.e., DataCam) and the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera, 
which is used for CLD Flame with a narrow bandpass filter to image CH* 
chemiluminesence.  Use of the IPSU-G was recovered by astronaut Scott Tingle on 
May 7 (18127) by the removal of that primary drive.  While this occurred during E-
FIELD Flames testing, the removed drive was reinstalled on Aug. 14 (18226) by 
astronaut Ricky Arnold.  Although the hard drive was installed in the secondary 
position, the IPSU-G surprisingly again became unusable.  Therefore, it was removed 
on Aug. 22 (18234) by astronaut Alex Gerst, returning it to use, albeit without the 
intended storage capacity. 
 
Flame testing was prevented on June 21 (18172) because the Mass Flow Controllers 
(MFCs) on the ACME insert were inoperable due to a cable mating issue, where the 
chamber insert had been temporarily removed by astronaut Ricky Arnold for burner 
cleaning two days earlier, on June 19 (18170).  The cable mating was corrected by 
Arnold on June 25 (18176). 
 
The CIR’s IPSU-1 Image Processing and Storage Unit, which is used with the High Bit-
Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera and the collimated illumination package, was 
only intermittently operable in Sept. 2018, at the end of CLD Flame’s second round.  
Those capabilities were not seen as critical for CLD Flame, so the testing continued 
unabated.  It was not functioning on Sept. 6 (18249) or Sept. 10 (18253) but did work 
on Sept. 14 (18257).  It was later determined to be an issue with a cable connection, 
which was corrected by astronaut Alex Gerst on Oct. 22 (18295) when he was 
conducting other ACME tasks. 
 
2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data   
CLD Flame tests sometimes automatically abort (due to the controlling software 
script), where that is typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter.  As a 
result, there is little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt.   The aborts 
normally occur because of communication issues with IPSU-1.  These are infrequent, 
but there are some days when tests abort repeatedly.  
 
Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite.  The first test of 
the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been 
sufficiently primed.  Ignition is sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the 
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of 
the igniter glow rather than a flame.  As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
47 
 
is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite.  
This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* 
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module.  The OH* 
chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited 
flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible 
spectrum.  However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to 
false ignition detection. 
 
Ignition failure repeatedly occurred in early testing, where it was determined in 
December 2017 that the igniter arm was not properly aligned with the burner.  This 
was corrected by astronaut Joe Acaba with the help of Mark Vande Hei on Jan. 5, 2018 
(18005).  The alignment helped enable the ignition of 57 flames that month in contrast 
to the 15 and 11 flames ignited in November and December 2017, respectively. 
 
While not an anomaly, the hot-wire igniter tips do degrade with repeated use and 
sometimes fail.  That occurred twice during the first round of CLD Flame testing, 
where the failures were discovered on Nov. 29, 2017 (17333) and Feb. 15, 2018 
(18046).  Those failures prevented success with flame testing on both of those days, 
so as a result they are not listed in Table 1.  The failed igniter tips were replaced by 
astronauts Randy Bresnik and Scott Tingle on Dec. 6, 2017 (17340) and Feb. 20, 2018 
(18051), respectively.  Care is normally taken to limit igniter heating and to quickly 
withdraw it after ignition, where the igniter tip degrades significantly when it is 
energized while remaining within the flame.  The script running the tests is normally 
set to automatically retract the igniter when ignition is detected (as previously 
discussed).   Furthermore, the igniter tip is proactively replaced on a periodic basis, 
when the crew are making other changes on the ACME chamber insert.  As a result, 
no additional ACME igniter tips have failed thus far. 
 
ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and 
synthetic air (i.e., 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen, on a volume basis) have 
unfortunately not always performed adequately.  The MFC used for the ‘air’ coflow 
behaves as if it is sticking in a few places, where the flow rate won’t linearly ramp 
when commanded.  It tends to stick in some places and then abruptly overshoot 
where that has sometimes been seen to extinguish the flame.  Furthermore, the fuel 
and especially nitrogen flows sometimes oscillate.  Adjustments are often then made 
to (1) the settings that control when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-
Derivative (PID) settings.  Adjustments are often then made to the settings that 
control when the valves open and of the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) 
settings.  This activity has involved significant testing, separate from flame tests, and 
has taken place on 17333, 17334, 17347, 17354, 18008, 18022, 18038, 18046, 18143, 
and 18241.  In this regard, there are an assortment of MFCs with different flow ranges 
for each of the three gases.  While the MFC tuning has been beneficial in some cases, 
it has not eliminated all gas flow problems.  It was seen that nitrogen oscillations tend 
to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow was implemented so that the oscillations

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
48 
 
would typically end before the flame measurements.  That approach has been 
partially successful and was introduced between CLD Flame’s first and second rounds.  
Later, a procedure of re-zeroing the MFCs prior to each test was also implemented, 
but that didn’t occur until after CLD Flame’s second round.  A replacement MFC for 
the ‘air’ coflow is being prepared for spaceflight, where a limited third round of CLD 
Flame testing is being planned to accomplish the extinction limit objective.  
 
The first round of E-FIELD Flames tests were conducted from March to May 2018 with 
the same coflow burner used by the CLD Flame experiment.  The final day of testing 
was conducted with highly sooty ethylene flames and a positively charged mesh, 
which tends to push the flame down toward the burner.  A significant amount of soot 
deposited on the burner, both on the inner tube from which the fuel issues as well as 
the honeycomb in the burner annulus from which the air flows.  The extent of the 
soot wasn’t appreciated until CLD Flame testing with flames resumed on May 25 
(18145).  Additional evaluation tests were performed on May 31 (18151), and the 
decision was made to have the crew clean the soot from the burner because it was 
clear that the gas flow from the burner was affected by the soot buildup.  A cleaning 
procedure was developed, approved, and carried out by astronaut Ricky Arnold on 
June 19 (18170).  The cleaned burner was imaged with the CIR cameras on June 21 
(18172), but the evaluation testing was deferred because of a cable mating issue.  The 
cable mating was corrected by Arnold on June 25 (18176) and the evaluation testing 
of the cleaned burner was conducted on the following day, June 26 (18177).  Regular 
flame testing in the second round finally commenced on July 5 (18186), six weeks after 
the soot accumulation was identified as an issue.  However, useful scientific results 
were obtained on the June 26 evaluation day, so the burner cleaning effectively led 
to a 1-month delay. 
 
C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The number of flames ignited far exceeds the originally planned tests that were specified 
as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD).  In contrast, 
to the 82 CLD Flame tests identified as required in the ISRD, 292 flames were ignited in 
Increments 53-56 for the CLD Flame experiment.  In other words, 250% more flames were 
ignited than had been planned. 
 
The breadth of fuel concentrations tests was also much greater than those originally 
planned, i.e., were required in the ACME ISRD.  The required methane tests were limited 
to low fuel concentrations (on a volume basis, with a balance of nitrogen) of 15%, 20%, 
and 30% and high concentrations of 80%, 90%, and 100%.  Methane concentrations 
between 30% and 80% were specified as desired or highly desired.  While tests were 
conducted at required concentrations, they were also conducted at intermediate 
concentrations, e.g., 40% and 50% methane.  Meanwhile, the required ethylene tests 
were at concentrations (again on a volume basis, with a balance of nitrogen) of only 10%, 
15%, 20%, and 50%.  Tests were conducted at those four concentrations, at intermediate 
concentrations between 20% and 50% (e.g., 30% and 40%), and at higher concentrations,

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
49 
 
e.g., 60%, 80%, and 100%.  While tests with 20% and 30% ethylene were specified as 
desired, there were originally no plans for tests with ethylene concentrations greater than 
50%.  Nonetheless, a large number of tests were conducted at those conditions. 
 
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not available for all tests.  As 
discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 ceased to work during the second round of testing, 
preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination package.  
Those are not critical for CLD Flame, so tests continued without their use. 
 
Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is 
done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be 
managed per test day.  Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice 
some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.  
This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing 
within the project constraints. 
 
Preliminary tests with flames are sometimes conducted on days during testing and tuning 
(i.e., adjustment) of mass flow controllers, where the recorded image data is typically 
limited to just the analog operations (ops) camera, i.e., which is downlinked in near real 
time.  The six flames ignited on Aug. 29, 2018 (18241) are an example of such testing.  
These tests are conducted to check flow performance, verify ignition parameters, etc.   In 
other words, they are conducted to gain basic information to prepare for subsequent 
tests. 
 
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware.  But neglecting that 
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually 
become ‘hot’ over time.  While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, 
they are a degradation of the image quality. 
 
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there 
is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available 
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).  In this regard, 
note that the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is 
equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS).  
 
Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has 
been secured and CLD Flame is considered to be highly successful with the exception of 
the objective to determine extinction limits. 
 
D. Status of Data Analysis 
The CLD Flame group and the ops team at GRC successfully obtained unique data sets for 
non-premixed methane/air and ethylene/air coflow flames in microgravity. The data sets 
include a wide range of flow conditions varying fuel mixture velocities, coflow velocities, 
and fuel mixture concentrations. From these measurements it will be possible to obtain

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
50 
 
flame temperatures and ACME data camera light calibration data from thin filament 
pyrometry (TFP), as well as CH* mole fractions, soot temperatures, and soot volume 
fractions. Preliminary results have been obtained from these measurements and have 
been presented at conferences throughout the year. However, much of these preliminary 
results are still being verified since it is first necessary to analyze the data set as a whole 
to assess the ACME data camera performance over the 11 months of CLD Flame testing 
and to confirm the absolute light calibration. 
 
The CLD Flame group is looking forward to a third round of testing where our main focus 
will be to obtain trusted data on flame extinction limits of microgravity flames. Previous 
attempts at testing extinction limits were found to be undependable due to poor 
performance of mass flow controllers during the dilution stages. Light calibration 
measurements using the fiber array would also be necessary for these extinction limit 
measurements as well as further verification of the ACME data camera’s performance and 
light calibration. 
 
Aside from the ISS flight data, steps have been taken to produce ground-based equivalent 
data for direct comparison of the effect of gravity on flame structure, stability, 
temperature, extinction limits, and sooting characteristics. This will be done using the 
ground-based copy of ACME’s coflow burner and a Prosilica camera of the same model as 
the ACME data camera. Steps are also being made to begin work on the numerical 
simulation of the microgravity study. 
 
E. Preliminary Research Findings 
Due to the importance of fiber measurements for analyzing the ACME data camera’s 
performance and being the source of light calibration for quantitative measurements, our 
initial focus has been on fiber test points. For some of our weak flames with low overall 
intensity, images were obtained with the maximum available lens aperture. For these 
cases, a slight defocusing of the fiber images was used to ensure that the fiber intensity 
was recorded in all three color channels. For highly sooting (hence highly luminous 
flames) a smaller aperture (higher f-number) was used, resulting in a large depth of field. 
For fiber images with these settings, defocusing the image was not feasible, and a method 
for dealing with data where the fiber image is smaller than the camera’s pixel size was 
needed. In these cases, the fiber vanishes from the red and blue channels as the fiber 
sweeps through the flame due to the Bayer color filter array structure of the camera 
sensor. To solve this problem, a combination of color ratio and intensity ratio pyrometry 
on images demosaiced by binning 2x2 pixel blocks was used.  
 
For the series of fiber images obtained during a fiber sweep, the camera signals of the 
green and red channels were combined into two composite single-color images. Color 
ratio pyrometry was then used to calculate the 2D temperature profile. Fig. 1(a) shows a 
color ratio temperature map obtained from a sweep where the fiber is defocused enough 
to provide reasonable color ratio temperature measurements. However, using the same 
approach on data from highly focused images gives the result shown in Fig. 2(a). Here,

where the red signal dropped out. By considering only regions where both the red and 
green channels have locally large signals, it is possible to obtain a limited set of valid color-
ratio temperatures. These reference temperatures, in turn, can be used with the signal 
levels of the green channel to generate an intensity ratio temperature lookup table. The 
improved temperature map is then obtained using the intensity ratio lookup table to get

30 March 2022 
57 
 
Appendix C. 30-Day Operational Accomplishments Report for ISS 
Increment 64 
25 June 2021 
30-day Operational Accomplishments Report  
… for International Space Station (ISS) Increment 64 
 
ACME 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments 
CLD Flame 
Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame 
CLD Flame is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, which 
uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels in the 
ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  The investigation was carried out in three separate 
rounds, where the rounds were respectively conducted during Increments 53-54, 55-56, and 64.   
The third round was limited in scope and was carried out with a replacement 20-slpm mass flow 
controller for the oxidizer coflow to make up for the poor coflow performance in the first two 
rounds.  While this report was prepared for Increment 64, it comprehensively addresses the 
operations in all five increments. 
 
Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project 
Scientist, who is the primary contact for CLD Flame and ACME information. 
 
 
 
Principal Investigator (PI): 
Prof. Marshall B. Long, Yale University, New Haven, CT 
Co-Investigator (Co-I): 
Prof. Mitchell D. Smooke, Yale University, New Haven, CT 
PI team member: 
 
Dr. Jesse A. Tinajero, Jr., Yale University, New Haven, CT 
Lead collaborator: 
Prof. Sergey Minaev, Far Eastern Federal University, Vladivostok, 
Russia 
Project Scientist (PS):  
Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH 
PS team member: 
Dr. Uday G. Hegde, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, 
OH 
 
 
 
I.  Introduction 
The Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is conducted in the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via 
Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  In this experiment, the flame - burning a gaseous fuel 
- is surrounded by air flowing in the same direction as the fuel.  More specifically, the gaseous 
fuel flows from an inner tube which is centered within a much larger outer tube, where a 21/79 
mixture of oxygen and nitrogen (on a volume basis) flows from the annulus.  The testing is

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
58 
 
generally conducted where the fuel and velocities are matched.  Measurements are made of 
flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and stability.  Conducting the 
tests in microgravity allows for great simplifications in the analysis, enabling new understanding 
and the development of more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for use on 
Earth. 
 
The overall goal is to improve our understanding of the physical and chemical processes 
controlling diffusion (i.e., non-premixed) flame structure and lifting phenomena (i.e., 
stabilization) and to provide for rigorous testing of numerical models, including thermal 
radiation, soot formation, and detailed chemical kinetics.  Such understanding allows for detailed 
computational predictions, e.g., of pollutant formation, and enables the improvement of 
combustion efficiency and reduction of pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion. 
 
Research conducted in microgravity has revealed that our current predictive ability is significantly 
lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute 
flames that are near extinction. The general goal of the CLD Flame experiment is to extend the 
range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally 
verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels.  The dependence of normal coflow 
flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution is carefully examined for flames at both very dilute 
and highly sooting conditions.  Measurements are made of the structure of methane and 
ethylene flames in an air coflow, where the fuels are often diluted with nitrogen. Lifted flames 
are used as the basis for the research to avoid flame dependence on heat loss to the burner. The 
results of this experiment are directly applicable to practical combustion issues such as turbulent 
combustion, ignition, flame stability, and more. 
 
In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational 
models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, CLD Flame has the following objectives: 
A. Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as 
a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off 
heights, temperatures and extinction limits. 
B. Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a 
function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas 
temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, 
and soot volume fractions. 
 
The experiment characterizes the structure of the flame, especially its base (i.e., stabilizing 
region), from attached through lifted conditions as a function of the fuel (including nitrogen 
dilution) and flow conditions. The velocity limits where the flame detaches from the burner and 
later extinguishes are similarly identified as a function of the fuel.  An understanding of lifting 
and lifted behavior is valuable, because of the importance of flame stability to the safe operation 
of practical combustion systems. 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e.,

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
59 
 
gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  Length 
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.  
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be 
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger 
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in 
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot 
free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and 
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  With these advantages, microgravity 
testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the 
gravitational environment of the combustion application. 
 
A precursor to the CLD Flame experiment was carried out during Expedition 30 in early 2012, 
namely the Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE).  The SLICE tests were conducted 
in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using the hardware from the Smoke Point In Coflow 
Experiment (SPICE).  The SPICE hardware was based on the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) 
investigation which was conducted in the Middeck Glovebox (MGBX) on STS-87 in 1997.  The ELF, 
SPICE, and SLICE experiments investigated coflow flames by placement of a gas-jet burner within 
a small fan-driven flow duct open to the glovebox facility.  Meanwhile, the CLD Flame experiment 
is carried out with a coflow burner within a sealed 100-liter chamber, with a coflow of 
compressed gas. 
 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
  
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
CLD Flame and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS 
crew.  The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  The 
most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) 
and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it may alternately 
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry 
stream.  For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or 
soot limit.  This was not done during Increments 53-56, where the console commanding 
during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed (in the analog 
ops video) that the flame had extinguished. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment.

ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
60 
 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. 
  
Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
Neglecting hardware set-up and engineering preparation, the first round took place from 
Nov. 2017 to Feb. 2018, during Increments 53-54, when 130 methane flames were 
ignited.  ACME testing subsequently shifted to the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar 
Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment, and afterward returned for a  second 
round of CLD Flame tests, which took place from May to September 2018, during 
Increments 55-56, when 162 ethylene flames were ignited.  The ‘interruption’ in the CLD 
Flame testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review 
the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to 
maximize its scientific outcome. 
 
Poor performance in ramping the oxidizer coflow during early testing inhibited 
determination of extinction limits.  The decision was made to launch a replacement Mass 
Flow Controller (MFC) and conduct a limited third round of tests to address that 
shortcoming.  The third round with the replacement MFC was conducted in Feb.-March 
2021, during Increment 64, when 52 ethylene and methane flames were ignited.  As a 
result, a total of 344 flames were ignited during the three rounds and five increments. 
 
CLD Flame does not have subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are 
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  Both 
are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) 
is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the 
absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because 
of its carbon double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel and fuel 
mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel and 
nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched with 
methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a 
volume basis).  Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 
50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  But the ACME 
hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing 
for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.  In all cases, 
the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  
 
There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for CLD Flame, where all of the ISS results 
are electronically transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all currently 
planned ACME experiments.

B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
1. Mission anomalies  
The primary hard drive for the CIR’s IPSU-G Image Processing and Storage Unit - for 
Gigabit Ethernet (GigE) cameras – failed to boot on 27 April 2018 (18117).  For ACME 
experiments, the IPSU-G is used for two key cameras, the ACME color digital ‘data’ 
camera (i.e., DataCam) and the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera, 
which is used for CLD Flame with a narrow bandpass filter to image CH* 
chemiluminesence.  Use of the IPSU-G was recovered by astronaut Scott Tingle on 7 
May 2018 (18127) by the removal of that primary drive.  While this occurred during 
E-FIELD Flames testing, the removed drive was reinstalled on 14 Aug. 2018 (18226) by 
astronaut Ricky Arnold.  Although the hard drive was installed in the secondary 
position, the IPSU-G surprisingly again became unusable.  Therefore, it was removed 
on 22 Aug. 2018 (18234) by astronaut Alex Gerst, returning it to use, albeit without 
the intended storage capacity. 
 
Flame testing was prevented on 21 June 2018 (18172) because the Mass Flow 
Controllers (MFCs) on the ACME insert were inoperable due to a cable mating issue, 
where the chamber insert had been temporarily removed by astronaut Ricky Arnold 
for burner cleaning two days earlier, on 19 June 2018 (18170).  The cable mating was 
corrected by Arnold on 25 June 2018 (18176).

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
63 
 
The CIR’s IPSU-1 Image Processing and Storage Unit, which is used with the High Bit-
Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera and the collimated illumination package, was 
only intermittently operable in Sept. 2018, at the end of CLD Flame’s second round.  
Those capabilities were not seen as critical for CLD Flame, so the testing continued 
unabated.  It was not functioning on 6 Sept. (18249) or 10 Sept. (18253) but did work 
on 14 Sept. (18257).  It was later determined to be an issue with a cable connection, 
which was corrected by astronaut Alex Gerst on 22 Oct. 2018 (18295) when he was 
conducting other ACME tasks.  In round 3 testing, the HiBMs camera, illumination 
package, and IPSU-1 were not even used which is an indication of their limited value 
to the investigation. 
 
During Increment 64, the slow leak of argon carrier gas made the CIR’s Gas 
Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) unavailable for measurements 
during CLD Flame’s third round.  As a result of the leak, the bottle valves for all of the 
instrument’s gas bottles were closed on 29 Dec. 2020 (GMT 364).  However, these 
measurements were not planned for CLD Flame, so that not a loss to the investigation.  
 
2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data   
CLD Flame tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the controlling software 
script), where that is typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter.  As a 
result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt.   The aborts 
normally occurred because of communication issues with IPSU-1.  These are 
infrequent, but there are some days when tests have aborted repeatedly.  
 
Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite.  The first test of 
the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been 
sufficiently primed.  Ignition is sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the 
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of 
the igniter glow rather than a flame.  As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter 
is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite.  
This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* 
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module.  The OH* 
chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited 
flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible 
spectrum.  However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to 
false ignition detection. 
 
Ignition failure repeatedly occurred in early testing, where it was determined in 
December 2017 that the igniter arm was not properly aligned with the burner.  This 
was corrected by astronaut Joe Acaba with the help of Mark Vande Hei on 5 Jan. 2018 
(18005).  The alignment helped enable the ignition of 57 flames that month in contrast 
to the 15 and 11 flames ignited in November and December 2017, respectively.

items.title: CLD_Flame_final_report_20220330.pdf
items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
64 
 
While not an anomaly, the hot-wire igniter tips do degrade with repeated use and 
sometimes fail.  That occurred, for example, twice during the first round of CLD Flame 
testing, where the failures were discovered on 29 Nov. 2017 (17333) and 15 Feb. 2018 
(18046).  Those failures prevented success with flame testing on both of those days, 
so as a result they are not listed in Table 1.  The failed igniter tips were replaced by 
astronauts Randy Bresnik and Scott Tingle on 6 Dec. 2017 (17340) and 20 Feb. 2018 
(18051), respectively.  Care is normally taken to limit igniter heating and to quickly 
withdraw it after ignition, where the igniter tip degrades significantly when it is 
energized while remaining within the flame.  The script running the tests is normally 
set to automatically retract the igniter when ignition is detected (as previously 
discussed).   Furthermore, the igniter tip is proactively replaced on a periodic basis, 
when the crew are making other changes on the ACME chamber insert. 
 
ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and 
synthetic air (i.e., 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen, on a volume basis) have 
unfortunately not always performed adequately.  The MFC initially used for the ‘air’ 
coflow behaved as if it momentary stuck in a few places, where the flow rate wouldn’t 
linearly ramp (with time) when commanded.  It tended to stick in some places and 
then abruptly overshoot where that has sometimes been seen to extinguish the flame.  
Furthermore, the fuel and especially nitrogen flows were sometimes found to 
oscillate.  Adjustments are often then made to (1) the settings that control when the 
MFC valves open and (2) their Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) settings.  This 
activity has involved significant testing, separate from flame tests, and has taken 
place, for example, on 17333, 17334, 17347, 17354, 18008, 18022, 18038, 18046, 
18143, and 18241.  In this regard, there are an assortment of MFCs with different flow 
ranges for each of the three gases.  While the MFC tuning has been beneficial in some 
cases, it has not eliminated all gas flow problems.  It was seen that nitrogen 
oscillations tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow was implemented so that 
the oscillations would typically end before the flame measurements.  That approach 
was partially successful and was introduced between CLD Flame’s first and second 
rounds.  Later, a procedure of re-zeroing the MFCs prior to each test was also 
implemented between CLD Flame’s second and third rounds. 
 
The first round of E-FIELD Flames tests were conducted from March to May 2018 with 
the same coflow burner used by the CLD Flame experiment.  The final day of testing 
was conducted with highly sooty ethylene flames and a positively charged mesh, 
which tends to push the flame down toward the burner.  A significant amount of soot 
deposited on the burner, both on the inner tube from which the fuel issues as well as 
the honeycomb in the burner annulus from which the air flows.  The extent of the 
soot wasn’t appreciated until CLD Flame testing with flames resumed on May 25 
(18145).  Additional evaluation tests were performed on May 31 (18151), and the 
decision was made to have the crew clean the soot from the burner because it was 
clear that the gas flow from the burner was affected by the soot buildup.  A cleaning 
procedure was developed, approved, and carried out by astronaut Ricky Arnold on 19

ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
65 
 
June 2018 (18170).  The cleaned burner was imaged with the CIR cameras on June 21 
(18172), but the evaluation testing was deferred because of a cable mating issue.  The 
cable mating was corrected by Arnold on June 25 (18176) and the evaluation testing 
of the cleaned burner was conducted on the following day, June 26 (18177).  Regular 
flame testing in the second round finally commenced on July 5 (18186), six weeks after 
the soot accumulation was identified as an issue.  However, useful scientific results 
were obtained on the June 26 evaluation day, so the burner cleaning effectively led 
to a 1-month delay. 
 
During Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) testing on 23 Dec. 2020, it was discovered that 
the lowest of the 14-micron silicon carbide fibers on the Thin Filament Pyrometry 
(TFP) fiber array had broken.  Recovery plans were developed and enacted on 18 Jan. 
2021 to remove the broken fragments from the harp-like array.  Unfortunately, the 
next fiber was broken during the delicate operations where the fibers are only spaced 
5 mm apart.  Although ACME does have alternate arrays, it also has months of 
remaining testing, so the decision was made to continue testing with only 3 fibers 
(instead of 5) for the final BRE testing and the subsequent CLD Flame tests.  This was 
viewed as a minor loss to CLD Flame given the small size of the experiment’s flames. 
 
As planned because of shortcomings discussed above, a replacement MFC for the 
oxidizer coflow was prepared, launched, and installed for the CLD Flame investigation 
on 3 Feb. 2021 (21034).  The replacement’s control of the flow rate was much better 
as was verified during MFC testing on the subsequent day.  
 
C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The number of flames ignited far exceeds the originally planned tests that were specified 
as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD).  In contrast, 
to the 82 CLD Flame tests identified as required in the ISRD, 344 flames were ignited for 
the CLD Flame experiment.  While not all of them provided useful data, 320% more flames 
were ignited than had been planned. 
 
The breadth of fuel concentrations tests was also much greater than those originally 
planned, i.e., were required in the ACME ISRD.  The required methane tests were limited 
to low fuel concentrations (on a volume basis, with a balance of nitrogen) of 15%, 20%, 
and 30% and high concentrations of 80%, 90%, and 100%.  Methane concentrations 
between 30% and 80% were specified as desired or highly desired.  While tests were 
conducted at required concentrations, they were also conducted at intermediate 
concentrations, e.g., 40% and 50% methane.  Meanwhile, the required ethylene tests 
were at concentrations (again on a volume basis, with a balance of nitrogen) of only 10%, 
15%, 20%, and 50% and during dynamic dilution toward even lower concentrations.  Tests 
were conducted at those four concentrations, at intermediate concentrations between 
20% and 50% (e.g., 30% and 40%), and at higher concentrations, e.g., 60%, 80%, and 
100%.  While tests with 20% and 30% ethylene were specified as desired, there were

items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
66 
 
originally no plans for tests with ethylene concentrations greater than 50%.  Nonetheless, 
a large number of tests were conducted at those conditions. 
 
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not available for all tests.  As 
discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 ceased to work during the second round of testing, 
preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination package.  
Those are not critical for CLD Flame, so tests continued without their use.  Similarly, the 
HiBMs camera and illumination package were not used during the round 3 testing.  
 
Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is 
done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be 
managed per test day.  Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice 
some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.  
This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing 
within the project constraints. 
 
Preliminary tests with flames are sometimes conducted on days during testing and tuning 
(i.e., adjustment) of mass flow controllers, where the recorded image data is typically 
limited to just the analog operations (ops) camera, i.e., which is downlinked in near real 
time.  The six flames ignited on 29 Aug. 2018 (18241) are an example of such testing.  
These tests are conducted to check flow performance, verify ignition parameters, etc.   In 
other words, they are conducted to gain basic information to prepare for subsequent 
tests. 
 
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware.  But neglecting that 
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually 
become ‘hot’ over time.  While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, 
they are a degradation of the image quality. 
 
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there 
is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available 
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).  Note that 
although the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is 
equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS) it was not utilized for CLD Flame 
(or any ACME) testing because of the crew time needed to enable and disable the 
isolation before and after testing. 
 
Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has 
been secured and CLD Flame, as a whole, is considered to be highly successful. 
 
D. Status of Data Analysis [prepared by the investigator team] 
The CLD Flame experiment produced a comprehensive data set of microgravity methane 
and ethylene flames over three rounds of testing.  Round one focused on methane flames 
while looking at the full range of dilution from pure fuel to near the dilution extinction

items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
67 
 
limit.  Round two targeted ethylene flames, also ranging in dilution from pure fuel to near 
the dilution extinction limit.  Round three focused on determining the dilution limits of 
both methane and ethylene flames which were not obtainable during rounds one and 
two because of MFC instability issues.  The improved gas delivery allowed the limits to be 
determined and allowed for stable flame measurements near these extinction limits. 
 
A substantial amount of effort has been made to evaluate the absolute light calibration 
method which is needed to perform quantitative flame measurements.  Because the light 
calibration was performed through thin filament pyrometry (TFP), improvements were 
made to the demosaicing procedures in order to optimize the light calibration test results.   
Improvements were also made to the algorithms for fixing hot pixels; hot pixels were a 
minor issue during rounds one and two but were significantly worse during round three. 
 
Quantitative measurements have been made on tests from all three rounds.  Light 
calibration and gas temperature measurements were obtained from 53 fiber tests.  Soot 
temperature and volume fraction measurements were obtained from 69 ethylene flames.  
Measurements of flame characteristics, such as flame heights, flame structures and lift-
off heights were made and analyzed for both sooty and non-sooty flames, including 39 
methane flames. Preliminary calculations of CH* mole fractions were performed on 19 
methane flames at fuel mixture concentrations between 30-50% CH4.  Dilution extinction 
limits were obtained for three flame conditions using methane and three conditions using 
ethylene.  
 
In parallel with the microgravity data, substantial efforts have been made on the normal 
gravity experimentation front, where many of the flame conditions were recreated on 
earth to determine the effects of gravity.  The measurements performed include flame 
temperature measurements using TFP, soot temperature and soot volume fractions of 
ethylene flames, and flame images to analyze flame characteristics. 
 
E. Preliminary Research Findings [prepared by the investigator team] 
The processing procedure for obtaining flame temperature measurements is summarized 
in Fig. 1.  An image of a heated SiC fiber taken during a space station fiber test is shown 
in Fig 1(a).  This is a single image taken from a series of images capturing a fiber sweeping 
through the center of the flame.  From the consecutive fiber images, a 2-D composite 
image is constructed and is shown in Fig. 1(b).  From this composite image, the 
temperature of the fiber is determined by performing color ratio pyrometry as seen in 
Fig. 1(c).  From these fiber temperatures, a light calibration is performed to determine the 
absolute light calibration constant.  Figure 2 shows the calibration results for this fiber 
test and shows an excellent fit to the pixel data and reasonably low deviations.

From the light calibration, reference parameters of signal and temperature could be 
obtained and used to perform intensity ratio pyrometry in order to get an improved 
signal-to-noise ratio fiber temperature measurement, as shown in Fig. 1(d).  The flame 
temperature measurement is obtained by applying a radiation correction to the fiber 
temperature results; see Fig. 1 (e).  The radiation correction uses an energy balance 
between radiation and convection at the surface of the fiber, while assuming conduction 
is negligible. 
 
Figure 3 shows telemetry data from a microgravity test to determine the dilution limits of 
a nitrogen-diluted methane flame.  The flame is ignited at 40% CH4 by volume and slowly 
diluted with excess nitrogen at constant velocity.  As identified by the telemetry data, the 
opening of the valve connected to the excess nitrogen MFC is delayed, which causes an 
unintentional drop in total fuel mixture velocity.  However, the valve eventually does 
open, and the conditions of fuel mixture gas flow fully recovers.  Sometime after the 
recovery, the flame extinction event occurs.  Assessment of the recovery determined that 
the initial drop in fuel mixture velocity did not affect the extinction event.  In all cases that 
were tested for methane flames diluted with nitrogen, the extinction event occurred

Figure 3. Telemetry data of a microgravity dilution limit test for a nitrogen-diluted 
methane flame at 40% CH4 by volume slowly diluted with excess nitrogen until extinction.  
The region enclosed in the dashed circle indicates an initial flow issue where the nitrogen 
MFC valve struggles to open at the start of the dilution ramping stage.  However, the MFC 
eventually recovers, and the dilution limit is determined. 
 
Stable flames in microgravity were achievable at a dilution of 30% CH4.  As a comparison, 
stable flames in normal gravity are unachievable at this dilution.  This demonstrates the 
extension of the dilution limits when buoyancy is not present.  Microgravity flames were 
stabilized at 30% and flame and fiber images were obtained.  Results from these tests are 
shown in Fig. 4.  The color flame images in these figures show the deconvoluted signal 
after applying an Abel inversion.  This reveals the internal structure of the flame. The lift-
off behavior of these very weak flames is also observed as a function of increasing gas 
velocity.  The flame temperatures were measured and will be important for the analysis 
when studying the stabilization mechanism that creates the lift-off behavior.

The contrast in stability behavior of microgravity flames vs normal gravity flames is shown 
in Fig. 6.  The lift-off behavior of normal gravity flames is more sensitive to increasing 
flowrate than the microgravity flames.  The normal gravity flames quickly lift-off and 
become very unstable.  Above 30 cm/s, stable flames were unachievable in normal 
gravity.  The microgravity flames, however, display increased stability due to the absence 
of a buoyancy-driven gas acceleration.  The improved stability results in flame conditions 
that were unobtainable in normal gravity and stabilization at higher lift-off locations.

Microgravity flames were observed to grow taller as a function of fuel concentration 
compared to normal gravity flames.  The pure fuel condition in Fig. 7(d) and 8(d) showed 
a height difference of nearly 1 cm.  Classic flame models, such as the Burke and Schumann 
flame model, have predicted that flame heights should be unaffected by gravity, however, 
these models have not carefully accounted for temperature dependent transport 
properties.  
 
Because the lack of buoyancy increases residence times, the soot loads in microgravity 
are higher, and thus, thermal radiative energy losses are higher in microgravity. The 
flames in microgravity are measured to have soot loads a factor of five to eight times 
higher in microgravity than in normal gravity. This results in the microgravity flames 
decreasing in temperature more rapidly as the flames grow in volume and as soot loads 
increase.  
 
The measured soot temperatures were used to estimate transport properties, which were 
then applied to a nondimensional analysis of flame heights proposed by Lin and Faeth 
(AIAA J. 37, 759–765, 1999).  The results are shown in Fig. 9.  An empirical constant, Cf, is 
determined through a linear-least-squares fit with the experimental data, where a value 
of Cf equal to unity represents a perfect fit to the theoretical flame model.  This figure 
demonstrates that when accounting for temperature dependent transport properties, 
the flame heights of microgravity and normal gravity flames can be effectively described 
by this simple flame model, since Cf is nearly unity in both cases.

items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
82 
 
Week 12: Nov. 10-16 
On GMT 319, we successfully began the first ACME experiment! ACME, or Advanced Combustion via 
Microgravity Experiments, is a set of five independent studies of gaseous flames to be performed in CIR. 
We performed ten successful ACME CLD (Coflow Laminar Diffusion) Flame test points. CLD Flame uses a 
burner that can simultaneously flow air and a gaseous fuel mixture. In a combustion chamber 
environment of air, the GMT 319 tests used various flow conditions with a 40% methane fuel mixture 
diluted with nitrogen. 
 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG 
For this test point, the flow rate of the gaseous fuel was held steady, while the flow of air started 
at zero and was gradually increased throughout the test. This increase in the air flow causes the 
flame to detach and lift away from the burner. The flame’s shape changes dramatically as it 
detaches, where the flame becomes increasingly premixed and then disk-shaped.  
 
CLD Flame studies lifted flames because they are advantageous for computational modeling. The 
general goal of CLD Flame is to extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately 
predicted, especially under conditions where the flame is sooty or could become unstable. The 
results will be directly applicable to practical combustion issues such as turbulent combustion, 
ignition, flame stability, and more. 
 
Week 13: Nov. 17-23 
On GMT 324, we performed ACME CLD Flame (Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame) test points to identify 
conditions under which ignition could be achieved. We performed five successful test points in which the 
fuel and air velocities increased to lift the flame from the burner. CLD Flame studies lifted flames because 
they are advantageous for computational modeling. 
 
 
Example monochrome image of a lifted disk-shaped flame from GMT 324, where the gas velocities were 
such that combustion could not be sustained at the burner despite the presence of both air and methane 
(the primary component of natural gas).

On GMT 356, we performed ACME CLD Flame (Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame) test points. Typically in a 
CLD Flame test, the flame is lifted from the burner by increasing the fuel and air flow velocities through 
the burner. However, these tests reduced the velocities after a lifted flame was established. Rather than 
settling on the burner and increasing in size, the lifted flame remained small and became very faint at the 
end of the tests. This flame behavior—when ramping the flow velocities downward—is significantly 
different than when ramping them upward.

1. Introduction 
The purpose of this report is to describe the data acquired for ACME’s CLD Flame experiment to facilitate 
its analysis.  The data is all digital, where the fuel was gaseous and there was no collection of soot or the 
combustion gases.  For each test, the key data consists of image files and a file with the non-imaging 
measurements.  Additional files such as chamber calculator output, camera metadata, and operational 
logs provide information that can support the analysis. 
 
It is recommended that readers interested in analyzing the CLD Flame data begin by familiarizing 
themselves with the hardware and instrumentation, either through the overview in the CLD Flame Final 
Report or the more comprehensive description found in the ACME Engineering Implementation 
document. 
 
Those seeking to analyze the data should next review this document.  To interpret the non-imaging data, 
it is suggested that a sample data file be opened, named for example 21050R1_data.csv, which has 
comma-separated values and can be opened with spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel.  The data 
is in raw voltages, where conversion to engineering units requires study of ACME’s Software Interface 
Design Description, i.e., ACME-DOC-010 (where the latest version at the time of this writing is revision D).

The BRE and Cool Flames radiometer characterization reports are not applicable to CLD Flame because 
the experiment didn’t use that instrumentation.  Instead, CLD Flame made use of the standard 
radiometers addressed in ACME-RPT-011. 
 
Also note that the Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) was not used during CLD Flame 
testing, and as such interpretation of its data is not addressed herein. 
 
 
2. CLD Flame Overview 
This text is the “Overview” from the ACME/CLD Flame Final Report, which also provides descriptions of the 
science, preliminary results, and more.  It is strongly suggested that it be reviewed by those interested in 
analyzing the CLD Flame data. 
 
The Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is one of six independent experiments that 
make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are 
conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). 
 
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) and Co-Investigator are respectively Profs. Marshall B. Long 
and Mitchell D. Smooke, who are both in the Department of Mechanical Engineering & Materials Science 
at Yale University.  The ISS research benefitted greatly from the work of Dr. Jesse Tinajero, who was a Yale 
postdoctoral researcher during the spaceflight operations, and Dr. Davide Giassi, who as a Yale doctoral 
student did important preparatory work.  
 
Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME 
including CLD Flame and the rest of the ACME investigations.  In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki 
Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist.  For 
ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam 
who are also with CWRU. 
 
The ISS operations for CLD Flame were conducted in three separate rounds of testing, where the rounds 
were respectively conducted during Increments 53-54, 55-56, and 64. The third round was limited in scope 
and was carried out with a replacement 20-slpm mass flow controller for the oxidizer coflow to make up 
for the poor coflow performance in the first two rounds. 
 
Note that there was a direct precursor to the CLD Flame investigation, namely the Structure & Liftoff In 
Combustion Experiment (SLICE), which was conducted in the ISS’ Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) 
during Expedition 30 in early 2012.  Prof. Long was the Principal Investigator, while Smooke, Takahashi, 
and Stocker were Co-Investigators.  For more information about SLICE, readers are encouraged to consult 
its final report.

items.text:
ACME/CLD Flame Data Interpretation 
 
25 Aug. 2023 
 
4 
 
3. Tests Conducted 
This text is an excerpt from the “Results” section of the ACME/CLD Flame – 30-Day Operation 
Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 64 (which is included in the ACME/Flame Design Final Report). 
 
Neglecting hardware set-up and engineering preparation, the first round took place from Nov. 2017 to 
Feb. 2018, during Increments 53-54, when 130 methane flames were ignited.  ACME testing subsequently 
shifted to the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment, and 
afterward returned for a second round of CLD Flame tests, which took place from May to September 2018, 
during Increments 55-56, when 162 ethylene flames were ignited.  The ‘interruption’ in the CLD Flame 
testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in 
detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. 
 
Poor performance in ramping the oxidizer coflow during early testing inhibited determination of 
extinction limits.  The decision was made to launch a replacement Mass Flow Controller (MFC) and 
conduct a limited third round of tests to address that shortcoming.  The third round with the replacement 
MFC was conducted in Feb.-March 2021, during Increment 64, when 52 ethylene and methane flames 
were ignited.  As a result, a total of 344 flames were ignited during the three rounds and five increments. 
 
CLD Flame does not have subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently 
conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  Both are simple hydrocarbon gases 
for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and 
tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene 
(C2H4), is highly sooting because of its carbon double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with 
pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel and 
nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched with methane 
concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  Similarly, 
bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 50%, and 100%, again with a balance of 
nitrogen (on a volume basis).  But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and 
nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel 
concentrations.  In all cases, the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  
 
There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for CLD Flame, where all of the ISS results are electronically 
transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all currently planned ACME experiments. 
 
A summary log of the flames ignited for the CLD Flame experiment during the three rounds (Increments 
53-56 and 64), including a limited overview of the test conditions, is found in Table 1.

(where any late-hour transition to the next day is neglected). 
2The columns labelled MFC identify the maximum flow rate of the specified ACME Mass 
Flow Controller (MFC) in slpm on a nitrogen basis. 
3Fuel conc. (as diluted with nitrogen on a volume basis) was varied between tests and 
sometimes during tests, where the listing here accounts for both.  However, it does not 
account for extinction that sometimes occurred before the flame fully reached the 
lowest concentration. 
4Flames ignited is the number ignited on that test day. 
 
Pre-flight and post-flight activities are generally not addressed in this report. 
 
 
4. Data Interpretation 
This key section provides (1) a general description of the raw experimental data and associated files and 
(2) guidance on data conversions, e.g., to engineering units.  Only limited guidance is provided for the 
processing of image data, with the important exception of the conversion of the ACME DataCam images 
from the raw Halcon object (HOBJ) format. 
 
A. Non-Imaging Data 
Data and files discussed in this section include the following: 
Data Output File 
Mass Flow Controller (MFC) Setpoint File 
Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data 
 
1. Data Output File 
The basic ACME non-imaging measurements for each test are together in a file described in 
Section 8.1 Data Output File on page 124 of Software Interface Design Description (ACME-
DOC-010 Rev D).  The test number is made up of the year (2-digts), day of year (3 digits), and 
test (a letter and single-digit number).  As such, the example, 21062D2 is test D2 conducted 
on the 62nd day of 2021.  But the test could also be early on the next (e.g., 63rd) day because 
the day portion of ACME test numbers is not changed when operations continue past 
midnight (whether GMT or Eastern) into the start of the next day. 
 
Tests numbers that only differ by the final digit (e.g., 21050D1, 21050D2, and 21050D3) are 
typically similar and occasionally identical, where the number is indicative of the variant or

aside, ACME tests are often not conducted in order and some planned tests are regularly not 
conducted at all.  The latter results in additional letter gaps if the tests from a day are sorted

The ACME MFCs are Hastings HFC-D-302 with default standard temperature and pressures 
(STP) of 0 Celsius and 760 torr for computations of volumetric flow or velocity.  It is very 
important to understand that slpm, i.e., standard liters per minute, is a measurement of the

may be helpful as a check in this regard.

3. Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data 
The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) in which the experiment was conducted, was equipped 
with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS), but it was not utilized for ACME testing because 
of the need for crew time to enable and disable the isolation (by respectively removing and 
installing alignment guides) on each test day.  However, the CIR was equipped with a 3-axis 
SAMS sensor head.  The acceleration archives, along with relevant documentation, are 
accessible from https://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/pims/home/, the home page for the Principal 
Investigator Microgravity Services (PIMS). 
 
The following guidance for the SAMS data was provided by Kenneth Hrovat (NASA Glenn):  In 
addition to the documentation and links from the PIMS home page, we introduce a few ways 
below to get started with exploring the CIR microgravity environment taking the perspective 
of SAMS measurements from within the rack. 
 
Roadmap Spectrograms 
To get a high-level, spectral roadmap view within two days after measurement, you can: 
a. Use your browser and start at this link: http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/roadmap 
b. In the upper left pane, you can navigate by GMT date to see a list of plots (PDF files) 
in the right pane for the GMT date of your choice.  We refer to these PDFs as roadmap

good way to look at patterns, structures and boundaries in both time and frequency 
for long time spans -- nominally, 8 hours per plot.  These spectrograms are mostly 
qualitative and crudely quantitative three-dimensional plots in that a color scale 
attempts to map power spectral density magnitude as a color for the 3rd dimension. 
NOTE: Ticking the Navigation Filter for “es05” in the bottom pane will then only 
highlight days in yellow in the upper left pane when the operations team powered on 
the SAMS sensor in the CIR to take measurements. 
c. You might want to navigate directly to a GMT day of interest for your science 
operations or run, but you can also browse day-by-day too in order to get some 
context comparing various 8-hour spans to get a feel for the environment under 
various conditions.

B. Image Files 
Image data and files discussed in this section are associated with the following cameras: 
Analog, operations (ops), internal camera 
ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera 
 
High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package 
 
The Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera is not addressed herein because it was not used 
for CLD Flame.  Of the ACME investigations, the LLL-UV camera was only used by the Structure 
and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) study. 
 
1. Analog, internal, operations (ops) camera  
This color analog camera is mounted on the ACME chamber insert, and as such is within the 
combustion chamber during testing and is sometimes referred to as the internal camera.  Its 
primary purpose is to support the operations, e.g., to visualize the burner and igniter, and as 
such is also often referred to as the operations or ops camera. 
 
The NTSC video (named for the National Television System Committee) from the ops camera 
is at 29.97 frames per second (fps) or nominally 30 fps.  It is not recorded on the space station 
but is streamed to the ground in near real time and is recorded on CIR consoles at the Glenn 
ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in a Transport Stream (TS) format using VLC Media 
Player, which can be freely downloaded from https://www.videolan.org/vlc/.  That software 
has a snapshot function allowing for convenient extraction of still images, e.g., for making 
measurements of flame dimensions. 
 
2. ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
ACME’s primary camera is a high-definition (1360 x 1024), 12-bit color camera mounted 
outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench.  It is equipped with a motorized lens with 
independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus.  It has a filter barrel with a fused silica 
window (for color imaging), a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, and bandpass filters for 
imaging CH* and CH2O (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence. 
 
It was characterized prior to launch to enable temperature measurements via soot pyrometry 
and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP), soot volume fraction, and quantitative determination of 
the CH* concentration. 
 
Soot temperatures can be determined from this camera’s images via techniques such as those

Images were normally downlinked within a week of the testing, but selected images were 
often downlinked during a test day.  Regardless, the images were downloaded in a wrapped 
Halcon object (HOBJ) format, which is not readily opened with typical image processing 
software.  The image data was made available in that raw format and later in a converted TIFF 
format, where the NASA conversion was carried out without each of the following: 
• 
color balancing (to avoid possible saturation as subsequently discussed)  
• 
dark frame subtraction 
• 
removal of hot spots from dead pixels (e.g., resulting from radiation damage)  
Furthermore, the NASA conversion employed a standard bilinear demosaicing process which 
is detrimental when determining temperature profiles via Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) as it 
will average pixels both on and off the glowing fibers.  The priority in the NASA conversion 
was to make the images more readily accessible, not to meet all needs. 
 
Most ACME investigators are processing the raw HOBJ files using the OMA2 software 
developed by Prof. Marshall Long (Yale U.), the lead for ACME’s CLD Flame experiment.   The 
OMA2 software is freely available in both Mac and cross-platform (Qt) versions, where the 
latter can be used with both PC and Linux operating systems.  A tutorial was prepared by Dr. 
Jesse Tinajero on the use of OMA2 to process ACME’s HOBJ image files, where it can be found 
at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RMtu3KEXNiI.  It has also been broken up and posted 
in three parts in which the image resolution may be better: 
 
Part 1 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdQHeQwokvY 
 
Part 2 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mua_8CfqhfM 
 
Part 3 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BGRqgbIxZL4 
 
The OMA2 read-hobj function was also rewritten by Tinajero as a Python function, where 
Python is an open source programming language that is easily obtainable for MacOS, Linux, 
and Windows operating systems.  The Python script to open the HOBJ files can be downloaded 
from https://github.com/mblong/hobjExample. A tutorial for this function may be found at 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4wbgWeJSilc. 
 
The HOBJ files can also be readily viewed and processed using ImageJ or its preloaded Fiji

However, imported DataCam images will be monochrome unless a Bayer filter (e.g., as 
described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayer_filter) is subsequently implemented.  It 
should be possible to install a plug-in to accomplish that color conversion.  As another option, 
Python and Matlab both have image demosaicing functions. 
 
To use the ACME DataCam for quantitative measurements other than dimensions, it is critical 
to avoid saturation, for example by using a camera gain of zero.  Another employed approach 
was to not use the camera’s white balance which by default multiplies the red and blue by 
1.41 and 1.68, respectively, because that could inadvertently lead to saturation.  Such 
multiplication can be done after the HOBJ file is converted and the colors demosaiced, where 
in OMA2 the white balancing is accomplished with the commands: 
*rgb 1.41 1 1.68 
clip 4095 
In summary, the white balance, if desired, needs to be done after the fact through software 
because the color balancing was at least generally not done with the hardware to avoid the 
risk of saturation.  
 
However, in carrying out color-ratio pyrometry calculations for the ISS data from ACME’s CLD 
Flame experiment, the investigators determined that the three color ratios (e.g., blue/red) 
didn’t result in the same temperature profile until the green channel was adjusted by 10%.  
This notably differs from the camera’s default of multiplication by 1 (i.e., no multiplication) 
for the green color plane. 
 
For Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP): “After rigorous testing, it was determined [by Tinajero and 
Long] that a modified version of the bilinear method could be used to optimize the conversion 
of raw fiber images to full resolution color images.  This modified version biases the linear 
interpolation along the length of the fiber.  This method combined with moderate use of 
defocusing was found to reduce artifacts created by standard demosaicing algorithms and 
was used in all of the fiber measurements described below.” 
Jesse Tinajero and Marshall Long. “Dilution Limits of Coflow Laminar Methane and 
Ethylene Flames in Microgravity Versus Normal Gravity,” 12th U.S. National Combustion 
Meeting, 24-26 May 2021. 
 
Note that the ACME images will be naturally dark because of the use of the 16-bit file format 
with 12-bit image data.  As such, adjustments to the image brightness will generally be 
necessary even if the images are not demosaiced.  Furthermore, cameras’ CCD arrays are 
susceptible to radiation damage while in orbit.  As a result, the images feature hot pixels which 
increased in number over the months and years in space.  As such, it will appear as if there is 
a star field within the combustion chamber.  Therefore, the images should ideally be 
processed to remove the bright outlying hot spots.  Radiation damage is also obvious in the 
ops camera imaging.

Although the DataCam was typically set for imaging at 30 fps, that is trumped by the exposure 
settings which were often long because of the dim nature of the microgravity flames.  As a 
result, the framing rate was typically far less.  Different exposures are often selected for 
different phases of the tests, e.g., prior to ignition and during the test, so the framing rate 
may not be consistent.  Bracketed imaging could also be employed, where a repeating 
sequence of different exposure durations is used to enable appropriate photography under 
uncertain or varying flame intensities.  Bracketing could also used to simultaneously 
accomplish multiple imaging objectives, e.g., to appropriately image both brightly glowing 
soot (or TFP fibers) as well as the much dimmer blue portion of the flame. 
 
In interpreting the image data, it may be helpful to check a test’s ACME DataCam metadata 
file, if available, e.g., to verify the exposure duration.  These files are in a comma-delimited 
(CSV) format and can be opened with spreadsheet software or alternately as a text file.  
Column headings are found in the first row of such files.

rate.  In this example case, the 0.1-s exposure time means that the framing rate (at the test’s 
start) was nominally 10 fps rather than the 30 indicated by FrameRate.  It is furthermore 
important to understand that the exposure time (and thus actual framing rate) was often 
varied during the test, where that could be seldom or often if bracketing was employed, i.e., 
where a repeated sequence of images was taken at different exposures.  
 
Unfortunately, it has been seen during bracketing that the reporting of exposure times in the 
metadata files is, or at least can be, offset.  Therefore, it is important to identify the brightest

bracketed exposure times.  
 
The parameter files, with names like ‘as run21062M1.txt,’ control the DataCam exposures 
and much more.  However, these files have not always saved as intended and were sometimes 
corrected after the fact.  In contrast, the text-file logs, with names such as 2021-03-03_23-
22_ACME.log, are a reliable source for the parameters which specified the imaging settings 
and much more.  There is normally a single file of this type for each test day (but sometimes 
more) and the parameters are a small fraction of the automated log content, but one can 
search for a test by its number.  Log files like this are discussed in section 4.C.5 of this 
document. 
 
Due to the use of a turning mirror, the DataCam images should be flipped vertically if upright 
images are desired, i.e., where the burner is at the bottom and the flame extends upward.  In 
this regard, note that the DataCam provides images in a ‘landscape’ format with the image’s 
long dimension orthogonal to the burner and chamber axis.  This is contrary to an ACME 
science requirement specifying that the long dimension be aligned with the experimental axis 
to provide images in a ‘portrait’ format.  In this regard, the science requirements were not 
always met, e.g., because of design tradeoffs. 
 
There is some variation in the ACME camera zoom, where its setting is not completely 
reproducible.  Therefore, the scaling of the image data should ideally be established for each 
subset of tests if more than one zoom setting was used within a test day.  The scaling can 
typically be carried out using images regularly taken of the ceramic fibers for Thin Filament 
Pyrometry (TFP), where such imaging is normally made at two fiber array positions.  
Meanwhile, the other cameras used in ACME testing had fixed lenses. 
 
3. Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera  
During ACME testing, this intensified camera was typically configured with a CH* bandpass 
filter and was generally archived at 23 fps. 
 
The grayscale image files are in a Tagged Image File Format (TIFF) format and can be opened 
readily, where brightness/contrast adjustment may again be required. 
 
Note that this camera’s Field of View (FOV) is partially blocked by the arms of the fiber array 
for Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) when it is moved to position the fibers across the flame. 
 
As with the ACME DataCam, it might be useful to check the metadata for the CFI intensified 
camera, which is in a comma-delimited (CSV) format and can be opened with spreadsheet 
software or alternately as a text file. 
 
CFI intensified camera metadata 
An example file name is INTNS_21062M1.mdipsug where INTNS designates the CFI intensified 
camera.  Presented below are the column headings and example values from the test’s first 
image (numbered 00000), and the corresponding camera parameter name and a description:
