ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
80 
 
 
Figure 1. E-FIELD Flames with (left) and without (right) a Simultaneous Flow of Air 
(Flames actually dim blue; colored & brightened here for clarity) 
 
The “red” flame in Figure 1 benefited from the oxygen supplied by the simultaneous flow of air from the 
burner; in contrast, the “blue” flame relied on entrainment and diffusion for its oxygen supply. Although 
the fuel velocity is the same in both tests, the small “red” flame is attached to the burner, while the “blue” 
oxygen-starved flame is much wider and is lifted from the burner. These characteristics help the “blue” 
flame get the oxygen required to consume the fuel. Meanwhile, the “red” flame gets that oxygen in a 
much smaller zone thanks to the presence of the simultaneous flow of air. 
 
 
Figure 2. E-FIELD Flames at Increasing Fuel Velocity (No Simultaneous Flow of Air) 
(Flames actually dim blue; colored & brightened here for clarity) 
 
Figure 2 shows flames at increasing fuel velocities. Although the positive electric field tends to force the 
flames downward toward the burner, the flames are lifted from the burner because they are oxygen 
starved without the simultaneous flow of air. More oxygen is required to burn higher fuel flow rates, and 
the diameter at the base of the flame correspondingly increases. The distance that the flame is lifted from 
the burner also increases with the fuel velocity, where the separation allows more oxygen to reach the 
flame. The flame length is another measure of the oxygen transport, where the flame extends until it gets 
enough oxygen to consume all of the fuel. 
 
Week 09: April 20-26 
On GMT 113, we again performed ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion 
Flames) test points using pure methane, but this time with a positively charged electrode mesh. Like we 
observed with 30% ethylene tests (GMT 095), these tests also showed the strong effect that an electric 
field can have on soot within the flame.

items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
81 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG  
In this test, just after ignition, the electric field is energized at a very low voltage. The small flame, 
with its yellow/orange top, stabilizes for several seconds. Then, the voltage is quickly increased to 
1 kilovolt. Under the influence of this electric field, you can see the flame broaden, turn all blue 
in color (i.e., become soot free), and become quite dim at the tip. When the electric field is 
deactivated just before the end of the test, the flame quickly returns to its initial condition—with 
its sooty top. 
 
Week 10: April 27 – May 3 
On GMT 117, the boot drive in the FCF Image Processor failed. As this hard drive stores all our science 
image data, we were unable to perform the planned ACME E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on 
Laminar Diffusion Flames) test points. Next week, the crew will remove this hard drive, so we can boot up 
the FCF Image Processor from its other hard drive. Once this hard drive is ready to go as the new boot 
drive, we plan to get back to performing test points. 
 
ACME E-FIELD Flames Test Point Early Results 
 
Figure 1. E-FIELD Flames with and without a Simultaneous Flow of Air at Increasingly Negative Electric-
field Potential (100% Methane) 
 
Figure 1 shows how the flame changes as the potential of the negatively-charged electric field is increased. 
The top row of flames benefitted from the oxygen supplied by air flowing from the burner at the same 
time as the fuel. The bottom row of flames had no extra flow of air—only the oxygen in the air-like 
environment of the Combustion Chamber. In both cases, the effect of the electric field on the flame shape 
and size is dramatic. The ion wind, an upward flow created by the negatively-charged electric field, 
enhances oxygen transport to the flame causing it to become narrower and shorter. 
 
The negatively-charged electric field also affects the ion current, or the electric current that passes 
through the flame due to the motion created by the ion wind. As the electric field continues to increase 
in strength, the ion current peaks then sharply drops to a lower ion current and the flame size increases 
correspondingly. In comparable testing in normal gravity, the ion current peaked at a lower current then 
plateaued instead of sharply dropping like the microgravity tests. Figure 2 below compares the 
microgravity tests with and without the simultaneous flow of air. The flames without the simultaneous 
flow of air peak at a lower ion current and at a lower field strength compared to flames with a 
simultaneous flow of air.

items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 
 
10 April 2021 
83 
 
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG  
At the start of this test, the 100% ethylene flame is broad and bright with soot “horns.” These 
soot “horns” are caused by heavy soot production just within the flame. As the positively charged 
electric-field starts to strengthen, the flame starts to vigorously oscillate. You can see hot soot 
particles stream from the flame, where they would normally be consumed as they pass through 
the flame sheet. 
  
At about 3 kilovolts, the flame steadies and flattens because the positively charged electric-field 
tends to push the flame toward the burner. It appears that the soot is trapped within the flame 
by thermophoresis, in which the soot particles are driven from hot to cold. At about 8 kilovolts, 
the flame begins to pulse strongly in an axisymmetric fashion; whereas, the earlier oscillations 
were asymmetric. Finally, when the electric field is deactivated, the soot streams from the top of 
the flame.  
 
One of the goals of E-FIELD Flames is to gain a fundamental understanding of using electric fields 
to control soot production in flames. Results could ultimately lead to more efficient and less 
polluting combustion technology for use on Earth.

E-FIELD Flames round 2 featuring the 2.1-mm gas-jet burner

items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
11 
1.0 
SCOPE 
1.1 
Identification 
The purpose of this document is to identify the design of the communication interfaces used by 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME). 
1.2 
System Overview 
 
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) is mini-facility designed to 
support Principal Investigators (PI) interested in studying various aspects of advanced 
combustion in a microgravity environment.  ACME will be integrated into the Fluids and 
Combustion Facility’s (FCF) Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) onboard the International Space 
Station in the US Lab Module.   
ACME will perform microgravity experiments to study fire suppression/flame extinguishment 
via 5 experiments: s-flame, Flame design, CLD Flame, E-Field Flames, and Burning Rate 
Emulator Flames as described in the ACME Baseline Description Document, ACME-DOC-004.  
ACME will allow investigation using pure as well as mixtures of gaseous fuels at various 
chamber atmosphere pressures, compositions, and oxygen concentrations.  The microgravity 
environment allows for observation and measurement of flame formation and extinguishment 
processes that cannot be made in sustained gravity.  The modular design of ACME allows for 
flexibility in configuration for specific experiments and easy maintainability of the hardware.  
The core elements of gaseous combustion are included in the ACME design as a basis for current 
and future gaseous combustion studies.  These elements are establishment of gas flow through 
various exchangeable mass flow controllers, ignition of gas at the burner and the use of 
appropriate diagnostic measurement devices.  The five identified experiments, and any future 
experiments, use these core elements to build a unique set of requirements for the study of 
various phenomena distinctive to gaseous combustion.  The goal of ACME is to improve the 
fundamental understanding of combustion processes in order to enable increased efficiency and 
reduce pollutant emission in practical combustion. 
 
1.3 
Document Overview 
This document is divided into interfaces used to communicate with the ISS (i.e., external 
communication interfaces) and interfaces used to communicate with devices within ACME that 
require a protocol (i.e., internal communication interfaces).

and IPSU-Gs go through the FCFCommunications application (Base Classes) which fills in the 
Command Sequence Count and Time Fields in the FCF Command Header before submitting the

Because it is a CIR PI package, ACME Package Command IDs in the FCF Command Header are assigned the range 0xC000-0xCFFF.  
The table below lists the commands, their IDs, and mnemonics. 
Detailed descriptions and parameter lists for each command follow the table.  In the parameter list for each command the parameter 
name is the variable name in the code, which is useful to know when Qt scripts are being written.  The name of the command, for 
example ‘NullCommand’, is also the name in code, in Qt scripts, and in log messages announcing the reception and completion of

Regarding parameters of type String, the entire available length can be used for characters without a terminating zero character.  If a

this transparent to the normal user.

items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
21 
3.1.2 
ACME Common Group Command Details 
These commands are called ‘common’ because they are  implemented using code shared 
between several payloads.  The detailed descriptions below are derived from the original 
documentation for these commands in Appendix K of FCF-ICD-0076, Rev C or later.  As stated 
in that appendix the high order bytes of the command ID are replaced by the command group 
number assigned to ACME common commands, which is 0xC0.  In that appendix the command 
IDs range from 0x0001 to 0x0038.  For ACME they range from 0xC001 to 0xC038. 
3.1.2.1 
NullCommand 
The NullCommand does nothing.  It can be used to test communication paths. 
Command ID: 0xC001 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_NULL 
3.1.2.2 
ExternalCommand 
The ExternalCommand command allows an avionics Main Processor (MP) CSCI to have no 
knowledge of this command and make use of the External Module feature. The command is 
passed to an External Module without intervention. This command enforces the requirement that 
an External Module requires a “module identifier” as the first parameter. The command group 
portion of the command ID, XX, depends on the module. 
Command ID: 0xXX02 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_EXTERNAL_PASS_THRU 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Description 
moduleIdentifier 
2 
Uint16 
Identifier (e.g. camera number 1,2) 
Command parameters 
80 
Area for module command-dependent parameters. 
 
3.1.2.3 
GoToIdle 
The GoToIdle command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the IDLE state. 
Command ID: 0xC003 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_IDLE 
 
3.1.2.4 
GoToExp 
The GoToExp command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the EXPERIMENT state. 
Command ID: 0xC004 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_EXPERIMENT

3.1.2.6

The GoToUpDownLink command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the 
UPLINK/DOWNLINK state. 
Command ID: 0xC006 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_UPLINK_DOWNLINK

GoToSafed 
The GoToSafed command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the SAFED state. 
Command ID: 0xC007 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_SAFED 
 
3.1.2.8 
SetRegistryItem 
The SetRegistryItem command selects an item in the registry file, 
/payload/app/config/AcmeConfig.ini, for modification by the SetRegistryValue command. The 
full path including group is required.  In Table 32, AcmeConfig.ini Contents, the full path is 
/Group/Key. 
Command ID: 0xC008 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON _REGISTRY_SET _ITEM 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Description 
registryName 
82 
String 
/Group/Key in AcmeConfig.ini (e.g. 
/EField/OutputFactorA) 
 
3.1.2.9 
SetRegistryValue 
The SetRegistryValue command selects the key set via the SetRegistryItem command and 
modifies it with the supplied value.  All software sub-systems are notified of the change and 
apply it used in the sub-system.  This is just a temporary change. It must be saved with the 
SaveRegistry command to become permanent in the AcmeConfig.ini file.  See Table 32. 
Command ID: 0xC009 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_REGISTRY_SET_VALUE

AbortCli 
The AbortCli command terminates the command running in the shell started by the RunCli 
command. It terminates any child processes the command may have started and the shell itself. It 
restarts the shell (SH) with the /payload working directory as the current directory.  
Command ID: 0xC00E 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_CLI_ABORT 
 
3.1.2.15 
FtpLocalFile 
The FtpLocalFile command stores the path for later use with the FtpSendFile command. It may 
be an absolute file path or a relative file path. If a relative path is given it is combined with the 
absolute directory set via the FtpLocalDirectory command to form the complete path.

items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
26 
3.1.2.21 
FtpSendFile 
The FtpSendFile command uses the information set via the FtpLocalFile, FtpLocalDirectory, 
and FtpRemoteDirectory commands. If an absolute path is provided in the FtpLocalFile 
command the result of the FtpLocalDirectory command is ignored, otherwise the two are 
combined to form an absolute file path for the source. The destination is provided as an absolute 
path from the FtpRemoteDirectory command. The file is sent from the local machine to the 
remote machine. 
Command ID: 0xC015 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_SEND_FILE 
 
3.1.2.22 
FtpSendDirectory 
The FtpSendDirectory command uses the absolute paths set via the FtpLocalDirectory command 
and the FtpRemoteDirectory command to copy a directory recursively from the local machine to 
the remote machine.  
Command ID: 0xC016 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_SEND_DIRECTORY 
 
3.1.2.23 
FtpGetFile 
The FtpGetFile command uses the information set via the FtpRemoteFile and 
FtpRemoteDirectory commands and the FtpLocalDirectory command. If an absolute path is 
provided in the FtpRemoteFile command the result of the FtpRemoteDirectory command is 
ignored, otherwise the two are combined to form an absolute file path for the source. The 
destination is provided as an absolute path from the FtpLocalDirectory command. The file is 
sent from the remote machine to the local machine.  
Command ID: 0xC017

SystemOpenTestPoint 
The SystemOpenTestPoint command prepares the software for recording data.  A directory is 
created at /payload/sci/testpointName to accept files, where testpointName is the supplied 
parameter.  If that directory already exists then ‘_x’ is appended to the name, where x is 1 or 2 or 
3 or more until a non-existent directory is found.  In this directory a file is created named 
testpointName_x_data.csv, where testpointName_x matches the directory name.   Two lines of 
header are written to the file and it is left open ready to accept data once an DataRecordingStart

The SystemCloseTestPoint command marks the end of the test point started with the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command.  Data recording is stopped, if it has not been stopped already 
using the DataRecordingStop command. The recorded data file, current command log file, and 
current message log file are compressed into the file 
/payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x.zip, where testpointName_x is as described 
under the SystemOpenTestPoint command. 
 
Command ID: 0xC103 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_TEST_POINT_CLOSE

SystemResetMotionController 
The SystemResetMotionController command resets the motion control board in the CIA that 
controls the igniter arm and TFP motors.  Any current motion and waveforms are stopped, the 
board is reset, and the board version is reported in the log.  This is a ‘soft reset’ as referenced in 
the Prodigy PC-104 Users Guide.  Hard resets of the individual motor stepper drivers are 
achieved using the IgniterMotorSetState and TfpMotorSetState commands. 
 
Command ID: 0xC104 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_RESET_MOTION_CONTROLLER

The SystemCirFlowState command is designed to be sent from the IOP to inform the ACME 
software about the state of the CIR manifolds.  Scripts can access this information as shown: 
 
If ( SystemCirFlowState.diluentManifoldState == 1) 
{ 
// Diluent manifold is opened 
}

3.1.4.38 
IntensifiedCameraSafe 
The IntensifiedCameraSafe command  places the intensified camera in a state that is safe for 
turning on lights without harming the camera by sending commands to the IPSUG.  The filter is 
commanded to home position and a fixed delay occurs to allow this to finish (without checking 
that it is finished).  Then the filter is sent to a safe position with another fixed delay.  The gain is 
set to 2048 (reporting back 2500).  Gate type is set to pulsed and gate width is set to zero 
(reporting back 20).  The delays and safe parameters are defined in the Intensifier group in 
AcmeConfig.ini. 
 
Command ID: 0xC226 
Mnemonic: ACME_INTENSFIED_CAMERA_SAFE 
 
3.1.5 
ACME Igniter Group Command Details 
3.1.5.1 
IgniterDisable 
The IgniterDisable command shuts down power to the igniter.  Specifically, it pulls low the 
primary control (PC) pin on the DC-DC converter that supplies the igniter.  For more 
information see the data sheet for the Vicor V24C12C100BL2 DC-DC converter. 
 
Command ID: 0xC301 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_DISABLE 
 
3.1.5.2 
IgniterPulse 
The IgniterPulse command turns on the igniter for a specified duration and power and then shuts 
it off.  Specifically, it sets the secondary control (SC) pin on the DC-DC converter that supplies 
the igniter to the specfied power voltage and then sets to primary control (PC) pin to 5V which 
enables output to the igniter.  After the specified pulse duration the PC pin is set to 0V, disabling 
output to the igniter.

3.1.5.3 
IgniterMove 
The IgniterMove command moves the igniter arm to the specified absolute postion.  The 
velocity, acceleration, and deceleration values used for the move are specified in 
AcmeConfig.ini.  See Table 32, Group: Igniter, Keys: VelocityCountsPerSec, 
AccelerationCountsPerSecSquared, and DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared.  To go to the home 
(retracted) position specify zero as the position.  In this case the keys used are 
HomeVelocityCountsPerSec, HomeAccelerationCountsPerSecSquared, and 
DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared. 
 
The igniter arm is moved using a trapezoidal velocity versus time profile.  If the acceleration 
parameter is greater than zero then movement begins with a ramp up until the specified velocity 
is achieved.  If the deceleration parameter is greater than zero then there is a ramp down to zero 
velocity.  The duration of the movement is calculated to reach the desired position. 
 
This command takes a few seconds to execute. To shorten the duration between command and 
movement use the IgniterSetupMove or IgniterSetupMoveWithParameters command followed by 
the IgniterExecuteSetupMove command when ready to move. 
 
The motor is a Haydon Kerk 25544-05-004ENG captive linear actuator.  There is no encoder. 
 
Command ID: 0xC303 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_MOVE

IgniterExecuteSetupMove 
The IgniterExecuteSetupMove command executes a move previously set up with the 
IgniterSetupMove or IgniterSetupMoveWithParameters commands. 
 
Command ID: 0xC306 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_EXECUTE_SETUP_MOVE 
 
3.1.5.7 
IgniterMotorSetState 
The IgniterMotorSetState command disables or enables the igniter motor by setting the RST line 
on the stepper driver to 0 V or 5 V respectively.  In normal operations this command should not 
be necessary because the motor is automatically enabled as soon as the cube is active (the signal 
originates in the cube), and is disabled when the software shuts down.  For reference, the stepper 
driver module is an Intelligent Motion System (IMS) XIM481H installed on an IMS INT-481 
board with MS0, MS2, and MS3 in the on position. 
 
To reset the motion controller board instead use the SystemResetMotionController command. 
 
Command ID: 0xC307

ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
61 
3.1.6 
ACME Flow Group Command Details 
For flow group commands refer to the latest revision of drawing S1101MFS004, “ACME/CIR 
Integrated Pneumatic Schematic” to see how flow devices are connected to each other.  A screen 
shot of the ACME CIA portion of this drawing (Rev A) is shown below.  Gas from the CIR 
comes in at the bottom of the diagram; fuel through QD11, nitrogen bypass through QD12, and 
static mixer through QD13. 
 
Figure 2  ACME CIA Flow Schematic 
 
3.1.6.1 
FlowEnableMfcs 
The FlowEnableMfcs command turns the mass flow controllers on or off.  Initially they are all 
turned on as soon as the cube boots.  After this first power-on the MFCs are queried for their 
configuration, including full scale flow which appears in telemetry.  Subsequent commanded 
power-ons do not cause a query of configuration.

3.1.6.2 
FlowSetMfcRate 
The FlowSetMfcRate command sets the flow rate setpoint for the selected mass flow controller.  
The flow rate specified in the command is in standard liters per minute which is converted to 0 to 
5V that is applied to the analog input control on the mass flow controller according to the 
equation: 
 
 
Analog input control (V) = flowSlm / fullScaleValue * 5.0 
 
,where fullScaleValue depends on the installed mass flow controller and is retrieved from the 
unit during the configuration query after power-on and is reported in telemetry for each MFC.

FlowZeroMfcs 
The FlowZeroMfcs command issues the ZRO serial command to the selected mass flow 
controllers.  From the Teledyne Hastings Digital 300 Software Guide the description of this 
command is as follows: 
This command adjusts the offset value of the flow meter such that the indicated flow reads zero 
flow at the present flow rate. Updates user offset value. This command should be executed 
periodically on flow meters when the flow rate is known to be zero. If this command is sent 
when the flow rate is non-zero this can cause significant flow reading errors. Flow controllers 
typically have the “autozero” function enabled and will not need to be re-zeroed.  
ACME mass flow controllers have the autozero function TBD.

ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
64 
 
3.1.6.5 
FlowMfcSerialCommand 
The FlowMfcSerialCommand command sends the specified raw serial command to the daisy-
chained mass flow controllers.  The start of the string is the address that determines the 
destination controller:  ‘*00’ = MFCA1 Static Mixer, ‘*01’ = MFCA2 Bypass, ‘*02’ = MFCA3 
Fuel.  The command follows the address, for example ‘*01ZRO’ to zero MFCA2, ‘*02MS’ to 
get the state of MFCA3, ‘*00sfl’ to get a status of all configuration items (the command sent 
after power-on) from MFCA1.  See the Teledyne Hastings Digital 300 Software Guide for 
available commands.  Replies to commands are placed in the telemetry text area. 
 
Serial commands are queued.  A command will not be issued until a response is received from 
any prior command or until the prior command response times out.  The response time out is 
specified by the registry value: Flow/MfcSerialCommandTimeoutMsec.  See Table 32. 
 
Command ID: 0xC405 
Mnemonic: ACME_FLOW_MFC_SERIAL_COMMAND 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Values 
Description 
serialCommand 
81 
String

The FlowSetSolenoidValveState command opens or closes the specified ACME solenoid valve. 
A valve is opened (allowing flow) by applying 5 V.  A valve is closed (stopping flow) by

FlowOpenAll 
The FlowOpenAll command sets MFCA1, MFCA2, and MFCA3 to full scale flow and opens 
solenoid valves SVA1 through SVA9. 
 
Command ID: 0xC408 
Mnemonic: ACME_FLOW_OPEN_ALL 
 
3.1.6.9 
FlowCloseAll 
The FlowCloseAll command sets MFCA1, MFCA2, and MFCA3 to zero flow and closes 
solenoid valves SVA1 through SVA9.  Any flow waveforms started with the FlowStepped, 
FlowRamped, FlowRectangularWave, or FlowRampedWave commands are stopped. 
 
Command ID: 0xC409 
Mnemonic: ACME_FLOW_CLOSE_ALL 
 
3.1.6.10 
FlowConfigForFill 
The FlowConfigForFill command configures ACME mass flow controllers and solenoid valves 
for filling the chamber.  MFCA1, MFCA2, and MFCA3 are set to full scale flow and SVA1, 
SVA2, and SVA3 solenoid valves are opened.  SVA4 through SVA9 are closed. 
 
Command ID: 0xC40A 
Mnemonic: ACME_FLOW_CONFIG_FOR_FILL

3.1.6.11 
FlowStepped 
The FlowStepped command steps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or not at all, 
by a specified step size, waits a specified duration, and steps again, repeating until each specified 
maximum flow (or minimum flow if stepping down) is reached, and then leaving the mass flow 
controller at the last flow. 
 
For positive step sizes the setpoints start at the minimum flow and step up until the maximum is 
reached, and does not go above.  For negative step sizes the setpoints start at the maximum and 
step down until the minimum is reached, and does not go below.  
 
Stepping can be stopped with the FlowStopWaveform command, which leaves the flow setpoints 
where they were last, or with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and closes 
all valves, with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the flow at 
the setpoint specified by the command.  Stepping is stopped for a MFC by any other flow 
waveform command if the parameters say to control that MFC, otherwise ongoing stepping 
continues until complete.

3.1.6.12 
FlowRamped 
The FlowRamped command ramps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or not at 
all, at a specified ramp rate for a specified duration, waits a specified hold duration, and ramps 
again, repeating until each specified maximum flow (or minimum flow if ramping down) is 
reached, and then leaving the mass flow controller at the last flow. 
 
For positive ramp rates the setpoints start at the minimum flow and ramp up until the maximum 
is reached, and does not go above.  For negative ramp rates the setpoints start at the maximum 
and ramp down until the minimum is reached, and does not go below.   During the ramp the 
control voltage of the mass flow controller is updated every millisecond. 
 
Ramping can be stopped with the FlowStopWaveform command, which leaves the flow setpoints 
where they were last, with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and closes all 
valves, or with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the flow at 
the setpoint specified by the command.  Ramping is stopped for a MFC by any other flow 
waveform command if the parameters say to control that MFC, otherwise ongoing ramping 
continues until complete.

3.1.6.13 
FlowRectangularWave 
The FlowRectangularWave command steps the flow of each mass flow controller a value, A, up, 
down, or not at all, waits a specified A duration, steps another value, B, up, down, or not at all, 
and waits a specified B duration.  This sequence is repeated until the maximum or minimum 
flow is reached or until stopped by a command. 
 
Rectangular waves can be stopped with the FlowStopWaveform command, which leaves the flow 
setpoints where they were last, with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and 
closes all valves, or with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the 
flow at the setpoint specified by the command.  Rectangular waves are stopped for a MFC by 
any other flow waveform command if the parameters say to control that MFC.

The FlowRampedWave command ramps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or 
not at all, at a specified ramp rate A for a specified duration A, waits a specified hold duration  
A, then ramps up or down or not at all at a specifried ramp rate B for a specified duration B, 
waits for a hold duration B, and repeats the sequence until specified maximum or minimum flow 
is reached or until stopped by command.

setpoints where they were last, with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and 
closes all valves, or with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the 
flow at the setpoint specified by the command.  Ramped waves are stopped for a MFC by any

3.1.7 
ACME Diagnostic Group Command Details 
3.1.7.1 
DataRecordingStart 
The DataRecordingStart command starts recording analog input and output data to a file at a rate 
defined by the Diagnostics/SampleTimeMsec registry entry, see Table 32, which defaults to 8 
msec for 125 Hz sampling. Prior to this command the SystemOpenTestPoint command must be 
issued to define the file name, otherwise the command fails.  The testpointName parameter in the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command results in the data being save to a path and file named 
/payload/sci/testpointName/testpointName_data.csv.   See section 8.1 for the file contents. 
 
Command ID: 0xC501 
Mnemonic: ACME_DATA_RECORDING_START 
 
3.1.7.2 
DataRecordingStop 
The DataRecordingStop command stops acquistion of data started with the DataRecordingStart 
command.  The resultant data file is left open until the SystemCloseTestPoint command is 
received.  Issuing another DataRecordingStart command instead will append data to the existing

differences in the data, which, for example, could include a tell-tale signature in the E-Field 
control voltage. 
 
Command ID: 0xC502 
Mnemonic: ACME_DATA_RECORDING_STOP 
 
3.1.7.3 
FiberMove 
The FiberMove command translates the thin filament pyrometry (Fiber) fiber array to the 
specified position at the specified velocity or translation rate. Movement acceleration and 
deceleration are registry values specified in AcmeConfig.ini, see Table 32, items 
Fiber/AccelerationCountsPerSecSquared and Fiber/DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared.  The 
response time to start movement is on the order of seconds.  To start movement closer to an 
event use the FiberSetupMove command followed by the FiberExecuteSetupMove command 
when ready to move. 
 
If the specified position exceeds the limit the command is not performed.  The position limit is 
the Fiber/MaxPosition registry value minus the Fiber/FiberToBurnerOffsets registry value (a 
comma-separated string of offsets in order of burner type number) for the burner type specified 
in the SystemDefineSetup command.  See the descriptions of these registry values in Table 32 for 
more information. 
 
Motion can be stopped prematurely using the FiberHaltMove command. 
 
The motor is an Ultramotion HT17 stepper motor linear actuator with 6 inch stroke and encoder.

The rest of the details of this command are the same as for the FiberMove command except that 
acceleration and deceleration are command parameters.

the stepper driver to 0 V or 5 V respectively.  In normal operations this command should not be

The PMTs are Hamamatsu part number H10722-10-MOD2.  PMT1 has a 310nm bandpass 
interference filter.  PMT2 has a UV fused silica broadband filter.  PMT3 has a 430nm bandpass 
interference filter.

PmtSetGain 
The PmtSetGain command sets the gain of the specified photo multipler tube. 
 
The gain parameter in this command specifies the volts out of the cube DNx-AO-333 board 
channels AO-25, AO-26, and AO-27, see Table 18.  These voltages are fed through a voltage 
divider of 10 Kohms and 1.21 Kohms before entering the control input on the PMT.  According 
to the PMT data sheet the recommended control voltage is 0.5 V to 1.1 V, corresponding to 4.63 
V to 10.19 V for the gain command parameter, which is limited to a maximum of 10 V. 
 
The equation to convert PMT control input, x, to PMT gain is: 
PMTGain = 2,000,000 * x ^ 8.643856 
,which gives a range of PMTGain from 5000 to 3,500,000 for 0.5 V to 1.1V control input, or 
4.63 V to 10.19 V command gain parameter. 
 
The equation to convert command gain parameter, gain, to PMT gain is: 
 
 
PMTGain = 2,000,000 * (gain/9.2645) ^ 8.643856 
 
The equation to convert PMT gain to command gain parameter, gain, is: 
 
 
gain = 10 ^ (0.115689 * log(PMTGain) + 0.23786213)

The ExtinctionDetectionConfigure command defines the limits, averaging duration, and method 
of extinction detection.  Detection of extinction using this configuration does not begin until the 
ExtinctionDetectionSetState command enables detection.  It ends when extinction is detected  or 
when the ExtinctionDetectionSetState command is used to force detection or disable detection.

averaged over the specified duration.  These averages are compared to the specified limts.  The 
numberOfInstruments parameter is used to indicate how many instrument averages must go

ACME E-Field Group Command Details 
3.1.8.1 
EFieldEnable 
The EFieldEnable command enables or disables the high voltage supply that powers the electric 
field mesh.  This command also effectively performs a EFieldSetVoltage command with voltage 
parameter equal to zero prior to an enable and after a disable.  Any waveforms are stopped by a 
disable. 
 
This command controls the cube DNx-AO-333 board AO-6 (HV2_EN) signal.  See Table 18. 
 
The high voltage supply is an Ultravolt part number 20A12-N4-Y6-C. 
 
Command ID: 0xC601 
Mnemonic: ACME_EFIELD_ENABLE 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Values 
Description

1 
Uint8 
0 = Disable 
1 = Enable 
Disable sets HV_EN to 0V.  Enable sets 
HV_EN to 5V. 
 
3.1.8.2 
EFieldSetVoltage 
The EFieldSetVoltage command controls the voltage present on the electric field mesh.  The 
voltage parameter, which is desired voltage on the mesh, is converted to control voltage output to 
the cube DNx-AO-333 board AO-4 (HV_CTRL) signal. See Table 18.  The conversion is 
according to the equation: 
 
𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑟𝑜𝑙 𝑉𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒= −𝐵+ √𝐵2 −4𝐶(𝐴−𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒)
2𝐶
 
 
,where A, B, and C are items in AcmeConfig.ini, See Table 32, and depend on whether the 
negative or positive supply is being used.  For the negative supply the names are: 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorA 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorB 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorC 
For the positive supply the names are: 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorA 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorB 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorC 
The SystemDefineSetup command tells the software which polarity of E-Field supply is installed. 
 
The reverse equation is: 
𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒= 𝐶∗𝑐𝑣2 + 𝐵∗𝑐𝑣+ 𝐴 
, where cv is control voltage and A,B,andC are as above. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply.

3.1.8.3 
EFieldSteppedSignal 
The EFieldSteppedSignal command steps the electric field voltage between a specfied minimum 
and maximum voltage with steps of a specified size and duration and back down (or up) for a 
specified number of cycles.  One cycle is a series of steps in one direction, therefore set cycles to 
a factor of 2 to perform complete up and down waveforms. 
 
The maximum and minimum voltages are not violated even if the step voltage does not divide 
evenly between them. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply. 
 
Special cases: 
-

> 1). 
- 
Cycles = 1 produces a single staircase. 
- 
stepVoltage = (maxVoltage – minVoltage) produces a square waveform.

National Aeronautics and Space Administration

7 
BRE 
 
 
 
 
•
Burning Rate Emulator 
– Jim Quintiere & Peter Sunderland (both U. Maryland) 
•
Concept 
– Flat-plate burner with gaseous fuel flow simulating the 
vaporization and combustion of condensed fuels 
– Heat flux to the burner is measured, where the flux 
vaporizes condensed-phase fuels 
–
Fuels to be simulated include paper, plastic, alcohols 
•
Goals  
– Quantify the burning and extinction behavior of 
condensed fuels in microgravity 
– Quantify the effects of increased O2 concentrations, 
e.g., for exploration atmospheres, on µg combustion. 
•
Why? 
– Spacecraft fire prevention through improved

Concept 
– Spherical (1D) flame, normal and inverse flow config.

Goals  
– Evaluate the effects of flame structure on soot 
inception and flame extinction 
– Obtain a correlation of sooting limits with 
stoichiometric mixture fraction, Zst, and adiabatic 
temperature, Tad 
– Determine the importance of gas-phase oxidation on 
soot inception for high Zst flames 
– Demonstrate the existence of steady spherical flames 
– Identify pseudo-flammability limits for diffusion flames 
in terms of  Zst and Tad 
•
Why? 
– To reduce soot and NOx through nitrogen exchange

National Aeronautics and Space Administration

Why Study Combustion? 
•
Energy 
– While we might  associate fire with the Stone Age, we still make 
extensive use of combustion in our daily lives. 
• Electricity – about 70% in the U.S. from combustion 
• Heating of buildings, water, food, and in manufacturing processes 
• Transportation 
– Our reliance on imported fuel contributes to our national trade 
deficit and affects our national security. 
•
Environment 
– Combustion is a source of greenhouse gases. 
– Soot contributes to global warming and is a health problem. 
•
Fire Safety 
 
Given its pervasive use with annual U.S. fuel costs on the order 
of a trillion dollars even small improvements in combustion 
technology can significantly reduce fuel needs and 
pollution production!

items.text:
Electric field, ions, and flames 
Background and motivation 
•  Hydrocarbon flame’s inherent electrical property 
was reported more than two centuries ago. 
•  Most of the theories with regard to the electrical 
charge carriers and ionization process were not 
extensively elaborated until after the 1950s. 
•  The book, written by Lawton and Weinberg, on 
the electrical aspects of combustion integrated 
the knowledge at the time (1969) of a flame’s 
systematic ion generation as well as electrical 
control of flames based on laboratory tests and 
observations. 
•  Pederson and Brown (among others) identified 
chemi-ionization mechanisms in hydrocarbon 
flames in 1993. 
Why microgravity?

Software Interface Design Description, ACME-DOC-010 Rev C (August 2016) 
 
 
8. Output Files 
 
 
4. Internal Interfaces (which includes Tables 15-17*) 
*where Table 17 describes channels A0-4 of the DNx-AO-333 analog output board as discussed in 8.1 below. 
 
8.0 
Output FILES 
8.1 
Data Output File 
Data output files are created using the SystemOpenTestPoint command which creates a file named and stored at 
/payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x_data.csv, where testpointName is the parameter received in the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command and _x is optional to avoid duplicate files, where x = 1,2,3, etc.  
The file contains a two-line header.  The first line has the date and time, documentation of the setup received in a 
SystemDefineSetup command, and the PMT gains.  The second line has the column headings for the subsequent rows of data.  The 
text of the column headings is defined by the Diagnostics/Header registry entry or the Diagnostics/BreHeader entry depending on 
whether the SystemDefineSetup command experimentType parameter was BRE or not. The column headings should match the data 
which is the following: 
- 
A timestamp in the format HH:MM:SS:mmm, where mmm is milliseconds. 
- 
11 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-207 board in the order shown in Table 1. 
-

items.text:
3 
 
8.2 
Message Log File 
Software messages are logged to files named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-DD_hh-mmACME.log, where YYYY 
is year, MM is month, DD is day of month, hh is hour, and mm is minutes.  The date in the name is when the log file is 
created, soon after software startup. 
Each message line in the file begins with a timestamp and a logging category.  The timestamp is of the format YYYY-MM-
DD DDD hh:mm:ss:mmm, where DDD is day of the year, mmm is milliseconds, and the rest are self-explanatory.  See 
section Error! Reference source not found. for information about the logging category and how to filter them out if 
desired. 
8.3 
Command Log File 
The message log file, section 8.2, includes messages showing commands received and their parameters.  Command log 
files contain only the details of each command received.  The files are named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-
DD_hh-mmACMECommands.log.  The format is for each command received a timestamped line of text with the 
command name followed by timestamped lines of text showing each parameter name and parameter value, including 
header information.

Why Study Combustion? 
•
Energy 
– While we might  associate fire with the Stone Age, we still make 
extensive use of combustion in our daily lives. 
• Electricity – about 70% in the U.S. from combustion 
• Heating of buildings, water, food, and in manufacturing processes 
• Transportation 
– Our reliance on imported fuel contributes to our national trade 
deficit and affects our national security. 
•
Environment 
– Combustion is a source of greenhouse gases. 
– Soot contributes to global warming and is a health problem. 
•
Fire Safety 
 
Given its pervasive use with annual U.S. fuel costs on the order 
of a trillion dollars even small improvements in combustion 
technology can significantly reduce fuel needs and 
pollution production!

condensed fuels in microgravity.

conditions in microgravity.

– Spacecraft fire prevention through improved

– To reduce soot and NOx through nitrogen exchange

items.title: PSI-22_Reports_PS_00538  Unlocking Mysteries.pdf
items.text:
Unlocking Mysteries in Microgravity:
NASA Glenn Provides the Keys With the Fluids 
and Combustion Facility
What Is Microgravity?
	
Gravity is a force that governs motion 
throughout the universe. It holds us to the 
ground and keeps the Earth in orbit around the 
Sun. Microgravity describes the environment 
in orbital space flight, which has very weak 
gravitational effects (one-millionth of what is 
felt on Earth) and which is sometimes referred 
to as a state of “weightlessness.” The condition 
of microgravity occurs when an object is in 
“free fall.” In free fall, an object falls faster and 
faster, accelerating with exactly the speed of 
attraction caused by gravity. Objects travelling 
around the Earth in a state of continuous free 
fall, or orbit, are essentially weightless even 
though their mass remains the same.
	
Conducting research in a microgravity 
environment gives researchers a unique oppor­
tunity to study the true nature of processes and 
materials without having to consider the effects 
of Earth’s gravity. Thus, physics theories can be 
tested at levels of accuracy that are impossible 
on Earth. Microgravity experiments uncover the 
mystery of how gravity affects processes such 
as combustion science and fluid physics. This 
knowledge can then help to improve the way 
we do things on Earth.
Astronaut Michael Fincke, Expedition 18 commander, works on the Combustion Integrated Rack in the Destiny 
Laboratory of the International Space Station.

items.title: PSI-22_Reports_PS_00538  Unlocking Mysteries.pdf
items.text:
Powering the Future	
2	
NASA Facts
A World-Class Orbiting Laboratory
	
The term “microgravity” will become more com­
monplace when the International Space Station (ISS) is 
fully operational. The ISS will be the largest orbiting space 
structure and the largest international scientific and tech­
nological endeavor in history. Sixteen countries, including 
the United States, are participating in this record-breaking 
project. The ISS is a permanent laboratory in space where 
studies can be performed without the effects of gravity.
	
The space station provides researchers with all the 
laboratory space and equipment and electrical power 
needed for safe, long-term research by human beings in 
space. The ISS enables larger and longer experiments than 
were possible on the typical 2-week space shuttle mission. 
This gives scientists time for more detailed observation in 
the microgravity environment.
	
The knowledge gained from ISS microgravity experi­
ments is benefiting research on Earth in many fields. Our 
understanding of theories relevant to everything from high-
temperature superconductivity to weather prediction will 
be advanced. New insights into areas such as human health 
and disease prevention and treatment will be achieved. In 
addition, scientists are using the microgravity environment 
to uncover other, more subtle forces and interactions in flu­
ids and materials. By essentially taking gravitational effects 
out of the equation, researchers are able to study as primary 
characteristics what would have been secondary behaviors 
on Earth.
	
Simple investigations of fluid interfaces and combus­
tion processes can be addressed in small, contained experi­
ments, such as the shuttle Glovebox experiments. However, 
more complex and challenging investigations require dedi­
cated facilities to contain fluids and products of combustion 
in a controlled and safe environment.
The ISS Fluids and Combustion Facility
	
The United States Laboratory Module on the ISS con­
tains the Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF), designed 
and built at NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, 
Ohio. The FCF was developed to accommodate the unique 
challenges of working with fluids and combustion pro­
cesses in microgravity, as well as to provide services and 
capabilities comparable to those found in traditional Earth-
based laboratories.
	
Glenn was an ideal choice for this project because of 
their reputation for award-winning research, particularly in 
the areas of fluids and combustion, as well as their long-
standing experience in developing experiment hardware and 
world-class test facilities. Glenn engineers and scientists 
have been involved in designing, producing, and manag­
ing space-based hardware and facilities since the 1960s. 
As pioneers in rocket research, they had tested high-energy 
propellants even before the United States officially entered 
into the space business. Glenn Research Center advanced 
the propulsion technology that helped make space travel 
possible.
	
The Center’s unique Zero Gravity Research Facility 
and other drop towers and laboratories were the source of 
foundational work in microgravity research. NASA’s Zero 
Gravity Trainer aircraft occasionally operates out of NASA 
Glenn in support of Glenn’s ground-based microgravity 
research. Some flights include astronauts participating in 
crew training so they can have low-gravity experience with 
experiment hardware and materials prior to shuttle mis­
sions. In all, these facilities give Glenn a unique ability to 
develop and test microgravity experiments.
	
Glenn Research Center is NASA’s center of excellence 
for fluid physics and combustion science and has been 
responsible for 153 experiments on 47 shuttle flights. In 
addition to providing the FCF, they are a major contributor 
to the investigations onboard the FCF, in gloveboxes, and 
in other ISS facilities. A forerunner of the FCF, the Glenn-
developed Combustion Module–1 (CM–1), which flew 
onboard the Shuttle Columbia, STS–83, in April 1997, laid 
the groundwork for the combustion portion of the new FCF 
with several hardware innovations.
	
The FCF is ushering in a new era of fluids and com­
bustion research. It is a modular, multi-user, permanent 
microgravity science laboratory that is making it possible 
for researchers on the ground, with the assistance of the 
astronauts in space, to schedule and perform studies of how 
fluids and flames behave in the absence of gravity at a cost 
that is not out of this world.
	
The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) was delivered 
by the Space Shuttle Endeavour in November 2008 dur­
ing mission STS–126.  The Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR)
was delivered by Space Shuttle Discovery in August 2009 
during mission STS–128. The two racks provide the basic 
physical and functional framework required to perform 
combustion science, fluid physics, and associated science 
Glenn researchers working on Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) during 
development.

items.title: PSI-22_Reports_PS_00538  Unlocking Mysteries.pdf
items.text:
Powering the Future	
3	
NASA Facts
onboard the ISS. The environmental control subsystems 
will provide temperature and pressure control for air and 
water systems, as well as safety measures and fire detection.
	
The end result is true facility operations with all of the 
capabilities that serious researchers expect on the ground 
without the effects of gravity. 
Combustion Science
	
Combustion, or burning, is a process in which a sub­
stance reacts with oxygen to give off heat and light. Com­
bustion meets almost 85 percent of the U.S. energy needs. 
While it does a good job of powering how we live on Earth, 
combustion is a major contributor to air pollution. 
	
The cost of combustion energy is about $450 billion 
each year in the United States. In any area of the economy 
where a huge amount of money is spent, even the small­
est improvements in efficiency can mean savings of very 
large amounts of money. A mere 1 percent increase in 
fuel efficiency, like improving your gas mileage from 25 
miles per gallon to 25.25 miles per gallon, would translate 
into a savings to America of nearly 100 million barrels of 
oil a year (roughly $5.5 million per day at today’s cost). 
Although today combustion is vital to transportation, mate­
rials processing, hazardous waste disposal, and many other 
areas, there is still only limited understanding of many of 
its fundamental characteristics. 
	
There are over 2500 fatalities and tens of billions of 
dollars in property damage each year in accidental fires. 	
	
Combustion research in microgravity can lead to 
advances in fire prevention, detection, and fighting. In addi­
tion, combustion research in microgravity can lead to more 
efficient use of energy, reduced pollution, and improved 
processes for making high-technology materials. Glenn 
Research Center’s experience with jet engines provides a 
solid background in combustion and Glenn scientists have 
already begun to study combustion in space. 
	
A simple example of microgravity’s effect in combus­
tion is the behavior of flames in space. On Earth, hot air 
rises around a candle flame, which causes the flame to 
flicker and take on an elongated shape. In microgravity, 
however, no such distortion takes place. The flame, without 
the effects of gravity, has a steady, spherical shape. The 
FCF allows researchers to study aspects of combustion, 
such as flame behavior, that are impossible to observe on 
the ground. Their research will lead to a better understand­
ing of whole processes, such as soot production, which will 
aid development of improvements in fire fighting and pollu­
tion reduction. 
Fluid Physics
	
Of the four states of matter—solid, liquid, gas, and 
plasma—three are fluid, meaning they flow in response 
to an applied force. An understanding of fluid physics is 
not only vital to advancing aircraft and spacecraft applica­
tions, such as airflow and propellant management, but is 
also essential to understanding the human body, aspects of 
everyday life, and many industrial processes. In micrograv­
ity, fluid positioning and flow characteristics can be studied 
from a new perspective. 
	
Scientists at NASA Glenn Research Center have 
played an important role in fluid physics research since the 
1940s. With orbiting spacecraft, microgravity fluid phys­
ics became an important research area in which NASA 
Glenn has always played a leading role. Glenn is currently 
focusing its research on the enabling technology for space 
exploration (water and fuel flow, life support systems, tem­
perature control, etc.) as well as on using the space environ­
ment (reduced gravity) to provide insight into phenomena 
that are important for Earth-based applications. One spinoff 
of the special nonintrusive instruments and techniques 
developed to perform the fluid experiments is a dynamic 
light scattering (DLS) probe and Hruby lens holder that 
make early detection of cataracts and other eye diagnoses 
easier. 
	
Glenn researchers have also experimented with the 
behavior of colloidal suspensions. A colloid is a system of 
fine particles suspended in a fluid. Italian salad dressing 
provides a simple illustration of the effects of micrograv­
ity on the behavior of colloidal suspensions. In space you 
would need to shake the dressing only once, rather than 
between uses, which is needed on Earth. Paint, ink, milk, 
and orange juice are also common examples. Though these 
products are routinely produced and used, scientists know 
little about the underlying structure of colloidal systems 
because they are difficult to study in ground-based labora­
tories. Understanding their structures may allow scientists 
to manipulate the physical properties of colloids for the 
creation of new materials and products or to improve the 
manufacturing of known products. 
Flame in microgravity.

FS–2011–06–035–GRC
National Aeronautics and Space Administration
Glenn Research Center
21000 Brookpark Road
Cleveland, Ohio 44135
	
NASA Facts
PS–00538–0611
Experiments by Remote Control
	
While the astronauts perform their roles in experiment 
setup, operation, observation, evaluation, and feedback, the 
FCF is teleoperated from the NASA Glenn Research Cen­
ter. Operation of experiments via remote control is coor­
dinated through the Telescience Support Center (TSC) at 
Glenn. Telescience is the systematic monitoring, command, 
and control of an experiment from a remote location and 
has already been implemented successfully by NASA on 
the shuttle/Spacelab and the Russian Mir Space Station. In 
concert with the work performed by the astronauts in space 
and the Cleveland-based operations team, the FCF principle 
investigator’s (PI’s) experiment can remotely monitor and 
control from the PI’s home site through Glenn’s TSC. 
	
The concept of telescience offers several advantages. 
Typically, the development of an experiment takes years 
and involves a varied group of scientists, engineers, and 
support personnel. Only a few of these people need to be on 
the operations team that travels to a NASA center to sup­
port actual mission operations. A major benefit of remote 
operations is that the entire team that developed and built 
the experiment can be connected to the operations team to 
support data analysis, command decisions, anomaly resolu­
tion, and other real-time considerations. Also, some facili­
ties that are not physically located at NASA centers can be 
included (e.g., colleges, universities, and industrial labs). 
Additional benefits are reductions in travel requirements 
and increases in the amount of science data acquired.
The Sky Is Not the Limit!
	
With over 10 years of continuous occupation, the ISS 
was assembled by over 100 launches of Russian vehicles, 
the American space shuttles as well as European and Japa­
nese vehicles. Over 150 spacewalks have been conducted 
in support of space station assembly totaling more than 944 
hours.  It has been visited by over 200 individuals, coming 
from 8 different countries. The newest star in the night sky  
continues to grow brightly, demonstrating to the world that 
its nations can work together in peace.
	
Researchers at NASA Glenn, world leaders in micro­
gravity science, continuously define scientific requirements 
and develop hardware for microgravity space experiments 
that will eventually have an impact on many areas of life 
here on Earth. Microgravity research aboard the ISS’s FCF, 
developed by NASA Glenn, is helping to improve indus­
trial processes, increase fundamental knowledge, advance 
our health care technologies, and make space exploration 
easier and safer. NASA Glenn has delivered and conducted 
18 investigations on ISS with many more in the pipeline. 
This research is helping create new ideas for tomorrow’s 
products, today.
	
Microgravity research on the ISS is showing life on 
Earth to us in ways we have never seen before. The sky is 
not the limit at NASA Glenn Research Center.
Telescience Support Center.

ACME CLD burner hot wire anemometry measurements - 12/26/16 
 
This report summarizes the results of the hot wire anemometry measurements performed on the revised 
version of the flight unit of the ACME CLD burner to assess the symmetry of the flow profiles. 
• A cold flow of air was employed for the coflow, and a cold flow of nitrogen was used for the fuel flow. 
• With respect to the following figure, the arrows identify the scanning directions followed to probe the 
velocity profiles on the burner. With reference to the plots in the following pages, the scanning 
directions are labeled and colored as follows. 
• Direction “A” 
• Direction “B” 
• Direction “C” 
• Direction “D” 
 
 
 
 
 
 
ACME CLD burner top view and hot wire scanning directions. 
 
• The flow velocity was measured with a TSI 1212-T.15 90° probe. 
• The teal arrow identifies the camera viewing direction. 
 
The measurements were performed in accordance to the Integrated Science Requirements Document 
(ISRD), and listed in the following. 
 
1.4.9: The burner shall have a uniform flow profile that is axisymmetric, i.e., where the velocity is 
independent of the angular position, especially (at radial positions) near the burner center. For the coflow 
burner, axisymmetric flow means that the variation in axial velocity with angular position (e.g., as measured 
in 1.4.11) shall be less than 10% of the (mean) velocity, where this shall hold for all radial positions from 0 to 
10 mm.  
•   verified 
1.4.11: The burner’s flow profile, across a plane orthogonal to the burner axis and within 0.5 mm 
downstream of the inner tube outlet, shall be well documented. The spatial uniformity shall be verified by 1g 
measurement of the velocity field using a cold flow (i.e., with no flame) simultaneously through both the 
annulus and the inner tube. The axial velocity shall be measured across a diameter of 30 mm at increments 
of no greater than 5 mm, especially within 5 mm of the burner axis where the increments shall be no greater 
than 1 mm. Unless otherwise specified, measurement across one diameter is sufficient. 
•   verified 
• The increments used were 0.25 mm, for both coflow and fuel tube regions. 
• Three heights above the burner outlet were scanned: 0.5 mm, 5 mm, and 10 mm.

diameters (as just described) at increments of no greater than 45 degrees.

In the following pages, the velocity plots are reported as a function of the radial coordinate, for the

fuel tube I.D. of 2.16 mm and O.D. of 2.41 mm. The black dashed lines identify the boundaries of the fuel

items.title: PSI-22_Presentations_ACME_CSSCI_2014 - Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station.pdf
items.text:
*Corresponding author.  Email address: dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov 
 
1 
Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute 
Mar 16–18, 2014 
Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the 
International Space Station 
Dennis P. Stocker1,*, Fumiaki Takahashi2, J. Mark Hickman1,  
and Andrew C. Suttles1 
1NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, Ohio 44135, USA 
2Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, Ohio 44106, USA 
Thus far, studies of gaseous diffusion flames on the International Space Station (ISS) have been limited to 
research conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) in mid-2009 and early 2012.  The 
research was performed with limited instrumentation, but novel techniques allowed for the determination of 
the soot temperature and volume fraction.  Development is now underway for the next experiments of this 
type.  The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project consists of five 
independent experiments that will be conducted with expanded instrumentation within the station’s 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  ACME’s goals are to improve our understanding of flame stability and 
extinction limits, soot control and reduction, oxygen-enriched combustion which could enable practical 
carbon sequestration, combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum performance and low 
emissions can be achieved, the use of electric fields for combustion control, and materials flammability. 
The microgravity environment provides longer residence times and larger length scales, yielding a broad 
range of flame conditions which are beneficial for simplified analysis, e.g., of limit behavior where 
chemical kinetics are important.  The detailed design of the modular ACME hardware, e.g., with 
exchangeable burners, is nearing completion, and it is expected that on-orbit testing will begin in 2016. 
1. Introduction 
Microgravity, i.e., apparent near weightlessness, is a unique environment for conducting 
combustion research.  Many flames are dramatically influenced by the effective elimination of 
buoyant convection, where the resulting effects are often advantageous.  For example, it is 
possible to create spherically symmetric flames enabling one-dimensional analysis.  More 
generally, the effective elimination of flicker yields quasi-steady flames.  Furthermore, the length 
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.  
Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere than normal-
gravity flames and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics.  For example, the long 
residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many 
microgravity flames are soot free.  Even neglecting soot, microgravity flames can be appropriate 
for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  It is also 
possible to study momentum-dominated flames at low velocities.  And of course, microgravity is 
the appropriate environment for studies related to spacecraft fire safety. 
Although microgravity combustion research has been conducted in drop facilities and research 
aircraft flying parabolic maneuvers, spacecraft like the International Space Station (ISS) offer 
significant advantages.  Drop durations, which are ~5 s or less in NASA facilities, are too short 
for soot to achieve quasi-steady conditions.  The drop durations are also too short to first 
establish a flame and then vary its flow rate, for example, to investigate stability or extinction

items.title: PSI-22_Presentations_ACME_CSSCI_2014 - Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station.pdf
items.text:
2 
 
limits.  Meanwhile, low-momentum flames can be dramatically disturbed by the g-jitter present 
in the aircraft testing, which is nominally ±0.02 g for a ~20 s duration.  The jitter can be avoided 
by floating an experiment within the aircraft, but that reduces the test duration to mere seconds.  
As a result, space-based testing is often necessary to get microgravity conditions of sufficient 
duration and quality for combustion research. 
Given the many advantages of space-based combustion research, five gas-fueled non-premixed 
flame experiments have thus far been conducted in space, where they are listed chronologically 
in Table 1.  Three experiments were conducted over a decade ago on the space shuttle, i.e., the 
Space Transportation System (STS).  The other two were conducted within the last five years on 
the ISS.  This past research was focused on gravity’s effects on the flame structure, soot and 
stability limits, and vortex interactions.  In each experiment, the flame configuration was the 
laminar gas-jet diffusion flame, where vortices were created in the TGDF experiment by varying 
the air entrainment (through mechanical control of an iris centered near the burner tube outlet).  
The research has included flames in both quiescent and coflowing atmospheres.  The LSP and 
TGDF experiments were conducted in sealed combustion chambers.  In contrast, the flame was 
enclosed within a small flow duct (with a 76-mm square cross-section) in the ELF, SPICE, and 
SLICE experiments.  The pressure was consistently ~100 kPa, with the exception of the LSP 
experiment which also included testing at lower values.  In all cases, the atmosphere consisted of 
~21% oxygen (by volume) with a balance of nitrogen.   Tests have been conducted with a variety 
of fuels (including dilutions) and burner diameters.

items.title: PSI-22_Presentations_ACME_CSSCI_2014 - Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station.pdf
items.text:
3 
 
The SPICE and SLICE experiments were both conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox 
(MSG) using common hardware which has since been used for the Burning and Suppression of 
Solids (BASS) experiment.  The manually-operated hardware, e.g., where the ISS crew 
controlled the flow with a potentiometer, was based on the preceding ELF experiment and was 
designed for exploratory studies.  The flame instrumentation was limited to a high-resolution 
digital still camera, an analog video camera, and a thermopile radiometer with a manually-
adjustable gain.  In addition to the radiometer output, the fuel flow, the coflow fan voltage, a 
coflow reference velocity, and a time stamp were both displayed and recorded through a video 
overlay.  Despite the limited instrumentation, pyrometric measurements were made in 2012 of 
the soot temperature and volume fraction using the innovative techniques discussed in [23-24].  
While these experiments proved to be valuable, more can be accomplished on the ISS. 
In 2008, the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) [25] was delivered to the International Space 
Station.  The facility is similar to a vending machine in size and includes a 100-liter combustion 
chamber capable of operation at pressures of up to 300 kPa.  The chamber features a ring of 8 
sapphire windows and is equipped with reconfigurable imaging systems (described later in this 
paper).  CIR includes a gas delivery system and provides venting, thermal control, electrical 
power, data handling, image processing and storage, and vibration isolation.  CIR experiments 
are conducted using unique hardware both inside and outside of the chamber.  Unlike the SPICE 
and SLICE experiments which were heavily dependent on the crew, the CIR experiments are 
commanded from the ground, limiting the crew’s responsibility to set up (e.g., exchange of gas 
bottles) and trouble shooting.   Since its launch, the CIR has been used for droplet combustion 
experiments, e.g., as seen in Figure 1, but future experiments are now in development.  
 
 
Figure 1: From left to right, the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) with the Multi-user Droplet 
Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) removed from the chamber for servicing by Expedition 34 
Commander Kevin Ford.  The photo was taken on Dec. 12, 2012 in the U.S. (Destiny) Laboratory  
of the International Space Station.  [NASA photo ISS034-E-007409]

items.title: PSI-22_Presentations_ACME_CSSCI_2014 - Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station.pdf
items.text:
4 
 
Gaseous flames will be investigated in the next set of CIR experiments as part of NASA’s 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  ACME currently 
includes five independent experiments, listed in Table 2, which are each focused on advanced 
combustion technology through fundamental research.  Although distinct, the experiments will 
be conducted with a single modular CIR insert similar to the MDCA seen in Fig. 1.  Laminar, 
non-premixed flames are used in all of the current ACME experiments.  To simplify analysis, the 
flames are either one or two dimensional, depending upon the experiment. 
 
Table 2: Planned ISS experiments investigating gaseous non-premixed flames,  
listed alphabetically.

(CLD Flame)
