Exploration Research) 
Flame Design 
PI Richard L. Axelbaum (Washington University in St. Louis) 
Co-I Beei-Huan Chao (University of Hawaii) 
Co-I Peter B. Sunderland (University of Maryland) 
Co-I David L. Urban (NASA Glenn Research Center) 
Structure and Response of Spherical 
Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) 
PI Chung K. Law (Princeton University) 
Co-I Stephen D. Tse (Rutgers University) 
Co-I Kurt R. Sacksteder (NASA Glenn Research Center) 
 
2. Science 
The current ACME experiments are primarily focused on energy and environmental concerns, 
but there is a secondary emphasis (with the BRE experiment) on fire prevention, especially for 
spacecraft.  The primary objective is to gain fundamental understanding that can enable 
improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion processes on Earth, for 
example through the development and verification of models for chemical kinetics and transport 
processes in computational simulations.  In addition to enhanced performance, improved 
modeling capability can lead to reductions in the time and cost for combustor design.  Some 
specific goals are to improve our understanding of combustion at fuel lean conditions where both 
optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, soot control and reduction, oxygen-
enriched combustion which could enable practical carbon sequestration, flame stability and 
extinction limits, the use of electric fields for combustion control, and materials flammability.   
Unlike the other current ACME experiments, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is 
focused on spacecraft fire prevention.  More specifically, BRE’s objective is to improve our 
fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as extinction behavior and the 
conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability

items.title: PSI-22_Presentations_ACME_CSSCI_2014 - Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station.pdf
items.text:
5 
 
test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.  A flat porous burner fed with gaseous 
fuel will simulate the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where measurements are made of the 
thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is 
dependent.  A small number of gaseous fuels (including mixtures with inert gases) will be used 
to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and alcohol by matching properties such 
as the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface temperature, and smoke point. 
Research, including that already conducted in microgravity, has revealed that our current 
predictive ability is significantly lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for 
sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction.  The goal of the Coflow 
Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is to extend the range of flame conditions 
that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and 
soot formation submodels.  The dependence of normal coflow flames on injection velocity and 
fuel dilution will be carefully examined for flames at both very dilute and highly sooting 
conditions.  Measurements will be made of the structure of diluted methane and ethylene flames 
in an air coflow.  Lifted flames will be used as the basis for the research to avoid flame 
dependence on heat loss to the burner.  The results of this experiment will be directly applicable 
to practical combustion issues such as turbulent combustion, ignition, flame stability, and more.  
The SLICE experiment was conducted as a precursor to ACME’s CLD Flame experiment, in 
order to maximize its science, e.g., through refinement of the test matrix. 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced by the 
combustion reactions.  The direct ion transport and the induced ion wind can modify the flame 
shape, alter the soot or flammability limits, direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutant emission.   
The purpose of the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) 
experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and investigate how 
the ions can be used to control non-premixed flames.  Outside reviewers concluded that the 
experiment “has great prospects of improving our understanding of nearly every practical 
combustion device.”  The experiment will be conducted with a simple gas-jet flame, where an 
electric field will be generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the 
burner and a flat circular mesh above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.  Measurements will be 
made of the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response to electric forcing as a 
function of the field strength, fuel, and fuel dilution. 
 
The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve our understanding of soot 
inception and control in order to enable the optimization of oxygen enriched combustion and the 
“design” of non-premixed flames that are both robust and soot free.  An outside review panel 
declared that Flame Design “… could lead to greatly improved burner designs that are efficient 
and less polluting than current designs."  Flame Design will investigate the soot inception and 
extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames created with porous spherical burners.  Tests 
will be conducted with various concentrations of both the fuel (i.e., ethylene or methane) and 
oxygen in order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot inception.  The effect of 
the flow direction on soot formation will be assessed by studying both normal flames and inverse 
flames, where in the latter case an oxygen/inert mixture flows from the spherical burner into a 
fuel/inert atmosphere.  The Flame Design experiment will explore whether the stoichiometric 
mixture fraction can characterize soot and flammability limits for non-premixed flames like the 
equivalence ratio serves as an indicator of those limits for premixed flames.

items.title: PSI-22_Presentations_ACME_CSSCI_2014 - Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station.pdf
items.text:
6 
 
The purpose of the Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) experiment is to 
advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot-free 
and sooty flames.  The spherical flames will be ignited at non-steady conditions and allowed to 
transition naturally toward extinction.  Tests will be conducted with various inert diluents, in 
both the fuel and chamber atmosphere.  The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane mixtures 
for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty flames.  One experiment objective is to identify the 
extinction limits for both radiative and convective extinction (i.e., at high and low system 
Damköhler numbers, respectively).  Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and 
nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in such flames 
with fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number. 
3. Experimental  
As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to 
accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners.  Besides the chamber insert, 
other ACME-unique hardware includes a high-definition color camera and an avionics package, 
which is for data acquisition and control. 
 
 
Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber 
insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS.

items.title: PSI-22_Presentations_ACME_CSSCI_2014 - Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station.pdf
items.text:
7 
 
ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety 
of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter.  
As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 
0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 
2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and 
two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm).  Most 
burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat 
flux transducers.  The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow 
monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface.  The igniter will have a crew-
exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will 
allow for precise positioning. 
 
 
Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, 
porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. 
 
The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the 
delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner.  
The maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 
slpm (on a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines.  The crew can 
exchange the mass flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow 
accuracy.  The gas delivery system enables on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both 
simultaneously), coflow, inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), 
and premixed flames, although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME 
experiments.  Gases can also be delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary 
in some circumstances, such as the blending of different fuel gases.  CIR’s standard bottle sizes 
are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to 
limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) that can be released into the combustion chamber. 
ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras 
and two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already 
in use on orbit.  All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber.  Collectively, the 
imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot 
volume fraction; and operational support.  However, it is unlikely that all functions would be 
exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. 
Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of 
the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning 
mirror).  Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development.  The analog

items.title: PSI-22_Presentations_ACME_CSSCI_2014 - Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station.pdf
items.text:
8 
 
camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations.  Light-
emitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both 
support the operations and provide reference images.  The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 
30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent 
control of the zoom, iris, and focus.  The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly 
with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging.  Color imaging can 
also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to 
avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green.  The natural flame 
color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and 
measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24].  Alternately, CH* 
imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm 
bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM).  A 450-nm 
bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively 
subtract interfering broadband soot emission.  However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so 
such subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible 
flame conditions. 
Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth 
Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which 
allows for imaging at multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each 
desired band.  This camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 
frames per second (fps).  Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary 
because of signal loss through the LCTF.  Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry 
(TFP) are possible, where ACME is equipped with a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide 
(SiC) fibers.  The fibers are orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the 
flame axis to the desired position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the 
analog video.  During set up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal to 
either ACME’s color digital camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF.  An alternate fiber 
array including a platinum wire will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination 
with preflight calibration will enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24]. 
CIR has a second HiBMs camera, without a filter, that will be used in combination with CIR’s 
illumination package for alternate measurements of the soot volume fraction.  This will be 
accomplished via an extinction technique previously employed in microgravity [3,6,26], where 
the camera and the collimated light source (with its two fiber-coupled laser diodes) are 
positioned at opposite windows.  The images are recorded at 1024x1024 and 30 fps.  Thus far, 
the primary purpose of this combined system has been the measurement of the droplet diameter 
for determination of the droplet burning rate. 
CIR’s Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) package is a monochrome camera with an 
intensifier (for 280-700 nm) and a 310-nm bandpass filter (with a 10-nm FWHM) for OH* 
imaging.  Again as a result of the signal loss through the filter, binning is employed such that the 
OH* images are recorded at 512x512 and 30 fps. 
The ACME chamber insert will also be equipped with non-imaging optical diagnostics including 
both thermopile radiometers and Photomultiplier Tubes (PMTs).  There is a crew-exchangeable 
linear array of radiometers of which there are two versions supporting the initial set of 
experiments.  The array has a fixed position which is parallel to the chamber axis and centered 
(along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows and thus most of the other

items.title: PSI-22_Presentations_ACME_CSSCI_2014 - Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station.pdf
items.text:
9 
 
instrumentation.  One array is equipped with a single wide-view radiometer with two narrow-
view radiometers that are downstream and two more that are upstream, where all views are 
orthogonal to the chamber axis, as depicted in Figure 4.  The narrow-view radiometers are 
intended to support studies of gas-jet flames, where ACME can accommodate shorter burners, 
making the “lower” detectors useful.  The other array, also seen in Fig. 4, provides for three 
wide-view measurements of the flame, where one view is masked to nominally block radiant 
emission from the burner.  It was specifically designed for the BRE experiment but will be a 
resource available to other ACME experiments.  Given that the radiometer array can be 
exchanged by the crew, alternate arrays could be developed.   
 
 
Figure 4: Crew-exchangeable radiometer arrays on the ACME chamber insert: (top) standard 
(ACME) array of 5 radiometers, and (bottom) array with three radiometers, designed for the BRE 
experiment, where the lowest detector is masked to avoid view of the burner.

items.title: PSI-22_Presentations_ACME_CSSCI_2014 - Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station.pdf
items.text:
10 
 
An additional wide-view radiometer, that is fixed and not crew exchangeable, is positioned 
downstream of the burner and flame at 30o from the chamber axis.  This detector is primarily 
intended to support the spherical flame experiments and will have a quicker response than the 
more sensitive detectors that will used in the linear arrays.   Like the radiometers on the two 
linear arrays, it will have a spectral range of nominally 0.2-11 micron and its field of view will 
be established by an appropriately selected aperture. 
To detect the quenching of dim flames, the chamber insert will be equipped with a set of three 
PMTs.  Each PMT will have a wide-angle view, a sight line that is orthogonal to the chamber 
axis, and will be centered (along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows so that it 
is aligned with most of the other instrumentation.  The PMTs’ spectral range will be 230-700 nm, 
i.e., visible and near ultraviolet, but one will have a 310-nm bandpass filter and another will have 
a 430-nm bandpass filter (where both are with a 10-nm FWHM).  The pair of detectors will 
enable measurement of OH* and CH* emission, respectively.  The third PMT will be equipped 
with a neutral density filter to prevent saturation.  Like many other components, the PMT array 
can be removed from the chamber insert by the crew. 
The chamber insert is also equipped with six far-field thermocouples to measure the spread of 
the thermal field in the spherical flame experiments.  They are of limited utility for other 
experiments because they are positioned upstream of the burner tip.  Therefore, they will 
generally not be installed by the crew to reduce the chance of accidental damage.  There will be 
two versions of a four-thermocouple rake to allow a choice of near and far measurements.  Other 
arrays could be designed to support future experiments, but they cannot extend downstream of 
the burner tip without interfering with other (e.g., optical) measurements. 
Experiment-unique hardware is also mounted on the chamber insert.  For example, to 
accommodate the E-FIELD Flames experiment, the insert is equipped with a high-voltage supply 
and a crew-removable electrode mesh which can be set between +10 and -10 kV.   The circular 
mesh is orthogonal to the chamber axis and is positioned (during set up) at either ~35 or ~50 mm 
downstream of the insulated burner.  The ion current between the burner and electrode mesh will be 
determined via measurement of the voltage drop across a known resistor and application of Ohm’s 
Law. 
Additional supporting measurements will be made, where the chamber pressure is a simple 
example.  The ACME experiments will use the CIR’s gas chromatograph for pre- and post-test 
analysis of the chamber atmosphere, e.g., for oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, carbon 
monoxide, and fuel gases.  Acceleration measurements will be provided by the Space 
Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) [27], which is the primary instrument for such 
measurements on ISS and previously served that role for the space shuttle. 
All ACME experiments will be constant volume (i.e., rather than constant pressure) studies, 
where the chamber’s free volume will be about 90 liters.  Burner flows will generally be 
constrained to limit the pressure rise, and tests will typically be 0.5-2 minutes in duration. 
The ACME experiments will be configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  Instead, the 
experiments will be commanded from the ground, specifically from the Telescience Support 
Center (TSC) at the NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio.  They can be conducted 
in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it will also be possible 
to effectively operate the experiments in a “manual” mode, where changes can be made in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream.

11 
 
For example, a flow rate could be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit.  Step and ramp 
changes can be made in the flow rate(s) or electric field potential.  The TFP fiber array can be 
translated uniformly through a soot-free flame to get a continuum measurement of the 
temperature field.  In summary, ACME’s experiment control will allow for broad flexibility.   
4. Concluding Remarks 
In January 2014, the Obama administration announced that ISS operations will continue until at 
least 2024.  It is currently expected that the five ACME experiments will be conducted from 
2016 to 2019.  While there are plans for subsequent CIR experiments, e.g., to study flame spread 
across solid fuels, future experiments could be conducted using the ACME hardware.  Although 
the current ACME experiments are limited to laminar non-premixed flames, turbulent and 
burner-stabilized premixed flames could also be studied using the ACME chamber insert.  Many 
of the hardware elements are exchangeable on orbit, including for example, the burner, igniter 
arm and tip, video cameras, radiometer array, PMT array, TFP fiber array, thermocouple rake, 
high-voltage supply, electrode mesh, and the gas chromatograph.  As such, the hardware can be 
customized to support a wide variety of future experiments.  Gaseous flames could continue to 
burn brightly on the ISS. 
Acknowledgments 
The authors are grateful for the critical contributions of both the ACME investigators (listed in 
Table 2) and the ZIN Technologies engineering team developing the ACME hardware and 
software, where key members include Brian Borowski, Adrian Drake, Timothy Gobeli, Stephen 
Lawn, Michael Medved, and Christopher Mroczka.  ACME also benefits significantly from the 
support of Eric S. Neumann and his microgravity facilities staff at the NASA Glenn Research 
Center in the conduct of ground-based microgravity tests to evaluate prototype burners, 
instrumentation, and of course flame behavior and in the design and assembly of the hardware to 
conduct those tests.

2011 7th US National Combustion Meeting

and Hosted by the Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA

Electric field induced convection in microgravity combustion  
K. Swenson1, S. Karnani2, D. Dunn-Rankin2, F. Takahashi3, D. Stocker1, and        
Z-G. Guang3 
1NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, Ohio 44135 
2Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, University of California at Irvine, 
Irvine, California 92617, USA 
3National Center for Space Exploration Research on Fluids and Combustion, Cleveland, Ohio 
92617, USA 
This paper describes measurements aimed at understanding the influence of electric fields on 
flames where buoyancy has been removed. Given that buoyancy and an electric field can have a 
similar influence on flames, buoyancy can obscure the contribution of an electric field in a normal 
gravity (1g) environment. Experiments were performed in the microgravity conditions of NASA’s 
2.2 Second Drop Tower on a simple jet diffusion flame to isolate the influence of an electric field. 
Results show similarities between the ion current response of a methane flame in an electric field 
in both 1g and microgravity (μg). Under some coflow velocities and electric fields strengths, it is 
possible to modify the flame shape so that it resembles a flame in 1g.  
1. Introduction 
 
When oxidized, hydrocarbon fuels produce a number of intermediate species, a small 
subset of which are charged. Hence, an electrostatic field applied across the flame zone creates a 
charge separation; opposites attract and ions move toward their respective opposite electrode. 
Acceleration of the ions is limited as momentum is transferred through collisions with neutral 
molecules. These repeated collisions induce a wind of companion neutral gas, which can 
potentially affect flame stability [1, 2], induce convection [3], and simulate microgravity [4-6]. 
 
In a 1g environment, the plume of hot gases from a flame naturally induces, through mass 
continuity, a convective flow to the neighboring cooler environment, giving rise to the flame’s 
characteristic teardrop shape. In a microgravity environment, buoyant convection, which in 1g is 
responsible for the transport of fresh oxidizer to a flame, is removed, leaving forced convection 
to dominate the flow field while species transport is a function of both that and molecular 
diffusion[7]. A number of experiments [8-10] have studied electric fields applied to flames in 
microgravity environments to measure mobility, its influence on burning rate constants, and the 
feasibility of inducing forced convection in a buoyancy free environment.  
 
The comparable influence of buoyant convection makes studying ion wind effects on 
flames in a 1g environment difficult. By removing buoyancy, the ion wind becomes a dominant 
force capable of creating similar flame shapes in a non-buoyant environment. This paper’s 
objective is to explore the different ion current regimes of a small diffusion flame when affected 
by an electric field in 1g and μg using the NASA Glenn 2.2-s Drop Tower.

2. Experimental  
The experimental drop rig (Figure 1) includes a cylindrical test chamber (24.6 cm i.d., 53.3 cm 
length), flow system, and data acquisition/control hardware. The burner is a stainless-steel fuel 
tube (2.1 mm i.d., 2.4 mm o.d.), coaxially positioned inside the cylindrical test chamber. For 
conditions requiring a coflowing annulus of gas, the stainless-steel fuel tube is coaxially 
positioned inside a Pyrex® converging nozzle (27.3 mm exit i.d.), through which air flows. Gas 
flow was controlled with a fixed orifice and upstream pressure. A hot-wire igniter (coiled 29-
gauge Kanthal, 11 cm length), which can be positioned over the burner by a rotary solenoid is 
used to ignite the fuel (CH4, 99.97%). Data signals from thermocouples, pressure transducers, 
radiometer (Dexter, ST150 Amplified), and a tri-axis accelerometer (Crossbow, CXL02TG3-S) 
are digitized and recorded at 20 Hz. The flame is observed by a CCD color camera (Hitachi HV-
D30), transmitted through a tethered optical fiber, and recorded using a digital video recorder 
placed atop the Drop Tower.  
 
To establish a steady flow through the flow orifice, fuel is introduced to the burner 8 seconds 
prior to the drop event (t = 0). Following ignition and igniter retraction, a selected high voltage is 
applied to the mesh electrode relative to the burner. The mesh screen was located 5 cm above the 
nozzle tip. The average strength of the electric field is approximated as:

3. Results and Discussion 
Flame response is presented in the following graphs by plotting the measured ion current as a 
function of the applied field. It should be noted that the burner is always grounded and electrical 
potentials are applied at the electrode. The polarity of the field is considered positive when the 
mesh electrode has a positive potential with respect to the burner electrode. All data points, 
except where noted, are averaged between t = 1.6 s to t = 2.1 s of the drop to avoid measuring the 
flame’s transient response. Data points were only included in the data set if a flame was present. 
Error bars represent the standard deviation of the shunt voltage in this same time period.  
Figure 3 shows the relationship between ion current and electric field strength for a 24 cm/s 
methane velocity in μg and 1g. Both conditions, regardless of polarity, show a sub-saturation 
region characterized by a near quadratic increase in ion current with voltage and a saturation 
region where ion current remains constant with increasing voltage. The ion current response 
exhibits minor differences in magnitude when changing gravity levels with a negative potential 
mesh in the sub-saturation and early saturation regions. At larger field strengths, initial transients 
from the voltage step can extinguish the flame.  Points that involve extinguishment are measured 
over different time periods and should not be considered accurate; however, the values are 
plotted for completeness and to show that extinguished flames have a clearly discernable 
behavior. For a positive potential mesh applied in μg, the ion driven wind forces the flame 
against the burner tube. The flames are partially quenched on the burner tube, reducing the

as a function of applied electric field strength and coflow velocity. The pink vertical line 
corresponds to the base location of a 1g flame without an applied field. The graphs show that a 
flame in μg with a -0.6 kV/cm average applied electric field or a coflow velocity of 24 cm/s will 
produce a flame with a similar area and flame base location as the unforced 1g flame. 
 
4. Conclusion 
The ion current response is nearly identical in μg and 1g environments, with the exception of the 
positive saturation plateau. This is expected considering that ion production is a global measure 
of flame behavior that is dependent on the flow field regardless of the driving mechanism. At 
electric field strengths greater than 1.8 kV/cm in μg, the flame begins to oscillate and the ion 
current jumps up significantly. At this point a faint corona glow is observed from the nozzle tip. 
At electric field strengths more negative than -1.6 kV/cm, the flame is unable to adjust to the 
abrupt change in flow conditions and extinguishes. Future research will include intermediate 
voltage steps or a ramp for testing at higher field strengths. Within the respective uncertainties, 
the surface area and flame base location of the images presented in Figure 4 are equal; where a    
-0.6 kV/cm electric field or a 24 cm/s coflow acting on a μg flame can produce a flame shape 
similar to that of a 1g flame without these influences.  The flames at these conditions are shown 
in Figure 4. A deeper understanding of how electric fields effect flames may lead to future 
applications such as soot control and applications where efficiency and stability can be actively 
controlled with electric fields.

items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
11 
1.0 
SCOPE 
1.1 
Identification 
The purpose of this document is to identify the design of the communication interfaces used by 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME). 
1.2 
System Overview 
 
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) is mini-facility designed to 
support Principal Investigators (PI) interested in studying various aspects of advanced 
combustion in a microgravity environment.  ACME will be integrated into the Fluids and 
Combustion Facility’s (FCF) Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) onboard the International Space 
Station in the US Lab Module.   
ACME will perform microgravity experiments to study fire suppression/flame extinguishment 
via 5 experiments: s-flame, Flame design, CLD Flame, E-Field Flames, and Burning Rate 
Emulator Flames as described in the ACME Baseline Description Document, ACME-DOC-004.  
ACME will allow investigation using pure as well as mixtures of gaseous fuels at various 
chamber atmosphere pressures, compositions, and oxygen concentrations.  The microgravity 
environment allows for observation and measurement of flame formation and extinguishment 
processes that cannot be made in sustained gravity.  The modular design of ACME allows for 
flexibility in configuration for specific experiments and easy maintainability of the hardware.  
The core elements of gaseous combustion are included in the ACME design as a basis for current 
and future gaseous combustion studies.  These elements are establishment of gas flow through 
various exchangeable mass flow controllers, ignition of gas at the burner and the use of 
appropriate diagnostic measurement devices.  The five identified experiments, and any future 
experiments, use these core elements to build a unique set of requirements for the study of 
various phenomena distinctive to gaseous combustion.  The goal of ACME is to improve the 
fundamental understanding of combustion processes in order to enable increased efficiency and 
reduce pollutant emission in practical combustion. 
 
1.3 
Document Overview 
This document is divided into interfaces used to communicate with the ISS (i.e., external 
communication interfaces) and interfaces used to communicate with devices within ACME that 
require a protocol (i.e., internal communication interfaces).

3.0 
EXTERNAL COMMUNICATION INTERFACES 
ACME commands originate from the ACME Ground Software (AGS) CSCI on a ground 
workstation at the Telescience Center (TSC) at Glenn Research Center (GRC).  These commands 
are then forwarded through a variety of systems until they eventually end up at the CIR on the 
ISS.   
 
Figure 1  ACME System Diagram 
 
 
3.1 
CIR Input/Output Processor (IOP) Interface 
Commands sent through the CIR IOP (Input Output Processor) are in the format required by 
FCF-ICD-0076A.  See section A.1, FCF Command Protocol for a listing of the required 
command formats, including all required headers.  All commands from the ground go to the IOP 
with the FCF Command Header and User Data filled in.  Commands from ACME to the IPSUs 
and IPSU-Gs go through the FCFCommunications application (Base Classes) which fills in the 
Command Sequence Count and Time Fields in the FCF Command Header before submitting the 
packet to the IOP for routing.

3.1.1 
ACME Commands 
Because it is a CIR PI package, ACME Package Command IDs in the FCF Command Header are assigned the range 0xC000-0xCFFF.  
The table below lists the commands, their IDs, and mnemonics. 
Detailed descriptions and parameter lists for each command follow the table.  In the parameter list for each command the parameter 
name is the variable name in the code, which is useful to know when Qt scripts are being written.  The name of the command, for 
example ‘NullCommand’, is also the name in code, in Qt scripts, and in log messages announcing the reception and completion of 
commands. 
Regarding parameters of type String, the entire available length can be used for characters without a terminating zero character.  If a 
string is less than the available length then a terminating zero character needs to be used.  The ground command software will make 
this transparent to the normal user. 
The Common Group is so-named because it is implemented in code shared between payloads.

ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
21 
3.1.2 
ACME Common Group Command Details 
These commands are called ‘common’ because they are  implemented using code shared 
between several payloads.  The detailed descriptions below are derived from the original 
documentation for these commands in Appendix K of FCF-ICD-0076, Rev C or later.  As stated 
in that appendix the high order bytes of the command ID are replaced by the command group 
number assigned to ACME common commands, which is 0xC0.  In that appendix the command 
IDs range from 0x0001 to 0x0038.  For ACME they range from 0xC001 to 0xC038. 
3.1.2.1 
NullCommand 
The NullCommand does nothing.  It can be used to test communication paths. 
Command ID: 0xC001 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_NULL 
3.1.2.2 
ExternalCommand 
The ExternalCommand command allows an avionics Main Processor (MP) CSCI to have no 
knowledge of this command and make use of the External Module feature. The command is 
passed to an External Module without intervention. This command enforces the requirement that 
an External Module requires a “module identifier” as the first parameter. The command group 
portion of the command ID, XX, depends on the module. 
Command ID: 0xXX02 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_EXTERNAL_PASS_THRU 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Description 
moduleIdentifier 
2 
Uint16 
Identifier (e.g. camera number 1,2) 
Command parameters 
80 
Area for module command-dependent parameters. 
 
3.1.2.3 
GoToIdle 
The GoToIdle command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the IDLE state. 
Command ID: 0xC003 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_IDLE 
 
3.1.2.4 
GoToExp 
The GoToExp command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the EXPERIMENT state. 
Command ID: 0xC004 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_EXPERIMENT

The FtpSendFile command uses the information set via the FtpLocalFile, FtpLocalDirectory, 
and FtpRemoteDirectory commands. If an absolute path is provided in the FtpLocalFile 
command the result of the FtpLocalDirectory command is ignored, otherwise the two are 
combined to form an absolute file path for the source. The destination is provided as an absolute 
path from the FtpRemoteDirectory command. The file is sent from the local machine to the 
remote machine.

FtpRemoteDirectory commands and the FtpLocalDirectory command. If an absolute path is 
provided in the FtpRemoteFile command the result of the FtpRemoteDirectory command is 
ignored, otherwise the two are combined to form an absolute file path for the source. The 
destination is provided as an absolute path from the FtpLocalDirectory command. The file is 
sent from the remote machine to the local machine.

communicated by this command is recorded in the header of each recorded data file.  The burner 
type is used to determine igniter limits. See the IgniterMove command.  The useIpsu parameters 
are used to determine which IPSUs to record images on. See the StartIpsus command.  This

3.1.3.2 
SystemOpenTestPoint 
The SystemOpenTestPoint command prepares the software for recording data.  A directory is 
created at /payload/sci/testpointName to accept files, where testpointName is the supplied 
parameter.  If that directory already exists then ‘_x’ is appended to the name, where x is 1 or 2 or 
3 or more until a non-existent directory is found.  In this directory a file is created named 
testpointName_x_data.csv, where testpointName_x matches the directory name.   Two lines of 
header are written to the file and it is left open ready to accept data once an DataRecordingStart

information about the headers.

3.1.3.3 
SystemCloseTestPoint 
The SystemCloseTestPoint command marks the end of the test point started with the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command.  Data recording is stopped, if it has not been stopped already 
using the DataRecordingStop command. The recorded data file, current command log file, and 
current message log file are compressed into the file 
/payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x.zip, where testpointName_x is as described 
under the SystemOpenTestPoint command. 
 
Command ID: 0xC103 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_TEST_POINT_CLOSE 
3.1.3.4 
SystemResetMotionController 
The SystemResetMotionController command resets the motion control board in the CIA that 
controls the igniter arm and TFP motors.  Any current motion and waveforms are stopped, the 
board is reset, and the board version is reported in the log.  This is a ‘soft reset’ as referenced in 
the Prodigy PC-104 Users Guide.  Hard resets of the individual motor stepper drivers are 
achieved using the IgniterMotorSetState and TfpMotorSetState commands. 
 
Command ID: 0xC104 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_RESET_MOTION_CONTROLLER 
 
3.1.3.5 
SystemCirFlowState 
The SystemCirFlowState command is designed to be sent from the IOP to inform the ACME 
software about the state of the CIR manifolds.  Scripts can access this information as shown: 
 
If ( SystemCirFlowState.diluentManifoldState == 1) 
{ 
// Diluent manifold is opened 
} 
 
 
Command ID: 0xC107 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_CIR_FLOW_STATE

ACME Igniter Group Command Details 
3.1.5.1 
IgniterDisable 
The IgniterDisable command shuts down power to the igniter.  Specifically, it pulls low the 
primary control (PC) pin on the DC-DC converter that supplies the igniter.  For more 
information see the data sheet for the Vicor V24C12C100BL2 DC-DC converter. 
 
Command ID: 0xC301 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_DISABLE 
 
3.1.5.2 
IgniterPulse 
The IgniterPulse command turns on the igniter for a specified duration and power and then shuts 
it off.  Specifically, it sets the secondary control (SC) pin on the DC-DC converter that supplies 
the igniter to the specfied power voltage and then sets to primary control (PC) pin to 5V which 
enables output to the igniter.  After the specified pulse duration the PC pin is set to 0V, disabling 
output to the igniter. 
 
The power parameter is converted to a control voltage using the equation,

ConversionFactorB in the Igniter group of AcmeConfig.ini.  See Table 32. 
 
The power parameter is limited by MinPowerVolts and MaxPowerVolts in the Igniter group in 
AcmeConfig.ini. These are control voltages not voltages at the igniter.

3.1.5.3 
IgniterMove 
The IgniterMove command moves the igniter arm to the specified absolute postion.  The 
velocity, acceleration, and deceleration values used for the move are specified in 
AcmeConfig.ini.  See Table 32, Group: Igniter, Keys: VelocityCountsPerSec, 
AccelerationCountsPerSecSquared, and DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared.  To go to the home 
(retracted) position specify zero as the position.  In this case the keys used are 
HomeVelocityCountsPerSec, HomeAccelerationCountsPerSecSquared, and 
DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared. 
 
The igniter arm is moved using a trapezoidal velocity versus time profile.  If the acceleration 
parameter is greater than zero then movement begins with a ramp up until the specified velocity 
is achieved.  If the deceleration parameter is greater than zero then there is a ramp down to zero 
velocity.  The duration of the movement is calculated to reach the desired position. 
 
This command takes a few seconds to execute. To shorten the duration between command and 
movement use the IgniterSetupMove or IgniterSetupMoveWithParameters command followed by 
the IgniterExecuteSetupMove command when ready to move. 
 
The motor is a Haydon Kerk 25544-05-004ENG captive linear actuator.  There is no encoder. 
 
Command ID: 0xC303 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_MOVE

FlowMfcSerialCommand 
The FlowMfcSerialCommand command sends the specified raw serial command to the daisy-
chained mass flow controllers.  The start of the string is the address that determines the 
destination controller:  ‘*00’ = MFCA1 Static Mixer, ‘*01’ = MFCA2 Bypass, ‘*02’ = MFCA3 
Fuel.  The command follows the address, for example ‘*01ZRO’ to zero MFCA2, ‘*02MS’ to 
get the state of MFCA3, ‘*00sfl’ to get a status of all configuration items (the command sent 
after power-on) from MFCA1.  See the Teledyne Hastings Digital 300 Software Guide for 
available commands.  Replies to commands are placed in the telemetry text area. 
 
Serial commands are queued.  A command will not be issued until a response is received from 
any prior command or until the prior command response times out.  The response time out is

3.1.6.11 
FlowStepped 
The FlowStepped command steps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or not at all, 
by a specified step size, waits a specified duration, and steps again, repeating until each specified 
maximum flow (or minimum flow if stepping down) is reached, and then leaving the mass flow 
controller at the last flow. 
 
For positive step sizes the setpoints start at the minimum flow and step up until the maximum is 
reached, and does not go above.  For negative step sizes the setpoints start at the maximum and 
step down until the minimum is reached, and does not go below.  
 
Stepping can be stopped with the FlowStopWaveform command, which leaves the flow setpoints 
where they were last, or with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and closes 
all valves, with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the flow at 
the setpoint specified by the command.  Stepping is stopped for a MFC by any other flow 
waveform command if the parameters say to control that MFC, otherwise ongoing stepping 
continues until complete.

3.1.6.12 
FlowRamped 
The FlowRamped command ramps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or not at 
all, at a specified ramp rate for a specified duration, waits a specified hold duration, and ramps 
again, repeating until each specified maximum flow (or minimum flow if ramping down) is 
reached, and then leaving the mass flow controller at the last flow. 
 
For positive ramp rates the setpoints start at the minimum flow and ramp up until the maximum 
is reached, and does not go above.  For negative ramp rates the setpoints start at the maximum 
and ramp down until the minimum is reached, and does not go below.   During the ramp the 
control voltage of the mass flow controller is updated every millisecond. 
 
Ramping can be stopped with the FlowStopWaveform command, which leaves the flow setpoints 
where they were last, with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and closes all 
valves, or with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the flow at 
the setpoint specified by the command.  Ramping is stopped for a MFC by any other flow 
waveform command if the parameters say to control that MFC, otherwise ongoing ramping 
continues until complete.

3.1.7

3.1.7.1 
DataRecordingStart 
The DataRecordingStart command starts recording analog input and output data to a file at a rate 
defined by the Diagnostics/SampleTimeMsec registry entry, see Table 32, which defaults to 8 
msec for 125 Hz sampling. Prior to this command the SystemOpenTestPoint command must be 
issued to define the file name, otherwise the command fails.  The testpointName parameter in the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command results in the data being save to a path and file named 
/payload/sci/testpointName/testpointName_data.csv.   See section 8.1 for the file contents. 
 
Command ID: 0xC501 
Mnemonic: ACME_DATA_RECORDING_START 
 
3.1.7.2 
DataRecordingStop 
The DataRecordingStop command stops acquistion of data started with the DataRecordingStart 
command.  The resultant data file is left open until the SystemCloseTestPoint command is 
received.  Issuing another DataRecordingStart command instead will append data to the existing

differences in the data, which, for example, could include a tell-tale signature in the E-Field 
control voltage. 
 
Command ID: 0xC502

3.1.7.3 
FiberMove 
The FiberMove command translates the thin filament pyrometry (Fiber) fiber array to the 
specified position at the specified velocity or translation rate. Movement acceleration and 
deceleration are registry values specified in AcmeConfig.ini, see Table 32, items 
Fiber/AccelerationCountsPerSecSquared and Fiber/DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared.  The 
response time to start movement is on the order of seconds.  To start movement closer to an 
event use the FiberSetupMove command followed by the FiberExecuteSetupMove command 
when ready to move. 
 
If the specified position exceeds the limit the command is not performed.  The position limit is 
the Fiber/MaxPosition registry value minus the Fiber/FiberToBurnerOffsets registry value (a 
comma-separated string of offsets in order of burner type number) for the burner type specified 
in the SystemDefineSetup command.  See the descriptions of these registry values in Table 32 for 
more information. 
 
Motion can be stopped prematurely using the FiberHaltMove command. 
 
The motor is an Ultramotion HT17 stepper motor linear actuator with 6 inch stroke and encoder.

3.1.7.11 
PmtSetGain 
The PmtSetGain command sets the gain of the specified photo multipler tube. 
 
The gain parameter in this command specifies the volts out of the cube DNx-AO-333 board 
channels AO-25, AO-26, and AO-27, see Table 18.  These voltages are fed through a voltage 
divider of 10 Kohms and 1.21 Kohms before entering the control input on the PMT.  According 
to the PMT data sheet the recommended control voltage is 0.5 V to 1.1 V, corresponding to 4.63 
V to 10.19 V for the gain command parameter, which is limited to a maximum of 10 V. 
 
The equation to convert PMT control input, x, to PMT gain is: 
PMTGain = 2,000,000 * x ^ 8.643856 
,which gives a range of PMTGain from 5000 to 3,500,000 for 0.5 V to 1.1V control input, or 
4.63 V to 10.19 V command gain parameter. 
 
The equation to convert command gain parameter, gain, to PMT gain is: 
 
 
PMTGain = 2,000,000 * (gain/9.2645) ^ 8.643856 
 
The equation to convert PMT gain to command gain parameter, gain, is: 
 
 
gain = 10 ^ (0.115689 * log(PMTGain) + 0.23786213)

of extinction detection.  Detection of extinction using this configuration does not begin until the

averaged over the specified duration.  These averages are compared to the specified limts.  The

The EFieldSetVoltage command controls the voltage present on the electric field mesh.  The 
voltage parameter, which is desired voltage on the mesh, is converted to control voltage output to 
the cube DNx-AO-333 board AO-4 (HV_CTRL) signal. See Table 18.  The conversion is 
according to the equation: 
 
𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑟𝑜𝑙 𝑉𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒= −𝐵+ √𝐵2 −4𝐶(𝐴−𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒)
2𝐶
 
 
,where A, B, and C are items in AcmeConfig.ini, See Table 32, and depend on whether the 
negative or positive supply is being used.  For the negative supply the names are: 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorA 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorB 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorC 
For the positive supply the names are: 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorA 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorB 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorC 
The SystemDefineSetup command tells the software which polarity of E-Field supply is installed. 
 
The reverse equation is: 
𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒= 𝐶∗𝑐𝑣2 + 𝐵∗𝑐𝑣+ 𝐴 
, where cv is control voltage and A,B,andC are as above. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply.

3.1.8.3 
EFieldSteppedSignal 
The EFieldSteppedSignal command steps the electric field voltage between a specfied minimum 
and maximum voltage with steps of a specified size and duration and back down (or up) for a 
specified number of cycles.  One cycle is a series of steps in one direction, therefore set cycles to 
a factor of 2 to perform complete up and down waveforms. 
 
The maximum and minimum voltages are not violated even if the step voltage does not divide 
evenly between them. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply. 
 
Special cases: 
- 
stepVoltage < 0 starts at maxVoltage and steps to minVoltage (and back up if cycles 
> 1). 
- 
Cycles = 1 produces a single staircase. 
- 
stepVoltage = (maxVoltage – minVoltage) produces a square waveform.

3.1.8.5 
EFieldRectangularWave 
The EFieldRectangularWave command is an EFieldSteppedSignal command but there is a 
second step with its own size and duration.  The two step sizes can be the same or opposite 
polarity. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply. 
 
Special cases: 
- 
If (stepAVoltage + stepBVoltage) < 0 the sequence starts at maxVoltage. 
- 
Cycles = 1 produces a single step sequence between min and max voltage. 
- 
stepAVoltage = -1 * stepBVoltage produces a square wave between minVoltage and 
minVoltage + stepAVoltage.

Mnemonic: ACME_EFIELD_RECTANGULAR_WAVE

The IOP requests telemetry at 1 Hz from all packages in the system, including the PI Location (PIL).  See Section A.2, FCF Telemetry

items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 
 
1 
 
1 June 2019 
30-day Operational Accomplishments Report  
… for the International Space Station (ISS) Increments 57 and 58 
 
ACME 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments 
E-FIELD Flames 
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames 
E-FIELD Flames is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, 
which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels 
in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  The investigation was carried out in two rounds of 
tests, where the first (with ACME’s coflow burner) occurred in Increment 55 and the second (with 
a gas-jet burner) began in Increment 56 and ended in Increment 57.  As a result, there is nothing 
to be reported for Increment 58. 
 
Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project 
Scientist, who is the primary contact for E-FIELD Flames and ACME information. 
 
 
 
Principal Investigator (PI): 
Prof. Derek Dunn-Rankin, University of California, Irvine, CA 
PI project scientist: 
 
Dr. Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien, University of California, Irvine, CA 
Lead collaborator: 
Prof. Sergey Minaev, Far Eastern Federal University, Vladivostok, 
Russia 
NASA Project Scientist (PS): Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH 
PS team member: 
Dr. Uday G. Hegde, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, OH 
 
 
 
I.  Introduction 
The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment was 
conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  In this experiment, an 
electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts was established between the burner and a flat, 
circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.  The motion of the 
charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong 
electric field.  The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting 
behavior of the flame.  Measurements were made of electric-field strength, the ion current 
passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, 
soot, and stability.  Conducting the tests in microgravity allowed for great simplifications in the 
analysis of ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the 
development of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth.

items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 
 
2 
 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a 
result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the 
soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer.  The purpose of the E-FIELD Flames 
experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the 
electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical 
benefit.  For example, electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel-lean conditions 
with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the 
electric field.  As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic.  
It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the 
residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame.  The experiment contributes to our 
critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields. 
 
More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: 
A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as 
functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert 
(nitrogen) in the fuel. 
B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion 
current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) 
flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. 
C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of 
luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions 
of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to 
the fuel stream. 
D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize 
the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven 
wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. 
 
The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of 
flame and electric field conditions.  The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric-field voltage and 
polarity were the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment.  Tests were conducted 
with methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of 
soot-producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting.  They were carried out with both 
a simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion 
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  Tests with the coflow burner were conducted with and without 
a coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner 
to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame.  The coflow burner also provided a different 
electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane).  
In a typical test, the mesh electrode was energized at increasing potentials (relative to the 
burner), where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field 
strength was measured.  The field strength was changed in repeated steps or was instead 
smoothly ramped. 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-

items.title: PSI-22_Reports_2019 - E-FIELD Flames 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 20190601.pdf
items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 
 
3 
 
driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  
Therefore, the flicker in the E-FIELD Flames was a result of electric body forces alone.  Length 
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.  
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be 
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger 
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in 
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot 
free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and 
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  For example, chemi-ion species, 
electronically excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, 
making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry.  
With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex 
nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion 
application. 
 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
  
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the 
ISS crew.  The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  
The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it may alternately 
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry 
stream.  For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or 
soot limit.  This was not done during Increments 55-56 or 57-58, where the console 
commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed 
in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 
 
4 
 
III.  Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
A total of 219 flames were ignited for the E-FIELD Flames experiment, with 142 and 77 
respectively ignited during Increments 55-56 and 57-58.  Note that the investigation’s 
testing was completed during Increment 57, so no flames were ignited during Increment 
58.  The first and second rounds of testing respectively occurred in March-May 2018 and 
September-November 2018.  The two rounds of tests resulted in 120 and 99 ignited 
flames conducted with coflow and gas-jet burners, respectively.  The coflow burner was 
developed for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD 
Flames’ second round occurred between the two rounds of the E-FIELD Flames 
experiment.  The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was intentionally planned 
years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that 
knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. 
 
E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests 
are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  
Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane 
(CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot 
given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting 
because of its carbon double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel 
and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel 
and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched 
with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on 
a volume basis).  Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 
50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  But the ACME 
hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing 
for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.  In all cases, 
the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  
 
No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for E-FIELD Flames; all of the ISS results were 
electronically transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all currently 
planned ACME experiments. 
 
A summary log of the E-FIELD Flames ignited for E-FIELD Flames during Increments 55-57, 
including a limited overview of the test conditions, is found on the next page in Table 1.

B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
1. Mission anomalies  
The CIR’s IPSU-1 Image Processing and Storage Unit, which is used with the High Bit-
Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera and the collimated illumination package, was 
only intermittently operable at the end of Increment 56 and was not operable at the 
start of Increment 57.  Those capabilities were not seen as critical for E-FIELD Flames,

ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 
 
6 
 
where the illumination is significantly blocked by the mounting bracket for the mesh 
electrode.  Therefore, the tests on Sept. 26 (18269), Oct. 1 (18274), Oct. 9 (18282), 
Oct. 12 (18285), and Oct. 17 (18290) were conducted without HiBMs imaging or the 
CIR illumination.  It was later determined to be an issue with a cable connection, which 
was corrected by astronaut Alex Gerst on Oct. 22 (18295) when he carried out other 
ACME tasks.  As a result, the subsequent E-FIELD Flames tests were carried out using 
the HiBMs camera and illumination package. 
 
2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data   
E-FIELD Flames tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the controlling 
software script), where that was typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the 
igniter.  As a result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt.   
The aborts normally occurred because of communication issues with IPSU-1.  These 
are infrequent, but there are some days when tests aborted repeatedly.  
 
Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite.  The first test of 
the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been 
sufficiently primed.  Ignition was sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the 
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of 
the igniter glow rather than a flame.  As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter 
is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite.  
This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* 
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module.  The OH* 
chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited 
flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible 
spectrum.  However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to 
false ignition detection. 
 
ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and 
synthetic air (i.e., 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen, on a volume basis) have 
unfortunately not always performed adequately.  The fuel and especially nitrogen 
flows sometimes oscillate. Furthermore, the MFC used for the ‘air’ coflow behaves as 
if it is sticking in a few places, where the flow rate won’t linearly ramp when 
commanded (as required for the CLD Flame experiment).  It tends to stick in some 
places and then abruptly overshoot where that has sometimes been seen to 
extinguish the flame.  As a result, mass flow controllers are tested - without flames - 
after they are first installed.  Adjustments are often then made to (1) the settings that 
control when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) 
settings.  This ACME activity has involved significant testing, separate from flame 
tests, and has taken place on 17333, 17334, 17347, 17354, 18008, 18022, 18038, 
18046, 18143, 18241, 19059, and 19112.  In this regard, there are an assortment of 
MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gases.  While the MFC 
adjustments have been beneficial, they have not eliminated all gas flow problems.  It 
was seen that nitrogen oscillations tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow

items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 
 
7 
 
was implemented so that the oscillations would typically end before the flame 
measurements.  That approach was partially successful and was introduced during E-
FIELD Flames’ first round.  Later, a procedure of re-zeroing the MFCs prior to each test 
was also implemented during E-FIELD Flames’ second round.  A replacement MFC for 
the ‘air’ coflow is being prepared for spaceflight, where a limited third round of CLD 
Flame testing is being planned to accomplish its extinction limit objective.  
 
C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The number of flames ignited significantly exceeds the planned tests which were (1) 
specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD), 
using the gas-jet burner, and (2) later expanded to include tests with the coflow burner 
to partially make up for science loss resulting from the slow response time of the high-
voltage power supply.  Following the revision, a total of 74 E-FIELD Flames tests were 
identified as required.  In contrast, 219 flames were ignited in the experiment, so nearly 
three times as many flames were ignited than required.  
 
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not available for all tests.  As 
discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 was not working at the beginning of the second round 
of testing, preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination 
package.  Those are not critical for E-FIELD Flames, so tests continued without their use. 
 
Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is 
done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be 
managed per test day.  Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice 
some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.  
This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing 
within the project constraints. 
 
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware.  But neglecting that 
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually 
become ‘hot’ over time.  While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, 
they are a degradation of the image quality. 
 
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there 
is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available 
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).  In this regard, 
note that the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is 
equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS).  
 
Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has 
been secured and E-FIELD Flames is considered to be highly successful.

items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 
 
8 
 
D. Status of Data Analysis 
Data from the tests making up the E-FIELD Flames experiment includes video recordings 
from the operations camera for general flame behavior, high resolution images from the 
ACME data camera at various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame 
luminosity, intensified camera images, and non-imaging data at 125 Hz.  The non-imaging 
data file is processed using Matlab scripts (modified from those developed by CLD Flame 
researchers) to separately show trends of ion current and flame luminosity as a function 
of the applied field, and the flame parameters (fuel, flowrate, burner type).  The PMT data 
is also extracted to evaluate flame luminosity oscillations.  Image data is processed using 
the OMA software (also developed and used by CLD Flame researchers).   
 
The overall data volume is large with a storage limit of 127,000 MB per test day.  All of 
the data has been downloaded to the hard drive with a backup system at UC Irvine.  At 
this stage, the data has been sorted into appropriate segments so that comparisons can 
be made between burner geometries (jet versus coflow from the prior round of testing), 
fuel type and dilution (methane versus ethylene; no dilution, modest dilution, high 
dilution) and fuel flow velocity.  The fuel flow velocity and dilution conditions were 
sometimes selected to hold total carbon flux into the flame constant.  At this stage, the 
analysis remains comparative and qualitative, to show the major differences in behavior 
in microgravity and normal-gravity (1-g) flames, and to show particularly how buoyancy 
modifies the electrical response of the flames. 
 
E. Preliminary Research Findings 
Distinctly different results were seen in E-FIELD Flames’ second round tests with the gas-
jet burner when compared with the first round tests with the coflow burner.  For example, 
the ion current response to the electric field strength with an upward ion driven wind in 
microgravity is a clear parabolic trend (which is similar to the trend observed in 1-g flames 
with the coflow burner as presented in the prior report).  The parabolic behavior is evident 
even with the strong oscillations observed during the rise.  This rising trend is not 
observed with the coflow burner.   
 
The behavior of the soot and its charge state are complicated since in the regions of high 
field strength, particularly near the fuel tube where the field lines converge, soot can emit 
or collect free charges.  Hence, the soot transport is driven directly by the field and by the 
ion-driven wind (and thermophoresis) which means it can travel differentially to the bulk 
flow.  These various transport elements can push the soot through the flame to burnout, 
hold it in stasis in the flame for additional growth, or drive it to the burner where it 
accumulates.  More work is needed to sort through these elements. 
 
Positive electric field for 100% methane fuel with jet burner  
The preliminary findings for the gas-jet burner in this section highlight the representative 
information of electric fields applied to a small hydrocarbon flame in the 0-g condition.  
The ISS tests covered a wide range of conditions which allowed the flame to settle as its

image was captured with the color camera and the intensified camera.  The total flame 
luminosity and the ion current were also recorded in all cases.  Figure 1 shows example 
flame images representative of the jet tests conducted with methane as fuel.  The voltage 
is indicated as the nominal field strength (kV/cm).  Since the physical spacing from the 
burner to the mesh is 35 mm, 1.16 kV/cm represents nominal potential of around 4000 V 
across the flame.  It is important to note that with the sharp-edged jet burner, there is an 
electric field concentration near the burner tip, so the field in that region will be stronger 
than is indicated by the nominal field strength and stronger than would be seen for the 
coflow burner where the coflow portion of the burner acts as a planar electrode to 
mitigate the field concentration at the jet burner’s tip. 
 
 
Figure 1. Flame images observed from the data camera at 19 cm/s methane jet with 
positive field applied. (Unit: kV/cm) 
 
The very first image of each condition, e.g., at 0.05 kV/cm, demonstrates the initial 
voltage stage before the voltage sweep test commences.  The jet flames are relatively 
more stable initially and less stable under high voltage than the previously reported 
flames using a coflow burner with no coflow [Chien et al., Ion Current and Flame Changes 
with Electric Fields in Microgravity, WSSCI Pasadena 2019].  As the positive field is applied 
to the jet, the flame becomes both narrower and shorter.  An immediate change is the 
appearance of bright soot at the flame tip.  With an increase of electric field strength, the 
soot region diminishes as the flame shrinks. 
 
The voltage was increased 350 volts per step and held at each voltage for two seconds. 
The ion current data rate was 125 Hz and the monitored current fluctuation at the same 
voltage step is shown in the graph.  The ion current to electric field strength (i.e., i-v) graph 
is plotted for 24 and 19 cm/s flow velocity in Figure 2, where the current initially increases 
parabolically with the applied voltage.  The ion current corresponds to the flame 
appearance in that the current increases and reaches a peak at the most compact flame, 
e.g., at a field strength of 1.36 kV/cm for a 19 cm/s burner flow (as seen in Figure 2b).  At

items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 
 
10 
 
that maximum, the soot is almost gone (as seen in Figure 1).  The flame base starts rising 
slightly around the current peak and lifts higher, with one side of the reaction wing 
attached to the tube, as the electric field increases further.  The flame is not always lifted 
at the same edge of the burner tube; therefore, the attached reaction wing sometimes 
rotates along the tube edge with approximately the same lift angle under the same 
electric field strength.  Otherwise, the lifted edge flame remains relatively stable.  With 
further increases in the electric field strength, the flame starts fluctuating and a distinct 
dancing phenomenon can be seen from the i-v curve where the ion current oscillates 
strongly at the same field strength.  The fluctuation crosses more than 3.5 A (between 
~1.2 to 5 A) and reaches 5.0 A for the 24 cm/s case.  Similarly, this oscillation at the 
same voltage is observed for 19 cm/s with the ion current spanning around 2.5 A (~1.4 
to 4 A) and reaching 4.0 A; corresponding flame images are shown as 1.86 and 2.16 
kV/cm in Figure 1.  These very high peak values may represent an incipient corona or 
discharge event.  The combustion extinguishes with the oscillations at 1.95 kV/cm for 24 
cm/s and 2.16 kV/cm for 19 cm/s.  
 
The flame geometries and soot distribution under the electric field influence clearly differ 
when comparing the gas-jet burner results with those from the earlier coflow burner tests 
without a coflow (i.e., with the same jet flow for each), where the annulus of the coflow 
burner acted as a planar electrode.  But the maximum amount of ions produced within 
the flame (as evidenced by the ion current reaching the plateau) is similar for the case 
where the fuel flow velocity matches at 19 cm/s.  The current also peaks around the same 
field strength per unit distance.  Moreover, the oscillation behavior only exists in the jet 
burner experiment and furthermore influences the ion current monitoring due to the 
unstable flame behavior responding to the high field strength.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 
 
12 
 
 
Figure 3. Flame appearance as a function of field strength observed from the data camera 
at 19 cm/s methane jet with negative field applied. (Unit: kV/cm) 
 
The ion current (as seen in Figure 4’s i-v curve) also increases with the field strength but 
differently than with the positive field at is has no clear curved slope.  Instead, it decreases 
parabolically after reaching the current peak.  The current peak corresponds to the most 
compact flame at 0.34 kV/cm for 19 cm/s and 0.43 kV/cm for 24 cm/s.  The peak ion 
current is 0.53 and 0.55 A, as shown in Figures 6b and 6a, respectively.  Soot also appears 
at the flame tip but with a wider distribution along the reaction sheet.  The soot reduces 
with increasing negative field strength, and it disappears at 0.84 kV/cm (as seen in Figure 
3) along the parabolic decay line after passing the ion current peak.  The flame width and 
height also expand after the most compact flame (at the peak current).  This trend is 
demonstrated in the second-row of images in Figure 4.  Notice that there are several 
sparkler-like particles, presumably of soot, at 1.24 and 2.04 kV/cm.  Further evaluation of 
this sparking is underway.
