items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 
 
14 
 
 
 
Figure 5. Flame appearance as a function of field strength observed from the data camera 
at 19 cm/s methane jet with negative field applied. (Unit: kV/cm) 
 
The ion current to the electric field strength graph of 19 cm/s, shown in Figure 6, reveals 
a similar trend to Figure 2 for the 100% methane jet, and further details appeared in this 
condition.  The ions are extracted from the flame gradually by the electric field, and with 
the increasing electric field the current rises.  After reaching the ion current peak around 
1.1 kV/cm, the flame has not yet oscillated as had occurred in the pure methane case.  
The ion current reduces and then rises back up in a parabolic behavior.  The flame starts 
fluctuating around 1.75 kV/cm with the positive field strength increase.  Further analysis 
is needed to understand the field strength to current behavior as a function of 
hydrocarbon content, and also with the influence from burner geometries in the 
microgravity environment. 
Figure 6. Ion current as a function of the field strength and fuel velocity at 19 cm/s 
methane.

items.title: PSI-22_Reports_2019 - E-FIELD Flames 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 20190601.pdf
items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 
 
15 
 
 
In all of the i-v curves, the ion current data points at each field strength stretch across 
~0.1 A for each step, which are the jagged features from the spikes following a voltage 
step change that are mostly associated with the transient capacitance of the system when 
a rapid voltage step is requested.  These overshoots notwithstanding, the i-v curves follow 
smooth and reproducible trajectories. The wide range of the ion current after the 
saturation plateau is due instead to the flame oscillation.  
 
This report shows the initial results of the E-FIELD Flames experiment using the gas-jet 
burner in the International Space Station (ISS).  The positive field allows the soot to 
concentrate and compresses the flame into a high current density thermal source.  The 
flames demonstrate an unpredicted oscillation before extinguishing with increasing field 
strength.  This oscillating phenomenon was not observed during the tests with the coflow 
burner from the first round, with the exception of a case that introduced the airflow at 
30 cm/s which increased the surface reaction while the flame tended to balance between 
electric field effects, ions, and charged soot. The negative field allows the flame to 
maintain its spherical characteristic in microgravity. The yellow soot appears for both of 
the electric field directions within the flame around the tip and disappears with increasing 
field strength after reaching the current peak.  The role of soot in the i-v behavior of these 
flames requires further investigation. 
 
Early E-FIELD Flame results from the ISS testing were presented in following oral and 
poster presentations: 
1. Derek Dunn-Rankin and Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien, “Electrical Field Effects on Laminar 
Diffusion Flames,” 11th Multi-Agency Coordinating Committee for Combustion 
Research (MACCCR) Annual Fuel and Combustion Research Review, Livermore, 
CA, 9-11 April 2018. (oral presentation) 
2. Chien, Y.-C., Tinajero, J., Stocker, D., Hegde, U. and Dunn-Rankin, D. “Electric Field 
Effects on Flames in Microgravity on the International Space Station,” Central 
States Section Combustion Institute Spring Technical Meeting, St. Paul, MN, 20-22 
April 2018. (conference paper and oral presentation) 
3. Chien, Y.-C., Tinajero, J., Stocker, D., Hegde, U. and Dunn-Rankin, D. “Small 
Diffusion Flames under the influences of Electric-Field: Microgravity and Gravity,” 
37th International Symposium on Combustion, Dublin, Ireland, 29 July to 3 Aug. 
2018.  (Work-in-Progress poster) 
4. Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien, Jesse Tinajero, Dennis Stocker, Uday Hegde, Derek Dunn-
Rankin, “Microgravity Experiments of Electric Field Effects on Laminar 
Ethylene/Air Diffusion Flames,” 34th Annual Meeting of the American Society for 
Gravitational and Space Research (ASGSR) Meeting, Rockville, MD, 31 Oct. to 3 
Nov. 2018. (oral presentation) 
5. Chien, Y.-C., Tinajero, J., Stocker, D., Hegde, U. and Dunn-Rankin, D. “Ion Current 
and Flame Changes with Electric Fields in Microgravity,” 11th U.S. National 
Combustion Meeting, Pasadena, CA, 24-27 March 2019. (conference paper and 
oral presentation)

items.text:
Soot and Electric Fields
Soot particle charge
Soot particles may be originally charged, especially if they are formed 
through an ionic route 
Soot particles gain a net charge through ion-attachment 
Measurements indicate that in the hottest zone, soot particles may be 
charged to equilibrium, but this is not always the case and the initial 
particle charge seems to depend upon the material burnt 
Net charge of soot particles in flames is generally positive even in the 
flame region where a large excess of electrons exist
Soot particle primary size is found to be ~20 nm in non-electric flames; 
size can be reduced in electric fields
Electric field effects on soot in laminar diffusion flames
Ion wind can induce partial premixing (changes reaction zone)
Ion precursors can be removed or reduced in number
Soot residence time can be changed (increased or decreased)

Microgravity Justification
• High Quality Microgravity -- confounding effects of 
buoyancy
– Ion driven wind velocity approximately equal to buoyant wind 
velocity so convection and mixing effects are difficult to separate
– Complex flow patterns created in 1-g
– Stability of weak flames (liftoff and blowout) – as in CLD Flame
• Extended Duration -- time scales to reproducible state
– Electrical response (RC time constant)
– Ion transport time
– Ion wind convection
– Soot formation and transport
– Flow field establishment
– Thermal inertia effects

items.text:
Extended Microgravity –
Experience of other investigators
•
CLD Flame discussion showed the necessity for high quality microgravity for 
near limit lifted co-flow flames (i.e., buoyant mixing has substantial effect)
•
Co-flow flame experiments showed problems with g-jitter on parabolic flights
•
Z.-G. Yuan et. al showed difficulties in achieving steady flames in a 2.2 sec. 
drop tower.
Graph reproduced from: 1100 AIAA-
2003-0812, Z. Yuan and U. Hegde
Note: if not carried out 
sequentially, a single EFIELD 
Flame measurement requires 
both time to reach a stable 
initial condition and time to 
reach the final condition

items.text:
Experimental Objectives
Understand flame ion production and use ions to control 
diffusion flames by modifying local convection (via the ion 
wind) and local species transport (via direct ion drift)
A) Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and 
chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel flow rate and the 
amount of inert in the fuel.
B) Obtain the time response of flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, 
and ion current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of 
total fuel flow rate and amount of inert added to the fuel stream.
C) Evaluate and control sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction 
and location of luminous soot) in relation to the electric field 
voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel flow rate 
and amount of inert added to the fuel stream.
D) Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied 
voltage to characterize and control the combustion behavior of 
near-limit lifted flames in a coflow burner.

items.title: PSI-22_Presentations_Lopez-Camara et al 2018 Numerical Simulations of Laminar Non-premixed CH4-Air Jet Flames.pdf
items.text:
•
The extruded burner geometry shows an I-V curve similar to the one obtained in the experiments in a 1g 
environment. Changes in the boundary condition have to still be performed.
•
The saturation point in the I-V curve obtained using the flush burner geometry simulation is aligning with 
the one obtained experimentally. The peak of positive charges (H3O+) that reach the upper electrode (anode) 
is displaced from the center, aligning with the experimental observations. However, simulations at sub-
saturation regimes show that higher e-fields are needed in the simulation in order to get the same ion 
currents (z-direction) than the ones obtained experimentally. This might be caused by the interaction 
between burner (positive electrode) and reaction zone. More investigation has to be performed in order to 
clarify this phenomena.
Next steps:
•
Define why sub-saturation flush burner geometry simulations show that higher electric fields are needed to 
achieve the ion currents obtained experimentally.
•
Proceed by simulating jet geometry burner flames at 1g.

IAC-08-A2.1.07 
 
COMBUSTION RESEARCH ON THE INTERNATIONAL SPACE STATION 
 
Terence F. O’Malley 
NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, USA 
tfomalley@nasa.gov  
 
William A. Sheredy 
NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, USA 
William.A.Sheredy@nasa.gov 
 
Dennis P Stocker 
NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, USA 
Dennis.P.Stocker@nasa.gov 
 
ABSTRACT 
 
This paper will discuss recent and future plans for combustion research on the International Space 
Station (ISS). Results from the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), will be discussed and 
future utilization plans for the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) will be detailed 
 
The initial payload in the CIR is the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), which will perform 
the Droplet Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity experiment (FLEX). MDCA will also perform the FLEX-2 
set of experiments which include the following objectives: Investigate bi-component fuels, Examine the 
influence of sub-buoyant convective flows, Study practical fuels, Extend single droplet studies to binary 
arrays of droplets. 
 
The next payload being developed for the CIR is the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments 
(ACME) insert. This group of investigations will focus on gaseous combustion experiments. Some of the 
objectives of this research include: combustion structure and stability near flammability limits; soot 
inception, surface growth, and oxidation processes; emission reduction through nitrogen exchange; and 
combustion stability enhancements via an electric field. 
 
The third payload envisioned for the CIR is the Flammability Assessment of Materials for Exploration 
(FLAME) insert. FLAME will examine critical parameters for modeling material flammability in three flow 
configurations: boundary layer, wake and stagnation flows. 
 
 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
With the launch and installation of both the 
European Space Agency’s Columbus Research 
Laboratory 
and 
the 
Japan 
Aerospace 
Exploration 
Agency’s Japanese 
Experiment 
Module/Kibo in the past year, the opportunities 
for research onboard the International Space 
Station 
(ISS) 
are 
increasing. 
Combustion 
research in micro-gravity is one of NASA’s 
significant research disciplines on ISS. This 
paper will outline recent research and current 
plans for combustion research in micro-gravity.  
 
SMOKE AND AEROSOL MEASUREMENTS 
EXPERIMENT 
 
The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment 
(SAME) 
is 
a 
combustion 
science 
flight 
experiment that investigates the formation of 
smoke aerosol (solid particulate and liquid 
droplets) in microgravity.   The Principal 
Investigator (PI) is Dr. David Urban, NASA 
Glenn Research Center.   The purpose of SAME 
is to make measurements of smoke particle size 
distributions in order to enable the design of 
future smoke detection systems that are more 
sensitive and specific.   The SAME data is

items.text:
2
important to the success of the Vision for Space 
Exploration by improving crew health, safety and 
mission assurance in that it provides data 
necessary to ensure reliable detection of 
incipient spacecraft fires should one occur 
during an exploration mission.    
 
The absence of buoyant flow increases the 
residence time in microgravity fires, causing 
substantial changes in flame structure and 
consequently, changes in the properties of the 
smoke produced. In particular, the increased 
residence time in the high temperature zone 
where the smoke is formed can increase the 
opportunity for growth in the size of the smoke 
particulate.  However, no measurements of the 
properties of smoke from microgravity fires had 
been made at the time when the detectors were 
designed for both the space shuttle and the 
International Space Station (ISS).  This absence 
of data caused the designers to base the 
designs on 1-g information and the current state 
of the art. As a result, the two detectors were 
designed using different detection technologies 
which 
have 
very 
different 
particle 
size 
sensitivities.  
 
The SAME experiment studied smoke produced 
from four typical spacecraft materials including 
Teflon™, 
Kapton™, cellulose and silicone 
rubber, and a reference material, dibutyl-
phthalate (which was deposited on a porous 
wick). The samples of each of these materials 
were tested at different airflow rates, pyrolysis 
temperatures and smoke aging durations. SAME 
measured moments of smoke particulate size 
distributions using three separate instruments. 
Two 
are 
industrial 
hygiene 
instruments 
manufactured by TSI, Inc. and one is a modified 
residential smoke detector. Smoke detectors 
used on the ISS and Space Shuttle were 
included in the SAME system in order to 
characterize 
their 
microgravity performance 
under controlled conditions. 
 
SAME was launched for delivery to the ISS on 
STS-118 on August 8, 2007, and it was installed 
in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) on 
September 5, 2007.   Flight operations began on 
September 9 and were completed on October 5, 
2007.   In all, 47 test points were conducted with 
the 30 samples provided, with 17 additional 
repeat points being conducted primarily with the 
reference sample material (dibutyl-phthalate). 
Data analysis is underway, but initial results 
indicate that the experiment was very successful 
and will provide the intended measurements 
needed to guide the rational design of future 
spacecraft smoke detectors.  Preliminary results 
indicate that the smoke particulate produced in 
low-gravity from the four solid materials all had 
count mean diameters smaller  than 300 nm, 
suggesting that discriminating smoke from 
spacecraft dust could possibly be achieved by 
detecting in the sub-micrometer range.  This 
would require the design of a detector that was 
more sensitive to small particulate than the ISS 
detector, but was not overly sensitive to large 
particulate (dust). 
 
 
Fig. 1 SAME  in the MSG onboard the ISS. 
 
COMBUSTION INTEGRATED RACK  
 
The 
cornerstone 
of 
NASA’s 
combustion 
research program is the Fluids and Combustion 
Facility (FCF) Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR). The FCF is designed to support physical 
and biological research as well as technology 
experiments in space that will support both the 
vision for space exploration and non-exploration 
research.  The FCF consists of two modular, 
reconfigurable racks: the CIR, shown in Fig.2 
and the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR). The initial 
payload in the CIR is the Multi-User Droplet 
Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) and the initial

3
FIR payload is the Light Microscopy Module 
(LMM) These payloads along with the racks will 
be in the U. S. Laboratory Module and will 
operate primarily by telescience with only 
reconfiguration and maintenance performed by 
the crew. 
 
 
Fig.  2:  The Fluids and Combustion Facility 
Combustion Integrated Rack.  At the top 
is 
the 
Fuel/Oxidizer 
Management 
Assembly, 
in 
the 
center 
is 
the 
combustion chamber, and at the bottom 
are the Electrical Power Conversion Unit 
(left) and Input/ Output Processor (right). 
 
The CIR will accommodate experiments that 
address critical needs in the areas of spacecraft 
fire prevention, detection and suppression, as 
well as basic research. 
 
 
 
COMMON RACK COMPONENTS 
 
This section describes the subsystems common 
to both FCF racks.  The use of common 
hardware reduces the design, development and 
life cycle costs, increases crew efficiency by 
using common procedures, and allows for 
common sparing on orbit.  (The sections on 
each individual rack describe the subsystems 
unique to each one.) 
 
International Standard Payload Rack 
The International Standard Payload Rack (ISPR) 
provides the supporting and mounting elements 
for the CIR and FIR subsystems and mechanical 
connections to the U. S. Laboratory Module.  A 
set of slides mounted on the vertical sides of the 
rack provides attachment for an optics bench.  
The optics bench can translate out and rotate 
down for access to both sides as shown in Fig. 
3.  Both racks provide bi-fold doors with upper 
and lower halves. The doors are closed during 
powered operations. 
 
Electrical Power System 
The Electrical Power Conversion Unit (EPCU) 
functions as the main power conditioning unit 
and power supply for each rack.  The EPCU 
takes the 120 VDC power provided by the ISS 
and converts it to the 28 VDC required by most 
FCF packages.  In addition, it makes available 
120 VDC for the Fire Detection and Suppression 
System smoke detector, the Active Rack 
Isolation System controller, and, if it is required, 
to the sub-rack experiment.  A total of 1600 W is 
available at 28 VDC and 1450 W at 120 VDC. 
 
Environmental Control Subsystems 
The 
FCF 
provides 
environmental 
control 
subsystems (ECS) that remove heat, provide fire 
detection 
and 
suppression, 
and 
provide 
interfaces to the ISS-supplied gases and 
vacuum vent lines. 
 
The Water Thermal Control System (WTCS) 
provides water-cooling of all FCF equipment by 
removing their heat and transferring it to the ISS 
Internal Thermal Control System Moderate 
Temperature Loop.  The WTCS provides cooling 
to the Air Thermal Control Unit (ATCU) and 
other FCF hardware in the primary loop.  A 
secondary loop may cool payload hardware as 
required.  Flexible hoses with quick disconnects 
allow for reconfiguration.  The WTCS can 
remove up to 3000 Watts of waste thermal 
energy.

4
 
Fig. 3:  The Combustion Integrated Rack with 
the optics bench translated and rotated.  
Visible on the back of the optics bench is 
the combustion chamber. 
 
The ATCU resides in the top of each rack.  It 
contains an air/water heat exchanger and two 
fans that circulate cooling air to the rack 
packages.  In the CIR, the fans draw warm air 
from the rear of the rack and push it through the 
heat exchanger into the optics bench.  In the 
FIR, the fans draw air from the optics bench in 
the rear of the rack and push it through the heat 
exchanger into the front of the rack.  The ATCU 
can remove up to 1650 Watts of waste thermal 
energy. 
 
The Fire Detection and Suppression System 
provides detection and suppression in case of 
fire in the rack.  The ATCU provides rack air 
circulation past an ISS smoke detector.    The 
ISS shuts off power to the rack if the detector 
triggers.  Then, if required, a crewmember could 
discharge an ISS Portable Fire Extinguisher 
containing carbon dioxide into a hole on the front 
panel of the rack to extinguish any fire. 
 
The Gas Interface Subsystem provides access 
to ISS-provided gaseous nitrogen and Vacuum 
Exhaust and Resource Systems.  Nitrogen gas 
is available up to 827 kPa (120 psia).  The VES 
provides for removal of waste gases from the 
system.  The VRS is a low-flow system used 
primarily to maintain rack sub-systems at a 
vacuum.  The rack sub-systems or experiment 
gases must meet ISS-allowable limits for 
contaminants to be eligible for venting through 
the ISS vent line. 
 
Avionics Subsystems 
The CIR and the FIR use several common 
avionics 
subsystems: 
 
the 
Input/ 
Output 
Processor (IOP), Image Processing and Storage 
Unit (IPSU), and the Station Support Computer 
(SSC). 
 
The IOP is the main processor within the CIR 
and the FIR.  It provides rack-level health and 
status 
monitoring, 
command 
and 
data 
processing, data management, control functions, 
and time synchronization.  The IOP provides 
communications with the ISS through Ethernet 
and low and high rate data lines.  It stores data 
on two 180 GB removable hard drives prior to 
downlinking by the ISS.  The IOP accepts 
commands from either the ground by uplink to 
the ISS, or from the SSC. 
 
Either rack can use common IPSUs.  The IPSU 
supports a variety of camera formats.  Two 
models of the common IPSU are available:  the 
C-IPSU and the C-IPSU-A.  The C-IPSU 
supports image acquisition from high-speed 
digital and IEEE 1394 (Firewire).  The C-IPSU-A 
supports image acquisition from IEEE 1394 or 
analog video.  The IPSUs have two 36 GB hard 
drives and provide analog video output for 
experiment monitoring. 
 
The SSC is a laptop computer supplied by the 
ISS that connects to the IOP.  It mounts on the 
front of the rack.  The SSC allows the crew to 
view all science, health and status, and 
command screens.  The crew can use the SSC 
to communicate with the FCF racks. 
 
Space Acceleration Measurement System 
A Space Acceleration Measurement System 
(SAMS) triaxial sensor head measures the 
microgravity acceleration environment in the 
rack at its location on the optics bench.  SAMS 
can measure microgravity accelerations from 
1x10-6 to 0.01 g and provide three orthogonal 
measurements from 0.01 to 200 Hz.

Software 
The FCF makes extensive use of software 
because it is designed to operate primarily 
without crew involvement.  The Telescience 
Support Center (TSC) at the NASA Glenn 
Research Center will support flight and ground 
operations.  The software accommodates new 
hardware and software upgrades.  It is modular 
to minimize the amount of new software required 
for a new configuration.  The ground operators 
can modify the flight software by uplinking new 
software from the ground. 
 
The FCF flight software performs command and 
data processing, control, caution and warning, 
health and status monitoring, and timing 
functions.  The operating system is VxWorks®.  
Programming languages are C++ and Java.  
Common subsystems software interacts with the 
IOP, ATCU, WTCS, C-IPSU, C-IPSU-A, and 
SSC.  Packages unique to the CIR or the FIR 
have rack-specific software written for them. 
 
The 
FCF 
ground 
software 
performs 
commanding of the flight unit, and receiving and 
viewing telemetry.  FCF sends much of the data 
to the Earth via downlinking.  The TSC receives 
and processes the payload data, and provides it 
to the experiment team, who can then use it to 
plan further experiment operations.  The FCF 
operators at the TSC will have operator 
interfaces to display health and status, data, 
command and control, crew display, operator 
logs, and reporting.  The TSC will archive the 
data for a ten-year period.  Ground support 
units, crew trainers, and simulators also use 
ground software.   
 
 
CIR COMPONENTS 
 
The CIR contains most of the hardware and 
software necessary for conducting combustion 
experiments.  It will accommodate a range of 
combustion experiments while meeting the ISS 
requirements and limitations such as safety, 
power and energy, cooling, mass, crew time, 
stowage, resupply flights, and data downlink.  
The major subsystems of the CIR are the ISPR, 
Passive Rack Isolation System, optics bench, 
combustion chamber, diagnostics, fuel/ oxidizer 
management assembly, environmental control 
subsystems, electrical power system, avionics 
subsystems, flight and ground software, and 
interfaces for experiment-specific hardware.   
 
Each investigation will customize the facility with 
experiment packages that contain a small 
amount of hardware and software.  The CIR 
design allows for the removal and replacement 
of different experiment packages within the 
combustion chamber.  A replaceable Principal 
Investigator (PI) Avionics box mounts on the 
optics bench and provides for PI command and 
control of the experiment. 
 
Passive Rack Isolation System 
The ISPR contains a Passive Rack Isolation 
System (PaRIS) to isolate it from ISS and U. S. 
Laboratory vibrations.  PaRIS isolates the entire 
ISPR.  The PaRIS system provides passive 
attenuation by eight spring-damper isolators.  
 
Optics Bench                                            
The optics bench provides structural support, 
electrical connections, and mounting locations 
for other hardware, such as a chamber, gas 
handling system, and diagnostics.  It spans two-
thirds of the rack vertically and mounts on slides 
so that it slides out from the rack and folds down 
for access to both sides.  The wiring harnessing 
and cooling airflow are internal to the bench.  
Diagnostics are interchangeable via a quick-
latch mechanism at any of eight universal 
mounting locations around the combustion 
chamber.  These locations provide air-cooling, 
electrical power, and communication and data 
interfaces. 
 
Combustion Chamber 
The combustion chamber is a cylindrical 
pressure vessel with domed end caps that 
mounts centrally to the optics bench.  It has a 
volume of 100 liters and an internal diameter of 
0.40 m and a length of 0.78 m.  The front lid 
opens for on-orbit access to the inside of the 
chamber.  The chamber has eight replaceable 
windows.  The first launch set is made of 
sapphire.  The chamber has a maximum design 
pressure differential of 827 kPa (120 psia).  Four 
pressure transducers provide for pressure 
measurements.  Electrical, vacuum, gas, venting 
and other resources connect through an 
interface resource ring near the front of the 
chamber. 
 
Diagnostics 
The diagnostics measurement systems perform 
measurements of the combustion phenomena 
and are segmented into two categories.  The 
CIR provides one set entirely, including the 
measurement device, power, control, and data

items.title: PSI-22_Presentations_CIR Paper 59th IAC 2008 - Combustion Research on the International Space Station.pdf
items.text:
6
collection and storage.  These include visible 
and ultraviolet imaging, pressure measurement, 
gas composition, and accelerometry.  The 
experiment team and the CIR jointly provide the 
other set of diagnostics.  The diagnostics may 
include infrared and color imaging, temperature 
measurements, and flame radiation. 
 
The diagnostic devices provided by the CIR are 
the 
High-Bit 
Depth 
Multispectral 
Imaging 
Package (HiBMs), the Illumination Package, and 
the Low-Light Level Ultraviolet Imaging Package 
(LLL-UV).  The HiBMs consists of a telecentric 
optical system and a high resolution, 12-bit 
digital camera.  The initial use of the HiBMs is 
for viewing backlit droplet images.  A tunable 
liquid crystal spectral filter in conjunction with the 
Illumination Package allows for soot volume 
fraction and soot temperature measurements.  
The 
Illumination 
Package 
provides 
an 
illumination source that consists of a collimated 
optical system and two identical light-emitting 
diode sources.  The initial use of the Illumination 
Package is as a backlight source for the viewing 
of droplet images.  The LLL-UV provides images 
of flames or objects at low radiance levels.  The 
LLL-UV has an intensifier with a spectral range 
of 280 to 700 nm coupled to a monochrome 
camera.  A filter at 310 nm provides for imaging 
of OH emission from flames. 
 
Fuel/ Oxidizer Management Assembly 
The Fuel/ Oxidizer Management Assembly 
(FOMA) provides gaseous fuels, oxidizers, and 
diluents to the combustion chamber.  The FOMA 
also provides gas sampling and analysis of the 
chamber contents, and cleanup and venting to 
space through the ISS vacuum exhaust system. 
 
The gas delivery system contains gas supply 
bottles, 
valves, 
pressure 
regulators 
and 
switches, and mass flow controllers.  The gas 
bottles may be 1.0, 2.25, or 3.8 liters and mount 
on the front of the optics bench for easy 
replacement by the crew.  Up to four bottles may 
be used at one time.  The maximum mole 
fraction of oxygen allowed in the bottle depends 
on its size:  1.0 liter up to 80% O2, 2.25 liters up 
to 50% O2, and 3.8 liters up to 30% O2. The 
maximum oxidizer flow rate is 30 standard Liters 
per minute (slpm) per manifold for a total of 90 
slpm (using three manifolds); maximum fuel flow 
rate is two slpm for propane.  The gas delivery 
system performs on-orbit gas mixing by either 
partial pressure or by dynamic blending in the 
chamber. 
 
A gas chromatograph (GC) analyzes the 
chamber contents.  The GC is a repackaged 
commercial unit with three independent column 
modules that use helium and argon carrier 
gases.  Two 500 mL bottles, which are 
changeable by the crew, contain the carrier 
gases.  The GC can detect oxygen, inerts such 
as nitrogen or helium, fuels such as hydrogen, 
methane, 
methanol, 
and 
propane, 
and 
combustion products such as carbon dioxide, 
carbon monoxide, benzene, and formaldehyde 
at compositions ranging from 0.1 to 100%.  The 
GC is not planned for use at initial installation of 
the CIR in ISS. 
 
A filter cartridge removes particulates, water, 
and other contaminants from the gas to 
condition it for the next test point or prior to 
venting.  The recirculation pumps pull the gas 
through the cartridge at a rate of 9 slpm.  Each 
experiment customizes the adsorber cartridge, 
which may contain substances such as lithium 
hydroxide, activated carbon, silica gel, and 
molecular sieve.  
 
FOMA Control Unit 
The FOMA Control Unit (FCU) controls the 
FOMA components in the CIR.  It monitors and 
stores all pressures, temperatures, and mass 
flow rates during gas blending and experiment 
operations, controls the GC for chamber 
sampling, and monitors the status of all FOMA 
hardware for transmittal to the ground via the 
IOP.  The FCU commands set points of devices 
such as valves and mass flow controllers. 
  
 
 
 
MULTI-USER DROPLET COMBUSTION 
APPARATUS 
 
The MDCA is the initial payload in the CIR. It 
contains the hardware and software required to 
conduct unique droplet combustion experiments 
in microgravity.  The first experiment is the 
Flame 
Extinguishment 
Experiment, 
which 
involves assessing the effectiveness of flame 
suppressants in microgravity, quantifying the 
effect of candidate exploration atmospheres on 
fire suppression characteristics, and providing 
data to develop simplified combustion models.  
MDCA consists of a Chamber Insert Assembly, 
an Avionics Package, and a suite of diagnostics. 
Its modular approach permits on-orbit changes

for accommodating different fuels, fuel flow 
rates, 
and 
varying 
droplet 
support 
and 
translation 
mechanisms 
to 
accommodate 
multiple investigations. 
 
Single combustible fuel droplets of varying sizes, 
freely deployed or supported by a tether are 
planned for study using the MDCA.  Such 
research supports how liquid-fuel-droplets ignite, 
spread, 
and 
extinguish 
under 
quiescent 
microgravity conditions. 
 
MDCA Subsystems 
The MDCA Chamber insert Assembly (CIA) 
provides all necessary hardware and interfaces 
to perform PI science on one platform.  Most 
experimental functions occur within the CIA 
structure.  The CIA consists of two major 
components: 
an 
Experimental 
Mounting 
Structure (EMS) and an Internal Apparatus (IA).   
 
The EMS provides the main structure for the CIA 
and acts as the primary mechanical interface 
with the CIR combustion chamber.  The IA 
provides the primary mounting platform for all 
experiment specific hardware and functions 
including droplet dispensing, deployment, and 
ignition.   
 
The IA encompasses all motors used for the 
operation of the experiment, water-cooling, 
radiometers, and an internally mounted color 
camera. Other subsystems on the CIA include 
the 
Droplet 
Dispensing 
System, 
Droplet 
Deployment System, Fiber Support System and 
Ignition System.  There are two independent 
replaceable dispenser systems on the IA.  Each 
system consists of a motor housing, replaceable 
fuel reservoir filled with the PI specific fuel, and 
fuel isolation valve.  Flexible tubing connects the 
fuel system to the deployment needles.  Fuel is 
dispensed by means of a lead screw on the 
motor, which in turn pushes the plunger on the 
syringe.  The Chamber Insert Assembly is 
shown in Figure 4. 
 
 
 
Fig.  4.  The chamber insert assembly is used 
for studying flame suppression with 
droplet combustion. 
 
Principal Investigator (PI) Avionics Package 
The 
PI 
Avionics 
Package 
provides 
the 
processing and control interface hardware for 
controlling the MDCA and communicating with 
the CIR hardware.  The avionics controls the 
CIA motors, provides the functions for input and 
output data control, and is the source for 
experimental data collection.  The package will 
receive electrical power at 28 VDC from the CIR.  
DC-DC converters within the avionics will 
convert the voltage necessary for MDCA 
operation.  The package will acquire health and 
status data from 
the CIA via dedicated 
input/output lines.  The data will be downloaded 
to the CIR Input/Output Processor (IOP) via the 
ethernet connection for downlink.  MDCA 
commands will be uplinked from the ground to 
the IOP, or issued from a Station Support 
Computer (SSC) to the IOP.  The IOP will 
transmit the commands to the avionics package 
via the ethernet.  The enclosure of the avionics 
package 
will 
provide 
the 
Electromagnetic 
Interference (EMI) shielding and provide the 
grounding to the CIR optics bench. 
 
MDCA Diagnostics 
MDCA provided diagnostics hardware includes: 
The Color Camera is mounted on the CIA and 
provides enhanced color imaging of combustion 
experiments and an overall view of the droplet 
combustion. 
 
The radiometers are mounted on the CIA 
providing measurement of wide band and 
narrow band radiation during combustion.

MDCA Operations 
Once on-orbit, the MDCA is managed from the 
GRC Telescience Support Center (TSC).  The 
MDCA and FLEX operations team reside at the 
TSC.  Data is transmitted to the PI’s at their 
home sites by means of workstations, allowing 
direct interaction between the PI and operations 
staff to maximum science.  Upon completion of 
the FLEX experiment, the MDCA is reconfigured 
for the next experiment or ultimately removed 
from the CIR, placed into stowage, and returned 
to Earth.  
 
FLAME EXTINGUISHMENT EXPERIMENT 
 
The overall objectives of FLEX are to (1) assess 
the effectiveness of different suppressants to 
suppress a fire in microgravity, (2) quantify the 
effect of candidate exploration atmospheres for 
the habitable volume on fire suppression 
characteristics, and (3) provide data that can be 
used to direct the development of and define fire 
suppression system verification tests in both 
ground-based low-gravity facilities and future 
flight experiments. The MDCA facility will deploy 
single droplets of fuel of predetermined and 
reproducible sizes (i.e., 2.0 mm to 6.0 mm) for 
combustion studies designed to determine the 
efficacy of fire suppressants under varying 
oxygen and pressure combinations and the 
propensity of a range of proposed habitable 
atmospheres to support combustion. The use of 
a droplet configuration for these experiments is 
significant because it allows a large number of 
test conditions to be performed while minimizing 
the up-mass and crew time. For this screening 
of fire suppressants in long-duration reduced 
gravity, the parameter space includes the 
variation of suppressant type (3), fuel type (2), 
flow velocity (3) and various combinations of O2 
concentration and ambient pressure (230 test 
conditions). 
Furthermore, 
the 
droplet 
configuration is amenable to modeling which will 
allow us to more fully understand the results so 
they can be extended to more challenging 
models of fire suppression on solids in later flight 
experiments. 
 
FLAME EXTINGUISHMENT EXPERIMENT-2 
 
The FLEX-2 experiments involve dispensing, 
deploying and igniting either a single droplet or a 
pair of droplets, depending on the experiment 
configuration, 
in 
a 
known 
and 
controlled 
gaseous environment. The ignited droplets 
either 
burn 
to 
completion 
or 
the 
flame 
extinguishes at a finite droplet radius in a 
quiescent ambient. During the experiments 
involving binary droplet arrays, two droplets are 
placed along a support fiber at known locations 
and the droplets are ignited simultaneously and 
the subsequent burning is recorded.  In the 
convective flow tests a single droplet is 
subjected to a known and controlled sub-
buoyant flow.  
The following discussion of the research 
objectives is grouped by the four basic 
experimental 
configurations 
which 
will 
be 
employed on the ISS.  These configurations 
comprise (i) the pure fuel experiments, (ii) the 
fuel mixture experiments, (iii) the convective flow 
experiments, and (iv) the binary droplet array 
experiments.     
 
Pure Fuel Experiments: The objectives of the 
pure fuel studies are to examine steady and 
unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena, 
flame extinction, soot formation mechanisms 
and radiative heat transfer.  Decane (C10H22) 
and ethanol (C2H5OH) fuels were chosen 
because of their combustion properties and to 
build on results from earlier flight experiments 
(i.e., DCE, FSDC-1 and FSDC-2) which also 
used an alkane and an alcohol; i.e., heptane and 
methanol.  In these experiments droplet burning 
rates, flame dimensions, radiative emissions, 
and soot volume fraction are measured as a 
function of time and initial droplet size for 
different 
ambient 
conditions. 
When 
flame 
extinction occurs, the diameter of the unburned 
droplet at extinction is also determined. The 
objectives for these experiments are as follows: 
 
• Determine the diffusive and radiative flame 
extinction boundaries for ethanol and decane 
droplets in test atmospheres containing N2 or 
He at pressures ranging from 0.5 atm to 2.5 atm.  
• Measure droplet extinction diameters for 
ethanol and decane fuels for validation of 
detailed and reduced chemical kinetic models. 
• Measure soot volume fractions and soot 
temperatures for a range of initial conditions to 
determine influence on droplet burning and 
flame extinction. 
• Measure radiant emissions from both luminous 
and non-luminous flames in test atmospheres 
containing N2 or He and at pressures ranging 
from 0.5 atm to 2.5 atm. 
 
Fuel Mixture Experiments:  Bi-component fuel 
mixtures are chosen to examine the role of liquid 
phase transport effects as well as to study the

items.text:
9
burning characteristics of simulated ‘real’ fuels 
(i.e, surrogate fuels).  Propanol/glycerol and 
heptane/hexadecane mixtures are used to 
examine the role of liquid phase diffusion, 
preferential evaporation, and mixing on the 
burning 
characteristics 
of 
fuel 
mixtures. 
Heptane/octane 
and 
decane/propylbenzene 
experiments 
focus 
on 
simulating 
the 
characteristics of ‘real’ fuels, like gasoline and 
jet fuels, which contain a variety of hydrocarbons 
with differing volatilities.  The measurements 
made during these experiments are similar to 
the pure fuel studies; however, the initial fuel 
composition and the interpretation of the results 
are different. The primary objectives for this set 
of experiments are as follows: 
 
• Measure the droplet diameter, dc , at the onset 
of flame contraction relative to the initial droplet 
diameter 
d0. 
 
Correlate 
with 
theoretical 
predictions and provide estimates for effective 
liquid diffusivities.  
• Measure burning rate, burning time, extinction 
diameter, and flame luminosity for the JP8 
surrogate fuel mixtures.  
 
Convective Droplet Experiments:  The overall 
objectives for this set of experiments are to 
investigate the effects of slow convective flows 
on the burning characteristics of liquid-fuel 
droplets. The imposed flow velocities are such 
that the Reynolds number based on initial 
droplet diameter is of the order unity. The 
specific 
objectives 
of 
the 
present 
flight 
experiments are as follows:  
 
• Obtain radiative and diffusive flame extinction 
limits in the low Reynolds number flow regime 
over a range of ambient test pressures and 
oxygen concentrations.  
• Measure droplet regression rates for sooting 
(decane) and non-sooting (ethanol) fuels as a 
function of imposed flow at low velocities over a 
range of ambient oxygen concentrations and 
pressures.  
• Measure flame stand-off distance, flame 
shape, and temperature field measurements in 
low flow velocities under a range of test 
atmospheres for use in validation of detailed 
theoretical models (i.e., radiative and finite-rate 
chemical kinetic effects).  
 
Droplet Arrays Experiments:  The objectives of 
the droplet array experiments are to investigate 
the droplet droplet interactions on the diffusive 
and radiative extinction of the flame surrounding 
the droplets for various L/D0 ratios using pure 
fuels. The specific microgravity experimental 
objectives are as follows: 
  
• Determine the flammability map (diffusive and 
radiative extinction limits) for a binary droplet 
array as function of L/D0 ratio.  
• Measure variations in the burning rate 
constant, K , as a function of L/D0 for a range of 
ambient 
conditions 
to 
verify 
theoretical 
predictions. 
 
ADVANCED COMBUSTION VIA 
MICROGRAVITY EXPERIMENTS 
 
ACME is now under development with a set of 
four independent experiments which are each 
focused on advancing combustion technology 
through fundamental research.  The current 
ACME experiments are specifically directed at 
addressing energy and environmental concerns.  
The 
overall 
goals 
are 
to 
improve 
our 
understanding of (1) combustion at fuel lean 
conditions where both optimum performance 
and low emissions can be achieved, (2) 
combustion of fuels with increased hydrogen 
content which could enable reduced greenhouse 
emission, (3) soot control and reduction, (4) 
oxygen enriched combustion which could enable 
practical carbon sequestration, and (5) use of 
electric fields for combustion control.  Unlike 
FLEX-1, 
ACME 
is 
not 
focused 
on 
the 
advancement 
of 
spacecraft 
fire 
safety 
technology, although it is likely that some ACME 
findings will be relevant.  While distinct, the 
experiments share several significant traits.   
The principal unifying feature of the ACME 
experiments is their use of gaseous fuels (e.g., 
methane and ethylene) rather than liquid or solid 
fuels.  With this in common, the experiments will 
be conducted within CIR through the use of a 
single modular insert.  In addition to the fuel 
state, the current set of ACME experiments all 
use 
laminar, 
non-premixed 
(i.e., 
diffusion) 
flames for their studies.  To simplify analysis, 
these flames are either one or two dimensional, 
depending upon the experiment. 
 
The purpose of the Spherical Flame (s-Flame) 
experiment is to advance our ability to predict 
the structure and dynamics, including extinction, 
of both soot-free and sooty flames.  The 
spherical flame, which is only possible in 
microgravity, will be created through use of a 
porous spherical burner from which a fuel/inert 
gas mixture will issue into the CIR chamber.

items.title: PSI-22_Presentations_CIR Paper 59th IAC 2008 - Combustion Research on the International Space Station.pdf
items.text:
10
Flames will be ignited at non-steady conditions 
and allowed to transition naturally toward 
extinction.  Tests will be conducted with various 
inert diluents, in both the fuel and chamber 
atmosphere.  The fuel gases include hydrogen 
and methane for soot-free flames, and ethylene 
for sooty flames.  One experiment objective is to 
identify the extinction limits for both radiative and 
convective extinction (i.e., at high and low 
system 
Damkohler 
numbers, 
respectively).  
Another objective is to determine the existence, 
onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that 
have been theoretically predicted to occur in 
such flames with fuel/diluent mixtures that are 
above a critical Lewis number. 
 
The 
primary 
goal 
of 
the 
Flame 
Design 
experiment is to improve our understanding of 
soot inception and control in order to enable the 
optimization of oxygen enriched combustion and 
the “design” of non-premixed flames that are 
both robust and soot free.  An outside review 
panel recently declared that Flame Design “… 
could lead to greatly improved burner designs 
that are efficient and less polluting than current 
designs."  Flame Design will investigate the soot 
inception and extinction limits of spherical 
microgravity flames, created in the same 
manner as for the s-Flame experiment.  Tests 
will be conducted with various concentrations of 
both the injected fuel (i.e., ethylene or methane) 
and the oxygen enriched atmosphere in order to 
determine the role of the flame structure on soot 
inception.  The effect of the flow direction on 
soot formation will be assessed through the use 
of a coflow burner which can allow for either 
normal or inverse flames.  In the case of the 
inverse flames, the oxygen/inert mixture is 
injected from a central tube, while the fuel is 
ejected from a surrounding annulus.  The Flame 
Design experiment will explore whether the 
stoichiometric mixture fraction can characterize 
soot and flammability limits for non-premixed 
flames like the equivalence ratio serves as an 
indicator of those limits for premixed flames. 
 
Research, especially including that already 
conducted in microgravity, has revealed that our 
current predictive ability is significantly lacking 
for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, 
namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute 
flames that are near extinction.  The general 
goal of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) 
Flame experiment is to extend the range of 
flame 
conditions 
that 
can 
be 
accurately 
predicted by developing and experimentally 
verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation 
submodels.  The dependence of normal coflow 
flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution will 
be carefully examined for flames at both very 
dilute 
and 
highly 
sooting 
conditions.  
Measurements will be made of the structure of 
diluted methane and ethylene flames in an air 
coflow.  Lifted flames will be used as the basis 
for the research to avoid flame dependence on 
heat loss to the burner.  The results of this 
experiment will be directly applicable to practical 
combustion 
issues 
such 
as 
turbulent 
combustion, ignition, flame stability, and more. 
 
Electric fields can strongly influence flames 
because of its effect on the ions present as a 
result of the combustion reactions.  The direct 
ion transport and the induced ion wind can 
modify the flame shape, alter the soot or 
flammability limits, direct heat transfer, and 
reduce pollutant emission.   The purpose of the 
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion (E-
FIELD) Flames experiment is to gain an 
improved understanding of flame ion production 
and investigate how the ions can be used to 
control non-premixed flames.  Outside reviewers 
recently concluded that the experiment “… will 
contribute to our critical understanding to our 
knowledge of combustion processes in the 
presence of electric fields.”  The experiment will 
be conducted with a normal coflow flame (as in 
the CLD Flame experiment) or perhaps with a 
simple gas-jet flame, where there is no 
surrounding coflow.  An electric field will be 
generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 
kV) differential between the burner and a flat 
circular 
mesh 
suspended 
above 
(i.e., 
downstream of) the burner.  Measurements, as 
a function of field strength and fuel dilution, will 
be made of the ion current through the flame 
and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. 
 
A general goal of the current ACME experiments 
is to gain fundamental understanding that can 
enable 
improved 
efficiency 
and 
reduced 
emissions in practical combustion processes, for 
example 
through 
the 
development 
and 
verification of models for chemical kinetics and 
transport 
processes 
in 
computational 
simulations. 
 
In 
addition 
to 
enhanced 
performance, improved modeling capability can 
lead to reductions in the time and cost for 
combustor design.  In summary, microgravity 
investigations of non-premixed flames cou

Flammability Assessment of Materials for 
Exploration 
 
The Objective of FLAME is to develop a small-
scale 
facility 
for 
study 
of 
solid 
material 
flammability in low-gravity. Material flammability 
for thick practical fuels has received limited 
study to date. FLAME will examine critical 
parameters for modeling material flammability in 
three flow configurations: boundary layer, wake 
and stagnation flows. The experiment will 
establish and validate CFD models to extend 
data usability, and use results to establish 
advanced fire prevention strategies for low-g 
and reduced-g environments. 
 
 
 
 
DEVELOPMENT STATUS 
 
NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, 
Ohio is develops the experiment hardware under 
a prime contract with ZIN Technologies, Inc. The 
CIR, and  MDCA/FLEX, have been delivered to 
the NASA Kennedy Space Center and have 
completed launch processing. The current 
schedules show launch of the CIR/MDCA on 
ULF-2 in November 2008. Launch of the Flex-2 
in December 2009, and ACME in 2011. 
 
 
 
ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS 
 
The NASA Headquarters Exploration Systems 
Directorate provides funding for the FCF, MDCA 
and LMM and support for combustion and fluid 
physics experiments.  The authors gratefully 
acknowledge the project teams at NASA Glenn 
Research Center and ZIN Technologies, Inc. for 
their excellent work and contributions to develop 
the Combustion Research on the ISS.

PDR RFA-001 Disposition  
RFA # 01 
Originator: Anita Tenteris 
Originator Concurrence:  23 September 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
One of the criteria for PDR is a preliminary limited 
life items list. Just because other experiments may 
not have such a list does not mean ACME should not 
have such a list. ACME presents a unique situation 
where experiments will occur in the same chamber 
as the Cube is located as well as tubing, wiring, 
cooling lines, etc. The project should to start 
identifying their materials lists from the Computer-
Aided Design (CAD) drawings so that compatibility 
issues/soft goods shelf life/limited life items can be 
identified early in the design cycle. Maybe testing 
would also be needed as well for materials with 
unknown compatibility? 
 
Identify the material 
compatibility and shelf life limits 
for the soft goods used in 
ACME and CIR 
 
It has been determined by the 
project that a materials analysis 
would not be done for PDR due to 
funding and resource limitations.  
The plan is to have this analysis 
and MIUL completed at CDR. 
  
Although the analysis was not 
complete at PDR, the ACME 
project is aware of potential issues 
with the Data Cube and other 
electronics and their compatibility 
with the gaseous fuels.  These 
issues are currently being tracked 
in the Risk Management 
Implementation Tool database.

PDR RFA-002 Disposition  
RFA # 02 
Originator: Anita Tenteris 
Originator Concurrence:  23 September 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
In many of the presentations, the presenters 
indicated CIR heritage for a choice of hardware. It 
seemed as though CIR was treated as a ‘black box’ 
that ACME hooks into. ACME fuels need to be 
compatible with CIR and also cause no issues to 
CIR. 
The following items need to be investigated further to 
assess compatibility: 
• ACME Venting compatibility with CIR hardware 
• Are the gases/liquids compatible with CIR 
hardware, particularly with the soft goods in the 
solenoid valves? The board was told the solenoid 
valves contained FKM o-ring. For the ACME 
gases, NBr is the recommended rubber for most of 
the gases, if not all. 
• What are the limited life items for CIR? Do any of 
the items need be replaced prior to ACME use? 
An assessment of the venting 
compatibility has been addressed 
and was deemed acceptable. 
 
As the project matures, CIR will 
assess compatibility of materials in 
their system with ACME gasses, 
products of combustion and any 
other applicable interactions. 
 
ACME anticipates this will be 
completed by CDR.

RFA # 03 
Originator: Al Linne 
Originator Concurrence:  7 November 2013 
Statement of 
Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
There are no warnings to 
eliminate damage to the 
test hardware 
To minimize the likelihood of 
hardware damage, the flight & 
ground software designs 
should incorporate software 
requirements to identify invalid 
commands and command 
parameters that are outside of 
allowable limits and to alert 
operations personnel that 
invalid commands were 
entered. 
 
A complete software command list for the ACME hardware has 
been derived from operational requirements for the ACME 
system.  Operational limits have been defined for each 
command and incorporated into the software requirement set.  
The software requirements are documented in the Software 
section of the ACME Engineering Requirements Document 
(ERD) ACME-REQ-001.   
This list of signals is also documented in the ACME Data 
Dictionary Document (ACME-DOC-008).   
These documents will be available for NASA review and 
comment during the CDR.   
The approved operational limitations will be built into the 
ACME ground command station software at the TSC.  Every 
command sent by an operator will be checked against these 
established limits.  Commands that violate safe ranges will be 
rejected (on the ground) and the operator will receive an error 
message.  This ground software will be verified, as part of the 
overall ACME test and verification  campaign, to ensure no 
command can ever reach the ACME hardware that is outside 
of these safely established limits.

Perform a detonation analysis on the 
expected ACME gas mixtures. This 
should be done prior to the ACME Phase 
0/1 Flight Safety Review, since it may 
inform some of the hazard analysis. Also, 
the results of this analysis could drive the 
consumables usage and could limit the 
amount of science performed. 
An ACME detonation analysis has been performed 
for the Inverse Flame Experiment, which is the the 
worst case hazard.  It was chosen because of the 
possible oxygen interaction with ACME CIA 
hardware (i.e. materials compatibility).  The 
analysis validated that the present configuration 
could safely meet requirements.  The analysis has 
not impacted the design. 
 
A full detonation analysis of all experiments will be 
completed prior to the Phase 2 Flight Safety 
Review.

Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
A number of different oxygen 
percentages were discussed & 
identified in the PDR presentation 
and documentation. What oxygen 
percentage was used in the 
design and does this cover the 
ranges requested by the PI. 
Determine the worst case oxygen 
percentage (and pressure) that could 
potentially be in the CIR chamber with 
ACME installed, based on credible failures 
to CIR & ACME equipment and use this 
oxygen percentage as the design point for 
ACME. This will drive integrated 
safety/hazard analyses as well as ACME 
material compatibility. 
Also, based on the resulting worst case 
oxygen percentage determine if an 
oxygen compatibility assessment needs to 
performed for the ACME Chamber Insert 
Assembly. 
Oxygen compatibility with the ACME CIA has 
been assessed and is documented in the 
Draft Materials Identification/ Usage List 
(MIUL), which is a review item for the CDR.  
An Integrated Hazard Analysis has been 
completed and the worst-case oxygen 
percentages and pressures have been 
identified and addressed in the Hazard 
Report (see ACME Hazard Report 5, 
documented in ACME-SDP-001).

Originator Concurrence:  25 October 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
CIR hazards mitigations are being 
used by ACME. It was not clear 
that the ACME team had reviewed 
the CIR hazards and confirmed 
the mitigation steps are applicable 
to ACME.  There were no 
integrated hazards included in the 
ACME Phase 0/1 Flight Safety 
Data Package safety hazard 
analysis (ACME-SDP-001. 
The ACME and CIR teams should provide 
an integrated CIR/ACME Safety story. 
There are likely integrated safety hazards 
that exist in the integrated system and 
these should be identified and 
documented. Perform an integrated 
hazard analysis and prepare integrated 
hazard reports. The integrated CIR/ACME 
hazard analysis should be part of the 
Phase 0/1 Flight Safety Review. 
Also, a pressure switch, a solenoid valve, 
and a pressure regulator in the ACME 
system were included in the design on the 
N2 input to the chamber. Perform a 
integrated hazard analysis of this system 
(CIR & ACME hardware) to ensure system 
meets the intent of CIR hazard analyses. 
The Integrated Hazard Analysis has been 
completed with the participation of the CIR 
Team.  An Integrated Safety Data Package 
has been prepared and was included as input 
to the ACME Phase 0/1 Flight Safety Review.

ACME Critical Design Review– 27 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
PDR RFA-007 Disposition  
RFA # 07 
Originator: Terry O’Malley 
Originator Concurrence:  25 October 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
The ACME project plan did not provide 
sufficient detail of the end-to-end project 
planning. There was no evidence of a 
bottoms up cost estimate or a bottoms 
up schedule. Both of these are vital in 
ensuring the project has been thought 
through and that sufficient resources are 
available to successfully complete the 
project. The only budget shown was the 
program budget, and it may not be 
adequate complete the current scope of 
the ACME project. 
The ACME Systems Engineering 
Management Plan also did not provide 
sufficient detail of the end-to-end project 
technical management. It provided 
details through PDR/CDR, but not the 
project lifecycle. 
Update the Project Plan. Complete a 
bottoms up cost estimate and a 
bottoms up end-to-end schedule. 
Consider performing a parametric cost 
estimate. To be of value, these should 
be performed within 6 months of the 
PDR. 
 
Update the SEMP to include technical 
details through launch. Include things 
as spare required, environmental 
testing required, Ground/Flight Support 
Equipment etc. 
An updated Project Plan has been 
baselined, which includes a bottoms-up 
cost estimate and schedule.  An 
independent cost estimate by the GRC 
Cost & Economic Analysis Office has 
been performed and is in-line with the 
project plan.    
 
Updates to the SEMP will be made 
regularly as more information becomes 
available to the project team.  The SEMP 
is a living document that will be revisited 
as necessary.

ACME Critical Design Review– 28 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
PDR RFA-008 Disposition  
RFA # 08 
Originator: Terry O’Malley 
Originator Concurrence:  25 October 2013 
Statement of Concern 
Recommended Action 
Closure Rationale 
The ACME Engineering requirements 
document is incomplete. While it appears 
that the Science requirements have been 
thoroughly addressed, carrier 
requirements (both CIR & ISS) and 
safety and mission assurance have not 
been addressed in the ACME ERD. It is 
important to thoroughly identify all 
requirements which are imposed on the 
system and subsequently must be 
verified. A related concern is the number 
of requirements that must be verified. 
There are a large number of 
requirements on the system and the 
verification program could be extensive. 
Complete the ERD. This should be 
done within 6 months of the PDR to 
ensure the CDR design meets all 
requirements that are levied on the 
system. Environmental testing 
requirements should be included as 
part of this, waivers for fragile 
equipment should be identified early. 
When developing the verification 
program look for ways to combine & 
streamline the verification process. 
The document FCF-ICD-CIR-ACME 
addresses carrier requirements (both CIR 
and ISS).  ACME-REQ-001 points there. 
 
Safety and Mission Assurance 
requirements will be detailed in the ACME 
Hazards and Integrated CIR-ACME 
hazard reports.  Following the Phase 0/1 
Flight Safety Review, where these Hazard 
Reports are approved, the requirements 
will be incorporated into ACME-REQ-001. 
 
The verification process will group 
requirements by discipline identified to 
facilitate verification and validation.

The project has done a good job of 
writing operational requirements, but they 
have not yet been vetted with the PIs. 
This concern stems from RDR when the 
PIs were assuming operational 
requirements that the GRC science and 
engineering teams were not aware of. 
This concern follows on from the ACME 
RDR-004 RFA which has not been 
closed out as of the PDR. 
It is imperative that: 1) the currently 
documented operational requirements 
are vetted with each of the PIs; 2) the 
engineering team talks with each of the 
PIs. This will ensure that both parties 
fullly understand what is meant by 
each of the requirements, and also 
give the engineering team a chance to 
uncover additional operational 
requirements. 
 
Close out the RFA ACME RDR-004. 
The Project Scientist, Dennis Stocker, has 
vetted the operations requirements 
documented in ACME-SRD-001 with the 
respective Pis.  Dennis has also 
discussed the Ops requirements with the 
ACME engineering team to be sure they 
are well understood. 
 
The ERD revision including the updates 
with the operations requirements has 
been completed and released. 
 
This information should be sufficient to 
close RFA ACME-RDR-004.

ACME Critical Design Review– 62 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center

Spherical Burner
 
Spherical Burner 
The upper part of the spherical burner will be supplied by Princeton 
University under the following conditions: 
 
1) Princeton University: Fabricate a 1/4”, 3/8”, and 1/2” spherical burner head with supply tube per ACME 
ISRD 1.2.1, 1.2.2, 1.2.5, and 1.2.6.  
2) Princeton University: Perform preliminary tests on the above spherical burner heads following ACME 
ISRD 1.2.3 as a guide and conferring with NASA ACME Project Scientist.  
3) Princeton University: Deliver accepted spherical burner heads to NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC).  
4) NASA GRC performs additional acceptance tests as necessary (microgravity).  
5) NASA GRC deliver acceptable spherical burner heads to ZIN Technologies Inc. as government furnished 
equipment (GFE.) via C727.  
6) Zin Technologies Inc.: Accept and serialize spherical burner heads from NASA GRC.  
7) Zin Technologies Inc.: Perform additional fabrication on S1101MFA1218, S1101MFA1223, and 
S1101MFA1228 per ACME ISRD 1.2.4, 1.2.6, and 1.2.7. This fabrication will produce the following top level 
assemblies: S1101MFA1216: 1/4” spherical burner assembly, S1101MFA1220: 3/8” spherical burner 
assembly, S1101MFA1225: 1/2” spherical burner assembly  
8) Zin Technologies Inc.: Deliver S1101MFA1216, S1101MFA1220, and S1101MFA1225 to NASA GRC via 
a DD1149.  
9) NASA GRC: Test and verify S1101MFA1216, S1101MFA1220, and S1101MFA1225 per ACME ISRD 
1.2.3.  
10) NASA GRC: Deliver verified spherical burner assemblies along with verification certification documents 
to Zin Technologies Inc. as GFE via C727.

items.text:
ACME Critical Design Review– 151 
Glenn Research Center
 
Glenn Research Center 
ZIN Technologies 
Depress / Repress 
• Unless part of a pressurized system, all volumes are designed to 
adequately vent due to station / vehicle depressurization 
• Vented Containers will be verified by the stored energy method (SDP 
STD-ACME-1 17.a) where the volume has a stored energy < 3,063 ft-
lbs.  Volumes with a stored energy > 3,063 ft-lbs will have a depress 
rate calculated. 
 
• Depress rates are calculated* for each volume to show that the 
volume’s depress rate is greater than maximum station / vehicle 
depress rate so no pressure load is generated 
• Maximum depress rate is defined in section 3.1.1.2.1.5 part B of SSP-
50835 Rev C as 13.3kPa/s (1.93psi/sec) 
 
 
 
*AIAA Journal, October 1986, Vol. 24, No. 10, pg 1709-1711, “Formulas for Venting or Charging 
Gas from a Single Volume”, H.T. Yang

Goal 
 Use the space environment as a laboratory for strategic 
research & technology experiments in physics, chemistry 
and biology to support Agency goals & the Nation’s vision 
new for space exploration.

• Develop the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the 
Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) to support physical and 
biological research on board the ISS. 
• Develop the Ground Infrastructure, Integration, 
Operations, Logistics & Maintenance plans required for 
FCF sustaining engineering and operations. 
• CIR provides the only large environmental chamber (100 
liters) on ISS in which the space environment, Lunar, Mars 
or other desired environment may be simulated (i.e., 
pressure, temperature, gaseous atmospheres, 
particulates, etc.) for long duration, on-orbit investigations 
and technology validations. 
• CIR provides easily reconfigurable diagnostics, 
customizable software, passive rack-level vibration 
isolation, and other subsystems that will support a wide 
range of investigations

Combustion Chamber Atmosphere 
Mixing 
The oxidant MFC can provide up to 30 slpm (based on nitrogen (N2)) 
flow. The oxygen gas concentration is a function of the gas bottle size, 
as listed below.  
•
2.25 liter bottle provides a maximum of 50% O2, balance diluent at 
2000 psia. 
•
3.8 liter bottle provides a maximum of 30% O2, balance diluent at 
2000 psia. 
  
A Nitrogen manifold can supply inert gas types such as N2, He, and 
CO2, as well as oxidant blends below 30% oxygen, to the chamber. In 
addition, this manifold provides the interface for the utilization of the ISS 
supplied N2. This manifold also can directly route the pressurized gas to 
the chamber, by-passing the regulator. The N2 MFC can provide up to 
30 slpm (based on nitrogen (N2)) flow.

ACME Risk Summary 
•
Risk ID: ACME-014 
•
Risk Title: IPSU to IOP image transfer rates take too long 
•
Risk Statement: Given that the current data transfer rates from the IPSU 
to the IOP is severely limited, transfer of ACME data may take an 
unacceptable amount of time and may reduce obtainable science for the 
allotted operational time on board ISS. 
•
Likelihood: 4 
•
Consequence: 3 
•
Approach: Watch. Need to keep an eye on this and follow up  
with the CIR team to keep updated on transfer improvements. 
•
Latest Status: 09/17/13 - The IPSU-G is going to have their  
PDR September 26th 2013. The IPSU-G will eliminate  
the need to transfer image data from an IPSU to the IOP for downlink  
because the IPSU-G will be able to directly downlink image data to  
the ground. A trigger for this risk would be the cancellation of the  
IPSU-G project that would require ACME to mitigate, accept, etc...

ACME hardware will not create noise exposure hazard causing 
damage to hardware, injury to crew, or interfere with communications 
or caution/alarm detection.

measurements and leakage check under vacuum to DNA battery. 
Perform functional check of Lippert Board Assembly (with soldered 
button battery) and visual inspection of Lippert Board battery. 
•Capacitors used as energy storage devices - ACME does not utilize 
asymmetric, lithium-based or free electrolyte capacitors as energy 
storage devices.

FCF-ACME-04 
Title: Adiabatic Combustion Ruptures CIR Combustion Chamber or CIR Exhaust 
Vent Package during ACME experiments (except for the Inverse Flame Experiment) 
Description: Rapid overpressurization during the combustion of ACME gaseous 
fuel and oxidizer/diluent exceeds the MDP of the CIR Combustion chamber and/or 
exhaust vent package resulting in damage to CIR or ISS hardware or injury to the 
crew. 
Note (on hazard report):   
1.
This hazard report works in conjunction with CIR hazard report FCF-C07, “Adiabatic Combustion 
ruptures the chamber walls, causing damage to station and/or injury to crew.“  Overpressurization due 
to combustion will be controlled by limiting the fuel volume in each gas bottle.  The CIR Valve Timers 
will be placed in the fuel mode.  The chamber will be pre-filled with gaseous oxidizer and gaseous fuel 
will flow through the ACME burner. 
2.
CIR is responsible for filling the experiment gas bottles.  The ACME detonation analyses determine the 
limits on fuel volumes in each bottle.  The fuel gas volumes will be chosen such that even if the entire 
contents of a bottle were to be released into the CIR Combustion Chamber, any adiabatic combustion 
would result in a pressure less than the MDP of the CIR Combustion chamber.  The MDP of the CIR 
chamber is 135 psia. 
3.
The CIR bottle leakage hazard controls and verifications are covered in CIR hazard report FCF-C08 
Leakage of Pressurized System. 
4.
The CIR system rupture hazard controls and verifications are covered in CIR hazard report FCF-C10 
Rupture of Pressurized Systems.

1. Introduction 
The purpose of this report is to describe the data acquired for ACME’s E-FIELD Flames experiment to 
facilitate its analysis.  The data is all digital, where the fuel was gaseous and there was no collection of 
soot or the combustion gases.  For each test, the key data consists of image files and a file with the non-
imaging measurements.  Additional files such as camera metadata and operational logs provide 
information that can support the analysis. 
 
It is recommended that readers interested in analyzing the E-FIELD Flames data begin by familiarizing 
themselves with the hardware and instrumentation, either through the overview in the E-FIELD Flames 
Final Report or the more comprehensive description found in the ACME Engineering Implementation 
document. 
 
Those seeking to analyze the data should next review this document.  To interpret the non-imaging data, 
it is suggested that a sample data file be opened, named for example 18073A3_data.csv, which has 
comma-separated values and can be opened with spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel.  The data 
is in raw voltages, where conversion to engineering units requires study of ACME’s Software Interface 
Design Description, i.e., ACME-DOC-010 (where the latest version at the time of this writing is revision D).

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 
 
2 Oct. 2020 
 
3 
 
 
Additional documents that may be important include: 
ACME-RPT-010 A 
Data Camera Characterization Report, Rev. A 
ACME-RPT-011 
Radiometer Characterization Report 
ACME-RPT-013 
PMT Characterization Report 
However, the BRE Radiometer Characterization Report, ACME-RPT-012, is not relevant because the BRE 
radiometer was developed specifically for ACME’s Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment.  E-FIELD 
Flames instead made use of the standard radiometers addressed in ACME-RPT-011. 
 
 
2. E-FIELD Flames Overview 
This text is the “Overview” from the ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report, which provides descriptions of the 
science, preliminary results, and more.  It is suggested that it be reviewed by those interested in analyzing 
the E-FIELD Flames data. 
 
The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is one of six 
independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) 
project for which tests are conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International 
Space Station (ISS). 
 
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Derek Dunn-Rankin of the University of California, 
Irvine (UC Irvine).  Dr. Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien, also of UC Irvine, served as the Project Scientist at the 
university.  Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is NASA’s Project Scientist 
(PS) for ACME including E-FIELD Flames and the rest of the ACME investigations.  In preparatory drop 
testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy 
Project Scientist.  For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde 
and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. 
 
The experiment had two Co-Investigators, the first of which was Prof. Felix Weinberg of London’s Imperial 
College.  Prof. Weinberg was a pioneer in researching the effects of electrical fields on flames in 
microgravity, but unfortunately died in 2012 (see http://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/117808/tribute-felix-
weinberg/) before the hardware was built and the tests were conducted on the ISS.  The second Co-
Investigator was Dr. Sunny Karnani who did his doctoral research in preparation of the spaceflight 
experiment and afterward worked for ClearSign Combustion Corp., which markets Electrodynamic 
Combustion Control (https://www.clearsign.com/technology/electrodynamic-combustion-control/).  The 
corporation provided some support to the E-FIELD Flames research effort, but Karnani left ClearSign to 
conduct research for the U.S. Army, effectively ending his intimate role in the project prior to the 
spaceflight operations.  He remains a collaborator. 
 
E-FIELD Flames operations were conducted in two rounds of testing during Increments 55-57, which were 
more specifically in March-May and September-November 2018.  The break in testing (from May to 
September) was intentional and planned years in advance to allow the research team to analyze early 
results and use the insights obtained from the analysis to plan the second round so as to maximize its 
scientific output.

items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 
 
2 Oct. 2020 
 
4 
 
 
3. Tests Conducted 
This text is an excerpt from the “Results” section of the ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation 
Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 (which is included in the ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final 
Report). 
  
A total of 219 flames were ignited for the E-FIELD Flames experiment, with 142 and 77 
respectively ignited during Increments 55-56 and 57-58.  Note that the investigation’s testing was 
completed during Increment 57, so no flames were ignited during Increment 58.  The first and 
second rounds of testing respectively occurred in March-May 2018 and September-November 
2018.  The two rounds of tests resulted in 120 and 99 ignited flames conducted with coflow and 
gas-jet burners, respectively.  The coflow burner was developed for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion 
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD Flames’ second round occurred between the two 
rounds of the E-FIELD Flames experiment.  The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was 
intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail 
and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. 
 
E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are 
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  Both are 
simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) is the 
primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of 
carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because of its carbon 
double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen 
over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel and nitrogen was premixed on the 
ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 
45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  Similarly, bottles were launched 
with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a 
volume basis).  But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to 
the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.  
In all cases, the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  
 
No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for E-FIELD Flames; all of the ISS results were 
electronically transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all currently planned 
ACME experiments.

items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 
 
2 Oct. 2020 
 
6 
 
 
4. Data Interpretation 
This key section provides (1) a general description of the raw experimental data and associated files and 
(2) guidance on data conversions, e.g., to engineering units.  Only limited guidance is provided for the 
processing of image data, with the important exception of the conversion of the ACME DataCam images 
from the raw Halcon object (HOBJ) format. 
 
A. Non-Imaging Data 
Data and files discussed in this section include the following: 
Data Output File 
Mass Flow Controller (MFC) Setpoint File 
Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) data 
Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data 
 
Some ACME experiments featured measurements made with the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph 
Instrumentation Package (GCIP), but it was not used for the E-FIELD Flames experiment and a such 
that data type is not addressed in this document. 
 
1. Data Output File 
The basic ACME non-imaging measurements for each test are together in a file described in 
Section 8.1 Data Output File on page 124 of Software Interface Design Description (ACME-
DOC-010 Rev D).  The test number is made up of the year (2-digts), day of year (3 digits), and 
test (a letter and single-digit number).  As such, the example, 18073A3 is test A3 conducted 
on the 73rd day of 2018.  But the test could also be early on the next (e.g., 74th) day because 
the day portion of ACME test numbers is not changed when operations continue past 
midnight (whether GMT or Eastern) into the start of the next day. 
 
Tests numbers that only differ by the final digit (e.g., 18073A1, 18073A2, and 18073A3) are 
normally similar and occasionally identical, where the number is indicative of the variant or 
repeat.  Letters I and O are not used because of their similarity to 1 and 0.  While initially used 
in ACME testing, the letter E ceased to be used because Excel software (for example) by 
default interpreted it as representing an exponential which was inconvenient.  As a related 
aside, ACME tests are often not conducted in order and some planned tests are regularly not 
conducted at all.  The latter results in additional letter gaps if the tests from a day are sorted 
alphabetically.  However, ACME testing often begins with test A1, where the final digit begins 
with 1 and is increased from there with variant or repeat tests for the same letter. 
 
The basic data is in a CSV format, i.e., with comma-separated values, which can be opened by 
spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel.  The first row is a header and provides a limited 
summary of the hardware and operational conditions.  The header is explained in Section 10.1 
Metadata Header of ACME-DOC-010 Rev D, which begins on page 126.
