items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 
 
2 Oct. 2020 
 
8 
 
 
Additional conversion is required for the measurements of the gas flow rates found in second 
through fourth columns of the data file.  By column (e.g., in Excel), the flow rates are for: 
 
B 
MFCA1StaticMixerFlow  
oxidizer (or inert) gas 
 
C 
MFCA2BypassFlow 
 
nitrogen 
 
D 
MFCA3FuelFlow 
 
fuel 
 
The ACME MFCs are Hastings HFC-D-302 with default standard temperature and pressures 
(STP) of 0 Celsius and 760 torr for computations of volumetric flow or velocity.  It is very 
important to understand that slpm, i.e., standard liters per minute, is a measurement of the 
mass (or alternatively molar) flow rate which is independent of the actual temperature or 
pressure.  This is discussed for example in the MFC manual, where chapter 9 (on page 39) is 
“Volumetric vs. Mass Flow.” 
 
Conversions for the actual gases can be made with information provided in the manual on 
subsequent pages and the spreadsheets GasDataTables.xls and Inside gas mix calculator.xls 
which were both provided by the MFC manufacturer.  First, open GasDataTables.xls and 
enable content, and then open Inside gas mix calculator.xls and enable content.  From this, 
one should be able to enter mixtures and compute appropriate Gas Conversion Factors 
(GCFs). 
 
Alternatively, the conversions above can be made with spreadsheets prepared by the ACME 
engineering team, where options include the following: 
ACMEFlowCalculator.xlsx 
ACMEFlowAndPressuresRawDataConversion.xlsx 
  
Computation of gas velocities, for example for the gas-jet and coflow burners, depends on 
burner dimensions.  For the coflow burner, ACME mechanical design engineer Adrian Drake 
indicated the following: 
 
“The inner diameter of the inner tube is .085 inches.  Its cross sectional area is .00567 
in^2, or 3.66 x 10^-6 m^2.  
  
The flow of the outer tube is a little tricky to calculate, based on where and how you 
measure.  There’s an internal step in the outer tube that can’t be seen from outside, and 
blocks the flow to the outer honeycombs.  Because of this, when we calculated the cross-
sectional are of the outer tube, it measures from the inner step.   
  
The outer tube’s outer diameter at that step is 0.984 inches.  Its cross section area at that 
diameter is .7605 in^2.  From this we have to subtract the inner tube’s outer 
diameter:  .095 inch diameter, so area is .00709.  Subtract from the Outer Diameter and 
we get .7534 in^2, or .000486 m^2.”

4. Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data 
The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) in which the experiment was conducted, was equipped 
with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS), but it was not utilized for ACME testing because 
of the need for crew time to enable and disable the isolation (by respectively removing and 
installing alignment guides) on each test day.  However, the CIR was equipped with a 3-axis 
SAMS sensor head.  The acceleration archives, along with relevant documentation, are 
accessible from https://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/pims/home/, the home page for the Principal 
Investigator Microgravity Services (PIMS). 
 
The following guidance for the SAMS data was provided by Kenneth Hrovat (NASA Glenn):  In 
addition to the documentation and links from the PIMS home page, we introduce a few ways 
below to get started with exploring the CIR microgravity environment taking the perspective 
of SAMS measurements from within the rack. 
 
Roadmap Spectrograms 
To get a high-level, spectral roadmap view within two days after measurement, you can: 
a. Use your browser and start at this link: http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/roadmap

b. In the upper left pane, you can navigate by GMT date to see a list of plots (PDF files) 
in the right pane for the GMT date of your choice.  We refer to these PDFs as roadmap 
plots.  For SAMS, these are acceleration spectrograms, which for vibratory data are a 
good way to look at patterns, structures and boundaries in both time and frequency 
for long time spans -- nominally, 8 hours per plot.  These spectrograms are mostly 
qualitative and crudely quantitative three-dimensional plots in that a color scale 
attempts to map power spectral density magnitude as a color for the 3rd dimension. 
NOTE: Ticking the Navigation Filter for “es05” in the bottom pane will then only 
highlight days in yellow in the upper left pane when the operations team powered on 
the SAMS sensor in the CIR to take measurements. 
c. You might want to navigate directly to a GMT day of interest for your science 
operations or run, but you can also browse day-by-day too in order to get some 
context comparing various 8-hour spans to get a feel for the environment under 
various conditions. 
 
Binary Data 
To download actual SAMS measurement data for use with your models or to correlate 
acceleration measurements with your science or support data, you can… 
a. Use your browser and start at this link: http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/ftp/pad 
b. Navigate by GMT date, for example you can follow year, month and day links to end 
up at: https://pims.grc.nasa.gov/ftp/pad/year2020/month06/day18/  where you see 
a list of SAMS sensor directories.  The sensor subdirectory of interest for CIR is 
samses_accel_es05. 
c. Once you click into that directory link, you will see data and header files listed for the 
CIR sensor. 
d. The instructions at the following link help you to read these data: 
http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/plots/user/mohan/how2read_pad_binary_files.html 
 
 
B. Image Files 
Image data and files discussed in this section are associated with the following cameras: 
Analog, operations (ops), internal camera 
ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera 
 
High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package 
 
The Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera is not addressed herein because it was not used 
for E-FIELD Flames or most of the current ACME experiments.  Thus far, the Structure and 
Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) investigation is the only ACME study to use the 
LLL-UV camera. 
 
1. Analog, internal, operations (ops) camera  
This color analog camera is mounted on the ACME chamber insert, and as such is within the 
combustion chamber and is sometimes referred to as the internal camera.  Its primary 
purpose is to support the operations, e.g., to visualize the burner and igniter, and as such is 
also often referred to as the operations or ops camera.

2 Oct. 2020 
 
13 
 
 
The NTSC video (named for the National Television System Committee) from the ops camera 
is at 29.97 frames per second (fps) or nominally 30 fps.  It is not recorded on the space station 
but is streamed to the ground in near real time and is recorded on CIR consoles at the Glenn 
ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in a Transport Stream (TS) format using VLC Media 
Player which can be freely downloaded from https://www.videolan.org/vlc/.  That software 
has a snapshot function allowing for convenient extraction of still images, e.g., for making 
measurements of flame dimensions. 
 
2. ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
ACME’s primary camera is a high-definition (1360 x 1024), 12-bit color camera mounted 
outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench.  It is equipped with a motorized lens with 
independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus.  It has a filter barrel with a fused silica 
window (for color imaging), a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, and bandpass filters for 
imaging CH* and HCHO (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence. 
 
It was characterized prior to launch to enable temperature measurements via soot pyrometry 
and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP), soot volume fraction, and quantitative determination of 
the CH* concentration. 
 
Soot temperatures can be determined from this camera’s images via techniques such as those 
described in the following references: 
a. S. De Iuliis, M. Barbini, S. Benecchi, F. Cignoli, and G. Zizak, Determination of the Soot 
Volume Fraction in an Ethylene Diffusion Flame by Multiwavelength Analysis of Soot 
Radiation, Combustion and Flame 115 (1998) 253–261. 
b. B. Ma and M. B. Long, Combined Soot Optical Characterization Using 2-D Multi-Angle 
Light Scattering and Spectrally Resolved Line-of-Sight Attenuation and Its Implication 
on Soot Color-Ratio Pyrometry, Applied Physics B 117 (2014) 287–303. 
c. B. Ma, S. Cao, D. Giassi, D. P. Stocker, F. Takahashi, B. A. V. Bennett, M. D. Smooke, 
and M. B. Long, An Experimental and Computational Study of Soot Formation in a 
Coflow Jet Flame under Microgravity and Normal Gravity, Proceedings of the 
Combustion Institute 35 (2015) 839–846. 
d. N. J. Kempema, B. Ma, and M. B. Long, Investigation of In-Flame Soot Optical 
Properties in Laminar Coflow Diffusion Flames Using Thermophoretic Particle 
Sampling and Spectral Light Extinction, Applied Physics B 122 (2016). 
e. N. J. Kempema and M. B. Long, Effect of Soot Self-Absorption on Color-Ratio 
Pyrometry in Laminar Coflow Diffusion Flames, Optics Letters 43 (2018) 1103. 
 
Meanwhile, TFP measurements can be made using approaches such as those discussed in:  
f. V. Vilimpoc and L. P. Goss, SiC-Based Thin-Filament Pyrometry: Theory and Thermal 
Properties, Symposium (International) on Combustion 22 (1989) 1907–1914. 
g. W. M. Pitts, Thin-Filament Pyrometry in Flickering Laminar Diffusion Flames, 
Symposium (International) on Combustion 26 (1996) 1171–1179. 
h. J. D. Maun, P. B. Sunderland, and D. L. Urban, Thin-Filament Pyrometry with a Digital 
Still Camera, Applied Optics 46 (2007) 483–488.

Particularly when making quantitative measurements, implementation of an Abel transform 
or similar is likely appropriate given the axisymmetry of the flames in the E-FIELD Flames 
investigation.  In fact, all six of the current ACME experiments feature axisymmetric or 
spherically symmetric flames.   Approaches are compared in this paper: 
k. C. J. Dasch, One-Dimensional Tomography: A Comparison of Abel, Onion-
Peeling, and Filtered Backprojection Methods, Applied optics 31 (1992) 1146–
1152. 
 
The a-k references above were taken from the following conference paper on early ACME 
results from the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment: 
Jesse Tinajero, Davide Giassi, Dennis Stocker, and Marshall Long. “Experimental Study on 
the Influence of Gravity on Highly Diluted and Sooting Coflow Flames,” 11th US National 
Combustion Meeting of the Combustion Institute, Pasadena, CA, 24-27 March 2019.   
 
Meanwhile, this paper on an ISS precursor to the CLD Flame experiment is an appropriate 
reference for determination of CH* concentration. 
D. Giassi, S. Cao, B.A. Bennett, D.P. Stocker, F. Takahashi, M.D. Smooke, and M.B. Long, 
“Analysis of CH* Concentration and Flame Heat Release Rate in Laminar Coflow Diffusion 
Flames under Microgravity and Normal Gravity,” Combustion and Flame, Vol. 167, pp. 
198-206 (2016). 
 
Images are normally downlinked within a week of the testing, but selected images are often 
downlinked during a test day.  Regardless, the images are downloaded in a wrapped Halcon 
object (HOBJ) format, which are not readily opened with typical image processing software. 
 
Most ACME investigators are processing the HOBJ files using the OMA2 software developed 
by Prof. Marshall Long (Yale U.), the lead for ACME’s CLD Flame experiment.   The OMA2 
software is freely available in both Mac and cross-platform (Qt) versions, where the latter can 
be used with both PC and Linux operating systems. 
 
The OMA2 read-hobj function was also rewritten as a Python function by Dr. Jesse Tinajero 
(Yale U.), where Python is an open source programming language that is easily obtainable for 
MacOS, Linux, and Windows operating systems.  The Python script to open the HOBJ files can 
be downloaded from https://github.com/mblong/hobjExample.

2 Oct. 2020 
 
15 
 
 
The HOBJ files can also be readily viewed and processed using ImageJ or its preloaded Fiji 
variant, where both can be freely downloaded.  In either software package, the HOBJ files can 
imported (rather than opened) as raw files with the following settings: 
 
Image type 
16-bit unsigned 
 
Width 
1360 
 
Height 
1024 
 
Offset to first image 
6244 
However, imported DataCam images will be monochrome unless a Bayer filter (e.g., as 
described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayer_filter) is subsequently implemented.  It 
should be possible to install a plug-in to accomplish that color conversion.  As another option, 
Python and Matlab both have image demosaicing functions. 
 
NASA is also working (at the time of this writing) toward providing converted images from the 
ACME DataCam, where the general priority is to support the ongoing ACME testing rather 
than covert images for experiments like E-FIELD Flames which have already been completed. 
 
In order to use the ACME DataCam for quantitative measurements it is critical to avoid 
saturation, for example by using a camera gain of zero.  Another employed approach was to 
not use the camera’s white balance which by default multiplies the red and blue by 1.41 and 
1.68, respectively, because that could inadvertently lead to saturation.  Such multiplication 
can be done after the HOBJ file is converted and the colors demosaiced, where in OMA2 the 
white balancing is accomplished with the commands: 
*rgb 1.41 1 1.68 
clip 4095 
In summary, the white balance, if desired, needs to be done after the fact through software 
because it was generally not done with the hardware to avoid the risk of saturation.  
 
Note that the ACME images will be naturally dark because of the use of the 16-bit file format 
with 12-bit image data.  As such, adjustments to the image brightness will generally be 
necessary even if the images are not demosaiced.  Furthermore, cameras’ CCD arrays are 
susceptible to radiation damage while in orbit.  As a result, the images feature hot pixels which 
increase in number over the months and years in space.  As such, it will appear as if there is a 
star field within the combustion chamber.  Therefore, the images should ideally be processed 
to remove the bright outlying pixels.  The radiation damage is also obvious in the ops camera 
imaging. 
 
Although the DataCam was typically set for imaging at 30 fps, that is trumped by the exposure 
settings which were often long because of the dim nature of the microgravity flames.  As a 
result, the framing rate was typically far less.  Different exposures could have been selected 
for different phases of the tests, e.g., prior to ignition and during the test, so the framing rate 
may not be consistent.  Bracketed imaging could also be employed, where a repeating 
sequence of different exposure durations is used to enable appropriate photography under 
uncertain or varying flame intensities.  Bracketing is also used to simultaneously accomplish 
multiple imaging objectives, e.g., to appropriately image both brightly glowing soot (or TFP 
fibers) as well as the much dimmer blue portion of the flame. 
 
In interpreting the image data, it may be helpful to check the ACME DataCam metadata file

Regardless of the version, it is very important to understand that the exposure time, in 
microseconds, trumps the specified framing rate (in fps), i.e., where long exposures will lead 
to a shorter actual framing rate.  In this example case, the 0.1-s exposure time means that the 
framing rate (at the test’s start) was nominally 10 fps rather than the 30 indicated by 
FrameRate.  It is furthermore important to understand that the exposure time (and thus 
actual framing rate) was often varied during the test, where that could be seldom or often if 
bracketing was employed, i.e., where a repeated sequence of images was taken at different 
exposures.  
 
For the DataCam, the exposures times, etc. can also be found in files with names like 
18073A3_ACME_CAM3_Exposures.txt, where such files are discussed in section 4.A.3 of this 
document because (despite the file naming) they primarily include pressures, flow rates, and 
temperatures from the CIR’s Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA). 
 
The parameter files, with names such as 18073A3_VoltageSweep.txt, control the DataCam 
exposures and much more.  However, these files were not always saved as intended and were 
sometimes corrected after the fact.  In contrast, the text-file logs, with names such as 2018-
10-17_12-26ACME.log, are a reliable source for the parameters which specified the imaging 
settings and much more.  There is a single file of this type for each test day (at least normally) 
and the parameters are a small fraction of the automated log content, but one can search for 
a test by its number.  Log files like this are discussed in section 4.C.4 of this document. 
 
Due to the use of a turning mirror, the DataCam images should be flipped vertically if upright 
images are desired, i.e., where the burner is at the bottom and the flame extends upward.  In 
this regard, note that the DataCam provides images in a ‘landscape’ format with the image’s 
long dimension orthogonal to the burner and chamber axis.  This is contrary to an ACME 
science requirement specifying that the long dimension be aligned with the experimental axis 
to provide images in a ‘portrait’ format.  In this regard, the science requirements were not 
always met, e.g., because of design tradeoffs, etc. 
 
There is some variation in the ACME camera zoom, where its setting is not completely 
reproducible.  Therefore, the scaling of the image data should be established for each day of 
testing, or each subset of tests if more than one zoom setting was used within a day.  The 
scaling can typically be carried out using images regularly taken of the ceramic fibers for Thin 
Filament Pyrometry (TFP), where such imaging is normally made at two fiber array positions.  
However, the fiber array was not used for the E-FIELD Flames experiment because of the

interference of the electric field and electrode mesh.  Therefore, scaling must be carried out 
using the burner or other visible hardware.  Meanwhile, the other cameras had fixed lenses. 
 
Note that files named for example 20180314_162445.789_ACME_18073A3.next are not 
useful for data interpretation, where such text files simply indicate the next ACME image 
number that would have been archived, i.e., until that test’s image archiving came to an end. 
 
3. Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera 
This intensified camera was typically configured with a CH* bandpass filter and was generally 
archived at 23 fps.  The grayscale image files are in a Tagged Image File Format (TIFF) format 
and can be opened readily, where brightness/contrast adjustment may again be required. 
 
While it wasn’t an issue for E-FIELD Flames, this camera’s Field of View (FOV) is partially 
blocked by the arms of the fiber array for Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) when it is moved to 
position the fibers across the flame.  But E-FIELD Flames didn’t use the fiber array because of 
interference with the electrode mesh and the electric field itself. 
 
As with the ACME DataCam, it might be useful to check the metadata for the CFI intensified 
camera.  This was similarly revised in early 2018 (between mid-March and early April) when 
the first round of E-FIELD Flames tests (with the coflow burner) was being conducted, such 
that there are two version of this file relevant to the experiment.  Although they are largely 
similar, the latter has two additional parameters, BitShift and CameraSpeed, and some 
additional changes, e.g., where some parameter names changed and where the parameter 
order has changed.  Therefore, detailed information on both versions will be presented where 
the parameter descriptions and names of the corresponding camera parameters were 
provided by ACME software engineer Jeffrey Eggers.  Both versions are in a comma-delimited 
(CSV) format and can be opened with spreadsheet software or alternately as a text file.

Note that ‘next’ files named for example 20180314_162445.789_INTNS_18073A3.next are 
not useful for data interpretation, where such text files simply indicate the next image 
number that would have been archived, i.e., until that test’s image archiving came to an end. 
 
4. High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package 
The HiBMs camera was used in combination with an opposed backlight, i.e., the CIR’s 
collimated illumination package.  The resultant imaging was used in preceding droplet 
combustion experiments for measuring droplet diameter, but it may also be useful for 
determining the soot volume fraction via light extinction.  However, the camera’s red filter, 
corresponding to the red illumination, is broad enough to permit significant soot 
incandescence to pass through the filter.  As a result, this imaging is unlikely to be useful for 
soot volume fraction measurements for all conditions.  After post-processing on the ground, 
the images were made available in the TIFF format and as such are readily opened.  The 
grayscale images were typically archived at 15 fps.

items.title: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 
 
2 Oct. 2020 
 
24 
 
 
It is important to understand that this camera’s images are notably of limited value for E-
FIELD Flames because the bracket for the electrode mesh significantly blocked the 
illumination.  ACME’s cameras and other optical instruments encircle the burner and made it 
difficult to avoid optical interference in all circumstances, where design trade-offs were 
necessary.  However, the soot volume fraction can also be computed using images from the 
ACME DataCam as discussed in that camera’s section.  
 
In initial ACME testing with the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, the 
monochrome camera was used without a filter, but that was abandoned because the camera 
is nearly insensitive to blue.  The red filter was used throughout E-FIELD Flames testing. 
 
 
C. Test Parameters and Other Files 
Files discussed in this section include the following: 
Test parameter file 
Notes 
Test timing 
Logs 
 
1. Test parameter file 
Each E-FIELD Flames test was controlled by a software script and corresponding parameter 
file, named for example 18073A3_VoltageSweep.txt, specifying settings for imaging, ignition, 
gas flow, and more.    The parameter file and script are discussed extensively in the ACME/E-
FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure document, which should be referred to for information 
on this file type.  But note that the ACME.log files should be the best way to verify the as-run 
test parameters, where the separate parameter files are unfortunately not completely 
reliable.  They were not always saved and as a result were sometimes recreated after the fact. 
 
2. Notes 
Notes of various types are available for test days, where not all types were collected or 
necessarily prepared for each test day.  It is important to understand that the notes, whether 
handwritten or typed, may include mistakes.  It is better to rely on automated logs, metadata 
files, and parameter files or of course the measurements themselves when possible. 
 
The daily test point logs, with names such as ‘18087 daily test point log.pdf,’ chronologically 
list the tests and the image data acquired which was to be downlinked.  Typically, image data 
was not downlinked without successful, i.e., sustained, ignition.  As an example, image data 
wasn’t downlinked if the test aborted prior to ignition.  However, the reverse is not always 
true.  Image data was sometimes downlinked when ignition was unsuccessful and as a result 
the test point log is only a clue as to what transpired.  Furthermore, note that image data 
from certain selected cameras, typically the HiBMs and/or CFI intensified camera(s), was 
sometimes not downlinked due to the limit of how much data could be reasonably 
downlinked in a subsequent two-shift day. 
 
Notes with names such as ‘18087 efield & velocities traces.pdf’ include preliminary plots of 
the electrode mesh voltage and flow rates (as seen on a console during testing), typically along 
with additional information about the tests.

4. Logs 
There are four primary types of automated logs of which two, with names like the following, 
may be helpful. 
 
2018-10-17_12-26ACME.log 
 
2018-10-17_12-51_IPSUG.log 
As a reminder, the IPSU-G is the processing and storage unit for the images from the ACME 
DataCam and CFI intensified camera. 
 
Meanwhile, the two logs of commands, with names like the following, are unlikely to be useful 
for interpreting the E-FIELD Flames results. 
 
2018-10-17_12-59ACMECommands.log 
 
2018-10-17_12-51_IPSUGCommands.log 
 
Each of the four log files are created for each day of testing, rather than for each test.  They 
are text files (despite the log suffix) and as such can be readily opened.

items.text:
19 May 2018 
 
 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) 
 
PURPOSE:  ACME is focused on advanced combustion 
technology via fundamental microgravity research.  The 
primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant 
emission in practical terrestrial combustion.  A secondary 
objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft. 
 
RESEARCH:  ACME includes six independent experiments 
investigating laminar, gaseous, non-premixed flames.  They 
are being conducted with a single set of modular hardware 
in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International 
Space Station (ISS). 
STATUS:  ACME set-up and check-out was carried out by the 
ISS crew in Sept.-Oct. 2017, where science testing began in 
November.  The first round of testing for the Coflow Laminar 
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment of Marshall B. Long 
et al. was completed in Feb. 2018, where 130 methane 
flames (at a range of concentrations) were ignited.  The first 
round of testing for the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar 
Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment of Derek 
Dunn-Rankin et al. was completed on May 18, where 120 
coflow flames were ignited.  On May 20, burners and 
additional hardware for the next three ACME experiments 
are scheduled to launch.  The ACME hardware should be 
reconfigured on May 22 by astronaut Ricky Arnold (NASA) 
for CLD Flame’s second round, where the ethylene flame 
testing should begin later in the week. 
 
WEB SITE:  http://spaceflightsystems.grc.nasa.gov/acme/ 
UPDATES:  www.facebook.com/space.flames  
PHOTOGRAPHS:  www.flickr.com/photos/space-flames

items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 
 
23 July 2020 
2 
 
1. Introduction 
The narrative description of the experimental procedure is from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ section of 
the following conference paper: 
Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on Flames in 
Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States 
Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. 
This description also appears in Section 4.B Overview of Experiment Test Operations of the E-FIELD Flames 
Final Report.  Note that the referenced Figure 4 (showing the coflow burner geometry) is not included in 
this document. 
 
The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  Thus far, ACME’s activity has 
included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities.  Most often the astronauts 
and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips.  In the latter case, the igniter 
tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the crew already has changes to 
make changes in the interior of the insert.  While these activities may seem mundane, the crew play a 
critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment.  As an extreme example, there were crew 
activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME 
experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  In contrast, only two 
crew days were required to reconfigure the hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the 
initial use of the same coflow burner.  Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks 
in advance, for which detailed procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. 
 
All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center 
(GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio.  Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the testing.  The CIR 
hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer (DMO) consoles, and the 
ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console.  Two shifts of personnel are 
scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they typically last 14 hours with the many 
pre- and post-testing activities.  Given that the tests are remotely commanded, the operations are carried 
out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., from 7 AM to 9 PM.  A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are 
normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less.  Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per 
two weeks.  On intervening weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both 
gas bottles.  Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2-shift day for the RO 
and DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and 
that data is not missing.  Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew activity.  As 
a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week.  A team of four carry 
out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily operational plans typically 
exceed 50 pages on days including testing. 
 
The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in near real 
time but doesn’t allow for commanding.  In the case of E-FIELD Flames, arrangements were made so that 
the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the research team to participate 
in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters.  That team does not 
see the telemetry during the testing, but is in communication via phone and e-mail with their NASA 
research partners at the GRC ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC).  While there are many preparatory 
steps, the tests are ultimately conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files.  In 
advance of the test day, the UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep 
script and specifies other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings.

items.title: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723.pdf
items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 
 
23 July 2020 
3 
 
It is also possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in 
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry.  For example, the electric field potential can be 
adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. 
 
Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, the low 
rate results from several unavoidable factors.  After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz non-imaging data is 
downlinked for immediate review by the science team.  A small sample of images are often downlinked 
to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for those images are typically 
selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples.  The review helps to verify parameters 
or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the voltage range after determining where the 
ion current saturates for the given flame conditions.  After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber 
atmosphere after which the chamber is vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed.  
Midway through a day’s E-FIELD Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter 
cartridge filled with molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion 
products, e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products.  The tests are only 
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay 
Satellite (TDRS) System.  Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic communication outages with 
a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite to another) or can last as long as 30 
minutes. 
 
A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a daily basis.  
The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame spread and material 
flammability.  That follow-on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, where each ACME experiment 
is allotted four months for testing.  Although it requires additional crew time, these allotments are split 
into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from testing for careful review of the early results 
so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of their second round.  This paper reports on early results 
from the first round of E-FIELD Flames. 
 
While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the available gas 
bottles that were and are launched to support the tests.  For E-FIELD Flames and most of ACME’s 
experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established in 2010.  At that time, 
NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of focused experiments with limited 
objectives rather than comprehensive experiments.  As such, the general target was 50 tests per 
experiment.  For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used 
to fill the chamber.  This resource constraint is exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair 
of redundant safety timers to limit the fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers 
can be set for the oxidizer flow in the case of inverse flame testing).  The timers can only be reset by 
venting the combustion chamber.  Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively 
corresponds to the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant).  For 
E-FIELD Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 
10 tests typically completed per day. 
 
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, such as 
the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours.  When necessary for the research, NASA 
does have continuous 24-hour/day operations for some non-CIR experiments.  But as discussed, the ACME 
tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is almost always limited to the planned 
durations.

items.title: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723.pdf
items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 
 
23 July 2020 
4 
 
Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on-orbit hardware can store a limited amount of data.  
More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two-shift transfer and 
downlink day.  Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where image data from select 
cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge.  Nonetheless, the limit sometimes 
forces decisions to abandon recorded images. 
 
This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME 
experiments are conducted.  Their complexity makes the flame conditions seem trivial in comparison.  It 
is a simple coflow flame, with just a small jet of fuel surrounded by a weak coflow of ‘air’ which also fills 
the chamber, but where tests are also conducted with no coflow.  A test includes starting the gas flows to 
prime the system, energizing the igniter to initiate a flame, retracting the igniter, and allowing the flame 
to steady slightly before energizing the electric field to its initial value.  The flame is again allowed to 
steady before beginning a voltage sweep over a specified range with steps or smooth ramps of specified 
voltage changes and durations.  The sweep can be in one direction or can include cycles of sweeps.  After 
each test, a duplicate field sweep is made to ensure that there are no current leaks, i.e., other than the 
ion current through the flame. 
 
The first phase tests in E-FIELD Flames employ the coflow burner geometry shown in Figure 4, with the 
fuel tube extending slightly above the burner surface.  The results shown in this paper are for tests 
conducted with 100% methane in a chamber atmosphere and coflow (when used) of synthetic ‘air’ (i.e., 
21/79 oxygen/nitrogen by volume) at a nominal pressure of 100 kPa.  The mesh is held at a negative 
potential relative to the burner in these tests.  The sweeps shown in this paper extend to at least -7 kV, 
where the voltage is increased in small steps (e.g., of 100 V) lasting 1-2 seconds.  The details of the voltage 
changes can be seen in the resulting plots.

items.title: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723.pdf
items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 
 
23 July 2020 
5 
 
2. Test Sequences and ParametersAll E-FIELD Flames tests conducted on the ISS 
were carried out using automated software which had its roots in ACME’s Integrated Science 
Requirements Documents (ISRD, RDR version, Rev. B) and Science Operations Requirements 
Documents (SORD, Rev. A).  The E-FIELD Flames Science Requirements Document (SRD) is of course 
pertinent but only that which was incorporated in the ISRD and SORD was used by the engineering 
team in developing the control software. 
 
Multiple software scripts and corresponding parameter files were prepared to address the various 
objectives explained in this excerpt from section 4.2 of the ACME ISRD.  The section is fully included with 
the important exception of the tables detailing the envisioned operational sequences.  Given that they 
were conceptual, they were left out to reduce the chance of a confused understanding of the engineering 
implementation.  For example, excessive electromagnetic interference (EMI) led to a change in the design 
of the electric field system limiting the voltage to a single polarity on a given test day.  As a result, the step 
response procedure could not be carried out as detailed in Table 4.2.2 of the ISRD.   
 
The E-FIELD experiment consists of 4 objectives corresponding to 4 series of tests using 2 different 
diffusion flame burner configurations. The first three test series provide the key fundamental 
information regarding the electrical character of diffusion flames and the influence of electric fields on 
soot formation; the final series focuses on electric field sensing and control of flames. 
 
General Operations 
Before any of the electric field experiments, the high voltage mesh should be installed (or moved into 
position). Leak current should be measured by sweeping the voltage from 0 to 10kV and 0 to -10kV 
with no flame present. A steep rise in current under these conditions indicates corona discharge and 
sets the upper limit on the potential. The test sequence involves a complete repeat voltage sweep 
with no flame to provide a point-by-point current leak measurement. A similar sweep should be 
completed following flame extinguishment at the end of a test set. Only ion current would need to be 
measured during the no-flame sweep. In addition, excessive leak current at relatively low voltage may 
indicate electron emission from carbon buildup on the gas jet flame tip. If the leak current exceeds 
10% of the flame ion current, cleaning of the gas jet tip is requested. Cleaning consists of a manual 
wiping or possibly burning off the carbon with a modified flame condition. We expect this to be a rare 
request, but the continuous monitor of flameless ion current provides a reliable in-situ monitor. We 
assume that the chamber will be emptied and refilled approximately every 7-8 tests to minimize the 
oxygen concentration uncertainty in the test chamber. The exact times for settling and voltage steps 
may vary (they should be reconfigurable from the ground), but a nominal expected operational 
sequence for one chamber fill and the key measurement data sets are shown below. 
 
(A) Voltage Sweep – collection of VI curves (or VCC curves) -- where the voltage is swept from 0-±5kV 
(or until flame blowout) and the ion current is monitored and recorded. The sweep will consist of a 
series of discrete steps, where a settling time is allowed after each voltage change. At the same time, 
color and OH* video records the flame shape and luminosity (both broadband flame and soot 
luminosity and OH* chemiluminescence) throughout the sweep. A typical step sweep might comprise: 
15 second ignition & stabilization; 100 V/step, 0.3 sec settle between steps, and a 0.25 sec. ion current 
measurement at each point, to ±5kV or blowout. Blowout can be detected by a sharp drop in ion 
current. Expected run time is 50 seconds per sweep (not including a background current sweep with 
the flame off). However, the time between voltage steps for flame adjustment and data collection 
shall be adjustable via uplink between the values of 0-10 seconds.

items.title: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723.pdf
items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 
 
23 July 2020 
6 
 
 
(B) Step Response—This test will involve the rapid change of voltage from a base level to a much 
higher (or lower) level, while the ion current (and flame luminosity and shape) is monitored in time 
as it settles to its new steady value. The key measurable is the ion current as a function of time through 
the voltage step change and the flame’s subsequent settling. As in test set (A), video, luminosity, and 
chemiluminescence will record flame behaviors in response to an instantaneous change in the electric 
field. A typical experiment sequence might comprise a 15 second ignition and stabilization, step 
changes on the order of hundreds of volts, and recording ion current for 2 seconds between step 
changes (where steps will not be limited to a single polarity). Settling time for these step changes in 
zero gravity (particularly, for soot related phenomena) may need to be adjusted via uplink; the test 
procedures shown are based on a nominal settling time observed in preliminary testing at 1g and the 
2.2 Second Drop Tower. The range of times between voltage steps may vary between 0-100 seconds. 
 
(C) Electric Field Effects on Soot – The following tests will demonstrate the effects of electric fields on 
soot (measured by broadband emission from the flame and soot volume fraction) by slowly increasing 
the coflow air velocity, comparing the flame structure at each step to a flame affected purely by 
electric forcing. Conditions will be uplinked and derived from experiments (A) and (B). Timing will 
depend on the burner, but each test will be allowed at least 100 seconds. Also, note that the step 
time between one coflow velocitity and the next shall be adjustable via uplink between the values of 
0-10 seconds. Broad solid angle collection luminosity, flame images along with soot volume fraction 
and soot pyrometry will be collected. 
 
(D) Open Loop Sensing and Control – The experiments associated with control will be uplinked, based 
on the results of the above baseline mapping experiments (A) and (B) above. Timing will depend on 
the condition, but each test will be allowed at least 70 seconds. The procedure is a series of voltage 
ramps (or small steps with continuous data collection). Ion current and luminosity (broadband and 
CH*) fluctuations will be collected as well as flame images. The time between voltage changes for 
flame adjustment and data collection shall be adjustable via uplink between the values of 0-10 
seconds. 
 
Although four types of E-FIELD Flames tests are discussed above, it was determined by 2017 that three 
types of tests could be used to address the four experimental objectives, where a separate script to 
investigate effects on the soot was not needed. 
 
While scripts were developed for the three remaining sequences, it was later determined that the open 
loop objectives could be accomplished by proper selection of parameter values with the voltage sweep 
script, e.g., limiting the voltage range.  Furthermore, the step response script was ultimately not employed 
because of the slow response time of the high-voltage power supply.  As such, all of the experiment’s 
flame tests were conducted with the voltage sweep script.  Therefore, that procedure is the only one to 
be further discussed in this document. 
 
The major phases of the test sequence are graphically displayed in Figure 1, where the green and gold 
lines represent the oxidizer coflow (if any), nitrogen flow (if any), and fuel flow.   The gold lines represent 
optional changes to flow rates, e.g., for a change in the fuel dilution after ignition.  The phases are 
described in detail at the bottom of the schematic, where the nomenclature throughout the figure 
generally corresponds to parameter names.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 
 
23 July 2020 
40 
 
4. Test Matrices 
For all ACME experiments, including E-FIELD Flames, the test planning is refined in multiple steps as 
described in this section.  Despite refinement, the experiments are always expected to address the science 
objectives approved in the ACME ISRD. 
 
A. Test Matrices: Years in Advance 
The test matrices found in section 5 of the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document 
(ISRD, RDR version, Rev. B) were the basis for planning the equipment and resources, such as gas 
bottles, needed to carry out each of the NASA-selected ACME experiments.  For E-FIELD Flames, 
the test matrices are found in section 5.2.  The investigators were each directed to define matrices 
with required testing which included at most one burner configuration and no more than 
nominally 50 flames ignited.  Regarding these constraints specified by Project Scientist Dennis 
Stocker, the intent was to conduct focused rather than comprehensive research given the 
considerable resources required for testing on the International Space Station.    Meanwhile, there 
were no limits put on desired or highly desired tests because of NASA’s plan to only carry out tests 
designated as required. 
 
However, in the case of E-FIELD Flames, the science loss associated with the slow response time 
of the developed electric field system led to the decision to allow a second burner type and an 
increased number of required tests.  Specifically, the matrix was expanded to 74 flames rather 
than the planned 58, where it must be understood that voltage sweep tests as defined in the ISRD 
require 2 flames, where the voltage is increased in one test and decreased in the other.  As a result 
of this allowance, E-FIELD Flames was carried out with both the coflow burner (developed for the 
CLD Flame experiment) and a gas-jet burner with the same tube size as the coflow burner’s inner 
tube.  This enabled testing with and without the coflow and in the absence of the outer tube (i.e., 
with the gas-jet burner) in order to assess latter’s coupled effect on the electric field distribution 
and oxidizer entrainment. 
 
NASA Glenn’s ISS Control Board later decided to limit ACME testing to nominally 4 months of ISS 
testing per experiment which with preparatory operations, minor delays, repeat testing due to 
science loss, etc. were expected to typically occur in a total of 5 months.  This decision was made 
with the expectation that the required testing, e.g., as specified in the ISRD, could at least mostly 
be accomplished in that time period assuming the availability of crew and other needed 
resources. 
 
As part of his planning, Stocker instigated an alternating sequence of experiment testing, wherein 
investigators would get a break in their testing in order to analyze early results in depth and with 
that knowledge achieve higher science outcomes in their second round of testing.  As a result, 
each experiment was expected to get 2 months of testing per round, which meant nominally 8 
test days per round of testing.  Within that time constraint and available resources, experiments 
were ultimately permitted to plan for and conduct more tests than had been specified as required 
in the ISRD, despite the initial planning which ignored desired and highly desired testing. 
 
B. Test Matrices: Months in Advance 
At least a few months in advance of testing, ACME investigators are directed to submit a refined 
test matrix for the upcoming round corresponding to available hardware, gas bottles, and the 
agreed number of test days.  The refinement can be based on what is learned from experimental,

items.title: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD_Flames_procedure_20200723.pdf
items.text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 
 
23 July 2020 
41 
 
analytical, or computational efforts subsequent to the 2013 ISRD.  Generally, this planning has 
been done in detail comparable to that found in the ISRD, with the important exception that it 
must furthermore establish the required hardware, including the specific mass flow controllers 
(and thus specification of the flow ranges) and gas bottles so that overall experiment operations, 
including crew activity, can be adequately planned.  In this regard, it must establish operational 
plans for the chamber atmosphere on each day of testing including filling, scrubbing (via 
circulation through the adsorber cartridge), venting (whether partial or complete), and 
measurements, if any, with the Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP).  However, 
GCIP measurements were not made during the E-FIELD Flames or CLD Flame experiments. 
 
C. Test Matrices: Days in Advance 
The investigators are required to submit their test parameters for all planned tests by noon 
Eastern at least three business days in advance of each scheduled test day.  That submission 
includes all of test parameters within the script and additional ones which are outside of the script  
Most of the latter deal with camera settings which don’t change during a test, for example the 
filters used with the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) and the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) 
intensified camera.  Outside of the script, the investigators must again specify the chamber 
atmosphere(s) and when GCIP measurements, if any, are planned where those must correspond 
to the plan submitted months earlier.  The script parameters, e.g., specifications of flow rates, 
don’t need to correspond to those previously specified, but they must correspond to the 
hardware and gas bottles planned months earlier and generally the chamber atmospheres as well 
by extension. 
 
Some specific examples of non-script parameters are listed here. 
chamber fill 
IPSU1 (HiBMS) Exposure (ms) 
IPSU1 (HiBMS) CIR Illumination 
IPSU1 Gain (V) 
IPSU1 Binning 
HiBMs Archiving 
Intensified camera frame rate 
 
D. Test Matrices: As-Run 
Within constraints, the ACME tests conducted can use different parameter values than those 
specified in advance.  While the planning is critically important, the plans themselves are not 
particularly useful for interpreting the data.  This is because most tests were conducted with 
parameters that differed in at least a few ways from those planned days earlier. 
 
While it may seem obvious and simple enough to focus attention on the as-run parameter values 
(where an example E-FIELD Flames file name is 18073A3_VoltageSweep.txt), that is unfortunately 
not the case for ACME.  The record of the as-run script parameters was initially reliant on the 
console staff to record the values.  That didn’t always occur as planned and the values were 
sometimes recreated from other records.  Given this shortcoming, the software was altered such 
that the as-run parameters values would automatically be saved.  However, it has been found 
that the software fails to save all parameter values.  The most assured way to get the as-run 
parameter values is presumably from the test day’s automated ACME log file, where an example 
name is 2018-10-17_12-26ACME.log.

items.text:
National Aeronautics and Space Administration
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)
www.nasa.gov
advanced combustion via microgravity experiments 
Burning Rate Emulator (BRE)
• Objective: Fire Safety—To improve our fundamental understanding of materials ﬂammability, such 
   as extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the 
   relevance of existing ﬂammability test methods for low- and partial-gravity environments.
• Flame/Burner: Flat perforated disk fed with gaseous fuel to simulate the burning of solid and 
   liquid fuels, where measurements are made of the thermal feedback upon which the vaporization 
   of such fuels depend.
• Investigators: Profs. James G. Quintiere and Peter B. Sunderland, University of Maryland; and 
   Dr. John L. deRis, FM Global (retired)
• Objective: Energy and Environment—To extend the range of ﬂame conditions that can be 
   accurately predicted by computational models, especially for highly dilute and heavily 
   sooting conditions.
• Flame/Burner: Coﬂow ﬂame where the gaseous fuel issues from an inner tube, which is centered 
   within a much larger outer tube, where an oxygen/nitrogen mixture issues from the annulus. 
• Investigators: Profs. Marshall B. Long and Mitchell D. Smooke, Yale University
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames)
• Objective: Energy and Environment—To gain an improved understanding of ion production in ﬂames 
   and investigate how an electric ﬁeld can be used to control ﬂames through the ion-driven wind.
• Flame/Burner: Gas-jet ﬂame, where (1) the gaseous fuel issues from a small circular tube into a 
   still atmosphere and (2) a high-voltage electric ﬁeld is established between the burner and a 
   disk-shaped copper mesh located a few centimeters downstream of the burner. 
• Investigator: Prof. Derek Dunn-Rankin, University of California, Irvine
Coﬂow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame)
• Objective: Energy and Environment—To improve our understanding of soot inception and control in 
   order to enable (1) the “design” of nonpremixed ﬂames that are both robust and soot free and (2) the 
   optimization of oxygen-enriched combustion.
• Flame/Burner: Spherical ﬂame where the burner gas issues from a porous spherical burner. Tests 
   are planned for both (1) normal ﬂames, where the fuel ﬂows into an oxygen/inert atmosphere and 
   (2) inverse ﬂames, where an oxygen/inert mixture ﬂows into a fuel atmosphere.
• Investigators: Prof. Richard L. Axelbaum, Washington University in St. Louis; Prof. Beei-Huan Chao, 
   University of Hawaii; Prof. Peter B. Sunderland, University of Maryland; and Dr. David L. Urban, 
   NASA Glenn Research Center
Flame Design
PURPOSE: ACME is focused on advanced combustion technology via fundamental microgravity research. The primary goal is to 
improve efﬁciency and reduce pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion. A secondary objective is ﬁre prevention, 
especially for spacecraft.
RESEARCH: ACME includes ﬁve independent experiments investigating laminar, gaseous, nonpremixed ﬂames. They will be 
conducted with a single set of modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station 
(ISS). An ACME precursor, the Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE), was conducted on ISS in 2012.
STATUS: ZIN Technologies, under the direction of the NASA Glenn Research Center, has completed the design and is now 
fabricating the space ﬂight hardware. On-orbit testing is expected to begin in 2017 and continue for a few years.
WEB SITE: http://spaceﬂightsystems.grc.nasa.gov/acme/   
• Objective: Energy and Environment—To advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, 
   including extinction, of both soot-free and sooty ﬂames.
• Flame/Burner: Spherical ﬂame—which is only possible in microgravity—where the gaseous fuel (fed 
   through a small tube) issues from a porous spherical burner into a still oxygen/inert atmosphere.
• Investigators: Prof. C.K. Law, Princeton University;  Prof. Stephen D. Tse, Rutgers University; and 
   Dr. Kurt R. Sacksteder, NASA Glenn Research Center
Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame)

items.text:
National Aeronautics and Space Administration
Glenn Research Center
21000 Brookpark Road
Cleveland, Ohio 44135
PS–01548–0515
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments
Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs)
• Three MFCs for the delivery of fuel, oxidizer, and/or nitrogen to the burner (and 
   chamber for ﬁlling)
• Capable of on-orbit dilution of fuel or oxidizer (but not both at once), coﬂow ﬂames, 
   inverse ﬂames, and premixed ﬂames
Igniter
• Resistively heated, retracting with stepper-motor drive for precise positioning, with an 
   exchangeable tip and arm 
High-Voltage Supply and Electrode Mesh—for E-FIELD Flames
• –10 to +10 kV to crew-removable mesh downstream of burner where the ion current 
   between mesh and burner is determined from the voltage drop across a known resistor
Thermocouples (TCs)
• Six far-ﬁeld TCs to measure the thermal ﬁeld spread, where two versions of a 
   four-TC rake allow varied proximity to the burner
Radiometers (speciﬁcally thermopile detectors)
• One ﬁxed wide-view sensor plus a crew-exchangeable array with up to ﬁve additional 
   radiometers, where all sensors are sensitive from 0.2 to 11 microns
Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) Modules
•Three wide-view PMTs: (1) broadband, 230 to 700 nm, (2) OH* emission, 310-nm ﬁlter, 
   and (3) CH* emission, 430-nm ﬁlter
Analog Color Camera (hidden from view)
• Downlinked in near real time to support operations, with an array of light-emitting diodes 
   (LEDs) to illuminate the burner position, etc.
OH* Camera (not shown)
• Intensiﬁed monochrome camera, 310-nm ﬁlter, 30 frames per second binned at 512512
Digital Color Camera (not shown)
• 12-bit, up to 30 frames per second at 13601024
• Motorized lens with independent control of zoom, iris, and focus 
• Four ﬁlters: (1) clear for color imaging, (2) blue-green ﬁlter to balance color planes for 
   pyrometry and soot volume fraction measurements, and (3-4) 430- and 450-nm ﬁlters 
   for CH* imaging, where the combination enables subtraction of interfering soot emission
Color-Ratio Soot and Thin Filament Pyrometry
• (1) Compare color planes of digital color camera (see above) and/or (2) compare frames from a second monochrome camera (not shown) 
   equipped with a liquid-crystal tunable ﬁlter, 30 frames per second binned at 512512
• Translating array of ﬁve silicon carbide ﬁbers (5 mm apart) with alternate arrays for absolute light calibration
Soot Volume Fraction
• Determined from (1) digital color camera (see above) using pyrometry results and absolute light calibration and/or (2) light extinction using a third 
   monochrome camera (not shown), 30 frames per second at 10241024, and a light source with two ﬁber-coupled laser diodes
Gas Chromatograph (GC)
• Pre- and post-test analysis of chamber atmosphere for oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and fuel gases
ACME Hardware
ACME Operations
• ACME experiments are constant volume, with ~85 liters free, where tests are 
   typically 0.5 to 2 minutes long to limit the pressure rise
• Tests manually set up by ISS crew and then remotely commanded from the 
   NASA Glenn Research Center (Cleveland, OH)
• Tests conducted in (1) a nominally automated mode using preprogrammed 
   scripts and/or (2) a “manual” mode where changes can be made, for example, 
   to ﬂow(s) in response to video downlink and telemetry (e.g., to approach a 
   soot or stability limit)

items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
3 
 
1. Introduction 
The purpose of this report is to provide a description of the experimental hardware and operations of 
used in the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project that is sufficient for 
informed interpretation of the experimental results.  In contrast, it is not the intent of this document to 
review the project management, engineering development, design process, etc. although such aspects 
may be briefly addressed. 
 
The ACME suite of experiments are being carried out on the International Space Station (ISS) in the 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  ACME features investigations with gaseous fuels, such as methane and 
ethylene.  In addition to the fuel state, the current ACME experiments use laminar, non-premixed (i.e., 
diffusion) flames for their studies.  To simplify analysis, these flames are furthermore either axisymmetric 
or spherically symmetric, depending upon the experiment. 
 
Currently, ACME includes six independent experiments of which the first five were selected for testing in 
spaceflight by NASA while the sixth was selected by the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space 
(CASIS) and the National Science Foundation (NSF). 
 
The CIR facility was launched in 2008 and with the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) was 
used for a series of liquid-fueled experiments from 2009 to 2017.  The facility was reconfigured and set 
up for ACME testing by the ISS crew in September and October 2017, where over 25 astronauts from 
Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and the United States have thus far supported the project’s 
research.  As of this writing, over one thousand ACME flames have been ignited on the ISS, where that 
began in Nov. 2017.    It is expected that the planned ACME testing will be completed in 2021, when the 
CIR operations should subsequently shift to the Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) project. 
 
The discussion of the CIR hardware herein is limited, but the research facility is described in various 
documents, such as those listed below.  These are listed in reverse chronological order, where the oldest 
predate the facility’s completion and have become outdated in some regards.  References 1, 2 and 4 also 
discuss ACME, but were all prepared prior to the completion of ACME’s spaceflight hardware. 
1. Suleyman A. Gokoglu, Daniel L. Dietrich, Dennis P. Stocker, Paul V. Ferkul, Sandy L. Olson, Michael 
C. Hicks, Amelia Rai (editor), Neesha Hosein (editor), and Cory Duke (designer), “Combustion 
Science: A Researcher’s Guide to International Space Station,” NASA Publication NP-2015-10-034-
JSC (2015). 
2. J.M. Hickman, D.L. Dietrich, M.C. Hicks, V. Nayagam, V., and D. Stocker, “FLEX: A Decisive Step 
Forward in NASA's Combustion Research Program,” 1st Annual International Space Station 
Research and Development Conference, Denver, Colorado 26-28 June (2012). 
3. “Unlocking Mysteries in Microgravity: NASA Glenn Provides the Keys with the Fluids and 
Combustion Facility,” NASA fact sheet FS-2011-06-035-GRC, PS-00538-0611 (2011). 
4. T.F. O'Malley, W.A. Sheredy, and D.P. Stocker, “Combustion Research on the International Space 
Station,” 59th International Astronautical Congress, Vol. 2, pp. 756-766 (2008). 
5. Terence F. O’Malley, Karen J. Weiland, Craig A. Myhre, Frank G. Gati, Myron E. Hill, and John H. 
Snead, “The Fluids and Combustion Facility and First Payloads: The Multi-User Droplet 
Combustion Apparatus and the Light Microscopy Module: Enabling Research on the ISS,” 57th 
International Astronautical Congress,  IAC-06-A2.1.07, 2-6 Oct. 2006, Valencia, Spain (2006). 
6. T. O’Malley and C. Myrhe, “The Fluids and Combustion Facility Combustion Integrated Rack and 
the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus: Microgravity Combustion Science Using Modular

items.text:
ACME Engineering Implementation 
 
19 May 2022 
4 
 
Multi-User Hardware,” 53rd International Astronautical Congress, The World Space Congress 
2002, IAC-02-J.5.05, 10-19 Oct. 2002, Houston, Texas (2002). 
7. Terence F. O'Malley and Karen J. Weiland, “The FCF Combustion Integrated Rack: Microgravity 
Combustion Science Onboard the International Space Station,” NASA Technical Memorandum 
TM--2002-210981, AIAA-2001-4927, September 2002. 
8. Robert L. Zurawski and Nora G. Bozzolo, “ISS Fluids and Combustion Facility: Combustion 
Integrated Rack: Payload Accommodations - Principal Investigator’s Guide,” NASA report, 
September 2000. 
 
The CIR facility was preceded by the Combustion Module (CM) which flew on the space shuttle Columbia.  
In 1997, the combustion research facility was within Spacelab on the STS-83 and STS-94 (Microgravity 
Science Laboratory) missions.  It was subsequently reconfigured and flew in 2003 within SPACEHAB, again in 
the shuttle’s payload bay, in the STS-107 mission.  The Combustion Module investigations included Laminar 
Soot Processes (LSP), Structure Of Flame Balls At Low Lewis-number (SOFBALL), and the Water-Mist Fire 
Suppression Experiment (Mist).  Although all three experiments burned gaseous fuel, each had its own 
chamber insert, whereas ACME features a single modular chamber insert to accomplish multiple 
investigations.  A significant difference between the CIR and its shuttle precursor is that the ISS tests are 
remotely commanded from the ground without crew involvement, which wasn’t the case with the 
Combustion Module research.  But in all cases the crew are required to configure the necessary hardware. 
 
While extensive, this report is far from exhaustive but there are other reports which provide additional 
detail useful for interpreting ACME’s experimental results.  Some key examples include the following:   
Camera characterization 
 
CFI Intensified Camera Package Characterization Report  
DRAFT REPORT

ACME-RPT-011

ACME-VER-002 Rev. B

ACME-VER-001 Rev. A 
Software and non-imaging data

ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D 
 
Abbreviations are addressed at the end of this report, but ERD stands for Engineering Requirements 
Document and many of the engineering requirements were directly derived from ACME’s science 
requirements.  Meanwhile, key hardware dimensions, for example of the burners, and other details are 
confirmed in the Inspection Verification Report.  Also note that the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) and Cool 
Flames radiometer reports are specific to certain ACME experiments, whereas the other reports are 
general to all of ACME. 
 
ACME Project Scientist Dennis Stocker (216-433-2166, dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov) may be contacted 
with questions about the ACME project.
