3.0  EXPERIMENT REQUIREMENTS 
 
3.1  Requirements Discussion 
 
This section does not include any requirements, but instead describes their importance in 
achieving the experiment objectives. The requirements have been incorporated into the merged 
ACME Science Requirements. 
3.1.1  Experiment Configuration Requirements 
3.1.1.1  Spherical Burner 
The burner will produce flames (up to 4cm radius) with spherical and concentricity 
characteristics meeting or exceeding that presently capable of the spherical burner presently 
provided by the PI.  The burner design includes the spherical, porous burner and the supply tube.   
3.1.1.2  Gas Supply 
Studies will be conducted with gaseous fuels, i.e., hydrogen, methane, and ethylene, all 
diluted with inert(s).  Additional inert(s) can be variably introduced into the final fuel mixture 
stream. 
The fuel/inert mixtures in the experiment include both H2 and CH4, or H2 or CH4 alone, aimed 
at addressing chemical kinetic aspects.  The inert concentrations are all fixed at 55% for all tests 
for baseline comparison.  Higher flow rates are used to examine radiative extinction.  Ramping 
down to lower flow rates are used to examine kinetic extinction.  Flame sooting experiments 
utilize C2H4.  The fuel component (C2H4) concentration is varied from 20-30%.  Since 
characteristic residence time will affect sooting tendencies, two flow rates are investigated. 
The use of the different inerts, i.e. N2, He, CO2, will alter the characteristic flame temperature 
and radiative properties, affecting extinction characteristics.  Additionally, since the different 
inerts directly affect the diffusive properties (and radiative heat loss), flame stability issues can 
be addressed. 
The oxidizing atmospheres will be 21% O2 based, simulating “normal air.”  The balancing 
inerts will correspond to the same used for the fuels. 
3.1.1.3  Burner Gas Delivery 
Flow system shall deliver fuel, inert(s), and oxygen to the burner, in the various combinations 
as stipulated in the Test Matrix (see §3.3).  System must allow different total-flow rates and 
mixture compositions to be delivered to the burner during the course of a single test.  One test is 
estimated to last less than 25s.  A requirement to provide gas at the maximum flow rate for at 
least 25s has been established. 
Flow control of fuel during testing is required.  In some tests, flow rates change within the 
course of the test. 
For a consistent basis of comparison, as well as well-defined modeling conditions, the supply 
temperature of fuel mixture shall be the same for all tests.  Fuel supply temperature affects the 
flame temperature and hence extinction characteristics.

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame_SRD_20100125.pdf
items.text:
29
3.1.1.4  Ignition 
The ignition system (e.g. a hot wire) shall ignite the fuel dispensed from the burner within the 
specified flow ranges, at approximately 3 mm from the burner surface.  50W for 200 ms have 
been shown in drop-tower studies using hot wire to properly ignite the mixtures to be 
investigated.  Since the fuel/oxidizer concentration at the igniter is not known a priori for such 
diffusion flames, ground-based testing is to be conducted to verify the ignition parameters. An 
ignition system with sufficient power shall be required.  Depending on the actual ignition system 
to be utilized, a maximum power requirement will be determined to ensure minimal effects on 
subsequent flame behavior, as well as practical considerations such as wire burnout.  Having the 
flame initially situated near the burner surface, the flame structure is of limited size, providing a 
clear initial condition for computational and theoretical modeling. 
A retractable igniter shall accomplish ignition.  Flame disturbance during deployment and 
retraction of ignition system (e.g., induced wakes, heat transfer into mechanism) should be 
minimal.  Igniter should retract out of performance volume. 
3.1.1.5  Ambient Environment 
The chamber air shall be dry with an initial oxygen mole fraction corresponding to that for 
medical dry air.  In order to accurately quantify the combustion species it is important that the 
initial composition of the chamber atmosphere is precisely known.  This requirement ensures that 
the results of the experiment are not affected by contaminants such as particulate, moisture, or 
trace presence of other species.  Furthermore, it is important to ensure that each test point is 
performed with the same starting conditions in order to allow each test point to be “cross 
referenced” to other test points and to allow for accurate model correlation.  Of particular 
importance is the starting O2 concentration in the chamber prior to each test. 
In the interest of conserving valuable gas resources, the initial ambient gas composition may 
be established by scrubbing the chamber atmosphere between tests as long as repeatable initial 
conditions are achieved.  In this case, ambient concentrations of CO2, H2O, other combustion 
products, and unburned fuel must be reduced to below 0.02% mole fraction combined.  For the 
“CO2-air” cases, H2O, other combustion products, and unburned fuel must be reduced to below 
0.02% mole fraction combined. 
For a consistent basis of comparison, as well as well-defined modeling conditions, the initial 
ambient pressure shall be the same for all tests.  Chamber pressure can vary from 101325 Pa to 
303975 Pa (i.e. 1 to 3 atm) during constant volume combustion.  It is desirable to limit pressure 
increase because pressure affects the thermal diffusivity, density, radiative properties, and 
chemical reaction rates. 
For a consistent basis of comparison, as well as well-defined modeling conditions, the initial 
ambient temperature shall be the same for all tests.  Ambient temperature affects the flame 
temperature and hence extinction characteristics. 
The specified free volume allows up to 25s of constant volume flame evolution without a drop 
in oxygen concentration at 20cm radius (see §Appendix 5.1).  Such duration has been deemed 
sufficient to study the aforementioned flame responses. 
Chamber volume should be sufficient to allow a spherical flame field to develop in a manner 
that is not affected by the chamber walls.  The specified dimensions of volume should allow for

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame_SRD_20100125.pdf
items.text:
30
sufficient distance from the chamber walls to the flame zone so that species and temperature 
gradient fields are not affected (see §Appendix 5.1). 
The large volume of hot gas present in the flame front is very sensitive to disturbance by 
accelerations, characterized by large Grashof numbers.  The maximum allowable acceleration is 
set by the need for the expected local buoyancy-induced flow velocity to be smaller than the 
local fuel flow rate velocity.  See §Appendix 5.5. 
Currently, there are requirements for emission measurements, e.g. with PMTs in the UV and 
visible.  However, knowing the actual emissivity values for the chamber walls and all other 
internal surfaces in direct view of the flame is important because it can affect radiative transport 
to/from the flame.  The requirements for UV and visible wavelengths is based on avoiding 
reflections that would impact imaging quality.  The requirement at IR wavelengths is to mimic a 
large system by avoiding multiple passes of radiation corresponding to photon emission from the 
combustion product species through the flame zone.  Having a high emissivity greatly simplifies 
radiation modeling.  It is desired that actual spectral emissivity values of the internal surfaces are 
provided to the PI. 
 
3.1.2  Monitoring Measurements Requirements 
3.1.2.1  Chamber Pressure 
The measurement of ambient pressure in the chamber is needed to understand the quasi-
steady conditions of the test and the knowledge of the chamber gas pressure.  Measurements of 
the ambient pressure during constant volume combustion are requisite to assess its impact on 
thermal diffusivity, density, radiative properties, and chemical reaction rates. 
3.1.2.2  Chamber Oxygen Concentration (Desired) 
The O2 concentration near the chamber “wall” and at a 10cm radius is desired to be measured.  
These boundary conditions are important for modeling purposes.  10cm radius corresponds to the 
“free area” performance volume specification.  Measurements of the oxygen concentration near 
the chamber wall assess the size of the flame structure, as well as oxygen depletion effects on the 
flame.  
3.1.2.3  Gas Flowrates 
Measurement of the gas flow rate issuing from the burner is a requisite boundary condition for 
the problem. 
3.1.2.4  Acceleration 
Flame Front Motion—Measurement of acceleration is needed in order to determine if changes 
in the flame front velocity or flame shape are due to acceleration or some other factor.  
Continuous measurement of the g-vector will correlate any buoyancy induced flame response, 
e.g. g-jitter. 
Quasi-Steady Extinction—Continuous measurements of the g-vector will correlate any 
buoyancy induced altering of the flame dynamics and structure, affecting the extinction limits.

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame_SRD_20100125.pdf
items.text:
31
Instability and Extinction—Continuous measurement of the g-vector will correlate any 
buoyancy-induced instability. 
Sooty Flames—Continuous measurement of the g-vector will correlate any buoyancy induced 
flame response directly affecting soot formation and transport. 
 
3.1.3  Science Diagnostics Requirements 
3.1.3.1  Optical access  
A minimum of two views along orthogonal axes (normal to support axis of burner) of the 
spherical flame is required in order to allow flame imaging and optical diagnostics, and to assess 
symmetry.  Imaging and optical diagnostics systems include color imaging and UV imaging.  All 
windows shall allow for light transmittance in the specified wavelength range of the 
corresponding imaging equipment. 
3.1.3.2  Color Imaging 
Spatial distribution history of visible emission (0.4 µm to 0.7 µm) from the flame shall be 
imaged from one and if possible, two (2) orthogonal views.  The required field of view (FOV) is 
120 mm in diameter, and an adjustable iris or gain is needed to accommodate varying flame 
intensities.  In addition to flame radius and shape from visible chemiluminescence, some soot 
formation and extinction processes should be observable from visible incandescence.  The 
perpendicular views characterize the symmetry of the flame.  The field of view is set by the need 
to resolve the largest flames anticipated, and the framing rate is set by the need to resolve the 
fastest events anticipated. 
Flame Front Motion—Measurement of the visible radiation from the flame assesses flame 
symmetry and visible “flame radius” to be compared with peak temperature and peak heat 
release rate locations.  Possible soot formation and extinction processes can be assessed from 
incandescence.  Since the visible images will not be deconvoluted (as with case of the UV 
images), the focal depth of the system shall be kept as narrow as possible to ensure imaging of 
the flame at its cross-sectional center “plane.” 
Quasi-Steady Extinction—Lack of visible flame radiation is not a good indicator of flame 
extinction.  See Tse et al. (2001).  The possible discrepancy between the intensity of visible 
flame radiation and magnitude of temperature of the field of the flame structure will be 
compared. 
Instability and Extinction—Visible “flame radius” oscillation may be captured.  Image allows 
for assessment of flame instability induced by the edge flame created by the burner support tube. 
Sooty Flames—In addition to “flame radius” and shape from visible chemiluminescence, soot 
presence should be observable from visible incandescence. 
3.1.3.3  UV Imaging 
Ultraviolet imaging of gas-phase chemiluminescence provides information on the spatial and 
temporal distribution of intermediate product species, i.e. OH* at 310 nm (presently planned) or 
CH* at 431 nm (highly desired)).  Ultraviolet imaging will capture hydrogen/oxygen/inert flame

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame_SRD_20100125.pdf
items.text:
32
images, which cannot be visualized using direct color imaging.  This requirement will be met by 
using the CIR’s Low Light Level UV (LLL-UV) Camera Package.  The LLL-UV package 
covers the spectral range of 200 – 750 nm but will launch with a filter for viewing only the OH* 
line at 310 nm. 
Species concentrations within the flame structure are needed to compare with the detailed 
chemistry computations.  Moreover, OH* emission from the flame often corresponds to the peak 
heat release position, thereby providing the flame location. 
Flame Front Motion—UV imaging of chemilluminescence from electronically excited species 
such as OH* (for all fuels mixtures) and CH* (for fuel mixtures containing elemental carbon) 
provides for the assessment of both detailed chemistry and (to a much lesser degree) flame 
structure, when compared with the computational simulations.  Axisymmetric Abel 
deconvolution of the projection image of the flame chemilluminescence within the focal depth of 
the camera (with appropriate narrow band filters) produces a map of excited species 
concentration as a function of radius (see §Appendix 5.4).  Comparisons with computational 
simulations will allow for possible refinement of the kinetic parameters associated with the 
formation of these excited species, as well as the extrapolation of the distribution of the non-
excited species (for further flame structure assessment).  The peak locations of these excited 
species will be tracked and compared with peak heat release rate location (from computations) 
and peak temperature (from experimental measurement and computations). 
Quasi-Steady Extinction—Measurements of OH* or CH* field, when compared with 
computational simulations, provide for the assessment of the chemistry near the extinction state. 
Instability and Extinction—Measurements of OH* or CH* field allow tracking of the flame 
front near the peak heat release location. 
Sooty Flames—Measurements of the OH* or CH* fields are needed to assess the reaction 
zone profile of the flame structure.  Such measurement allows for the identification of the onset 
of sooting as the flame expands outward from a non-sooty one to a sooty one. 
3.1.3.4  Spherical Burner Temperature 
Transient measurement of the burner surface temperature provides a requisite initial and 
boundary condition for the problem.  The temperature at the burner surface assesses the heat 
transfer to the burner, which affects the flame temperature and hence extinction characteristics.  
Moreover, in order to perform an accurate energy balance it will be necessary to quantify heat 
transfer from the flame, requiring accurate measurements of the temperature at the burner 
surface. 
3.1.3.5  Gas-Phase Temperature Distribution 
The diagnostic should allow for determination of peak temperature position, as well as 
provide flame structure information.  The final diagnostic should provide the density/temperature 
field (1-D radial is sufficient) history, so that local assessment of extinction can be made (based 
on the precipitous drop in temperature). 
Flame Front Motion—Measurements of the temperature/density field are requisite to assess 
the transient flame structure.  Analyses (Tse et al. 2001) have shown that transient response of 
the flame is dependent on the flame structure rather than simply the flame front radius.  Flames

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame_SRD_20100125.pdf
items.text:
33
with the same flame front radius can possess vastly different flame structures; for example, 
compare the infinitely large diffusion flame structure at steady state with the localized one at 
ignition.  The experimental data will then be directly compared to the transient computational 
simulations for both density and temperature distribution.  Additionally, from a mapping of the 
temperature/density profile, the location of peak temperature can be easily identified and tracked.  
Analyses have shown that for above atmospheric pressure, the location of peak temperature, 
rather than that of peak chemiluminescent emission (Tse et al. 2001), corresponds well with the 
location of peak heat release rate, for the mixtures examined.  As a result, the location of peak 
temperature shall be taken to be the flame front radius, one of whose transient response will be 
examined. 
Quasi-Steady Extinction—Measurements of the temperature field are critical for the 
assessment of the moment of flame extinction.  Analyses (Tse et al. 2001) have shown the lack 
of correspondence between chemiluminescent flame intensity and actual flame strength (as 
described by flame temperature and heat release rate).  For example, chemiluminescent flame 
intensity has been shown to decrease under circumstances where the flame temperature is 
increasing. 
Instability and Extinction—Temperature field measurements allow for the assessment of and 
comparison between the magnitude of oscillation of the entire flame structure and that of the 
local flame front location (max T), as well as oscillation in peak temperature. 
Sooty Flames—Measurements of the temperature field are needed to assess the local 
temperature at which soot is formed.  Additionally, the maximum flame temperature for different 
ethylene concentrations can be assessed. 
3.1.3.6  Far-Field Temperature Measurement 
Six (6) locations are specified, with one at each orthogonal-component “of wall” and one at 
each orthogonal-component “of 10cm radius.”  Ambient temperature affects the flame 
temperature and hence extinction characteristics.  10cm radius corresponds to the “free area” 
performance volume specification. 
Measurements of the ambient temperature near the chamber walls provide a requisite 
boundary condition for the problem and allow for the assessment of the growth of the flame 
structure.  Concurrently, such measurements allows for the assessment of possible radiative 
heating of the chamber walls from the flame. 
3.1.3.7  Radiant Emission 
Global flame radiation needs to be measured in order to obtain the radiative heat loss from the 
entire flame.  The spectral response should include CO2 and OH* emission.  Higher than video 
data acquisition rates are needed in order to capture oscillation phenomena.  For measuring total 
flame emission as a function of time, a radiometer viewing the entire flame is envisioned.  
Radiative loss affects the flame temperature and hence extinction characteristics.  Moreover, in 
order to perform an accurate energy balance it will be necessary to quantify heat transfer from 
the flame, requiring accurate measurements of the global flame radiation. 
Flame Front Motion—Measurements of the radiative flux at a fixed position contribute to the 
assessment of the total thermal radiative loss rate, which should increase with the size of the 
flame structure.  It is assumed that radiative heat loss from chemilluminescence is negligible.

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame_SRD_20100125.pdf
items.text:
34
Quasi-Steady Extinction—Measurements of the radiative flux at a fixed position will aid in 
determining the moment of extinction. 
Instability and Extinction—Measurement of the radiative flux at a fixed position captures 
flame oscillations in the heat release rate, whose frequency and magnitude may be difficult to 
capture via direct imaging (i.e., cameras).  Consequently, the rate of date acquisition for this 
diagnostic should be higher than that for direct imaging.  The measured radiative flux will also 
be compared to directly imaged oscillations. 
Sooty Flames—The radiative heat flux is expected to change at the onset of soot formation. 
3.1.3.8  Post-Test Gas Composition (Desired) 
The gas composition should be analyzed (e.g. with GC) locally near the wall at the end of an 
experiment.  This will determine the validity of the imposed boundary condition.  Additionally, 
the gases within the chamber should be well mixed and then analyzed to determine total oxygen 
consumption. 
 
3.2  Operational Sequence 
I. 
Establish chamber at constant pressure and species concentration. 
II. Discharge fuel mixture through porous burner at the initial flow rate. 
III. Ignite fuel mixture with hot wire coil and retract upon successful ignition. 
IV. Allow for spherical diffusion flame to evolve. 
V. Apply one of the following: 
a. Maintain flow rate with same initial mixture for duration of test (25s) or until 
extinction.  See §5 for justification of this duration. 
b. Single step decrease in flow rate with same initial mixture at specified time, 
maintaining new flow rate for duration of test (25s) or until extinction. 
VI. 
Terminate fuel supply to the burner after 25s. 
The proposed flight experiment plan maximizes the value of a single test by satisfying 
multiple scientific objectives.  The priority of the scientific objectives to be examined are 
ordered as listed in §2.1, for both non-sooty and sooty flames: 
(A)  Transient phenomenon leading toward steady flame 
(B)  Extinction phenomenon at “quasi-steady”-states 
(C)  Instability phenomenon, e.g. Le > 1 oscillations and Le < 1 wrinkling 
By ignition with the flame not situated at the steady flame location, we will automatically 
observe (A).  In studying (B), we may perhaps observe (C).  So objectives (A), (B), and (C) may 
all be addressed by conducting a single experiment.

3.4  Test Matrix Summary 
The test matrix (given above in §3.3) is designed to meet the complete success criteria, 
addressing all scientific objectives listed above. 
All experimental sets will address transient phenomenon, as the flame evolves from localized 
ignition towards “steady” behavior, corresponding to Objective (A).  The flames evolve in a 
quasi-steady state manner (becoming history independent), after a short initial transient.  This 
issue is discussed in §Appendix 5.2. 
The rationale for this test matrix is to utilize various mixtures to assess both chemical and 
transport effects (including radiative) on flame behavior.  Pure H2 and pure CH4 are utilized to 
assess kinetic mechanisms associated with each.  Additionally, pure H2 only produces H2O as its 
radiative product, thereby isolating its radiative properties.  Mixtures composed of both H2 and 
CH4 are used to examine their combined chemical and transport effects.  Various inerts which 
affect characteristic flame temperature and transport (molecular and radiative), all in the same 
mole fractions, are utilized for comparison.  C2H4 allows for the examination of a fuel with 
nominal unity Le number.  Additionally, its characteristic sooting nature directly addresses our 
basic science objectives focusing on (A) spreading of flame sheets, (B) dual extinction states, 
and (C) flamefront instabilities. 
The fuel/inert mixtures in the REQUIRED experiment sets 1-2 include H2/CH4 mixtures (see 
subsets a, b, c) and H2 and CH4 as pure fuels (see subsets d, e) aimed at addressing chemical 
kinetic aspects.  The inert mole fractions are all fixed at 55% for baseline comparison.  As can be

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame_SRD_20100125.pdf
items.text:
37
seen, the difference between sets 1 and 2 is the inert (N2 versus He), which is chosen to assess 
transport (e.g. diffusive properties) effects on flame stability.  For example, experimental set 2 is 
aimed at inducing the pulsating instability for Le > 1, corresponding to Objective (C).  The fuel 
components and their relative compositions are the same for sets 1-2, with different inert species 
in balance; similarly, the ambient composition reflects the use of a different inert species in the 
fuel mixture.  It is noted that the characteristic flame temperatures (which will affect the 
Zeldovich number, Ze) will be different for the two experimental sets affecting stability and 
extinction. 
Experiment sets 1-2 will also assess radiative extinction for high flow rates (see i, ii, iii under 
the flow rate category) and kinetic extinction for low flow rates (see iv and v under the flow rate 
category), corresponding to Objective (B).  With regard to radiative extinction, mixture 
compositions of 25%H2/20%CH4, 20%H2/25%CH4, and 30%H2/15%CH4 have been shown in 
drop-tower experiments to be characterized by different radiative extinction times.  These 
mixtures also eschew sooty ignition (due to strong H2 presence), which can otherwise result in 
asymmetrically trapped soot that deteriorates flame sphericity.  With respect to kinetic 
extinction, note that a step change from a higher flow rate to a lower one is needed because 
starting with a flow rate below the extinction limit would preclude flame establishment in the 
first place. 
The HIGHLY DESIRED experiment sets 3-4 utilize C2H4 as fuel.  With a nominal Le of unity 
with respect to air for this fuel, a baseline case (experiment set 3) for flame stretch and thermal-
diffusive stability effects is established.  The fuel and inert mole fractions for the C2H4/inert are 
varied to address different fuel concentration effects on sooting, which can impact Objectives 
(A) flame spread behavior, (B) extinction, and (C) flame stability.  Soot will also enhance flame 
radiation.  Since characteristic residence times will affect sooting tendencies, two flow rates are 
investigated for each mixture.  Experiment set 4 replaces the inert, N2, of set 3 with He, to better 
isolate Le>1 instabilities, corresponding to Objective (C), as well as examine extinction for 
characteristically higher flame temperatures. 
The DESIRED experiment sets 5-6 examine the same fuel mixtures of the REQUIRED and 
HIGHLY DESIRED experiment sets, but with CO2 as inert, including that for the ambient.  N2 
and He are radiatively transparent gases; while CO2 is an optically participating gas.  While use 
of CO2 should result in a characteristically lower flame temperature, the highly reabsorptive CO2 
species can minimize net radiative heat loss affecting flame dynamics and extinction.  Objectives 
(A)-(C) are addressed by these experiments. 
The maximum duration of any test is 25s.  See §5 for justification of this duration.  A test is 
terminated early if the flame extinguishes. 
 
3.5  Success Criteria 
Success of the s-Flame Experiment will be judged on meeting the stated science objectives.  
Three different levels, minimal, substantial, and complete success, are defined below.

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame_SRD_20100125.pdf
items.text:
38
3.5.1  Minimal Success  
Minimal success is defined to mean sufficient scientific data return from the experiment to 
perform a direct comparison with the numerical flame simulation and publish a single archival 
journal article.  This minimal level of success may be achieved by obtaining (for example): 
1. Observations of transient flame phenomena leading toward steady state flames for 1 
CH4 case and 1 C2H4 case.  Such observations must include, at a minimum, the flow 
and boundary condition measurements, flame temperature data and image sequences 
from at least two orthogonal imaging systems; or 
2. Observations of flame extinction at both low and high system Damkohler number for 
1 case.  Such observations must include, at a minimum, the flow and boundary 
condition measurements, flame temperature data and image sequences from at least 
two orthogonal imaging systems; or 
3. Observations of spherical soot formation in 1 C2H4 case.  Such observations must 
include, at a minimum, the flow and boundary condition measurements, flame 
temperature data and image sequences from at least two orthogonal imaging systems. 
3.5.2  Significant Success 
Significant Success is defined to mean sufficient scientific data return from the experiment to 
perform direct comparison with the numerical flame simulation resulting in multiple archival 
journal publications, but less return that defined for complete success.  This significant level of 
success may be achieved by obtaining (for example): 
1. Observations of at least two instances of flame front instabilities including at least one 
hydrocarbon fuel.  Such observations must include, at a minimum, the flow and 
boundary condition measurements, and data quantifying the flame front oscillations 
from image sequences from at least two of the three imaging systems and from the 
radiometer instrument; or 
2. Combinations or extensions (in terms of number of mixture ratios for a single 
hydrocarbon fuel or number of hydrocarbon fuels) of at least two of items 1 through 3 
defined for minimum success; or 
3.5.3  Complete Success 
Complete Success is defined as meeting all of the experiment objectives, including as a 
minimum: 
1. Observations of transient flame phenomena leading toward steady state flames for at 
least three different mixture ratios of each of two hydrocarbon fuels and two diluents.  
Such observations must include, at a minimum, the flow and boundary condition 
measurements, flame temperature data, image sequences from two orthogonal imaging 
systems, and radiometer data; and 
2. Observations of flame extinction at both low and high system Damkohler number for 
at least three different mixture ratios of each of two hydrocarbon fuels and two 
diluents.  Such observations must include, at a minimum, the flow and boundary

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame_SRD_20100125.pdf
items.text:
39
condition measurements, flame temperature data, image sequences from two 
orthogonal imaging systems, and radiometer data; and 
3. Observations of at least two instances of flame front instabilities each including at 
least one hydrocarbon fuel.  Such observations must include, at a minimum, the flow 
and boundary condition measurements, and data quantifying the flame front 
oscillations from image sequences from at least two orthogonal imaging systems and 
from the radiometer instrument; and 
4. Observations of soot formation. Such observations must include the flow and 
boundary condition measurements, flame temperature data, image sequences from all 
imaging systems, temperature data, and radiometer data. 
3.6  Post Flight Data Analysis Plan 
Each test conducted on orbit will produce unique digital and imaging data – all of which are 
to be directly compared to the results of numerical simulations of the identical test conditions 
using the transient code developed under this program.  These processed data sets are derived 
from the raw data produced by the experiment hardware, data acquisition, and imaging systems 
and conveyed to the investigator team through the flight hardware systems, space to ground 
communications systems, ground-based data handling systems, and the ground-based project 
operations team.  These specific data sets are required to describe and evaluate the results of the 
flight experiments and to perform the comparisons between the experimental results and 
underlying detailed simulations of flames.  In many instances, these data sets are required for 
analysis between successive test runs in order to either confirm or change the test conditions for 
the later tests.  In each case, the data must be synchronized to a common time base that can be 
referenced to the ISS time standard.  Except for the digital imaging data (i.e., items 2-4 and 6 
below), the data must be provided to the investigator team in standard engineering units and in 
tabular electronic files such as a spreadsheet. 
There are specific data sets that are needed: 
1. 
Flow and Boundary Conditions, establishing the operating parameters of each test: 
a. Burner flow rate and composition vs. time for each test, derived from the monitoring 
data of one or more gas sources (fuel(s), diluent(s), oxygen).  Establishes boundary 
conditions. 
b. Ambient oxygen concentration vs. time, derived from monitoring data obtained in the 
far field of the test chamber.  Establishes boundary conditions. 
c. Pressure vs. time, derived from monitoring data obtained in the test chamber. 
d. Three-axis accelerations vs. time, derived from monitoring data obtained near the 
chamber.  Establishes body forces imposed on flames. 
e. Ambient temperature vs. time, derived from monitoring data obtained in the far field 
of the test chamber.  Establishes boundary conditions and heat loss rate to the far field. 
f. Burner surface temperature vs. time, derived from thermocouple or alternative 
measurements.  Establishes flow boundary conditions and heat loss rate to the burner.

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame_SRD_20100125.pdf
items.text:
40
2. 
Flame temperature vs. radius and time, derived from imaging data by the PI’s – e.g. 
thin filament pyrometry.  Provides flame structure and the primary indication of flame 
extinction. 
3. 
UV intensity vs. radius and time, related to emissions/concentrations of OH* and CH*, 
derived from digital images.  Provides flame structure and one indicator of extinction. 
4. 
Visible Image vs. time, derived from digital images.  Provides visualization of flame 
behavior including symmetry, flame front velocities, extinction radius. 
5. 
Radiation flux vs. time, derived from calibrated radiometer data.  Provides estimate of 
total radiative flux from the flame and one indicator of flame extinction. 
6. 
Soot Volume Fraction vs Radius and Time, derived from laser extinction 
measurements.  Provides assessment of soot presence, especially that which may be at 
temperatures below the threshold for visible observation from incandescence. 
Table 3.6 shows the relationship between these data sets and the Experiment Objectives.  Data 
Sets 1, 2, and 5 are to be compared directly to the results of the numerical simulations.  Image 
sequences 3 and 4 require complex processing including extraction of line intensity data along 
axi-symmetric chords, data inversion (Abel Transform) to obtain axi-symmetric distributions, 
conversion to relative species number density or temperature units.

Within the framework of gas-phase quasi-steadiness, the flamefront motion process can be 
described as follows.  Since the flame is initially situated close to the porous burner and far from 
the steady-state flame position, the fuel mass consumption rate at the flame is smaller than the 
fuel production rate from the burner.  Consequently, the flamefront spreads outwardly, as it seeks 
the steady-state position where the fuel consumption and fuel production rates are equal, 
resulting in an accumulation of the fuel vapor between the droplet surface and flame.  It is the 
flamefront motion itself, adjusting its velocity in order to completely consume the mass flow of 
fuel entering its reaction zone that governs the quasi-steady expansion behavior.

5.3  Heat Transfer to Burner Considerations 
 
To attempt to address the worst-case scenario, we examine the adiabatic case (at constant 
pressure) with no radiative loss.  Note that the burner represents only the solid material and not 
the gas inside it.  Ideally, the burner should be adiabatic such that all of the heat conducted 
toward it from the flame is directly transferred to the gas mixture within it, with its only purpose 
being to provide a uniform flow field.  Consequently, the entire flow-field temperature 
distribution including an adiabatic burner should be the same as that for a point source issuing 
fuel mixture at zero radius.  Here, we assume that the initial mixture temperature is 300K.  
Figure A.6 compares the initial temperature profiles (where a flame is ignited a few millimeters 
away from the burner surface) for an adiabatic case and one where the temperature at the burner 
surface is measured to be 350K (20%H2-25%CH4-55%N2, 15.72 mg/s).

5.4  UV Imaging:  Comparison with Experiment and Computation 
 
A nearly-spherical, “inverse” hydrogen flame was formed by issuing a 9%O2/91%N2 mixture 
of mass flow rate m = 0.078 g/s into a pure hydrogen environment at a chamber pressure of 
0.079 atm.  A chemiluminescence image of electronically-excited hydroxyl radical was captured 
by a Xybion IMC-201 intensified multispectral video camera with a 50-mm, UV-transmissive 
lens and narrowband interference filter centered at 310nm with full-width, half maximum of 
20nm.  Flame luminosity was always contained within the focal depth of the camera system, so 
that the image could be treated as a line-of-sight projection.  After digital image filtering and 
processing, the 2-D projections were spatially deconvoluted (separately for half of the 
“symmetric” projections) to map local luminosity as a function of radial position. A “3-
dimensional” images of the flame chemiluminescence were then constructed from vertical stacks 
of Abel deconvoluted two-dimensional slices.  Figure A.10(a) shows the OH* flame projection 
image, and Fig. A.10(b) shows the Abel deconvoluted image. 
 
   
   r - ←→r +
 
(a)                                       (b) 
Figure A.10 
 
The experimental flame was computationally simulated using the Sandia burner-stabilized 
premixed flame code, with boundary conditions modified for nonpremixed burning.  The mass 
flow rate, burner surface temperature, and ambient temperature were specified by the 
experiment, along with the boundary mixture compositions. Additionally, the computational 
domain size was set so that the computed maximum temperature location corresponded to that 
measured experimentally.  As it turned out, the resulting computational domain size equaled the 
effective spherical radius (24.8cm), calculated from the physical volume of the non-spherical 
chamber. 
The reaction mechanism used was based on the H2/O2/N2 mechanism developed by Mueller 
[1], which consists of 9 species and 21 elementary reaction steps, obtained at conditions ranging 
from 0.3 to 15.7atm and 850–1040K. OH* chemiluminescence reactions were added to the 
above mechanism.  OH* in the first electronically excited state is produced primarily from the 
reaction H + O + M → OH* + M.  At the same time OH* disappears by the quenching step OH* 
+ M → OH + M and by photon emission OH* → OH + hν, corresponding to the transition 2Σ+ 
→ 2Π, observable at 305.4nm.  The rate constants for these steps were taken from Refs. [2, 3], 
with the heat of formation for OH* set at 93kcal/mol above that of ground-state OH.

items.text:
ACME/s-Flame Experimental Procedure 
 
8 April 2021 
2 
 
1. Introduction 
The narrative description of the experimental procedure is an excerpt from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ 
section of the following conference paper. 
Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on Flames in 
Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States 
Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018. 
 
While the paper was written for the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) 
experiment, much of the discussion applies to ACME in general, including the s-Flame investigation.  The 
figure referenced in this excerpt is not included herein.  Clarifications and additional information, not in 
the conference paper, are included in boxed notes like this. 
 
The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  Thus far, ACME’s activity has 
included the majority of the crew members, regardless of their nationalities.  Most often the astronauts 
and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips.  In the latter case, the igniter 
tip exchange can occur after failure or proactively before failure when the crew already has changes to 
make changes in the interior of the insert.  While these activities may seem mundane, the crew play a 
critical role in setting up the hardware for each experiment.  As an extreme example, there were crew 
activities on 8 separate days in Sept.-Oct. 2017 to configure the CIR and ACME hardware for the first ACME 
experiment, namely the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  In contrast, only two 
crew days were required to reconfigure the hardware for the first E-FIELD Flames tests because of the 
initial use of the same coflow burner.  Planning is critical because crew activity is scheduled three weeks 
in advance, for which detailed procedures must be prepared and uplinked to the ISS. 
 
Similarly, the s-Flame experiment was conducted using the same burner as the Flame Design investigation 
which preceded it.  However, there was hardware reconfiguration for s-Flame to enable use of an 
additional intensified camera for imaging OH* chemiluminescence, namely the Low Light Level Ultraviolet 
(LLL-UV) camera. 
 
All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center 
(GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio.  Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the testing.  The CIR 
hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer (DMO) consoles, and the 
ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console.  Two shifts of personnel are 
scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they typically last 14 hours with the many 
pre- and post-testing activities.  Given that the tests are remotely commanded, the operations are carried 
out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., from 7 AM to 9 PM.  A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are 
normally conducted in a period of 10 hours of less.  Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per 
two weeks.  On intervening weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both 
gas bottles.  Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2-shift day for the RO 
and DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors and 
that data is not missing.  Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew activity.  As 
a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week.  A team of four carry 
out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily operational plans typically 
exceed 50 pages on days including testing. 
 
The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in near real 
time but doesn’t allow for commanding.  In the case of E-FIELD Flames, arrangements were made so that

items.title: PSI-23_Engineering Documents_s-Flames_procedure_20210408.pdf
items.text:
ACME/s-Flame Experimental Procedure 
 
8 April 2021 
3 
 
the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the research team to participate 
in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters.  That team does not 
see the telemetry during the testing, but is in communication via phone and e-mail with their NASA 
research partners at the GRC ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC).  While there are many preparatory 
steps, the tests are ultimately conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files.  In 
advance of the test day, the UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep 
script and specifies other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings.  
It is also possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in 
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry.  For example, the electric field potential can be 
adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. 
 
Provisions have been made to enable the investigators from all ACME experiments to remotely view the 
analog video while they communicated verbally with NASA science personnel in the operations center.  
Thus far, all ACME flame tests, including those for s-Flame and E-FIELD Flames, have been conducted in an 
automated manner using software scripts and extensive parameter files. 
 
Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, the low 
rate results from several unavoidable factors.  After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz non-imaging data is 
downlinked for immediate review by the science team.  A small sample of images are often downlinked 
to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for those images are typically 
selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples.  The review helps to verify parameters 
or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the voltage range after determining where the 
ion current saturates for the given flame conditions.  After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber 
atmosphere after which the chamber is vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed.  
Midway through a day’s E-FIELD Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter 
cartridge filled with molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion 
products, e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products.  The tests are only 
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available through NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay 
Satellite (TDRS) System.  Depending on the various orbits, there are periodic communication outages with 
a loss of signal (LOS) that can be a short handover (from one satellite to another) or can last as long as 30 
minutes. 
 
In contrast to E-FIELD Flames, an average of 15 flames were ignited per test day for s-Flame, but they were 
of even shorter durations. The pressure rise with an s-Flame test was small and the chamber was rarely 
vented after a test unless the chamber atmosphere was being adjusted for other purposes.  In this regard, 
the chamber atmosphere was sometimes scrubbed for the s-Flame investigation by recirculating it through 
the adsorber cartridge, but this was not a regular routine as in the case of E-FIELD Flames.  The chamber 
was also sometimes partially or completely vented and refilled during s-Flame operations, for example to 
adjust the atmosphere’s oxygen concentration. 
 
Unlike E-FIELD Flames, the s-Flame experiment also made use of the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph 
Instrumentational Package (GCIP) to measure species concentrations of the atmosphere in the combustion 
chamber.  There is no sampling probe and measurements are only made before, between, or after tests 
when the chamber atmosphere was ‘stirred’ through use of a fan.  For s-Flame, the GC measurements 
were made on most but not all test days, but they were limited in scope because of the significant time 
required.  The GC measurements were sometimes only made at the end of the test day but were 
occasionally made earlier in the day, for example prior to an adjustment of the chamber atmosphere.

items.title: PSI-23_Engineering Documents_s-Flames_procedure_20210408.pdf
items.text:
ACME/s-Flame Experimental Procedure 
 
8 April 2021 
4 
 
A variety of constraints limit the number of tests that can be performed, both overall and on a daily basis.  
The next combustion experiments in the CIR will feature solid fuels and focus on flame spread and material 
flammability.  That follow-on plan limits the duration of ACME operations, where each ACME experiment 
is allotted four months for testing.  Although it requires additional crew time, these allotments are split 
into two rounds so that the investigators have a break from testing for careful review of the early results 
so that they can maximize the scientific outcome of their second round.  This paper reports on early results 
from the first round of E-FIELD Flames. 
 
In contrast to earlier plans, the two rounds of the s-Flame experiment occurred sequentially because of 
limited crew availability.  Due to delays in commercial crew transport, the space station had three rather 
six crew members through much of 2020.  As a result of the reduced crew size, the s-Flame investigators 
did get a 3-month break (in Feb. to April) between their two rounds of flame tests allowing them to study 
early results and prepare for the second round.   Hardware issues also stretched out s-Flame operations in 
the latter half of 2019.   
 
While nitrogen is available from the space station, the combustion testing is limited by the available gas 
bottles that were and are launched to support the tests.  For E-FIELD Flames and most of ACME’s 
experiments, the test matrices used to plan those gas resources were established in 2010.  At that time, 
NASA limited the scope of the ACME tests matrices with the intent of focused experiments with limited 
objectives rather than comprehensive experiments.  As such, the general target was 50 tests per 
experiment.  For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used 
to fill the chamber.  This resource constraint is exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair 
of redundant safety timers to limit the fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers 
can be set for the oxidizer flow in the case of inverse flame testing).  The timers can only be reset by 
venting the combustion chamber.  Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively 
corresponds to the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant).  For 
E-FIELD Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 
10 tests typically completed per day. 
 
The second round of the s-Flame experiment featured helium dilution of both the fuel and the oxidizer, so 
its testing was also limited by the oxygen/helium bottles launched for that purpose. 
 
The 999-second limit on the valve safety timers has thus far been common for all ACME testing.  However, 
the timers can be reset to 999 by nearly completely venting the chamber.  Sufficient time and gas resources 
are needed to vent and refill the chamber and still conduct tests afterward and that was only occasionally 
done for s-Flame. 
 
Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, such as 
the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours.  When necessary for the research, NASA 
does have continuous 24-hour/day operations for some non-CIR experiments.  But as discussed, the ACME 
tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is almost always limited to the planned 
durations. 
 
Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on-orbit hardware can store a limited amount of data.  
More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two-shift transfer and 
downlink day.  Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where image data from select

cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge.  Nonetheless, the limit sometimes 
forces decisions to abandon recorded images. 
 
This detailed description of operations and hardware provides the context under which the ACME 
experiments are conducted.  …  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2. Test Sequence and Parameters 
All s-Flames tests conducted on the ISS were carried out using automated software which had its roots in 
ACME’s Integrated Science Requirements Documents (ISRD, RDR version, Rev. B) and Science Operations 
Requirements Documents (SORD, Rev. A).  The s-Flame Science Requirements Document (SRD) is of course 
pertinent but only that which was incorporated in the ISRD and SORD was used by the engineering team 
in developing the control software. 
 
The major phases of the test sequence are graphically displayed in Figures 1 and 2, which are respectively 
for the two-rounds of s-Flame testing.  The first round was carried out with nitrogen dilution of the fuel 
and atmosphere, where that inert gas was available from the space station.  Meanwhile, the second round 
was carried out with fuel diluted in advance (on the ground) with helium.  Similarly, bottles of 30% oxygen 
with a balance of helium (on a volume basis) were launched for this testing, where that was often diluted 
with 100% helium (also launched for s-Flame) to conduct tests in a 21% oxygen atmosphere. 
 
The lines appearing in the Figures 1 and 2 represent the inert (i.e., nitrogen or helium) flow rate, the fuel 
flow rate, the igniter position and power.  The lines that are more lightly shaded represent some optional 
changes to flow rates, for example for a change in flow rate(s) following ignition.  However, the flow 
variations in the darkly shaded lines are also optional.  The phases are described in detail at the bottom 
of each schematic, where the nomenclature throughout these figures generally corresponds to the script 
parameter names.

ACME/s-Flame Experimental Procedure 
 
8 April 2021 
37 
 
NASA Glenn’s ISS Control Board later decided to limit ACME testing to nominally 4 months of ISS 
testing per experiment which with preparatory operations, minor delays, repeat testing due to 
science loss, etc. were expected to typically occur in a total of 5 months.  This decision was made 
with the expectation that the required testing, e.g., as specified in the ISRD, could at least mostly 
be accomplished in that time period assuming the availability of crew and other needed 
resources. 
 
As part of his planning, Stocker instigated an alternating sequence of experiment testing, wherein 
investigators would get a break in their testing in order to analyze early results in depth and with 
that knowledge achieve higher science outcomes in their second round of testing.  As a result, 
each experiment was expected to get 2 months of testing per round, which meant nominally 8 
test days per round of testing.  Within that time constraint and available resources, experiments 
were ultimately permitted to plan for and conduct more tests than had been specified as required 
in the ISRD, despite the initial planning which ignored desired and highly desired testing. 
 
B. Test Matrices: Months in Advance 
At least a few months in advance of testing, ACME investigators are directed to submit a refined 
test matrix for the upcoming round corresponding to available hardware, gas bottles, and the 
agreed number of test days.  The refinement can be based on what is learned from experimental, 
analytical, or computational efforts subsequent to the 2013 ISRD.  Generally, this planning has 
been done in detail comparable to that found in the ISRD, with the important exception that it 
must furthermore establish the required hardware, including the specific mass flow controllers 
(and thus specification of the flow ranges) and gas bottles so that overall experiment operations, 
including crew activity, can be adequately planned.  In this regard, it must establish general 
operational plans for the chamber atmosphere on each day of testing including filling, scrubbing 
(via circulation through the adsorber cartridge), venting (whether partial or complete), and 
measurements, if any, with the Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). 
 
C. Test Matrices: Days in Advance 
The investigators are required to submit their test parameters for all planned tests by noon 
Eastern at least three business days in advance of each scheduled test day.  That submission 
includes all of the test parameters within the script and additional ones which are outside of the 
script  Most of the latter deal with the camera settings which don’t change during a test, for 
example the filters used with the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) and the Cool Flames Investigation 
(CFI) intensified camera.  Outside of the script, the investigators must again specify the chamber 
atmosphere(s) and when GCIP measurements, if any, are planned where those must correspond 
to the plan submitted months earlier.  The script parameters, e.g., specifications of flow rates, 
don’t need to correspond to those previously specified, but they must correspond to the 
hardware and gas bottles planned months earlier and generally the chamber atmospheres as well 
by extension. 
 
Non-script parameters specified in advance for s-Flame are listed here. 
chamber fill pressure (psia) 
chamber fill O2% 
chamber fill He% 
GC Sample (Before, After or No) 
GC Sample Method (O2, Byproducts or Both)

D. Test Matrices: As-Run 
Within constraints, the ACME tests conducted can use different parameter values than those 
specified in advance.  While the planning is critically important, the plans themselves are not 
particularly useful for interpreting the data.  This is because most tests were conducted with 
parameter values that differed in at least a few ways from those planned days earlier. 
 
While it may seem obvious and simple enough to focus attention on the as-run parameter values 
(where an example s-Flame file name is as run20176A1.txt), that is unfortunately not the case for 
ACME because the as-run values were not always completely recorded, despite the 
implementation of automated recording.  The most assured way to get the as-run parameter 
values is presumably from the test day’s automated ACME log file, where an example name is 
2020-06-24_15-10_ACME.log.

items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
11 
1.0 
SCOPE 
1.1 
Identification 
The purpose of this document is to identify the design of the communication interfaces used by 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME). 
1.2 
System Overview 
 
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) is mini-facility designed to 
support Principal Investigators (PI) interested in studying various aspects of advanced 
combustion in a microgravity environment.  ACME will be integrated into the Fluids and 
Combustion Facility’s (FCF) Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) onboard the International Space 
Station in the US Lab Module.   
ACME will perform microgravity experiments to study fire suppression/flame extinguishment 
via 5 experiments: s-flame, Flame design, CLD Flame, E-Field Flames, and Burning Rate 
Emulator Flames as described in the ACME Baseline Description Document, ACME-DOC-004.  
ACME will allow investigation using pure as well as mixtures of gaseous fuels at various 
chamber atmosphere pressures, compositions, and oxygen concentrations.  The microgravity 
environment allows for observation and measurement of flame formation and extinguishment 
processes that cannot be made in sustained gravity.  The modular design of ACME allows for 
flexibility in configuration for specific experiments and easy maintainability of the hardware.  
The core elements of gaseous combustion are included in the ACME design as a basis for current 
and future gaseous combustion studies.  These elements are establishment of gas flow through 
various exchangeable mass flow controllers, ignition of gas at the burner and the use of 
appropriate diagnostic measurement devices.  The five identified experiments, and any future 
experiments, use these core elements to build a unique set of requirements for the study of 
various phenomena distinctive to gaseous combustion.  The goal of ACME is to improve the 
fundamental understanding of combustion processes in order to enable increased efficiency and 
reduce pollutant emission in practical combustion. 
 
1.3 
Document Overview 
This document is divided into interfaces used to communicate with the ISS (i.e., external 
communication interfaces) and interfaces used to communicate with devices within ACME that 
require a protocol (i.e., internal communication interfaces).

EXTERNAL COMMUNICATION INTERFACES 
ACME commands originate from the ACME Ground Software (AGS) CSCI on a ground 
workstation at the Telescience Center (TSC) at Glenn Research Center (GRC).  These commands 
are then forwarded through a variety of systems until they eventually end up at the CIR on the 
ISS.   
 
Figure 1  ACME System Diagram 
 
 
3.1 
CIR Input/Output Processor (IOP) Interface 
Commands sent through the CIR IOP (Input Output Processor) are in the format required by 
FCF-ICD-0076A.  See section A.1, FCF Command Protocol for a listing of the required 
command formats, including all required headers.  All commands from the ground go to the IOP 
with the FCF Command Header and User Data filled in.  Commands from ACME to the IPSUs 
and IPSU-Gs go through the FCFCommunications application (Base Classes) which fills in the 
Command Sequence Count and Time Fields in the FCF Command Header before submitting the 
packet to the IOP for routing.

ACME Commands 
Because it is a CIR PI package, ACME Package Command IDs in the FCF Command Header are assigned the range 0xC000-0xCFFF.  
The table below lists the commands, their IDs, and mnemonics. 
Detailed descriptions and parameter lists for each command follow the table.  In the parameter list for each command the parameter 
name is the variable name in the code, which is useful to know when Qt scripts are being written.  The name of the command, for 
example ‘NullCommand’, is also the name in code, in Qt scripts, and in log messages announcing the reception and completion of 
commands. 
Regarding parameters of type String, the entire available length can be used for characters without a terminating zero character.  If a 
string is less than the available length then a terminating zero character needs to be used.  The ground command software will make 
this transparent to the normal user.

items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
21 
3.1.2 
ACME Common Group Command Details 
These commands are called ‘common’ because they are  implemented using code shared 
between several payloads.  The detailed descriptions below are derived from the original 
documentation for these commands in Appendix K of FCF-ICD-0076, Rev C or later.  As stated 
in that appendix the high order bytes of the command ID are replaced by the command group 
number assigned to ACME common commands, which is 0xC0.  In that appendix the command 
IDs range from 0x0001 to 0x0038.  For ACME they range from 0xC001 to 0xC038. 
3.1.2.1 
NullCommand 
The NullCommand does nothing.  It can be used to test communication paths. 
Command ID: 0xC001 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_NULL 
3.1.2.2 
ExternalCommand 
The ExternalCommand command allows an avionics Main Processor (MP) CSCI to have no 
knowledge of this command and make use of the External Module feature. The command is 
passed to an External Module without intervention. This command enforces the requirement that 
an External Module requires a “module identifier” as the first parameter. The command group 
portion of the command ID, XX, depends on the module. 
Command ID: 0xXX02 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_EXTERNAL_PASS_THRU 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Description 
moduleIdentifier 
2 
Uint16 
Identifier (e.g. camera number 1,2) 
Command parameters 
80 
Area for module command-dependent parameters. 
 
3.1.2.3 
GoToIdle 
The GoToIdle command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the IDLE state. 
Command ID: 0xC003 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_IDLE 
 
3.1.2.4 
GoToExp 
The GoToExp command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the EXPERIMENT state. 
Command ID: 0xC004 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_EXPERIMENT

3.1.2.6 
GoToUpDownLink 
The GoToUpDownLink command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the 
UPLINK/DOWNLINK state. 
Command ID: 0xC006 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_UPLINK_DOWNLINK 
 
3.1.2.7 
GoToSafed 
The GoToSafed command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the SAFED state. 
Command ID: 0xC007 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_SAFED 
 
3.1.2.8 
SetRegistryItem 
The SetRegistryItem command selects an item in the registry file, 
/payload/app/config/AcmeConfig.ini, for modification by the SetRegistryValue command. The 
full path including group is required.  In Table 32, AcmeConfig.ini Contents, the full path is 
/Group/Key. 
Command ID: 0xC008 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON _REGISTRY_SET _ITEM 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Description 
registryName 
82 
String 
/Group/Key in AcmeConfig.ini (e.g. 
/EField/OutputFactorA) 
 
3.1.2.9 
SetRegistryValue 
The SetRegistryValue command selects the key set via the SetRegistryItem command and 
modifies it with the supplied value.  All software sub-systems are notified of the change and 
apply it used in the sub-system.  This is just a temporary change. It must be saved with the 
SaveRegistry command to become permanent in the AcmeConfig.ini file.  See Table 32. 
Command ID: 0xC009 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_REGISTRY_SET_VALUE

The AbortCli command terminates the command running in the shell started by the RunCli

items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
26 
3.1.2.21 
FtpSendFile 
The FtpSendFile command uses the information set via the FtpLocalFile, FtpLocalDirectory, 
and FtpRemoteDirectory commands. If an absolute path is provided in the FtpLocalFile 
command the result of the FtpLocalDirectory command is ignored, otherwise the two are 
combined to form an absolute file path for the source. The destination is provided as an absolute 
path from the FtpRemoteDirectory command. The file is sent from the local machine to the 
remote machine. 
Command ID: 0xC015 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_SEND_FILE 
 
3.1.2.22 
FtpSendDirectory 
The FtpSendDirectory command uses the absolute paths set via the FtpLocalDirectory command 
and the FtpRemoteDirectory command to copy a directory recursively from the local machine to 
the remote machine.  
Command ID: 0xC016 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_SEND_DIRECTORY 
 
3.1.2.23 
FtpGetFile 
The FtpGetFile command uses the information set via the FtpRemoteFile and 
FtpRemoteDirectory commands and the FtpLocalDirectory command. If an absolute path is 
provided in the FtpRemoteFile command the result of the FtpRemoteDirectory command is 
ignored, otherwise the two are combined to form an absolute file path for the source. The 
destination is provided as an absolute path from the FtpLocalDirectory command. The file is 
sent from the remote machine to the local machine.  
Command ID: 0xC017 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_GET_FILE 
 
3.1.2.24 
FtpGetDirectory 
The FtpGetDirectory command uses the absolute paths set via the FtpRemoteDirectory 
command and FtpLocalDirectory commands to copy a directory recursively from the remote 
machine to the local machine.  
Command ID: 0xC018 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_GET_DIRECTORY

common filesystem commands to the given path. The path may be an absolute path or a relative

SystemOpenTestPoint 
The SystemOpenTestPoint command prepares the software for recording data.  A directory is 
created at /payload/sci/testpointName to accept files, where testpointName is the supplied 
parameter.  If that directory already exists then ‘_x’ is appended to the name, where x is 1 or 2 or 
3 or more until a non-existent directory is found.  In this directory a file is created named 
testpointName_x_data.csv, where testpointName_x matches the directory name.   Two lines of 
header are written to the file and it is left open ready to accept data once an DataRecordingStart

The SystemCloseTestPoint command marks the end of the test point started with the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command.  Data recording is stopped, if it has not been stopped already 
using the DataRecordingStop command. The recorded data file, current command log file, and 
current message log file are compressed into the file 
/payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x.zip, where testpointName_x is as described 
under the SystemOpenTestPoint command. 
 
Command ID: 0xC103 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_TEST_POINT_CLOSE

The SystemResetMotionController command resets the motion control board in the CIA that 
controls the igniter arm and TFP motors.  Any current motion and waveforms are stopped, the 
board is reset, and the board version is reported in the log.  This is a ‘soft reset’ as referenced in 
the Prodigy PC-104 Users Guide.  Hard resets of the individual motor stepper drivers are 
achieved using the IgniterMotorSetState and TfpMotorSetState commands. 
 
Command ID: 0xC104 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_RESET_MOTION_CONTROLLER

The SystemCirFlowState command is designed to be sent from the IOP to inform the ACME 
software about the state of the CIR manifolds.  Scripts can access this information as shown: 
 
If ( SystemCirFlowState.diluentManifoldState == 1) 
{ 
// Diluent manifold is opened 
}

3.1.4.38 
IntensifiedCameraSafe 
The IntensifiedCameraSafe command  places the intensified camera in a state that is safe for 
turning on lights without harming the camera by sending commands to the IPSUG.  The filter is 
commanded to home position and a fixed delay occurs to allow this to finish (without checking 
that it is finished).  Then the filter is sent to a safe position with another fixed delay.  The gain is 
set to 2048 (reporting back 2500).  Gate type is set to pulsed and gate width is set to zero 
(reporting back 20).  The delays and safe parameters are defined in the Intensifier group in 
AcmeConfig.ini. 
 
Command ID: 0xC226 
Mnemonic: ACME_INTENSFIED_CAMERA_SAFE 
 
3.1.5 
ACME Igniter Group Command Details 
3.1.5.1 
IgniterDisable 
The IgniterDisable command shuts down power to the igniter.  Specifically, it pulls low the 
primary control (PC) pin on the DC-DC converter that supplies the igniter.  For more 
information see the data sheet for the Vicor V24C12C100BL2 DC-DC converter. 
 
Command ID: 0xC301 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_DISABLE 
 
3.1.5.2 
IgniterPulse 
The IgniterPulse command turns on the igniter for a specified duration and power and then shuts 
it off.  Specifically, it sets the secondary control (SC) pin on the DC-DC converter that supplies 
the igniter to the specfied power voltage and then sets to primary control (PC) pin to 5V which 
enables output to the igniter.  After the specified pulse duration the PC pin is set to 0V, disabling 
output to the igniter. 
 
The power parameter is converted to a control voltage using the equation,

items.title: PSI-23_Reference Data_ACME-DOC-010_D Software Interface Design Description.pdf
items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
57 
 
Vcontrol = B * power + A, where A and B are ConversionFactorA and 
ConversionFactorB in the Igniter group of AcmeConfig.ini.  See Table 32. 
 
The power parameter is limited by MinPowerVolts and MaxPowerVolts in the Igniter group in 
AcmeConfig.ini. These are control voltages not voltages at the igniter. 
 
Command ID: 0xC302 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_PULSE 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Values 
Description

4 
Float

Igniter voltage corresponding to -
0.6 to 0.8V control voltage.

4

Pulse duration in milliseconds. 
 
3.1.5.3 
IgniterMove 
The IgniterMove command moves the igniter arm to the specified absolute postion.  The 
velocity, acceleration, and deceleration values used for the move are specified in 
AcmeConfig.ini.  See Table 32, Group: Igniter, Keys: VelocityCountsPerSec, 
AccelerationCountsPerSecSquared, and DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared.  To go to the home 
(retracted) position specify zero as the position.  In this case the keys used are 
HomeVelocityCountsPerSec, HomeAccelerationCountsPerSecSquared, and 
DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared. 
 
The igniter arm is moved using a trapezoidal velocity versus time profile.  If the acceleration 
parameter is greater than zero then movement begins with a ramp up until the specified velocity 
is achieved.  If the deceleration parameter is greater than zero then there is a ramp down to zero 
velocity.  The duration of the movement is calculated to reach the desired position. 
 
This command takes a few seconds to execute. To shorten the duration between command and 
movement use the IgniterSetupMove or IgniterSetupMoveWithParameters command followed by 
the IgniterExecuteSetupMove command when ready to move. 
 
The motor is a Haydon Kerk 25544-05-004ENG captive linear actuator.  There is no encoder. 
 
Command ID: 0xC303 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_MOVE

IgniterMotorSetState 
The IgniterMotorSetState command disables or enables the igniter motor by setting the RST line 
on the stepper driver to 0 V or 5 V respectively.  In normal operations this command should not 
be necessary because the motor is automatically enabled as soon as the cube is active (the signal 
originates in the cube), and is disabled when the software shuts down.  For reference, the stepper

board with MS0, MS2, and MS3 in the on position.

3.1.6 
ACME Flow Group Command Details 
For flow group commands refer to the latest revision of drawing S1101MFS004, “ACME/CIR 
Integrated Pneumatic Schematic” to see how flow devices are connected to each other.  A screen 
shot of the ACME CIA portion of this drawing (Rev A) is shown below.  Gas from the CIR 
comes in at the bottom of the diagram; fuel through QD11, nitrogen bypass through QD12, and 
static mixer through QD13. 
 
Figure 2  ACME CIA Flow Schematic 
 
3.1.6.1 
FlowEnableMfcs 
The FlowEnableMfcs command turns the mass flow controllers on or off.  Initially they are all 
turned on as soon as the cube boots.  After this first power-on the MFCs are queried for their 
configuration, including full scale flow which appears in telemetry.  Subsequent commanded 
power-ons do not cause a query of configuration.

3.1.6.5 
FlowMfcSerialCommand 
The FlowMfcSerialCommand command sends the specified raw serial command to the daisy-
chained mass flow controllers.  The start of the string is the address that determines the 
destination controller:  ‘*00’ = MFCA1 Static Mixer, ‘*01’ = MFCA2 Bypass, ‘*02’ = MFCA3 
Fuel.  The command follows the address, for example ‘*01ZRO’ to zero MFCA2, ‘*02MS’ to 
get the state of MFCA3, ‘*00sfl’ to get a status of all configuration items (the command sent 
after power-on) from MFCA1.  See the Teledyne Hastings Digital 300 Software Guide for 
available commands.  Replies to commands are placed in the telemetry text area. 
 
Serial commands are queued.  A command will not be issued until a response is received from 
any prior command or until the prior command response times out.  The response time out is 
specified by the registry value: Flow/MfcSerialCommandTimeoutMsec.  See Table 32.

3.1.6.11 
FlowStepped 
The FlowStepped command steps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or not at all, 
by a specified step size, waits a specified duration, and steps again, repeating until each specified 
maximum flow (or minimum flow if stepping down) is reached, and then leaving the mass flow 
controller at the last flow. 
 
For positive step sizes the setpoints start at the minimum flow and step up until the maximum is 
reached, and does not go above.  For negative step sizes the setpoints start at the maximum and 
step down until the minimum is reached, and does not go below.  
 
Stepping can be stopped with the FlowStopWaveform command, which leaves the flow setpoints 
where they were last, or with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and closes 
all valves, with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the flow at 
the setpoint specified by the command.  Stepping is stopped for a MFC by any other flow 
waveform command if the parameters say to control that MFC, otherwise ongoing stepping 
continues until complete.

3.1.6.12 
FlowRamped 
The FlowRamped command ramps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or not at 
all, at a specified ramp rate for a specified duration, waits a specified hold duration, and ramps 
again, repeating until each specified maximum flow (or minimum flow if ramping down) is 
reached, and then leaving the mass flow controller at the last flow. 
 
For positive ramp rates the setpoints start at the minimum flow and ramp up until the maximum 
is reached, and does not go above.  For negative ramp rates the setpoints start at the maximum 
and ramp down until the minimum is reached, and does not go below.   During the ramp the 
control voltage of the mass flow controller is updated every millisecond. 
 
Ramping can be stopped with the FlowStopWaveform command, which leaves the flow setpoints 
where they were last, with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and closes all 
valves, or with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the flow at 
the setpoint specified by the command.  Ramping is stopped for a MFC by any other flow

3.1.7

3.1.7.1 
DataRecordingStart 
The DataRecordingStart command starts recording analog input and output data to a file at a rate 
defined by the Diagnostics/SampleTimeMsec registry entry, see Table 32, which defaults to 8 
msec for 125 Hz sampling. Prior to this command the SystemOpenTestPoint command must be 
issued to define the file name, otherwise the command fails.  The testpointName parameter in the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command results in the data being save to a path and file named 
/payload/sci/testpointName/testpointName_data.csv.   See section 8.1 for the file contents. 
 
Command ID: 0xC501 
Mnemonic: ACME_DATA_RECORDING_START 
 
3.1.7.2 
DataRecordingStop 
The DataRecordingStop command stops acquistion of data started with the DataRecordingStart 
command.  The resultant data file is left open until the SystemCloseTestPoint command is 
received.  Issuing another DataRecordingStart command instead will append data to the existing

differences in the data, which, for example, could include a tell-tale signature in the E-Field 
control voltage.

3.1.7.3 
FiberMove 
The FiberMove command translates the thin filament pyrometry (Fiber) fiber array to the 
specified position at the specified velocity or translation rate. Movement acceleration and 
deceleration are registry values specified in AcmeConfig.ini, see Table 32, items 
Fiber/AccelerationCountsPerSecSquared and Fiber/DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared.  The 
response time to start movement is on the order of seconds.  To start movement closer to an 
event use the FiberSetupMove command followed by the FiberExecuteSetupMove command 
when ready to move. 
 
If the specified position exceeds the limit the command is not performed.  The position limit is 
the Fiber/MaxPosition registry value minus the Fiber/FiberToBurnerOffsets registry value (a 
comma-separated string of offsets in order of burner type number) for the burner type specified 
in the SystemDefineSetup command.  See the descriptions of these registry values in Table 32 for 
more information. 
 
Motion can be stopped prematurely using the FiberHaltMove command. 
 
The motor is an Ultramotion HT17 stepper motor linear actuator with 6 inch stroke and encoder.

until a FiberExecuteSetupMove command is received.  This command pair can be used to place

The rest of the details of this command are the same as for the FiberMove command except that 
acceleration and deceleration are command parameters.

PmtSetGain 
The PmtSetGain command sets the gain of the specified photo multipler tube. 
 
The gain parameter in this command specifies the volts out of the cube DNx-AO-333 board 
channels AO-25, AO-26, and AO-27, see Table 18.  These voltages are fed through a voltage 
divider of 10 Kohms and 1.21 Kohms before entering the control input on the PMT.  According 
to the PMT data sheet the recommended control voltage is 0.5 V to 1.1 V, corresponding to 4.63 
V to 10.19 V for the gain command parameter, which is limited to a maximum of 10 V. 
 
The equation to convert PMT control input, x, to PMT gain is: 
PMTGain = 2,000,000 * x ^ 8.643856 
,which gives a range of PMTGain from 5000 to 3,500,000 for 0.5 V to 1.1V control input, or 
4.63 V to 10.19 V command gain parameter. 
 
The equation to convert command gain parameter, gain, to PMT gain is: 
 
 
PMTGain = 2,000,000 * (gain/9.2645) ^ 8.643856 
 
The equation to convert PMT gain to command gain parameter, gain, is: 
 
 
gain = 10 ^ (0.115689 * log(PMTGain) + 0.23786213)
