The ExtinctionDetectionConfigure command defines the limits, averaging duration, and method 
of extinction detection.  Detection of extinction using this configuration does not begin until the 
ExtinctionDetectionSetState command enables detection.  It ends when extinction is detected  or 
when the ExtinctionDetectionSetState command is used to force detection or disable detection.

averaged over the specified duration.  These averages are compared to the specified limts.  The 
numberOfInstruments parameter is used to indicate how many instrument averages must go

3.1.8.1 
EFieldEnable 
The EFieldEnable command enables or disables the high voltage supply that powers the electric 
field mesh.  This command also effectively performs a EFieldSetVoltage command with voltage 
parameter equal to zero prior to an enable and after a disable.  Any waveforms are stopped by a 
disable. 
 
This command controls the cube DNx-AO-333 board AO-6 (HV2_EN) signal.  See Table 18. 
 
The high voltage supply is an Ultravolt part number 20A12-N4-Y6-C. 
 
Command ID: 0xC601 
Mnemonic: ACME_EFIELD_ENABLE 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Values 
Description

1

Disable sets HV_EN to 0V.  Enable sets 
HV_EN to 5V. 
 
3.1.8.2 
EFieldSetVoltage 
The EFieldSetVoltage command controls the voltage present on the electric field mesh.  The 
voltage parameter, which is desired voltage on the mesh, is converted to control voltage output to 
the cube DNx-AO-333 board AO-4 (HV_CTRL) signal. See Table 18.  The conversion is 
according to the equation: 
 
𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑟𝑜𝑙 𝑉𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒= −𝐵+ √𝐵2 −4𝐶(𝐴−𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒)
2𝐶
 
 
,where A, B, and C are items in AcmeConfig.ini, See Table 32, and depend on whether the 
negative or positive supply is being used.  For the negative supply the names are: 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorA 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorB 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorC 
For the positive supply the names are: 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorA 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorB 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorC 
The SystemDefineSetup command tells the software which polarity of E-Field supply is installed. 
 
The reverse equation is: 
𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒= 𝐶∗𝑐𝑣2 + 𝐵∗𝑐𝑣+ 𝐴 
, where cv is control voltage and A,B,andC are as above. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply.

3.1.8.3 
EFieldSteppedSignal 
The EFieldSteppedSignal command steps the electric field voltage between a specfied minimum 
and maximum voltage with steps of a specified size and duration and back down (or up) for a 
specified number of cycles.  One cycle is a series of steps in one direction, therefore set cycles to 
a factor of 2 to perform complete up and down waveforms. 
 
The maximum and minimum voltages are not violated even if the step voltage does not divide 
evenly between them. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply. 
 
Special cases: 
- 
stepVoltage < 0 starts at maxVoltage and steps to minVoltage (and back up if cycles 
> 1). 
- 
Cycles = 1 produces a single staircase. 
- 
stepVoltage = (maxVoltage – minVoltage) produces a square waveform.

This analog input layer in the UEI PowerDNA Cube has 16 differential input channels with an input range of +/-10 Volts and 18-bit

BRE 
 
 
 
 
•
Burning Rate Emulator 
– Jim Quintiere & Peter Sunderland (both U. Maryland) 
•
Concept 
– Flat-plate burner with gaseous fuel flow simulating the 
vaporization and combustion of condensed fuels 
– Heat flux to the burner is measured, where the flux 
vaporizes condensed-phase fuels 
–
Fuels to be simulated include paper, plastic, alcohols 
•
Goals  
– Quantify the burning and extinction behavior of 
condensed fuels in microgravity 
– Quantify the effects of increased O2 concentrations, 
e.g., for exploration atmospheres, on µg combustion. 
•
Why? 
– Spacecraft fire prevention through improved 
assessment for materials selection (currently based on 
1g testing, where flames can exist in µg and not in 1g)

CLD Flame 
 
 
 
 
•
Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame 
– Marshall B. Long & Mitchell D. Smooke (both Yale U.) 
•
Concept 
– Lifted coflow (2D) flame, so little/no heat loss to burner 
• enabling improved modeling of the flame 
•
Goals  
– Generation of modified kinetic mechanisms for 
hydrocarbon fuels that are able to model effectively 
diffusion flame structure under a larger parameter 
range than existing mechanisms. 
– Development of submodels for soot formation that are 
capable of predicting both high and low soot loading 
levels in hydrocarbon flames of various fuels. 
•
Why? 
– Improved design capability through validation of  
combustion models over wider parameter range

– Derek Dunn-Rankin (UC Irvine) 
•
Concept 
– Gas-jet or coflow (2D) flame with high-voltage mesh (up 
to ±10 kV) electrode above (downstream of) burner 
•
Goal 
– Understand chemi-ionization behavior and the resulting 
ion driven winds sufficiently well so that electrical 
properties of flames can be used to characterize (by 
monitoring ion current) and control them (via direct 
chemical or local convective influences). 
•
Why? 
– Advanced control capability enabling improved 
combustion performance

Flame Design 
•
A novel approach to clean, efficient diffusion flames 
– Rich Axelbaum (Washington U., St. Louis), Beei-
Huan Chao (U. Hawaii), Peter Sunderland (U. 
Maryland), David L. Urban (NASA Glenn) 
•
Concept 
– Spherical (1D) flame, normal and inverse flow config. 
•
Goals  
– Evaluate the effects of flame structure on soot 
inception and flame extinction 
– Obtain a correlation of sooting limits with 
stoichiometric mixture fraction, Zst, and adiabatic 
temperature, Tad

Why Study Combustion? 
•
Energy 
– While we might  associate fire with the Stone Age, we still make 
extensive use of combustion in our daily lives. 
• Electricity – about 70% in the U.S. from combustion 
• Heating of buildings, water, food, and in manufacturing processes 
• Transportation 
– Our reliance on imported fuel contributes to our national trade 
deficit and affects our national security. 
•
Environment 
– Combustion is a source of greenhouse gases. 
– Soot contributes to global warming and is a health problem. 
•
Fire Safety 
 
Given its pervasive use with annual U.S. fuel costs on the order 
of a trillion dollars even small improvements in combustion 
technology can significantly reduce fuel needs and 
pollution production!

items.title: PSI-23_Presentations_ACME fact sheet 20180519.pdf
items.text:
19 May 2018 
 
 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) 
 
PURPOSE:  ACME is focused on advanced combustion 
technology via fundamental microgravity research.  The 
primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant 
emission in practical terrestrial combustion.  A secondary 
objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft. 
 
RESEARCH:  ACME includes six independent experiments 
investigating laminar, gaseous, non-premixed flames.  They 
are being conducted with a single set of modular hardware 
in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International 
Space Station (ISS). 
STATUS:  ACME set-up and check-out was carried out by the 
ISS crew in Sept.-Oct. 2017, where science testing began in 
November.  The first round of testing for the Coflow Laminar 
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment of Marshall B. Long 
et al. was completed in Feb. 2018, where 130 methane 
flames (at a range of concentrations) were ignited.  The first 
round of testing for the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar 
Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment of Derek 
Dunn-Rankin et al. was completed on May 18, where 120 
coflow flames were ignited.  On May 20, burners and 
additional hardware for the next three ACME experiments 
are scheduled to launch.  The ACME hardware should be 
reconfigured on May 22 by astronaut Ricky Arnold (NASA) 
for CLD Flame’s second round, where the ethylene flame 
testing should begin later in the week. 
 
WEB SITE:  http://spaceflightsystems.grc.nasa.gov/acme/ 
UPDATES:  www.facebook.com/space.flames  
PHOTOGRAPHS:  www.flickr.com/photos/space-flames 
EDUCATION:  https://tinyurl.com/space-flames

Goals
• Use spherical diffusion flames in long-duration mg 
environment to: 
– obtain experimental data of exceptional quality in 
simple, well-defined flow fields.
– understand various key elemental diffusion flame 
processes.
• Compare these data with those obtained through 
independent computational simulation with detailed

s-Flame Merits of One-Dimensional Flames 
for Fundamental Studies
• Flame structure fundamentally affected by 
aerodynamics.
• Simple flow and flame configuration facilitate 
experimentation, computation, analysis, and 
comparison, with enhanced accuracy and reliability.
• Reduced effort in describing flows allows more 
detailed study of other aspects of flames such as 
chemistry.
• A one-dimensional flame is the simplest possible 
configuration.

items.text:

s-Flame
II. Flame Extinction: 
Experimental, Low Da
• Fuel/inert mixtures will be issued from the spherical burner and 
ignited at initial flow rates expected (or known/observed) to form 
flames that evolve toward idealized steady-state conditions
• Following ignition and initial flame front movement, the fuel/inert 
flow rate will be abruptly reduced to a second flow rate below the 
expected extinction limit
• Quasi-steady extinction is expected to occur as the flame adjusts to 
the reduced flow rate
• To refine the determination of the extinction flow rate for each 
fuel/diluent mixture, repeated tests are to be conducted at 
successively lower initial flow rates and higher secondary flow 
rates.

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame SCR 200802.pdf
items.text:
14
14
s-Flame
II. Flame Extinction: 
Experimental, High Da
• Fuel/inert mixtures will be issued from the spherical burner 
and ignited at flow rates slightly above and beyond that of 
the radiation extinction limit.
• Upon ignition the flame will grow and subsequently 
extinguish at the radiation extinction limit. 
• Rates of radiative emissions from the flame and radiative 
reabsorption elsewhere are to be accentuated in some cases 
by using a radiatively active diluent such as CO2.

items.text:

s-Flame
III. Flamefront Instabilities: 
Phenomenology
• Stoichiometry constraint and lack of chemistry render 
diffusion flame sheets absolutely stable.
• However, chemistry becomes important for near-limit 
burning. Will flame become unstable? 
• Recent theories & experiments show instability 
characteristics similar to those of premixed flames for 
near-limit burning
• Since (positive) stretch suppresses cellular instability 
while promotes pulsating instability, the (stretchless) 
spherical flame is well suited for such studies.

detection and flame control

Fundamental Needs in Computational 
Aerothermochemistry
• Satisfactory quantitative description of 
combustion phenomena depends on: 
– Accurate input of physics & chemistry
– Computationally accessible
• Components of input:
– Turbulence (DNS & modeled)
– Chemistry (detailed & reduced)

Complexities in 
Description of Chemistry
• Fuel oxidation is highly nonlinear and nonmonotonic in terms 
of temperature, pressure, and species concentrations
• Oxidation mechanisms consist of large number of species and 
reactions
• Characteristic reaction rates span over many orders of 
magnitude, hence computationally stiff
• Multicomponent diffusive transport can also be 
computationally expensive

Targets for Comprehensiveness in 
Experimental Data
• Broad coverage of thermodynamic states: temperature,

• Ignition (homogeneous and diffusive): low-temperature

items.text:

s-Flame The Role of mg Spherical Diffusion Flame in 
Comprehensive Mechanism Development
• Substantial research on homogeneous systems (shock 
tubes, flow reactors, etc.) and premixed flames
• Diffusion flame experiments mostly involve counter-
and stagnation flows, and droplet flames
• Burner-supported spherical flame is 1D and steady state
• Experiments of interest to chemistry are those involving 
ignition and extinction.
• Experiments for situations away from extinction would 
yield information on the diffusion and radiation 
parameters.

– Elimination of unimportant species & reactions
– Time-scale analysis (steady-state and partial equilibrium 
assumptions)
– Diffusion coefficient lumping
• Example: Detailed n-heptane mechanism with 561 
species and 2539 elementary reactions reduced to 
55 species and 51 lumped reactions

s-Flame
Experimental Approach  (2/6)
• Objective A – Flame Structure Evolution
–Fuel/diluent mixtures will be issued from the spherical 
burner and ignited at flow rates expected to form flames 
that evolve toward idealized steady-state conditions.
–As the flame spreads outward, transient measurements of 
flame front velocity and flame structure will be obtained 
using imaging and radiometric systems.  
–The flame characteristics will be compared with the 
predictions of the transient numerical simulation of 
spherical diffusion flames for evaluations of detailed 
chemical kinetic and transport models.

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame SCR 200802.pdf
items.text:
40
40
s-Flame
Experimental Approach  (3/6)
• Objective B – Quasi-Steady Extinction Limits, Low Da
–Fuel/inert mixtures will be issued from the spherical burner and 
ignited at initial flow rates expected (or known/observed) to 
form flames that evolve toward idealized steady-state conditions.  
–Following ignition and initial flame front movement, the 
fuel/inert flow rate will be abruptly reduced to a second flow 
rate below the expected extinction limit.  
–Quasi-steady extinction is expected to occur as the flame adjusts 
to the reduced flow rate.  
–To refine the determination of the extinction flow rate for each 
fuel/diluent mixture, repeated tests are to be conducted at 
successively lower initial flow rates and higher secondary flow 
rates.

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame SCR 200802.pdf
items.text:
41
41
s-Flame
Experimental Approach  (4/6)
• Objective B – Quasi-Steady Extinction Limits, Low Da
–At the low Da extinction limit, chemical kinetic rates are 
retarded with respect to flow rates by inert gas in the 
fuel stream that decreases the flame temperature.
–Based on theoretical predictions, fuel/inert mixtures are 
to be chosen for which the extinction flame radius is 
large enough to minimize the effects of heat loss to the 
burner.
–The surface temperature of the burner will be directly 
measured to quantify this loss.

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_s-Flame SCR 200802.pdf
items.text:

Experimental Approach  (5/6)
• Objective B – Quasi-Steady Extinction Limits, High Da
–Fuel/inert mixtures will be issued from the spherical 
burner and ignited at flow rates above and beyond those 
expected (or known/observed) to form steady flames 
when radiative loss is considered.  
–The quasi-steady extinction is expected to occur as the 
flame moves outward before reaching the adiabatic
steady-state radius.
–Rates of radiative emissions from the flame and radiative 
reabsorption elsewhere are to be accentuated in some 
cases by using a radiatively active diluent such as CO2.

items.text:

s-Flame
Experimental Approach  (6/6)
• Objective C – Flame Front Instabilities
–Pulsating flame front instabilities are predicted to occur 
near the extinction conditions at both low and high Da.
–The approach taken to observe the instabilities is similar to 
the approach for observing extinction except fuel/diluent 
mixtures with large system Lewis numbers (Le) are used.
• Low Da: moderate initial flow rate, abrupt change to flow rate 
below predicted extinction rate.
• High Da: initial flow rate above predicted extinction flow rate 
with radiation.
• Instabilities are expected to appear before extinction.
–Radiating diluents are used to further encourage the 
instabilities.

items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
11 
1.0 
SCOPE 
1.1 
Identification 
The purpose of this document is to identify the design of the communication interfaces used by 
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME). 
1.2 
System Overview 
 
The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) is mini-facility designed to 
support Principal Investigators (PI) interested in studying various aspects of advanced 
combustion in a microgravity environment.  ACME will be integrated into the Fluids and 
Combustion Facility’s (FCF) Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) onboard the International Space 
Station in the US Lab Module.   
ACME will perform microgravity experiments to study fire suppression/flame extinguishment 
via 5 experiments: s-flame, Flame design, CLD Flame, E-Field Flames, and Burning Rate 
Emulator Flames as described in the ACME Baseline Description Document, ACME-DOC-004.  
ACME will allow investigation using pure as well as mixtures of gaseous fuels at various 
chamber atmosphere pressures, compositions, and oxygen concentrations.  The microgravity 
environment allows for observation and measurement of flame formation and extinguishment 
processes that cannot be made in sustained gravity.  The modular design of ACME allows for 
flexibility in configuration for specific experiments and easy maintainability of the hardware.  
The core elements of gaseous combustion are included in the ACME design as a basis for current 
and future gaseous combustion studies.  These elements are establishment of gas flow through 
various exchangeable mass flow controllers, ignition of gas at the burner and the use of 
appropriate diagnostic measurement devices.  The five identified experiments, and any future 
experiments, use these core elements to build a unique set of requirements for the study of 
various phenomena distinctive to gaseous combustion.  The goal of ACME is to improve the 
fundamental understanding of combustion processes in order to enable increased efficiency and 
reduce pollutant emission in practical combustion. 
 
1.3 
Document Overview 
This document is divided into interfaces used to communicate with the ISS (i.e., external 
communication interfaces) and interfaces used to communicate with devices within ACME that 
require a protocol (i.e., internal communication interfaces).

EXTERNAL COMMUNICATION INTERFACES 
ACME commands originate from the ACME Ground Software (AGS) CSCI on a ground 
workstation at the Telescience Center (TSC) at Glenn Research Center (GRC).  These commands 
are then forwarded through a variety of systems until they eventually end up at the CIR on the 
ISS.

3.1 
CIR Input/Output Processor (IOP) Interface 
Commands sent through the CIR IOP (Input Output Processor) are in the format required by 
FCF-ICD-0076A.  See section A.1, FCF Command Protocol for a listing of the required 
command formats, including all required headers.  All commands from the ground go to the IOP 
with the FCF Command Header and User Data filled in.  Commands from ACME to the IPSUs 
and IPSU-Gs go through the FCFCommunications application (Base Classes) which fills in the 
Command Sequence Count and Time Fields in the FCF Command Header before submitting the 
packet to the IOP for routing.

ACME Commands 
Because it is a CIR PI package, ACME Package Command IDs in the FCF Command Header are assigned the range 0xC000-0xCFFF.  
The table below lists the commands, their IDs, and mnemonics. 
Detailed descriptions and parameter lists for each command follow the table.  In the parameter list for each command the parameter 
name is the variable name in the code, which is useful to know when Qt scripts are being written.  The name of the command, for 
example ‘NullCommand’, is also the name in code, in Qt scripts, and in log messages announcing the reception and completion of 
commands. 
Regarding parameters of type String, the entire available length can be used for characters without a terminating zero character.  If a 
string is less than the available length then a terminating zero character needs to be used.  The ground command software will make 
this transparent to the normal user.

3.1.2 
ACME Common Group Command Details 
These commands are called ‘common’ because they are  implemented using code shared 
between several payloads.  The detailed descriptions below are derived from the original 
documentation for these commands in Appendix K of FCF-ICD-0076, Rev C or later.  As stated 
in that appendix the high order bytes of the command ID are replaced by the command group 
number assigned to ACME common commands, which is 0xC0.  In that appendix the command 
IDs range from 0x0001 to 0x0038.  For ACME they range from 0xC001 to 0xC038. 
3.1.2.1 
NullCommand 
The NullCommand does nothing.  It can be used to test communication paths. 
Command ID: 0xC001 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_NULL 
3.1.2.2 
ExternalCommand 
The ExternalCommand command allows an avionics Main Processor (MP) CSCI to have no 
knowledge of this command and make use of the External Module feature. The command is 
passed to an External Module without intervention. This command enforces the requirement that 
an External Module requires a “module identifier” as the first parameter. The command group 
portion of the command ID, XX, depends on the module. 
Command ID: 0xXX02 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_EXTERNAL_PASS_THRU 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Description 
moduleIdentifier 
2 
Uint16 
Identifier (e.g. camera number 1,2) 
Command parameters 
80 
Area for module command-dependent parameters. 
 
3.1.2.3 
GoToIdle 
The GoToIdle command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the IDLE state. 
Command ID: 0xC003 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_IDLE 
 
3.1.2.4 
GoToExp 
The GoToExp command requests an avionics MP CSCI to be set to the EXPERIMENT state. 
Command ID: 0xC004 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_STATE_EXPERIMENT

The SetRegistryItem command selects an item in the registry file, 
/payload/app/config/AcmeConfig.ini, for modification by the SetRegistryValue command. The

modifies it with the supplied value.  All software sub-systems are notified of the change and 
apply it used in the sub-system.  This is just a temporary change. It must be saved with the 
SaveRegistry command to become permanent in the AcmeConfig.ini file.  See Table 32. 
Command ID: 0xC009

items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
26 
3.1.2.21 
FtpSendFile 
The FtpSendFile command uses the information set via the FtpLocalFile, FtpLocalDirectory, 
and FtpRemoteDirectory commands. If an absolute path is provided in the FtpLocalFile 
command the result of the FtpLocalDirectory command is ignored, otherwise the two are 
combined to form an absolute file path for the source. The destination is provided as an absolute 
path from the FtpRemoteDirectory command. The file is sent from the local machine to the 
remote machine. 
Command ID: 0xC015 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_SEND_FILE 
 
3.1.2.22 
FtpSendDirectory 
The FtpSendDirectory command uses the absolute paths set via the FtpLocalDirectory command 
and the FtpRemoteDirectory command to copy a directory recursively from the local machine to 
the remote machine.  
Command ID: 0xC016 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_SEND_DIRECTORY 
 
3.1.2.23 
FtpGetFile 
The FtpGetFile command uses the information set via the FtpRemoteFile and 
FtpRemoteDirectory commands and the FtpLocalDirectory command. If an absolute path is 
provided in the FtpRemoteFile command the result of the FtpRemoteDirectory command is 
ignored, otherwise the two are combined to form an absolute file path for the source. The 
destination is provided as an absolute path from the FtpLocalDirectory command. The file is 
sent from the remote machine to the local machine.  
Command ID: 0xC017 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_GET_FILE 
 
3.1.2.24 
FtpGetDirectory 
The FtpGetDirectory command uses the absolute paths set via the FtpRemoteDirectory 
command and FtpLocalDirectory commands to copy a directory recursively from the remote 
machine to the local machine.  
Command ID: 0xC018 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FTP_GET_DIRECTORY 
 
3.1.2.25 
ChangeDirectory 
The ChangeDirectory (linux ‘cd’) command moves the notion of the current directory for the 
common filesystem commands to the given path. The path may be an absolute path or a relative

items.title: PSI-23_Reference Data_ACME-DOC-010_D.pdf
items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
27 
path. Relative path ChangeDirectory commands can be chained to traverse a deep directory 
structure. The path must exist for the command to successfully complete. 
Command ID: 0xC019 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FS_CHANGE_DIR 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Description 
path 
82 
String 
Directory path 
 
3.1.2.26 
MakeDirectory 
The MakeDirectory (linux ‘mkdir -P’) command creates a new directory(s). The path may be an 
absolute path or a relative path. All parent directories necessary to create the full path are made. 
If a relative path is given it is combined with the current working directory from a single or 
series of ChangeDirectory commands to form the complete path.  
Command ID: 0xC01A 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FS_MAKE_DIR 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Description 
path 
82 
String 
Directory path (e.g. /tmp/a/b/c or  a/b/c) 
 
3.1.2.27 
RemoveSingleEmptyDirectory 
The RemoveSingleEmptyDirectory (linux ‘rmdir’) command removes a directory. The given 
directory path must be empty for the command to succeed. The path may be an absolute path or a 
relative path. If a relative path is given it is combined with the current working directory from a 
single or series of ChangeDirectory commands to form the complete path. 
Command ID: 0xC01B 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FS_REMOVE_SINGLE_EMPTY_DIR 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Description 
path 
82 
String 
Directory path 
 
3.1.2.28 
RemoveMultipleEmptyDirectories 
The RemoveMultipleEmptyDirectories (linux ‘rmdir -p’) command removes all parent directories 
in the path, provided they are empty. The path may be an absolute path or a relative path. If a 
relative path is given it is combined with the current working directory from a single or series of 
ChangeDirectory commands to form a complete path. This command is the opposite of the

items.title: PSI-23_Reference Data_ACME-DOC-010_D.pdf
items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
28 
MakeDirectory command. This command performs actions to the best of its ability and will stop 
if/when it finds a non-empty directory.  Actions completed to that point are not rolled back. 
Command ID: 0xC01C 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FS_REMOVE_MULTIPLE_EMPTY_DIRS 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Description 
path 
82 
String 
Directory path 
 
3.1.2.29 
MoveFiles 
The MoveFiles (linux ‘mv SRC DIR’) command moves SRC(s) to DIR. Source directory is set 
via the SetSource command and the destination directory is set via the SetDestination command. 
Wildcards * (any number of unknown characters) and ? (one unknown character) may be used in 
the filter. A blank filter or a filter consisting of a single * is interpreted as all files. If a single file 
move is desired, give filenames in the source and destination. A better solution is to use the 
RenameFile command. If moving an entire directory tree is desired, use the RenameDirectory 
command.  
Command ID: 0xC01D 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FS_MOVE_FILES 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Description 
filter 
82 
String 
Name filter (e.g. *.jpeg  or  image?003.jpeg) 
 
3.1.2.30 
RenameFile 
The RenameFile command renames a source file set via the SetSource command to a destination 
file set via the SetDestination command.  
Command ID: 0xC01E 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FS_RENAME_FILE 
 
3.1.2.31 
RenameDirectory 
The RenameDirectory command renames a source directory set via the SetSource command to a 
destination directory set via the SetDestination command.  
Command ID: 0xC01F 
Mnemonic: ACME_COMMON_FS_RENAME_DIR

The RemoveFiles (linux ‘rm’) command removes files from a directory. Source directory is set

SetSource command and the destination is set via the SetDestination command. Wildcards * (any 
number of unknown characters) and ? (one unknown character) may be used in the filter. A

The SetSource command provides the source for filesystem commands. The path may be an

3.1.3.2 
SystemOpenTestPoint 
The SystemOpenTestPoint command prepares the software for recording data.  A directory is 
created at /payload/sci/testpointName to accept files, where testpointName is the supplied 
parameter.  If that directory already exists then ‘_x’ is appended to the name, where x is 1 or 2 or 
3 or more until a non-existent directory is found.  In this directory a file is created named 
testpointName_x_data.csv, where testpointName_x matches the directory name.   Two lines of 
header are written to the file and it is left open ready to accept data once an DataRecordingStart

information about the headers.

Any whitespace characters are trimmed

3.1.3.3 
SystemCloseTestPoint 
The SystemCloseTestPoint command marks the end of the test point started with the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command.  Data recording is stopped, if it has not been stopped already 
using the DataRecordingStop command. The recorded data file, current command log file, and 
current message log file are compressed into the file 
/payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x.zip, where testpointName_x is as described 
under the SystemOpenTestPoint command. 
 
Command ID: 0xC103 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_TEST_POINT_CLOSE 
3.1.3.4 
SystemResetMotionController 
The SystemResetMotionController command resets the motion control board in the CIA that 
controls the igniter arm and TFP motors.  Any current motion and waveforms are stopped, the 
board is reset, and the board version is reported in the log.  This is a ‘soft reset’ as referenced in 
the Prodigy PC-104 Users Guide.  Hard resets of the individual motor stepper drivers are 
achieved using the IgniterMotorSetState and TfpMotorSetState commands. 
 
Command ID: 0xC104 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_RESET_MOTION_CONTROLLER 
 
3.1.3.5 
SystemCirFlowState 
The SystemCirFlowState command is designed to be sent from the IOP to inform the ACME 
software about the state of the CIR manifolds.  Scripts can access this information as shown: 
 
If ( SystemCirFlowState.diluentManifoldState == 1) 
{ 
// Diluent manifold is opened 
} 
 
 
Command ID: 0xC107 
Mnemonic: ACME_SYSTEM_CIR_FLOW_STATE

The IntensifiedCameraSafe command  places the intensified camera in a state that is safe for 
turning on lights without harming the camera by sending commands to the IPSUG.  The filter is 
commanded to home position and a fixed delay occurs to allow this to finish (without checking 
that it is finished).  Then the filter is sent to a safe position with another fixed delay.  The gain is 
set to 2048 (reporting back 2500).  Gate type is set to pulsed and gate width is set to zero 
(reporting back 20).  The delays and safe parameters are defined in the Intensifier group in 
AcmeConfig.ini.

3.1.5 
ACME Igniter Group Command Details 
3.1.5.1 
IgniterDisable 
The IgniterDisable command shuts down power to the igniter.  Specifically, it pulls low the 
primary control (PC) pin on the DC-DC converter that supplies the igniter.  For more 
information see the data sheet for the Vicor V24C12C100BL2 DC-DC converter. 
 
Command ID: 0xC301 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_DISABLE 
 
3.1.5.2 
IgniterPulse 
The IgniterPulse command turns on the igniter for a specified duration and power and then shuts 
it off.  Specifically, it sets the secondary control (SC) pin on the DC-DC converter that supplies 
the igniter to the specfied power voltage and then sets to primary control (PC) pin to 5V which 
enables output to the igniter.  After the specified pulse duration the PC pin is set to 0V, disabling 
output to the igniter. 
 
The power parameter is converted to a control voltage using the equation,

items.title: PSI-23_Reference Data_ACME-DOC-010_D.pdf
items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
57 
 
Vcontrol = B * power + A, where A and B are ConversionFactorA and 
ConversionFactorB in the Igniter group of AcmeConfig.ini.  See Table 32. 
 
The power parameter is limited by MinPowerVolts and MaxPowerVolts in the Igniter group in 
AcmeConfig.ini. These are control voltages not voltages at the igniter. 
 
Command ID: 0xC302 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_PULSE

# Bytes 
Type

4 
Float

Igniter voltage corresponding to -
0.6 to 0.8V control voltage.

3.1.5.3 
IgniterMove 
The IgniterMove command moves the igniter arm to the specified absolute postion.  The 
velocity, acceleration, and deceleration values used for the move are specified in 
AcmeConfig.ini.  See Table 32, Group: Igniter, Keys: VelocityCountsPerSec, 
AccelerationCountsPerSecSquared, and DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared.  To go to the home 
(retracted) position specify zero as the position.  In this case the keys used are 
HomeVelocityCountsPerSec, HomeAccelerationCountsPerSecSquared, and 
DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared. 
 
The igniter arm is moved using a trapezoidal velocity versus time profile.  If the acceleration 
parameter is greater than zero then movement begins with a ramp up until the specified velocity 
is achieved.  If the deceleration parameter is greater than zero then there is a ramp down to zero 
velocity.  The duration of the movement is calculated to reach the desired position. 
 
This command takes a few seconds to execute. To shorten the duration between command and 
movement use the IgniterSetupMove or IgniterSetupMoveWithParameters command followed by 
the IgniterExecuteSetupMove command when ready to move. 
 
The motor is a Haydon Kerk 25544-05-004ENG captive linear actuator.  There is no encoder. 
 
Command ID: 0xC303 
Mnemonic: ACME_IGNITER_MOVE

For flow group commands refer to the latest revision of drawing S1101MFS004, “ACME/CIR 
Integrated Pneumatic Schematic” to see how flow devices are connected to each other.  A screen 
shot of the ACME CIA portion of this drawing (Rev A) is shown below.  Gas from the CIR 
comes in at the bottom of the diagram; fuel through QD11, nitrogen bypass through QD12, and 
static mixer through QD13. 
 
Figure 2  ACME CIA Flow Schematic 
 
3.1.6.1 
FlowEnableMfcs 
The FlowEnableMfcs command turns the mass flow controllers on or off.  Initially they are all 
turned on as soon as the cube boots.  After this first power-on the MFCs are queried for their 
configuration, including full scale flow which appears in telemetry.  Subsequent commanded 
power-ons do not cause a query of configuration.

The FlowMfcSerialCommand command sends the specified raw serial command to the daisy-
chained mass flow controllers.  The start of the string is the address that determines the 
destination controller:  ‘*00’ = MFCA1 Static Mixer, ‘*01’ = MFCA2 Bypass, ‘*02’ = MFCA3 
Fuel.  The command follows the address, for example ‘*01ZRO’ to zero MFCA2, ‘*02MS’ to 
get the state of MFCA3, ‘*00sfl’ to get a status of all configuration items (the command sent 
after power-on) from MFCA1.  See the Teledyne Hastings Digital 300 Software Guide for 
available commands.  Replies to commands are placed in the telemetry text area. 
 
Serial commands are queued.  A command will not be issued until a response is received from 
any prior command or until the prior command response times out.  The response time out is 
specified by the registry value: Flow/MfcSerialCommandTimeoutMsec.  See Table 32.

3.1.6.11 
FlowStepped 
The FlowStepped command steps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or not at all, 
by a specified step size, waits a specified duration, and steps again, repeating until each specified 
maximum flow (or minimum flow if stepping down) is reached, and then leaving the mass flow 
controller at the last flow. 
 
For positive step sizes the setpoints start at the minimum flow and step up until the maximum is 
reached, and does not go above.  For negative step sizes the setpoints start at the maximum and 
step down until the minimum is reached, and does not go below.  
 
Stepping can be stopped with the FlowStopWaveform command, which leaves the flow setpoints 
where they were last, or with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and closes 
all valves, with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the flow at 
the setpoint specified by the command.  Stepping is stopped for a MFC by any other flow 
waveform command if the parameters say to control that MFC, otherwise ongoing stepping 
continues until complete.

3.1.6.12 
FlowRamped 
The FlowRamped command ramps the flow of each mass flow controller up or down, or not at 
all, at a specified ramp rate for a specified duration, waits a specified hold duration, and ramps 
again, repeating until each specified maximum flow (or minimum flow if ramping down) is 
reached, and then leaving the mass flow controller at the last flow. 
 
For positive ramp rates the setpoints start at the minimum flow and ramp up until the maximum 
is reached, and does not go above.  For negative ramp rates the setpoints start at the maximum 
and ramp down until the minimum is reached, and does not go below.   During the ramp the 
control voltage of the mass flow controller is updated every millisecond. 
 
Ramping can be stopped with the FlowStopWaveform command, which leaves the flow setpoints 
where they were last, with the FlowCloseAll command, which sets all flows to zero and closes all 
valves, or with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the flow at 
the setpoint specified by the command.  Ramping is stopped for a MFC by any other flow

down, or not at all, waits a specified A duration, steps another value, B, up, down, or not at all,

closes all valves, or with the FlowSetMfcRate or FlowSetAllMfcRates commands which leave the

3.1.7 
ACME Diagnostic Group Command Details 
3.1.7.1 
DataRecordingStart 
The DataRecordingStart command starts recording analog input and output data to a file at a rate 
defined by the Diagnostics/SampleTimeMsec registry entry, see Table 32, which defaults to 8 
msec for 125 Hz sampling. Prior to this command the SystemOpenTestPoint command must be 
issued to define the file name, otherwise the command fails.  The testpointName parameter in the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command results in the data being save to a path and file named 
/payload/sci/testpointName/testpointName_data.csv.   See section 8.1 for the file contents. 
 
Command ID: 0xC501 
Mnemonic: ACME_DATA_RECORDING_START 
 
3.1.7.2 
DataRecordingStop 
The DataRecordingStop command stops acquistion of data started with the DataRecordingStart 
command.  The resultant data file is left open until the SystemCloseTestPoint command is 
received.  Issuing another DataRecordingStart command instead will append data to the existing

items.title: PSI-23_Reference Data_ACME-DOC-010_D.pdf
items.text:
ACME-DOC-010 Rev D 
71 
file.  However, there is no indication in the file between the two acquisition periods except for 
differences in the data, which, for example, could include a tell-tale signature in the E-Field 
control voltage. 
 
Command ID: 0xC502 
Mnemonic: ACME_DATA_RECORDING_STOP 
 
3.1.7.3 
FiberMove 
The FiberMove command translates the thin filament pyrometry (Fiber) fiber array to the 
specified position at the specified velocity or translation rate. Movement acceleration and 
deceleration are registry values specified in AcmeConfig.ini, see Table 32, items 
Fiber/AccelerationCountsPerSecSquared and Fiber/DecelerationCountsPerSecSquared.  The 
response time to start movement is on the order of seconds.  To start movement closer to an 
event use the FiberSetupMove command followed by the FiberExecuteSetupMove command 
when ready to move. 
 
If the specified position exceeds the limit the command is not performed.  The position limit is 
the Fiber/MaxPosition registry value minus the Fiber/FiberToBurnerOffsets registry value (a 
comma-separated string of offsets in order of burner type number) for the burner type specified 
in the SystemDefineSetup command.  See the descriptions of these registry values in Table 32 for 
more information. 
 
Motion can be stopped prematurely using the FiberHaltMove command. 
 
The motor is an Ultramotion HT17 stepper motor linear actuator with 6 inch stroke and encoder.

The FiberSetupMove command sets up a move of the Fiber fiber array.  Movement is not started 
until a FiberExecuteSetupMove command is received.  This command pair can be used to place 
the start of movement closer to an event since setup takes on the order of seconds to complete. 
 
The rest of the details of this command are the same as for the FiberMove command except that 
acceleration and deceleration are command parameters.

The FiberMotorSetState command disables or enables the Fiber motor by setting the RST line on 
the stepper driver to 0 V or 5 V respectively.  In normal operations this command should not be 
necessary because the motor is automatically enabled as soon as the cube is active (the signal 
originates in the cube), and is disabled when the software shuts down.  For reference, the stepper 
driver module is an Intelligent Motion System (IMS) XIM481H installed on an IMS INT-481

The PmtPower command turns all three photo multiplier tubes (PMTs) on or off. 
 
The PMTs are Hamamatsu part number H10722-10-MOD2.  PMT1 has a 310nm bandpass 
interference filter.  PMT2 has a UV fused silica broadband filter.  PMT3 has a 430nm bandpass 
interference filter.

3.1.7.11 
PmtSetGain 
The PmtSetGain command sets the gain of the specified photo multipler tube. 
 
The gain parameter in this command specifies the volts out of the cube DNx-AO-333 board 
channels AO-25, AO-26, and AO-27, see Table 18.  These voltages are fed through a voltage 
divider of 10 Kohms and 1.21 Kohms before entering the control input on the PMT.  According 
to the PMT data sheet the recommended control voltage is 0.5 V to 1.1 V, corresponding to 4.63 
V to 10.19 V for the gain command parameter, which is limited to a maximum of 10 V. 
 
The equation to convert PMT control input, x, to PMT gain is: 
PMTGain = 2,000,000 * x ^ 8.643856 
,which gives a range of PMTGain from 5000 to 3,500,000 for 0.5 V to 1.1V control input, or 
4.63 V to 10.19 V command gain parameter. 
 
The equation to convert command gain parameter, gain, to PMT gain is: 
 
 
PMTGain = 2,000,000 * (gain/9.2645) ^ 8.643856 
 
The equation to convert PMT gain to command gain parameter, gain, is: 
 
 
gain = 10 ^ (0.115689 * log(PMTGain) + 0.23786213)

3.1.7.13 
ExtinctionDetectionConfigure 
The ExtinctionDetectionConfigure command defines the limits, averaging duration, and method 
of extinction detection.  Detection of extinction using this configuration does not begin until the 
ExtinctionDetectionSetState command enables detection.  It ends when extinction is detected  or 
when the ExtinctionDetectionSetState command is used to force detection or disable detection. 
 
During detection the instruments that have limits in this command have their values continuously 
averaged over the specified duration.  These averages are compared to the specified limts.  The 
numberOfInstruments parameter is used to indicate how many instrument averages must go 
below their limits before extinction is detected.  Instruments can be assigned no influence on the 
detection state by specifying negative one limit.

3.1.8 
ACME E-Field Group Command Details 
3.1.8.1 
EFieldEnable 
The EFieldEnable command enables or disables the high voltage supply that powers the electric 
field mesh.  This command also effectively performs a EFieldSetVoltage command with voltage 
parameter equal to zero prior to an enable and after a disable.  Any waveforms are stopped by a 
disable. 
 
This command controls the cube DNx-AO-333 board AO-6 (HV2_EN) signal.  See Table 18. 
 
The high voltage supply is an Ultravolt part number 20A12-N4-Y6-C. 
 
Command ID: 0xC601 
Mnemonic: ACME_EFIELD_ENABLE 
 
Parameter 
# Bytes 
Type 
Values 
Description 
state 
1 
Uint8 
0 = Disable 
1 = Enable 
Disable sets HV_EN to 0V.  Enable sets 
HV_EN to 5V. 
 
3.1.8.2 
EFieldSetVoltage 
The EFieldSetVoltage command controls the voltage present on the electric field mesh.  The 
voltage parameter, which is desired voltage on the mesh, is converted to control voltage output to 
the cube DNx-AO-333 board AO-4 (HV_CTRL) signal. See Table 18.  The conversion is 
according to the equation: 
 
𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑟𝑜𝑙 𝑉𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒= −𝐵+ √𝐵2 −4𝐶(𝐴−𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒)
2𝐶
 
 
,where A, B, and C are items in AcmeConfig.ini, See Table 32, and depend on whether the 
negative or positive supply is being used.  For the negative supply the names are: 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorA 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorB 
EField/NegativeOutputFactorC 
For the positive supply the names are: 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorA 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorB 
EField/PositiveOutputFactorC 
The SystemDefineSetup command tells the software which polarity of E-Field supply is installed. 
 
The reverse equation is: 
𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒= 𝐶∗𝑐𝑣2 + 𝐵∗𝑐𝑣+ 𝐴 
, where cv is control voltage and A,B,andC are as above. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply.

3.1.8.3 
EFieldSteppedSignal 
The EFieldSteppedSignal command steps the electric field voltage between a specfied minimum 
and maximum voltage with steps of a specified size and duration and back down (or up) for a 
specified number of cycles.  One cycle is a series of steps in one direction, therefore set cycles to 
a factor of 2 to perform complete up and down waveforms. 
 
The maximum and minimum voltages are not violated even if the step voltage does not divide 
evenly between them. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply. 
 
Special cases: 
- 
stepVoltage < 0 starts at maxVoltage and steps to minVoltage (and back up if cycles 
> 1). 
- 
Cycles = 1 produces a single staircase. 
- 
stepVoltage = (maxVoltage – minVoltage) produces a square waveform.

3.1.8.5 
EFieldRectangularWave 
The EFieldRectangularWave command is an EFieldSteppedSignal command but there is a 
second step with its own size and duration.  The two step sizes can be the same or opposite 
polarity. 
 
The EfieldEnable command must be issued first to enable the supply. 
 
Special cases: 
- 
If (stepAVoltage + stepBVoltage) < 0 the sequence starts at maxVoltage. 
- 
Cycles = 1 produces a single step sequence between min and max voltage. 
- 
stepAVoltage = -1 * stepBVoltage produces a square wave between minVoltage and 
minVoltage + stepAVoltage.

This analog input layer in the UEI PowerDNA Cube has 16 differential input channels with an input range of +/-10 Volts and 18-bit 
resolution.  Several gains are available but ACME is using a gain of 1.

* MFCA1_FULL_SCALE.  Device is Teledyne Hastings HFC-D-302.

Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Structure and Response of Spherical

To gain an initial understanding of this experiment, refer to the documents “ACME non-imaging data file 
description.pdf” and “s-Flame_final_report_20210729.pdf” located in “Final Report” of the “Resulting Products” 
section on the “Pubs & Docs” tab.  
 
The s-Flame data is organized in PSI by diluent and fuel composition. Raw data, and video & image data are 
available on the “Scientific Data and Information Tab” of each of the eight “Experiment Data” records:  
 
 
1 Nitrogen-diluted Hydrogen and Oxygen 
 
2 Nitrogen-diluted Methane and Oxygen 
 
3 Nitrogen-diluted Hydrogen-Methane mixtures and Oxygen 
 
4 Nitrogen-diluted Ethylene and Oxygen 
 
5 Helium-diluted Hydrogen and Oxygen 
 
6 Helium-diluted Methane and Oxygen 
 
7 Helium-diluted Hydrogen-Methane mixtures and Oxygen 
 
8 Helium-diluted Ethylene and Oxygen 
 
Within each “Experiment Data” record, “Raw Data”, “Images” and “Audio/Video Files” are available on the 
“Scientific Data and Information” tab. Test names are formatted YYDDDX# where YY identifies year, DDD identifies 
day of year (GMT), X identifies a letter and # identifies a number  – where the different numbers can be for repeats 
but are typically variants, e.g., with different flow rate(s) or instrumentation setting(s), e.g. 19308F1. Record 
naming and listings are based on the detailed information in the test conditions table below (page 2). 
 
Test specific raw data files are located on the “Raw Data and Information” tab of the “Raw & Analyzed Data” 
record. The first row of the .csv files provides information about the test configuration. The headers of the basic 
data in .csv files is explained in Section 10.1, beginning on page 126 of the “ACME-DOC-010 Rev D.pdf” located in 
the “Data Organization Document(s)” section of the “Scientific Data and Information” section on the “Data” tab of 
the ACME s-Flames “Investigations” record. Associated videos are located on the “General” tab and associated 
images are located on the “Image Data and Information” tab of the “Videos & Images” record. 
 
There are various other supporting engineering documents, videos, reports and publications available on the other 
tabs of the “Investigations” record.

primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant

investigating laminar, nonpremixed flames of gaseous

items.text:
PS–02788–0319
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments
Diffusion flames with a weak air coflow as a function of the electric field strength, where an open copper mesh above the 
flame is negatively and positively charged in the top and bottom rows, respectively. Flames naturally include ions which can 
be affected by a powerful electric or magnetic field. In ACME’s E-FIELD Flames experiment, the copper mesh is energized 
up to 10,000 volts. This technology could be used to stabilize fuel-lean flames under conditions which are less polluting.
Canadian astronaut David Saint-Jacques preparing the 
ACME chamber insert for the BRE experiment.
ACME chamber insert within the CIR facility (above left) and two 
examples (above middle and right) of lifted flames that are 
detached from CLD Flame’s coflow burner, as a function of the 
fuel and air velocities. The false color in the image to the right 
indicates the CH* concentration as function of the radius and 
height above the burner. CH* is an excited species and emits blue 
light as it drops to a lower energy level in a process known as 
chemiluminescence. It is the primary source of the blue that is the 
natural color of hydrocarbon flames (neglecting the broadband 
thermal radiation from the soot).

items.text:
20 August 2018 
 
 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) 
 
PURPOSE:  ACME is focused on advanced combustion 
technology via fundamental microgravity research.  The 
primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant 
emission in practical terrestrial combustion.  A secondary 
objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft. 
 
RESEARCH:  ACME includes six independent experiments 
investigating laminar, non-premixed flames of gaseous fuels.  
The experiments are being conducted with a single set of 
modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) 
on the International Space Station (ISS).  While the ISS 
astronauts set up the experimental hardware, the ACME tests 
are remotely commanded from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center. 
STATUS:  ACME setup and checkout were carried out by the 
ISS crew in Sept.-Oct. 2017.  Thus far, a dozen astronauts 
from Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and the United States 
have supported the ACME research.  Since November 2017, 
over 300 flames have been ignited for the Coflow Laminar 
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) and Electric-Field Effects on 
Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiments led 
respectively by Profs. Marshall B. Long (Yale University) and 
Derek Dunn-Rankin (University of California, Irvine).   
 
A second round of CLD Flame tests is currently underway and 
should end in September when the testing will transition 
back to the E-FIELD Flames experiment.  In late 2018, the 
hardware will be reconfigured for the Burning Rate Emulator 
(BRE) experiment led by Prof. Jim Quintiere (University of 
Maryland).  While the first two ACME experiments are 
focused on improving practical combustion on Earth, BRE is 
aimed at improving spacecraft fire safety. 
Italian astronaut Paolo Nespoli installing the ACME 
chamber insert into the CIR’s combustion chamber. 
U.S. astronaut Joe Acaba aligning the retracting hot-wire 
igniter to the burner on the ACME chamber insert. 
Example image of a lifted coflow flame from the CLD Flame 
experiment led by Prof. Marshall B. Long (Yale University). 
German astronaut Alex Gerst exchanging a mass flow 
controller (for the nitrogen used to dilute the gaseous fuel) 
on the ACME chamber insert.

National Aeronautics and Space Administration 
www.nasa.gov 
Why Study Combustion? 
•
Energy 
– While we might  associate fire with the Stone Age, we still make 
extensive use of combustion in our daily lives. 
• Electricity – about 70% in the U.S. from combustion 
• Heating of buildings, water, food, and in manufacturing processes 
• Transportation 
– Our reliance on imported fuel contributes to our national trade 
deficit and affects our national security. 
•
Environment 
– Combustion is a source of greenhouse gases. 
– Soot contributes to global warming and is a health problem. 
•
Fire Safety 
 
Given its pervasive use with annual U.S. fuel costs on the order 
of a trillion dollars even small improvements in combustion 
technology can significantly reduce fuel needs and 
pollution production!

Flame Design 
•
A novel approach to clean, efficient diffusion flames 
– Rich Axelbaum (Washington U., St. Louis), Beei-
Huan Chao (U. Hawaii), Peter Sunderland (U. 
Maryland), David L. Urban (NASA Glenn) 
•
Concept 
– Spherical (1D) flame with nitrogen exchange 
•
Goals  
– Evaluate the effects of flame structure on soot 
inception and flame extinction 
– Obtain a correlation of sooting limits with 
stoichiometric mixture fraction, Zst, and adiabatic 
temperature, Tad 
– Determine the importance of gas-phase oxidation on 
soot inception for high Zst flames 
– Demonstrate the existence of steady spherical flames 
– Identify pseudo-flammability limits for diffusion flames 
in terms of  Zst and Tad

The data is generally explained through 2 excerpts from the Software IDD, i.e., 
Software Interface Design Description, ACME-DOC-010 Rev C (August 2016) 
 
 
8. Output Files 
 
 
4. Internal Interfaces (which includes Tables 15-17*) 
*where Table 17 describes channels A0-4 of the DNx-AO-333 analog output board as discussed in 8.1 below. 
 
8.0 
Output FILES 
8.1 
Data Output File 
Data output files are created using the SystemOpenTestPoint command which creates a file named and stored at 
/payload/sci/testpointName_x/testpointName_x_data.csv, where testpointName is the parameter received in the 
SystemOpenTestPoint command and _x is optional to avoid duplicate files, where x = 1,2,3, etc.  
The file contains a two-line header.  The first line has the date and time, documentation of the setup received in a 
SystemDefineSetup command, and the PMT gains.  The second line has the column headings for the subsequent rows of data.  The 
text of the column headings is defined by the Diagnostics/Header registry entry or the Diagnostics/BreHeader entry depending on 
whether the SystemDefineSetup command experimentType parameter was BRE or not. The column headings should match the data 
which is the following: 
- 
A timestamp in the format HH:MM:SS:mmm, where mmm is milliseconds. 
- 
11 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-207 board in the order shown in Table 1. 
- 
25 channels of analog input from the cube DNx-AI-225 board in the order shown in Table 2.  (The names of 
many of these values change depending on whether it is a BRE test or not, hence the two options for header.) 
- 
Channel AO-4 of the DNx-AO-333 analog output board.  This is the E-Field control voltage. 
Rows of comma-separated data is added to the file between DataRecordingStart and DataRecordingStop commands at a 
rate defined by the Diagnostics/SampleTimeMsec registry entry, see Error! Reference source not found., defaulting to 8 
msec for 125 Hz sampling.

items.title: PSI-23_Science Documents_ACME non-imaging data file description.pdf
items.text:
3 
 
8.2 
Message Log File 
Software messages are logged to files named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-DD_hh-mmACME.log, where YYYY 
is year, MM is month, DD is day of month, hh is hour, and mm is minutes.  The date in the name is when the log file is 
created, soon after software startup. 
Each message line in the file begins with a timestamp and a logging category.  The timestamp is of the format YYYY-MM-
DD DDD hh:mm:ss:mmm, where DDD is day of the year, mmm is milliseconds, and the rest are self-explanatory.  See 
section Error! Reference source not found. for information about the logging category and how to filter them out if 
desired. 
8.3 
Command Log File 
The message log file, section 8.2, includes messages showing commands received and their parameters.  Command log 
files contain only the details of each command received.  The files are named and stored at /payload/logs/YYYY-MM-
DD_hh-mmACMECommands.log.  The format is for each command received a timestamped line of text with the 
command name followed by timestamped lines of text showing each parameter name and parameter value, including 
header information.

20 September 2021

ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 
 
 
Prepared by: 
Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center 
dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov, 216-433-2166 
 
 
 
 
Dennis Stocker, the ACME Project Scientist, at the science console for the 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) in NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations 
Center (GIPOC).  In this photo, he is reviewing data from an s-Flame test.

1. Introduction 
The purpose of this report is to describe the data acquired for ACME’s s-Flame experiment to facilitate its 
analysis.  The data is all digital, where the fuel was gaseous and there was no collection of soot or the 
combustion gases.  For each test, the key data consists of image files and a file with the non-imaging 
measurements.  Additional files such as chamber calculator output, camera metadata, and operational 
logs provide information that can support the analysis. 
 
It is recommended that readers interested in analyzing the s-Flame data begin by familiarizing themselves 
with the hardware and instrumentation, either through the overview in the s-Flame Final Report or the 
more comprehensive description found in the ACME Engineering Implementation document. 
 
Those seeking to analyze the data should next review this document.  To interpret the non-imaging data, 
it is suggested that a sample data file be opened, named for example 19254A1_data.csv, which has 
comma-separated values and can be opened with spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel.  The data 
is in raw voltages, where conversion to engineering units requires study of ACME’s Software Interface 
Design Description, i.e., ACME-DOC-010 (where the latest version at the time of this writing is revision D). 
Additional documents that may be important include:

ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 
 
20 September 2021 
 
3 
 
 
ACME-RPT-010 A 
Data Camera Characterization Report, Rev. A 
ACME-RPT-011 
Radiometer Characterization Report 
ACME-RPT-013 
PMT Characterization Report 
MDC-XXX-1866-R1 
CFI Intensified Camera Package Characterization Report  
Meanwhile, the BRE and Cool Flames radiometer characterization reports are not applicable to s-Flame 
because it used the standard radiometers addressed in ACME-RPT-011.  
 
 
2. s-Flame Overview 
This text is the “Overview” from the ACME/s-Flame Final Report, which provides descriptions of the science, 
preliminary results, and more.  It is suggested that it be reviewed by those interested in analyzing the s-
Flame data. 
 
The Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment is one of six independent 
experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for 
which tests are conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station 
(ISS). 
 
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Chung K. Law of Princeton University.  The experiment 
has two Co-Investigators (Co-Is), namely Prof. Stephen D. Tse of Rutgers University and Dr. Kurt R. 
Sacksteder of the NASA Glenn Research Center.  While Sacksteder was actively engaged in defining the 
experiment, he had transitioned to other NASA work long before the spaceflight operations limiting his 
overall contributions.  
 
Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME 
including s-Flame and the rest of the ACME investigations.  In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki 
Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist.  For 
ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Vedha Nayagam and Uday G. Hegde 
who are also with CWRU. 
 
The s-Flames operations were conducted in two rounds of testing during Increments 60-63, where there 
was no testing during Increment 62 due to limited crew availability.  More specifically, the first round of 
testing was conducted from Sept. 2019 to Jan. 2020, while the second-round testing – featuring helium 
rather than nitrogen dilution - occurred from May to July 2020. 
 
 
3. Tests Conducted 
This text is an excerpt from the “Results” section of the ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation 
Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63 (which is included in the ACME/s-Flame Final Report). 
 
A total of 276 flames were ignited for the s-Flame experiment, with 29, 116, and 131 respectively 
ignited during Increments 60, 61, and 63.  These numbers neglect some flames which quenched 
promptly after ignition.  In this regard, science testing began at the end of Increment 60 and the 
first round of tests were completed during Increment 61.  No tests were conducted in Increment 
62 due to a lack of crew time, where the second round of tests were fully conducted during 
Increment 63.

items.title: PSI-23_Engineering Documents_s-Flame_data_interpretation_20210920.pdf
items.text:
ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 
 
20 September 2021 
 
4 
 
 
The tests were conducted in two rounds, where the first was conducted in increments 60 and 61 
featured 145 flames (nominally) in which the fuel and oxygen (i.e., in the chamber atmosphere) 
were diluted with nitrogen.  The second round conducted in increment 63 featured 131 flames 
(nominally) in which the fuel and oxygen were instead diluted with helium.   
The s-Flame experiment does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests 
are independently conducted with various gaseous fuels, including hydrogen, methane, 
hydrogen/methane blends, and ethylene.  These are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the 
chemistry is relatively well understood. 
 
No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for s-Flame; all of the ISS results were electronically 
transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all currently planned ACME 
experiments.

A. Non-Imaging Data 
Data and files discussed in this section include the following: 
Data Output File 
Mass Flow Controller (MFC) Setpoint File 
Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) data 
Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data 
 
1. Data Output File 
The basic ACME non-imaging measurements for each test are together in a file described in 
Section 8.1 Data Output File on page 124 of Software Interface Design Description (ACME-
DOC-010 Rev D).  The test number is made up of the year (2-digts), day of year (3 digits), and 
test (a letter and single-digit number).  As such, the example, 19254A1 is test A1 conducted 
on the 254th day of 2019.  But the test could also be early on the next (e.g., 255th) day because 
the day portion of ACME test numbers is not changed when operations continue past 
midnight (whether GMT or Eastern) into the start of the next day. 
 
Tests numbers that only differ by the final digit (e.g., 19254H1, 19254H2, and 19254H3) are 
normally similar and occasionally identical, where the number is indicative of the variant or 
repeat.  Letters I and O are not used because of their similarity to 1 and 0.  While initially used 
in ACME testing, the letter E ceased to be used because Excel software (for example) by 
default interpreted it as representing an exponential which was inconvenient.  As a related 
aside, ACME tests are often not conducted in order and some planned tests are regularly not 
conducted at all.  The latter results in additional letter gaps if the tests from a day are sorted 
alphabetically.  However, ACME testing often begins with test A1, where the final digit begins 
with 1 and is increased from there with variant or repeat tests for the same letter. 
 
The basic data is in a CSV format, i.e., with comma-separated values, which can be opened by 
spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel.  The first row is a header and provides a limited 
summary of the hardware and operational conditions.  The header is explained in Section 10.1 
Metadata Header of ACME-DOC-010 Rev D, which begins on page 126.

(displayed in two columns rather than a long row):

These files can be analyzed with the INFICON’s EZ IQ software for its 3000 Micro GC (version 
3.3.2 SP2) which only works under Windows 7 or XP SP3 (with the NET Framework 3.0 and/or 
3.5). INFICON has indicated that their newer software for the Micro GC Fusion will not work 
with 3000 Micro GC files.  However, it is possible that software developed by Agilent may be 
able to work with these files, where they apparently developed the EZ IQ software initially.  
 
NASA plans to analyze the files to determine species concentrations and make those results 
available, but the agency abandoned use of Windows 7 and earlier operating systems which 
has thus far prevented the planned analysis.  As a result, species concentration results are not 
yet available from the GCIP measurements, where the instrument was not used in the 
experiments preceding ACME.  It has furthermore only been used in a fraction of the ACME 
experiments, but s-Flame is one for which data was collected.  
 
4. Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data 
The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) in which the experiment was conducted, was equipped 
with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS), but it was not utilized for ACME testing because 
of the need for crew time to enable and disable the isolation (by respectively removing and 
installing alignment guides) on each test day.  However, the CIR was equipped with a 3-axis 
SAMS sensor head.  The acceleration archives, along with relevant documentation, are 
accessible from https://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/pims/home/, the home page for the Principal 
Investigator Microgravity Services (PIMS). 
 
The following guidance for the SAMS data was provided by Kenneth Hrovat (NASA Glenn):  In 
addition to the documentation and links from the PIMS home page, we introduce a few ways 
below to get started with exploring the CIR microgravity environment taking the perspective 
of SAMS measurements from within the rack. 
 
Roadmap Spectrograms 
To get a high-level, spectral roadmap view within two days after measurement, you can: 
a. Use your browser and start at this link: http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/roadmap 
b. In the upper left pane, you can navigate by GMT date to see a list of plots (PDF files) 
in the right pane for the GMT date of your choice.  We refer to these PDFs as roadmap 
plots.  For SAMS, these are acceleration spectrograms, which for vibratory data are a 
good way to look at patterns, structures and boundaries in both time and frequency 
for long time spans -- nominally, 8 hours per plot.  These spectrograms are mostly 
qualitative and crudely quantitative three-dimensional plots in that a color scale 
attempts to map power spectral density magnitude as a color for the 3rd dimension. 
NOTE: Ticking the Navigation Filter for “es05” in the bottom pane will then only 
highlight days in yellow in the upper left pane when the operations team powered on 
the SAMS sensor in the CIR to take measurements. 
c. You might want to navigate directly to a GMT day of interest for your science 
operations or run, but you can also browse day-by-day too in order to get some 
context comparing various 8-hour spans to get a feel for the environment under 
various conditions.

items.text:
ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 
 
20 September 2021 
 
10 
 
 
 
Binary Data 
To download actual SAMS measurement data for use with your models or to correlate 
acceleration measurements with your science or support data, you can… 
a. Use your browser and start at this link: http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/ftp/pad 
b. Navigate by GMT date, for example you can follow year, month and day links to end 
up at: https://pims.grc.nasa.gov/ftp/pad/year2020/month06/day18/  where you see 
a list of SAMS sensor directories.  The sensor subdirectory of interest for CIR is 
samses_accel_es05. 
c. Once you click into that directory link, you will see data and header files listed for the 
CIR sensor. 
d. The instructions at the following link help you to read these data: 
http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/plots/user/mohan/how2read_pad_binary_files.html 
 
 
B. Image Files 
Image data and files discussed in this section are associated with the following cameras: 
Analog, operations (ops), internal camera 
ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera 
 
Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera 
 
 
High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package 
 
1. Analog, internal, operations (ops) camera  
This color analog camera is mounted on the ACME chamber insert, and as such is within the 
combustion chamber and is sometimes referred to as the internal camera.  Its primary 
purpose is to support the operations, e.g., to visualize the burner and igniter, and as such is 
also often referred to as the operations or ops camera. 
 
The NTSC video (named for the National Television System Committee) from the ops camera 
is at 29.97 frames per second (fps) or nominally 30 fps.  It is not recorded on the space station 
but is streamed to the ground in near real time and is recorded on CIR consoles at the Glenn 
ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in a Transport Stream (TS) format using VLC Media 
Player which can be freely downloaded from https://www.videolan.org/vlc/.  That software 
has a snapshot function allowing for convenient extraction of still images, e.g., for making 
measurements of flame dimensions. 
 
2. ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
ACME’s primary camera is a high-definition (1360 x 1024), 12-bit color camera mounted 
outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench.  It is equipped with a motorized lens with 
independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus.  It has a filter barrel with a fused silica 
window (for color imaging), a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, and bandpass filters for 
imaging CH* and CH2O (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence. 
 
It was characterized prior to launch to enable temperature measurements via soot pyrometry 
and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP), soot volume fraction, and quantitative determination of 
the CH* concentration.  However, the flames in s-Flame testing were soot-free with the

Particularly when making quantitative measurements, implementation of an Abel transform 
or similar is likely appropriate given the axisymmetry of the flames.  In fact, all six of the

items.text:
ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 
 
20 September 2021 
 
12 
 
 
current ACME experiments feature axisymmetric or spherically symmetric flames.   
Approaches are compared in this paper: 
k. C. J. Dasch, One-Dimensional Tomography: A Comparison of Abel, Onion-Peeling, 
and Filtered Backprojection Methods, Applied Optics, 31 (1992) 1146–1152.  
https://doi.org/10.1364/AO.31.001146 
 
The a-k references above were taken from the following conference paper on early ACME 
results from the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment: 
Jesse Tinajero, Davide Giassi, Dennis Stocker, and Marshall Long. “Experimental Study on 
the Influence of Gravity on Highly Diluted and Sooting Coflow Flames,” 11th US National 
Combustion Meeting of the Combustion Institute, Pasadena, CA, 24-27 March 2019.   
 
Meanwhile, this paper on an ISS precursor to the CLD Flame experiment is an appropriate 
reference for determination of CH* concentration. 
D. Giassi, S. Cao, B.A. Bennett, D.P. Stocker, F. Takahashi, M.D. Smooke, and M.B. Long, 
“Analysis of CH* Concentration and Flame Heat Release Rate in Laminar Coflow Diffusion 
Flames under Microgravity and Normal Gravity,” Combustion and Flame, Vol. 167, pp. 
198-206 (2016).  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.combustflame.2016.02.012 
 
Images are normally downlinked within a week of the testing, but selected images are often 
downlinked during a test day.  Regardless, the images are downloaded in a wrapped Halcon 
object (HOBJ) format, which is not readily opened with typical image processing software.  
The image data was made available in that raw format and later in a converted TIFF format, 
where the NASA conversion was carried out without each of the following: 
• 
color balancing (to avoid possible saturation as subsequently discussed)  
• 
dark frame subtraction 
• 
removal of hot spots from dead pixels (e.g., resulting from radiation damage)  
Furthermore, the NASA conversion employs a standard bilinear demosaicing process which is 
detrimental when determining temperature profiles via Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) as it 
will average pixels both on and off the glowing fibers.  The priority in the NASA conversion 
was to make the images more readily accessible, not to meet all needs. 
 
Most ACME investigators are processing the raw HOBJ files using the OMA2 software 
developed by Prof. Marshall Long (Yale U.), the lead for ACME’s CLD Flame experiment.   The 
OMA2 software is freely available in both Mac and cross-platform (Qt) versions, where the 
latter can be used with both PC and Linux operating systems.  A tutorial was prepared by Dr. 
Jesse Tinajero on the use of OMA2 to process ACME’s HOBJ image files, where it can be found 
at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RMtu3KEXNiI.  It has also been broken up and posted 
in three parts in which the image resolution may be better: 
 
Part 1 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdQHeQwokvY 
 
Part 2 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mua_8CfqhfM 
 
Part 3 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BGRqgbIxZL4 
 
The OMA2 read-hobj function was also rewritten by Tinajero as a Python function, where 
Python is an open source programming language that is easily obtainable for MacOS, Linux, 
and Windows operating systems.  The Python script to open the HOBJ files can be downloaded 
from https://github.com/mblong/hobjExample. A tutorial for this function may be found at

items.text:
ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 
 
20 September 2021 
 
13 
 
 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4wbgWeJSilc. 
 
The HOBJ files can also be readily viewed and processed using ImageJ or its preloaded Fiji 
variant, where both can be freely downloaded.  In either software package, the HOBJ files can 
imported (rather than opened) as raw files with the following settings: 
 
Image type 
16-bit unsigned 
 
Width 
1360 
 
Height 
1024 
 
Offset to first image 
6244 
However, imported DataCam images will be monochrome unless a Bayer filter (e.g., as 
described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayer_filter) is subsequently implemented.  It 
should be possible to install a plug-in to accomplish that color conversion.  As another option, 
Python and Matlab both have image demosaicing functions. 
 
To use the ACME DataCam for quantitative measurements, it is critical to avoid saturation, 
for example by using a camera gain of zero.  Another employed approach was to not use the 
camera’s white balance which by default multiplies the red and blue by 1.41 and 1.68, 
respectively, because that could inadvertently lead to saturation.  Such multiplication can be 
done after the HOBJ file is converted and the colors demosaiced, where in OMA2 the white 
balancing is accomplished with the commands: 
*rgb 1.41 1 1.68 
clip 4095 
In summary, the white balance, if desired, needs to be done after the fact through software 
because it was at least generally not done with the hardware to avoid the risk of saturation.  
 
However, in carrying out color-ratio pyrometry calculations for the ISS data from ACME’s CLD 
Flame experiment, the investigators determined that the three color ratios (e.g., blue/red) 
didn’t result in the same temperature profile until the green channel was adjusted by 10%.  
This notably differs from the camera’s default of multiplication by 1 (i.e., no multiplication) 
for the green color plane. 
 
For Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP): “After rigorous testing, it was determined [by Tinajero and 
Long] that a modified version of the bilinear method could be used to optimize the conversion 
of raw fiber images to full resolution color images.  This modified version biases the linear 
interpolation along the length of the fiber.  This method combined with moderate use of 
defocusing was found to reduce artifacts created by standard demosaicing algorithms and 
was used in all of the fiber measurements described below.” 
Jesse Tinajero and Marshall Long. “Dilution Limits of Coflow Laminar Methane and 
Ethylene Flames in Microgravity Versus Normal Gravity,” 12th U.S. National Combustion 
Meeting, 24-26 May 2021. 
 
Note that the ACME images will be naturally dark because of the use of the 16-bit file format 
with 12-bit image data.  As such, adjustments to the image brightness will generally be 
necessary even if the images are not demosaiced.  Furthermore, cameras’ CCD arrays are 
susceptible to radiation damage while in orbit.  As a result, the images feature hot pixels which 
increase in number over the months and years in space.  As such, it will appear as if there is a 
star field within the combustion chamber.  Therefore, the images should ideally be processed

items.title: PSI-23_Engineering Documents_s-Flame_data_interpretation_20210920.pdf
items.text:
ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 
 
20 September 2021 
 
14 
 
 
to remove the bright outlying hot spots.  Radiation damage is also obvious in the ops camera 
imaging. 
 
Although the DataCam was typically set for imaging at 30 fps, that is trumped by the exposure 
settings which were often long because of the dim nature of the microgravity flames.  As a 
result, the framing rate was typically far less.  Different exposures are often selected for 
different phases of the tests, e.g., prior to ignition and during the test, so the framing rate 
may not be consistent.  Bracketed imaging could also be employed, where a repeating 
sequence of different exposure durations is used to enable appropriate photography under 
uncertain or varying flame intensities.  Bracketing can also used to simultaneously accomplish 
multiple imaging objectives, e.g., to appropriately image both brightly glowing soot (or TFP 
fibers) as well as the much dimmer blue portion of the flame. 
 
In interpreting the image data, it may be helpful to check the ACME DataCam metadata file 
which should be available for each successful flame test, e.g., to verify the exposure duration.  
These files are in a comma-delimited (CSV) format and can be opened with spreadsheet 
software or alternately as a text file.  Column headings are found in the first row of such files.
